Methods: Hospitals from CMS Care Compare were classified using a strict definition (heart transplant and ECMO), reflecting capability for definitive CS care, and a broad definition (transplant or ECMO), capturing any advanced mechanical circulatory support capability. We computed 60-minute drive-time isochrones and overlaid block-group adult population data from the American Community Survey 5-year estimates. County cardiac mortality (CDC WONDER, 2018-2022) was examined for four mortality outcomes: cardiogenic shock, acute myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, and cardiac arrest. Getis-Ord Gi* identified mortality hot spots; the care-desert association was tested with Fisher's exact tests on empirical-Bayes-smoothed rates and spatial-error regression. Analysis was restricted to the contiguous U.S. Results: 108 hospitals met the strict definition, and 289 met the broad definition. Of 257.9 million contiguous-US adults, 114.1 million (44.2%) lived more than 60 minutes from a strict-definition center, and 73.1 million (28.4%) from a broad-definition center. Of 3,144 counties, 2,456 were complete care deserts under the strict definition. Care-desert counties had higher odds of being mortality hot spots across all outcomes: ischemic heart disease, odds ratio 6.76 (95% CI 3.48-15.04); acute myocardial infarction, 3.92 (2.38-6.89); cardiogenic shock, 2.87 (1.24-8.17); and cardiac arrest, 8.25 (3.07-31.22). Spatial-error regression confirmed positive associations for all four outcomes. Conclusions: More than 2 in 5 U.S. adults live beyond 60-minute access to a Level-1 CS center, and county cardiac mortality is spatially associated with low access. These care deserts identify regions to target for systems-of-care or capability expansion.
title: Abstract 10757: Cardiogenic Shock Care Deserts: National Access to Advanced Circulatory Support and Cardiac Mortality

abstract: Introduction: ST-segment elevation in lead aVR with diffuse ST-segment depression is a high-risk electrocardiographic (ECG) pattern classically associated with left main coronary artery (LMCA) occlusion or severe multivessel coronary artery disease, often prompting urgent catheterization. Less commonly, this pattern may arise from reversible, non-obstructive causes such as severe anemia, which produces myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch that mimics high-risk acute coronary syndrome and creates uncertainty regarding invasive management. Patient Information: An 89-year-old woman with moderate aortic stenosis presented with exertional dyspnea, near-syncope, melena, and hypotension. She had been taking aspirin. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Initial evaluation showed blood pressure of 85/49 mm Hg, hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, hematocrit 15.1%, and troponin 0.106 ng/mL. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with ST-segment elevation in aVR and diffuse ST-segment depression, consistent with circumferential subendocardial ischemia and concerning for left main coronary artery occlusion. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: The combination of profound anemia, active gastrointestinal bleeding, hypotension, modest troponin elevation, and clinical context supported type 2 myocardial injury from oxygen supply-demand mismatch rather than primary plaque rupture. Because of active bleeding and high procedural/antithrombotic risk, antiplatelet escalation, anticoagulation, and immediate coronary angiography were deferred while serial electrocardiograms and biomarkers were monitored. Therapeutic Intervention: The patient received three units of packed red blood cells. Follow-Up and Outcomes: Within approximately 4 hours, hemodynamics stabilized, symptoms improved, hemoglobin increased to 7.8 g/dL, and troponin decreased to 0.066 ng/mL. Repeat electrocardiography showed complete resolution of ST-segment elevation in aVR and diffuse ST-segment depression. Echocardiography demonstrated normal biventricular systolic function without regional wall motion abnormalities. Endoscopy subsequently identified a duodenal ulcer as the bleeding source; proton pump inhibitor therapy was subsequently started. Discussion and Synthesis: Severe anemia can mimic a left main coronary artery occlusion pattern on electrocardiography through reversible global subendocardial ischemia. This case highlights the importance of integrating clinical context, hemodynamics, bleeding risk, serial electrocardiography, biomarkers, and echocardiography before pursuing invasive management when a correctable cause of supply-demand mismatch is evident. Close monitoring remains essential because this electrocardiographic pattern can also represent true high-risk coronary disease.
title: Abstract 10764: Reversible Electrocardiographic Pattern of Left Main Coronary Artery Occlusion in a Patient with Severe Anemia Treated with Blood Transfusion: A Case Report

abstract: Background: Risk scores are widely used for prognostication in cardiac surgery and are increasingly applied to patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, contemporary surgical and TAVR-specific scores remain incompletely validated in external TAVR cohorts. We evaluated the performance of contemporary risk scores for predicting 1-year mortality after TAVR. Methods: Consecutive patients with native aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR at Cleveland Clinic from 2019-2020 were included. Fifteen contemporary surgical and TAVR-specific risk scores were retrospectively calculated, including EuroSCORE I/II, STS-AVR PROM, STS/ACC TVT, France-2, FTS, German Aortic Valve Score I/II, Observant, TARI, TARIS, TAVI 2, TAVI futility risk models 1 and 3, and UK TAVI. Discrimination for 1-year all-cause mortality was assessed using area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve. Calibration was assessed using observed/expected ratios when applicable. Results: Among 1,035 patients, mean age was 78.9±8.9 years, 430 were women (41.5%), and 998 (96.4%) underwent transfemoral TAVR. Mortality occurred in 5 patients (0.5%) at 30 days, 71 (6.9%) at 1 year, and 240 (23.2%) during a mean follow-up of 2.1±0.9 years. Patients with 1-year mortality had greater symptomatic burden and higher prevalence of cardiovascular comorbidities, including prior cardiac surgery, coronary heart disease, atrial fibrillation/flutter, heart failure, cardiac implantable electronic devices, smoking history, and chronic liver disease. Among surgical scores, STS-AVR PROM had the highest discrimination for 1-year mortality (AUC 0.616, 95% CI 0.546-0.687). Among TAVR-specific scores, TARIS, FTS, and TAVI futility risk model 3 performed best, with AUCs of 0.701, 0.696, and 0.668, respectively. Calibration for 1-year mortality was assessable for FTS, TARI, and TARIS, with observed/expected ratios of 1.35, 0.68, and 0.35, respectively. Conclusion: In this contemporary TAVR cohort, available surgical and TAVR-specific risk scores demonstrated only modest discrimination for 1-year mortality. TAVR-specific models, particularly TARIS, FTS, and TAVI futility risk model 3, performed better than most surgical scores, although calibration was suboptimal. Further refinement and external validation are needed before these scores can be routinely used as stand-alone tools for risk stratification and clinical decision-making after TAVR. Clinical Implication: Improved TAVR-specific risk models incorporating frailty, right-heart function, pulmonary hypertension, anatomic risk features, and non-cardiovascular comorbidities may better identify high-risk patients and support individualized treatment planning.
title: Abstract 10765: Prognostic Utility of Contemporary Risk Scores for 1-Year Mortality After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Introduction: Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) is managed by preserving preload, maintaining afterload, and reducing contractility. With myocardial bridging, severe left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and systolic anterior motion (SAM)-mediated mitral regurgitation (MR) can raise filling pressures and contribute to ischemic apical stunning, complicating preload support. Case Presentation: A 79-year-old woman with known oHCM on metoprolol presented with chest pain and lightheadedness. She was initially stable and appeared dry. Troponin peaked at 6,752 ng/L and ECG showed inferior and V2-V6 T-wave inversions, concerning for NSTEMI. Early management included heparin, metoprolol tartrate and intravenous fluids to support preload. Within hours, she became hypoxic to 85%, hypotensive to 83/51 mmHg and bradycardic to 58 bpm. Chest X-ray confirmed pulmonary edema. Diagnosis: TTE showed LVEF 30-35%, apical akinesis, severe SAM, peak LVOT gradient 90 mmHg, and severe MR. LHC showed nonobstructive coronaries, significant mid-to-distal LAD myocardial bridging, LVEDP 25 mmHg, LVEF 35%, apical ballooning and basal hypercontractility, and elevated LV-aortic gradient. These findings suggested severe oHCM with elevated filling pressures and apical stunning from bridge-associated ischemia versus primary Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TCM). Interventions: Management shifted from preload loading to phenylephrine-supported cautious diuresis while continuing beta-blockade. Given phenylephrine-dependent shock, hypoxic respiratory failure, severe SAM-MR, and prohibitive surgical risk, she underwent mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) on hospital day 2 to reduce SAM and relieve LVOT. Outcome: M-TEER was performed without complications. Hemodynamics improved, phenylephrine was discontinued, and oxygen was weaned. Post-M-TEER TTE showed LVOT gradient improved to 35 mmHg despite persistent apical akinesis. At one week, LVEF recovered to 55-60%, LVOT gradient was 25 mmHg standing and 18 mmHg with Valsalva, with mild residual MR. Discussion: This case highlights a dilemma where oHCM management was complicated by myocardial bridging and ischemia-driven apical stunning. Initial beta-blockade and preload support were appropriate for dynamic LVOT obstruction. However, elevated LVEDP and apical stunning quickly reduced preload tolerance and precipitated pulmonary edema. LVOT gradient improved first post-M-TEER, followed by apical wall motion recovery. This timeline supported bridge-associated ischemic stunning in severe oHCM rather than TCM. Conclusion: In oHCM with myocardial bridging, severe SAM-mediated LVOT obstruction can drive ischemia, pulmonary edema, and apical stunning. When medical therapy is insufficient and surgery is prohibitive, urgent M-TEER may rescue the hemodynamic crisis by relieving obstruction.
title: Abstract 10769: Rescue Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair for Cardiogenic Shock in Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy with Bridge-Associated Apical Stunning

abstract: Leukostasis is an oncologic emergency driven by microvascular obstruction from leukemic cell proliferation resulting in impaired circulation. Although pulmonary vascular involvement is rare, it can be rapidly fatal. Here we discuss the clinical decision-making and course of a young woman with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) who developed leukostasis leading to group 5 pulmonary hypertension (PH) and acute right ventricular (RV) failure. A 26-year-old female with newly diagnosed AML was admitted with neutropenic fever. Initial labs revealed WBC 212 х10 9 /L (55% monocytes, 34% blasts), platelets 17 х10 9 /L, acute kidney injury, and an acute myocardial injury pattern. Infectious workup was unrevealing. She was started on hydroxyurea for cytoreduction but developed progressive hypoxic respiratory failure requiring ICU transfer and mechanical ventilation by hospital day 4. This prompted initiation of emergent induction chemotherapy with leuprolide, daunorubicin, and cytarabine. Worsening oxygenation and RV dilatation and dysfunction on echocardiography prompted right heart catheterization, performed with transfusion support. Isolated elevation in right-sided pressures (RA 15mmHg, PA 62/23 with mean 46mmHg; PCWP 18mmHg, PVR 4.4 Woods, RV stroke volume index 3.8 mL/m2) confirmed precapillary PH with resultant RV failure and was attributed to pulmonary leukostasis. With preserved cardiac index of 3.1 L/min/m 2 by thermodilution, the predominant driver of her hypoxemia was felt to be acute respiratory distress syndrome. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was considered due to this and worsening RV function but deferred due to severe anemia and thrombocytopenia. She was treated with IV diuresis and inhaled nitric oxide for RV afterload reduction and oxygenation support. Her respiratory status gradually improved, allowing for extubation after ten days. Repeat echocardiogram showed mild RV recovery. Hospital course was prolonged by C. difficile infection and bilateral vocal cord paresis but she was eventually discharged after a 30-day admission. Leukostasis can cause significant pulmonary microvascular obstruction and endothelial injury, leading to sudden increases in pulmonary vascular resistance and RV strain. Our patient’s isolated RV dysfunction supported a primary pulmonary vascular process, and the clinical course underscores the importance of maintaining suspicion for leukostasis-related PH in leukemia patients with new respiratory compromise. Early recognition of RV failure and prompt initiation of supportive therapy, including diuresis and inhaled pulmonary vasodilation, were key strengths, along with treatment of the underlying leukemia. While rare, leukostasis-associated PH can be reversible with rapid cytoreduction, consistent with the partial improvement observed in this case, underscoring the need of coordinated multidisciplinary care.
title: Abstract 10771: Leukostasis in Setting of Acute Leukemia: A Rare Cause of Right Ventricular Failure & Group 5 Pulmonary Hypertension

abstract: Caseous calcification of mitral annulus (CMAC) is rare variant of mitral annular calcification (MAC). The exact prevalence of CMAC) is not clearly known. CMAC was found in approximately 0.06-0.07% of population. A 73-year-old female patient was referred to a cardiologist during the planning of her eye surgery. The patient's ECG showed right bundle branch block. The patient’s echocardiographic examination revealed appearance of a mass adherent to the mitral valve and severe mitral insufficiency. Cardiac MRI showed a 2.5 cm x 5 cm hypo-intense mass involving the mitral valve, on all sequences of posterior-leaflet. Via a standard cardiac surgical procedure, distal anastomosis was performed on the patient's Right coronary artery and Circumflex coronary arteries for coronary bypass surgery and a performed right atriotomy and visualized the mitral valve via a trans-septal approach. We opened the cavity at the junction of the posterior leaflet and annulus. We aspirated a large, white, toothpaste-like material collected inside the mass and cleaned the cavity. After meticulous debridement of the cavity, the defect was closed by plication. Mitral valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve and tricuspid ring annuloplasty were subsequently performed. Pathological examination revealed amorphous basophilic material of specimens derived from the mass and intra-mass material conclusive with caseous calcification of the mitral annulus. CMAC can be appear as a smooth, round, peri-annular mass with a central echolucent area and a surrounding hyper-echogenic rim. The exact etiology of caseous mitral annular calcification CMAC remains unclear and can often be confused with vegetation, infective endocarditis and tumors. Some cases may be asymptomatic, however most commonly present as palpitations and dyspnea. Syncope has rarely been reported as a presenting complaint. Neurological deficits due to recurrent embolism can occur very rarely. The presence of a mass localized to the posterior aspect of the mitral annulus, demonstrating a hypoechoic appearance on echocardiography and no internal flow on Doppler imaging, should raise suspicion for CMAC. In such cases, further evaluation with magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography may be considered. Although no definitive treatment protocol has been established due to the limited number of reported cases, surgical intervention may be warranted given the potential for adverse outcomes. Published case reports have described both conservative follow-up and surgical management strategies. This rare clinical condition may need to be intervened surgically in patients with huge calcifications and additional cardiac pathologies.
title: Abstract 10792: Caseous Mitral Annular Calcification Diagnostic Challenges and Surgical Management of a Rare Cardiac Mass

abstract: Introduction: Newborn mouse cardiomyocytes retain mitotic capacity and can generate new muscle cells to repair myocardial injury during early postnatal life. However, proliferative capacity ceases later in postnatal development as they transition from a fetal glycolytic phenotype into differentiated adult myocytes that rely on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). During that transition they undergo mitochondrial biogenesis, raising the question of whether inhibition of mitochondrial function that forces a return to glycolytic metabolism would re-awaken mitotic capacity in adult cells. Hypothesis: Genetic inhibition of mitochondrial OXPHOS in adult mouse cardiomyocytes should force a return to glycolytic metabolism and restore mitotic capacity. Methods: Mitochondrial function was abolished by a tamoxifen-inducible Cre-Lox, conditional genetic deletion of Ndufs2 , a subunit required for complex I function in adult mouse cardiomyocytes. Mice were studied at 100 days post-tamoxifen, when residual Ndufs2 protein was virtually absent. Results: The progressive depletion of Ndufs2 in adult cardiomyocytes caused an increase in glycolytic metabolism and activation of mTOR, yet produced no evidence of bioenergetic deficiency at rest. Transcriptional and proteomic analysis signatures revealed cardiomyocyte de-differentiation, a return of mitotic cell division and cytokinesis resulting in hyperplastic remodeling of the heart without evidence of cellular hypertrophy, fibrosis or inflammation. Heart weight/body weight ratios exceeded 2.5X that of littermate controls, but heart structure was otherwise normal. Metabolomic analyses revealed both increases in lactate and the ratio of S-adenosylmethionine/S-adenosylhomocysteine and decreases in the ratios of α-ketoglutarate/succinate and α-ketoglutarate/fumarate, which promoted significant changes in DNA CpG methylation. Genes that were both differentially methylated and differentially expressed were closely linked with cardiac developmental processes including activation of the Hippo/Yap-Taz pathway, an established mechanism of cardiomyocyte regeneration. These findings suggest that the metabolic consequences of mitochondrial electron transport chain inactivation cause a re-awakening of mitotic function that had terminated shortly after birth. Conclusions: Mitochondrial signals regulate the developmental transition of hearts as they shift from a fetal glycolytic phenotype into an adult OXPHOS-dependent cells state through the alteration of methylation state of genes regulating that transition.
title: Abstract 10802: Mitochondria Regulate Cardiomyocyte Proliferation and Heart Regeneration

abstract: Background: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a major cause of cardiovascular death. Despite expanded eligibility for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), equitable changes in AS-related mortality across regulatory eras remain unclear. We aim to evaluate temporal trends in AS-related mortality across TAVR eras and assess whether trends differed by sex, age, race, region, and urbanization. Methods: We analyzed Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) Multiple Cause of Death data, 1999-2024. Adults aged ≥25 years were included when International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes I06.0, I06.2, I35.0, or I35.2 were underlying or contributing causes. Age-adjusted mortality rate (AAMR) was standardized to the 2000 U.S. population. Joinpoint regression estimated annual percent change (APC) and average annual percent change (AAPC). Eras were pre-TAVR (1999-2011), intermediate/high-risk expansion (2012-2018), and low-risk (2019-2024). Era-specific rate ratios (RRs) used Poisson methods. Urbanization analyses were limited to 1999-2020. Results: From 1999 to 2024, 673,926 AS-related deaths occurred. Overall AAMR changed from 11.51 to 10.93 per 100,000, with a stable full-period trend (AAPC, -0.18%; P=.317). AAMR rose during 2006-2013 (APC, 1.02%; P<.001), declined during 2013-2018 (APC, -1.72%; P<.001), and declined during 2021-2024 (APC, -2.26%; P=.001). Era-specific mortality was stable before TAVR (AAPC, 0.25%; P=.059), decreased during intermediate/high-risk expansion (AAPC, -1.27%; P<.001), and plateaued during the low-risk era (AAPC, -0.56%; P=.308). Mortality decreased in women (AAPC, -0.29%; P=.008) and was stable in men (AAPC, -0.05%; P=.795). Mortality increased at ages 45-54 years (APC, 2.07%; P<.001), 55-64 years (APC, 2.35%; P<.001), and 65-74 years (APC, 0.96%; P<.001), decreased at ages 75-84 years (AAPC, -0.86%; P=.001), and increased modestly at ages ≥85 years (AAPC, 0.29%; P=.040). Non-Hispanic Black versus non-Hispanic White RRs were 0.270, 0.256, and 0.281 across eras; Hispanic versus non-Hispanic White RRs were 0.195, 0.204, and 0.222. AS-related mortality was higher among residents of nonmetropolitan than metropolitan counties, with RRs increasing from 1.287 to 1.405. Through 2020, mortality among residents of metropolitan areas decreased (AAPC, -0.37%; P=.008), whereas mortality among residents of nonmetropolitan areas increased (AAPC, 0.53%; P=.025). Conclusion: During TAVR expansion, overall AS-related mortality was stable, but trends differed by age and geography. Increasing mortality among middle-aged and early older adults and worsening mortality among residents of nonmetropolitan counties support improved AS detection, referral, valve-intervention access, procedural quality surveillance, and disparity monitoring.
title: Abstract 10812: Disparities in Aortic Stenosis-Related Mortality During Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Expansion in the United States, 1999-2024

abstract: Introduction/Background: Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a condition associated with high morbidity and mortality. Surgical intervention is recommended in selected cases; however, many patients are not suitable candidates for operative management. Methods/Approach: We describe the case of a 91-year-old female who presented with an embolic stroke and was subsequently diagnosed with native mitral valve infective endocarditis due to Streptococcus agalactiae with vegetation enlargement (3.0х1.2 cm) and progression to moderate-severe regurgitation despite 6 weeks of antibiotics. Given extreme operative risk, with a Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) predicted mortality of 61.6% and combined morbidity/mortality of 90.2%, surgical intervention was deferred. Percutaneous transseptal AlphaVac™-assisted vegetation debulking was performed, using a 26-French AlphaVac™ catheter under intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) and fluoroscopic guidance, with adjunctive cerebral embolic protection using the SENTINEL device (Fig 2a, 2b) (Fig 3a,3b). No veno-venous bypass was used. Results/Data: Pre-procedural ICE demonstrated a vegetation measuring 3.4 х 1.1 cm (Fig 1a,1b). Aspiration debulking resulted in near-complete removal, with only a small residual remnant at the mitral valve base. No debris was identified within the cerebral protection filters. A brief vasovagal response occurred (resolved with phenylephrine). No stroke, bleeding, vascular complication, or hemodynamic compromise occurred. Post-procedure, no new neurologic deficits were identified. Conclusion: This case adds to the limited literature describing the use of percutaneous transseptal AlphaVac™ in debulking extreme high-risk left-sided infective endocarditis in elderly patients with prohibitive risk; and highlights the potential utility of cerebral embolic protection during left-sided aspiration procedures. Further prospective studies are warranted to define optimal patient selection, procedural standardization, safety, efficacy, and long-term clinical outcomes. Keywords: AlphaVac; Infective Endocarditis; Aspiration Debulking; Transseptal approach; Elderly
title: Abstract 10813: Vac-ing Against the Odds: Percutaneous Transseptal AlphaVac Debulking of Native Mitral Valve Endocarditis in a Prohibitive-Risk Nonagenarian

abstract: Introduction: Commercial insurance deductibles decrease utilization of recommended medical care. Little is known about how the deductible reset in January of each year affects cardiac rehabilitation (CR) enrollment and adherence, which is usually initiated in the weeks or months following a cardiovascular event or procedure. Research Question: Does the annual deductible reset affect CR enrollment and adherence for patients with commercial insurance compared to those with Traditional Medicare (TM)? Methods: Administrative claims data from the Michigan Value Collaborative multipayer registry were used to identify beneficiaries undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) between 01/2021-12/2023 discharged alive with continuous coverage for ≥12 months following discharge. CR enrollment (≥1 session) and adherence (number of sessions attended) were assessed within one year of discharge. Univariate and bivariate analysis compared CR enrollment and adherence between commercial and TM insurance by month of CABG/PCI. Logistic and Poisson regression was used to compare CR enrollment and adherence, respectively, in each month relative to July (referent month), adjusting for patient demographics, comorbidities, and hospital clustering. Results: The sample included 10,875 beneficiaries, of whom 4,540 (41.7%) were commercially insured. Commercially insured beneficiaries were younger, more likely to be male, and less likely to have comorbidities relative to TM beneficiaries. Compared to TM, those with commercial insurance had higher CR enrollment (47.6% vs 40.6%, p<0.001) but lower CR adherence (mean sessions: 19.9±12.3 vs. 24.0±15.0, p<0.001). After adjustment, CR enrollment did not differ significantly by month in the commercial or TM populations. However, CR adherence remained significantly lower for commercially insured beneficiaries with CABG/PCI in December versus July (relative rate, RR=0.83, 95% CI: 0.75-0.91, p<0.001), while TM beneficiaries had significantly higher adherence (RR=1.09, 95% CI: 1.02-1.16, p=0.010) (Figure). This corresponds to a 24% lower RR of adherence among commercially insured beneficiaries relative to TM beneficiaries, when comparing December to July. Conclusion: Among patients undergoing CABG/PCI, CR adherence declined among commercially insured patients and this observation corresponded to the time of the annual deductible reset. Enrollment was not impacted by the deductible reset for either TM or commercially insured patients. These findings highlight a predictable period of vulnerability for CR dropout, suggesting opportunities for targeted interventions to sustain adherence among commercially insured patients.
title: Abstract 10822: Association Between Annual Deductible Reset and Cardiac Rehabilitation Enrollment and Adherence

abstract: Background: Intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) is evident in ~40% of reperfused ST-elevation myocardial infarctions and is the strongest predictor of Major Adverse Cardiac Events. Free heme released from extravasated erythrocytes can drive iron-dependent oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction through mechanisms distinct from classical ischemia-reperfusion injury. We hypothesized that dexrazoxane (DXZ), an FDA-approved iron chelator, can protect cardiomyocytes against heme-mediated myocardial injury Methods: Sprague-Dawley rats underwent 90-min LAD ligation, followed by reperfusion; DXZ group received 30 mg/kg IV DXZ immediately before reperfusion. Myocardial injury and DXZ effect were evaluated by H&E, Prussian Blue, and Masson’s trichrome staining at 60 min, 24 h, 48 h, and 8 days; ejection fraction was quantified by echocardiography (n=5). For mechanistic studies, human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) were matured for 7 days, exposed to 90 min simulated ischemia (1% O 2 ), and reperfused with 2.5 or 5 μM hemin; the treatment group received 10 μM DXZ 30 min before 5 μM hemin exposure (n=5/group). Cardiomyocyte injury was assessed by viability assay and cardiac troponin-I (cTn-I) release. RNA-seq was performed at 24 h followed by DESeq2 differential expression analysis (adj. p<0.05), hierarchical clustering, GO, KEGG, and GSEA. Results: In vivo histopathology confirmed time-dependent myocardial injury following IMH — acute red blood cell extravasation at 60 minutes, early collagen deposition at 48 hours, and dense fibrotic remodeling by 8 days with iron deposition. DXZ preserved ejection fraction versus untreated hemorrhagic MI by 13.44±4.36 percentage points at day 1 (p<0.05) and 16.99±3.58 percentage points at day 3 (p<0.01). At 48 hours, DXZ also preserved myocardial architecture, reduced infarct size, and improved myofiber organization. In vitro, exogenous heme increased cTn-I secretion ~by over 20-fold above I/R alone (190.29±73.37 vs. 8.39±2.41 ng/mL, p<0.01) and reduced viability (p<0.01) at 24H. RNA-seq identified 6,404 heme-dysregulated genes (3,025 up, 3,379 down). DXZ pretreatment restored cell viability, suppressed cTn-I release by >50% (82.19±20.59 ng/mL, p<0.01), and reversed 68% (2,055 genes) of the heme-induced transcriptional signature. Key stress-response genes MAP3K14 (4.55±0.69-fold, p<0.01) and OSGIN1 (6.62±0.72-fold, p<0.01) were strongly induced by exogenous heme and significantly attenuated by DXZ (p<0.01). Pathway analyses showed rescue of mitochondrial electron transport chain, NADH dehydrogenase activity, and oxidative stress response programs (FDR<0.01). Conclusions: DXZ attenuates heme-mediated myocardial injury by preserving cardiac function, reducing cTn-I release, improving cardiomyocyte viability, and restoring mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathways. *PAD and GY contributed equally.
title: Abstract 10825: Dexrazoxane for Protection from Hemorrhagic Myocardial Infarction in Rats

abstract: Background: Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD) hearts sustain ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) which can be modulated with Cyclosporin A (CyA) treatment at reperfusion. We observed significant decrease in infarct size but no functional improvement in DCD hearts treated with CyA on Langendorff setup perfused for 60 minutes. We hypothesize that longer duration of reperfusion will manifest the benefits of CyA treatment of DCD hearts. Methods: Sprague-Dawley rats (n = 8 to 17 per group) were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine. Respiratory support was established with ventilator via tracheal intubation. Carotid artery cannulated to administer heparin and vecuronium. Release from ventilator marked the start of DCD ischemia time. DCD hearts were procured after 25 minutes of ischemia and were reanimated on Langendorff setup primed with Kreb-Henseleit (KH) buffer perfused at 74mmHg pressure for 60 minutes. A balloon tip catheter inserted into left ventricle transduced to LabChart measured hemodynamics. Hearts were then procured for infarct size measurement. CyA treated hearts received 0.5 μM CyA mixed in KH buffer, for the first 15 minutes of perfusion. Control non-ischemic hearts, continuous heart-beating donation (CBD) were procured before termination of ventilator support. A similar set of rats were assigned to undergo heterotopic heart transplantation following 25 minutes of in-situ ischemia. CyA (0.5 μM) was administered to the DCD hearts via carotid cannula at the time of procurement. Hearts were heterotopically transplanted into the recipient abdomen by attaching aorta to aorta and pulmonary artery to inferior vena cava (Figure). Recipient rats were allowed to recover for 48 hours and were then anesthetized with isoflurane (2-3%). Transplanted heart function was measured with balloon tip catheter transduced to LabChart software, then procured to measure infarct size. Results: In buffer-perfused hearts, cardiac function was impaired in the DCD group compared to the CBD group, as indicated by a decreased rate pressure product (RPP). Infarct size was larger in DCD hearts compared to CBD hearts (Table 1 & 2). While CyA treatment reduced infarct size in buffer-perfused DCD hearts (Table 2), it did not improve cardiac function (Table 1). In transplanted hearts, cardiac function was also impaired in the DCD group compared to the CBD group and the infarct size was larger (Table 1 & 2). However, CyA treated transplanted DCD hearts had reduced infarct size and improved cardiac function (Table 1 & 2). Conclusions: CyA administered to DCD hearts at reperfusion decreases IRI. Functional improvement requires longer duration of reperfusion. Future studies should explore stunned myocardium as the possible mechanism of this observation.
title: Abstract 10828: Longer Reperfusion Results in Improved Heart Function in Donation After Circulatory Death Hearts Treated with Cyclosporine A

abstract: Introduction: Sex differences in outcomes after left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) are incompletely characterized, and crude event rates conflate sex with differences in age and comorbidity. Whether men and women face the same risk profile, or diverge across competing outcomes, has direct implications for counseling and antithrombotic management. Methods: We analyzed 2,750 patients undergoing LAAO at 8 centers participating in the National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry. We fit a multistate survival model with four mutually exclusive outcome states (major bleeding, stroke/transient ischemic attack/systemic embolism, cardiac complications, and death), using flexible parametric models on the log cumulative hazard scale with spline-based baseline functions to estimate 2-year risks separately for men and women. To enable a fair comparison by sex, we applied regression standardization, calculating the sex-specific 2-year risk for each outcome as if men and women shared the same overall distribution of age, comorbidities, and other clinical risk factors observed in the full cohort. This approach removes differences attributable to men and women presenting with different case mixes, so that any remaining contrast in standardized risks reflects the effect of sex itself under the assumption of adequate covariate control. We then estimated the absolute 2-year risk difference between men and women for each outcome, along with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Results: Adjusted two-year risks diverged in opposite directions across outcomes. Women had higher bleeding incidence than men (3.27%, 95% CI 2.39 to 4.47 vs 1.72%, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.46), a difference of –1.55 percentage points (95% CI –2.75 to –0.35) favoring men. Conversely, men had higher mortality (7.43%, 95% CI 6.27 to 8.79 vs 4.64%, 95% CI 3.57 to 6.04), a difference of +2.79 percentage points (95% CI +1.02 to +4.55) favoring women. Both differences excluded zero. Cardiac complication incidence was effectively identical (1.16% vs 1.17%; difference –0.01, 95% CI –0.74 to +0.72), and the stroke difference was not significant (–0.25, 95% CI –1.12 to +0.62). Conclusions: After LAAO, women and men occupy distinct risk profiles rather than differing in overall severity. Women carry higher adjusted bleeding risk, men carry higher adjusted mortality, and periprocedural cardiac and stroke risks are statistically indistinguishable. These opposing gradients indicate that sex shapes the balance of competing risks after LAAO and support sex-specific framing of bleeding-versus-mortality tradeoffs in patient selection and antithrombotic decisions.
title: Abstract 10837: Sex-Specific Divergence in Bleeding and Mortality Risk After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion

abstract: Background: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair devices, such as MitraClip™, have emerged as a viable option for treatment of severe mitral regurgitation (MR) in patients who are at prohibitive surgical risk. The incidence of device detachment, most often single leaflet detachment, is estimated to occur in 1-2% of patients and is typically diagnosed shortly after device deployment. Case Summary: A 63-year-old man with a history of severe primary mitral regurgitation treated with mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) using two MitraClips™ in 2022 presented with chest pain and syncope two months after returning from a cruise. Shortly after returning from his cruise he developed diarrhea, fevers, and chills and was diagnosed with Enterococcus faecalis bacteremia. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed chronic moderate aortic insufficiency (AI), mild MR, and no evidence of infective endocarditis (IE). He was treated with six weeks of intravenous antibiotic therapy using ampicillin and ceftriaxone. Several weeks later he presented to the hospital with chest pain and rapidly developed acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock manifested by acute kidney injury and ischemic hepatitis. TTE showed severe MR, moderate AI and severe pulmonic regurgitation (PR). Only one MitraClip™ was visible on the valve. Cross-sectional imaging identified his missing MitraClip™ lodged at the takeoff of his right superficial femoral artery. He continued to decompensate, therefore he was cannulated for left atrial venoarterial ECMO (LAVA-ECMO) prior to transfer to a center with surgical expertise in multi-valvular shock. He was transferred to our facility and underwent aortic valve replacement, mitral valve replacement, tricuspid valve repair, pulmonic valve replacement, left atrial appendage closure and right superficial femoral artery cutdown for removal of the embolized Mitraclip™. Surgical pathology confirmed E. faecalis with significant destruction of the mitral and pulmonic valves. His post-operative course was largely uncomplicated and he was discharged from the hospital approximately three weeks later to a rehabilitation center. Discussion: This is the first documented case of infective endocarditis-related embolization of a MitraClip™. This case demonstrates a rare presentation of bilateral IE involving the pulmonary and mitral valves causing valvular shock with multiorgan failure. This case also highlights the use of LAVA-ECMO as a bridge for patients presenting in refractory multi-valvular shock requiring mechanical circulatory support, where commonly utilized options for left ventricular decompression, such as intra-aortic balloon pump or Impella® are precluded. Finally, this case reinforces the importance of timely surgical intervention for critically ill patients with valvular shock.
title: Abstract 10860: A Tale of Two Valves: Mitral and Pulmonic Valve Infective Endocarditis Complicated by MitraClip™ Embolization

abstract: Introduction: Risk scores used to select patients for left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) typically treat prior major bleeding and prior stroke as nonspecific markers of higher overall risk. Whether these histories signal a globally vulnerable patient or instead forecast recurrence of the same specific event is unknown and has direct implications for how prior events should inform LAAO patient selection and counseling. Methods: We studied 2,750 patients undergoing LAAO at 8 centers participating in the National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) LAAO Registry. Using a multistate survival model with four outcome states (major bleeding, stroke/transient ischemic attack/systemic embolism, cardiac complications, and death), we estimated 2-year risks for each outcome according to the presence of prior major bleeding and, separately, prior stroke or TIA. To enable fair comparisons, we applied regression standardization, calculating each group’s risk as if all patients shared the same overall distribution of age, comorbidities, and other clinical risk factors observed in the full cohort, so that any remaining differences reflect the prognostic effect of the specific history itself. We then estimated absolute risk differences and corresponding 95% confidence intervals for each outcome. Results: Prior events selectively increased the risk of their own recurrence rather than global risk. Patients with a history of major bleeding had higher 2-year major bleeding risk than those without (2.73% vs 1.08%; risk difference +1.66 percentage points, 95% CI +0.61 to +2.70), while their standardized risks of stroke/systemic embolism, cardiac complications, and death did not differ significantly (all risk-difference confidence intervals included zero). A parallel pattern was observed for prior stroke or TIA: patients with such a history had higher 2-year stroke/systemic embolism risk (2.18% vs 0.78%; risk difference +1.40 percentage points, 95% CI +0.24 to +2.57), with no significant differences in major bleeding, cardiac complications, or death. Neither prior bleeding nor prior stroke/TIA was associated with higher 2-year mortality. Conclusions: After LAAO, a history of major bleeding and a history of stroke/TIA each predict recurrence of the same event type rather than a broadly elevated risk profile, and neither is associated with excess mortality. These findings suggest that prior events mark organ- or system-specific vulnerability rather than global frailty. Accordingly, using prior bleeding or stroke solely as generic severity markers may mischaracterize risk, whereas incorporating a patient’s specific event history can better identify which complication they are most likely to face after LAAO.
title: Abstract 10885: A History of Bleeding or Stroke Predicts Recurrence of the Same Event, Not Global Risk, After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion

abstract: Introduction: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) due to systolic anterior motion (SAM) is a recognized complication after mitral valve repair, typically occurring early and managed with medical therapy or re-intervention. Late or persistent LVOTO driven by subvalvular/chordal mechanisms is less commonly described. The role of myosin inhibition in non-hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) LVOTO, at present remains unclear. Patient Information: A 61-year-old man with a history of severe mitral regurgitation due to myxomatous mitral valve prolapse of the P2 scallop underwent mitral valve repair with posterior leaflet resection and annuloplasty. Clinical Findings & Timeline: One year post-surgery, the patient experienced dizziness and exertional dyspnea. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed normal left ventricular ejection fraction (60-65%) with new dynamic LVOTO (resting peak gradient 52 mmHg), moderate mitral regurgitation, and SAM of the mitral valve, which was not seen on immediate post-op TTE. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a stable annuloplasty ring and redundant chordae to the anterior leaflet, causing chordal SAM and LVOTO. Cardiac MRI showed no hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or fibrosis. The mechanism was progressive chordal myxomatous degeneration, leading to excessive mobility of redundant chordae, thereby increasing the risk of late SAM and LVOTO. Therapeutic Intervention(s): Given persistent symptoms despite beta-blocker therapy, Mavacamten 2.5 mg daily was initiated. Follow-Up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: At 1-month follow-up, TTE showed reduction in LVOT gradient to 18 mmHg (22 mmHg with Valsalva), with subsequent improvement to 9 mmHg at two months. The patient reported significant improvement in dyspnea and functional capacity and no adverse events were observed. Discussion & Synthesis: This case highlights a novel method to treat late postoperative LVOTO due to chordal SAM following mitral valve repair. In select patients without underlying HCM, Mavacamten may offer a non-surgical therapeutic option for refractory SAM-related obstruction. Our case highlights the potential application of myosin inhibition beyond classic HCM and underscores the importance of detailed imaging to guide mechanism-driven management strategies.
title: Abstract 10914: Chordal Systolic Anterior Motion Causing Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction After Mitral Valve Repair: A Novel Therapeutic Role for Myosin Kinase Inhibitor

abstract: Introduction: Arterial calcification complicates vascular intervention, decreasing drug penetration and increasing the risk of stent underexpansion. Despite its clinical relevance, mechanical properties and composition of vascular calcium remain inconsistently characterized. Published elastic modulus values vary from Mega to Giga Pascals, likely reflecting methodological inconsistency in sample preparation and the use of specimens from anatomically diverse vascular regions. To address these gaps, this study introduces an enzymatic digestion protocol to isolate pure calcified deposits from three distinct vascular sites - aorta, coronary, and femoral arteries. Methods: Human calcified aorta, coronary and femoral arteries were extracted from cadavers (n=5) received within 24h of death. Calcified segments were incubated in collagenase type I (450U/ml, 3-6hrs), rinsed, and air-dried. For phase analysis, samples were ground into powder and analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD; PANalytical Empyrean; Cu Kα; 5-90° 2θ; ICDD PDF5+). For mechanical analysis, samples were embedded in epoxy, polished to a mirror finish, and tested by nanoindentation (Berkovich tip; 2,000,000 μN; 10x10 arrays, 5 μm spacing, 500 nm depth), generating spatially resolved hardness (H) and Youngs’ modulus (YM) maps. Surface morphology and elemental composition were analyzed using SEM (Crossbeam340, Zeiss; 10kV) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, X-Max 50, Oxford Instruments; 15kV). Results: Gross morphology differed markedly: aortic samples were large, flat sheets; coronary specimens formed irregular incomplete arcs reflecting focal asymmetric calcification; femoral samples were complete 360° tubular rings (concentric medial pattern). XRD confirmed hydroxyapatite as the dominant phase (HA ≥92%) at all vascular sites. EDS-derived Ca/P ratios (aorta 1.8±0.1, coronary 1.4±0.4, femoral 1.1±0.3, p=0.02) showed coronary and femoral values below the stoichiometric HA ratio of 1.67, and higher femoral Mg content (0.7±0.3%) suggesting a greater proportion of substituted or immature mineral phases. Crystallite size decreased from aorta (~30nm) to coronary (~21nm) and femoral (~18nm), indicating a site-specific variability in mineral maturity. Nanoindentation revealed comparable H (~1 GPa) and YM (10-30 GPa) across vascular sites (p=ns), with bimodal distributions suggesting nanoscale compositional heterogeneity. Conclusions: This study provides the first systematic regional characterization of human vascular calcification. Despite distinct gross morphology and mineral maturity, mechanical properties were comparable across vascular sites, with observed variability reflecting inter-patient variability. These findings offer biomechanical data to support computational modeling and optimization of intravascular lithotripsy.
title: Abstract 10946: Mechanical and Compositional Study of Human Vascular Calcification Across Aorta, Coronary and Femoral Arteries

abstract: Introduction: Pulmonary vein stenosis (PVS) after cardiac surgery is rare and under-recognized. We report a case of iatrogenic right upper pulmonary vein (RUPV) stenosis following mitral valve replacement (MVR), successfully treated with percutaneous stenting. Patient Information: A 63-year-old woman with hypertension and prior smoking history presented with exertional dyspnea and intermittent lower-extremity edema. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Preoperative transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) showed severe eccentric mitral regurgitation from a flail A2 scallop (PISA radius 0.92cm) with pulmonary vein flow reversal, and markedly elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure. Coronary angiography was unremarkable. She underwent MVR with a 29-mm bioprosthesis; an intravenous vent was placed in the RUPV during left atrial closure. Postoperatively, she had persistent severe pulmonary hypertension (systolic pulmonary artery pressures > 90 mmHg) and new moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation. A right MCA ischemic stroke prompted further workup. Diagnostic Assessment: Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated elevated RUPV inflow velocities but no thrombus (Figure 1). Cardiac CT angiography confirmed focal RUPV stenosis at ~4.1 x 5.0 mm (Figure 2). Selective hemodynamic assessment revealed a wedge pressure gradient: left PCWP 18 mmHg versus RUPV wedge pressure 30 mmHg, confirming outflow obstruction. Therapeutic Intervention: Selective PCWPs were performed to confirm RUPV stenosis (Figure 3A and 3B). Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) was used to characterize the lesion (Figure 4). Via transseptal approach, the RUPV was predilated with an 8 x 20 mm balloon, followed by a drug-coated balloon. An 8 x 27 mm bare-metal biliary stent was deployed and post-dilated with a 9 x 20 mm balloon (Figure 5B and 5C). The ostium was post dilated with a 9x20mm balloon (Figure 5C). Post-stent pulmonary artery systolic pressure decreased from 60 to 52 mmHg. Follow-Up & Outcomes: The patient reported significant symptomatic improvement. Follow-up transthoracic echocardiography showed reduced pulmonary pressures and improved tricuspid regurgitation severity. No procedural complications occurred. Discussion: Iatrogenic PVS from pulmonary vein cannulation or venting is likely underdiagnosed. Multimodality evaluation including CT angiography, selective wedge pressure sampling, and intravascular ultrasound is essential. Endovascular stenting can achieve meaningful anatomic and hemodynamic improvement. Persistent postoperative pulmonary hypertension disproportionate to clinical expectations should prompt PVS evaluation. Conclusion: Iatrogenic PVS is a treatable cause of post-surgical pulmonary hypertension. Early recognition and percutaneous intervention can restore hemodynamics and relieve symptoms.
title: Abstract 10948: Beyond the Valve: Iatrogenic Right Upper Pulmonary Vein Stenosis Following Mitral Valve Replacement

abstract: Background: Risk stratification after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains critical for identifying patients at risk for recurrent cardiovascular events. Although invasive coronary angiography is routinely used to define coronary anatomy and guide revascularization, its long-term prognostic value in contemporary ACS populations remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated the prognostic significance of angiographic disease burden on short- and long-term outcomes among patients presenting with ACS. Methods: In this prospective observational study, 766 consecutive patients with ACS (STEMI, NSTEMI, or UA) underwent invasive coronary angiography. Baseline clinical, laboratory, electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and angiographic data were collected. Angiographic assessment included obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD), multivessel disease, left main CAD, chronic total occlusions, and disease complexity. Patients were followed at 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, and beyond 12 months. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as all-cause mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction, unplanned revascularization, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Multivariable Cox regression identified independent predictors of adverse outcomes. Results: Mean age was 59±12 years and 62% were male. Obstructive CAD was present in 83%, multivessel disease in 46%, left main disease in 8%, and chronic total occlusions in 14%. MACE occurred in 7.8% at 1 month, 11.9% at 3 months, and 15.6% at 6 months. During long-term follow-up (median 4.1 years), 212 patients (27.7%) experienced MACE, including 98 deaths, 61 recurrent myocardial infarctions, 74 heart failure hospitalizations, and 85 repeat revascularizations. Patients with multivessel disease had significantly higher event rates than those with single-vessel disease at 1 month (11.2% vs. 4.9%), 6 months (22.4% vs. 9.1%), and long-term follow-up (38.5% vs. 17.8%; all p<0.001). Independent predictors of long-term MACE included multivessel disease (HR 1.92, 95% CI 1.48-2.50), left main CAD (HR 2.41, 95% CI 1.71-3.38), lower left ventricular ejection fraction (HR 1.31 per 10% decrease), diabetes mellitus (HR 1.46), and chronic kidney disease (HR 1.58) (all p≤0.004). Patients with left main or three-vessel disease demonstrated the poorest survival. Conclusions: Among patients with ACS, angiographic disease burden provides powerful prognostic information from the acute phase through long-term follow-up. Multivessel disease left main involvement, and greater angiographic complexity independently predict adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Incorporating detailed angiographic assessment into contemporary risk stratification models may improve identification of high-risk patients who could benefit from intensified surveillance and secondary prevention.
title: Abstract 10949: Incremental Prognostic Value of Invasive Coronary Angiographic Findings in Patients Presenting with Acute Coronary Syndromes: Short- and Long-Term Outcomes from a Contemporary Real-World Cohort

abstract: Introduction: Atrial fibrillation (AF) pattern is often treated as a single axis of disease severity, with more sustained AF assumed to confer uniformly higher risk. Whether paroxysmal, persistent, and permanent AF differentially shape the competing risks of bleeding, thromboembolism, cardiac complications, and death after left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) remains poorly defined. Methods: We studied 2,750 patients undergoing LAAO at 8 centers participating in the National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry. We fit a multistate survival model with four outcome states (major bleeding, stroke/transient ischemic attack/systemic embolism, cardiac complications, and death), using flexible parametric models on the log cumulative hazard scale with spline-based baseline functions to estimate 2-year risks according to AF pattern (paroxysmal, persistent, and permanent). To enable fair comparisons, we applied regression standardization, calculating each pattern’s 2-year risk as if all patients shared the same distribution of CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc scores and other clinical covariates observed in the full cohort, so that residual differences reflect AF pattern rather than case mix. We then estimated absolute risk differences relative to paroxysmal AF, with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Results: AF pattern differentiated patients only with respect to mortality, and only for persistent AF. Patients with persistent AF had higher 2-year mortality than those with paroxysmal AF (9.01%, 95% CI 6.76-11.95 vs 5.72%, 95% CI 4.79-6.82; risk difference +3.29 percentage points, 95% CI +0.53 to +6.05), while risks of major bleeding, stroke/systemic embolism, and cardiac complications did not differ significantly (all confidence intervals included zero). Permanent AF was not significantly associated with any outcome, including mortality (2-year mortality 6.05%; risk difference vs paroxysmal AF +0.33 percentage points, 95% CI –2.40 to +3.06), indicating that the excess mortality signal was confined to persistent AF. Conclusions: After LAAO, AF pattern does not behave as a simple ordinal severity gradient. Persistent AF specifically marks higher 2-year mortality without measurable increases in stroke, bleeding, or cardiac complications, whereas permanent AF is not associated with excess risk across outcomes. These findings support persistent AF as a distinct prognostic phenotype that may warrant closer postprocedural surveillance and follow-up.
title: Abstract 10951: Atrial Fibrillation Pattern and Competing Outcomes After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: Persistent Disease Marks Mortality Risk

abstract: Introduction: End-diastolic forward flow (EDFF) across the pulmonic valve is classically linked to restrictive right ventricular (RV) physiology after repaired tetralogy of Fallot but is rarely described in carcinoid pulmonic valve disease. We report a three-patient series in which EDFF was identified intraoperatively in advanced carcinoid heart disease. Case Presentation: Three adults with metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors and carcinoid valve disease were referred for surgery. The first patient was a 62-year-old woman with severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and pulmonic regurgitation (PR), moderate RV dilation, mildly reduced RV function, and no marked pulmonary hypertension. The second was a 64-year-old man with chronic right-sided heart failure, recurrent volume overload, severe TR and PR, moderate mitral regurgitation, severe RV dilation, and moderately to severely reduced RV function. The third was a 74-year-old woman with acute decompensated heart failure, severe TR, moderate aortic regurgitation, obstructive coronary artery disease, and elevated right-sided filling pressures. Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography in all patients showed advanced carcinoid pulmonic valve involvement, with thickened, retracted, restricted leaflets, incomplete coaptation, and severe PR. The shared operative echo finding was late-diastolic antegrade flow across the pulmonic valve. Color Doppler demonstrated end-diastolic flow, and spectral Doppler showed a reproducible antegrade signal after the P wave and before the next QRS complex, confirming flow during atrial contraction rather than ventricular systole. All patients underwent pulmonic and tricuspid valve replacement. Concomitant procedures included mitral repair and coronary bypass in one patient and aortic valve replacement with coronary bypass in another. Discussion: This series demonstrates that EDFF in carcinoid heart disease is a clinically relevant perioperative marker of severe pulmonic valve involvement, not merely an unusual Doppler pattern. The key mechanism is atrial contraction transmitting flow through a fixed-open, incompletely coapting pulmonic valve, with possible contribution from altered RV compliance. This finding is more likely to be seen in a carcinoid patient with normal sinus rhythm and severe TR and PR. EDFF requires an effective atrial contraction and therefore depends on sinus rhythm. It is further accentuated by severe TR, which increases diastolic forward flow, and by severe PR, because pulmonic regurgitation has already occurred before atrial systole contributes to EDFF. Because the PR index depends on regurgitant-flow duration relative to diastole, recognizing EDFF after the P wave and before the QRS complex may prevent Doppler mistiming, misclassification as systolic flow, and underestimation of PR severity during operative assessment.
title: Abstract 10953: End-Diastolic Forward Flow Across the Pulmonic Valve in Carcinoid Heart Disease: A Three-Patient Case Series

abstract: Background: Factor XIa inhibition has emerged as a promising antithrombotic strategy that may reduce thromboembolic events while minimizing bleeding complications. We performed an systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of asundexian across cardiovascular populations. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CENTRAL were searched through April 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing asundexian with placebo or active anticoagulant therapy in adults with cardiovascular disease were included. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Results: Five randomized controlled trials involving 31,301 participants were included. Asundexian did not significantly affect all-cause mortality compared with control (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.85–1.14) or ischemic stroke (RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.66–2.66). No significant differences were observed for cardiovascular death (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.74–1.04), ISTH major bleeding (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.30–2.09), major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.37–1.61), serious adverse events (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91–1.05), or overall adverse events (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.97–1.01). Significant heterogeneity was observed for several thromboembolic and bleeding outcomes. Sensitivity analyses excluding an influential trial reduced heterogeneity substantially and demonstrated a lower risk of stroke or systemic embolism (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.84). Conclusions: Across 31,301 patients with cardiovascular disease, asundexian demonstrated a safety profile comparable to control without significant effects on mortality or major bleeding. Sensitivity analyses suggest a potential reduction in thromboembolic events; however, findings remain influenced by study-level heterogeneity. Further adequately powered trials are needed to define the role of factor XIa inhibition in cardiovascular prevention.
title: Abstract 10967: Efficacy and Safety of Asundexian in Cardiovascular Diseases, Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Simple biochemical markers that capture systemic stress could refine short-term risk stratification after TAVR. We evaluated whether an elevated AST/ALT (De Ritis) ratio predicts early adverse outcomes following transfemoral TAVR. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 733 consecutive patients undergoing transfemoral TAVR. The exposure was the preprocedural AST/ALT ratio categorized as low (<1.4; n=478) or high (≥1.4; n=255). Baseline characteristics were compared using t/Wilcoxon tests and χ 2 /Fisher’s exact tests. Thirty-day endpoints included all-cause mortality, acute kidney injury (AKI), ischemic stroke, and new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF). Kaplan-Meier failure curves were compared by the log-rank test. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs; candidate covariates were prespecified and further refined with LASSO (10-fold cross-validation). Model assumptions were checked with Schoenfeld residuals. Results: High AST/ALT was associated with greater 30-day risk of AKI (adjusted HR 3.18, 95% CI 1.80-5.63), stroke (adjusted HR 2.73, 95% CI 1.31-5.69), and new-onset AF (adjusted HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.57-3.51). For mortality, the unadjusted association trended positive (HR 2.07, = 0.084) but was not independent after adjustment (HR 1.74, 95% CI 0.75-4.04). Additional adjusted associations included higher AKI risk with high-intensity statins (HR 3.51, 95% CI 1.75-7.06) and baseline complete right bundle-branch block (HR 3.77, 95% CI 1.49-9.57). Conclusions: An elevated preprocedural AST/ALT ratio independently identifies TAVR recipients at increased 30-day risk of AKI, stroke, and new-onset AF, but not mortality. Incorporating this inexpensive marker into routine assessment may help tailor periprocedural strategies and early surveillance after TAVR.
title: Abstract 10972: De Ritis (AST/ALT) Ratio as a Predictor of Early Adverse Outcomes Following TAVR

abstract: Introduction: Given the variety of significant changes in atherosclerotic plaques (ASP) in ACS, study by non-invasive imaging methods their further dynamics, it’s relationship with clinical factors, including prognosis, is important and relevant. Purpose: Assessment of the dynamics of ASP remaining after PCI, according to CT angiography (CTA) in patients (pts) with ACS. Materials and Methods: The study included 80 pts with ACS (81.3% of men, age 58.9±9.5 years). MI occurred in 33.3% of pts, unstable angina - in 66.7%. After PCI a primary CTA scan was performed by 320 - row CT scanner on the 3rd-7th day of ACS. Repeated scan was performed after 22 [13.7; 28] months. The degree of stenosis (DS) was determined in most ASP, and structural characteristics, as well as known CT instability signs (IS) of plaques were determined in non-calcified ASB (NASB). Standard therapy was performed. Results: Initially there were 219 ASP. Plaque type changes from soft to calcified were detected in 34 (15.5%) plaques, 197 NASP were further analyzed. During the study period an increase in DS from 55.2±16.5% to 59.8±16.7% (p=0.007) and a decrease in ASP minimum density from 33.2±15.7 HU to 28.1±14.3 HU (p <0.001) were detected. There were no significant changes in the mean values of length, burden, average density and remodeling index of ASP. Fig. 1 shows 3 types of individual ASP dynamics based on DS changes, as well as the frequency of accompanying unidirectional changes in other characteristics according two types of DS dynamics. In ASP group with an DS increase, there was a significant decrease in the minimum density by -6 [-16;8;0] HU (p<0.001), which confirms the "worst" plaque dynamics (Fig1). Among the plaques with DS decrease, 13 ones showed a reduction in all 3 "dimensional" characteristics (6.6% of all ASP), which is likely due to involutional processes. Fig. 2 demonstrated the variants of ASP changes in the pts coronary bed. In pts the detection of ASP with a minimum density of <30 HU increased from 42.8% to 58.2% (p=0.0032), while other qualitative characteristics, including IS, did not change significantly. Conclusion: The revealed significant changes in the structure of ASP are natural for the development of the atherosclerotic process in the CA after ACS. At the same time, the study showed that plaques with multidirectional changes usually coexist in the coronary bed of patients, which are realized both in the "worst-case" and relatively favorable scenarios.
title: Abstract 10991: Structural Features of Atherosclerotic Plaques According to Computed Tomography of Coronary Arteries and Their Dynamics in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Introduction: As the use of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has expanded beyond traditional high-risk patient profiles and surpassed surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) volume, incorporating patient-specific predictors of readmission into outcome analysis has become increasingly important. Furthermore, because death outside hospitalizations is not recorded in administrative claims data, traditional readmission analyses misestimate readmission risk, particularly in older populations with high comorbidity. Research Question: We sought to develop fixed-window models of readmission and time-to-event models of both readmission and post-discharge mortality after SAVR and TAVR using patient-level and hospital-level predictors. Methods: Using the 2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD), we constructed regularized logistic regression models from index-admission demographic, clinical, and hospital predictors to predict readmission within 6 months after SAVR and TAVR. Models were validated using held-out data. Additionally, we built Weibull proportional hazards models to predict time-dependent risk of readmission and mortality. Both events shared covariate effects, with the magnitude of the model coefficients linked by a single scaling factor. Death parameters were calibrated to independently reported mortality rates. Results: The isolated cohort contained 27,125 total SAVRs and 54,397 total TAVRs, of which 5,337 (19.7%) and 12,153 (22.3%) were readmitted within the same calendar year. The logistic regression models demonstrated modest discrimination on held-out validation data, with AUCs of 0.67 for SAVR and 0.66 for TAVR. However, these logistic regression models are limited to prediction of readmission before a fixed time point using a single threshold for classification. In contrast, by modeling death and readmission as competing outcomes using time-to-event analysis, we computed patient-specific predicted time courses for readmission and death (see Image 1). Cumulative readmission probability adjusted for death flattened at long horizons, particularly for high-hazard patients, adhering more closely to real trends of readmission (see Image 2, panel A ). Probabilities of readmission exhibited wide patient heterogeneity and were validated by observed readmission timelines (see Image 2, panel B ). Though trained only on the 2022 NRD, this model accurately extrapolated for 5 years to previously published readmission rates (see Image 3). Trends for SAVR (not shown) matched qualitatively. Conclusion: We developed logistic regression models for predicting readmission after SAVR and TAVR, and Weibull proportional hazards models that provide patient-specific longitudinal predictions of readmission and unobserved death.
title: Abstract 11005: Joint Modeling of Readmission and Post-Discharge Mortality After Surgical and Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Introduction: Diastolic mitral regurgitation (MR) is uncommon and generally reflects reversal of the left atrial-left ventricular pressure gradient. In aortic valve infective endocarditis (IE), eccentric aortic regurgitation (AR) may produce a distinct mechanism of diastolic MR through direct interaction with the mitral valve. Patient Information: A 69-year-old man with recent ischemic stroke and newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation presented with palpitations and was found to have Streptococcus anginosus bacteremia. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular (LV) systolic function with normal LV end-diastolic volume (indexed end-diastolic volume, 69 mL/m 2 ), severe MR (effective regurgitant orifice area, 0.50 cm 2 ; regurgitant volume, 80 mL), and a mobile abnormality involving the anterior mitral leaflet (AML). Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) demonstrated destructive aortic valve IE with severe eccentric AR and an AML abscess with perforation, producing severe systolic MR. Doppler imaging demonstrated additional early and late diastolic MR components. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Severe eccentric AR in the setting of normal LV end-diastolic volume supported acute severe AR. The eccentric AR jet was directed toward the AML perforation and passed through it during early diastole, accounting for the early diastolic MR component. Late diastolic MR also occurred through the same perforation after atrial contraction and was most consistent with reversal of the transmitral pressure gradient from elevated LV end-diastolic pressure in the setting of severe AR. This biphasic pattern reflected flow through a common anatomic lesion driven by distinct diastolic mechanisms. Therapeutic Intervention: Given destructive multivalvular IE with severe AR and MR, the patient underwent aortic and mitral valve replacement with concomitant MAZE procedure and left atrial appendage closure. Follow-Up and Outcomes: Surgical inspection demonstrated vegetation and perforation involving the aortic valve and AML. He was discharged on antimicrobial therapy and remained clinically stable at one-month follow-up. Discussion and Synthesis: Although diastolic MR has been described in acute AR and IE, recognition of biphasic diastolic MR in this case clarified the interaction between AR jet trajectory, mitral valve destruction, and abnormal diastolic hemodynamics. In acute severe AR, diastolic MR should prompt careful assessment of regurgitant jet trajectory and mitral valve integrity.
title: Abstract 11008: Biphasic Diastolic Mitral Regurgitation Associated with an Eccentric Aortic Regurgitation Jet in Infective Endocarditis

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) frequently co-exist and increase thromboembolic and bleeding risk, making long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC) difficult to use safely in this population. Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) may provide stroke prevention while reducing dependence on chronic anticoagulation. Given the limited randomized evidence in this high-risk population, we aimed to compare LAAO versus OAC for mortality, bleeding, stroke, and net adverse clinical events (NACE) in patients with AF and CKD. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane through January 2026 for studies comparing LAAO and OAC in adults (≥18 years) with concomitant AF and CKD. Outcomes assessed included all-cause mortality, major bleeding, ischemic stroke, and NACE, defined as a composite of death, stroke and major bleeding with component definitions likely varying across studies. Index date was recorded for each arm wherever reported. We calculated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using random-effects meta-analysis. We assessed heterogeneity using the I 2 statistic and evaluated risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Results: Four retrospective cohort studies comprising 8,588 patients (LAAO, 2,427; OAC, 6,161) were included. Compared with OAC, LAAO was significantly associated with lower hazards of all-cause mortality (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.68, 0.95; p=0.01; I 2 =66%), major bleeding (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.57, 0.70; p<0.00001; I 2 =11%), stroke (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.55, 0.84; p=0.0005; I 2 =13%), and NACE (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.75, 0.84; p<0.00001; I 2 =0%). The NOS scores ranged from 7 to 8 of 9, indicating moderate to high methodological quality but persistent susceptibility to confounding by indication and selection bias. Conclusions: Although LAAO was associated with lower mortality, bleeding, stroke, and NACE, the consistent direction of benefit across endpoints, especially the all-cause mortality signal, is more compatible with confounding by indication than with a true causal effect. Notably, the observed mortality and stroke benefits exceed prior randomized evidence, which demonstrated noninferiority rather than superiority for LAAO. Thus, our retrospective findings are hypothesis-generating and remain vulnerable to residual confounding and immortal time bias. Randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm benefit, clarify stroke subtype-specific effects, and define optimal patient selection and antithrombotic strategies.
title: Abstract 11028: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion versus Oral Anticoagulation in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation and Chronic Kidney Disease: A Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Preprocedural anemia is common in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and has been consistently associated with worse outcomes in prior studies, including analyses from large registries. However, less is known about the potential interactions with valve characteristics. Objective: To evaluate the association between pre-TAVR hemoglobin and outcomes after TAVR, including 30 day mortality, 1 year mortality, and length of stay (LOS), with emphasis on any interaction with valve morphology (bicuspid vs tricuspid), valve type ( self-expandable vs balloon-expandable) and left ventricle ejection fraction (LVEF). Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of 3,030 TAVR patients. Patients were stratified into two cohorts based on pre-procedural hemoglobin levels: Hb <10 g/dL and Hb ≥10 g/dL. Outcomes included 30-day mortality, 1-year mortality, and hospital LOS. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate associations between hemoglobin and mortality outcomes, while linear regression was used for LOS. Models were adjusted for Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) risk score, demographic characteristics, comorbidities, valve type and valve morphology. Interaction terms were included in multivariable models to assess whether the association between hemoglobin category and outcomes differed by valve type, aortic valve morphology, or LVEF. Results: Among 3,030 patients undergoing TAVR, 395 had baseline Hb <10 g/dL and 2,635 had Hb ≥10 g/dL. Baseline characteristics were similar between the two cohorts. In unadjusted analyses, Hb ≥10 g/dL was associated with lower odds of 30 day mortality (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.23-0.65; p<0.001) and 1 year mortality (OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.25-0.49; p<0.001). After multivariable adjustment, Hb ≥10 g/dL remained associated with lower 30 day mortality (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.28-0.86; p=0.012) and 1 year mortality (adjusted OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30-0.62; p<0.001). Hb ≥10 g/dL was also associated with shorter hospital LOS. In interaction analyses, the association between Hb and mortality was not modified by valve type (30 day mortality (p=0.787); 1 year mortality (p=0.340) ). Similarly, no significant interaction was identified between hemoglobin category and aortic valve morphology (1 year mortality p=0.930) or LVEF (1-year mortality p=0.904). Conclusion: Preprocedural hemoglobin <10 g/dL was independently associated with increased 30 day and 1 year mortality following TAVR. The association between anemia and mortality remained consistent regardless of valve type, aortic valve morphology, or LVEF. However, our analysis was limited to hemoglobin measured before TAVR and does not account for changes in anemia after TAVR. Further studies are needed to determine whether worsening anemia during/after the TAVR, or treatment of anemia following TAVR influences clinical outcomes.
title: Abstract 11050: Association of Baseline Hemoglobin with Mortality After TAVR: The Role of Valve Type and Aortic Valve Morphology

abstract: Background: Transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) is increasingly performed in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation. About one fourth of these patients have pre-existing cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs). Expert consensus supports lead extraction before TTVR to avoid mechanical interaction and to preserve future lead management options. Contemporary real world lead management strategies and subsequent device-related outcomes remain poorly characterized. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, a federated electronic health record platform spanning 172 healthcare organizations. Adults aged ≥18 years with pre-existing CIEDs who subsequently underwent TTVR were identified using standardized diagnosis and procedure codes. Patients were classified as having retained transvalvular leads if no lead extraction occurred within one year before TTVR and as "extracted" otherwise. The primary outcome was a composite CIED lead reintervention occurring 1 to 365 days after TTVR, and cumulative incidence was reported with a Clopper-Pearson exact 95% confidence interval. Results: A total of 203 patients with pre-existing CEIDs underwent TTVR. Of these, 173 (85.2%) underwent TTVR with retained transvalvular leads whereas 30 (14.8%) underwent extraction before TTVR. Amongst patients with retained transvalvular leads, 16 of 173 patients (9.2%, 95% CI 5.4-14.6) experienced a CIED lead reintervention within 365 days after TTVR. The composite outcome captured transvenous lead repositioning, repair, or new insertion; subcutaneous or extravascular defibrillator placement or revision; leadless pacemaker placement or removal; and subsequent lead extraction. Conclusions: In a large real world cohort of patients undergoing TTVR with a pre-existing CIED, lead retention strategy was substantially more common contrary to current expert recommendations. Significant percentage of patients (1 in 11) required a subsequent lead-related procedure within one year of TTVR. These findings provide contemporary real-world data regarding lead management strategies during TTVR and support further prospective studies evaluating optimal management of transvalvular CIED leads in patients undergoing tricuspid valve intervention.

title: Abstract 11072: Management of Transvenous CIED Leads During Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement: Real-World Practice Patterns and Outcomes
