abstract: Background: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has emerged as an evolving treatment option for patients with high-risk and intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (PE). Systemic thrombolysis (ST), the traditional reperfusion strategy for high-risk PE, is associated with significant bleeding complications, including gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) and intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). MT offers a localized, minimally invasive approach that may reduce systemic adverse effects while providing effective clot removal. We evaluated national trends in the utilization of MT and ST for PE from 2016-2023 using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) database. Methods: Using ICD-10 codes, we queried the NIS database from 2016-2023 to identify adult hospitalizations with PE undergoing either MT or ST. National trends in the utilization of MT and ST were evaluated over the study period. Survey-weighted (SVY) analysis was used for the primary analysis, while propensity score matching (PSM) analysis was performed as a secondary analysis. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included length of stay (LOS), total hospitalization charges (TOTCHG), GIB, ICH, acute kidney injury (AKI), and cardiac arrest. Results: A total of 101,145 weighted hospitalizations underwent MT or ST for PE from 2016-2023, including 58,845 MT and 42,300 ST hospitalizations. MT utilization increased from 16.9% in 2016 to 83.1% in 2023, while ST utilization decreased from 83.1% to 16.9%. In-hospital mortality was significantly lower with MT compared with ST (4.38% vs 17.05%; aOR 0.24, 95% CI 0.21-0.27; p<0.001). MT was also associated with lower odds of AKI (aOR 0.58), cardiac arrest (aOR 0.16), GIB (aOR 0.68), and ICH (aOR 0.44), all p<0.001. MT was associated with approximately 28% higher TOTCHG and 4.7% longer LOS compared with ST (both p<0.001). PSM analysis demonstrated findings consistent with the primary SVY analysis. Conclusion: Utilization of MT for PE increased substantially from 2016-2023 and was associated with lower in-hospital mortality, bleeding complications, AKI, and cardiac arrest compared with ST, although with higher TOTCHG and slightly longer LOS. These findings suggest that MT is a promising and potentially safer reperfusion strategy for PE; however, prospective randomized studies are needed to further validate these findings.
title: Abstract 13569: National Trends & In Hospital Outcomes of Mechanical Thrombectomy vs Systemic Thrombolysis in Pulmonary Embolism

abstract: Background: The optimal temporary mechanical circulatory support strategy for acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) remains uncertain. Although Impella provides greater hemodynamic support than intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), comparative effectiveness data in routine clinical practice remain limited. We compared clinical outcomes associated with Impella and IABP in a large real-world cohort of patients with AMI-CS. Methods: Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, we identified adults with AMI complicated by cardiogenic shock who received Impella or IABP support. Patients receiving both devices, early extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, or durable ventricular assist devices were excluded. One-to-one propensity score matching was performed using demographics and major cardiovascular comorbidities, yielding 2,413 patients in each group. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, acute kidney injury (AKI), renal replacement therapy (RRT), major bleeding, transfusion, ischemic stroke, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation escalation, and recurrent myocardial infarction (MI). Results: Among 4,826 propensity-matched patients, Impella was associated with higher all-cause mortality compared with IABP (44.1% vs. 38.1%; RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.24; HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.32-1.57; p<0.001). AKI occurred more frequently with Impella (46.2% vs. 41.7%; RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04-1.18; HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.21-1.44; p=0.002). Ischemic stroke demonstrated a higher hazard with Impella (HR 1.47, 95% CI 1.21-1.78; p<0.001). Rates of RRT and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation escalation were similar between groups. Major bleeding showed a higher hazard with Impella (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.15-1.44; p<0.001). Recurrent MI was less frequent among Impella-treated patients (64.6% vs. 74.2%; RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.84-0.91; p<0.001). Conclusions: In this large propensity-matched real-world cohort of patients with AMI-CS, Impella use was associated with higher mortality, AKI, ischemic stroke, and bleeding hazards compared with IABP. Although recurrent MI occurred less frequently among Impella-treated patients, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for residual confounding related to shock severity and treatment selection. Prospective studies are needed to better define the optimal mechanical circulatory support strategy in AMI-CS.

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective TriNetX cohort, propensity-matched 1:1, 2,413 patients in each group (4,826 matched).
appraisal.main_limitation: Matching omitted shock severity and lactate, so residual confounding by indication is probable, as the authors acknowledge; outcomes rely on coded data.
appraisal.one_line: Propensity-matched network analysis found Impella associated with worse mortality than IABP in AMI-CS.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Impella was associated with higher all-cause mortality compared with IABP (44.1% vs. 38.1%; RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.24; HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.32-1.57; p<0.001).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Runs against the direction of randomised evidence for microaxial pumps and illustrates the confounding that target trial emulation with severity data would need to address.

title: Abstract 13583: Impella versus Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump in Acute Myocardial Infarction-Related Cardiogenic Shock: A Propensity Matched Real World Analysis

abstract: Background: Melnick–Needles Syndrome is a rare X-linked skeletal dysplasia caused by pathogenic FLNA variants. Although cardiovascular abnormalities have been described, pulmonary vascular disease remains poorly characterized. We report a fatal case of severe precapillary pulmonary hypertension (PH) complicated by refractory right ventricular (RV) failure. Case Summary: A 33-year-old man with genetically confirmed Melnick–Needles syndrome presented with progressive dyspnea, hypoxemia, and right-sided heart failure. Echocardiography demonstrated severe RV enlargement and dysfunction with severe PH. Right heart catheterization revealed pulmonary artery pressure 91/69 mmHg (mean 76 mmHg), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 13 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance 22.7 Wood units, RV pressure 101/33 mmHg, and right atrial pressure 39/37 mmHg (mean 35 mmHg), confirming severe precapillary PH. Fick cardiac output was 2.76 L/min with cardiac index 1.9 L/min/m 2 and pulmonary artery oxygen saturation 44%. Simultaneous aortic pressure was 64/43 mmHg (mean 49 mmHg), consistent with cardiogenic shock. Evaluation for secondary causes of PH, including chronic thromboembolic disease, connective tissue disease, left-sided heart disease, and significant parenchymal lung disease, was unrevealing. Despite aggressive diuresis, inhaled epoprostenol, and intensive care support, he developed progressive RV failure and refractory shock resulting in death. Discussion: This case demonstrates an extreme hemodynamic phenotype of precapillary PH associated with Melnick–Needles syndrome. Markedly elevated pulmonary artery and right atrial pressures, severe pulmonary vascular resistance elevation, low cardiac output, and profound mixed venous desaturation reflected advanced pulmonary vascular disease with end-stage RV failure. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for PH in patients with Melnick–Needles syndrome presenting with dyspnea or exercise intolerance, as delayed recognition may result in irreversible RV dysfunction and poor outcomes.
title: Abstract 13601: Fatal Precapillary Pulmonary Hypertension and Refractory Right Ventricular Failure in Adult Male Melnick-Needles Syndrome

abstract: Background: The role of pulmonary artery catheterization (Swan-Ganz catheterization) in cardiogenic shock remains controversial. We evaluated the association between Swan-Ganz catheter use and clinical outcomes in a large contemporary real-world cohort. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults with cardiogenic shock were identified and stratified by Swan-Ganz catheter use within one day before through three days after shock diagnosis. One-to-one propensity score matching was performed for age, sex, race/ethnicity, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and systolic heart failure, yielding 12,318 patients in each cohort. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included acute kidney injury (AKI), acute respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation escalation, cardiac arrest, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) escalation, and dialysis/renal replacement therapy (RRT). Results: Among 24,636 propensity-matched patients, Swan-Ganz catheterization was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with no catheterization (44.9% vs. 47.7%; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.92-0.97; HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.79-0.84; p<0.001). Swan-Ganz use was associated with higher rates of AKI (51.0% vs. 45.2%; RR 1.13, p<0.001), acute respiratory failure (42.7% vs. 37.8%; RR 1.13, p<0.001), mechanical ventilation escalation (53.0% vs. 37.8%; RR 1.40, p<0.001), ECMO escalation (7.7% vs. 2.8%; RR 2.74, p<0.001), and dialysis/RRT (12.1% vs. 8.9%; RR 1.37, p<0.001). Cardiac arrest rates were similar between groups (15.3% vs. 15.4%; RR 0.99, p=0.737). Conclusions: In a large propensity-matched cohort of patients with cardiogenic shock, Swan-Ganz catheterization was associated with lower mortality but higher rates of organ-support and escalation-of-care outcomes. These findings likely reflect residual confounding by illness severity and should not be interpreted as causal. Prospective studies are needed to further define the role of invasive hemodynamic monitoring in cardiogenic shock.
title: Abstract 13603: Use of Swan-Ganz Catheterization in Cardiogenic Shock and Associated Outcomes: A Propensity-Matched Analysis

abstract: Background: Acute-on-chronic heart failure (HF)-related cardiogenic shock (CS) may represent a distinct clinical phenotype; however, data describing presentation, management, and outcomes remain limited, particularly among underserved populations underrepresented in contemporary CS studies. We compared clinical characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes among CS patients with and without pre-existing HF at an urban safety-net academic medical center. Methods: Retrospective cohort of 128 consecutive adults with adjudicated CS treated at the Howard University Hospital between 2022 and 2025. Patients were stratified by pre-existing HF status. Primary outcome: in-hospital mortality. Statistical Analysis: Chi-square/Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for comparisons. Multivariable logistic regression assessed the independent association between pre-existing HF and mortality, adjusting for age and admission lactate. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) were reported with 95% CI. Analyses were performed and independently verified in R. AI-assisted tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used for figure rendering based on verified results; all analytical decisions and final text were reviewed and approved by the authors. Results: Among 128 predominantly Black (95%) CS patients (mean age 67±15), pre-existing HF was present in 79 (62%). Patients with pre-existing HF had higher BNP (median 2148 vs 641 pg/mL, p<0.001) and lower LVEF (25% vs 42%, p=0.005), and were more likely to receive CCU admission (47% vs 17%, p=0.001), RHC (30% vs 12%, p=0.03), and inotropic support (65% vs 35%, p=0.005). Sepsis preceded CS more frequently in those without pre-existing HF (43% vs 23%, p=0.03). Patients with pre-existing HF had numerically lower in-hospital mortality (39% vs 53%, p=0.18) and a trend toward higher de novo renal replacement therapy use (32% vs 15%, p=0.055). LOS was similar (11 vs 10 days, p=0.68). After adjustment for age and admission lactate, pre-existing HF was not independently associated with mortality (aOR 0.55, 95% CI 0.24-1.23, p=0.14). Conclusions: Pre-existing HF was associated with more advanced cardiac dysfunction and greater HF-directed care intensity, yet mortality and LOS did not significantly differ. These findings highlight phenotype-specific differences in CS presentation and management within a predominantly Black underserved population that remains underrepresented in contemporary CS registries. Limitations: single-center, modest sample size, limited covariate adjustment, and heterogeneous comparator group (including sepsis-preceded CS) that may confound the outcome comparison.
title: Abstract 13616: Cardiogenic Shock With and Without Pre-Existing Heart Failure: Characteristics, Care Intensity, and Outcomes in an Underserved Urban Cohort

abstract: TAVI/TAVR ; Valvuloplasty ; Structural heart disease intervention ; Valvular heart disease ; Aortic valve stenosis Introduction: Valve in valve Transcatheter Aortic Valve (ViV-TAVR) is established for failed surgical bioprostheses. The Perceval sutureless bioprosthesis has a tall self-expanding nitinol frame which poses unique challenges with difficult anatomy like horizontal aorta and severe aortic calcification further complicating valve delivery and alignment. We describe a snare assisted technique to achieve successful ViV-TAVR when standard methods failed. Patient Information (De-identified): An 81-year-old female with multiple comorbidities presented with NYHA Class III heart failure. Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) predicted mortality was 22.3%. She had prior surgical aortic valve replacement with a Perceval bioprosthesis, complicated by structural degeneration and severe prosthetic aortic stenosis. Clinical Findings and Timeline: TTE demonstrated mean gradient 47 mmHg and peak gradient 71 mmHg across the failed prosthesis. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) was 22 mmHg. Prohibitive surgical risk prompted referral for ViV-TAVR. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Perceval structural degeneration causing severe prosthetic aortic stenosis was confirmed. Anatomic risk factors like annular calcification, horizontal aortic root and unfavorable arch angulation predicted difficulty for coaxial transcatheter delivery. Therapeutic Intervention: Right femoral access was obtained via 18-French sheath. After retrograde crossing and wire positioning, balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) was performed at 160 bpm. A 26 mm self-expanding transcatheter valve failed to achieve coaxial alignment through the Perceval frame despite sequential escalation with techniques like exchange to a stiffer wire (Lunderquist), rotational maneuvers, sheath upsizing to 20-French, and dual buddy wire support. A goose-neck snare then engaged the delivery system nose cone, mechanically redirecting its trajectory. Deployment was achieved at 120 bpm with excellent frame-in-frame alignment. Follow up, Outcomes and Adverse Events: Post procedural TTE confirmed no paravalvular leak, peak velocity 1.6 m/s, mean gradient 6.3 mmHg. The patient was discharged in stable condition. Discussion and Synthesis: The Perceval frame’s nitinol profile and tall self-anchoring architecture create a narrow corridor resisting standard delivery. Goose-neck snares are established for device retrieval; their use as a directional guide represents a bailout strategy. Other techniques such as transseptal antegrade access carry greater risk. Snare-assisted delivery is a safe, reproducible option for structural heart teams managing degenerated Perceval valves.
title: Abstract 13620: Snare Assisted Deployment of Self Expanding Transcatheter Aortic Valve in a Failed Perceval Sutureless Bioprosthesis

abstract: Introduction: Cardiac masses encompass a broad spectrum of pathology, including primary benign and malignant tumors, metastatic disease, thrombi, and vegetations. Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in approximately 0.02% of the population, with papillary fibroelastoma (PFE) and myxoma being the most common benign subtypes. Left-sided cardiac masses carry significant embolic risk, with embolization rates as high as 25%, frequently involving the cerebral and retinal vasculature. Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) as the initial manifestation of a cardiac mass is even more rare. Here we present a case of a large mitral valve mass discovered after recurrent embolic events. Case Description: An 82-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, history of carotid endarterectomy, and CAD developed acute left-sided upper visual field loss. Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed an inferior BRAO with embolus at the optic disc. He was referred for stroke workup, started on DAPT and high-intensity statin, and discharged with instructions to obtain outpatient routine echocardiogram after MRI brain showed no acute abnormalities. One month later, he re-presented with unresponsiveness and aphasia. MRI brain demonstrated multifocal acute infarcts in the left frontal lobe. Echocardiogram revealed a 2.7 x 1.9 cm mass on the ventricular side of the posterior mitral leaflet, confirmed on cardiac MRI. Blood cultures, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and autoimmune workup were unremarkable. He was discharged to rehab and underwent mitral valve replacement six weeks later. Biopsy results remain pending. Discussion: Retinal artery occlusion (RAO) is increasingly recognized as a stroke equivalent, with up to 22% of patients with BRAO developing ischemic cerebrovascular disease and stroke risk as high as 25%. The American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends urgent referral to a stroke center for systemic evaluation including echocardiography. Cardiac MRI is the reference standard for tissue characterization of cardiac masses, with 89-98% accuracy in distinguishing benign from malignant lesions, as recommended by ACR Appropriateness Criteria for cardiac masses of unknown etiology. The differential for a mitral valve mass includes PFE, myxoma, thrombus, vegetation, and malignancy. Negative cultures, autoimmune, and malignancy workup further narrow the differential. Surgical excision is recommended at high-volume centers for low-risk patients, with valve preservation in up to 98% of cases. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of urgent echocardiographic evaluation in patients presenting with RAO, particularly when an embolic source is suspected. A BRAO may serve as a sentinel event for an underlying cardiac mass. Timely echocardiography during the initial presentation may have identified the mass earlier and potentially prevented the subsequent embolic stroke.
title: Abstract 13635: Left Sided Cardiac Mass Presenting as a Case of Branch Retinal Artery Occlusion

abstract: Introduction: Acute Type A aortic dissection rarely presents as acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Coronary malperfusion usually arises from dissection extension into an ostium, false-lumen compression, or a mobile intimal flap, most often in the right coronary artery. A circumferential intimal tear causing intimo-intimal intussusception is far rarer and left main coronary artery (LMCA) involvement rarer still. We report such a case mimicking NSTEMI. Patient Information: A lifelong non-smoking 40-year-old man with controlled migraine presented with acute left-sided chest pain radiating to the jaw and shoulder and dyspnea on light exertion. Family history included premature coronary disease. A cardiac evaluation four years earlier for similar symptoms was unremarkable. Findings: On arrival he was asymptomatic and hemodynamically stable. ECG showed new dynamic inferolateral T-wave inversions, and high-sensitivity troponin I was mildly elevated near 150 ng/L, prompting a provisional NSTEMI diagnosis. Diagnostic assessment: Coronary angiography suggested LMCA compromise without an atherosclerotic culprit. Aortography revealed aortic-root dissection with Sellers 4+ aortic regurgitation. Non-gated CT angiography was non-diagnostic owing to aortic-root motion artifact. Intraoperative TEE and direct surgical inspection confirmed a circumferential aortic-root dissection intermittently occluding the LMCA ostium. Intervention: Given the aortographic findings, the patient underwent emergent open repair of the ascending aorta. Outcome: Resected tissue showed degenerative aortic valve change and mild aortic-wall atherosclerosis, with no connective tissue disorder. The ECG changes and troponin normalized, and he remained well at three months with preserved left ventricular function. Discussion: Coronary malperfusion complicates 7-15% of Type A dissections; LMCA obstruction is rare but portends high risk of shock and sudden death. It is a convincing ACS masquerade; standard therapy is hazardous: antiplatelets, anticoagulation, and above all thrombolysis can precipitate hemorrhage, tamponade, or rupture. Biomarker-severity mismatch and left main compromise without plaque should prompt suspicion. Non-gated CT can be equivocal from aortic-root motion artifact; aortography gave real-time views of the intimal flap and flow, identified the dynamic LMCA mechanism, and enabled direct progression to repair. Management prioritizes restoring true-lumen flow and repairing the primary tear; immediate surgical repair is standard and must not be delayed for percutaneous revascularization, a bridge only in profound instability. The patient lacked traditional risk factors, suggesting subclinical idiopathic aortopathy despite only mild degenerative change. Recognition in young, low-risk patients is essential; delay is often fatal.
title: Abstract 13652: Circumferential Type A Aortic Dissection with Dynamic Left Main Coronary Occlusion Masquerading as NSTEMI

abstract: Introduction: Cardiac myxomas are the most common primary cardiac tumors and carry significant embolic risk, yet myxoma-induced coronary embolism causing STEMI remains exceedingly rare. In Carney complex, an autosomal dominant syndrome of myxomas, endocrine tumors, and pigmentation, myxomas tend to be larger, multifocal, and more prone to embolization than sporadic cases. We report a case of embolic STEMI in a young patient with Carney complex, managed with emergent PCI and multidisciplinary intervention. Case Presentation: A 20 year old male with Carney complex (Cushing syndrome s/p bilateral adrenalectomies, pituitary adenoma, testicular masses) presented with 3 days of progressive exertional dyspnea, and nonproductive cough. Known 8х5 cm left atrial myxoma with MVP and moderate-severe MR was previously identified. At presentation BP 108/49 mmHg, HR 60 bpm, SpO2 99%, BMI 39. Exam unremarkable. On day two, he developed acute chest pain with ECG showing ST-elevation in II, III, aVF, V5 and V6. Troponin T 77 ng/L, NT-proBNP 1324 pg/mL, Hb 10.4 g/dL. Pre-cath echo: EF 55%, mildly dilated LA, borderline RV enlargement, dilated IVC. Management: Emergent coronary angiography revealed a left-dominant system with subtotal mid-LCx occlusion and total OM3 occlusion due to thrombus, without atherosclerosis. Emergent PCI with aspiration thrombectomy (Export catheter) and balloon angioplasty restored TIMI 3 flow in LCx and TIMI 2 in OM3. No stent was placed given embolic etiology. Aspirated thrombus pathology confirmed myxoma fragments, establishing embolic STEMI etiology. Surgical resection (July 30): 8х5 cm LA myxoma excised, MV repair with 34 mm annuloplasty ring, LAA clip performed. Post-op atrial flutter with RVR required DCCV х2, amiodarone load, and temporary-permanent pacemaker (VVI, 50 bpm). He received stress dose steroids for his adrenal insufficiency in the post op period. Follow up: Discharged August 2025 in stable condition. At 2-week follow-up: asymptomatic, EF 55%, trace MR, sinus bradycardia with 49% pacing. Pacemaker explanted January 2026; loop recorder implanted for arrhythmia monitoring. No recurrent emboli or ACS. Genetic counseling and family screening initiated. Discussion: This case illustrates myxoma embolization as a rare but life-threatening cause of STEMI in young patients without atherosclerosis. Key learning points: (1) Myxoma fragments confirmed by thrombectomy pathology establish embolic etiology and inform management; (2) Urgent PCI per ESC ACS guidelines achieves revascularization, while surgical resection prevents recurrence; (3) Carney complex necessitates multidisciplinary care encompassing cardiology, cardiac surgery, and endocrinology; (4) Post-operative arrhythmia and adrenal insufficiency require anticipatory management. This case underscores the embolic risk of cardiac myxoma and the importance of genetic evaluation.
title: Abstract 13663: Coronary Embolism from Left Atrial Myxoma in Carney Complex: A Rare Cause of ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare obstetric complication featuring cardiopulmonary collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC) in labor. Its pathophysiology involves an anaphylactoid response to amniotic material and the release of procoagulant and hyperfibrinolytic factors from amniotic fluid, leading to consumptive coagulopathy, pulmonary vasospasm, right ventricle (RV) failure, and circulatory arrest. Case Presentation: A 37-year-old woman at 40 weeks’ gestation experienced cardiac arrest minutes after spontaneous rupture of membranes. Following resuscitation and emergent cesarean delivery, laboratory results revealed severe coagulopathy ( Table 1 ), and thromboelastography (TEG) was consistent with DIC ( Figure 1 ), suggesting AFE. Despite uterotonics, tranexamic acid, and massive transfusion, heavy uterine bleeding required hysterectomy for hemostasis. Echocardiography revealed significant RV dilation and strain. Due to ongoing cardiogenic shock and vasopressor requirements, a Swan-Ganz catheter was placed and showed right atrial pressure (RAP) exceeding pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP; Table 2 ). Computed tomography demonstrated extensive bilateral pulmonary emboli (PE), further contributing to RV failure. Dobutamine and inhaled epoprostenol were initiated, and therapeutic heparin was started once the hemorrhage resolved. She was successfully extubated and weaned off vasopressors, with improved RV size and function on interval echocardiogram. She was discharged on hospital day eight with a six-month course of warfarin. Discussion: This case illustrates successful resuscitation and recovery from AFE-induced acute RV failure and cardiogenic shock complicated by PE. While AFE classically triggers DIC with platelet-rich thrombi in the pulmonary microvasculature, this patient developed bilateral macrovascular PE - a rarer occurrence that added diagnostic and management complexity. TEG results at the time of arrest were an indispensable diagnostic tool, indicating AFE, rather than PE, was the driver of this patient’s presentation. The clinical challenge was managing severe RV dysfunction from concurrent AFE and PE amid life-threatening hemorrhage and DIC, where fibrinolytics were contraindicated and anticoagulation carried increased risk. Elevated RAP > PCWP and evidence of RV uncoupling from the pulmonary artery were key hemodynamic findings, prompting aggressive inotropic and vasodilator therapy to support the failing RV while hemorrhage control and DIC treatment proceeded. This allowed RV recovery without necessitating catheter-based therapies for PE or escalation to mechanical circulatory support. Successful management required multidisciplinary collaboration to address coagulation abnormalities, control maternal hemorrhage, and restore hemodynamic stability.
title: Abstract 13683: Right Ventricle Failure from Amniotic Fluid Embolism with Pulmonary Emboli: A Case Report

abstract: Introduction: Cancer patients who develop Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) are a high-risk group with poorly characterized long-term cardiovascular risk. Outcome data beyond the index hospitalization are scarce, and whether tumor biology modifies the post-TTS risk trajectory is unknown. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that TTS confers substantial, durable excess cardiovascular and systemic risk in cancer patients, with hematopoietic malignancy patients bearing a greater burden than solid tumor patients. Methods: Retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study using a federated electronic health record network (~250 million patients, 120 health systems). Adult cancer patients with incident TTS were matched 1:1 to cancer patients without TTS, stratified by malignancy type: solid tumor (5,886 pairs) and hematopoietic (1,215 pairs). Patients with TTS preceding cancer diagnosis or with <30 days of follow-up were excluded. Matching used age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidities, and healthcare utilization (standardized mean differences <0.001 post-match). Ten outcomes were assessed at 1, 3, and 5 years using Cox proportional hazards regression and Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results: TTS was associated with elevated risk across all outcomes and both cancer types. In solid tumor patients, 1-year mortality was 27.3% vs 7.9% (hazard ratio [HR] 4.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.65-4.49; p<0.001), intensive care unit (ICU) admission 29.5% vs 4.8% (HR 7.37), mechanical ventilation 10.8% vs 0.9% (HR 13.01), and sepsis 19.1% vs 4.2% (HR 5.33). Hematopoietic patients fared worse: 1-year mortality 34.2% vs 8.7% (HR 4.56, 95% CI 3.68-5.65) and sepsis 31.6% vs 6.0% (HR 6.50). HRs attenuated but remained markedly elevated at 5 years (mortality HR 3.02 solid, 3.63 hematopoietic). Cardiogenic shock reached HR 7.17 (95% CI 4.06-12.67; p=0.002) at 3 years in solid tumor patients. Conclusions: TTS confers substantial, durable cardiovascular and systemic risk in cancer patients that persists for at least 5 years and is greatest among hematopoietic malignancy patients. These findings reframe TTS as a long-term prognostic marker and support dedicated long-term cardio-oncology surveillance.
title: Abstract 13710: Long-Term Cardiovascular Outcomes of Takotsubo Syndrome in Cancer Patients: A Propensity Matched Analysis of Solid versus Hematopoietic Malignancies

abstract: Background: Consensus statements endorse the use of multi-disciplinary cardiogenic shock (CS) teams; however, contemporary U.S. data describing practice patterns and outcomes associated with CS teams remain limited. Methods: We examined baseline characteristics, management strategies, and clinical outcomes of CS patients stratified by site-reported CS team activation using the AHA CS Registry from 2022-2025. A logistic regression model to assess the association of CS team activation and in-hospital mortality was adjusted for for differences in demographics, co-morbidities, and shock severity. Results: Among 7,466 patients with CS, 4,198 ( 56.2% ) were managed with CS teams. These patients were younger (66 vs 69 years), had lower rates of chronic kidney disease (23.8% vs 30.1%), and less likely to present with HF-related CS (39.1% vs 49.9%). Most CS team activations (61.4%) occurred within 6h of CS onset and 84.5% of activations occurred within 24 hours. Patients managed by CS teams had similar presenting lactate levels (2.7 vs 2.7 mmol/L), but were more likely to experience preceding cardiac arrest (21.9% vs 18.4%) and present with SCAI Stage D/E shock (27.0% vs 16.7%). CS team activation was associated with greater use of right heart catheterization (56.4% vs 49.1%), mechanical ventilation (64.3% vs 53.4%), and renal replacement therapy (24.4% vs 16.1%). Patients managed with CS teams received more temporary mechanical circulatory support (44.4% vs 27.1%); specifically ( Figure ): Impella CP (27.4% vs 10.7%), Impella 5.5 (8.8% vs 2.8%), and VA-ECMO (10.7% vs 4.0%), more so than intra-aortic balloon pump (15.6% vs 15.4%). Clinical outcomes were comparable between patients treated with or without CS team involvement, including: hospital length of stay (10.2 vs 9.5 days), heart transplant (2.0% vs 1.4%), and mortality (32.7% vs 31.2%). After multivariable adjustment ( Figure ), CS team activation was not associated with in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.92 - 1.20; p=0.49). Conclusions: In a contemporary national registry, multi-disciplinary CS team activation occurred in over half of CS patients, generally in patients with more severe shock presentations. CS team care was associated with greater use of invasive hemodynamic assessment and advanced temporary MCS therapies. In the setting of wide use of CS teams, adjusted in-hospital mortality was similar with or without CS team involvement.

appraisal.design_and_n: AHA Cardiogenic Shock Registry 2022 to 2025, 7,466 patients with CS, of whom 4,198 (56.2%) were managed with CS teams.
appraisal.main_limitation: Site-reported activation is confounded by shock severity and selection, and the abstract does not address timing or team composition.
appraisal.one_line: National registry describes shock-team activation patterns and finds no adjusted mortality difference.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: After multivariable adjustment, CS team activation was not associated with in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.92 - 1.20; p=0.49).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Contemporary systems-of-care data in a field where shock teams are endorsed by consensus but lack comparative outcome evidence.

title: Abstract 13726: Contemporary Patterns of Cardiogenic Shock Team Activations and Associated Management Strategies: Insights from the American Heart Association Cardiogenic Shock Registry

abstract: Patients with myocardial infarction (MI) are at risk for developing a cardiac ventricular thrombus (CVT), which may embolize, leading to ischemic stroke. Although oral anticoagulation has been demonstrated to be effective at reducing CVT after MI, it may increase the risk of bleeding. We hypothesized that milvexian, a novel Factor XIa inhibitor, may reduce CVT without increasing major or non-major clinically relevant bleeding. The Librexia ACS randomized trial (NCT05754957) evaluated whether milvexian (25mg bid) vs placebo could reduce the composite of CV death, MI, or ischemic stroke when initiated within 7 days of an ACS, in conjunction with standard-of-care antiplatelet therapy. Results of that study have been reported separately. As a preplanned, exploratory investigation, CVT cases were identified from investigator-reported adverse events coded with the preferred term of cardiac ventricular thrombosis. We used a time-to-first event analysis in the intention-to-treat population (n=14,194). A total of 80 CVTs were detected, 24 of 7,094 patients (0.3%) in the milvexian group versus 56 of 7,100 patients (0.8%) in the placebo group (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.27-0.69, p<0.001). Of these, 77 (96%) were observed in patients with ST-segment elevation MI and 76 (95%) in those treated with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). The benefit was observed early and persisted throughout follow-up (Figure). Major bleeding (BARC 3b,3c, 5) in the safety population (n=14,035), on-treatment plus 2 days, was infrequent and similar in both groups (0.9% vs 0.9%, HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.68, 1.37), while non-major clinically relevant bleeding (BARC 2) tended to be higher with milvexian although not significantly so (5.2% vs 4.5%, HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.98, 1.33, p=0.083). In the safety population with CVT, numerically fewer ischemic strokes (1 vs. 3), myocardial infarctions (1 vs. 4), and BARC type 3c/5 bleeding events (0 vs. 2) were observed with milvexian compared with placebo, respectively. In post-MI patients, milvexian at 25mg bid on background DAPT was associated with significantly lower risk of CVT without increased major bleeding vs placebo.

appraisal.design_and_n: Pre-planned exploratory analysis of the Librexia ACS randomised trial (NCT05754957), intention-to-treat population n=14,194; 80 events.
appraisal.main_limitation: Events were investigator-reported adverse events rather than imaging-adjudicated, and the analysis was exploratory.
appraisal.one_line: Exploratory Librexia ACS analysis found fewer cardiac ventricular thrombosis events with milvexian than placebo after acute coronary syndrome.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Cardiac ventricular thrombosis occurred in 24 of 7,094 patients (0.3%) with milvexian versus 56 of 7,100 patients (0.8%) with placebo (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.27-0.69, p<0.001). Major bleeding (BARC 3b,3c, 5) was 0.9% vs 0.9% (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.68, 1.37).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Provides a factor XI inhibitor signal for LV thrombus prevention after MI, relevant to antithrombotic strategy in interventional populations.

title: Abstract 13728: Milvexian Prevents Cardiac Ventricular Thrombosis in Patients with Myocardial Infarction: Insights from the Librexia ACS Trial

abstract: BACKGROUNDRenal sympathetic denervation (RDN) lowers blood pressure in sham-controlled trials, but reported pooled effects vary substantially across published syntheses. Earlier meta-analyses, including our own prior analyses, reported a tightly consistent ≈3 mmHg reduction in 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure (ABPM SBP) with near-zero heterogeneity. We re-examined this conclusion using a complete, independently verified set of sham-controlled trials.METHODSWe pooled all sham-controlled randomized trials reporting between-group differences (RDN minus sham) in 24-hour ABPM SBP, identified from recent systematic reviews, society statements, and registries. The SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED population (combined pilot+pivotal, n=331) was entered once to avoid double-counting. Random-effects models with REML τ 2 estimation, Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman variance correction, and 95% prediction intervals were used. Prespecified subgroups examined region (China, Western, Japan), device (radiofrequency, ultrasound, alcohol-mediated), and antihypertensive medication status. A secondary analysis pooled daytime ABPM SBP across three ultrasound (RADIANCE) trials.RESULTSEight trials (n≈2,120) reporting 24-hour ABPM SBP were included. The pooled effect was –3.55 mmHg (95% CI –6.17 to –0.93; Hartung-Knapp –6.86 to –0.24; P=0.039) , with substantial heterogeneity ( I 2 =75%; τ=3.3 mmHg ); the 95% prediction interval (–12.2 to +5.1) crossed zero. Heterogeneity was explained largely by region and device: two Chinese radiofrequency trials demonstrated –9.07 mmHg (95% CI –11.61 to –6.53; I 2 =0%), whereas five Western trials showed only –2.52 mmHg (–3.81 to –1.23; I 2 =27%). The Japanese ultrasound trial (REQUIRE) was neutral (–0.10 mmHg). Leave-one-out analysis confirmed that removal of either Chinese trial shifted the pooled estimate to approximately –2.8 mmHg. Among three ultrasound trials, daytime ABPM SBP was reduced by –5.90 mmHg (–7.83 to –3.97; I 2 =0%), though the prediction interval (1 df) was uninterpretable. Published meta-analyses span –2.6 to –4.4 mmHg depending on trial inclusion.CONCLUSIONSAcross all sham-controlled trials, RDN reduces 24-hour ABPM SBP, but the effect is heterogeneous, not uniform. For Western, FDA-relevant populations the effect is modest (≈2-3 mmHg). The markedly larger effects in Chinese radiofrequency trials are outliers warranting scrutiny before generalization. The evidence supports a measured, adjunctive role for RDN and a research agenda centered on durability, hard cardiovascular outcomes, and elucidating the between-region variation.
title: Abstract 13756: Renal Denervation and Ambulatory Blood Pressure Reduction: A Complete, Heterogeneity-Aware Meta Analysis of Sham-Controlled Randomized Trials

abstract: Introduction: As transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) use expands, management of transcatheter heart valve (THV) failure has become increasingly important. We present a case of failed TAVR with challenging coronary anatomy, successfully managed with a SURPLUS procedure. Case Presentation: An 82-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis status post TAVR in 2021 presented with progressive dyspnea and acute decompensated heart failure. Echocardiography demonstrated severe prosthetic valve dysfunction with peak/mean gradients of 48/31 mmHg, valve area of 0.45 cm 2 , moderate-to-severe paravalvular leak, and new left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 20-25%). CTA TAVR performed to determine appropriate Transcatheter valve size revealed a 23mm Sapien valve was recommended. The initial TAVR valve was implanted in 2021, at that time, commissure alignment technique was not available in our hospital. CTA of estimated commissure and coronary ostia orientation revealed superimposed RCA and LAD with 2 TAVR commissures, indicating severe commissure misalignment. Given the inability to cannulate the coronaries, unfavorable valve-to-coronary anatomy with commissural misalignment, the catheterization team recommended careful consideration of redo TAVR (TAV-in-TAV), noting BASILICA or UNICORN techniques would likely not be feasible. The patient's STS risk score was calculated at 53.4% indicating prohibitive surgical risk. The patient underwent a SURPLUS procedure involving urgent aortic valve replacement within the existing TAVR prosthesis. This included femoral cannulation for cardiopulmonary bypass, followed by sternotomy, aortotomy, surgical resection of Evolut valve leaflets, and implantation of a 23 mm SAPIEN S3 Ultra valve. Postoperative echocardiography demonstrated marked improvement in valve function with gradients reduced to 12/7 mmHg, a calculated valve area of 1.72 cm2 and trivial paravalvular leak. After temporary inotropic support, LVEF improved to 35%, and the patient was discharged to cardiac rehabilitation. Discussion: Management of THV failure depends on the mechanism of valve dysfunction, patient risk, and anatomic considerations. While redo-TAVR and surgical explantation remain standard options, complex anatomy and hemodynamic instability may necessitate alternative approaches. The SURPLUS procedure combines surgical leaflet resection with transcatheter valve implantation under cardiopulmonary bypass support, offering a less invasive alternative to complete valve explantation in selected high-risk patients. Conclusion: This case demonstrates the successful use of the SURPLUS procedure in a patient with failed TAVR, and unfavorable coronary anatomy. Hybrid strategies may provide an effective treatment option for complex THV failure when conventional approaches are not feasible.
title: Abstract 13758: Beyond Valve-in-Valve: SURPLUS Procedure for Failed TAVR in Patients with Complex Coronary Anatomy

abstract: Background: Aspirin remains a cornerstone of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Aspirin hypersensitivity presents a significant therapeutic challenge, particularly in community hospitals where allergy consultation may not be readily available. We describe successful cardiologist-led aspirin desensitization following primary PCI and the subsequent development of an institutional pathway to facilitate guideline-directed therapy. Case: A 47-year-old man with hypertension and gout presented with exertional chest pain and elevated cardiac biomarkers. He reported a remote history of aspirin-induced angioedema but had tolerated other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. He was loaded with ticagrelor without aspirin. During hospitalization, he developed lateral STEMI with a peak troponin of 15,000 ng/L. Emergent coronary angiography demonstrated a critical proximal left anterior descending artery lesion, which was successfully treated with PCI. Decision-Making: The patient remained at high risk for stent thrombosis without aspirin-based DAPT. Allergy consultation was unavailable, and no institutional desensitization protocol existed. Given the absence of equivalent alternatives to aspirin in guideline-directed therapy, the cardiology team developed and implemented an ICU-based desensitization strategy. The patient received pretreatment with methylprednisolone, diphenhydramine, famotidine, and montelukast followed by stepwise aspirin administration (1 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, and 100 mg) under continuous telemetry, pulse oximetry, and close hemodynamic monitoring (Table 1 and 2) Intravenous tirofiban was maintained throughout the protocol to ensure uninterrupted platelet inhibition. The patient completed desensitization without respiratory, cutaneous, or hemodynamic complications and was successfully transitioned to aspirin and ticagrelor. Conclusion: Community hospitals frequently manage high volumes of acute coronary syndrome patients but may lack immediate access to allergy specialists. This case demonstrates that cardiologist-led aspirin desensitization can be safely performed in a monitored ICU setting following primary PCI for STEMI. The experience led to the development of a standardized institutional pathway aimed at improving access to guideline-directed DAPT in patients with aspirin hypersensitivity. Broader adoption of similar protocols may help overcome resource limitations and reduce barriers to optimal cardiovascular care.
title: Abstract 13763: Developing a Cardiologist-Led Aspirin Desensitization Pathway Following Primary PCI for STEMI in a Community Hospital Without Allergy Support

abstract: Background: In AZALEA-TIMI 71, the novel factor XI inhibitor abelacimab significantly reduced the risk of bleeding compared with rivaroxaban in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Those with AF and a history of bleeding are at elevated risk for recurrent bleeding, often resulting in interruption or even permanent discontinuation of anticoagulation. Purpose: To evaluate the safety of abelacimab vs rivaroxaban among patients with and without a history of bleeding. Methods: AZALEA-TIMI 71 randomized patients with AF at moderate-to-high risk of stroke to one of two abelacimab doses (90 or 150 mg) administered subcutaneously monthly or to oral rivaroxaban (20 mg daily, dose reduced to 15 mg in patients with creatinine clearance ≤50 mL/min). The individual abelacimab dosing arms were pooled for this analysis. Outcomes of interest included ISTH major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (CRNM), major bleeding alone, and major GI bleeding, as adjudicated by an independent, blinded clinical events committee. Outcomes were examined using Cox proportional hazards models with an interaction term between baseline history of bleeding and treatment allocation. Results: Among 1,276 patients, 99 patients (7.8%) had a prior history of bleeding. Those with prior bleeding were older (median age 77 vs. 74 years), with lower creatinine clearance (CrCl <50 ml/min 28.3% vs. 19.9%) and higher HAS-BLED scores (median 4 vs. 2). In the rivaroxaban arm, the rate of major/CRNM bleeding was >2-fold higher in those with a prior history of bleeding than in those without (crude IR 19.7 vs. 7.6 per 100 PY). Abelacimab consistently reduced the relative rate of major/CRNM bleeding vs. rivaroxaban both in those with and without a history of bleeding (HR 0.29 [95% CI 0.11, 0.78] and HR 0.35 [95 % CI 0.23, 0.52] respectively; p-interaction 0.65), with a numerically greater absolute risk reduction in those with a history of bleeding (ARR 14.4 vs 4.9 per 100 PY) ( Fig 1A ). Results were consistent when comparing the individual abelacimab doses to rivaroxaban (p-interaction = 0.95). A similar pattern was seen for major bleeding alone and major GI bleeding ( Figs 1B and 1C ). Premature permanent study drug discontinuation rates were similar in those with and without a history of bleeding randomized to abelacimab (4.5% vs. 6.1% per year) but were approximately twice as high in those with vs. without a history of bleeding randomized to rivaroxaban (9.1% vs 4.7% per year). Conclusion: Inhibition of factor XI with abelacimab consistently reduced incident bleeding irrespective of bleeding history, with numerically greater absolute risk reduction and possibly enhanced tolerability in those with a history of bleeding at baseline compared to rivaroxaban. These data suggest that the safety profile of abelacimab may be particularly advantageous in vulnerable patients with AF with a history of bleeding.

appraisal.design_and_n: Secondary analysis of AZALEA-TIMI 71 (randomised, abelacimab 90 or 150 mg monthly vs rivaroxaban), 1,276 patients, 99 patients (7.8%) with prior bleeding.
appraisal.main_limitation: Only 99 patients had prior bleeding, so the subgroup estimate is imprecise, and the trial population is atrial fibrillation rather than interventional.
appraisal.one_line: Prespecified-style subgroup analysis of a randomised factor XI trial by bleeding history in atrial fibrillation.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Abelacimab consistently reduced the relative rate of major/CRNM bleeding vs. rivaroxaban both in those with and without a history of bleeding (HR 0.29 [95% CI 0.11, 0.78] and HR 0.35 [95 % CI 0.23, 0.52] respectively; p-interaction 0.65).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Supports factor XI inhibition in patients at high bleeding risk, relevant to antithrombotic strategy after LAAO and structural procedures.

title: Abstract 13770: History of Bleeding and Safety of Abelacimab vs. Rivaroxaban in Atrial Fibrillation:A Secondary Analysis of AZALEA-TIMI 71

abstract: Background: Current prosthetic mitral valves, including mechanical and bioprosthetic valves, often provide a smaller effective orifice area than the native mitral valve, potentially impairing left ventricular filling and limiting cardiac output after mitral valve replacement. We developed a novel cylinder-type prosthetic valve designed to preserve physiologic transmitral flow. This study evaluated whether the novel valve reproduces native mitral valve hemodynamics across a wide range of heart rates. Methods: Porcine native mitral valves (n=12) and novel prosthetic valves (n=12) were evaluated using a pulsatile mock circulatory loop. Hemodynamic performance was assessed at heart rates of 70, 100, and 130 bpm while maintaining a target mean flow of 3 L/min. Systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), forward flow, and net flow were measured and compared between valve types using two-way ANOVA. Results: The novel prosthetic valve demonstrated a bicuspid closing configuration resembling that of the native mitral valve. Across all tested heart rates, hemodynamic parameters were comparable between the novel prosthetic and native mitral valves. There was no difference between valve types in SBP/DBP at 70, 100, and 130 bpm with 119±7.1/91±5.7, 106±4.8/90±3.7, and 97±5.1/83±4.5 mmHg for native valves, compared with 119±7.9/91±2.9, 106±5.5/89±4.1, and 99±7.9/85±6.6 mmHg for novel prosthetic valves (all p>0.05). SBP significantly differed by heart rate but no significant effect valve type-heart rate interaction was observed for SBP or DBP. Forward flow was also comparable between native and prosthetic valves at all heart rates (70 bpm: 3.7±0.4 vs. 3.6±0.2 L/min; 100 bpm: 3.5±0.5 vs. 3.4±0.2 L/min; 130 bpm: 3.3±0.6 vs. 3.3±0.6 L/min), with no significant valve-type effect or interaction (p=0.324 and p=0.954).Similarly, net flow was preserved with the prosthetic valve and was comparable to native valve performance at 70 bpm (3.1±0.4 vs. 3.0±0.2 L/min), 100 bpm (2.8±0.4 vs. 2.7±0.2 L/min), and 130 bpm (2.4±0.5 vs. 2.4±0.4 L/min), without significant differences between valve types or interaction effects (p=0.210 and p=0.978). Conclusions: The novel cylinder-type prosthetic valve reproduced native-like hemodynamics across physiologic and tachycardic heart rates in the ex vivo study. Preservation of blood pressure, forward flow, and net flow suggests that this design maintains transmitral flow after mitral valve replacement. These findings support the potential of this next-generation prosthetic valve to address a fundamental limitation of conventional mitral valve prostheses and provide more physiologic postoperative hemodynamics.
title: Abstract 13783: Hemodynamic Comparison of a Novel Prosthetic Valve and the Native Mitral Valve in a Pulsatile Flow Model

abstract: Introduction: Isolated cardiac sarcoidosis is an elusive condition with an unpredictable clinical course. Ventricular arrythmias are a recognized but uncommon complication associated with high morbidity and mortality. We describe a case of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) due to cardiac sarcoidosis complicated by ventricular tachycardia (VT) storm and cardiogenic shock, requiring VA-ECMO as a bridge to orthotopic heart transplant (OHT). Case Presentation: A 46-year-old male with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented with subacute dyspnea and palpitations. Initial evaluation showed elevated troponins, frequent polymorphic ventricular ectopy and interventricular conduction delay (IVCD) on EKG (Fig 2) and biventricular systolic dysfunction on echo. Right and left heart catheterization revealed widely patent coronary arteries, mildly elevated filling pressures, and severely reduced cardiac indices. Cardiac MRI demonstrated myocardial edema and multifocal late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) involving the RV, suggestive of myocarditis (Fig 1). Endomyocardial biopsy revealed granulomatous myocarditis consistent with cardiac sarcoidosis (Fig 2). FDG-PET demonstrated biventricular perfusion defects with FDG uptake in the septum, inferior wall, and RV free wall without extracardiac involvement (Fig 1). Despite immune suppression with high-dose corticosteroids and mycophenolate mofetil, the patient developed VT storm refractory to antiarrhythmics (Fig 2). Due to cardiogenic shock, VA-ECMO was initiated as a bridge to OHT. Outcomes and Follow-up: His post-operative course was complicated by primary allograft dysfunction requiring inotropes, VAV-ECMO, and Impella 5.5 support; acute renal failure; stroke; and prolonged ventilator dependence due to pulmonary hemorrhage. Ultimately, he recovered and was discharged home post-op day 47 after completion of inpatient rehabilitation with normal allograft function, off dialysis, with normal end organ function. Conclusion: This case highlights the malignant arrhythmic potential of cardiac sarcoidosis and the importance of early recognition, particularly in patients with significant right ventricular LGE burden, which is independently associated with increased VT risk. Clinicians should maintain a low threshold for tissue sampling when evaluating suspected isolated CS. Clinically, it illustrates a rare presentation of isolated CS with in extremis cardiogenic shock associated with electrical storm at index hospitalization, ultimately necessitating mechanical circulatory support and urgent OHT. Mechanical circulatory support is an established therapy in cardiogenic shock and refractory VT. However, its use in cardiac sarcoidosis remains uncommon. These findings underscore the critical role of timely multidisciplinary management in the early recognition and treatment of cardiogenic shock in CS.
title: Abstract 13791: Cardiac Sarcoidosis-Associated Ventricular Tachycardia Storm and Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Background: Initiating potent lipid-lowering regimens at the time of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) hospitalization may curb the heightened recurrent-event risk of the early post-ACS window. Whether adding a PCSK9 inhibitor (PCSK9i) or ezetimibe to background statin therapy confers greater protection remains unresolved in the absence of direct head-to-head trials. Hypothesis: Early initiation of PCSK9i plus statin during index ACS hospitalization reduces major adverse cardiovascular events more effectively than ezetimibe plus statin or statin monotherapy. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and Embase were searched from inception to December 2025 for randomized or observational studies enrolling ACS patients in whom combination lipid-lowering therapy was initiated during index hospitalization and continued for ≥6 months. A random-effects Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA) generated risk ratios (RRs) and 95% credible intervals (CrIs); treatment hierarchy was assessed via surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA). Results: Thirteen studies (5 randomized, 8 observational) comprising 26,048 patients were included. Compared with statin monotherapy, ezetimibe plus statin did not significantly reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (RR 0.89, 95% CrI 0.63-1.05), whereas PCSK9i plus statin significantly reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (RR 0.59, 95% CrI 0.45-0.76), myocardial infarction (RR 0.50, 95% CrI 0.33-0.74), and revascularization (RR 0.63, 95% CrI 0.46-0.82). All-cause death and stroke did not differ significantly across strategies. In indirect comparison, PCSK9i plus statin was favored over ezetimibe plus statin for myocardial infarction (RR 0.57, 95% CrI 0.29-0.99). SUCRA ranked PCSK9i plus statin highest across all outcomes (range 73.7%-97.5%). Conclusions: Early PCSK9i initiation after ACS was associated with the most favorable clinical profile in this NMA. Given the indirect nature of cross-treatment comparisons and the inclusion of observational data, prospective randomized trials directly comparing both strategies are essential before practice-changing recommendations can be made.
title: Abstract 13796: Early PCSK9 Inhibitor-Statin versus Ezetimibe-Statin Therapy After Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Periprocedural stroke during cardiac catheterization is rare (incidence 0.05-0.1% for diagnostic angiography; 0.18-0.44% for PCI). Classical mechanisms include aortic atheroma, catheter-surface thrombus, or air embolism. Stroke arising solely from intracoronary thrombus dislodgement during diagnostic angiography without interventional instrumentation remains poorly characterized. We present a distinct case of retrograde intracoronary thrombus embolization precipitating large-vessel occlusion stroke. Patient Information A 43-year-old male with hypertension and tobacco use presented with NSTEMI (troponin markedly elevated, blood pressure 200/110 mmHg). No prior cerebrovascular history was documented. Baseline neurological examination was entirely normal. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Urgent diagnostic coronary angiography with planned PCI was performed under continuous neurological monitoring. Left coronary angiography revealed collateral filling suggestive of RCA occlusion. Contrast injection into the RCA confirmed near-complete proximal thrombus. A second injection minutes later showed complete thrombus disappearance. Within 2-3 minutes, the patient developed acute aphasia and right facial droop. Diagnostic Assessment: Emergent CT angiography identified left MCA M1 occlusion. The temporal correlation between thrombus disappearance and neurological deterioration with no PCI instrumentation, balloon inflation, or stent deployment prior to stroke onset strongly supported retrograde embolization. High-pressure contrast injection is postulated to have generated sufficient shear force to dislodge the proximal thrombus retrograde into the aorta, enabling cerebral embolization. Interventions Emergent mechanical thrombectomy achieved complete left MCA recanalization (TICI score 3). No thrombolytics were administered. Rapid multidisciplinary coordination between interventional cardiology and neurointerventional teams was essential to the reperfusion strategy. FOLLOW-UP AND OUTCOMES Aphasia and right facial droop fully resolved by discharge. Mild right lower extremity weakness persisted as the sole residual deficit. No adverse events were recorded. The favorable outcome reflected immediate stroke recognition and pre-established catheterization laboratory protocols. Discussion This case establishes that diagnostic coronary angiography alone can precipitate large-vessel stroke via retrograde intracoronary thrombus embolization, a mechanism distinct from classical embolic pathways. Intracoronary thrombus burden is an underrecognized hazard even during purely diagnostic procedures. Continuous neurological monitoring, pre-established stroke response protocols, and rapid multidisciplinary coordination are essential in the catheterization laboratory to optimize reperfusion outcomes.
title: Abstract 13805: When Coronary Thrombus Travels Upstream: A Rare Case of Retrograde Cerebral Embolization During Diagnostic Coronary Angiography

abstract: Background: In patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), optimal stroke prevention strategy remains debated, particularly as left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) emerges as an alternative to oral anticoagulation. A comprehensive comparison among direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), warfarin, and LAAC within a unified analytical framework is lacking. Hypothesis: DOACs, warfarin, and LAAC differ meaningfully in mortality, thromboembolic, and bleeding outcomes in AF patients, with no single strategy dominating across all endpoints. Methods: A frequentist network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted following a systematic search of randomized controlled trials comparing DOACs, warfarin, or LAAC in AF patients. Incidence risk ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using mixed treatment comparisons. Eight trials comprising 76,199 patients were included. Results: For all-cause death, DOACs significantly reduced mortality versus warfarin (IRR 0.90, 95% CI 0.86-0.95), and LAAC significantly reduced mortality versus warfarin (IRR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65-0.99); DOACs and LAAC did not differ significantly (IRR 1.12, 95% CI 0.91-1.39). For cardiovascular death, both DOACs (IRR 0.86, 95% CI 0.76-0.97) and LAAC (IRR 0.67, 95% CI 0.49-0.93) outperformed warfarin; no significant difference was found between DOACs and LAAC (IRR 1.28, 95% CI 0.94-1.75). For stroke or systemic embolism, DOACs significantly reduced events versus warfarin (IRR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80-0.96). However, no significant difference was seen between DOAC vs LAAC (IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.00) and LAAC vs warfarin (IRR 1.21, 95% CI 0.87-1.68). Regarding safety outcomes, for major bleeding, DOACs were superior to warfarin (IRR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67-0.99); no significant differences were observed between LAAC and either comparator. However, regarding major or minor bleeding, LAAC was superior to both DOACs (IRR 0.71, 95% CI 0.53-0.94) and Warfarin (IRR 0.59, 95% CI 0.43-0.81) Conclusions: In this NMA of AF patients, DOACs demonstrated the most consistent benefit across stoke and thromboembolic outcomes, while LAAC showed a mortality advantage over warfarin without a significant stroke reduction benefit. Additionally, LAAC improved bleeding event compared to both oral anticoagulants. These findings highlight the need for individualized treatment selection based on patient-specific bleeding and thromboembolic risk profiles.
title: Abstract 13808: Left Atrial Appendage Closure Devices versus Oral Anticoagulation in Non Valvular Atrial Fibrillation: A Network Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction/Background: Post-myocardial infarction ventricular septal rupture (VSR) is a rare but catastrophic complication of acute myocardial infarction (MI) resulting from transmural septal necrosis, which can lead to left-to-right shunt, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and high mortality. Surgery is the definitive treatment, while mechanical circulatory support (MCS) and medical treatments can provide stability. Given the rarity of this condition, contemporary data remains limited. Research Questions/Hypothesis: We sought to describe the clinical characteristics, management strategies, and outcomes of patients with post-MI VSR at our institution. Methods/Approach: We conducted a retrospective single-center study of adults with ICD-identified post-MI VSR between 01/01/2015 and 02/26/2026. Patients younger than 18 years old or with non-MI-related VSR were excluded. Results/Data: We identified 27 patients with post-MI VSR, 81% male, mean age 68 ± 9 years, BMI 30.4 ± 4.9 kg/m 2 , and mean LVEF of 53.7%. The median time from symptom onset to admission was 12 hours. Patients’ presenting ECG demonstrated ST elevation (89%) and Q waves (81%). The most common culprit vessel was the right coronary artery (67%). Right heart catheterization was performed in 85% of patients, 63% received primary percutaneous coronary intervention, and 89% required ICU admission. In the first 24 hours in ICU, mean characteristics showed lowest systolic BP 88 ± 24 mmHg, lowest MAP 68 ± 20 mmHg, highest HR 110 ± 42 bpm, highest lactate 3.3 ± 5.5 mmol/L, highest NT-pro-BNP of 12023 ± 15862, and highest HS-troponin of 18165 ± 63207. VSR size ranged from 0.5 to 4.7 cm, with the most common location being inferior/basal (74%). Mechanical circulatory support was common, with IABP (52%), for a mean duration of 6.4 ± 7.7 days. Surgical repair was performed in 52% of patients, while 41% were managed medically. Outcomes differed dramatically by treatment approach. (Table 1) Conclusion: In this single-center cohort, post-MI VSR was associated with frequent ICU admission and high inpatient mortality without early surgical repair. Clinical trajectory and treatment decisions appeared to reflect overall hemodynamic instability, comorbid burden, and end-organ dysfunction rather than VSR size alone.
title: Abstract 13819: Clinical Characteristics, Management, and Outcomes of Post-Myocardial Infarction Ventricular Septal Rupture: A Single Center Experience

abstract: Background: Mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) improves mitral regurgitation (MR), but its effects on left ventricular (LV) intraventricular flow organization remain incompletely characterized. Doppler velocity reconstruction (DoVeR) enables quantitative assessment of LV flow dynamics from routine color Doppler echocardiography. Methods: We prospectively studied 24 patients undergoing intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography before and after TEER. Mid-esophageal 2-chamber and 3-chamber color Doppler acquisitions were processed using DoVeR to reconstruct 2-dimensional velocity fields and quantify flow energy loss (FEL), kinetic energy (KE), vortex strength (VS), FEL/KE ratio, and pressure-derived parameters. Flow metrics were compared before and after device implantation using paired nonparametric testing. Associations with postprocedural 3-dimensional vena contracta area (3D-VCA), used as an efficacy marker, and transmitral mean gradient (TMG), used as a safety marker, were assessed using Spearman correlation and exploratory univariate logistic regression. Results: TEER significantly altered LV flow dynamics. In the 3-chamber view, device implantation was associated with reductions in KE, VS, systolic FEL, E-wave velocity, suction pressure, and reversal pressure. In the 2-chamber view, reductions were most evident for systolic FEL, KE, VS, and total KE. FEL/KE ratios increased, particularly in diastolic and total-cycle measurements, consistent with greater flow disorganization after repair. Vector field analysis demonstrated disrupted vortex formation, wall impingement of postprocedural inflow jets, and complex interactions between dual jets. Higher postprocedural FEL/KE ratio was associated with lower 3D-VCA, most prominently for systolic peak FEL/KE in the 2-chamber view (ρ = -0.68, p < 0.001). Peak diastolic FEL/KE in the 3-chamber view was positively associated with TMG (ρ = 0.43, p = 0.038). On exploratory logistic regression, 2-chamber peak diastolic, peak systolic, and total FEL/KE ratios demonstrated unadjusted discriminative ability for increased residual MR defined by total VCA >0.3 cm 2 . Conclusions: Doppler-derived LV flow reconstruction demonstrated that TEER acutely reduces LV flow energy and vortex strength while increasing FEL/KE ratio, indicating altered flow organization. FEL/KE was associated with both residual MR and transmitral gradient, suggesting a potential hemodynamic trade-off between regurgitation reduction and inflow obstruction. These exploratory findings support further evaluation of echocardiographic flow metrics as adjunctive physiologic markers of TEER outcomes.
title: Abstract 13826: Doppler-Derived Left Ventricular Flow Remodeling After Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair

abstract: Background: Left ventricular unloading with Impella during venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECPELLA) has been proposed as a strategy to improve outcomes in cardiogenic shock, but existing evidence remains inconsistent. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that ECPELLA may improve short-term mortality compared with VA-ECMO alone. This study aimed to systematically evaluate comparative clinical outcomes. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception through May 18, 2026 identified studies comparing ECPELLA with VA-ECMO in adults with cardiogenic shock. The primary outcome was short-term mortality (In-hospital or 30-day mortality). Secondary outcomes included renal failure requiring continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), ventricular assist device (VAD) implantation or heart transplantation, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) weaning, hemolysis, and major bleeding. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: Ten studies comprising 1,419 patients were included in the analysis, with 520 patients in the ECPELLA group and 899 in the VA-ECMO group. Of these, eight were retrospective and two were prospective in design. There was no significant difference in short-term mortality between ECPELLA and VA-ECMO alone (RR = 0.91, 95% CI 0.80-1.04; p=0.15).). ECPELLA was associated with increased CRRT use (RR = 1.64, 95% CI 1.10-2.43; p = 0.01) and higher risk of hemolysis (RR = 1.73, 95% CI 1.24-2.40; p = 0.001). There was no difference in major bleeding events (RR = 1.19, 95% CI 0.80-1.77; p = 0.40). ECPELLA was associated with higher likelihood of VAD implantation or heart transplantation (RR = 2.05, 95% CI 1.51-2.80; p < 0.00001). ECPELLA was associated with higher rates of successful weaning from mechanical circulatory support compared with VA-ECMO alone (RR: 1.33; 95% CI: 1.01-1.75; p = 0.04). Conclusions: In patients with cardiogenic shock, ECPELLA did not demonstrate significant reduction in short-term mortality compared with VA-ECMO alone. Moreover, it was associated with higher rates of advanced therapy utilization and mechanical support weaning, but also with increased renal replacement therapy and hemolysis, without a difference in major bleeding. Overall, ECPELLA confers no clear survival benefit, and its use should be guided by careful patient selection and a balanced assessment of risks and benefits. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to define its optimal role in this patient population.
title: Abstract 13832: Left Ventricular Unloading with Impella in Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation versus Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Alone in Cardiogenic Shock: A Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Transapical off-pump NeoChord implantation is a minimally invasive repair strategy for degenerative mitral regurgitation that restores leaflet coaptation while preserving native mitral valve geometry. Its acute effects on left ventricular (LV) intraventricular flow dynamics remain incompletely characterized. Doppler velocity reconstruction (DoVeR) enables quantitative assessment of LV flow from routine color Doppler echocardiography. Methods: We prospectively studied 18 patients undergoing intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography before and after NeoChord implantation. Mid-esophageal 3-chamber color Doppler acquisitions were processed using DoVeR to reconstruct 2-dimensional velocity fields and quantify flow energy loss (FEL), kinetic energy (KE), vortex strength (VS) and intraventricular pressure-gradient metrics. Pre- and postprocedural flow variables were compared using paired nonparametric testing. Results: NeoChord implantation significantly reduced mitral regurgitation severity, with total 3-dimensional vena contracta area decreasing from 0.62 ± 0.15 cm 2 to 0.22 ± 0.09 cm 2 . Quantitative flow analysis demonstrated significant reductions in FEL, KE, and VS across the cardiac cycle after repair. Intraventricular pressure-gradient metrics also decreased significantly, whereas E-wave velocity remained unchanged. Notably, the reduction in FEL was proportional to the reduction in KE, and the reduction in diastolic average FEL was greater than the reduction in diastolic average. Qualitative vector-field analysis showed that preprocedural flow was characterized by a high-energy inflow jet, unstable vortical structures, and limited continuity between diastolic flow organization and systolic outflow. After repair, diastolic inflow was less energetic but generated a more coherent anterior vortex near the LV outflow tract, which persisted into late diastole and aligned with systolic outflow. Conclusions: Doppler-derived LV flow reconstruction showed that NeoChord implantation acutely reduces flow energy loss, kinetic energy, vortex strength, and pressure-gradient metrics. In diastole, FEL decreased to a greater extent than KE, suggesting a disproportionate reduction in dissipative flow losses relative to overall flow energy. These findings indicate that transapical chordal repair may lessen the energetic burden associated with regurgitant and disorganized flow while preserving efficient intraventricular flow organization. DoVeR-derived flow analysis may therefore provide a mechanistic echocardiographic framework for evaluating LV hemodynamic response after mitral valve repair.
title: Abstract 13835: Doppler-Derived Left Ventricular Flow Remodeling After Transapical NeoChord Mitral Valve Repair

abstract: Introduction: As transcatheter heart valves (THVs) are increasingly implanted in younger, lower risk patients, durability concerns arise. When THVs fail, optimal management, surgical explantation (TAVR explant), redo TAVR, or redo surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), remains unclear. This network meta-analysis compares their clinical outcomes. Methods: We systematically searched multiple medical databases from inception through June 2026 for studies comparing TAVR explant, redo TAVR, and redo SAVR in patients with failed transcatheter heart valves. A Bayesian network meta-analysis was conducted. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I tool. Results: Twenty studies comprising 18,742 patients with failed transcatheter heart valves were included. Network meta-analysis demonstrated that redo TAVR was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality compared with TAVR explant (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.31-0.57) and redo SAVR (OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.52-0.89). TAVR explant carried the highest mortality risk (rank probability 89%). For stroke, redo TAVR vs. redo SAVR was similar (OR 1.04; 95% CI 0.72-1.50), while TAVR explant showed increased risk vs. redo TAVR (OR 1.85; 95% CI 1.23-2.78). Coronary obstruction was more frequent with redo TAVR vs. TAVR explant (OR 3.12; 95% CI 1.87-5.21). Permanent pacemaker implantation was highest with redo TAVR vs. redo SAVR (OR 2.34; 95% CI 1.65-3.31). Acute kidney injury favored redo TAVR vs. explant (OR 0.54; 95% CI 0.38-0.77) and redo SAVR vs. explant (OR 0.61; 95% CI 0.44-0.85). Heart failure hospitalization was lower for redo TAVR vs. explant (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.31-0.71). Reintervention rates favored redo SAVR vs. redo TAVR (OR 0.31; 95% CI 0.18-0.53). Conclusion: Redo TAVR offered the lowest mortality but higher coronary obstruction and pacemaker risk. TAVR explant had the highest mortality. Treatment selection requires individualized risk stratification. Risk of bias was low.
title: Abstract 13836: Comparative Clinical Outcomes of TAVR Explantation, Redo-TAVR (TAVR-in-TAVR), and Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement for Failed Transcatheter Heart Valves: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: TAVR relies on precise CT planning for annular sizing and complication prediction, but conventional expert assessment is time-consuming and variable. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers automated, rapid analyses. However, the comparative impact of AI-assisted versus conventional CT planning on valve sizing accuracy, procedural efficiency, and clinical outcomes remains undefined. This meta-analysis addresses that gap. Methods: We systematically searched databases (inception-June 2026) for studies comparing AI-assisted versus conventional CT planning for TAVR. Primary outcome: correct valve sizing. Random-effects meta-analysis used Stata 18.0. Risk of bias assessed with ROB 2.0. Heterogeneity via I 2 . Results: Eleven studies (n=9,842 patients) met inclusion criteria. AI-assisted CT planning significantly improved correct valve sizing accuracy compared with conventional expert planning (OR 1.62; 95% CI 1.38-1.90; p<0.001; I 2 =34%). Rates of moderate-to-severe paravalvular leak were lower with AI assistance (OR 0.71; 95% CI 0.59-0.86; p=0.001; I 2 =28%). Patient-prosthesis mismatch did not differ between groups (OR 0.94; 95% CI 0.78-1.14; p=0.52; I 2 =0%). CT analysis time was significantly shorter with AI (mean difference -9.4 minutes; 95% CI -12.1 to -6.7; p<0.001; I 2 =89%). Procedural duration also favored AI (MD -6.2 minutes; 95% CI -9.8 to -2.6; p=0.001; I 2 =56%). Coronary obstruction prediction accuracy was comparable (OR 1.08; 95% CI 0.82-1.42; p=0.58). No significant differences were observed for pacemaker implantation (OR 0.92; 95% CI 0.76-1.11) or 30-day mortality (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.68-1.16). Heterogeneity was low to moderate for most outcomes. Conclusion: AI-assisted CT planning for TAVR improves valve sizing accuracy, reduces paravalvular leak, and shortens both CT analysis and procedural duration compared with conventional expert planning, without increasing adverse clinical events. These findings support AI integration into routine TAVR workflows to enhance efficiency and precision. Risk of bias was low.
title: Abstract 13844: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted versus Conventional Expert CT Planning for Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Valve Sizing Accuracy, Procedural Efficiency, and Clinical Outcomes

abstract: Background: Trastuzumab (TRZ), the first humanized monoclonal antibody targeting human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), is a cornerstone in the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer. However, its clinical application is limited by TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity. Hence, it is imperative to identify novel and effective therapeutic targets. Interferon regulatory factor 9 (IRF9) acts as a key regulatory molecular in inflammation, cancer, and cardiovascular diseases. Elucidating the role and mechanism of IRF9 in TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity could provide a strategy for preventing and TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity. Methods: An in vivo model of TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity was established. Differential proteomic analysis was used to identify the key proteins and pathways associated with TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity. Expression levels of IRF9, HER2, and pyroptosis-related effectors were examined in cardiac tissue and cardiomyocytes. To investigate the functional role of IRF9, cardiomyocyte-specific IRF9-overexpressing and IRF9-knockdown mouse models were generated, followed by the establishment of TRZ-induced cardiotoxicity model. Proteomic analysis in H9C2 cells was performed to screen the downstream targets of IRF9.
