ICI-associated AF may reflect a subclinical immune-cardiotoxic phenotype characterized by systemic inflammation, macrophage activation, myocardial injury, and sex-specific thyroid changes
title: Abstract 14257: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Associated Atrial Fibrillation and Subclinical Immune-Cardiotoxicity

abstract: Background: Secondary mitral regurgitation (SMR) remains a significant clinical challenge in patients with left ventricular dysfunction.Surgical mitral valve repair (SMVr) has historically been the standard intervention; however, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) has emerged as a less invasive therapeutic alternative for high-risk patients. This meta-analysis evaluates the comparative safety and efficacy of SMVr versus TEER in patients with symptomatic SMR. Methods: Systematic database search identified 3,149 studies reporting on TEER or SMVr for treatment of SMR from inception till May 2024. A total of 10 studies were included after screening according to PRISMA guidelines.Analysis was done using a randome effects model.The outcomes of interest were all-cause mortality,length of hospital stay,cardiovascular outcomes,NYHA functional class improvement, post operative LVEF changes etc. Results: A total of 10 postoperative outcomes and complications were analyzed. Compared to TEER, SMVr was associated with a significantly higher risk of all-cause mortality (RR 1.62, 95% CI 1.17-2.25,p=0.0035) and a longer length of hospital stay (SMD 0.91, 95% CI 0.22-1.60,p=0.0093).SMVr was also associated with increased rates of cardiac arrest (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.02-2.28,p=0.0417), prolonged mechanical ventilation (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.12-2.88, p=0.0143), and post-procedural cerebral infarction (RR 2.41;,95% CI 1.30-4.48, p=0.0054).No significant differences were observed between the two groups regarding in-hospital mortality (p=0.5275), cardiac tamponade (p=0.1635), post-procedural thrombosis (p=0.7776), NYHA functional class III/IV at 24 months (p=0.7668) or, post-procedural left ventricular ejection fraction (p=0.5738). Conclusion: In patients with secondary mitral regurgitation, TEER is associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality, shorter hospital stays, and reduced procedural morbidity compared to SMVr.While efficacy endpoints were comparable, TEER's superior safety makes it the preferred intervention for patients at high surgical risk.

register_verdicts.note: Compares surgical repair with TEER, not TEER with medical therapy outside COAPT criteria.

title: Abstract 14268: Comparative Analysis of Postoperative Outcomes Following Surgical vs. Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Mitral Valve Repair for Secondary Mitral Regurgitation

abstract: Background: GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reduce cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes (T2DM), and emerging evidence suggests potential neuroprotective effects. Myocardial infarction (MI) may represent a period of heightened vulnerability for cognitive decline; however, whether GLP-1 RA initiation after MI is associated with lower dementia risk, but the mechanism remains unclear. Hypothesis: Among patients with T2DM initiating glucose-lowering therapy after MI, GLP-1 RA initiation would be associated with a lower incidence of dementia than the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) initiation. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. Adults aged≥40 years with T2DM and acute MI who initiated a GLP-1 RA or DPP-4i within 180 days after MI were identified. Patients with type 1 diabetes, pre-index dementia, or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) were excluded. Cohorts were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics, comorbidities, cardiovascular risk factors, and medication use. The primary outcome was incident dementia over 3 years; secondary outcomes included MCI, vascular dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and all-cause mortality. Longer follow-up windows were assessed in sensitivity analyses. Risk ratios (RRs) and hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs were estimated; p<0.05 was considered significant. Results: After 1:1 propensity score matching, 7,419 patients were included in each cohort with adequate baseline balance (all SMDs <0.10). At 3 years, GLP-1 RA initiation was associated with lower cumulative incidence of dementia compared with DPP-4i initiation (1.2% vs 1.6%; RR, 0.75;95% CI, 0.57-0.98; P=0.04). Time-to-event analysis was directionally concordant but nonsignificant (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.66-1.14). Risk-based dementia findings remained significant at 5 years (RR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.49-0.79) and at the longest available follow-up (RR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.44-0.68). Secondary neurocognitive outcomes were directionally lower but not significant at 3 years. All-cause mortality was lower among GLP-1 RA initiators at 3 years (RR,0.82; 95% CI, 0.76-0.88; HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.85-0.99). Conclusions: Among patients with T2DM initiating therapy after MI, GLP-1 RA initiation was associated with a lower 3-year cumulative incidence of dementia than DPP-4i initiation, with consistent risk-based findings across longer follow-up windows. Attenuated time-to-event estimates for dementias support cautious interpretation. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant prospective evaluation of GLP-1 RA initiation for long-term neurocognitive outcomes after MI.
title: Abstract 14270: Post-Myocardial Infarction GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Initiation and Incident Dementia in Type 2 Diabetes: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Cardiac troponin T (cTnT) is the gold-standard biomarker for acute coronary syndrome. However, plasma cTnT elevation is detected in other settings, including endurance sports, heart failure, and pharmacologic stress. Recent work utilizing single-extracellular vesicle (EV) imaging indicates that cTnT may be associated with EVs, lipid-delimited particles secreted by all cell types, which have emerged as potential carriers of disease-relevant cargo. Isolating EVs from plasma presents technical challenges, and an effective approach for capturing and characterizing cTnT-associated EVs remains elusive. Here, we identify an optimized approach for characterizing EV-associated cTnT in human plasma across cardiovascular disease states. Methods: EVs were isolated from 500 μL of patient plasma using a size-exclusion chromatography-based approach selected following systematic comparison of EV isolation methods. EV and non-EV fractions were characterized by Western blot and cTnT ELISA. EV particle size and concentration were assessed by Microfluidic Resistive Pulse Sensing. For single-EV phenotyping, heart-enriched EVs (cardiovesicles) were immunocaptured via anti-CHRNE antibody from crude plasma, permeabilized, and co-stained for cTnT and tetraspanins. Single-EV imaging by super-resolution radial fluctuations microscopy demonstrated cTnT colocalization with cardiovesicles. Results: cTnT was detectable in EV and non-EV fractions and crude plasma across a pilot cohort of healthy controls, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and myocardial infarction (MI) patients (n=3 per group), confirming an EV-associated subset of circulating cTnT. The findings were enabled by an optimal EV isolation approach, outperforming alternative methods in EV purity and cTnT enrichment normalized to total protein. In bulk EVs, the EV:non-EV cTnT ratio was greater in healthy controls compared to HFrEF ( p < 0.01) and MI ( p < 0.001) patients. Resolution at the single-EV level, however, showed an increase in cTnT-positive cardiovesicles per region of interest in HFrEF patients compared to healthy controls ( p < 0.0001). Conclusions: These findings confirm an EV-associated pool of circulating cTnT in human plasma across cardiovascular disease states. The EV:non-EV cTnT ratio suggests utility as a metric for distinguishing necrotic from physiological cTnT release, with an observed inverse association with myocardial injury. Future studies will apply this EV isolation strategy to patient samples from clinical trials to evaluate whether medication-associated cTnT elevations reflect physiological EV-associated release rather than cardiomyocyte necrosis. Characterization of EV-associated cTnT may ultimately improve patient risk-stratification for subsequent procedures or discrimination of safety signals for novel therapies.
title: Abstract 14285: Optimization of Extracellular Vesicle Isolation from Human Plasma Enables Characterization of Circulating Extracellular Vesicle-Associated Cardiac Troponin T in Cardiovascular Disease

abstract: Introduction: All commercially available bioprosthetic heart valves are bovine or porcine and contain galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal), making alpha-gal syndrome a relative contraindication to their use. Risk stratification usually requires allergy or immunology expertise, which is unavailable at many centers. Case Presentation: A 79-year-old woman with critical aortic stenosis (valve area 0.82 cm2, mean gradient 52 mm Hg, peak velocity 5.0 m/s), severe multivessel coronary disease, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis required valve replacement but was at prohibitive surgical risk (Society of Thoracic Surgeons predicted mortality above 30%). A mechanical valve was precluded by operative risk and by the hazards of anticoagulation in dialysis, leaving a bioprosthetic transcatheter valve or palliation. Documented alpha-gal syndrome threatened candidacy. Alpha-gal-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) was 4.61 kU/L, down from about 24.50 kU/L seven years earlier, and pork-specific IgE was 2.97 kU/L (from 8.46), placing her in a low perioperative-risk category. With no inpatient allergy service and unsuccessful transfer attempts, the heart team performed a supervised oral pork challenge in the cardiac care unit, with bedside rescue medications and no premedication. She tolerated it without reaction and, five days later underwent uncomplicated transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement with a 29-mm Evolut porcine self-expanding valve. She tolerated systemic intravenous heparin without hypersensitivity. Postprocedural echocardiography showed normal prosthetic function (mean gradient 16 mm Hg, effective orifice area 1.41 cm2). She was discharged with improved ambulation and reported no hypersensitivity at follow-up. Discussion: To our knowledge, this is the first use of an oral meat challenge to gauge bioprosthetic valve candidacy, offering a pragmatic, reproducible pathway when allergy support is unavailable. A negative challenge establishes only acute, ingested-route tolerance, not parenteral or implant-route safety or long-term durability. A declining alpha-gal titer read against perioperative thresholds can help support candidacy. Because immune, renal, and metabolic factors may converge to accelerate structural valve deterioration in a patient who cannot undergo reoperation, structured echocardiographic surveillance and a valve-in-valve contingency during follow up are warranted.
title: Abstract 14289: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Alpha-Gal Syndrome Without Allergy Support: A Supervised Oral Meat Challenge to Guide Tissue-Valve Candidacy

abstract: Background: Acute pericarditis is generally considered a benign and self-limited condition; however, a substantial subset of patients experience recurrent hospitalization, hemodynamic compromise, and premature mortality. Frailty, a multidimensional syndrome reflecting diminished physiologic reserve, has emerged as a powerful determinant of adverse outcomes across cardiovascular diseases. Yet, its prognostic significance in acute pericarditis remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the association between frailty and long-term clinical outcomes among patients with acute pericarditis using a large multinational electronic health record network. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network. Adults (≥18 years) with acute pericarditis between 2005 and 2025 were identified. Frailty was defined using validated Johns Hopkins frailty-defining diagnoses recorded within one year before index diagnosis. We used propensity score matching for demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, medications, and procedural characteristics. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, hospitalization, cardiac tamponade, pericardiocentesis, or constrictive pericarditis. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, cardiac tamponade, all-cause readmission, and atrial fibrillation/flutter. Outcomes were assessed through 10 years using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards analyses. Results: Among 84,039 patients with acute pericarditis, 14,014 (16.7%) were frail. After propensity matching, cohorts were well balanced (all standardized mean differences <0.1). Frailty was associated with a higher risk of the primary outcome at 1 year (HR 1.63, 95% CI 1.46-1.81) and 10 years (HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.25-1.49). Frail patients had increased long-term all-cause mortality (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.36-1.49), readmission (HR 1.22, 95% CI 1.11-1.33), heart failure (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.01-1.18), and cardiogenic shock (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.08-1.49). Risk was greatest within the first year, with 63% and 53% increases in the primary outcome and mortality, respectively. Frailty was not associated with cardiac tamponade or atrial fibrillation/flutter. Conclusions: Frailty identifies a highly vulnerable phenotype among patients with acute pericarditis and is independently associated with significantly increased long-term risks of mortality, hospitalization, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and major adverse clinical events. Routine frailty assessment may provide valuable prognostic information beyond traditional cardiovascular risk factors and could facilitate earlier risk stratification, closer surveillance, and tailored multidisciplinary management strategies in patients with acute pericarditis.
title: Abstract 14296: Frailty and Long-Term Outcomes in Acute Pericarditis: A Global Propensity-Matched Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality due to progressive diastolic dysfunction and heart failure. The prognostic implications of concomitant non-rheumatic aortic stenosis (AS) in patients with RCM remain poorly characterized. Understanding the long-term interaction between these conditions may help identify patients at increased risk for adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network. Adult patients diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy (ICD-10-CM I42.5) between 2006 and 2024 were identified. Patients with cardiomyopathy due to amyloidosis (E85, I43) were excluded. The exposure cohort included patients with concomitant non-rheumatic aortic stenosis (ICD-10-CM I35.0, I35.2), while the control cohort consisted of patients with RCM without aortic stenosis.After 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, comorbidities, laboratory values, and baseline clinical characteristics with standardized mean differences <0.10) in all covariates. Outcomes were assessed at 1 year and long term 10 years. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Results: Following propensity matching, patients with RCM and concomitant AS demonstrated significantly higher risks of several clinically important cardiovascular outcomes. At 1 year, AS was associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.03-1.13; p=0.002), atrial fibrillation/flutter (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.25-1.44; p<0.001), acute MI (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.03-1.23; p=0.008), and cardiogenic shock (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.41-1.81; p<0.001). No significant differences were observed in heart failure, stroke, or MACCE.At 10 years, mortality was no longer significantly different between groups (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.05; p=0.118). However, patients with AS continued to experience higher risks of heart failure (HR 1.11, 95% CI 1.06-1.16; p<0.001), atrial fibrillation/flutter (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.19-1.30; p<0.001), stroke (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.04-1.17; p=0.001), and cardiogenic shock (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.30-1.51; p<0.001). Long-term risks of acute MI, MACCE, and mortality remained comparable between cohorts. Conclusions: Among patients with restrictive cardiomyopathy, concomitant non-rheumatic aortic stenosis identifies a high-risk phenotype associated with substantially increased risks of atrial arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, heart failure progression, and stroke. Although long-term mortality and MACCE were not significantly increased, the persistent excess burden of adverse cardiovascular events suggests that AS contributes importantly to disease progression in RCM. Enhanced surveillance and earlier consideration of valve-directed and heart failure therapies may be warranted in this vulnerable population.
title: Abstract 14304: Aortic Stenosis Identifies a High-Risk Phenotype in Non-Amyloid Restrictive Cardiomyopathy: A 10-Year Global Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Contemporary multi-society dyslipidemia guidelines recommend statin continuation in high-risk pregnant individuals with clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or familial hypercholesterolemia, a shift enabled by the removal of pregnancy as an absolute contraindication to statin use by the Food and Drug Administration in 2021. However, the prevalence and characteristics of statin-eligible pregnancies in real-world practice remain unknown. We used two large longitudinal pregnancy electronic health record (EHR)-based cohorts to characterize pregnancies meeting contemporary criteria for statin eligibility. Methods: We ascertained statin eligibility among pregnancies in two longitudinal, multi-institutional EHR pregnancy cohorts. Statin eligibility was defined as any diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) (identified by diagnosis codes or low-density lipoprotein [LDL] level ≥190 mg/dL) or diagnosis of clinical ASCVD (including angina, myocardial infarction, coronary or arterial revascularization, ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, and peripheral artery disease) prior to pregnancy. We examined age-adjusted annual trends in stability eligibility from 1999 to 2024. We summarized clinical characteristics and pregnancy-related cardiovascular outcomes by statin eligibility status. Results: Among 98,524 pregnancies across two EHR-based cohorts, 3.6% (n=2,735) in Mass General Brigham (MGB) and 3.4% (n=748) in Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) met contemporary criteria for statin eligibility. Age-adjusted statin-eligibility rates were stable over the study period ( Figure 1A ). Compared with pregnancies not meeting eligibility criteria, statin-eligible pregnancies occurred in individuals with higher burden of cardiometabolic risk factors, including older age, higher body mass index, and greater prevalence of preexisting hypertension and diabetes (all p<0.001). Statin eligible pregnancies also had higher rates of pregnancy-related major adverse cardiovascular events (14% vs 5% in MGB; 7% vs 3% in BIDMC; both p<0.001) and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (25% vs 15% in MGB; 24% vs 15% in BIDMC; both p<0.001). Of all statin-eligible pregnancies across both cohorts, 63% (n=2,186) met eligibility criteria based on FH and 39% (n=1,366) based on clinical ASCVD ( Figure 1B ). Conclusions: In two real-world EHR-based pregnancy cohorts, approximately 3% of pregnancies met contemporary guideline criteria for statin continuation, a proportion that has remained stable over the past two decades. Statin eligibility identified a higher-risk pregnancy population with greater cardiometabolic comorbidity and higher rates of pregnancy-related cardiovascular complications, underscoring the importance of incorporating dyslipidemia management into cardio-obstetric care.
title: Abstract 14308: Statin Eligibility in Pregnancy Under Contemporary Dyslipidemia Guidelines: Analysis of Two Longitudinal Real-World Pregnancy Cohorts

abstract: Background: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects approximately 1% of live births, and advances in surgical and catheter-based intervention have enabled a growing population of women with CHD to survive to reproductive age. While prior repair is presumed to confer hemodynamic benefit during pregnancy, large-scale real-world data comparing maternal cardiovascular outcomes in repaired versus unrepaired CHD are lacking. Methods: Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, comprising 67 healthcare organizations, we identified pregnant women with CHD and stratified them into two cohorts: those with prior surgical or catheter-based cardiac repair and those without documented repair. Repair was defined using a comprehensive set of CHD-specific CPT procedure codes, including septal defect closure, valvuloplasty, great vessel repair, and patent ductus arteriosus ligation. Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 ratio using 14 covariates, including age, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, CHD lesion type, and tobacco use. The index event was the first pregnancy encounter. Outcomes were assessed through 365 days of follow-up and included new-onset heart failure, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia, preterm delivery, postpartum cardiomyopathy, and all-cause mortality. Results: After propensity score matching, each cohort included 791 patients. Compared with women with unrepaired CHD, those with repaired CHD had significantly higher risks of new-onset heart failure (13.5% vs. 6.2%; RR 2.19, 95% CI 1.53-3.14; HR 2.07, 95% CI 1.42-3.00; p<0.001) and cardiogenic shock (3.3% vs. 1.5%; RR 2.13, 95% CI 1.08-4.21; HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.03-4.06; p=0.038). Arrhythmias were more frequent among women with repaired CHD by cumulative risk analysis (10.8% vs. 7.2%; RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.04-2.16; p=0.029), although time-to-event analysis did not reach statistical significance by Kaplan-Meier log-rank testing (p=0.099). Rates of preterm delivery, postpartum cardiomyopathy, and all-cause mortality were not significantly different between cohorts. Conclusions: In this propensity-matched analysis of pregnant women with CHD, repaired CHD was associated with approximately twofold higher risks of new-onset heart failure and cardiogenic shock compared with unrepaired CHD. This counterintuitive association likely reflects greater underlying lesion complexity, residual hemodynamic burden, and long-term sequelae among women requiring prior intervention, rather than risk attributable to repair itself. These findings underscore that anatomic repair should not be equated with physiologic risk normalization and support intensified peripartum cardiovascular surveillance for women with repaired CHD.
title: Abstract 14319: Repaired but Not Protected: Higher Maternal Cardiovascular Risk During Pregnancy in Women with Repaired Congenital Heart Disease

abstract: Introduction: Aconitum-containing herbal preparations can cause rapidly fatal sodium-channel-mediated cardiotoxicity. Early symptoms may mimic gastrointestinal illness or allergic reaction before progressing to malignant ventricular arrhythmias. Case 1 Summary: A 65-year-old woman presented 90 minutes after ingesting an Ayurvedic joint-pain preparation containing Aconitum with intractable nausea/vomiting, tachycardia, and hypotension. Workup noted QTc prolongation, premature ventricular contractions (PVCs), hypokalemia, normal magnesium, lactic acidosis, leukocytosis, normal serial troponins, and unremarkable chest X-ray and toxicologic evaluation. Bedside echocardiography showed preserved biventricular function. Initial management included IV fluids, electrolyte repletion, and vasopressors. The arrhythmia rapidly progressed to polymorphic VT (Figure 1). Despite IV magnesium, lidocaine, amiodarone, sodium bicarbonate, and repeated cardioversion, she developed refractory VT/VF storm with recurrent cardiac arrest. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and IV propafenone were attempted without improvement. Case 2 Summary: A 56-year-old man presented 1 hour after ingesting the same Aconitum-containing preparation with paresthesias, dizziness, dyspnea, burning abdominal pain, intractable nausea/vomiting, diaphoresis, and hypotension. He was initially treated for presumed anaphylaxis, but symptoms persisted. Serial ECGs showed progressive QTc prolongation and PVCs. Workup showed no major electrolyte derangements, normal serial troponins, leukocytosis, and unremarkable imaging and toxicologic evaluation. He then developed worsening agitation, encephalopathy, hypotension, and increasing PVC burden. Despite vasopressors, IV magnesium, amiodarone, and lidocaine, he developed recurrent polymorphic VT, progressing to VT/VF storm with recurrent cardiac arrest. CRRT could not be safely initiated. Outcomes: Both patients underwent ACLS and multiple defibrillations and were considered for veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. After family discussions, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) was declined. Both patients expired after transition to comfort-focused measures. Discussion: These cases highlight fulminant cardiovascular toxicity from Aconitum-containing herbal preparations. Aconitum toxicity should be considered in patients with unexplained hypotension, QTc prolongation, ventricular ectopy, or VT/VF storm after ingestion of herbal preparations, particularly when gastrointestinal, neurologic, or allergy-like symptoms precede rapid deterioration. Early toxicology consultation, telemetry monitoring, aggressive electrolyte optimization, sodium-channel targeted antiarrhythmic therapy, and prompt MCS evaluation may be critical. However, optimal therapy remains uncertain.
title: Abstract 14330: Refractory Ventricular Tachycardia/Fibrillation Storm After Aconitum-Containing Herbal Preparation Ingestion: A Two-Patient Case Series

abstract: Introduction: A total of 600,000 Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) devices has been implanted worldwide, but randomized trials enroll selected patients in experienced centers only. Real-world outcomes across unselected multicenter institutions remain underexplored. Furthermore, bedside tools to identify patients at high risk of adverse outcomes are limited in the real world. Hypothesis We evaluated real-world clinical outcomes after LAAO and hypothesized that routinely available baseline clinical variables could be used to derive a practical bedside mortality risk score. Methods: We analyzed adults undergoing percutaneous LAAO across 111 healthcare organizations from 2016 to 2026 using TriNetX, a global federated electronic-health-record network. The index date was the first qualifying LAAO procedure (CPT 33340). Incident ischemic stroke, major bleeding, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and all-cause death were estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Mortality prediction models were developed using a 70/30 train-test split. Penalized Cox regression and random survival forest models were compared with CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc using Harrell C-index, time-dependent area under the curve (AUC), calibration, and integrated Brier score. A simplified 0-19-point bedside mortality score was derived from baseline clinical predictors. Results: A total of 29,554 patients were identified (mean age 75.3±7.5 years, 39.9% women, mean CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc 4.9, mean HAS-BLED 2.6, heart failure 51.2%, chronic kidney disease 35.3%, and prior major bleeding 42.1%). Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence at 1 and 2 years was 6.9% and 13.5% for all-cause death, 2.0% and 3.7% for incident ischemic stroke, 3.9% and 5.7% for incident major bleeding, and 12.3% and 21.2% for MACE (Figure 1). Random survival forest showed the strongest mortality discrimination, with C-index 0.729 and AUCs of 0.754, 0.752, and 0.753 at 12, 24, and 36 months, respectively ( Figure 2a ). Penalized Cox also outperformed CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc (C-index 0.713 vs 0.602). Model calibration was acceptable, with integrated Brier score 0.0916 ( Figure 2b ). A bedside score incorporating age ≥75 years, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, prior major bleeding, vascular disease, cancer, and anemia stratified 12-month mortality from 2.8% in the low-risk group to 19.1% in the very-high-risk group; corresponding 24-month mortality increased from 6.3% to 32.4% ( Figure 3, Table1 ). Conclusion: In a large multicenter real-world LAAO cohort, incident ischemic stroke and major bleeding rates were low despite substantial baseline comorbidity. Machine-learning survival models improved mortality prediction compared with CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc, and a simple bedside score provided clinically practical mortality risk stratification.
title: Abstract 14377: Real-World Outcomes and Utility of a Bedside Score in Atrial Fibrillation Patients Undergoing Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO)

abstract: Hypotension frequently limits optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Midodrine is increasingly used off-label to support blood pressure and facilitate GDMT initiation or titration, but its cardiovascular safety relative to alternative pressor strategies remains uncertain. We compared outcomes associated with midodrine versus fludrocortisone in patients with HFrEF and hypotension.METHODSWe performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults with HFrEF (ICD-10 I50.2*) and hypotension (I95*) receiving midodrine or fludrocortisone were identified. Cohorts were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics and major comorbidities, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, obesity, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hyperlipidemia, prior stroke, peripheral vascular disease, and obstructive sleep apnea.Primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 1 month, 3 months, and 1 year. Secondary outcomes included cardiogenic shock, acute kidney injury (AKI), ventricular arrhythmias, hypokalemia, hypertension-related events, emergency department visits, observation encounters, and hospitalizations. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.RESULTSAfter propensity matching, baseline characteristics were well balanced between groups. Compared with fludrocortisone, midodrine was associated with increased mortality at 3 months (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.00-1.16; p=0.047) and 1 year (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.07-1.21; p<0.001), while 1-month mortality was similar. Midodrine was associated with higher risks of cardiogenic shock (HR 2.08 at 1 month; HR 2.29 at 3 months; both p<0.001), AKI (HR 1.41 and 1.34, respectively), and ventricular arrhythmias (HR 1.50 and 1.59, respectively). Fludrocortisone was associated with more hypokalemia and hypertension-related events. Midodrine users also experienced greater healthcare utilization, including emergency department visits, observation encounters, and hospitalizations.CONCLUSIONSAmong patients with HFrEF and hypotension, midodrine use was associated with increased mortality, cardiogenic shock, AKI, ventricular arrhythmias, and healthcare utilization compared with fludrocortisone. Although residual confounding cannot be excluded, these findings raise concerns regarding the safety of chronic vasoconstrictor-based blood pressure support in HFrEF and support prospective evaluation of patient selection strategies.
title: Abstract 14379: Comparative Safety of Midodrine versus Fludrocortisone in Hypotensive Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is intended for patients intolerance to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. However, some patients still end up on or having to restart OAC after LAAO. Real world data on clinical outcomes in such patients are not known. Hypothesis: We evaluated whether continued anticoagulation after LAAO was associated with lower ischemic stroke, major bleeding, or all-cause mortality compared with being successfully off OAC after implantation. Methods: We analyzed adults undergoing percutaneous LAAO from 2016 to 2026 using TriNetX, a federated electronic-health-record network. To reduce immortal-time bias, we used a 6-month landmark design. OAC exposure was defined using prescription fills 45 to 180 days after implantation and classified as continued/restarted OAC versus off OAC. Outcomes were incident ischemic stroke, incident major bleeding, and all-cause mortality. Patients with outcome events before the landmark were excluded from the corresponding outcome analysis. Associations were assessed using Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence, multivariable Cox models, and propensity-score inverse-probability-of-treatment-weighted (IPTW) Cox models as a supplement to main analysis. Covariate balance was assessed using standardized mean differences. P of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Among 29,554 LAAO patients, 23,128 survived the 6-month landmark. Of these, 1,956 (8.5%) were continued or restarted on OAC and 21,172 (91.5%) were off OAC. Among patients on OAC after LAAO, 97.1% were receiving a direct oral anticoagulant. IPTW achieved strong covariate balance (Figure 2). At 24 months after the landmark, cumulative incidence among on-OAC versus off-OAC patients was 13.8% versus 14.0% for mortality, 4.3% versus 3.5% for ischemic stroke, and 4.9% versus 3.8% for major bleeding (Figure 1). Continued or restarted OAC was not associated with lower mortality in adjusted analysis (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.82-1.04; P=0.201) or IPTW analysis (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80-1.07; P=0.296). OAC was also not associated with lower ischemic stroke (adjusted HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.96-1.55; P=0.101; IPTW HR 1.31, 95% CI 0.99-1.74; P=0.058) or major bleeding (adjusted HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.91-1.44; P=0.259; IPTW HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.86-1.49; P=0.391) (Figure 3). Conclusion: Our study shows continued or restarted OAC was not associated with lower ischemic stroke or increased all-cause mortality compared with successful discontinuation. Patients maintained on OAC likely represent a higher-risk subgroup with clinical indications such as device-related thrombus, peri-device leak, incomplete closure, or persistent thromboembolic risk. These findings support shared decision-making and careful patient selection when considering continued anticoagulation after LAAO.

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective TriNetX cohort of 29,554 LAAO patients, 23,128 of whom survived the 6-month landmark; 1,956 (8.5%) continued or restarted OAC and 21,172 (91.5%) were off OAC.
appraisal.main_limitation: Observational EHR data with confounding by indication and no adjudicated outcomes; the OAC group is small and probably selected for higher risk.
appraisal.one_line: TriNetX landmark analysis found no association between continued anticoagulation after LAAO and lower stroke or mortality.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Mortality HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.82-1.04 (adjusted) and HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80-1.07 (IPTW); ischemic stroke adjusted HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.96-1.55; major bleeding adjusted HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.91-1.44.
appraisal.why_it_matters: It bears on antithrombotic strategy after LAAO, where randomised evidence on residual OAC is lacking.

title: Abstract 14380: Continued Anticoagulation After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO) Was Not Associated with Lower Stroke or Mortality

abstract: Background: Sympathetic overactivation is an important mechanism of hypertension. Traditional renal denervation (RDN) reduces sympathetic activity through permanent nerve ablation. However, due to the invasiveness and uncertain long-term effects of RDN, its widespread application is limited. Wearable low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has been reported to reversibly modulate neural activity and demonstrates significant potential in regulating sympathetic nervous system activity. We hypothesized that daily bilateral renal hilum stimulation with a wearable device consisting of two ultrasound probes and an ultrasonic transmitter could lower blood pressure (BP) in patients with mild hypertension. Methods: In this prospective, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, we included 62 patients with diagnosed grade 1 hypertension, who were randomly assigned to the LIPUS treatment group (driving frequency: 0.7 MHz, sonic power of each probe: 0.75 W/cm 2 ) or the sham control group using a visually identical sham device. The patients used the device twice a day, 30 minutes each time, with an interval of at least 6 hours for 14 days. The primary endpoint was the change in 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure after 2 weeks of device use. Secondary endpoints included changes in 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure and clinic blood pressure at 14, 45 and 90 days after treatment initiation. Results: Among 62 patients, 58 completed the measurement of the primary endpoint. The reduction in ambulatory systolic BP was greater in the LIPUS group (mean, –11.80 mmHg [SD, 12.47 mmHg]) than in the sham group (mean, –1.50 mmHg [SD, 6.30 mmHg]) and similarly for ambulatory diastolic BP (mean, -7.73 mmHg [SD, 9.88 mmHg]) than the sham group (mean, 1.89 mmHg [SD, 7.73 mmHg]). After 14 days, the ambulatory BP control rate (24-hour average <130/80 mmHg) was 63.33% in the LIPUS group and 0.00% in the sham group (rate difference, 63.33 percentage points; 95% CI, 46.09 to 80.58; p < 0.0001). Clinic BP control rates (defined as <140/90 mmHg) were 63.33% and 7.41%, respectively (rate difference, 55.93 percentage points; 95% CI, 36.05 to 75.80; p < 0.0001). No serious device-related adverse events were reported in either group. Conclusion: This study suggests that LIPUS may represent a novel non-pharmacological treatment option for mild hypertension. Further studies are required to determine the persistence of treatment effects and long-term safety.
title: Abstract 14392: Wearable Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound Lowers Blood Pressure in Patients with Mild Hypertension by Stimulating the Renal Hilum

abstract: Introduction & Objective: Residual pulmonary regurgitation (PR) and subsequent right ventricular (RV) remodeling are common late complications after ToF repair. The aim of this study was to investigate the associations between echocardiographic parameters of right heart remodeling, valvular lesions, and clinical outcomes, in order to identify potential markers of clinical deterioration. Methods: Comprehensive echocardiography and clinical assessment were performed in 62 ToF patients (comprising 35 men and 27 women). The mean age of the study population was 28.8 ± 12.6 years. With the mean age at the time of surgical repair being 16.4 months (median 6 months), the estimated average time elapsed since the surgical correction was approximately 27.4 years. Patients were stratified by PR severity (≥moderate vs. none/mild) and the presence of heart failure (HF). Results: PR was the most frequent valvular lesion, with moderate to severe PR present in 40.0% of patients. Patients with PR ≥moderate had significantly larger RV outflow tract (RVOT) dimensions compared to those with none/mild PR (35 mm vs. 30 mm, p = 0.015). However, PR severity did not correlate significantly with 6MWT distance or NT-proBNP levels - Table. In contrast, tricuspid regurgitation (TR) severity was significantly correlated with right atrial area (RAA) (rho = 0.418, p = 0.0015) and NT-proBNP (rho = 0.331, p = 0.0136). Patients with HF exhibited significantly larger RAA (21 vs. 17 cm 2 , p = 0.018) and a trend toward lower RV systolic excursion velocity (RVs’) (10.0 vs. 11.0 cm/s, p = 0.057) - Figure. Conclusions: While pulmonary regurgitation is primarily associated with RVOT enlargement, it does not directly translate to immediate functional decline in this cohort. Conversely, right atrial enlargement and tricuspid regurgitation severity appear more closely linked to biomarker activation and clinical heart failure, suggesting RAA may be a sensitive marker of clinical deterioration in repaired ToF.
title: Abstract 14411: Impact of Pulmonary and Tricuspid Valvular Regurgitation on Right Heart Remodeling and Clinical Status in Post-Repair Tetralogy of Fallot

abstract: Introduction: Non-English primary language is associated with adverse healthcare outcomes, but its independent association with cardiogenic shock (CS) mortality—and potential amplification by social vulnerability, as quantified by the CDC’s social vulnerability index (SVI)—remains unclear. Hypothesis: Non-English primary language is independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality in CS, with this association amplified among patients with high-social-vulnerability. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 2,610 adults admitted with CS to a quaternary referral center (2013-2022); 2,424 had documented primary language (English n=2,004; non-English n=420). Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. We also assessed the interaction between primary language and high SVI (quartile 4). Multivariable logistic regression was performed with adjustments for demographics and shock severity. Additionally, patients with available pulmonary artery catheter data (n=692) underwent adjustment for cardiac index. Sensitivity analyses were performed with adjustments for race, ethnicity, and insurance status. Race and ethnicity were not strongly associated with primary language. Insurance status was reserved for sensitivity analysis because insurance type may itself reflect language-related access barriers and therefore lie on the causal pathway between language and mortality. Results: Unadjusted mortality was higher among non-English speakers (25% vs. 17%; P<0.001), and this finding persisted after adjustment (OR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.09-1.84; P=0.008) (Figure 1), and after adjusting for cardiac index (OR, 2.01; 95% CI, 1.03-3.76; P=0.034) (Table 1). Non-English speakers from the most socially vulnerable ZIP codes (quartile 4 SVI) had worse outcomes (OR, 3.19; 95% CI, 1.10-9.23; P=0.031). (Table 1) These findings held up across sensitivity analyses adjusting for ethnicity, race, and insurance type (OR range 1.39-1.48, all P<0.05). The likelihood of receiving an orthotopic heart transplant (OHT) was not different between the groups, after adjustment for shock severity. Conclusions: Non-English primary language is independently associated with increased CS mortality. Likelihood of receiving an OHT was equitable after adjustment for shock severity, arguing against OHT access as a driver of the observed mortality disparity. Patients with non-English language and high social vulnerability represent a high-risk subgroup, with disproportionate mortality, which warrants further investigation.
title: Abstract 14416: Primary Language and In-Hospital Mortality in Cardiogenic Shock: Interaction with Social Vulnerability

abstract: Background: Renal denervation (RDN) has re-emerged as a catheter-based device therapy for patients with uncontrolled hypertension following the landmarks SPYRAL HTN-OFF MED and SPYRAL HTN-ON MED sham-controlled trials, which demonstrated significant office and ambulatory systolic blood pressure (BP) reductions independent of antihypertensive medication. Despite this regulatory milestone, contemporary real-world data characterizing BP trajectory and post-procedural safety remain limited to highly selected trial populations, leaving critical gaps in understanding RDN effectiveness in heterogeneous clinical practice. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults ≥18 years with a hypertension diagnosis and objective evidence of elevated BP (SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg) at the index RDN date were included. RDN was identified using CPT, HCPCS, ICD-10-PCS, and SNOMED codes. BP control was defined as SBP <140 mmHg and DBP ≤90 mmHg, analyzed separately. The index event was the first qualifying RDN procedure per patient. Safety outcomes included MACE (all-cause mortality, acute MI, or ischemic stroke), incident hospitalization, and renal and bleeding complications. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days, 6 months, and 1 year using risk analysis and Kaplan-Meier survival methods; patients with prior occurrence of each outcome were excluded from that analysis. Results: BP control improved rapidly following renal denervation and was sustained throughout follow-up. Among 529 adults undergoing RDN across 32 healthcare organizations, systolic BP control (SBP <140 mmHg) increased from 43.2% at 30 days to 68.1% at 1 year, representing a 25-percentage-point absolute and 58% relative improvement. Diastolic BP control (DBP ≤90 mmHg) increased from 56.5% to 77.7% over the same period. Improvements were evident within weeks of the procedure, with median time to BP control was 20-24 days (diastolic) and 42-54 days (systolic). At 1 year, MACE occurred in 3.3% of eligible patients, with 95.3% Kaplan-Meier event-free survival; renal and bleeding complications were below reportable thresholds, consistent with very low event rates. Conclusions: In this large multicenter real-world cohort, RDN was associated with rapid, durable, and clinically meaningful improvements in BP control: more than two-thirds of patients achieved systolic control and nearly four-fifths achieved diastolic control by 1 year. These findings extend the efficacy observed in sham-controlled trials to a broader, less-selected clinical population. MACE rates were low and renal and bleeding complications exceedingly rare, providing reassuring post-market safety data and supporting catheter-based RDN as an adjunctive treatment strategy for uncontrolled hypertension, one of the largest contemporary real world evaluations following regulatory approval.
title: Abstract 14427: Real-World Blood Pressure Control and Safety After Renal Denervation for Uncontrolled Hypertension

abstract: Exercise intolerance is common in adults with repaired Tetralogy of Fallot (rTOF), even in the presence of preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF >50%). The mechanisms underlying this early functional decline remain incompletely understood and may precede overt structural myocardial disease. We aimed to determine whether reduced exercise capacity in adults with rTOF and preserved LVEF is associated with markers of diastolic dysfunction (DD), atrial remodeling, right ventricle (RV) dysfunction, and myocardial fibrosis (MF). We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with rTOF with preserved LVEF who underwent cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) within 18 months. Exercise capacity was assessed using percent-predicted peak oxygen uptake (ppVO 2 ) on CPET. A DD score (0-4) was calculated using the ratio of early to late atrial ventricular filling velocities (E/A), tissue Doppler velocity of the mitral annulus during early diastolic relaxation (e′), the ratio of transmitral E velocity to tissue Doppler e′ velocity (E/e′), left atrial volume index (LAVI), and tricuspid regurgitation max velocity (TR Vmax) using guideline-based thresholds. Pulmonary regurgitation (PR) fraction was also assessed. CMR assessed RV function and MF. Associations were assessed using non-parametric testing and Spearman correlation. Among adults with rTOF and preserved LVEF, reduced ppVO 2 was associated with multiple markers of adverse cardiac remodeling. Patients with LAVI >34 mL/m 2 demonstrated lower ppVO2 compared to those with normal LAVI (p < 0.001). Elevated E/e′ and reduced e′ velocity were also associated with lower ppVO 2 (both p < 0.05). LAVI demonstrated a moderate inverse correlation with ppVO 2 (ρ = –0.31, p < 0.001). Higher TR Vmax was weakly associated with lower ppVO 2 (ρ = –0.19, p < 0.05). The composite DD score demonstrated a graded relationship with ppVO 2 , with patients exhibiting ≥2 abnormal parameters having lower ppVO 2 than those with 0 or 1 abnormalities (both p < 0.01). Reduced RV function was associated with lower ppVO 2 (p < 0.001). PR fraction and MF were not associated with ppVO 2 . In adults with rTOF and preserved LVEF, reduced exercise capacity is associated with DD, atrial remodeling, TR Vmax, and RV dysfunction. These findings suggest that functional limitation may precede overt structural myocardial injury and identify a potentially reversible stage of myocardial remodeling.
title: Abstract 14430: Early Myocardial Remodeling Precedes Structural Disease in Adults with Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot

abstract: Background: Systemic thrombolysis remains a standard reperfusion strategy for high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) but is associated with substantial bleeding risk. Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has emerged as an alternative reperfusion strategy for high-risk PE, but comparative real-world effectiveness data relative to systemic thrombolysis remain limited. We compared clinical outcomes among patients with high-risk PE treated with MT versus systemic thrombolysis. Methods: Adult patients (≥18 years) with high-risk submassive or massive PE between January 2015 and September 2025 were identified using the TriNetX US Collaborative Research Network. Patients treated with MT were compared with those receiving systemic thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). One-to-one propensity score matching was performed using 69 demographic, clinical, comorbidity, and treatment-related variables. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included major bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, gastrointestinal bleeding, ischemic stroke, palliative care evaluation, and mechanical ventilation. Outcomes were assessed through 180 days using Cox proportional hazards models. Results: Among 18,965 patients with high-risk PE, 5,876 MT-treated patients were matched to 5,876 patients receiving systemic thrombolysis. Compared with thrombolysis, MT was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.45-0.56), mechanical ventilation (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.37-0.52), and palliative care evaluation (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.53-0.78) (all p<0.001). Rates of major bleeding (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.80-1.11), intracranial hemorrhage (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.64-1.54), gastrointestinal bleeding (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.61-1.03), and ischemic stroke (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.80-1.50) were similar between groups. Conclusion: In this large propensity-matched real-world cohort of patients with high-risk PE, mechanical thrombectomy was associated with substantially lower mortality and reduced need for mechanical ventilation without an increase in major bleeding or stroke compared with systemic thrombolysis. These findings suggest that MT may offer superior clinical outcomes compared with systemic thrombolysis in appropriately selected patients with high-risk PE and support its expanding role in contemporary PE management.

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective TriNetX cohort of 18,965 patients with high-risk PE; 5,876 thrombectomy patients matched 1:1 to 5,876 thrombolysis patients.
appraisal.main_limitation: Code-based identification and strong selection of patients for thrombectomy make residual confounding likely, and the effect size is implausibly large for a causal reading.
appraisal.one_line: TriNetX propensity-matched comparison associated mechanical thrombectomy with lower mortality than systemic thrombolysis in high-risk PE.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: All-cause mortality HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.45-0.56; major bleeding HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.80-1.11; intracranial hemorrhage HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.64-1.54.
appraisal.why_it_matters: It adds to the contested question of catheter-directed versus systemic reperfusion in high-risk PE, a domain with little randomised evidence.

title: Abstract 14443: Mechanical Thrombectomy versus Systemic Thrombolysis for High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis of Mortality and Clinical Outcomes

abstract: Background: The optimal treatment strategy for pediatric acute myocarditis has not been established, and clinical risk stratification, including causative pathogens, remains challenging. Furthermore, the need for long-term heart failure therapy after recovery is unclear. We established a nationwide pediatric myocarditis registry in Japan and analyzed its clinical characteristics and outcomes. Methods and Results: We analyzed registry data from patients younger than 18 years who were clinically diagnosed with myocarditis between 2012 and 2022 at 25 pediatric cardiology centers across Japan. A total of 276 patients were enrolled. The median age at diagnosis was 108 months (IQR, 51–153). Preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms were observed in 238 patients (86%), and chest symptoms were present in 183 (66%).Among 266 patients who underwent pathogen screening, causative pathogens were identified in 58 (22%). The most frequently detected pathogens were influenza A virus (12%), influenza B virus (14%), parvovirus B19 (12%), and SARS-CoV-2 (16%). Steroid pulse therapy and intravenous immunoglobulin were administered in 51 (18%) and 166 (60%) of patients, respectively. Mechanical ventilation was required in 167 cases (61%), and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) was used in 111 cases (40%).The in-hospital mortality rate was 13% (36 patients), and 5 patients (2%) were listed for heart transplantation. The median hospital stay was 22 days (IQR, 11–38). At discharge, persistent cardiac complications including LVEF<50% and ventricular aneurysm were observed in 35 patients (13%), and neurological sequelae in 17 (6%). β-blockers were prescribed in 23% of patients at discharge and in 20% at 1-year follow-up.Factors significantly associated with in-hospital mortality included admission and peak CK-MB levels (P<0.001), admission LVEF (P<0.001), identification of a causative pathogen (P=0.03), and steroid pulse therapy (P<0.001). Eight patients continued to have LVEF <50% at 3 years after onset; the only factor associated with persistent ventricular dysfunction was the use of MCS (P=0.048). Conclusions: Pediatric acute myocarditis in Japan required MCS in 40% of cases and in-hospital mortality rate of 13%. Influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2, and parvovirus B19 were the most frequently identified pathogens, and pathogen-positive cases had significantly higher mortality. One-fifth of patients remained on β-blocker therapy one year after onset, highlighting the need for long-term follow-up and identification of cardiovascular risks in adulthood.
title: Abstract 14449: Nationwide Pediatric Acute Myocarditis Registry in Japan

abstract: Background: Intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) has emerged as a non-ablative, sonic-pulse plaque-modification strategy for heavily calcified peripheral arterial disease (PAD), whereas atherectomy remains the dominant endovascular debulking technique. Despite growing clinical adoption of IVL, rigorous comparative real-world outcome data between these strategies are lacking. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults aged ≥18 years with PAD (ICD-10-CM I70.2, I73.9, E11.51) undergoing lower-extremity IVL (HCPCS: C9764, C9772) or atherectomy (CPT 37225, 37227, 37229, 37231, 37233, 37235, 0238T; SNOMED 415069007) were identified using diagnosis and procedure codes. Treatment groups were made mutually exclusive by excluding patients exposed to both procedures. Cohorts were 1:1 propensity-matched (nearest-neighbor) for demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity), comorbidities (smoking history, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, chronic ischemic heart disease, prior myocardial infarction, stroke/TIA, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, dialysis, COPD), PAD severity markers (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene), prior minor amputation, and baseline vascular medications (antiplatelet, statin, and cilostazol use).The primary endpoint was an amputation-related limb event composite; secondary endpoints included all-cause mortality, major cardiovascular events, kidney events, bleeding, and hospitalization. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days, 6 months, and 1 year using Kaplan-Meier and Cox proportional hazards models. Results: After propensity score matching, 2,626 patients per arm were well balanced across all covariates (all standardized mean differences <0.1). Atherectomy was associated with significantly higher amputation-related limb event rates at all time points: 30 days (5.0% vs. 3.2%; HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.19-2.12; p=0.001), 6 months (7.6% vs. 5.9%; HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03-1.64; p=0.025), and 1 year (8.9% vs. 7.1%; HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.03-1.55; p=0.026). No significant differences were observed in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, kidney events, or major bleeding at any time point. Conclusions: In this large, multi-institutional propensity-matched analysis, IVL was associated with a consistently lower risk of amputation-related limb events compared with atherectomy across 30-day, 6-month, and 1-year follow-up, without differences in mortality, cardiovascular, renal, or bleeding outcomes. These findings suggest a potential limb-safety advantage for peripheral IVL in PAD. Residual confounding from lesion morphology, calcification burden, anatomic distribution, and device selection cannot be excluded; prospective comparative trials are warranted.
title: Abstract 14452: Peripheral Intravascular Lithotripsy versus Atherectomy for Peripheral Artery Disease: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Implanting a prosthetic valve may require lifelong anticoagulation due to the risk of infection. Long-term postoperative anticoagulation is not necessary with aortic valve neocuspidization (AVNeo), an alternative procedure that involves pericardial restoration of aortic cusps. The process can be carried out using either autologous pericardium treated with glutaraldehyde or bovine pericardium utilizing a modified Batista approach. Patient Information: Preoperative advice was given to a patient with severe symptomatic aortic regurgitation regarding mechanical aortic valve replacement using a minimally invasive technique. Clinical Findings and timeline: The patient showed signs of significant aortic regurgitation, including increasing dyspnea and activity intolerance. With left ventricular function intact, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) verified significant regurgitation. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Mechanical valve replacement was proposed since preoperative TTE did not clearly show anatomy appropriate for valve reconstruction. The surgical plan was reevaluated after direct intraoperative evaluation showed well-preserved leaflet architecture that was not visible on preoperative imaging. Therapeutic Interventions: A less invasive upper mini-sternotomy was used to carry out a modified Batista AVNeo technique. All three aortic cusps were rebuilt using bovine pericardium, circumventing the need for long-term anticoagulation and prosthetic valve implantation. Adverse Events, Follow-up, and Outcomes The patient had no symptoms at the one-year follow-up, and an echocardiographic evaluation showed that the aortic valve was functioning properly. No adverse effects were noted, and no anticoagulation was necessary. Discussion and Synthesis: This case shows that even when preoperative imaging indicates otherwise, intraoperative anatomical reassessment may lead to a favorable modification in surgical technique. With good functional results and no need for anticoagulation, minimally invasive AVNeo employing the modified Batista approach is a practical and conservative substitute for mechanical valve replacement. Optimizing results in this situation requires customized intraoperative decision-making. Patient perspective: The predicted necessity for mechanical valve replacement and lifetime anticoagulation were properly explained to the patient prior to surgery. After a thorough anatomical evaluation, the intraoperative decision to pursue AVNeo was made in the patient’s best interest. The patient reported being satisfied with the outcome and quality of life at the one-year follow-up.
title: Abstract 14466: Modified Batista Procedure with Minimally Invasive Approach in Aortic Valve Neocuspidization: Respect Rather Than Resect

abstract: Introduction: Frailty is common in patients undergoing left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) and predicts death, but frailty alone does not show which patients have enough survival time to benefit from a stroke-prevention device. Hypothesis We hypothesized that a simple Frail-LAAO Benefit Score could stratify competing mortality risk among frail LAAO patients better than the Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS) or CHA2DS2-VASc. Methods: We analyzed frail adults, defined by HFRS >15, undergoing LAAO across 111 healthcare organizations from 2016 to 2026 using TriNetX, a federated electronic-health-record network . A Cox mortality model using 10 routinely available baseline factors assigned integer points proportional to log-hazard ratios. Mortality discrimination was compared with a full Cox model, HFRS alone, and CHA2DS2-VASc. Score bands were examined for 2-year mortality, 2-year survival, and 1-year incident ischemic stroke, representing competing mortality versus stroke prevention from LAAO. P <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Among 15,204 frail LAAO patients, 2,919 deaths occurred. The 0-16-point score included age >=80 years, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/oxygen dependence, body mass index <22 kg/m2, diabetes, metastatic cancer, malnutrition/weight loss, and anemia ( Table 1 ). The full Cox model had the highest discrimination (C-index 0.699). The simplified score retained strong discrimination (C-index 0.674), outperforming HFRS alone (0.580) and CHA2DS2-VASc (0.574). Across score bands, 2-year mortality rose from 4.4% in favorable patients (0-2 points; n=2,423, 15.9%) to 9.8% in intermediate patients (3-4 points; n=3,106, 20.4%), 16.1% in low-benefit patients (5-6 points; n=4,166, 27.4%), and 27.8% in very-low-benefit patients (>=7 points; n=5,509, 36.2%) ( Figure 1 ). In contrast, 1-year ischemic stroke remained low across groups (1.3%-2.5%). Two-year survival ranged from 95.6% to 72.2%. Conclusion: Among frail patients undergoing LAAO, a simple 10-item Frail-LAAO Benefit Score was able to risk stratify patients in whom competing mortality may outweigh expected stroke-prevention benefit from device implantation. Our FRAIL-LAAO bedside score had the best discrimination while being clinically applicable. These findings support individualized patient selection and shared decision-making when considering LAAO in frail patients.
title: Abstract 14481: A Simple Bedside Score Identifies Frail Patients with Increased Mortality Risk After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion

abstract: Background: Left ventricular pseudoaneurysm is an uncommon but potentially fatal complication of late presenting inferior wall myocardial infarction and may be difficult to detect by standard echocardiographic techniques. We report a case of incidentally detected large inferior wall pseudoaneurysm by intracardiac echocardiography at the time of emergent ventricular arrhythmia ablation. Case: A 76-year-old man presented after 3 days of ongoing chest pain and found to have inferior wall Q-waves with persistent ST elevations on the ECG, a severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 15%, inferior wall hypokinesis, severe posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation, and acute thrombotic occlusion of the right coronary artery that could not be revascularized. He was transferred to our intensive care unit for persistent cardiogenic shock and recurrent ventricular arrhythmias refractory to amiodarone, lidocaine and aggressive hemodynamic support. Recurrent ventricular fibrillation (VF) episodes persisted despite the initiation of VA-ECMO and cervical sympathetic blockade. Decision Making: There was significant conduction system disease with bradycardia in the 40s, and recurrent episodes of PVC-triggered ventricular fibrillation. Rather than prolonged QT and early coupled-PVCs, the mechanism was thought to be ongoing Purkinje irritation due to the late presenting and not revascularized inferior wall myocardial infarction. Outcome: Intracardiac echocardiography at the time of potential ventricular arrhythmia ablation uncovered an unexpected large, bi-lobulated inferior wall pseudoaneurysm, missed by both transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms. A monomorphic ventricular tachycardia was exiting at the area of the pseudoaneurysm, and this was burst terminated. Due to the high-risk of perforation if ablating in this friable area, he underwent temporary pacing (VVI 80) and the PVC-triggered ventricular fibrillation was addressed with quinidine, with no further ventricular arrhythmia recurrence. A subsequent CT angiogram confirmed the pseudoaneurysm. Mechanical correction was performed with a vascular plug to occlude the aneurysm neck (a 12mm ASO device) and a MITRAclip for the severe ischemic mitral regurgitation. Hemodynamics improved and he was able to come off ECMO. Conclusion: This case highlights the classical findings of late presenting inferior wall myocardial infarction with bradycardia, recurrent ventricular arrhythmia, ischemic mitral regurgitation, inferior wall pseudoaneurysm and cardiogenic shock, and the role of multidisciplinary collaboration in the critically ill cardiac patient. High-resolution intracardiac echocardiography with the probe in the right ventricle is uniquely poised to uncover structural abnormalities that may be missed by other imaging modalities and also guide interventional management.
title: Abstract 14494: Intracardiac Echocardiography Uncovers Unexpected Finding During Emergency Ventricular Arrhythmia Ablation - Large Inferior Wall Pseudoaneurysm Missed by Both Transthoracic and Transesophageal Echocardiograms

abstract: Background: Reperfused STEMI spans a spectrum of myocardial tissue injury, from reversible (edema-only) - CCS Stage 1; to injury to infarction without microvascular damage - CCS Stage 2; to infarction with microvascular obstruction - CCS Stage 3; to hemorrhagic myocardial infarction with intramyocardial hemorrhage - CCS Stage 4. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is used to identify these stages of injury but is typically performed 48-72 hours after PCI, limiting its real-time clinical utility. Hypothesis: Serial post PCI high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) kinetics can be used to identify the CCS stages of myocardial injury stages in reperfused STEMI patients. Methods: TROP-MI-STAGES was a prospective multicenter study comprising of 266 adults with STEMI undergoing primary PCI. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I was measured at 12 prespecified time points from pre-PCI through 48 hours after PCI. All patients underwent CMR 48-72 hours after PCI to adjudicate infarct size, microvascular obstruction, intramyocardial hemorrhage, and the stage of myocardial injury. Post-PCI and CMR readers were blinded. Diagnostic performance of time-indexed hs-cTnI values for injury stages was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results: Serial hs-cTnI profiles differed by stage of injury. CCS Stage 1 showed minimal release, CCS Stage 2 showed intermediate infarct-related release, CCS Stage 3 showed greater and more protracted release, and CCS Stage 4 showed the earliest and highest post-PCI hs-cTnI surge. At 1 hour after PCI, median hs-cTnI values increased stepwise across stages: 7.35 ng/mL in CCS Stage 1, 18.04 ng/mL in CCS Stage 2, 38.66 ng/mL in CCS Stage 3, and 139.69 ng/mL in CCS Stage 4. At 4 hours, corresponding values were 7.41, 29.42, 49.93, and 168.54 ng/mL, respectively (P<0.001 across stages). Peak hs-cTnI level was highest in CCS Stage 4 at 210.91 ng/mL, compared with 8.80, 36.33, and 71.77 ng/mL in CCS Stages 1-3 (P<0.001). CCS Stage 4 - hemorrhagic myocardial infarction - was identifiable early, with an area- under-the-curve of 0.875 at 4 hours and 0.871 at 6 hours after PCI. CMR confirmed progressive injury across stages, with larger infarct size, greater microvascular obstruction, intramyocardial hemorrhage only in CCS Stage 4, and lower left ventricular ejection fraction from CCS Stage 1 to Stage 4. Conclusion: In TROP-MI-STAGES, serial hs-cTnI kinetics enabled early bedside classification of CMR-defined myocardial tissue-injury severity after primary PCI and accurately identified CCS Stage 4 corresponding to hemorrhagic myocardial infarction within hours of reperfusion. Cardiac Troponin I based CCS staging of tissue injury may close a key diagnostic gap in STEMI care by enabling earlier risk stratification, monitoring intensity, and stage-specific therapeutic trial enrollment.

appraisal.design_and_n: TROP-MI-STAGES, a prospective multicentre study of 266 adults with STEMI undergoing primary PCI, with hs-cTnI at 12 time points and CMR at 48-72 hours.
appraisal.main_limitation: Diagnostic accuracy against CMR without reported clinical outcomes or external validation in the abstract.
appraisal.one_line: Serial hs-cTnI after primary PCI separated CMR-defined stages of reperfusion injury, with early identification of intramyocardial haemorrhage.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: CCS Stage 4 was identifiable early, with an area under the curve of 0.875 at 4 hours and 0.871 at 6 hours after PCI; median hs-cTnI at 1 hour was 7.35, 18.04, 38.66 and 139.69 ng/mL across Stages 1 to 4.
appraisal.why_it_matters: A bedside troponin rule for microvascular obstruction and haemorrhage could select patients for adjunctive STEMI therapies in trials.

title: Abstract 14504: Early Troponin Kinetics for Bedside CCS Classification of Myocardial Injury Stages After Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) presentations overlap with acute myopericarditis, posing significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We present a case in which complimentary multimodality imaging allowed for timely diagnosis of both entities and allowed for accurate and timely differentiation/management. Case: A 45-year-old with hyperlipidemia presented with worsening exertional acute chest pain. The patient had recent exposure to family with viral symptoms. ECG was notable for diffuse ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, aVF, and V2-V6, along with reciprocal ST depressions in aVR consistent with pericarditis. High sensitivity troponins (hsT) were initially 4.7 ng/L (reference range ≤ 35 ng/L), increasing to 92.9 ng/L two hours later. Echocardiogram showed left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction of 50% with abnormal LV segmental wall motion and apical hypokinesis. Intermittent chest pain continued on day of admission without development of new Q waves or T wave inversion on serial ECGs. However, subsequent hsT increased significantly, peaking at 16956.8 ng/L 20 hours later, which in the setting of wall motion abnormalities on echocardiogram prompted performance of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging to differentiate between myopericarditis and infarction. It revealed patchy late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) of the apex with mixed transmural and subepicardial involvement suggestive of myopericarditis, though infarction could not be ruled out. Coronary CTA (CCTA) was recommended to differentiate between infarction and myopericarditis, demonstrating a 70% stenosis of the mid-LAD. Subsequent left heart catheterization (LHC) showed a 90% thrombotic lesion in the mid-LAD, and a drug-eluting stent was placed. His overall clinical picture was consistent with concurrent type 1 myocardial infarction (T1MI) in the setting of myopericarditis. He was discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy plus beta blocker, spironolactone, and atorvastatin for coronary artery disease management, and colchicine for myopericarditis. Discussion: This case highlights the diagnostic and management challenges in a patient presenting with MI while simultaneously experiencing an inflammatory process. While diffuse ST segment elevations and CMR suggested a primary inflammatory driver for presentation, underlying ischemia was suspected given the subsequent rapidly rising hsT and wall motion abnormalities on echocardiogram, leading to an ultimate diagnosis of ACS on CCTA and LHC. A systematic, stepwise diagnostic approach uncovered more insidious pathology which facilitated implementation of appropriate interventions for this T1MI with an accompanying inflammatory process. We highlight the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for ACS in patients with biomarker elevations disproportionate to their presenting clinical symptoms.
title: Abstract 14508: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges for Acute Coronary Syndrome Initially Presenting as Myopericarditis

abstract: Background: Myopericarditis may closely mimic acute coronary syndrome (ACS), presenting with chest pain, electrocardiographic abnormalities, and substantial troponin elevation. Distinguishing inflammatory myocardial injury from ischemic disease is essential because management and prognosis differ significantly. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) has emerged as the noninvasive reference standard for tissue characterization and diagnosis of inflammatory myopericardial syndromes. Case Presentation: A 21-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with acute chest pain, fever, chills, and a single episode of non-bloody emesis occurring two days before presentation. Initial laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated high-sensitivity troponin levels of 11,000 ng/L, peaking at 12,168 ng/L. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm with diffuse ST-segment abnormalities involving the inferior and lateral leads. Viral testing and toxicology screening were unrevealing. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function without regional wall motion abnormalities or pericardial effusion. Given the marked biomarker elevation despite normal echocardiographic findings, CMR was pursued. CMR demonstrated subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement involving the basal inferolateral, inferior, and apical lateral segments with associated pericardial hyperenhancement, consistent with myopericarditis. The patient was treated with anti-inflammatory therapy and experienced clinical improvement. Decision-Making The degree of troponin elevation initially raised concern for ACS. However, the absence of regional wall motion abnormalities despite substantial myocardial injury prompted further evaluation with CMR. Tissue characterization demonstrated a nonischemic pattern of injury characterized by subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement and associated pericardial inflammation, establishing the diagnosis of myopericarditis and avoiding unnecessary invasive management. Conclusion: Marked troponin elevation does not necessarily indicate obstructive coronary disease. In patients with chest pain, elevated cardiac biomarkers, and preserved ventricular function, CMR can identify inflammatory myocardial injury and distinguish myopericarditis from ACS. Recognition of characteristic late gadolinium enhancement patterns is critical for diagnosis, risk stratification, and longitudinal follow-up
title: Abstract 14526: Marked Troponin Elevation with Preserved Ventricular Function: Cardiac MRI Reveals Myopericarditis Mimicking Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Introduction: Pheochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine secreting neuroendocrine tumor with an incidence of approximately 0.6 per 100,000 person years. While the classic triad of episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis is well recognized, cardiovascular complications including stress cardiomyopathy represent an important and potentially life threatening manifestation. Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) occurs in ~23% of pheochromocytoma-associated cardiomyopathies, with the reverse pattern-basal hypokinesis and apical sparing- far more common than in primary TTS (26-30% vs. 2.2%). We present a young male with pheochromocytoma presenting as reverse TTS mimicking Acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Patient Information: A 36 year old male presented with recurrent severe headaches, photophobia, diaphoresis, hypertension, and atypical chest pain. Clinical Finding: Elevated blood pressure 200/120 mmHg. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. High sensitivity troponin I peaked at 2,148 ng/L. Diagnostic assessment: Transthoracic echocardiography revealed LVEF 36% with extensive basal to apical hypokinesis in anterolateral, inferior, inferoseptal, and inferolateral walls, consistent with reverse Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.Coronary angiography showed normal coronaries. CT angiography abdomen pelvis identified a 6.1 х 4.8 х 6.1 cm left adrenal mass.Biochemistry confirmed catecholamine excess: plasma metanephrines 477 pg/mL, norepinephrine 812 pg/mL. Therapeutic Intervention: Myocardial injury was attributed to catecholamine mediated reverse TTS given normal coronaries and multi territory wall motion abnormalities. Preoperative alpha blockade was initiated before beta blockade.MIBG scintigraphy was planned, and genetic testing recommended as up to 40% of pheochromocytomas harbor hereditary variants. Follow up and outcomes: Post adrenal resection, pathology confirmed pheochromocytoma without malignant features. LVEF recovered to 55-60% with no wall motion abnormalities, confirming reversible catecholamine induced cardiomyopathy. Discussion: Pheochromocytoma induced reverse TTS is a rare but important cause of acute heart failure mimicking ACS, carrying higher rates of cardiogenic shock (43% vs. 22%) and cardiac arrest (32% vs. 5%) than typical TTS. Resection improves cardiomyopathy in 96% of cases, while failure to resect is associated with death or transplantation in 44%. Conclusion: Pheochromocytoma induced reverse Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a rare but important cause of acute heart failure mimicking ACS . This case underscores the importance of screening for pheochromocytoma in patients with unexplained nonischemic cardiomyopathy, particularly when accompanied by episodic hypertension, headache, and diaphoresis. Timely alpha adrenergic blockade and surgical resection are essential for recovery of ventricular function.
title: Abstract 14540: Pheochromocytoma Induced Reverse Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy Mimicking Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Introduction: Septal reduction therapy is indicated for hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) refractory to medical management. While alcohol septal ablation (ASA) is an alternative to surgical myectomy, long-term durability can be limited by anatomical remodeling. We present a case of salvage myectomy nine years after ASA, subsequent requirement for mechanical circulatory support (MCS), and terminal complications from systemic inflammation response and coagulopathy. Case Vignette: A 48-year-old male with a history of HOCM and prior ASA presented with severe angina, dyspnea, and recurrent syncope. Physical examination revealed a Grade IV/VI systolic murmur. Echocardiography confirmed asymmetric septal hypertrophy and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction (peak gradient 90 mmHg).
