Despite mid-septal akinesia from the previous ablation, an 18-20 mm fibromuscular ridge remained distal to the aortic valve plane.The patient underwent a Morrow procedure and subvalvular resection. The postoperative course was complicated by refractory mixed shock, requiring emergency peripheral veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO). During intensive care, the patient developed Stage 3 acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring continuous renal replacement therapy, and high-grade AV block necessitated a permanent dual-chamber pacemaker. Following 96 hours of support, the patient was successfully decannulated and extubated. While hemodynamics initially stabilized, the course was marked by progressive multisystem organ dysfunction (NT-proBNP 7,794 pg/mL; direct bilirubin 10 mg/dL). On postoperative day 38, the patient suffered a catastrophic upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. This precipitated refractory hypovolemic shock (BP 65/40 mmHg) compounded by acute anemia (Hb 9 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (Platelets 62,000/μL). Despite a massive transfusion protocol, the patient experienced terminal cardiovascular collapse secondary to exsanguination. Discussion: This case highlights the technical challenges of redo septal interventions. The persistence of a massive fibromuscular ridge a decade after ASA suggests that alcohol-induced necrosis may fail to address proximal subvalvular anatomy in certain phenotypes. Transitioning from a chronically high-afterload state to a low-pressure post-obstructive environment can trigger profound vasoplegia and low cardiac output, demanding temporary MCS. In this context, prolonged systemic anticoagulation, concurrent hepatorenal dysfunction, and intermittent hemodialysis significantly elevated the risk for fatal hemorrhage. The terminal outcome demonstrates that mortality risk in complex HOCM often shifts from primary mechanical obstruction to the cumulative systemic morbidity of prolonged circulatory and renal replacement therapy.
title: Abstract 14548: Salvage Morrow Procedure and Extracorporeal Life Support for Refractory HOCM: A Case Report on a Decade of Progression and Terminal Hemorrhagic Complications

abstract: Background: Plaque erosion (PE) and plaque rupture (PR) are distinct culprit lesion phenotypes in acute coronary syndromes, but whether they differ in clinical risk profile and angiographic disease burden remains incompletely defined. Research Question: We assessed whether optical coherence tomography-defined PE is associated with differences in age, sex, body mass index, cardiometabolic risk factors, smoking, and multivessel disease compared with PR. Methods: We performed a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of studies comparing PE/intact fibrous cap with PR/ruptured fibrous cap. Binary outcomes were pooled as odds ratios (OR) using Paule-Mandel random effects with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals (CIs). Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MD) using restricted maximum likelihood random effects with Hartung-Knapp CIs. Results: Fourteen studies contributed 1,748 PE and 3,240 PR patients for baseline clinical outcomes. Compared with PR, PE was associated with younger age (MD -2.70 years; 95% CI, -3.66 to -1.73; I 2 =20.5%) and higher odds of current smoking (OR 1.27; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.47; I 2 =17.6%). PE was associated with lower odds of hypertension (OR 0.80; 95% CI, 0.66 to 0.96; I 2 =41.2%) and diabetes (OR 0.81; 95% CI, 0.66 to 0.98; I 2 =29.8%). Male sex did not differ significantly between groups (OR 1.14; 95% CI, 0.97 to 1.34; I 2 =4.5%), and body mass index was similar (MD 0.10 kg/m 2 ; 95% CI, -0.25 to 0.46; I 2 =0%). In 11 studies with angiographic data, PE was associated with lower odds of multivessel disease (OR 0.55; 95% CI, 0.40 to 0.75; I 2 =63.3%). Conclusions: In acute coronary syndromes, PE was associated with a younger, more smoking-enriched phenotype with lower prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, and multivessel coronary disease, while sex distribution and body mass index were similar. These findings support PE as a clinically distinct culprit lesion phenotype rather than a milder variant of PR.
title: Abstract 14560: Clinical Risk Profile and Coronary Disease Burden in Plaque Erosion versus Plaque Rupture

abstract: Background: Recurrent pericarditis affects up to one-third of patients despite anti-inflammatory and corticosteroid therapy. Rilonacept, an interleukin-1 inhibitor approved in 2021, has significantly improved outcomes; however, a small subset of patients develop refractory disease. We report a case of recurrent post-cardiac injury syndrome (PCIS) requiring radical pericardiectomy despite extensive contemporary medical therapy. Case Summary: A 61-year-old man with bicuspid aortic valve disease and associated aortopathy underwent bicuspid aortic valve and ascending aortic replacement (26-mm tube graft) in 2014 for aortic regurgitation and ascending aortic aneurysm. His postoperative course was complicated by perimyocarditis consistent with PCIS, followed by recurrent episodes of perimyopericarditis characterized by pleuritic chest pain and CRP elevation. Extensive autoimmune evaluation was unrevealing. Over subsequent years, he required repeated courses of NSAIDs, colchicine, and corticosteroids, with recurrent flares during attempts to taper therapy. Rilonacept was initiated in May 2021 as a steroid-sparing strategy, allowing prednisone discontinuation by November 2021. After approximately two years of treatment, recurrence developed within 5-6 weeks of rilonacept withdrawal. Re-initiation failed to achieve durable remission, and multiple attempts to discontinue concomitant colchicine and NSAID therapy were unsuccessful (Figure 1). Initial and serial cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated persistent mild pericardial late gadolinium enhancement despite rilonacept therapy, while inflammatory markers increased during clinical flares without significant imaging progression (Figure 2). Concurrent echocardiography demonstrated progression to severe aortic stenosis, moderate-severe mitral regurgitation, and aortic root dilation to 4.6 cm. Given refractory pericarditis and the need for repeat valvular surgery, the patient underwent redo sternotomy in March 2026 with radical pericardiectomy, Bio-Bentall aortic root replacement, mitral and tricuspid valve repair, Maze procedure, and left atrial appendage clipping. Histopathology demonstrated a fibrotic pericardium with dense adhesions, consistent with chronic inflammatory remodeling. Discussion: This case illustrates refractory PCIS-associated recurrent pericarditis despite contemporary therapy, including prolonged IL-1 blockade with rilonacept. Imaging demonstrated persistent pericardial disease activity and provided assessment throughout treatment. Ultimately, the patient required repeat cardiac surgery and radical pericardiectomy for definitive management. Although IL-1 blockade has transformed recurrent pericarditis treatment, a small subset of patients with chronic post-surgical pericardial inflammation may require surgical intervention.
title: Abstract 14561: Recurrent Post-Cardiac Injury Syndrome Refractory to Rilonacept Requiring Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement & Pericardiectomy

abstract: Introduction: Ebstein’s anomaly is associated with several EKG abnormalities which are likely secondary to abnormal electrical features of the atrialized right ventricle (RV) myocardium. Prior studies show an association between EKG characteristics and pre-op structure and function. Small case studies have demonstrated improvement in QRS fragmentation (QRSf) after tricuspid valve (TV) repair, but no study has examined additional EKG features including QRS prolongation (QRSp) or the relationship with post-op structure and function. Question: To examine the relationship between pre and post-op EKG characteristics with post-op outcomes. Methods: Retrospective TTE and EKG data was collected on patients with Ebstein’s anomaly who underwent Cone procedure at our center between February 2016 and June 2025. Baseline characteristics and post-op echo outcomes were compared across EKG groups using the Wilcoxon Mann-Whitney test or Kruskal–Wallis test for continuous variables and the chi-square test or Fisher exact test for categorical variables. Within-patient changes in EKG were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for continuous variables and McNemar test for paired categorical variables. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratios (OR), and 95% confidence intervals (CI), after accounting for age at operation. Results: We identified 152 patients with an average follow-up of 44 days (IQR 35). Patients with pre-op QRSf had higher post-op rates of ≥ moderate tricuspid regurgitation (TR) (8.7% vs. 1.0%, p =0.0370) and severe post-op qualitative RV dilation (19.6% vs. 6.5%, p =0.0380). Additionally, pre-op QRSf had higher LV E/e’ (9.8 vs. 8.2, p =0.0281), while LVEDVi (37.1 vs. 46.3 mL/m2, p =0.0035) and LVSVi (23.9 vs. 29.0 mL/m2, p =0.0403) were significantly lower. QRSf had nearly 11 times higher odds (OR=10.95; 95% CI: 1.17-102.84; p =0.0362) of ≥ moderate TR and 4 times greater odds (OR=4.15; 95% CI: 1.34-12.86; p =0.0137) of severe RV dilation. Patients with improvement in post-op QRSf were significantly more likely to have normal post-op RV dilation ( p =0.0386). Patients with pre-op and post-op QRSf had the highest rate of severe post-op RV dilation ( p =0.0393). Patients with pre-op QRSp were significantly more likely to have severe post-op qualitative RV dilation (16.0% vs. 3.8%, p =0.0290), ≥ moderate post-op RV dysfunction (67.1% vs. 36.4%, p =0.0005), and ≥ moderate post-op qualitative right atrial (RA) dilation (42.7% vs. 21.8%, p =0.0388). Conclusions: Pre-op QRSf and QRSp are both strongly associated worse post-op RV dilation and dysfunction, however QRSf was additionally associated with worse post-op TR and decreased LV diastolic function. Resolution of QRSf was associated with improved post-op RV dilation suggesting these characteristics potentially represent useful clinical predictors of post-op function.
title: Abstract 14571: Relationship Between EKG Characteristics and Post-Operative Echocardiogram Findings in Ebstein’s Anomaly Patients Following Cone Repair

abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have shown cardiovascular benefit in randomized clinical trials, particularly among high-risk and secondary prevention populations with diabetes. However, real-world data on GLP-1 RA utilization in primary prevention and their impact of CVD and mortality outcomes is scarce. Research Question: We examined the association between GLP-1 RA use and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular outcomes in overweight or obese patients. Methods: Using EHR data from a multi-site healthcare network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study in overweight or obese (BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 ) patients from 2017 and 2025. Exposure to GLP-1 receptor agonists was defined as treatment at index or initiation during follow-up before the outcome of interest. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction (MI)/revascularization, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, ischemic stroke hospitalization, major adverse limb events (MALE), and all-cause mortality. To reduce confounding, GLP-1 RA users and non-users were balanced using 1:1 propensity score matching. Associations were evaluated using multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models and restricted mean event-free survival analyses. Results: Among 815,506 patients with BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 , approximately 15% received GLP-1 RAs. Following 1:1 propensity score matching, 233,018 patients were included in the matched cohort (mean age 52.4 years). Over a median follow-up of 7.1 years (IQR 4.0-8.5), incidence of the composite outcome and all individual outcomes was consistently lower among GLP-1 RA users throughout follow-up (Figure 1). Compared with non-users, GLP-1 RA use was associated with a lower risk of the composite outcome ( adjusted HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.41-0.43), all-cause mortality (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.35-0.38), MI/revascularization (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.64-0.69), HF hospitalization (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.40-0.44), ischemic stroke hospitalization (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.43-0.50), and MALE (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.69-0.82) (all P<0.001). Conclusion: In a large real-world cohort of adults with overweight or obesity, GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly lower risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, and major adverse limb events, as well as longer event-free survival.

register_verdicts.note: General overweight cohort of GLP-1 RA use, not post-MI incretin initiation.

title: Abstract 14577: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use and Its Association with Cardiovascular Outcomes in Overweight and Obese Adults

abstract: Background: Acute coronary syndrome in young patients without traditional risk factors presents a diagnostic challenge, particularly in distinguishing atherosclerotic plaque rupture from spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), as management strategies differ significantly. Case: A 25-year-old male with hemophilia A on emicizumab, nonsmoker, presented with acute chest pain. Family history was notable for myocardial infarction in both parents. Electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL and V2-V5, and troponin exceeded 26,000. Coronary angiography revealed an 80% ulcerated lesion in the proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) and a separate smooth, tapering distal LAD lesion concerning for type 2A SCAD, with additional luminal irregularities in the left circumflex and right coronary arteries. Decision-Making: Given the patient’s young age and mixed angiographic findings, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) was performed. Imaging of the proximal LAD demonstrated fibrotic plaque with ulceration, consistent with plaque rupture and identifying the culprit lesion. The distal LAD lesion showed morphology consistent with SCAD. Neither lesion improved with intracoronary nitroglycerin.Intervention: The proximal LAD lesion was treated with direct stenting using a zotarolimus-eluting stent, followed by post-dilation with a stent balloon and a 3.0 mm non-compliant balloon, achieving TIMI 3 flow without complications. Post-procedural IVUS confirmed adequate stent expansion and apposition without edge dissection. Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel was initiated in coordination with hematology to balance ischemic and bleeding risks. Outcome: The patient remained clinically stable, was monitored for 48 hours in the cardiac intensive care unit, and discharged home with close follow-up.Conclusion: This case highlights the coexistence of plaque rupture and SCAD in a young patient without traditional risk factors. Intravascular imaging was essential in identifying the culprit lesion and guiding appropriate revascularization. Multidisciplinary management is critical when balancing antiplatelet therapy in patients with inherited bleeding disorders.
title: Abstract 14582: Concurrent Plaque Rupture and Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection in a Young Adult with Hemophilia A Presenting with ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) have historically been considered at increased procedural risk due to dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction and altered loading conditions. Prior studies reported in-hospital mortality up to 18.6% with elevated cardiogenic shock rates, but were limited to small cohorts, in-hospital outcomes, and earlier procedural eras. Long-term outcomes remain poorly defined. Methods: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR (2015-2025). Patients with HCM were propensity score matched 1:1 to non-HCM controls on demographics, comorbidities, medications, and laboratory values. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 30 days, 1 year, and 5 years. Secondary outcomes included stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock, heart failure hospitalization, complete heart block, composite atrioventricular block (AVB), permanent pacemaker implantation, atrial fibrillation/flutter, and acute kidney injury. Sensitivity analyses included landmark analyses, falsification endpoints, restriction to the modern era (2020-2025), and exclusion of prior septal reduction therapy. Exploratory analyses compared obstructive and non-obstructive HCM. Results: Among 82,918 TAVR patients, 1,577 had HCM; 1,561 matched pairs were analyzed. Mortality was identical at 30 days (1.7% vs 1.7%; HR 1.00; p=0.99) and comparable at 1 year (HR 0.93; 95% CI 0.74-1.17; p=0.53) and 5 years (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.78-1.04; p=0.16). Stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock, heart failure hospitalization, pacemaker implantation, atrial arrhythmias, and acute kidney injury were comparable across all time points. However, composite AVB was consistently higher in HCM at 30 days (20.6% vs 16.2%; HR 1.30; p=0.002), 1 year (HR 1.21; p=0.006), and 5 years (33.1% vs 27.7%; HR 1.29; p<0.001). Excess AVB risk was present in both obstructive and non-obstructive HCM with no significant difference between phenotypes. Findings were consistent across all sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: HCM was not associated with increased mortality or major complications following TAVR through 5 years, contrasting with earlier reports. However, persistently higher composite AVB across both phenotypes suggests the shared myocardial substrate rather than obstruction alone underlies excess conduction risk, underscoring the importance of conduction surveillance in this population.

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective TriNetX cohort of 82,918 TAVR patients, 1,577 with HCM; 1,561 matched pairs analysed.
appraisal.main_limitation: Administrative coding of HCM and outcomes, and no data on valve type or septal anatomy.
appraisal.one_line: TriNetX matched cohort found no excess mortality after TAVR in patients with HCM, but a higher rate of atrioventricular block.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Mortality was 1.7% vs 1.7% at 30 days (HR 1.00), HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.74-1.17 at 1 year and HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.78-1.04 at 5 years; composite AVB at 5 years was 33.1% vs 27.7% (HR 1.29).
appraisal.why_it_matters: It challenges earlier small-series reports of high TAVR risk in HCM, a population excluded from the pivotal trials.

title: Abstract 14595: Clinical Outcomes Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

abstract: Background: Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) face substantial in-hospital mortality following acute myocardial infarction (AMI). While glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce long-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), their association with in-hospital outcomes during AMI remains incompletely defined in contemporary national datasets. Methods: We analyzed the 2023 National Inpatient Sample, the first dataset capturing a full calendar year of GLP-1 RA use (ICD-10-CM Z79.85). Adult T2DM hospitalizations with atherothrombotic AMI were included, excluding type 1 diabetes and demand ischemia. Patients with antecedent GLP-1 RA use (n=2,058) were matched 1:1 to controls using doubly robust propensity score methods, yielding 4,116 hospitalizations (20,580 weighted encounters) adjusted for 24 clinical and socioeconomic covariates, including comorbidity burden and hospital characteristics (Figure 1). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, MACE, respiratory failure, sepsis, and resource utilization. Results: Post-matching balance was excellent (mean standardized mean difference 1.6%). GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower mortality (2.5% vs 5.1%; aOR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.79; p=0.001). GLP-1 RA users also had lower odds of MACE-4 (aOR 0.57; p<0.001), cardiogenic shock (aOR 0.63; p=0.002), ischemic stroke (aOR 0.46; p=0.001), and cardiac arrest (aOR 0.71; p=0.046) (Figure 2). Non-cardiac complications, including respiratory failure (aOR 0.68; p<0.001) and sepsis (aOR 0.61; p=0.001), were also less frequent, while acute kidney injury was similar (aOR 0.94; p=0.470). GLP-1 RA users had shorter length of stay (4.27 vs 5.09 days; p<0.001) and lower hospital charges (p=0.019). Findings were directionally consistent across eight pre-specified clinical subgroups. A comprehensive summary of study design, outcomes, and interpretation is shown in Figure 3. Conclusions: Among hospitalized patients with T2DM and AMI, antecedent GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower odds of in-hospital mortality, cardiovascular events, and selected non-cardiac complications. These associations should be interpreted cautiously given the observational design and potential for residual confounding and healthy user effects, as patients receiving GLP-1 RAs may differ in access to care, treatment adherence, and baseline health status. The consistency and magnitude of these associations across outcomes and subgroups support the need for prospective studies to better define the relationship between GLP-1 RA therapy and acute cardiovascular outcomes.
title: Abstract 14612: Healthy User Effect or Measured Association? GLP-1 RA Use and In-Hospital Outcomes in Acute Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major cause of thromboembolism, and left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is an established strategy for stroke prevention in selected patients. Catheter ablation (CA) provides rhythm control, and performing CA concomitantly with LAAO may reduce procedural burden; however, its impact on peri-device seal, efficacy, and safety outcomes remains uncertain. We aimed to compare concomitant CA and LAAO with isolated LAAO for device-related, safety, and clinical outcomes. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies comparing concomitant catheter ablation and left atrial appendage occlusion (CA+LAAO) versus isolated LAAO in adults (≥18 years) with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Included studies consisted predominantly of retrospective observational cohorts, and no randomized controlled trials were identified. The primary outcome was peri-device leak (PDL). Secondary outcomes included complete left atrial appendage closure, device-related thrombus (DRT), pericardial effusion requiring intervention, major bleeding, stroke, and all-cause mortality. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects meta-analysis model. Results: A total of 110,244 participants from 7 studies were included, of whom 2,784 underwent concomitant catheter ablation and left atrial appendage occlusion (CA+LAAO) and 107,460 underwent isolated LAAO. Compared with isolated LAAO, concomitant CA+LAAO was associated with a higher rate of peri-device leak (RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.03-1.55; p=0.02), pericardial effusion requiring intervention (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.11-2.73; p=0.02), and major bleeding (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.14-2.33; p=0.008). No significant differences were observed between groups in complete left atrial appendage closure (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90-1.01; p=0.13), device-related thrombus (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.37-1.36; p=0.30), stroke (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.21-1.88; p=0.41), or all-cause mortality (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.50-3.08; p=0.64). Conclusion: Concomitant catheter ablation and left atrial appendage occlusion (CA+LAAO) was associated with higher rates of peri-device leak, pericardial effusion requiring intervention, and major bleeding compared with isolated LAAO, while complete left atrial appendage closure, device-related thrombus, stroke, and mortality rates were similar between groups. These findings suggest a trade-off between procedural efficiency and procedural risk with concomitant CA+LAAO, which may reduce procedural burden while modestly compromising peri-device seal and procedural safety. However, the included studies did not directly compare concomitant versus staged procedural strategies, where cumulative risks associated with multiple procedures may differ. Further prospective randomized studies are needed to define the optimal treatment approach.
title: Abstract 14621: Outcomes of Combined Catheter Ablation and Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion versus Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Alone in Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Pulmonary hypertension (PulHTN) and right heart failure (RHF) are prevalent comorbidities among patients undergoing mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER), but their impact on in-hospital outcomes remains unclear. Methods: Adult hospitalizations involving M-TEER were identified from the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2023). Patients with PulHTN and/or RHF were compared against a control group of M-TEER patients without PulHTN, RHF, or any congestive heart failure. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was used to assess adjusted in-hospital outcomes. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included cardiac, renal, respiratory, vascular, neurologic, and pericardial complications. A secondary analysis further stratified the patient group into PulHTN alone, PulHTN with RHF, and RHF alone to examine the differential impact of each subgroup on in-hospital mortality. Results: Among 29,770 M-TEER hospitalizations, 22,155 (74.4%) had PulHTN and/or RHF, with a significantly higher comorbidity burden across cardiovascular, metabolic, and renal domains (Charlson index 3.44 vs. 1.32, p<0.001)(Table 1a). After adjustment, PulHTN and/or RHF was associated with significantly higher odds of in-hospital mortality, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, cardiac dysrhythmias, cardiac tamponade, pericardial effusion, acute kidney injury, mechanical ventilation, and pleural effusion(Table 1b).On secondary analysis, the majority of the patient group had PulHTN alone (92.96%), followed by PulHTN with RHF (3.90%) and RHF alone (3.14%). In-hospital mortality was highest among those with concomitant PulHTN and RHF (6.9%), compared to RHF alone (5.0%) and PulHTN alone (2.5%). On adjusted analysis, concomitant PulHTN and RHF carried significantly higher mortality compared to PulHTN alone (aOR 2.38, 95% CI 1.183-4.772, p=0.015), whereas isolated RHF did not reach statistical significance (aOR 1.79, 95% CI 0.780-4.097, p=0.170). Conclusions: Pulmonary hypertension and/or right heart failure identify a high-risk population among patients undergoing M-TEER, and are associated with significantly increased in-hospital mortality, hemodynamic instability, pericardial complications, acute kidney injury, and need for mechanical ventilation. The co-existence of PulHTN and RHF conferred the highest mortality risk, suggesting that right ventricular decompensation may be a key determinant of adverse outcomes in this population.

title: Abstract 14626: Pulmonary Hypertension and Right Heart Failure as Determinants of In-Hospital Morbidity and Mortality Following Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair: A Population-Based Study of 29,770 Hospitalizations

abstract: Background: Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) lies in direct contact with the coronary arteries, and higher-attenuation (“inflamed”) EAT is thought to reflect a proinflammatory, lipid-poor phenotype. Whether inflamed EAT volume is associated with coronary artery calcium (CAC) and predicts cardiovascular events independent of CAC is unknown. We hypothesized that inflamed EAT volume is associated with CAC burden and with incident events beyond CAC. Methods: In the Houston Methodist HeartScan Registry, EAT was segmented from non-contrast ECG-gated CAC computed tomography using a deep-learning model (DeepFat 2.0; fat window –190 to –30 HU); inflamed EAT volume was the volume with attenuation –70 to –30 HU. We related inflamed EAT volume (per SD, 17 cm 3 ) to prevalent CAC≥100 and CAC≥300 by logistic regression (n=26,829) and to incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, or coronary revascularization) by Cox regression (n=18,342). Models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and type 2 diabetes (T2DM); MACE models additionally for CAC category, with non-cardiovascular death censored. Results: Mean inflamed EAT volume was 47±17 cm 3 ; mean age 57±11 years, 50% men, 10% T2DM. Each SD higher inflamed EAT volume was associated with greater odds of CAC≥100 (odds ratio [OR] 1.19, 95% CI 1.14-1.24) and CAC≥300 (OR 1.22, 1.16-1.28; both p<0.001), persisting after adjustment for race/ethnicity and without effect modification by BMI. Over a median of 3.2 years, 1,241 MACE occurred; 5-year incidence rose across inflamed EAT volume tertiles (5.9%, 8.2%, 12.0%). Higher inflamed EAT volume was associated with incident MACE independent of risk factors and CAC (hazard ratio 1.10 per SD, 1.03-1.18; p=0.005), whereas total EAT volume was not (1.00; p=0.90), localizing the association to the inflamed component. The MACE association persisted after excluding events within 6 months, after stratifying by CAC category, and in competing-risk analysis, but did not improve discrimination beyond CAC (C-statistic 0.735 vs 0.736). Conclusions: Inflamed EAT volume, quantified automatically from CAC computed tomography already obtained for risk stratification, is associated with coronary calcium and independently predicts incident cardiovascular events, suggesting that the inflamed epicardial fat phenotype captures cardiovascular risk not fully reflected by coronary calcium burden.
title: Abstract 14631: Artificial Intelligence -Derived Inflamed Epicardial Adipose Tissue Volume, Coronary Artery Calcium, and Incident Cardiovascular Events: The Houston Methodist HeartScan Registry

abstract: Introduction: The optimal strategy for revascularization in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) remains an area of debated controversy. We present a case of AMI-CS with multivessel CAD undergoing multi-disciplinary guided culprit vessel intervention with mechanical circulatory support (MCS) as a bridge to eventual complete revascularization. Case: A 59-year-old man with familial hyperlipidemia presented with exertional presyncope and was in extremis. Twelve lead ECG demonstrated ST elevation in aVR with precordial ST depressions, consistent with global subendocardial ischemia (Fig 1). Emergent coronary angiography demonstrated severe multivessel disease with thrombotic occlusion of the left main (LM) and circumflex arteries (LCx). The left anterior descending (LAD) and right coronary arteries (RCA) were chronically occluded (Fig 2A-D). Diagnostic Assessment: An Impella CP was placed for left ventricular unloading due to hypotension with escalating vasopressor requirements, consistent with SCAI D CS. The culprit LCx was treated with salvage balloon angioplasty, with restoration of TIMI 3 flow. He was subsequently transferred to the CICU, where he was intubated and required device-based and vasoactive support. A transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated severe biventricular dysfunction without valvular disease (LVEF 24%, TAPSE 1.3 cm). Management & Outcome: The multidisciplinary Heart Team determined the patient to be prohibitively high-risk for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) given refractory hemodynamic instability. He was referred for high risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and he underwent successful intravascular ultrasound-guided PCI of the LM and LCx with drug-eluting stents (Fig 3A-C, 4A-B). The LAD and RCA chronic total occlusions were deferred for staged revascularization. He was ultimately weaned from vasopressor support, and the Impella was removed the following day. He was discharged home in stable condition on guideline-directed medical therapy with heart failure and surgical follow-up with plans for staged CABG. Discussion: This case highlights the merits of a team-based and targeted approach to the management of AMI-CS with multivessel disease. Studies such as CULPRIT-SHOCK, DanGer SHOCK and the COMPLETE trial were incorporated to facilitate best practice for management of unstable AMI-CS. This patient underwent PCI of culprit lesions with Impella support, thereby facilitating acute left ventricular unloading and end-organ preservation, as a bridge to eventual staged complete revascularization, which is associated with long-term survival benefit. Staged revascularization in prevention of recurrent heart failure remains unclear and warrants further investigation.
title: Abstract 14648: Precision-Based Myocardial Unloading: Microaxial Flow Pump Supported High-Risk PCI in Acute Myocardial Infarction Related Cardiogenic Shock with Multivessel Disease

abstract: Background: VA-ECMO can restore systemic perfusion in cardiogenic shock, but retrograde aortic flow may increase left ventricular afterload, promote ventricular distension, and impair myocardial recovery. Whether active unloading with a percutaneous microaxial pump improves clinical outcomes remains a central unresolved question in contemporary shock care. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that combined VA-ECMO and Impella-mediated left ventricular unloading (ECMELLA/ECpella) would be associated with lower short-term mortality and improved liberation from support compared with VA-ECMO alone, with an offsetting increase in device-related morbidity. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception to June 2026 for comparative studies of adults with cardiogenic shock treated with ECMELLA/ECpella versus VA-ECMO alone. The primary outcome was short-term mortality. Secondary outcomes included successful weaning, major bleeding, renal replacement therapy, stroke, vascular complications, and bridging to durable left ventricular assist device or transplantation. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I. Random-effects meta-analysis generated odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: Sixteen comparative studies met eligibility criteria, of which 12 entered quantitative synthesis; all were observational. ECMELLA/ECpella was associated with lower short-term mortality than VA-ECMO alone (OR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58-0.89; p=0.003; I 2 =34%), with pooled mortality of 51% versus 64%, respectively. Successful weaning from support was more frequent with active unloading (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.20-2.10; p=0.001). Major bleeding was increased (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.10-1.90; p=0.016), highlighting the procedural trade-off of dual large-bore support. Bridging to durable left ventricular assist device or transplantation (OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.90-1.80; p=0.14) and stroke (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.60-1.40; p=0.81) did not differ significantly. Timing-stratified data favored early or simultaneous unloading rather than delayed rescue use. Most studies had moderate or serious risk of bias, principally from confounding by indication. Conclusions: In comparative evidence to date, ECMELLA/ECpella is associated with a clinically meaningful survival and weaning signal compared with VA-ECMO alone, counterbalanced by excess bleeding. These findings support early consideration of left ventricular unloading within protocolized shock pathways, while underscoring the need for randomized evidence to define optimal patient selection and timing.
title: Abstract 14664: ECMELLA versus VA-ECMO Alone in Adult Cardiogenic Shock: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Reporting performance metrics and clinical outcomes in AI-assisted CT analysis for TAVR planning studies is crucial to establishing clinical trust and accuracy. However, it is unclear whether clinical outcomes and Segmentation performance metrics (SPM) have been well reported in AI-based studies. Research Question: What evidence exists on anatomical measurements, segmentation performance metrics, and clinical outcomes in AI-assisted CT analysis in TAVR planning? Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, a literature search in PubMed focusing on AI-assisted CT analysis for TAVR planning identified nearly 700 studies. We screened the collected studies using titles/abstracts, followed by full-text screening. Descriptive analyses were performed using pooled data, frequencies, and percentages. We described the frequency of reporting the following performance metrics in the included studies: Dice Score (Dice), Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) and 95th Percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95). Reporting of the abovementioned metrics was stratified for the following anatomical components: Aortic Annulus, Sinus of Valsalva (SOV), Sinotubular Junction (STJ), Ascending Aorta (AA), Coronaries and Calcification. Moreover, clinical outcomes were summarized descriptively. Results: A total of 20 studies, including validation, prospective observational, and retrospective studies, involving 5430 cases, were analyzed. The pooled mean age across the studies was 77.34, and 2237 (41.2%) cases were females. Sample sizes across the studies ranged from 31 to 1352. 9 studies, including 2583 cases (47.57%), reported no conflict of interest (COI) between the vendor company and the first author. Anatomical measurements reporting is shown in Table 1. Frequencies of reporting SPM among the 5430 cases included in the studies for the six anatomical components were as follows: AA and calcifications: 1661 (30.59%) cases. This was followed by 1478 (27.22%) cases for coronaries, 1159 (21.34%) cases for annulus measurements, 614 (11.31%) cases for sinotubular junction (STJ), and 126 (2.32%) cases for sinus of Valsalva (SOV). Among studies that reported SPM, acceptable metrics were achieved most consistently for SOV and AA. Performance metrics reporting in detail is shown in Table 2 We found that none of the identified studies described stroke, permanent pacemaker, or in-hospital mortality as measured outcomes. Only one study, which included 105 cases (1.93%), reported a 30-day mortality of 6.8%. Conclusions: Among studies that focused on AI-Assisted CT Analysis in TAVR, SPM reporting was inconsistent among different anatomical parameters, and clinical outcomes were poorly described. These data suggest that further studies focusing on performance metrics and clinical outcomes are warranted to understand the implications of AI use for TAVR planning in clinical practice.
title: Abstract 14668: Technical Performance and Clinical Outcomes in AI-Assisted CT Analysis in TAVR Planning: A Systematic Review

abstract: Background: Frailty is a multidimensional clinical syndrome that predicts adverse outcomes following structural heart interventions. Contemporary nationally representative data on frailty's impact in patients undergoing transcatheter mitral valve edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) remain limited. Hypothesis: Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS)-defined frailty is independently associated with major adverse in-hospital events (MAIE) and greater resource utilization in adults undergoing M-TEER. Methods: We analyzed the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2017-2022, identifying M-TEER hospitalizations via ICD-10-PCS code 02UG3JZ. Frailty was defined as HFRS ≥5 (non-frail: <5). The primary outcome was MAIE, a composite of in-hospital mortality, ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, cardiogenic shock, major bleeding, and blood transfusion. Secondary outcomes included individual MAIE components, length of stay (LOS), total hospital costs (2022 USD), and non-home discharge. Multivariable survey-weighted logistic and linear regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and beta-coefficients, respectively, adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, payer, admission type, and hospital characteristics. Results: Among 60,165 M-TEER hospitalizations, 15,525 (25.8%) were frail. Frail patients had greater comorbidity burden (Elixhauser index 7.23 vs. 5.40), higher rates of non-elective admission (46% vs. 13%), and more renal failure (64% vs. 33%). Frailty was associated with substantially higher unadjusted MAIE (33.0% vs. 5.1%) and mortality (6.2% vs. 0.3%). After multivariable adjustment, frailty independently predicted MAIE (aOR 6.43, 95% CI 5.59-7.39), mortality (aOR 13.60, 95% CI 8.78-21.06), cardiogenic shock (aOR 5.12, 95% CI 4.28-6.13), major bleeding (aOR 5.87, 95% CI 5.11-6.74), ischemic stroke (aOR 2.41, 95% CI 1.68-3.46), and non-home discharge (aOR 6.52, 95% CI 5.60-7.60). Frail patients also had longer LOS (+5.2 days, 95% CI 4.8-5.6) and higher costs (+$23,445, 95% CI $20,731-$26,160). Conclusions: In a nationally representative M-TEER cohort, HFRS-defined frailty was highly prevalent and independently associated with markedly worse clinical outcomes and substantially greater resource utilization. Systematic frailty assessment using administrative data may improve pre-procedural risk stratification, patient counseling, and resource planning in M-TEER candidates.
title: Abstract 14677: Frailty Defined by Hospital Frailty Risk Score and In-Hospital Outcomes After Transcatheter Mitral Valve Edge-to-Edge Repair: A Nationwide Analysis

abstract: Introduction/Background: Right heart catheterization metrics are preload and afterload-dependent, masking underlying ventricular function. Single-beat estimation of the right ventricular (RV) pressure-volume loop yields load-independent metrics of intrinsic right ventricular (RV)-pulmonary vascular function that help guide care. These parameters are difficult to obtain, but we have developed a novel computational program that can extract these from the standard RV tracing image (Moon et al JACC HF 2026). We tested whether our program-derived RV end-systolic elastance (Ees), effective arterial elastance (Ea), and other pressure-volume loop metrics can predict poor outcomes in an Impella (Abiomed, MA) supported shock cohort. Methods: We retrospectively studied Impella-supported cardiogenic shock patients with baseline and subsequent hemodynamic data (n=55). Hemodynamic variables were collected at time 0 and 48 hours post-Impella implant (time 2d). RV waveforms collected at time 0 were inputted into the program alongside stroke volume to derive Ees, Ea, their ratio, as well as end-systolic volume (ESV), end-diastolic volume, and RV pressure-volume loops. Kruskal-Wallis and post-hoc testing compared program and hemodynamic metrics across three outcome groups: successful bridging to recovery or definitive surgery, need for MCS escalation, and death. We then investigated predictors of death. Results: Seven of the 55 patients died before successful bridging or MCS escalation. Outcomes were dichotomized into survivable (recovery or MCS escalation) and fatal (death). Pulmonary artery pulsatility index (log transformed PAPI), Ees, and ESV were significantly predictive of death (p<0.05). Change in RV cardiac power output (RV-CPO) from time 0 to time 2d was as well (p<0.05). The death group had the lowest change in RV-CPO (-0.02 ± 0.02 vs 0.06 ± 0.02) and lower logPAPI (0.29 ± 0.15 vs 0.89 ± 0.1), low Ees (0.32 ± 0.03 vs 0.59 ± 0.07), and elevated ESV (142.5 ±19.6 vs 91.6 ± 7.6) (Figure 1). Conclusion: Single beat-derived RV metrics, including Ees and ESV, helped supplement traditional metrics to predict death in an Impella-supported shock cohort. Low RV performance metrics and elevated RV ESV in those who died suggest that mortality may stem from biventricular failure not fully supported by univentricular mechanical support. Our program may add value to up front prognostication of shock patients undergoing Impella placement.
title: Abstract 14688: Leveraging a Novel Program to Obtain Load-Independent Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Metrics to Predict Clinical Response in Impella-Supported Cardiogenic Shock Patients

abstract: Introduction: Hypoattenuated leaflet thickening (HALT) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is common, usually subclinical, and anticoagulation responsive. We describe an anticoagulation-dependent prosthesis in which leaflet thrombosis recurred with every lapse in anticoagulation and, after years of stability, a brief interruption precipitated life-threatening obstruction within days. Patient Information: A 73-year-old man with bicuspid aortic stenosis underwent TAVR with a 29-mm balloon-expandable valve. A thrombophilia evaluation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene, antiphospholipid antibodies) was negative. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Early rising gradients prompted gated CT showing leaflet thickening with restricted motion; warfarin restored normal hemodynamics. Thrombosis recurred when anticoagulation was stopped and resolved again on resumption, after which apixaban maintained stable valve function for several years. Apixaban was held for noncardiac surgery; within five days he developed rest angina, dyspnea, and pulmonary edema. Diagnostic Assessment: ECG showed diffuse ST-depression with ST-elevation in aVR; troponin was elevated (peak 96.7 pg/mL), BNP was 822 pg/mL, and LVEF was near 20%. Coronary angiography showed only mild epicardial disease without a culprit. Echocardiography and repeat gated CT confirmed severe prosthetic obstruction with restricted leaflet motion. Therapeutic Interventions: He deteriorated despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Under a mechanical-support-ready (“protected”) strategy, he underwent TAVR explant and surgical aortic valve replacement. Operative findings were a completely thrombosed prosthesis with a pinhole orifice and left main ostial compression by valve struts, requiring concomitant left main ostial plasty. Follow-up and Outcomes: Gradients normalized and LVEF recovered from approximately 20% to greater than 50%. Apixaban was resumed; he remained stable on imaging. Discussion: Recurrent leaflet thrombosis after TAVR can progress within days of anticoagulation interruption to life-threatening prosthetic obstruction with coronary compromise, mimicking acute coronary syndrome. Most HALT, whether index or recurrent, responds to anticoagulation, and routine surgical explantation would expose many patients to unnecessary risk. This case instead illustrates a rare anticoagulation-dependent phenotype: the thrombus remained anticoagulation-responsive for years yet the valve tolerated no lapse, while a negative thrombophilia workup supported a localized device-host process. Recognition matters because it favors sustained, carefully bridged anticoagulation rather than interruption; explantation should be reserved for refractory or hemodynamically critical obstruction, as occurred here.
title: Abstract 14699: Recurrent Transcatheter Aortic Valve Thrombosis Causing Circulatory Collapse Following Temporary Interruption of Anticoagulation

abstract: Background: The Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) shock classification stratifies cardiogenic shock severity, but its independent prognostic value in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains incompletely defined. We evaluated whether SCAI stage independently predicts mortality after PCI in a contemporary high-acuity cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of consecutive adults undergoing PCI with documented SCAI shock staging between 2018 and 2023. Patients were categorized into SCAI Stages B-E. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included 30-day and 6-month mortality. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of mortality, adjusting for demographics, comorbidities, lactate, mechanical ventilation, and mechanical circulatory support use. Results: Among 294 patients, 10 (3%) were Stage B, 89 (30%) Stage C, 186 (63%) Stage D, and 9 (3%) Stage E. In-hospital mortality increased progressively across stages: 20% in Stage B, 11% in Stage C, 40% in Stage D, and 78% in Stage E (p<0.001). Similar gradients persisted at 30 days and 6 months. In multivariable analysis, Stage D independently predicted in-hospital mortality versus Stage C (adjusted OR [aOR] 4.22, 95% CI 1.63-10.91, p=0.003), while Stage E was associated with nearly tenfold higher mortality odds (aOR 9.60, 95% CI 1.16-79.63, p=0.036). Mechanical ventilation was the strongest non-SCAI predictor (aOR 5.15, 95% CI 2.39-11.10, p<0.001), followed by baseline lactate and older age. The prognostic significance of Stage D persisted across multiple sensitivity analyses and longer-term mortality models. Conclusions: SCAI shock stage may independently predict mortality after PCI beyond traditional clinical and hemodynamic markers. Stage D may confer > fourfold increase in in-hospital mortality risk compared with Stage C, supporting routine SCAI stage documentation during PCI for risk stratification, triage, and escalation of circulatory support strategies.
title: Abstract 14708: SCAI Shock Stage Independently Predicts Mortality After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Introduction: Cardiogenic shock (CS) represents a high-fatality emergency; however, contemporary patterns of premature mortality among adults with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) comorbidity remain insufficiently characterized. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that CS mortality among working-age adults with diabetes mellitus (DM), chronic kidney disease (CKD), or CKM features increased disproportionately during 2018-2024, with persistent sex disparities. Methods: A retrospective analysis of U.S. mortality data from 2018-2024 was conducted among adults aged 25-74 years. Deaths involving CS were stratified as overall CS, CS with CKM, CS with DM, and CS with CKD based on the extracted dataset. Outcomes included annual deaths, age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMR) per 100,000, percent change from 2018-2024, sex-specific mortality, and log-linear annual percent change (APC) in AAMR. Results/Data: Between 2018 and 2024, overall CS deaths increased from 16,329 to 21,822 (+33.6%), while AAMR rose from 6.6 to 8.2 per 100,000 (+24.2%; APC 3.7%, p=0.023). CS with CKM exhibited a greater increase in mortality, with deaths rising from 3,003 to 4,392 (+46.3%) and AAMR from 1.2 to 1.6 (+33.3%; APC 4.9%, p=0.027). CS with DM increased from 1,881 to 2,710 deaths (+44.1%), with AAMR rising from 0.7 to 1.0 (+42.9%; APC 6.0%, p=0.031). CS with CKD increased from 1,143 to 1,696 deaths (+48.4%), with AAMR increasing from 0.4 to 0.6 (+50.0%; APC 6.5%, p=0.011). In 2024, male AAMR exceeded female AAMR across all strata, including CKM (2.1 vs 1.2), DM (1.3 vs 0.7), and CKD (0.8 vs 0.4). Conclusion(s): Premature CS mortality increased substantially from 2018 to 2024, with larger relative increases observed among adults with CKM, DM, and CKD compared to overall CS. These findings identify CKM comorbidity as an expanding critical care mortality phenotype and underscore the importance of earlier cardiometabolic-kidney risk recognition prior to progression to fatal hemodynamic collapse.
title: Abstract 14724: Cardiogenic Shock with Diabetes or Chronic Kidney Disease: A Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Critical Care Mortality Analysis

abstract: Background: Neighborhood socioeconomic status influences cardiovascular outcomes, yet its relationship with mechanical circulatory support (MCS) use in cardiogenic shock (CS) remains unclear. We examined whether neighborhood income is associated with MCS utilization patterns and whether differences in device use are associated with income-related survival differences. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the 2023 National Inpatient Sample. Adults (≥18 years) with CS were identified using ICD-10-CM codes and stratified by ZIP code median household income quartiles (Q1-lowest to Q4-highest). Co-primary outcomes were MCS use and in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included device tier, total charges, and discharge disposition. Device-tier use (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) was evaluated using survey-weighted multinomial regression adjusted for age, sex, shock etiology, cardiac arrest, mechanical ventilation, comorbidity burden, and hospital characteristics. A 1:1 propensity-matched cohort (N=22,092) and mediation analysis assessed associations between device use and mortality. Results: Among 328,525 estimated CS admissions, higher neighborhood income was associated with greater and more advanced MCS use without proportional differences in survival (Figure 1). A stepwise gradient was observed with adjusted MCS use rising from 10.75% (Q1) to 13.80% (Q4) (P-trend<.001) (Figure 2A). Q4 patients had higher odds of any MCS (aOR 1.37; P<.001) and destination therapy (aOR 1.41; P=.007). Differences in escalation were most pronounced at higher tiers; compared with Q1, Q4 patients had higher relative risk of IABP (aRRR 1.39) and VA-ECMO (aRRR 1.83, P<.001) (Figure 2B). In the matched cohort, Q4 patients had lower mortality (30.7% vs 32.0%; OR 0.94; P=.03), ~8.4% higher charges (P<.001), and lower skilled-nursing discharge (OR 0.89; P<.001) (Figure 3A). In mediation analysis, differences in MCS use were associated with explaining ~6% of the survival difference (indirect-effect OR 0.996; P=.011), with ~94% attributed to non-device pathways (direct-effect OR 0.938; P=.049). High-volume centers used more MCS but did not significantly modify disparities (P-interaction=.12) (Figure 3B). Conclusions: Higher neighborhood income was associated with increased MCS use across all tiers, particularly advanced devices, but differences in device use were associated with only a small proportion of survival differences. These findings suggest that factors beyond device access contribute substantially to outcomes. As an administrative dataset, NIS cannot account for illness severity, individual-level socioeconomic status, or longitudinal outcomes; these hypothesis-generating findings warrant prospective evaluation.
title: Abstract 14762: The Illusion of the Machine: Device Access and Socioeconomic Differences in Cardiogenic Shock Outcomes - A 2023 National Inpatient Sample Analysis

abstract: Background: The optimal strategy for initiating mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in acute myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) remains uncertain. This study evaluated the clinical and economic outcomes of upfront direct Impella placement versus a stepwise intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) to Impella escalation strategy. Methods: Adult AMI-CS hospitalizations requiring Impella support were identified using the National Inpatient Sample (2020-2022). CS was defined by a concurrent diagnosis of cardiogenic shock and markers of acute end-organ dysfunction. A 1:1 propensity score match (PSM) was performed using baseline demographics, comorbidities, hospital characteristics, and STEMI presentation. A multivariable logistic regression was subsequently performed on the matched cohort, adjusting for indicators of end-organ failure and shock severityResults: The unadjusted cohort comprised 12,594 (86%) direct Impella and 2,056 (14%) escalation patients. PSM generated a highly balanced cohort of 1,825 matched patient pairs. In the matched cohort, the IABP-to-Impella escalation strategy was associated with significantly higher in-hospital mortality compared with direct Impella (52.6% vs. 39.7%, P<.001). There were no significant differences in procedural bleeding (7.7% vs. 5.5%, P=.22), vascular complications (2.19% vs. 1.92%, P=.79), or length of stay (13.25 vs. 12.07 days, P=.31). However, escalation was associated with higher total hospital charges ($635,765 vs. $539,230, P=.03). In the fully adjusted model, the escalation strategy remained a strong, independent predictor of in-hospital mortality (Adjusted Odds Ratio, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.13-2.19; P=.007).Conclusions: In a propensity-matched national cohort of AMI-CS, a stepwise strategy of IABP-to-Impella escalation was associated with significantly higher in-hospital mortality and resource utilization compared with upfront direct Impella support, without mitigating device-related complications.

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective National Inpatient Sample cohort (2020-2022) of 12,594 direct Impella and 2,056 escalation patients; 1,825 matched pairs.
appraisal.main_limitation: Escalation reflects clinical trajectory and shock severity that administrative data capture poorly, so the association may reflect confounding and immortal-time effects.
appraisal.one_line: National Inpatient Sample analysis associated stepwise IABP-to-Impella escalation with higher in-hospital mortality than direct Impella in AMI-CS.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: In-hospital mortality was 52.6% vs 39.7% (escalation vs direct Impella); adjusted odds ratio 1.57, 95% CI 1.13-2.19.
appraisal.why_it_matters: It addresses device timing and escalation in AMI-CS, a systems and strategy question with no randomised evidence.

title: Abstract 14772: Direct Impella versus Stepwise IABP-to-Impella Escalation in Acute Myocardial Infarction with Cardiogenic Shock: A Propensity-Matched Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Hypertension is an independent risk factor for mitral chordae tendineae rupture, but its role as an acute decompensating trigger of pre-existing valve incompetence is underrecognized. An afterload surge can dynamically magnify mitral regurgitation (MR), converting a tolerated lesion into cardiogenic shock. Patient Information: A 71-year-old man with hypertension, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and prior bioprosthetic aortic root replacement presented with acute dyspnea after two days of antihypertensive non-adherence. Blood pressure was 186/92 mmHg with diffuse pulmonary edema. On presentation no significant murmur was auscultated and he improved rapidly. The only prior echocardiogram, years earlier, showed mild MR. After roughly half a day of stability on nasal-cannula oxygen, he abruptly decompensated with a hypertensive surge, recurrent pulmonary edema, intubation, and vasopressor-dependent shock. At the time of decompensation a new harsh holosystolic murmur was appreciated. Investigations: Serial electrocardiograms and troponins showed no ischemia, and prior coronaries were normal. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed torn chordae with a flail P2-P3 posterior leaflet and severe eccentric MR with two jets and systolic pulmonary-vein flow reversal. Right heart catheterization showed a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 26 mmHg with prominent V waves and a cardiac index of 2.65 L/min/m 2 . Follow-up imaging demonstrated concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and a normally functioning aortic bioprosthesis. Interventions and Outcome: An intra-aortic balloon pump was placed. Given prohibitive surgical risk, salvage mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair was performed using a tailored hybrid construct—two PASCAL Ace devices medially and one PASCAL Precision laterally—reducing MR to mild-to-moderate, with a final mean transmitral gradient of 2 mmHg and restored antegrade pulmonary-vein flow. He was extubated on day eleven and discharged to rehabilitation, remaining well at five months with stable devices and mild residual MR. Discussion: The new harsh murmur and abrupt decompensation, both coinciding with the hypertensive surge, suggest the surge acutely worsened the regurgitant lesion; whether it completed a partial tear or decompensated an established flail cannot be resolved given the absent recent baseline, consistent with the established hypertension-chordal-rupture association. The ischemia-negative presentation excludes mechanical mimics, and hypertension supplied both substrate (hypertrophy) and trigger, while the normal prosthesis argues against an aortic contribution. An afterload surge can convert tolerated structural MR into shock within hours, warranting urgent echocardiography and, in prohibitive-risk patients, hybrid PASCAL repair.
title: Abstract 14777: Hypertensive Surge Precipitating Cardiogenic Shock from Mitral Chordae Rupture: Salvage Repair with a Hybrid PASCAL Construct

abstract: Background Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. It is frequently associated with myocardial injury and underlying structural heart disease, which may contribute to adverse cardiovascular outcomes that are now captured under the concept of stroke-heart syndrome. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is an established marker of myocardial fibrosis and structural remodeling; however, its prevalence and patterns in AIS have not been systematically quantified. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the pooled prevalence of LGE on CMR in patients with AIS. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception to May 20, 2026, for observational studies reporting LGE prevalence on CMR in adults with AIS. The primary outcome was the pooled prevalence of any LGE pattern. Secondary outcomes included prevalence stratified by LGE pattern (ischemic vs. non-ischemic). Two independent reviewers screened records and extracted data; methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Proportions were pooled using a random-effects model with the Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation. Heterogeneity was quantified using the I 2 statistic. This systematic review is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261401945). Results Five studies, including 901 patients, were analyzed. The pooled prevalence of any LGE on CMR was 28% (95% CI: 18-38%; I 2 = 84.6%, P < 0.0001), reflecting considerable between-study heterogeneity. Stratified by pattern, ischemic LGE was present in 17% of patients (95% CI: 14-20%; I 2 = 0.0%, P = 0.45; 5 studies, n = 901), with a narrow and homogeneous prediction interval of 13-21%. Non-ischemic LGE was identified in 7% of patients (95% CI: 2-13%; prediction interval: 0-27%; I 2 = 53.1%, P = 0.09; 4 studies, n = 359), indicating moderate heterogeneity. Conclusions LGE on CMR is detected in more than one-quarter of patients with AIS, with ischemic patterns predominating and showing high consistency across studies. Non-ischemic LGE, a marker of underlying structural myocardial disease, is present in approximately 1 in 14 patients. Although less prevalent, it identifies patients with underlying structural myocardial disease who may be at increased risk for arrhythmic and cardioembolic complications. These findings support the systematic evaluation of CMR as an adjunctive tool to refine cardiac risk stratification and guide post-stroke diagnostic and management strategies.
title: Abstract 14782: Prevalence and Pattern of Late Gadolinium Enhancement on Cardiac MRI After Acute Ischemic Stroke A Systematic Review and Meta Analysis

abstract: Background: Liver cirrhosis is present in a growing proportion of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement, driven by the convergence of metabolic liver disease, aging, and expanding procedure indications. Despite this, cirrhosis remains a near-universal exclusion from landmark trials including PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low-Risk, leaving real-world one-year outcome data largely absent. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that transcatheter aortic valve replacement in patients with pre-existing cirrhosis would be associated with higher one-year mortality and major bleeding compared with propensity-matched non-cirrhotic patients, reflecting the hemostatic and hepatic dysfunction inherent to advanced liver disease. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX Research Network spanning 111 healthcare organizations. Adults aged 18 or older who underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement with a prior cirrhosis diagnosis were compared with non-cirrhotic controls. Cirrhosis was defined by ICD-10 codes encompassing alcoholic, biliary, and unspecified cirrhosis. One-to-one propensity score matching on age, sex, race, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, portal hypertension, and hepatorenal syndrome yielded 2,144 patients per group. Outcomes were assessed from day one through day 365 and included all-cause mortality, major bleeding, acute kidney injury, and ischemic stroke. Results: After propensity matching, cirrhotic patients had significantly higher one-year mortality (14.2% vs. 12.0%; risk ratio 1.187; 95% CI, 1.017-1.385; hazard ratio 1.206; 95% CI, 1.022-1.424; p=0.026) and major bleeding (13.2% vs. 7.9%; risk ratio 1.669; 95% CI, 1.392-2.000; hazard ratio 1.721; 95% CI, 1.422-2.082; p<0.001). Acute kidney injury trended higher but did not reach significance (20.8% vs. 18.7%; risk ratio 1.115; 95% CI, 0.988-1.258; p=0.078). Ischemic stroke was numerically lower in the cirrhotic group (3.0% vs. 4.0%; risk ratio 0.765; 95% CI, 0.557-1.050; p=0.096). Conclusion: In this large propensity-matched real-world cohort of 4,288 patients, cirrhosis was independently associated with significantly higher one-year mortality and major bleeding following transcatheter aortic valve replacement, while stroke rates were equivalent. These findings provide the first large-scale one-year comparative outcome data for this systematically excluded population and underscore the need for individualized hepatic risk assessment and multidisciplinary heart-liver team evaluation before transcatheter aortic valve replacement in cirrhotic patients.
title: Abstract 14794: Clinical Outcomes After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients with Pre-Existing Cirrhosis: A Propensity-Matched Retrospective Analysis

abstract: Background: Elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) is commonly detected in patients with acute stroke and may reflect myocardial injury, underlying cardiovascular disease, or stroke-heart syndrome. Although hs-cTn has emerged as a potential prognostic biomarker, its association with adverse outcomes across ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke populations remains incompletely defined. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the prognostic significance of elevated hs-cTn in patients with acute strokes. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Embase (Ovid) was conducted from database inception through May 20, 2026. Observational studies evaluating hs-cTn measured during the acute phase of stroke and reporting clinical outcomes according to troponin status were included. The primary outcome was a major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). Secondary outcomes included coronary events, stroke recurrence, and 3-month all- cause mortality. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to estimate pooled risk ratios (RRs) and hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The study was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261408169). Results: Twenty studies involving 14,612 patients with acute stroke were included. Seventeen studies evaluated hs-cTnT, whereas three evaluated hs-cTnI. Elevated hs-cTn was associated with a significantly increased risk of MACE (RR 2.58, 95% CI 1.73-3.83; I 2 =79%), recurrent stroke (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.08-1.96; I 2 =0%), coronary events (RR 2.15, 95% CI 1.14-4.06; I 2 =0%), and 3-month mortality (HR 3.88, 95% CI 2.84-5.31; I 2 =0%). Patients with elevated hs-cTn had nearly fourfold higher mortality at 3 months compared with those with normal hs-cTn levels. Conclusions: Elevated hs-cTn is associated with substantially increased risks of MACE, recurrent stroke, and 3-month mortality following acute stroke. These findings support the use of hs-cTn as a valuable prognostic biomarker for risk stratification and may help identify patients who warrant closer cardiovascular monitoring and intensified secondary prevention strategies.
title: Abstract 14798: Clinical Outcomes Associated with Elevated High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin in Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm associated with increased thrombotic risk, with thrombotic events being the presenting manifestation in approximately 20% of patients. Acute coronary syndrome may be the initial presentation of disease. We report a case of previously undiagnosed PV presenting as ST Elevation MI (STEMI) with angiographic findings of multiple concurrent coronary pathophysiologic mechanisms. Patient Information: A 76-year-old man with hypertension and dyslipidemia presented with severe substernal chest pain radiating to both shoulders, associated with dyspnea, palpitations, and nausea. Clinical Findings & TimelineElectrocardiography demonstrated anterior STEMI. High-sensitivity troponin increased from 646.8 ng/L to 215,777 ng/L. Laboratory evaluation revealed hemoglobin 19.5 g/dL, hematocrit 61.2%, leukocyte count 17х10 9 /L, and platelet count 827х10 9 /L.Diagnostic Assessment and reasoning Coronary angiography showed complete proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery occlusion with severe distal LAD and diagonal disease. Percutaneous coronary intervention restored Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) 3 flow; however, there was persistent distal LAD pruning and poor distal vessel opacification. A dominant right coronary artery showed a chronic healed dissection. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30-35% with anterior, septal, and apical wall-motion abnormalities. JAK2 V617F mutation confirmed PV. Retrospective chart review identified persistent erythrocytosis and thrombocytosis for two years before presentation. Therapeutic Intervention: The patient underwent emergent PCI, therapeutic phlebotomy, hydroxyurea initiation, dual antiplatelet therapy, and guideline-directed medical therapy.Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events The patient remained clinically stable and was discharged with hematology and cardiology follow-up. No major in-hospital complications occurred. Discussion & Synthesis: This case highlights an unusual coronary phenotype in JAK2 V617F-positive polycythemia vera. In addition to acute proximal LAD thrombosis, angiography also showed persistent distal LAD pruning despite successful reperfusion and a chronic healed RCA dissection. While PV-associated thrombosis is common, these findings suggest involvement beyond a single culprit lesion. JAK2-mediated endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and prothrombotic signaling may have contributed to both acute coronary thrombosis and chronic vascular injury. Earlier investigation of longstanding erythrocytosis and thrombocytosis may have led to earlier diagnosis and prevention of the current presentation
title: Abstract 14803: Previously Undiagnosed Polycythemia Vera Presenting with ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction with Angiographic Evidence of Multiple Coronary Pathophysiologic Mechanisms

abstract: Introduction Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) causes acute coronary syndrome in younger women. Type 2 (diffuse) SCAD can mimic spasm and be missed on angiography. We present rapidly progressive multivessel type 2 SCAD defined by serial coronary CT angiography (CCTA) in a patient with Swyer syndrome, managed conservatively. Patient Information A 42-year-old phenotypic female with Swyer syndrome (46,XY gonadal dysgenesis) on intermittent oral estradiol, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prediabetes, and recent bariatric surgery presented with chest pain. Clinical Findings & Timeline Electrocardiogram showed an anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Initial angiography showed SCAD of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and diagonal with preserved TIMI 3 flow; LVEF was 45% with regional hypokinesis. With recurrent angina, repeat angiography showed a new obtuse marginal (OM1) stenosis with under 50% lumen gain after intracoronary vasodilators (SCAD vs superimposed spasm), with unchanged LAD and diagonal. An initial CCTA was unrevealing; repeat CCTA days later showed extensive intramural hematoma (type 2 SCAD) of the left main, LAD, diagonal, and circumflex with severe multivessel stenosis, no atherosclerosis. A small pulmonary embolism prompted anticoagulation. She was transferred for refractory pain. Diagnostic Assessment Although surgical revascularization was initially considered, all vessels were patent (TIMI 3 flow) with distal LAD, focal circumflex, and limited left main involvement, so conservative care was pursued. Fibromuscular dysplasia screening was negative. Therapeutic Interventions Estradiol was held given the acuity, with management deferred to outpatient care. Refractory angina required combination isosorbide mononitrate, intravenous nitroglycerin, and sodium nitroprusside with diltiazem and fentanyl; beta-blockers were ineffective. Dual antiplatelet therapy and heparin (for the embolism) were given. Follow-up & Outcomes LVEF recovered from 45% to 64% without wall-motion abnormality. She remained free of chest pain in cardiac rehabilitation. Discussion This case highlights three points. First, type 2 SCAD can mimic spasm and be angiographically occult; serial CCTA confirmed the diagnosis and revealed rapid multivessel progression. Second, multivessel type 2 SCAD with preserved flow and non-critical anatomy can be managed conservatively, with recovery of ventricular function. Third, angina responsive to nitrates and calcium channel blockers but not beta-blockers, with partial response to intracoronary vasodilators, suggests vasospasm. Swyer syndrome with chronic estrogen exposure is notable; although causality is unproven, hormonal influences are implicated in SCAD.
title: Abstract 14809: Hidden in Plain Sight: Serial CT Angiography Unmasks Rapidly Progressive Multivessel Type 2 SCAD in Swyer Syndrome

abstract: Introduction: Following left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), antithrombotic regimens to prevent device-related thrombosis vary. With limited comparative data, we sought to compare three common strategies—warfarin plus aspirin, direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) plus aspirin, and dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT; P2Y12 inhibitor plus aspirin)—using a large multicenter US electronic health record database to characterize post-procedural risk for major bleeding and secondary cardiovascular outcomes. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network. We compared three cohorts of patients who underwent LAAO with a history of atrial fibrillation: (1) warfarin plus aspirin, (2) DOAC plus aspirin, and (3) DAPT. Other drug regimens and conditions increasing bleeding risk (e.g., cancer, myocardial infarction) were excluded. We propensity score-matched to control for confounders according to CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores, including age, sex, cardiovascular comorbidities, liver disease, and clotting-related lab values. Primary outcomes included major bleeding and device thrombosis; secondary outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and mortality. Risk ratios (RR), confidence intervals (CI), and p-values were compared. Results: After matching, 2,996 patients were included in the DAPT vs DOAC comparison, 657 in DAPT vs warfarin comparison, and 683 in DOAC vs warfarin comparison. In the DAPT vs DOAC analysis, DOAC was associated with a significantly lower risk of major bleeding compared with DAPT (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56-0.96; p=0.021) and MACE (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60-0.95; p=0.017), with no significant differences in thrombosis, mortality, or other outcomes. In the DAPT vs warfarin comparison, there was no significant difference in major bleeding (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.58-1.52; p=0.807), but warfarin was associated with significantly greater mortality compared with DAPT (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.11-3.13; p=0.017). In the DOAC vs warfarin comparison, warfarin was associated with greater bleeding risk (RR 2.06, 95% CI 1.15-3.70; p=0.013) but no significant differences were observed in MACE or mortality. Discussion: In this propensity score-matched analysis, post-LAAO antithrombotic strategy was associated with differing safety profiles. Compared with DOAC, DAPT was associated with higher risks of major bleeding and MACE, without significant differences in device thrombosis, mortality, or cardiovascular outcomes. Warfarin was associated with increased mortality compared with DAPT, and with greater major bleeding risk compared with DOAC. While causality cannot be inferred, these findings suggest a potentially less favorable safety profile associated with warfarin-based regimens in this population. Together, these findings support consideration of DOAC-based strategies in contemporary post-LAAO management.
title: Abstract 14827: Comparative Safety of Post-Procedural Antithrombotic Regimens After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Real-World Cohort Study

abstract: Introduction: Atrial fibrillation is common in cardiogenic shock (CS), and electrical cardioversion (ECV) is often needed for rhythm control. Body mass index (BMI) influences cardioversion success in ambulatory populations, but its effect on procedural success and outcomes in CS is poorly defined. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of 68 adults with CS who underwent ECV for atrial fibrillation in an ICU in 2023. Procedural success was modeled with Bayesian logistic regression, reporting adjusted median odds ratios (OR) per 1-unit BMI increase with 95% credible intervals (CrI), adjusting for age, sex, cardiomyopathy type, and SCAI shock stage. Thirty-day mortality was compared for BMI ≥35 versus <35. Invasive hemodynamics were assessed within 6 hours before and after ECV. Results: Overall ECV success was 79.4%. Successful ECV was associated with lower mean BMI than unsuccessful ECV (28.4±6.5 vs 34.0±13.7 kg/m 2 ; p=0.029). In adjusted models, higher BMI was associated with lower odds of success (median OR 0.927 per +1 BMI; 95% CrI 0.852-0.999; 97.7% posterior probability of a negative association). By BMI group, post-ECV hemodynamics were similar for BMI ≥35 versus <35: cardiac index 2.71±0.71 vs 2.65±1.04 L/min/m 2 (p=0.869), right atrial pressure 16.7±7.3 vs 13.9±6.0 mmHg (p=0.206), and vasoactive-inotropic score 8.5±8.2 vs 12.1±19.2 (p=0.483). BMI ≥35 showed no clear survival disadvantage (adjusted median OR for 30-day death 0.676; 95% CrI 0.195-2.16; Pr[OR>1]=25.7%). No post-procedural strokes or bradycardia occurred in either group. Conclusions: In cardiogenic shock, higher BMI is associated with lower odds of successful electrical cardioversion. Once sinus rhythm is restored, post-procedural hemodynamics and 30-day survival are similar across BMI groups, though mortality estimates are imprecise. These findings suggest that obesity may reduce procedural success without clearly affecting short-term outcomes after cardioversion.
title: Abstract 14828: Body Mass Index and Outcomes of Electrical Cardioversion of Atrial Fibrillation in Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Background Ventricular fibrillation (VF) remains a leading cause of sudden cardiac death with incompletely characterized electrophysiologic substrate. Traditional large-animal VF models are limited by hemodynamic collapse and myocardial ischemia. This study establishes a reproducible swine model using dual mechanical circulatory devices to enable high-density electroanatomic mapping under non-ischemic conditions. Methods Five Yorkshire swine (55-65 kg) underwent sustained VF supported by veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO; 2.5-3.0 L/min) and percutaneous left ventricular unloading (Impella CP, P-2 to P-4). High-density electroanatomic mapping using CARTO 7 was performed at baseline sinus rhythm and after external defibrillation.
