abstract: Background. Decreased physical function is associated with worse outcomes in heart failure (HF). The 6-Clicks score is a standardized measure of mobility systematically assessed by physical therapists and nurses at multiple health systems. We evaluated the association between pre-discharge 6-Clicks score and outcomes in patients with HF across the range of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). Methods. The 6-Clicks score is a six-item assessment derived from the administered by physical therapists in hospitalized patients derived from the Activity Measure for Post-Acute Care (AM-PAC) that evaluates independence in mobility in hospitalized patients. The score has a range from 6 (worst function) to 24 (best function). Among adults with HF who were discharged across 12 hospitals from an integrated health system in Ohio and Florida, were free of cardiac amyloidosis, mechanical circulatory support, heart transplant, and who had echocardiogram during their index hospitalization, we evaluated the association between 6-Clicks score in quintiles using the highest (“very high”) as reference, and a composite outcome of all-cause readmission or all-cause death. Patients were then stratified by reduced EF (rEF; <40%) and LVEF ≥40%. All Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for sex, race, age group, eGFR, NT-proBNP, atrial fibrillation/flutter, and prior HF admission; HFrEF models additionally adjusted for a guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) score. Models for LVEF >40 additionally adjusted for sodium-glucose transporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) prescription. Results. Among 20,733 patients (predominant age group in the 65-89 range; 76% LVEF ≥40%). The 1-year composite occurred in a graded fashion across discharge 6-Clicks quintiles (Figure 1). In adjusted cox models, the lowest mobility quintile (“very low”) carried a markedly higher hazard of the composite versus the highest quintile (HR 1.65; 95% CI 1.55-1.75), of all-cause hospitalization (HR 1.59; 1.49-1.69), and of death (HR 3.21; 2.87-3.58; Figure 2). Per each point increase in 6-Clicks score, there was a lower risk of the composite outcome across phenotypes (HFrEF: HR 0.97; 95% CI 0.96, 0.98 and LVEF ≥40%: HR 0.97; 95% CI 0.96,0.97; Figure 3).Conclusions. In what is, to our knowledge, the largest analysis of standardized inpatient mobility assessment and HF outcomes, the discharge PT 6-Clicks score was a strong, graded, independent predictor of 1-year all-cause hospitalization and mortality that is consistent across LVEF strata.
title: Abstract 16167: Inpatient Physical Function and 1-Year Outcomes Across Heart Failure Phenotypes

abstract: Background: Renal transplant recipients remain at elevated risk for cardiovascular disease and acute coronary syndromes despite restoration of kidney function. Clinicians may be reluctant to pursue invasive coronary evaluation in these patients because of concerns regarding contrast-associated renal injury. We evaluated the utilization, safety, and outcomes of coronary angiography among renal transplant recipients hospitalized with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample from January 2016 through December 2023. Adult hospitalizations with NSTEMI were identified using ICD-10-CM codes. Renal transplant recipients were identified and stratified according to receipt of coronary angiography. Survey-weighted multivariable regression models adjusted for demographics, socioeconomic characteristics and comorbidities including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and obesity. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and acute kidney injury (AKI). Secondary outcomes included cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, length of stay, and hospitalization costs. Results: A weighted 10,580 renal transplant recipients were hospitalized with NSTEMI during the study period. Coronary angiography was performed in 59.5% of admissions, while PCI was performed in 11.1%. Overall in-hospital mortality was 4.5%. Among renal transplant recipients, coronary angiography was not associated with an increased risk of AKI (aOR 1.04, p=0.753). Coronary angiography was associated with longer hospitalization (+1.05 days, p<0.001) and greater hospitalization charges (+$49,592, p<0.001). In adjusted analyses restricted to patients undergoing coronary angiography, renal transplant recipients had higher in-hospital mortality compared with non-transplant NSTEMI patients (aOR 1.60, 95% CI 1.13-2.26; p=0.008). However, PCI utilization was similar between renal transplant and non-transplant patients undergoing coronary angiography (aOR 1.14, 95% CI 0.97-1.34; p=0.113). No significant difference in cardiac arrest was observed. Conclusion: Coronary angiography was utilized in the majority of renal transplant recipients hospitalized with NSTEMI and was not associated with an increased risk of acute kidney injury despite concerns regarding contrast exposure. These findings suggest that fear of renal complications alone should not preclude invasive coronary evaluation in appropriately selected renal transplant recipients presenting with NSTEMI. Further studies are needed to define the impact of invasive management on long-term cardiovascular outcomes in this high-risk population.
title: Abstract 16168: Coronary Angiography in Renal Transplant Recipients Presenting with NSTEMI: Is Concern for Kidney Injury Justified?

abstract: Background: Prehospital delay remains a major contributor to total ischemic time in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The Area Deprivation Index (ADI), a validated measure of neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation, may influence time to first medical contact through differences in symptom recognition, care-seeking behavior, and emergency medical services (EMS) activation. However, the association between ADI and prehospital delay in contemporary STEMI patients is not well characterized. Objective: To examine the association between neighborhood socioeconomic deprivation and prehospital delay among contemporary STEMI patients. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of first STEMI presentations from 2018, 2019, 2023, and 2024 across the Mayo Clinic network. Years 2020-2022 were excluded due to potential pandemic-related changes in care-seeking behavior. Patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, in-hospital or incidental STEMI, missing symptom-to-first medical contact (FMC) time, or symptom onset >24 hours were excluded. National ADI was categorized into quintiles from Q1, least deprived, to Q5, most deprived. Outcomes included symptom-to-FMC, symptom-to-emergency room (ER), and symptom-to-EMS arrival at scene times. Group comparisons were performed using nonparametric tests, and adjusted analyses used multivariable median quantile regression adjusted for age, sex, healthcare worker status, distance from hospital, diabetes, and STEMI location. Results: A total of 1,579 patients were included (Q1 n=129, Q2 n=253, Q3 n=546, Q4 n=467, Q5 n=184). Overall symptom-to-FMC time differed borderline across ADI quintiles (p=0.057), while symptom-to-ER time did not differ significantly (p=0.225). Symptom-to-EMS time differed significantly across ADI quintiles (p=0.004). Compared with Q1, median symptom-to-EMS time was longer in Q2 (68 [41-138] vs 34 [20-69] minutes) and Q3 (60 [34-125] vs 34 [20-69] minutes). After multivariable adjustment, Q2 was associated with longer overall symptom-to-FMC time compared with Q1 (β +23.7 minutes, 95% CI 3.6 to 43.8; p=0.021), while Q3 to Q5 were not significant. For symptom-to-EMS time, Q2 (β +36.4 minutes, 95% CI 10.1 to 62.7; p=0.007) and Q3 (β +29.4 minutes, 95% CI 5.3 to 53.4; p=0.017) remained associated with longer delays compared with Q1. No ADI quintile was independently associated with symptom-to-ER time. Conclusion: In this contemporary STEMI cohort, ADI was associated with variation in prehospital delay, driven primarily by longer symptom-to-EMS arrival times in selected ADI quintiles. No adjusted association was observed for symptom-to-ER time. These findings suggest that neighborhood-level socioeconomic factors may contribute to delays in EMS-mediated STEMI care and warrant further investigation into barriers to EMS activation and timely first medical contact.
title: Abstract 16184: Association of Neighborhood Socioeconomic Deprivation with EMS-Related Prehospital Delay in STEMI

abstract: Background: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) commonly receive direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) to reduce the risk of stroke or systemic embolism. Among individuals with concomitant AF and peripheral arterial disease (PAD), this risk is further amplified due to shared risk factors. Following lower extremity revascularization, aspirin is often added to DOAC therapy; however, the benefit of this combination remains uncertain, particularly given the potential for increased bleeding risk . Methods: Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, we identified adults (≥18 years) with PAD and AF who underwent lower extremity revascularization and were subsequently treated with a DOAC with or without aspirin. Patients with prior bleeding events were excluded. Outcomes were assessed after a 30-day blanking period following revascularization. The primary outcome was 5-year major adverse limb events (MALE), defined as repeat revascularization, amputation, or chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI). Results: We identified 870 patients receiving DOAC monotherapy and 2,214 receiving DOAC plus aspirin. After propensity score matching, 1,490 patients were included (745 per group). The mean age was 75.8 years, 59.4% were male, and 83.4% were White. With a median follow-up of 978 days, DOAC monotherapy was associated with a significantly lower risk of MALE compared with DOAC plus aspirin (19.2% vs. 27.2%; HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56-0.86; Figure 1A). This reduction was primarily driven by lower rates of repeat revascularization (HR 0.27, 95% CI 0.16-0.46) and CLTI (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.58-0.90). DOAC monotherapy was also associated with a lower incidence of any bleeding (26.6% vs. 31.8%; HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68-0.99; Figure 1B), including gastrointestinal bleeding (11.3% vs. 15.4%; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56-0.98; p=0.032). Rates of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. Conclusions: Among patients with AF and PAD undergoing lower extremity revascularization, compared to combination of DOAC and aspirin, DOAC monotherapy was associated with lower rates of MALE and bleeding, without an increase in mortality or ischemic events. These findings suggest that the addition of aspirin to DOAC therapy may provide no benefit while increasing bleeding risk. Prospective randomized trials are needed to validate these observations.
title: Abstract 16204: DOAC Monotherapy versus DOAC Plus Aspirin Following Lower Extremity Revascularization in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation and Peripheral Artery Disease

abstract: Introduction/hypothesis: Ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) drives adverse ventricular remodeling post myocardial infarction, with reperfusion damage substantially contributing to final infarct size. The bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) signals through nuclear receptors (FXR) and membrane receptors (TGR5) to modulate inflammation, apoptosis, and metabolism, and associates with reduced cardiovascular mortality in coronary artery disease. Yet, its role in IRI is undefined. Methods/Results: In STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, pre-intervention plasma CDCA associated with improved LVEF (18.4% relative increase;p=0.012) and reduced infarct size by late gadolinium enhancement (23.7% decrease;p=0.013) at 6 months. To determine causation, glycine-conjugated CDCA (GCDCA), the primary circulating form in humans, was administered to mice undergoing IRI. At 24h post-IRI, GCDCA increased LVEF (vehicle: 39.7±3.0; GCDCA: 53.2±2.7%;p<0.0001) and reduced infarct size (vehicle: 56.4±2.1; GCDCA: 25.8±3.6%;p=0.004). At 4 weeks, LVEF remained improved (vehicle: 55.3±2.8; GCDCA: 61.1±4.6%;p=0.003), with reduced fibrotic area (vehicle: 5.9±4.2; GCDCA: 0.9±0.6%;p=0.01) and cardiomyocyte hypertrophy (vehicle: 6578±852; GCDCA: 5019±527 μm 2 ;p=0.001). Human iPSC-derived cardiac organoids under hypoxia-reoxygenation showed improved viability (vehicle: 0.632±0.06; GCDCA: 0.729±0.02 au;p=0.01) and reduced mitochondrial superoxide (vehicle: 1.2±0.07; GCDCA: 1.02±0.07 au;p=0.002). iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes showed improved contractile amplitude 48h post hypoxia-reoxygenation (vehicle: 0.07±0.06; GCDCA: 0.15±0.1;p=0.006). Bulk proteomics of ischemic left ventricles 24h post-IRI revealed upregulation of mitochondrial ETC Complex I/IV assembly proteins (mean log 2 FC=1.25±0.66;p=0.0005), MICOS cristae organization proteins (mean log 2 FC=1.19±0.53;p=0.007), and MIA40 import factors (Chchd4: log 2 FC=2.09;p=0.0001; Cmc2: log 2 FC=0.59;p=0.02), indicating preserved ETC integrity. Together with reduced organoid mitochondrial ROS, these data suggest GCDCA preserves mitochondrial function. Upregulation of TGF-β target ECM proteins (Col4a1, Fbn1, Sparc; mean log 2 FC=1.29±0.45;p=0.000025), reductions in acute-phase proteins (SAA1, SAA2, CHI3L1, ficolin-1) and upregulation of complement inhibitors (CD59a, factor H), indicate GCDCA reshapes the post-IRI inflammatory microenvironment toward resolution. CDCA is a TGR5 agonist, and cardiomyocyte TGR5 overexpression reduces hypoxia/reoxygenation injury, suggesting CDCA may improve post-IRI cardiac function via TGR5 activation. Conclusion: GCDCA improves post-ischemic cardiac function and attenuates adverse ventricular remodeling, potentially through preservation of mitochondrial integrity and modulation of inflammatory responses.
title: Abstract 16209: The Bile Acid Glycochenodeoxycholic Acid Preserves Cardiac Function and Protects Against Adverse Remodeling Following Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is frequently encountered in cardiogenic shock (CS) and can further compromise cardiac output through loss of atrial contribution and rapid ventricular rates. Electrical cardioversion is often employed to restore sinus rhythm; however, contemporary data describing procedural success, recurrence, and clinical outcomes in CS are limited. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 666 adults admitted with CS at Cleveland Clinic. Patients who underwent cardioversion for AF during CS were included. Outcomes included acute cardioversion success (restoration of sinus rhythm), sinus rhythm at 24 hours and at discharge, AF recurrence during hospitalization, and all-cause mortality through 1 year. Kaplan-Meier methods were used to estimate cumulative mortality; unadjusted logistic regression evaluated factors associated with acute cardioversion success, and univariable Cox proportional hazards models evaluated factors associated with time-to-death. Results: Of 666 patients with CS, 68 (10.2%) underwent cardioversion for AF during CS. Mean age was 63.96 (± 12.24 years) and 26.5% of the cohort were female. Average LVEF was 29.72 (±16.69%). Acute cardioversion success occurred in 79.4%. Sinus rhythm was present in 57.4% at 24 hours and 72.1% at discharge. AF recurrence occurred in 41.5%. Kaplan-Meier cumulative mortality was 25.3% at 30 days, 37.8% at 3 months, 46.0% at 6 months, and 51.6% at 1 year. On unadjusted logistic regression, no baseline demographic, comorbidity, shock-severity, or mechanical support variables were significantly associated with acute cardioversion success. In univariable Cox analyses, higher lactate (HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.10-1.37), higher vasoactive-inotropic score at day 1 (HR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01-1.04), VA-ECMO use (HR 3.78, 95% CI 1.70-8.41), and sepsis (HR 3.19, 95% CI 1.52-6.70) were associated with increased mortality. Conclusions: In CS patients undergoing cardioversion for AF, acute rhythm restoration was frequently achieved, but AF recurrence was common and mortality remained high. Mortality was strongly associated with markers of shock severity and systemic illness, underscoring the importance of interpreting rhythm-control strategies within overall CS severity. Figure 1. Kaplan-Meier curves of all-cause mortality through 3 years following cardioversion for atrial fibrillation in patients with cardiogenic shock.
title: Abstract 16232: Electrical Cardioversion for Atrial Fibrillation During Cardiogenic Shock: Success, Recurrence, and Mortality

abstract: Background: The use of concomitant atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation with left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is increasing to provide comprehensive treatment for AF. 4D intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has emerged as an alternative to transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) for intraprocedural imaging; however, comparative data remain limited. Purpose: We sought to compare LAAO outcomes between ICE- and TEE-guided procedures using postoperative imaging. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of Emory Healthcare patients undergoing concomitant pulsed field AF ablation and device implantation between November 2024 and December 2025. Patients were grouped by intraprocedural imaging modality (ICE vs TEE). Baseline patient demographics and procedural characteristics were compared. Peridevice leak was defined as residual flow on postoperative imaging, and we categorized leaks as <3 mm, 3-5 mm, ≥5 mm. Significant shoulder was defined as peridevice flow involving ≥1/3 of the device circumference. Results: Of 145 patients who underwent concomitant AF ablation and LAAO, 45 underwent TEE-guided procedures and 100 underwent ICE-guided procedures. Baseline comorbidities were similar between groups. Periprocedural complications were infrequent, with 1 case each of acute heart failure, groin bleeding, chest pain, pericardial effusion, and stroke. Postoperative imaging at 45-90 days was performed in all patients. Peridevice leak occurred in 20 patients, with 13 leaks <3 mm, 5 leaks 3-5 mm, and 2 leaks ≥ 5 mm. Seven patients had 1/3 device shoulder involvement, and no device-related thrombi were identified. No significant differences existed in postoperative imaging between ICE and TEE groups (Figure 2, Table 1). Conclusions: ICE demonstrated comparable 45-90-day postoperative outcomes to TEE in concomitant AF ablation and LAAO. These findings support the efficacy of an ICE-only procedure in experienced operators; however, larger prospective studies are needed.
title: Abstract 16256: Outcomes of Concomitant Catheter Ablation and Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Procedures Using Transesophageal versus Intracardiac Echocardiography

abstract: Introduction: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) may recover with timely therapy; however, conception before left ventricular (LV) recovery can convert a reversible process into advanced heart failure. This case frames LV recovery as a preconception safety endpoint and reproductive planning as core HF care. Patient Information: A postpartum woman in her 20s (G2P2) presented 4.5 months after delivery and was found to be 6 weeks pregnant. Clinical Findings: She reported 2 weeks of dyspnea, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Examination revealed basilar rales and bilateral edema. Diagnostic Assessment: Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema. ECG showed sinus rhythm with left bundle branch block. Echocardiography revealed LVEF 30%, global hypokinesis, mild LV dilation, severe functional mitral regurgitation, and RVSP 41 mm Hg. NT-proBNP was 5,990 pg/mL. PPCM was diagnosed as new postpartum systolic dysfunction without another cause, complicated by conception before recovery. Interventions: After high-risk counseling, pregnancy termination was performed, followed by etonogestrel implant placement. Guideline-directed HF therapy was initiated. She later underwent CRT-D placement and mitral valve repair. Outcomes: Despite therapy, LVEF declined to 20%. Her course was complicated by persistent atrial fibrillation with left atrial appendage thrombi despite anticoagulation, amiodarone-associated pulmonary fibrosis, and cardiogenic shock from biventricular failure. Orthotopic heart transplantation was performed 33 months after presentation. Discussion: PPCM care must extend beyond decongestion. Diagnosis should trigger a reproductive safety plan including pregnancy testing, contraception counseling, shared decision-making, and early postpartum follow-up with primary care and cardiology to screen for new HF symptoms and prompt timely PPCM evaluation. The postpartum-to-cardiology transition is vulnerable: dyspnea may be normalized, diagnosis delayed, and subsequent pregnancy may occur before recovery is recognized. Postpartum dyspnea with orthopnea or elevated natriuretic peptides should prompt echocardiography. Counseling should distinguish symptom improvement from myocardial recovery; persistent LV dysfunction increases risk with subsequent pregnancy. Failure of EF recovery should prompt early advanced HF referral, as PPCM may progress to arrhythmia, thrombosis, biventricular failure, and transplantation. Functional mitral regurgitation reflects adverse remodeling and may not alter disease trajectory. Conclusion: Diagnosis of PPCM should trigger pregnancy testing, contraception counseling, shared decision-making, and a documented LV recovery target before future conception. Contraception and coordinated cardio-obstetric care are essential HF interventions to prevent irreversible progression.
title: Abstract 16309: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy Requiring Heart Transplantation After Subsequent Pregnancy Before LV Recovery

abstract: Background: Concomitant left atrial appendage (LAA) closure and atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation is increasingly performed. Objective: Evaluate the acute effects of AF ablation upon LAA geometry and long-term Watchman (WM) -LAA tissue interaction. Methods: Single-center cohort of 35 pts undergoing Concomitant AF ablation and then immediate WM device implantation. LAA os width and depth, LAA oval size, and LA ridge (Coumadin ridge) were measured by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) in 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135° views prior to and immediately after ablation. WM device compression (DComp) was measured at implantation and at 6-week post-implant (TEE or CT). CT evaluation utilized specialized software. DComp was also measured at implant and at 6-week imaging in a Control group (n=32) of pts who underwent WM LAAO but without AF ablation. Results: Concomitant pt features: 19 female; mean age 72; LVEF: 52%; CHADS-VASc 4±1; HAS-BLED 2±1; WM FLX Pro size 27.6 ± 4.7mm; LA pressure at implant 18 ± 5mmHg. There were no significant differences in LAA os width or depth (mm) pre- vs post-ablation (width: 18.62 ± 3.81 vs 18.43 ± 3.80, p=0.6; depth: 21.75 ± 3.7 vs 21.86 ± 3.98, p=0.3); or in LAA oval size. The LA ridge diameter increased significantly post- vs pre-ablation (7.75 ± 2.04 vs 6.44 ± 1.65mm, p<0.01). In the Concomitant group, percent DComp decreased from 21±5% at implant to 12±10% at 6-week imaging (mean 32% decrease p<0.001). In the Control group, DComp decreased from 22±6% to 20±7% (mean 10% decrease p<0.01). Reduction in DComp was significantly greater in Concomitant vs Control (p<0.001). Peridevice leak occurred in 2 Concomitant pts. Conclusion: AF ablation results in acute inflammatory thickening (~20%) along the LA ridge and minimally alters LAA os dimensions (~1%). There is significant reduction in DComp at 6- week imaging in Concomitant and Control groups; however, the degree of reduction in DComp is significantly greater in Concomitant. This suggests that ablation-related inflammation results in acute LAA remodeling/inflammation altering WM-LAA interaction. This change resolves during follow-up, reflected by a reduced DComp. These data may alter selection of WM device sizing with Concomitant AF ablation.
title: Abstract 16320: Impact of Atrial Fibrillation Ablation Upon Left Atrial Appendage Device Occlusion

abstract: Background: Left ventricular thrombus (LVT) is a serious complication of ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM). The morphological characteristics of LVT and size may impact the risk of embolization and the likelihood of resolution; however, data characterizing these relationships are limited. Methods: Patients with ICM and echocardiography confirmed LVT who were treated with anticoagulants (AC) between 2018 and 2023 were identified retrospectively. LVT morphologic features by echo were characterized (mobile, pedunculated, lobulated, calcified, laminated), size, and number of thrombi were recorded at the index echocardiogram. Embolic outcomes assessed were overall, at presentation (off AC), and during follow-up (on AC), as well as thrombus resolution. Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Optimal size thresholds were derived from ROC-AUC analysis. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for size, mobility, and thrombus multiplicity. Results: A total of 196 patients with ICM and acute/newly identified LVT were included (mean age 68.9 ± 12.4 years; 85.2% male). Median follow up time 33.2 months (IQR 19.2 - 47.8). Overall embolism occurred in 31 patients (15.8%), presenting embolism in 17 (8.7%), and follow-up embolism in 15 (7.7%). Pedunculated thrombus had the highest overall embolism rate (20.8%) followed by lobulated (20.0%) and mobile (19.3%), while laminated thrombus had the lowest (11.7); no morphological characteristic reached statistical significance versus mobile as reference (all p >0.05). A size threshold of ≥16 mm was optimal for overall and presenting embolism (AUC 0.610 and 0.66, respectively), and ≥24 mm for follow-up embolism (AUC 0.562). Thrombus ≥16 mm was associated with higher overall embolism (OR 3.2 [1.45-7.00]) and presenting embolism (OR 5.27 [1.77-15.68]); ≥24 mm with higher follow-up embolism (OR 4.0 [1.3-13.0]). On multivariable regression, size was the only independent predictor of embolism (overall: OR 3.3, p=0.005; presenting: OR 5.2, p=0.005; follow-up: OR 5.1, p=0.013) Table 1 . Resolution occurred in 162 patients (82.7%), with laminated thrombus having the lowest resolution rate. Conclusions: In patients with ICM-associated LVT treated with AC, thrombus size was the dominant imaging predictor of embolization. Other morphological features, including lamination, lobulation pattern, mobility, and echogenic characteristics, did not independently refine embolic risk.
title: Abstract 16337: Left Ventricular Thrombus Morphology and Embolic Risk in Patients with Ischemic Cardiomyopathies

abstract: Background: Aortic valve disease spans a continuum from sclerosis to severe aortic stenosis. Prior studies show stepwise increases in mortality, but population-level data remain limited. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) reports contain rich clinical detail but exist as unstructured text; large language models (LLM) now enable population-scale extraction and classification of disease severity. Understanding outcome gaps across this spectrum is critical to improving risk stratification and reducing disparities. Research Question: How do cardiovascular hospitalization and mortality vary across the aortic valve disease continuum, and which clinical and TTE factors independently predict events within each severity? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults who underwent TTE at a large integrated healthcare system in Southern California (2011–2021). Aortic valve disease was classified into sclerosis, mild, moderate, and severe aortic stenosis (AS) using a validated LLM applied to TTE reports; prior aortic valve replacement was excluded. Outcomes were identified using ICD-9/ICD-10 and procedural codes, with follow-up through December 2024. Hospitalization and valve replacement rates were calculated per 1,000 person-years; multivariable Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted associations with 99% confidence intervals. Results: Among 243,928 patients (sclerosis N=180,734; mild AS N=35,896; moderate AS N=16,616; severe AS N=10,682), mean age increased with disease severity, and 65% were ≥70 years. Rates of acute major CV hospitalization rose from 43.7 per 1,000 person-years in sclerosis to 205.2 in severe AS, while hospitalization for any CV disease increased from 57.8 to 568.8 per 1,000 person-years. Heart failure-specific events demonstrated similar gradients, increasing from 14.9 to 71.1 per 1,000 person-years. After multivariable adjustment, older age, heart failure, renal failure, and atrial fibrillation were strongly associated with increased risk of acute CV hospitalization or death across all severity strata. Heart failure conferred consistent risk (HR 1.54–1.86 across classes), while reduced LVEF was also independently associated with adverse outcomes. Male sex was associated with modestly higher CV risk (HR approximately 1.11–1.18 across severity strata). Hispanic and Asian patients had lower adjusted risks of CV events compared with non-Hispanic White patients, whereas Black patients had similar risk profiles. Conclusions: Cardiovascular morbidity increases markedly across the aortic valve disease continuum, with gradients beginning at early disease stages. Traditional clinical risk factors and echocardiographic parameters independently stratify risk across all severity classes. These findings support earlier risk identification and targeted strategies across the disease spectrum.
title: Abstract 16344: Population-Level Outcomes Across the Aortic Valve Disease Continuum: A Large Language Model-Enabled Retrospective Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Impella devices are increasingly used for temporary mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock, but national estimates of access-related vascular and bleeding complications remain limited. Research Question: What is the prevalence and outcome association of access-related complications during Impella-supported hospitalization? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2018-2022, identifying adult hospitalizations (≥18 years) involving Impella support. Patients were stratified based on the presence or absence of access-related vascular or bleeding complications, including acute limb ischemia, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula, retroperitoneal hematoma, post-procedural bleeding, device-related complications, and hemolysis. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, length of stay, total hospital charges. Secondary outcomes included sepsis, stroke, blood transfusion, and lower extremity amputation. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic and linear regression models were used to adjust for demographics, comorbidities, hospital characteristics, and temporal trends. Results: Among 106,570 Impella-supported hospitalizations, 19.4% had access-related complications. The most frequent were device-related complications (13.7%), acute limb ischemia or arterial thrombosis (2.7%), post-procedural bleeding (2.3%), and retroperitoneal hematoma (1.0%). Compared with hospitalizations without complications, those with complications had higher unadjusted mortality (34% vs 28%), longer median LOS (9 vs 6 days), and higher median charges ($445,159 vs $333,826; all p<0.001). After adjustment, access complications were associated with higher mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.32, 95% CI 1.22-1.43), absolute mortality increase of 5.7 percentage points (95% CI 4.0-7.3), stroke (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.32-1.79), sepsis (aOR 1.39, 95% CI 1.26-1.53), and transfusion (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.31-1.58; all p<0.001). LOS and charges were higher with access complications (LOS ratio 1.29; charge ratio 1.26; both p<0.001). Lower extremity amputation was uncommon but more frequent with access complications in unadjusted analysis (0.46%; OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.73-3.92). Conclusions: Access-related vascular and bleeding complications occurred in nearly one in five Impella-supported hospitalizations and were independently associated with higher mortality, stroke, sepsis, transfusion, LOS, and charges. These findings support access planning, early recognition, and targeted mitigation protocols during Impella support.
title: Abstract 16345: Access-Related Vascular and Bleeding Complications of Impella Support and Their Impact on Outcomes: A National Inpatient Sample 2018-2022 Analysis

abstract: Background: Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) demonstrates marked clinical heterogeneity, yet traditional classifications inadequately characterize patterns of cardiopulmonary decompensation, resource utilization, and escalation of care. We aimed to identify machine learning-derived deterioration phenotypes among hospitalized ACS patients using a nationwide real-world database and evaluate their temporal reproducibility and economic burden. Methods: Adult ACS hospitalizations were identified from the Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD) 2021-2022 (n=1,483,120). Unsupervised phenotyping applied K-Means, PAM with Gower distance, and hierarchical clustering across 31 clinical features encompassing demographics, comorbidities, ACS subtype, procedures, procedure-timing variables, and hospital characteristics. Cluster performance was assessed using silhouette analysis, Calinski-Harabasz index, and Davies-Bouldin metrics. Temporal reproducibility was evaluated using adjusted Rand index (ARI) and normalized mutual information (NMI) between independently derived 2021 and 2022 cluster solutions. Results: PAM with Gower distance achieved optimal clustering performance (silhouette 0.219) versus K-Means (0.132) and hierarchical clustering (0.086), identifying three clinically distinct deterioration phenotypes. Phenotype A ("Revascularization-Responsive," 39.5%): median age 67 years, STEMI 20.8%, mortality 6.0%, LOS 3 days, median cost $74,167. Phenotype B ("Respiratory-Predominant," 31.4%): oldest patients (median age 73 years), female-majority (52.7%), predominantly NSTEMI, ARF 30.4%, mortality 10.1%, LOS 5 days, median cost $80,458. Phenotype C ("Severe Multi-System Deterioration," 29.0%): highest cardiogenic shock (10.6%), ARF (59.5%), cardiac arrest (4.7%), mortality (16.8%), LOS 5 days, and median cost $87,228. Hospitalization cost increased 17.5% from Phenotype A to C, reflecting escalating resource utilization across the severity spectrum. Phenotype structure demonstrated strong temporal reproducibility (ARI 0.791, NMI 0.689). Conclusions: Machine learning identified three reproducible ACS deterioration phenotypes spanning low-risk revascularization-responsive presentations to severe multi-system cardiopulmonary failure, with a parallel gradient in mortality, resource utilization, and hospitalization costs. These findings support phenotype-guided approaches for precision risk stratification, individualized critical care escalation, and targeted interventions to reduce the economic burden of high-risk ACS deterioration.
title: Abstract 16359: Three Distinct Cardiopulmonary Deterioration Phenotypes in Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Machine Learning Analysis of 1.48 Million Hospitalizations

abstract: STEMI accounts for ~40% of CVD deaths in India, a country whose age-standardised CVD mortality already exceeds the global average. Rural populations bear a disproportionate burden- mortality higher than urban areas driven by delayed diagnosis, absent cath-lab access, and fragmented referral pathways. India's NP-NCD STEMI Guidelines mandate bolus thrombolysis within 30 minutes of detection at peripheral facilities, yet translating this policy into a uniform, functioning care pathway at scale remains the critical implementation gap. We describe a prospective, government-led, multi-state hub-and-spoke STEMI program across seven Indian states (174+ districts, 2800+ facilities, ~305 million population) with Tricog Health as the technology partner. Each spoke facility (PHC/CHC/TH) was equipped with a CDSCO-certified digital 12-lead ECG machine transmitting via cloud to a 24х7 cardiologist reporting centre, with AI pre-screening and human-verified reports within a median of 10 minutes. STEMI alerts triggered immediate care coordinator outreach; eligible patients received thrombolysis at the spoke within the 30-minute door-to-needle target before transfer to district hubs or tertiary cath-lab centres (if not contraindicated or had necessary thrombolytics available) for pharmacoinvasive or primary PCI. A centralised STEMI registry tracked door-to-needle, door-to-balloon, reperfusion strategy, and in-hospital mortality across all sites. Over 74,000 STEMI cases have been managed across active states. Program survival averaged ~88% against modelled no-intervention mortality of 25-27%. Spoke-level thrombolysis reduced mortality by ~23.8 percentage points versus no reperfusion (8.5% vs 27.6%; p<0.05). Facilitated PCI following spoke thrombolysis and thrombolysis alone conferred better survival rates than optimal medical therapy without reperfusion (91.9% & 74.8%; p<0.001, Kaplan-Meier). Median door-to-thrombolysis time declined by >35% over successive program quarters, achieving sub-30-minute guideline adherence at maturity. Over 23,000 healthcare workers were trained; program adoption exceeded 85% across most sites. Projected national scale-up to 10,000 facilities estimates 420,000-560,000 lives saveable annually. A government-led, technology-enabled hub-and-spoke STEMI program is clinically effective, replicable, and scalable across India's heterogeneous public health infrastructure. Standardised digital ECG acquisition, 24х7 AI-assisted remote reporting, and structured care coordination enable guideline-adherent reperfusion at the primary care periphery without on-site specialist capacity. Progressively declining treatment times confirm that system maturation compounds survival benefit over time. This model offers a transferable framework for equitable emergency cardiac care in low- and middle-income settings.
title: Abstract 16380: Scaling a Government-Mandated Hub-and-Spoke STEMI Care Network in India: Replicable Design, Technology-Enabled Implementation, and Impact at Population Scale

abstract: Introduction In 2022, the American Heart Association updated its cardiovascular health (CVH) framework to Life’s Essential 8 (LE8), adding sleep as a health behavior. The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI), launched in the 1990s, followed over 160,000 postmenopausal women to study prevention of major chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disease. However, researchers have not fully characterized the association between LE8-defined CVH and cardiovascular outcomes in this population. Research Question We sought to determine whether higher LE8-defined CVH was associated with lower risk of incident atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) among postmenopausal women in the WHI. Methods We included postmenopausal women enrolled in the WHI clinical trial and observational study cohorts from 1993-1998 with baseline data and no pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Baseline LE8 scores were derived from diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep, body mass index, blood glucose, cholesterol, and blood pressure, and categorized as low (0-49), moderate (50-79), or high (80-100). The primary outcome was incident ASCVD events (including ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, angina) and cardiovascular death. Cox proportional hazards models stratified by study enrollment period estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusted for age, race, ethnicity, and education. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation. Results Among 18,453 women included in the final cohort, the mean age was 63.6 years; 35% were Black and 16% were Hispanic. Overall, 4,893 (26.5%) had low CVH, 11,507 (62.3%) had moderate CVH, and 1,193 (6.5%) had high CVH scores. Compared with women with low CVH scores, women with high CVH scores had more favorable risk factor profiles (Table 1). Baseline CVH differed by race, with Black women most represented in low CVH (44.9%) and White women disproportionately represented in high CVH (70.7%). Over 18.7 years of follow-up, 4,908 primary outcome events occurred. In the fully adjusted model, there was a stepwise protective effect of increasing CVH on incident ASCVD events and cardiovascular death: moderate CVH was associated with 42% lower risk (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.54-0.61) and high CVH was associated with 65% lower risk (HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.30-0.40), compared with low CVH. Conclusion Among postmenopausal women in the WHI, higher baseline LE8-defined cardiovascular health was strongly associated with lower risk of incident ASCVD events and cardiovascular death. These findings support LE8, including sleep health, as a clinically relevant framework for cardiovascular risk assessment and prevention in postmenopausal women.
title: Abstract 16385: Life’s Essential 8 and Incident Cardiovascular Outcomes in Postmenopausal Women

abstract: Background: Patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remain at substantial risk for recurrent ischemic events despite advances in contemporary secondary prevention. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated cardiovascular benefits in patients with cardiometabolic disease; however, their impact on long-term outcomes following PCI remains incompletely characterized. Objective: To evaluate the association between GLP-1RA therapy and cardiovascular outcomes among patients with prior PCI. Methods: We conducted a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study using Global Collaborative Network. Adults with a history of PCI were stratified by GLP-1RA exposure and matched 1:1 across 73 demographic, comorbidity, medication, procedural, and laboratory variables. Outcomes were assessed over 730 days and included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, repeat revascularization, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, atrial arrhythmias, in-stent restenosis, in-stent thrombosis, and all-cause hospitalization/emergency department (ED) utilization. Results: Following propensity matching, 72,955 patients were included in each cohort. GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significantly lower risks of MACE (23.7% vs 31.1%; RR 0.76, OR 0.69, p<0.001), non-fatal MI (18.3% vs 25.0%; RR 0.73, OR 0.67, p<0.001), stroke (7.8% vs 9.4%; RR 0.82, OR 0.81, p<0.001), repeat revascularization (1.0% vs 1.5%; RR 0.68, OR 0.68, p<0.001), HF hospitalization (30.7% vs 39.5%; RR 0.78, OR 0.68, p<0.001), new-onset atrial fibrillation (15.6% vs 17.0%; RR 0.92, OR 0.90, p<0.001), atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence (17.4% vs 20.8%; RR 0.84, OR 0.81, p<0.001), and all-cause hospitalization/ED visits (58.1% vs 71.2%; RR 0.82, OR 0.56, p<0.001). No significant differences were observed in in-stent restenosis (RR 1.02, p=0.585) or in-stent thrombosis (RR 1.22, p=0.296). Conclusions: In this large propensity-matched real-world cohort, GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significantly lower risks of MACE, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure hospitalization, and repeat coronary revascularization following PCI. These findings suggest that GLP-1RAs may provide important cardiovascular benefits beyond glycemic control and support their potential role as adjunctive secondary prevention therapy in patients undergoing coronary revascularization.
title: Abstract 16393: Cardiometabolic Therapy After PCI: Real-World Outcomes Associated with GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use

abstract: Background: Cardiovascular risk is increased in women with Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), but whether risk differs among PMOS phenotypes remains uncertain. The Rotterdam Criteria stratifies PMOS into phenotypes by the presence of hyperandrogenism (A, B, C), ovulatory dysfunction (A, B, D), and polycystic ovarian morphology (A, C, D). We evaluated composite atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease events (CAE) across PMOS phenotypes. Methods: Using the TriNetX Research Network, women aged 18-45 years between 2010 and 2026 with phenotype A/B (hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction), phenotype C (hyperandrogenism without ovulatory dysfunction), and phenotype D (ovulatory dysfunction without hyperandrogenism) were compared with propensity score matched controls. The primary outcome was CAE, defined as a composite of ischemic heart disease, ischemic stroke, peripheral arterial disease, and atherosclerotic vascular disease. Secondary outcomes included acute coronary syndrome (ACS), heart failure (HF), and ischemic cerebrovascular accident (CVA). Results: A total of 220,335 PMOS patients (phenotype A/B, n=78,698; C, n=44,581; D, n=97,056) were matched to equal-sized control cohorts. After matching, baseline characteristics were well balanced (standardized mean differences <0.1), with a low-risk metabolic profile across cohorts (mean A1c 5.48±0.94%, LDL 105±30.9 mg/dL, HDL 58.1±15.8, Tg 102±70.3, Cr 0.757±1.05, BMI 28.6±7.5 kg/m 2 ). Phenotype A/B patients had higher rates of CAE (1.50% vs. 0.89%, RR 1.69, p<0.001) and ACS (0.19% vs. 0.12%, RR 1.58, p<0.001). Phenotype C demonstrated increased CAE (1.24% vs. 0.87%, RR 1.43, p<0.001) without significant differences in secondary outcomes. Phenotype D exhibited the highest cardiovascular burden, with increased CAE (1.73% vs. 1.05%, RR 1.65, p<0.001), ACS (0.26% vs. 0.15%, RR 1.73, p<0.001), HF (0.68% vs. 0.59%, RR 1.15, p=0.015), and ischemic CVA (0.09% vs. 0.05%, RR 1.80, p=0.005). Conclusions: Despite a low baseline cardiovascular risk profile, all PMOS phenotypes were associated with increased CAE. Phenotype D demonstrated the highest burden, including ACS, heart failure, and ischemic stroke. These findings support current literature describing PMOS as an independent cardiovascular risk factor and suggest higher ASCVD events for patients with PMOS and ovulatory dysfunction.
title: Abstract 16394: Composite Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Events Across Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Phenotypes

abstract: Introduction: Infective endocarditis (IE) complicated by acute valvular destruction often necessitates urgent surgery. However, concurrent intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) presents a critical therapeutic dilemma, as systemic heparinization for cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) risks catastrophic hematoma expansion. Current guidelines offer limited consensus on balancing imminent hemodynamic collapse from severe acute mitral regurgitation (MR) against neurological worsening. Patient Information: A 30-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use and partially treated MRSA tricuspid valve IE presented unresponsive following a brief period of self-discharge. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Imaging revealed a 5-cm right frontotemporal intracerebral hemorrhage, a 5-mm midline shift, and uncal herniation secondary to a ruptured distal cerebral mycotic aneurysm. She underwent emergent hematoma evacuation, aneurysm clipping, and external ventricular drain placement. Subsequent echocardiography revealed a 1.8 х 1.2 cm mitral valve vegetation with anterior leaflet (A1) perforation, culminating in severe MR and rapid progression to cardiogenic shock by hospital day 4. Acute limb ischemia further compounded the clinical course, while the recent ICH strictly precluded both urgent cardiac surgery and mechanical circulatory support. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Valvular surgery timing was guided by multimodal physiological and radiographic stability rather than a fixed empiric delay. Therapeutic Interventions: Cardiogenic shock was aggressively managed and optimized with targeted inotropic support and meticulous afterload reduction. Cardiac surgery was deferred until serial neuroimaging confirmed hematoma resolution, angiography verified complete aneurysm obliteration, and transcranial Doppler documented resolution of vasospasm (MCA velocity < 100 cm/s, Lindegaard ratio < 3). The patient maintained a stable neurological examination during blood pressure challenges, and bacteremia cleared. Follow-up, Outcomes, & Adverse Effects: On post-craniotomy day 18, under full heparinization for CPB, she underwent successful mitral valve repair utilizing autologous pericardial patches for the A1 perforation. Postoperative echocardiography demonstrated mild residual MR and no hematoma expansion. She completed antibiotics and was discharged to rehabilitation. Discussion and Synthesis: Acute severe MR causing cardiogenic shock can be successfully optimized medically to allow for the stabilization of a severe ICH. A structured, multimodal strategy tracking hematoma stability, aneurysm obliteration, and vasospasm can define a safe, individualized operative window for definitive cardiac repair.
title: Abstract 16416: Bridging Cardiogenic Shock to Surgical Repair: Managing Ruptured Intracranial Mycotic Aneurysm and Severe Mitral Regurgitation in Infective Endocarditis

abstract: Introduction: Acute myocardial infarction from an aortic root thrombus occluding a coronary ostium- Rare finding, particularly without dissection, aneurysm or plaque rupture.Coronary angiography may reveal the effect but miss the cause. We report an inferior wall MI caused by a floating aortic sinus thrombus that resolved with anticoagulation only. Patient Information: A 36yr old man, smoker, alcoholic, hepatitis B reactive with no history of diabetes or hypertension, presented 3 days after onset of epigastric pain,sweating,and anxiety. Clinical Findings: At initial evaluation was pain-free with normal hemodynamics and cardiovascular examination. Diagnostic Assessment: ECG showed sinus rhythm with deepened inferior Q waves (III, aVF) suggestive of inferior wall myocardial infarction. Troponin elevated. ECG showed inferoposterior wall hypokinesia with mild left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF 42%). Coronary angiography showed thrombotic occlusion of ostioproximal RCA with oscillating mass extending from ostium into right coronary sinus. Immediately, angiography was abandoned ,an urgent CT aortography was planned. CT aortography demonstrated a 12x6 mm mobile thrombus arising from the anterior sinus of Valsalva extending into the ascending aorta ,occluding the RCA ostium, with no dissection flap.Prothrombotic workup with homocysteine done Therapeutic Intervention: Thrombus floating in sinus, an urgent CTVS review was taken. Main culprit was a floating aortic thrombus rather than an atherosclerotic plaque, the heart team preferred conservative management with anticoagulation therapy over an aggressive surgical approach . Surgical management was considered if it persists even after anticoagulation on serial CT aortography.Unfractionated heparin was infused and titrated to APTT 50-75 seconds, then transitioned to low-molecular-weight heparin and an oral anticoagulant. Dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, and guideline-directed heart failure therapy given. Follow-up and Outcomes: Repeat CT aortography (after 5 days) - resolution of the aortic sinus thrombus with persistent ostial RCA occlusion. The patient - asymptomatic, hemodynamically stable and discharged on conservative management. At 1 month follow-up, patient is asymptomatic. Future plan- repeat CT aortography at 3 months and to consider for coronary intervention after cardiac stress testing. Discussion: Vital diagnostic lesson: angiography identified an occluded ostium, but CT aortography revealed its true embolic source while excluding dissection. In a non-aneurysmal aorta, a mobile thrombus needs for anticoagulation rather than reflexive intervention and may resolve entirely. Premature arterial thrombosis seen in a young adult also warrants evaluation for a prothrombotic state. Patient Perspective: Initially anxious over surgical intervention but was grateful medicines worked.
title: Abstract 16419: Case of a Floating Culprit Beyond the Coronary Aortic Sinus Thrombus Causing Ostial RCA Occlusion and Inferior Myocardial Infarction Resolved with Anticoagulation Alone

abstract: Background. New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is associated with excess mortality, but US population-scale data on oral anticoagulation (OAC) use and long-term outcomes in this population are limited. Methods. In the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we identified adults with STEMI who had a first recorded diagnosis of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter within 30 days of the index event in the available network record. OAC initiation within 30 days was compared with no recorded OAC using 1:1 propensity-score matching on prespecified covariates. Results. Among 36,965 eligible patients, OAC was prescribed to 36%; 10,566 pairs were matched. At 3 years, OAC was associated with lower all-cause mortality (15.2% vs 28.8%; HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.44-0.50; P<0.001), with absolute risk reduction 13.6 percentage points and number needed to treat of 7. The mortality association emerged at 30 days (HR 0.26, 95% CI 0.24-0.29; P<0.001) and persisted at 1 year (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.37-0.43; P<0.001). Ischemic stroke did not differ at 3 years (4.1% vs 4.0%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82-1.09; P=0.40). Major bleeding (6.8% vs 6.3%; P=0.71) and intracranial hemorrhage (1.4% vs 1.3%; P=0.76) were similar. Conclusions. In this US retrospective cohort of patients with documented NOAF after STEMI, OAC initiation within 30 days was associated with lower 3-year mortality without a statistically significant increase in coded major bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage. These findings highlight substantial treatment variation and support prospective studies to define optimal antithrombotic management in this population.
title: Abstract 16430: Association of Oral Anticoagulation with Long-Term Outcomes in New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation After ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Propensity-Score-Matched Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Sudden cardiac death (SCD) remains a major cause of mortality in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Although PCSK9 inhibitors (PCSK9i) reduce low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and major adverse cardiovascular events, their association with SCD-related and arrhythmic outcomes in ICM/HFrEF remains uncertain. Objective: To evaluate the association between PCSK9i therapy and SCD-related and cardiovascular outcomes in adults with ICM/HFrEF. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults aged 18-75 years with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and systolic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) diagnosed between January 2010 and May 2026 were identified. Patients with prior cardiac arrest, VT/VF, ICD/CRT-D implantation, or heart transplantation were excluded. PCSK9 inhibitor (PCSK9i) exposure was defined as ≥3 prescriptions for alirocumab, evolocumab, or inclisiran initiated within 5 years of ICM/HFrEF diagnosis. Propensity score matching (PSM) adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, medications, laboratory, echocardiographic, and device-related variables, including GDMT use and ICD/CRT-D status. Outcomes were assessed from 30 days after the index date through 5 and 10 years. The primary outcome was sudden cardiac death (SCD)-related mortality, identified by ICD-10 codes I46.2 and I46.9. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, VT/VF, ICD implantation, VT ablation, AMI, PCI, and CABG. Results: Before matching, PCSK9i users had substantially higher GDMT utilization. After PSM, cohorts were well balanced, with 1,946 patients per group (mean age 60.9 years; 67% male). PCSK9i therapy was associated with lower SCD-related mortality at 5 years (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27-0.71) and 10 years (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31-0.75). Risks of VT/VF were also reduced at 5 years (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.42-0.83) and 10 years (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43-0.83), as were rates of ICD implantation at 5 years (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.50-0.89) and 10 years (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51-0.91). No significant differences were observed for VT ablation, AMI, PCI, or CABG. All-cause mortality was significantly lower among PCSK9i users both before and after matching; after PSM, HRs were 0.46 (95% CI 0.37-0.57) at 5 years and 0.49 (95% CI 0.40-0.60) at 10 years (both p<0.001). (Figure 1, Table 2A-2B) Conclusions: In this large real-world PSM cohort of patients with ICM/HFrEF, PCSK9i therapy was associated with lower SCD-related mortality events, VT/VF, and ICD implantation after adjustment for GDMT and device-related covariates. Because this retrospective analysis remains vulnerable to residual confounding and administrative coding limitations, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.
title: Abstract 16439: PCSK9 Inhibitor Therapy and Sudden Cardiac Death-Related Outcomes in Ischemic Cardiomyopathy and Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction: A Propensity Score-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Background: Occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) represents a high-risk subset of ACS characterized by acute coronary artery occlusion or near-occlusion requiring urgent reperfusion. Conventional STEMI criteria fail to identify a substantial proportion of patients with OMI, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment. AI-ECG has emerged as a promising strategy to improve early recognition. Methods: A systematic review following PRISMA guidelines was performed using PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library, from databases’ inception through May 29, 2026, using terms related to artificial intelligence, ECG, myocardial infarction, coronary occlusion, and OMI. Studies were eligible if they included adults with suspected ACS, evaluated an AI-based ECG algorithm, and used angiographically confirmed culprit lesions with OMI definitions specified as reference standards. Only the studies from which true/false positive and true/false negative rates were able to be assessed, were included in the statistical analysis. Results: A total of 507 records were identified, from which 125 were duplicates. Finally, twenty-nine studies underwent full-text review, and 12 studies met inclusion criteria. Eight studies included direct comparisons with conventional ECG interpretation, STEMI criteria, or expert readers, while four studies assessed clinical outcomes. The 12 included studies encompassed 53,690 patients from North America and Europe and included retrospective single-center and multicenter cohorts. Deep learning and convolutional neural network architectures were the most employed AI models. Reported areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.72 to 0.95, compared with 0.27 to 0.84 for conventional ECG interpretation or STEMI-based approaches when reported. Across studies, sensitivity ranged from 28.8% to 100.0%, specificity from 50.7% to 98.9%, PPV from 26.2% to 89.9%, and NPV from 63.8% to 100.0%. AI-ECG algorithms consistently demonstrated improved identification of angiographically confirmed coronary occlusion, particularly among patients without diagnostic STEMI criteria, and several studies reported reductions in false-positive catheterization laboratory activations while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy. Conclusions: Current evidence supports AI-ECG as a promising diagnostic tool for the detection of OMI and acute coronary occlusion. Across diverse healthcare settings and patient populations, AI-ECG models demonstrated favorable diagnostic performance and frequently outperformed conventional ECG-based approaches. Future prospective implementation studies and randomized clinical trials are warranted to determine whether AI-assisted ECG interpretation improves clinical outcomes, reduces treatment delays, and optimizes utilization of invasive cardiovascular resources.

Abstract 16441: Beyond STEMI: AI-Enhanced Electrocardiography Consistently Improves Detection of Occlusion Myocardial Infarction -

abstract: Background- Prophylactic Impella support during complex high-risk PCI in reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) has been evaluated predominantly at 30 days, with limited literature across medium and long-term outcomes. To evaluate whether hemodynamic stabilization and complete revascularization achieved at the index procedure are associated with incremental clinical benefit across 30-day, 90-day, and >90-day follow-up periods. Methods- MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from January 2005 through March 2026 per PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies enrolled non-emergent patients with prophylactic Impella (2.5, CP, or ECP). Cardiogenic shock, bailout-only, and post-cardiotomy populations were excluded. Co-primary outcomes were MACCE (all-cause mortality, stroke, MI, unplanned revascularization) at 30 days, 90 days, and >90 days. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular hospitalization, NYHA functional class improvement, and completeness of revascularization at each horizon. Meta-regression analyses were conducted to identify determinants of temporal differences in clinical outcomes. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.5.0. Results- Eighteen studies met eligibility (N=7,412; 2 RCTs, 1 FDA post-approval study, 15 registries). Median LVEF 27%, median SYNTAX score 35. At 30 days, pooled MACCE was 11.3% (95% CI 8.6-14.4%; I 2 =58%), with mortality 3.2% and major bleeding 8.4%. In elective SIHD patients with pre-procedural placement, 30-day MACCE was 7.9%, driven by periprocedural MI and access complications rather than mortality. At 90 days, cumulative MACCE was 18.4% (95% CI 14.7-22.5%; I 2 =71%). Incremental 30-to-90-day event accrual was 7.1%, reflecting heart failure hospitalization and repeat revascularization rather than new mortality. In the elective pre-procedural subgroup, 90-day MACCE was 12.1% with a significant 29% relative risk reduction (RR 0.71; 95% CI 0.56-0.90; p=0.005). NYHA improvement ≥1 class was observed in 63% at 90 days. Beyond 90 days (4 studies; N=2,156; median follow-up 18 months), incremental events decelerated to 3.2% per 6-month interval versus 6.8% in the first 90 days (p=0.003), consistent with a durable plateau of benefit. Complete revascularization (residual SYNTAX ≤8) was the strongest independent predictor of freedom from MACCE beyond 90 days (adjusted HR 0.52; 95% CI 0.38-0.71). Conclusions- Prophylactic Impella-supported CHIP in elective reduced-LVEF patients demonstrates a consistent and progressive pattern of benefit: early hemodynamic and procedural safety at 30 days, reduced heart failure hospitalization and repeat revascularization at 90 days, and durable survival advantage beyond 90 days mediated by completeness of revascularization
title: Abstract 16446: Temporal Trajectory of Clinical Outcomes Following Prophylactic Impella-Supported Complex High-Risk PCI in Reduced LVEF: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Objective Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) requires computed tomography angiography (CTA)-based annular assessment for valve sizing, while traditionally surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) has not. The objective of this study was to determine whether routine use of CTA-based annular assessment for patients requiring aortic valve replacement (AVR) was associated with changes in SAVR valve sizing and outcomes over time. Methods/Approach We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 226 veterans who underwent SAVR at a Veterans Affairs Healthcare System from 2013 to 2025. Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative variables were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Outcomes included postoperative mean aortic valve gradient, all-cause mortality at 1 and 5 years, postoperative stroke, and postoperative acute kidney injury, with postoperative gradient prespecified as the primary hemodynamic outcome. Valve hemodynamic performance was assessed using the first available postoperative echocardiogram within 30 days of surgery. Annulus-implant discrepancy, defined as the difference between CTA-derived annular diameter and implanted valve size, was calculated for all patients with available preoperative CTA measurements. Temporal changes in valve sizing and surgical outcomes were evaluated by year of surgery. Multivariable regression models were used to assess associations. Results/Data Median implanted valve size increased from 23 mm in 2013 to 27 mm in 2025 (p<0.001). Mean annulus-implant discrepancy decreased from 3.0 mm to 0.3 mm over the study period (p<0.001). After adjusting for age, body surface area, sex, operative status, predicted operative mortality, and year of surgery, each 2 mm increase in implanted valve size was associated with a 2.3 mmHg lower postoperative gradient (β –2.3 mmHg; 95% CI, –3.0 to –1.6; p<0.001). Later year of surgery was also independently associated with lower postoperative gradient (β –0.26 mmHg/year; 95% CI, –0.44 to –0.08; p=0.005). Conclusions Among patients undergoing SAVR from 2013 to 2025, implanted valve size increased, annulus-implant discrepancy decreased, and postoperative valve hemodynamics improved over time. These trends coincided with institutional adoption of CTA-based annular assessment as the standard preoperative workup for patients undergoing AVR. These findings suggest that using CTA-based preoperative annular assessment may improve prosthetic valve selection and early postoperative hemodynamic performance following SAVR. Whether these changes translate into longer-term clinical benefit warrants further study.
title: Abstract 16470: Changes in Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement Prosthetic Sizing with Routine Use of Computed Tomography Angiography

abstract: Introduction: Acute instability of a transcatheter tricuspid prosthesis is an uncommon, high-risk complication with limited published bailout experience. Rescue is particularly complex in pacemaker-dependent patients with chronic transvalvular leads, in whom stabilization must preserve pacing and lead integrity. Patient Information: A 65-year-old woman with NYHA class III symptoms, torrential tricuspid regurgitation, severe right-sided enlargement, longstanding pacing/defibrillator leads, and prohibitive surgical and lead-extraction risk was referred for transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR). Clinical Findings & Timeline: Imaging showed severe annular dilation, marked leaflet restriction, posterior leaflet plastering, a 1.5-cm posterior commissural coaptation gap, and two transvalvular leads. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Multidisciplinary structural-heart and electrophysiology review favored TTVR with planned lead jailing, asynchronous device programming, left ventricular wire backup pacing, electrophysiology standby, and multimodality imaging. Therapeutic Intervention(s): After deployment, a 52-mm transcatheter tricuspid prosthesis demonstrated insufficient anterior anchoring, marked rocking, and partial embolization into the right ventricle. Via right internal jugular access, an endovascular snare captured a posterior anchoring element and stabilized the prosthesis within the annular plane. A 29-mm balloon-expandable valve was deployed within the unstable frame during rapid pacing, establishing a stable valve-in-valve construct. The snare became entrapped between the prostheses and was released with electrocautery using an externalized wire. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Final imaging showed no transprosthetic regurgitation, mild anterior paravalvular leak, and a mean gradient of 1 mm Hg. Postoperatively, right ventricular failure with cardiogenic shock required inotropes, and respiratory failure required temporary mechanical ventilation. She was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 30 days, lead function remained stable, the mean gradient was 3 mm Hg, right ventricular function improved from severely to moderately reduced, and symptoms improved to NYHA class II. Discussion & Synthesis: Published experience with bailout valve-in-valve rescue for unstable TTVR is limited to isolated reports; systematic safety, efficacy, and durability data are lacking. This case extends that experience by combining targeted snare stabilization, balloon-expandable valve-in-valve implantation, and electrocautery-assisted release of an entrapped snare. It highlights the importance of anticipatory non-tricuspid pacing support, multimodality imaging, and immediate access to complementary bailout tools in complex lead-bearing anatomy.
title: Abstract 16482: Snare-Assisted Valve-in-Valve Rescue After Partial Tricuspid Prosthesis Embolization in a Pacemaker-Dependent Patient

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock is a devastating complication among hospitalized patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), yet early identification of at-risk patients remains challenging. Traditional risk approaches may inadequately capture the complex cardiovascular interactions preceding hemodynamic deterioration. We developed and temporally validated an explainable machine learning model to stratify cardiogenic shock risk among hospitalized AF patients and characterize the cardiovascular vulnerability profile associated with shock development. Methods: Adult AF hospitalizations were identified from the Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD) 2021-2022 (n=5,267,332). XGBoost, LightGBM, logistic regression, and random forest models were trained on NRD 2021 (n=2,595,423) and temporally validated on NRD 2022 (n=2,671,909) using 118 clinical features. Model stability was confirmed by 5-fold cross-validation. Explainability was assessed via SHAP; clinical utility by decision curve analysis and subgroup analyses stratified by age, sex, heart failure, CKD, prior stroke, and AF subtype. Results: Cardiogenic shock occurred in 2.0% of hospitalizations (n=53,972 test cases). XGBoost achieved excellent discrimination (AUROC 0.913, sensitivity 83.8%, specificity 83.1%, NPV 99.6%, PR-AUC 0.281, Brier 0.120; 5-fold CV 0.9111±0.0013), outperforming LightGBM (0.912), random forest (0.901), and logistic regression (0.898). Decision curve analysis confirmed net clinical benefit over treat-all at clinically relevant thresholds. SHAP identified procedure burden (1.090), cumulative diagnosis count (0.565), heart failure (0.525), acute myocardial infarction (0.310), Elixhauser comorbidity score (0.295), service line (0.192), HFpEF (0.182), sepsis (0.158), HFrEF (0.153), and cardiomyopathy (0.130) as dominant shock predictors, confirming a convergent cardiovascular vulnerability profile defined by myocardial dysfunction, ischemic burden, and multimorbidity. Discrimination was robust across all subgroups (AUROC 0.895-0.919), with highest performance in younger patients (0.915) and patients without CKD (0.919). Conclusions: A temporally validated explainable ML model demonstrates excellent discrimination for cardiogenic shock across 5.2 million AF hospitalizations. SHAP reveals convergent myocardial dysfunction, ischemic burden, and multimorbidity as the primary shock drivers — a cardiovascular vulnerability profile that may support AI-assisted early identification of high-risk hospitalized AF patients.
title: Abstract 16507: Cardiogenic Shock in Hospitalized Atrial Fibrillation Patients: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach to Risk Stratification in 5.2 Million Hospitalizations

abstract: Background- ECPR achieves 30% overall survival in refractory cardiac arrest versus approximately 2% neurologically intact survival after 15-20 minutes of conventional CPR (CCPR), with a 30% decrease in neurologically favorable survival per decade of age. Whether meaningful absolute benefit persists across <45, 45-60, and >60 year strata and at what threshold incremental advantage attenuates remains the operative unanswered question for patient selection. Methods- MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from January 2000 through March 2026 per PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies comparing ECPR versus CCPR in adult refractory cardiac arrest with age-stratified outcomes were eligible. Co-primary outcomes were survival to discharge and favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) by age stratum. Random-effects meta-analysis with subgroup analyses by arrest location, initial rhythm, and low-flow time. Meta-regression assessed age as a continuous moderator of benefit. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.5.0 Results- Twenty-two studies (N=14,830; 3 RCTs, 8 propensity-matched cohorts, 11 registry analyses). Overall survival: 34.1% ECPR versus 18.6% CCPR (OR 2.21; 95% CI 1.74-2.81). <45 years: survival 51.3% versus 21.4% (OR 3.84; 95% CI 2.61-5.65); favorable neurological outcome 78%. 45-60 years: survival 38.7% versus 19.8% (OR 2.52; 95% CI 1.89-3.36); favorable neurological outcome 68% most consistent benefit across different settings. >60 years: survival 22.8% versus 14.1% (OR 1.79; 95% CI 1.31-2.44); favorable neurological outcome 23% through age 75, declining sharply beyond 75 (11%). Elderly patients lost survival probability when ECMO initiation was delayed beyond 21 minutes versus a substantially longer window in younger patients. ECMO complications did not differ across strata. Meta-regression confirmed age as a significant continuous moderator (β = –0.038/year; p<0.001); ROC-derived inflection at 63 years. Conclusions- ECPR confers significant survival benefit over CCPR across all strata with a steep age-dependent gradient greatest below 45, consistent through 60, attenuated but present through 75, near-absent beyond 75. Age alone is insufficient as an exclusion criterion; the interaction of age, low-flow time, shockable rhythm, and ACS etiology defines the true benefit window.

appraisal.main_limitation: Pools mostly observational data with likely selection bias and confounding by indication.
appraisal.one_line: ECPR versus conventional CPR meta-analysis stratified by age in refractory cardiac arrest.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Overall survival: 34.1% ECPR versus 18.6% CCPR (OR 2.21; 95% CI 1.74-2.81).
