title: Abstract 16532: Does Age Define the Benefit of Extracorporeal CPR in Refractory Cardiac Arrest? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Non-statin low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)-lowering therapies, including proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) monoclonal antibodies, ezetimibe, and bempedoic acid, demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in randomized trials. The recent VESALIUS-CV trial expanded evidence for LDL-C lowering into primary prevention populations. Research Question: Do non-statin LDL-C-lowering therapies reduce cardiovascular events and mortality compared with placebo, usual care, or background statin therapy in adults at cardiovascular risk, and do treatment effects differ between primary- and secondary-prevention populations? Methods: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were systematically searched from inception through May 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, ezetimibe, or bempedoic acid. Adults undergoing primary or secondary cardiovascular prevention were eligible. The primary outcome was adjudicated 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke). Secondary outcomes included trial-defined MACE, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, coronary revascularization, cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, serious adverse events (SAE), and discontinuation due to adverse events. Risk ratios (RRs) or Peto odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. A pre-specified subgroup analysis compared primary- versus secondary-prevention populations. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 . Results: Seven RCTs comprising 103,540 participants were included. Non-statin LDL-C-lowering therapy significantly reduced 3-point MACE (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.78-0.91; p<0.0001; I 2 =63%), trial-defined MACE (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.82-0.91; p<0.00001; I 2 =62%), MI (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.73-0.87; p<0.00001; I 2 =57%), stroke (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.75-0.88; p<0.00001; I 2 =0%), and coronary revascularization (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.76-0.90; p<0.0001; I 2 =74%). No significant reductions were observed in mortality or SAE. Discontinuation due to adverse events was also comparable between groups. For 3-point MACE, benefits were consistent across primary- and secondary-prevention populations (p=0.18). Similar findings were observed for trial-defined MACE (interaction p=0.11). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings. Conclusion: Non-statin LDL-C-lowering therapies significantly reduce MACE, MI, stroke, and coronary revascularization in adults at cardiovascular risk, with consistent benefits across primary- and secondary-prevention settings. No significant effects on mortality were observed, and overall safety remained comparable to control.
title: Abstract 16541: Cardiovascular Outcomes with Non-Statin LDL-Lowering Therapies: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials Including VESALIUS-CV

abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal anticoagulation strategy following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in patients requiring long-term oral anticoagulation remains uncertain. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) have emerged as an alternative to vitamin K antagonists (VKAs); however, randomized and observational studies have reported conflicting results regarding their safety and efficacy. HYPOTHESIS We sought to evaluate the comparative safety and efficacy of DOACs versus VKAs with respect to mortality, stroke, and major bleeding in patients undergoing TAVR who require long-term oral anticoagulation. METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar (2016-2026) identified 10 observational studies and 3 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DOACs and VKAs in patients undergoing TAVR who required long-term oral anticoagulation. Outcomes of interest included all-cause mortality, stroke, and major bleeding. Observational studies and RCTs were analysed separately. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic. Study quality was assessed using ROB-2, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. RESULTS: Ten observational studies and three randomized controlled trials involving over 50,000 patients were included. Outcomes were assessed at trial follow-up (1-12 months). In randomized trials, DOACs demonstrated comparable all-cause mortality compared with VKAs (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.95-1.33; p=0.18; I 2 =0%). A trend toward increased major bleeding was observed with DOAC therapy (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.99-1.67; p=0.06; I 2 =12%), while stroke risk was similar between groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.69-1.46; p=0.99; I 2 =4%). In observational studies, DOACs demonstrated a trend toward lower all-cause mortality compared with VKAs (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69-1.01; p=0.06; I 2 =48%). DOAC therapy was associated with significantly lower major bleeding (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.78-0.90; p<0.001; I 2 =19%), while stroke risk was comparable between groups (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.99-1.25; p=0.07; I 2 =0%). CONCLUSION: Among patients undergoing TAVR who require long-term oral anticoagulation, DOACs demonstrated comparable efficacy to VKAs for prevention of mortality and stroke. Observational studies suggested lower major bleeding and a trend toward lower mortality with DOAC therapy, whereas randomized trials demonstrated neutral efficacy outcomes and a trend toward increased bleeding. These findings highlight key differences between observational and randomized evidence and underscore the need for additional adequately powered randomized trials to define the optimal anticoagulation strategy following TAVR.

title: Abstract 16547: Direct Oral Anticoagulants versus Vitamin K Antagonists Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients Requiring Long-Term Oral Anticoagulation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Intravascular imaging (IVI)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been associated with improved outcomes in complex coronary lesions; however, recent randomized trials have reported conflicting findings. We performed a comprehensive meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate the impact of IVI guidance on clinical outcomes. Methods: We systematically identified RCTs comparing IVI-guided versus angiography-guided PCI in patients with complex coronary lesions. The primary outcomes were major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and cardiac death. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using random-effects models, with complementary Bayesian analyses. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: Nineteen RCTs involving 19,109 patients were included. Compared with angiography guidance, IVI-guided PCI significantly reduced MACE (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.83), cardiac death (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.44-0.93), myocardial infarction (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75-0.99), clinically driven target lesion revascularization (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51-0.99), and stent thrombosis (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.35-0.78). A significant interaction was observed by geographic region, with greater treatment effects among Asian trial populations (Pinteraction<0.01). Among studies reporting optimization outcomes, achievement of imaging-defined stent optimization was associated with substantially lower adverse event rates (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.28-0.58). Conclusions: In patients undergoing PCI for complex coronary lesions, IVI guidance significantly reduces adverse cardiovascular events compared with angiography guidance alone. These findings suggest that the clinical benefit of IVI may be mediated, in part, through achievement of imaging-defined stent optimization.

appraisal.design_and_n: Nineteen RCTs involving 19,109 patients.
appraisal.main_limitation: Conference abstract; a regional interaction was reported (Pinteraction<0.01), with larger effects in Asian trials, which limits transportability.
appraisal.one_line: Frequentist and Bayesian meta-analysis of intravascular imaging-guided versus angiography-guided PCI in complex lesions.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: IVI guidance was associated with lower MACE (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.83) and cardiac death (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.44-0.93).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Updates the pooled evidence on imaging guidance, relevant to guideline strength and to the question of transportability.

title: Abstract 16550: Intravascular Imaging-Guided Drug-Eluting Stenting for Complex Coronary Lesions: A Frequentist and Bayesian Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

abstract: Background: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease recognized as a cardiovascular risk-enhancing condition. Whether cardiovascular risk varies by psoriasis severity remains unclear. We evaluated the association between treatment-defined psoriasis severity and long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults with psoriasis diagnosed between 2016 and 2025 were stratified by treatment-defined severity: mild (topical therapy only), moderate (systemic non-biologic therapy), and severe (biologic therapy). Patients with prior cardiovascular events, systemic inflammatory diseases, malignancy, HIV infection, end-stage renal disease, or organ transplantation were excluded. Seborrheic dermatitis served as an active comparator to reduce healthcare utilization bias. Propensity score matching was performed separately within each severity stratum using 51 variables. The primary outcome was an expanded major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) composite including myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, and cardiac arrest. Secondary outcomes included acute myocardial infarction (AMI), stroke, heart failure (HF), NSTEMI, and STEMI. Outcomes were assessed for up to 10 years using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Results: After propensity score matching, analyses included 81,028 mild psoriasis-control pairs, 17,623 moderate psoriasis-control pairs, and 133,790 severe psoriasis-control pairs. Compared with controls, mild psoriasis was associated with increased risk of MACE (HR 1.52, 95% CI 1.46-1.58), AMI (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.50-1.76), stroke (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.26-1.46), and HF (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.51-1.67). Similar findings were observed in moderate psoriasis (MACE HR 1.53, 95% CI 1.42-1.65; AMI HR 1.77, 95% CI 1.53-2.04; stroke HR 1.56, 95% CI 1.36-1.79; HF HR 1.58, 95% CI 1.44-1.73) and severe psoriasis (MACE HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.44-1.54; AMI HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.56-1.80; stroke HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.33-1.51; HF HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.47-1.61). NSTEMI and STEMI risks were also elevated across all severity strata. No clear dose-response was observed across severity groups. Conclusions: Psoriasis was associated with significantly increased long-term risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure across all treatment-defined severity strata. Cardiovascular risk was evident even among patients managed with topical therapy alone and remained elevated among those receiving systemic or biologic therapy. The absence of a clear severity gradient suggests that treatment-defined severity may not fully capture underlying cardiovascular risk burden. These findings support psoriasis as a cardiovascular risk-enhancing condition and reinforce the importance of cardiovascular risk assessment.
title: Abstract 16564: Psoriasis and Long-Term Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events Across Treatment-Defined Severity Strata: A Global Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Anthracycline-based chemotherapy causes cardiotoxicity through oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and direct myocardial injury. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) increases this risk through impaired myocardial energetics and systemic inflammation. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) may counter these pathways, whereas dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4) are cardiovascularly neutral comparators. Real-world evidence remains lacking in oncology patients with T2DM. Hypothesis: We sought to determine whether GLP-1 RA use, compared with DPP-4 inhibitor use, was associated with a lower risk of incident heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) or dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in adults with T2DM receiving anthracycline-based chemotherapy. Methods: We used the TriNetX United States Collaborative Network, a federated EHR database spanning 67 health care organizations, to identify adults with T2DM who received anthracycline-based chemotherapy from 2015 through 2024 and later initiated a GLP-1 RA (including tirzepatide, a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor and GLP-1 RA) or DPP-4 inhibitor. Cohorts were mutually exclusive. After one-to-one propensity score matching, 878 matched pairs were analyzed over 365 days. The primary outcome was incident HFrEF or DCM. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality (ACM), three-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), composite arrhythmia, and incident atrial fibrillation (AF). Cox proportional hazards models were used, with results reported as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: After matching, most baseline characteristics were balanced; however, there were imbalances in body mass index (32.9 versus 30.3 kg/m 2 ) and left ventricular ejection fraction (58.1% versus 61.3%). The primary outcome did not differ significantly (2.5% versus 2.7%; HR 0.90, p=0.724). GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower ACM (9.8% versus 17.7%; HR 0.53, CI 0.41-0.69; p<0.001), lower MACE (10.8% versus 19.2%; HR 0.54, CI 0.41-0.71; p<0.001), lower AF (2.6% versus 4.8%; HR 0.52, CI 0.30-0.90; p=0.018), and lower composite arrhythmia (3.5% versus 6.1%; HR 0.55, CI 0.34-0.88; p=0.012). Conclusions: GLP-1 RA use was not associated with lower one-year risk of HFrEF or DCM, compared with DPP-4 inhibitor use. The null primary endpoint likely reflects insufficient follow-up, as anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy typically manifests over years. Nevertheless, GLP-1 RAs were associated with significantly lower ACM, MACE, and incident AF. These findings are limited by the observational design, post-matching imbalances, unmeasured confounding from cancer severity and performance status, and follow-up insufficient to capture anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy; prospective trials with extended follow-up are warranted.
title: Abstract 16588: Cardiovascular Outcomes of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists Compared with Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 Inhibitors in Adults with Type2 Diabetes Mellitus Receiving Anthracycline Based Chemotherapy: A Propensity Matched TriNetX Multicenter Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Left main bifurcation PCI remains technically challenging, particularly when accompanied by tandem downstream bifurcation disease. Although angiography guides procedural strategy, it may fail to detect clinically important complications. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) can provide critical information that directly influences management. We present a case in which OCT identified an angiographically occult complication that altered procedural outcome. Case: An 80-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with progressive exertional angina and a recent syncopal episode. Coronary angiography demonstrated unprotected distal left main bifurcation disease (Medina 1,1,1) involving the LAD and LCX, along with tandem LCX/OM1 bifurcation disease (Medina 1,1,1). Given advanced age and favorable anatomy, percutaneous revascularization was selected. To minimize metallic burden within the distal bifurcation, drug-coated balloon angioplasty was performed to the OM1 branch. The distal left main bifurcation was subsequently treated using a mini-crush two-stent technique. Following stent deployment, proximal optimization technique, LCX rewiring, non-compliant balloon post-dilation, final kissing balloon inflation, and repeat proximal optimization were performed. Final angiography demonstrated an excellent result with preserved distal flow and no apparent complication. OCT was performed for procedural assessment and demonstrated excellent stent expansion and apposition, preserved LCX ostial architecture, and favorable minimal stent areas. Importantly, OCT identified an angiographically unapparent distal LAD stent-edge dissection measuring approximately 6 mm. Given the potential risk of thrombosis and adverse ischemic events, an additional distal LAD stent was implanted. Repeat OCT confirmed complete sealing of the dissection with satisfactory final stent architecture. Discussion: This case highlights the evolving role of OCT as a decisional rather than merely confirmatory tool in complex PCI. A hybrid strategy combining drug-coated balloon therapy and mini-crush bifurcation stenting enabled treatment of serial left main double-bifurcation disease while limiting unnecessary metallic burden. Despite an apparently optimal angiographic result, OCT detected a clinically actionable stent-edge dissection that directly altered management. This case underscores that procedural success in complex bifurcation PCI should be defined not only by angiographic appearance but also by imaging-guided identification of occult complications requiring immediate correction.
title: Abstract 16605: Beyond Angiographic Success: OCT-Guided Detection of Occult Stent-Edge Dissection Following Complex Left Main Double-Bifurcation PCI

abstract: Introduction/Background: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is standard therapy for severe aortic stenosis. Conscious sedation/monitored anesthesia care (CS/MAC) has emerged as an alternative to general anesthesia (GA), with potential hemodynamic, recovery, and resource advantages. However, prior evidence is limited by observational design, selection bias, and a predominance of U.S.-based studies. Research Question/Hypothesis: We compared clinical, procedural, and resource-use outcomes of CS/MAC versus GA in patients undergoing TAVR. Methods/Approach: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched from inception to April 1, 2026, following PRISMA guidelines. Comparative TAVR studies were included. Analyses were performed using R version 4.5.2. Random-effects meta-analysis generated risk ratios (RRs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 . Subgroup, meta-regression, and leave-one-out analyses were performed when feasible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2.0 and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Results/Data: Thirty-three studies including 162,067 patients were included: 30 cohort studies and 3 prospective multicenter randomized controlled trials. Compared with GA, CS/MAC was associated with shorter intensive care unit stay (MD, -6.29; 95% CI, -11.06 to -1.53), hospital stay (MD, -1.13; 95% CI, -1.68 to -0.57), and procedural time (MD, -13.57; 95% CI, -21.65 to -5.49). CS/MAC was also associated with lower 30-day mortality (RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.63 to 0.72), 1-year mortality (RR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.62 to 0.91), acute kidney injury (RR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.63 to 0.92), hypotension (RR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.71), in-hospital mortality (RR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.86), vasopressor or inotrope use (RR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.48 to 0.94), Society of Thoracic Surgeons predicted risk (MD, -0.53; 95% CI, -0.99 to -0.07), rehospitalization (RR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.52 to 0.85), and fluoroscopy time (MD, -3.04; 95% CI, -6.02 to -0.06). No significant differences were found for myocardial infarction, stroke, respiratory or surgical complications, pacemaker implantation, major bleeding, vascular complications, procedural success, paravalvular leak, reintubation, VARC-2 safety, access-site complications, or contrast volume. Leave-one-out analyses supported key findings, but subgroup analysis and meta-regression did not explain heterogeneity. Conclusion(s): CS/MAC was associated with lower selected mortality endpoints, shorter procedural duration, reduced resource use, and lower rates of selected complications compared with GA, without compromising procedural success or major safety outcomes. These findings support CS/MAC as a feasible anesthetic strategy for selected TAVR patients, although further randomized evidence is needed.
title: Abstract 16613: Conscious Sedation/Monitored Anesthesia Care versus General Anesthesia in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Recurrent severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) after prior surgical annuloplasty is difficult to manage when valve anatomy prevents edge-to-edge repair and a leadless pacemaker is in place. Transcatheter valve-in-ring (TViR) implantation offers a useful alternative for high-risk patients. Patient Information: A 65-year-old woman with heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF), post-capillary pulmonary hypertension (PH), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hepatitis C cirrhosis, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) status post Watchman, prior stroke, non-obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD), and complete heart block status post Micra presented with recurrent volume overload. Clinical Findings & Timeline: She underwent tricuspid valve repair with a 26-mm MC3 Edwards ring 3 years prior. Recurrent severe TR with right heart failure developed, requiring multiple hospitalizations for intravenous (IV) diuresis. TriClip was attempted 4 months prior but failed due to ring proximity to leaflets limiting grasping. She was referred for transcatheter valve-in-ring replacement after heart team discussion. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Pre-procedure transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed well-seated ring with ruptured chordae and flail septal leaflet causing severe TR (vena contracta 12 mm, hepatic vein reversal). Right ventricle (RV) moderately dilated/reduced function; left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 50-55%. Prior right heart catheterization (RHC) confirmed post-capillary PH. TViR was selected given high surgical risk, failed interventions, and Micra pacemaker. Therapeutic Interventions: Elective transcatheter TViR replacement was performed under general anesthesia via right femoral access. A 26-mm Edwards Sapien 3 Ultra Resilia valve was deployed in reverse orientation within the ring using double-tap technique with rapid pacing via Micra. Intra-procedural TEE showed well-seated valve with near-complete TR resolution. She transitioned to apixaban monotherapy due to bleeding risk. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Marked dyspnea improvement occurred. Post-procedure transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed trace TR without effusion. Discharged day 3 on optimized heart failure (HF) therapy and apixaban. At 2-week follow-up, TTE showed well-seated 26-mm Edwards Sapien valve with no TR or stenosis. Discussion & Synthesis: This case shows transcatheter tricuspid valve-in-ring replacement with balloon-expandable valve successfully treats torrential TR after failed surgical annuloplasty and failed edge-to-edge repair despite a leadless pacemaker.
title: Abstract 16626: Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve-in-Ring Replacement After Failed Surgical Annuloplasty and Failed Edge-to-Edge Repair for Torrential Tricuspid Regurgitation

abstract: Background: Conduction disturbances requiring permanent pacing are a frequent complication of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Although right ventricular pacing (RVP) remains the conventional strategy, it may worsen ventricular dyssynchrony in a population already vulnerable to heart failure. Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) recruits the conduction system distal to TAVI-related injury and may better preserve physiologic ventricular activation. We compared electrophysiological and clinical outcomes of LBBAP versus RVP after TAVI. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through May 2026 for studies comparing LBBAP and RVP in patients requiring permanent pacing after TAVI. Random-effects meta-analysis using restricted maximum likelihood estimation with Hartung-Knapp adjustment was performed. Risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for clinical and electrophysiological outcomes. Results: Six studies (1 randomized and 5 observational) comprising 583 patients (294 LBBAP, 289 RVP) were included. Baseline demographic, clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic characteristics were comparable between groups. LBBAP resulted in significantly narrower paced QRS duration at follow-up compared with RVP (MD –31.0 ms, 95% CI –36.5 to –25.5; P<0.001), a finding that remained robust across sensitivity analyses. Device performance at follow up was similar between strategies, with no significant differences in capture threshold (MD +0.09 V, 95% CI –0.10 to +0.29), lead impedance (MD –27.5 Ω, 95% CI –132.5 to +77.6), or sensing amplitude (MD +0.35 mV, 95% CI –1.58 to +2.28). All-cause mortality was comparable between groups (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.61-1.22), and cardiovascular mortality remained inconclusive because of sparse events. Heart-failure hospitalization numerically favored LBBAP (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.15-2.32) but did not reach statistical significance under the primary random-effects model. Conclusion: Among patients requiring permanent pacing after TAVI, LBBAP consistently achieved superior electrical synchrony without sacrificing device performance. While current evidence remains insufficient to demonstrate a reduction in mortality or heart-failure hospitalization, the favorable electrophysiological profile and the observed signal toward fewer heart-failure events support further evaluation of LBBAP as a physiologic pacing strategy in this growing population.
title: Abstract 16648: Left Bundle Branch Area Pacing versus Right Ventricular Pacing After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil and capecitabine) are associated with cardiovascular adverse events (CVAEs) that frequently lead to treatment interruption. Evidence guiding rechallenge and alternative treatment strategies remains limited. Research Question: Among patients who develop fluoropyrimidine-associated CVAEs, how do different rechallenge and therapeutic substitution strategies influence recurrent cardiovascular toxicity and treatment continuation? Methods: We conducted a PRISMA-compliant systematic review using PubMed and Embase (01/2000-05/2026) for studies of adults with solid tumors who underwent fluoropyrimidine (FP) rechallenge or received a non-fluoropyrimidine alternative following FP-associated CVAEs (angina, chest pain, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, heart failure, coronary vasospasm, cardiogenic shock, or sudden cardiac death). We included prospective and retrospective observational studies. Our primary outcome of interest was recurrence of cardiovascular toxicity. Secondary outcomes included type and severity of recurrent CVAEs, treatment completion, and cardioprotective medication use. Results: Among 15 included studies, 870 patients had fluoropyrimidine-associated CVAEs, 485 underwent FP rechallenge and 110 received non-FP alternative (raltitrexed). Two FP rechallenge strategies (same-agent and S-1 switch) were identified. Overall recurrence of cardiovascular toxicity was 11.3% (55/485). By strategy, recurrence was 17.5% with same-agent rechallenge (43/246) and 5.0% with S-1 switch (12/239). No CVAEs were reported in the raltitrexed group (0/110). Recurrent CVAEs were predominantly troponin-negative chest pain or angina (≥31/55 events, 56%). All S-1 recurrences were grade 1-2, while ≥8 severe events were documented in 3 same-agent studies. No recurrence-related deaths were reported. Treatment completion ranged 71-95% for same-agent rechallenge and 98.5% for S-1 switch. Cardioprotective medications, predominantly CCBs and nitrates, were used heterogeneously across same-agent studies. Conclusion: The safety of fluoropyrimidine rechallenge after fluoropyrimidine-associated cardiovascular adverse events appears to depend on the selected strategy. Switching to S-1 or using raltitrexed may be associated with lower recurrent cardiovascular toxicity than same-agent rechallenge. Prospective studies are needed to define the optimal approach that balances cardiovascular safety with oncologic efficacy.
title: Abstract 16699: Cardiovascular Safety of Rechallenge and Substitution Strategies Following Fluoropyrimidine Cardiotoxicity

abstract: Background: Risk stratification in patients with suspected coronary artery disease remains challenging. Established circulating biomarkers and coronary flow reserve (CFR) have shown prognostic value, but their potential incremental benefit beyond traditional risk factors remains unclear. Research question: This study aimed to determine whether cardiac stress biomarkers and transthoracic Doppler echocardiography-derived CFR improve prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) beyond traditional risk factors. Methods: The CEVENT study is a prospective cohort of patients with chest pain referred for myocardial perfusion scintigraphy. CFR was assessed by adenosine stress transthoracic Doppler echocardiography of the left anterior descending artery. Cardiac stress biomarkers were analyzed using the Olink Target 96 Cardiovascular panel (GDF15 and NT-proBNP) and a Singulex assay (cTnI). In 361 patients (97 MACE events over 5 years), biomarkers were combined into a Cox-derived risk score and dichotomized into low (≤median) and high (>median) biomarker levels. Patients were categorized into four phenotypes based on biomarker level and CFR status: low/preserved (LP), low/impaired (LI), high/preserved (HP), high/impaired (HI), with preserved CFR defined as ≥2.0. Cox regression was used to assess the 5-year cumulative incidence of MACE (death, myocardial infarction, stroke, TIA, unstable angina, and revascularization), adjusted for age, sex and hypertension. In a separate analysis, patients were reclassified into four prediction models: (1) traditional risk factors (age, sex, hypertension, LDL, smoking, diabetes), (2) traditional risk factors plus cardiac stress biomarkers, (3) traditional risk factors plus CFR, and (4) a combined model including both biomarkers and CFR on top of traditional risk factors. Model performance was evaluated using AUC (DeLong’s test), continuous NRI, and IDI. Results: MACE incidence differed significantly between the groups (log-rank p<0.001). Comparing patients with low biomarkers and preserved CFR (LP), the risk was higher in LI (HR 3.86, 95% CI 1.71-8.70) and HP (HR 2.32, 95% CI 1.27-4.27), and highest in HI (HR 4.89, 95% CI 2.51-9.53). In the separate prediction model analysis, discrimination improved from AUC 0.760 (traditional model) to 0.781 with biomarkers (p=0.073) and 0.784 with CFR (p=0.111). The combined model achieved the highest discrimination (AUC 0.797; ΔAUC +0.037, p=0.035) and significantly improved reclassification (NRI 0.397, p=0.001; IDI 0.060, p<0.001). Conclusions: Cardiac stress biomarkers and CFR provide incremental prognostic information, with the highest performance achieved when combined. This integrated approach identifies a high-risk group with markedly increased 5-year MACE risk and may improve clinical risk stratification.
title: Abstract 16702: Integrating Biomarkers and Coronary Flow Reserve for Cardiovascular Risk Stratification

abstract: Introduction: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Its prognostic significance in patients with already-established atherosclerosis remains unclear. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (2006-2026). Adults aged 18 years or older with a diagnosis of atherosclerosis and a measured Lp(a) were classified as elevated (≥125 nmol/L or ≥50 mg/dL) or non-elevated (<125 nmol/L or <50 mg/dL). The index date was the date of atherosclerosis diagnosis. Cohorts were 1:1 propensity-score matched on demographics (age, sex, race, BMI) comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, tobacco use, chronic ischemic heart disease), medication (statins, PCSK9-I, ACE-I, ARB, anticoagulants) and stratified LDL cholesterol. Primary outcomes were carotid artery stenosis and myocardial infarction (MI). Secondary outcomes included peripheral artery disease (PAD), MACE and mortality. Outcomes were assessed from 30 days to 5 years after index. Hazard ratios (HR) were estimated by Cox proportional-hazards analysis. Results: After matching, 11,217 patients per group were well-balanced across all covariates (SMD<0.1), including age (65.2 vs 65.0), sex (51.0% male vs 51.3% male) and 6 different LDL buckets. Over 5 years, elevated Lp(a) was associated with higher risk of carotid artery stenosis (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.17-1.40, p<0.01), PAD (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.14-1.38, p<0.01), MI (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.03-1.27, p=0.01), and MACE (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04-1.24, p<0.01). No association was seen for stroke (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.94-1.16, p=0.39) or all-cause mortality (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.84-1.06, p=0.30). Conclusions: In a large, propensity-matched multinational cohort of patients with established atherosclerosis, elevated Lp(a) was independently associated with incident myocardial infarction, carotid artery stenosis, peripheral artery disease, and MACE, but not with stroke or mortality at 5 years. These findings suggest that elevated Lp(a) contributes to atherosclerotic progression across multiple vascular territories.
title: Abstract 16713: Lipoprotein(a) and Risk of Incident Cardiovascular Events in Patients with Established Atherosclerotic Disease

abstract: Introduction: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is predominantly an elective procedure. A small proportion of patients presenting with clinical decompensation may require urgent/emergent TAVR and generally represent a more clinically complex population. Data comparing outcomes between urgent/emergent and elective TAVR in underserved populations are limited. We present characteristics and clinical outcomes of urgent/emergent and elective TAVR cases at Bellevue Hospital, the largest public hospital in the United States. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that urgent/emergent TAVR would be performed in a sicker, higher-acuity patient population, while resulting in comparable clinical outcomes to those undergoing elective TAVR. Methods: We analyzed 100 consecutive patients receiving TAVR at Bellevue Hospital between March 2023 and October 2024, stratified by urgent/emergent cases (n=38) and elective cases (n=62). Demographics, socioeconomic factors, and clinical outcomes were evaluated. Results: All urgent/emergent TAVRs occurred in hospitalized patients, whereas all elective TAVRs occurred in outpatients. Urgent/emergent patients were younger (mean age 73.7 vs 78.2 years) with a similar percentage of female patients (47.4% vs 46.8%) to elective patients. Racial breakdown for urgent/emergent vs. elective cohort was, respectively: 21% vs 19% White, 26% vs 23% Black, 32% vs 11% Asian, and 21% vs 45% Hispanic. The urgent/elective cohort had a higher proportion of high-risk (STS>=8) patients (31.6% vs 12.9%) and higher rates of severely reduced LVEF (EF<30%) (21.1% vs 0%), cardiogenic shock at the time of procedure (5.3% vs 0%), syncope prior to procedure (11% vs 2%) and mechanical circulatory support at the time of procedure (2.6% vs 0%). The urgent/emergent cohort had a longer mean length of stay (13.8 vs 1.8 days) and a higher rate of Medicaid utilization (92.1% vs 79.0%). Regarding outcomes, urgent/emergent cases had higher rates of 30-day readmission (15.8% vs 11.3%), permanent pacemaker placement (10.5% vs 3.2%), and stroke at 30 days (2.6% vs 0%). The urgent/emergent group had lower 30-day mortality (0% vs 1.6%), major vascular complications (0% vs 1.6%), and major bleeding (2% vs 4%). No in-hospital mortality or conversion to surgery occurred in either cohort. Twelve-month mortality was 0% in the urgent/emergent cohort vs. 8.1% in the elective cohort. Functional improvement was seen in both groups: 73.7% of urgent/emergent cases and 88.7% of elective cases demonstrated improvement in NYHA or KCCQ scores. Conclusions: Despite greater clinical acuity and socioeconomic complexity among patients undergoing urgent/emergent TAVR, short-term mortality and functional improvement was comparable to those observed in elective cases. This suggests that a safety-net TAVR program may achieve favorable outcomes among medically complex and underserved patients.
title: Abstract 16737: Urgent/Emergent versus Elective Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: Clinical Outcomes in an Underserved Population at a Municipal Safety-Net Hospital

abstract: Background: Cardiomyocyte (CM) proliferation is a fundamental mechanism of heart growth and regeneration. Tetralogy of Fallot (ToF), a congenital heart disease, imposes biomechanical stress and chronic hypoxemia on the neonatal myocardium leading to CM loss and heart failure. CM proliferation can serve as a mechanism to replenish the loss of functional CMs. However, CM proliferation is also suppressed in ToF, which may be due to secretion of anti-proliferative mediators that inhibit CM cell division. While pro-proliferative mediators have been studied, anti-proliferative mediators are less known. One candidate, endothelin-1 (ET-1), an extracellular peptide hormone, is elevated in ToF and in experimental myocardial injury and acts through endothelin receptors A and B (ET-R A , ET-R B ) on CMs. Hypothesis: Upregulated ET-1 signaling in injured or diseased myocardium inhibits CM proliferation. Methods: Myocardial samples from infants with ToF and control samples were used to determine tissue ET-1 levels by ELISA. ET-1 expression in cryoinjured hearts from neonatal ICR-CD1 mice (male and female) was analyzed by PCR and ELISA. Neonatal rat ventricular myocyte (NRVM) cultures and organotypic cultures of patient-derived ToF tissue were used to evaluate the effects of ET-1 and the ET-R A inhibitor ambrisentan on CM proliferation using H3P staining. The effects of CM-specific ET-R A knockout and ambrisentan treatment on neonatal cryoinjured mouse hearts were evaluated by measuring H3P+ nuclei, scar area (AFOG), mortality, ejection fraction (MRI), and wall stress (MRI). The effects of ET-1 and ambrisentan on NRVM cultures were further analyzed by RNA sequencing and western blotting to identify the signaling mechanisms. Results: ToF hearts (n=5 heart; p=0.0339) and the injury zone of cryoinjured neonatal mouse hearts (n=4; p<0.0001) exhibited elevated ET-1 levels. ET-1 reduced the number of proliferating CMs in NRVM cultures (n=6; p<0.0001), while ambrisentan increased their proliferation (n=4; p=0.0093). In cryoinjured neonatal mouse hearts, ambrisentan increased CM proliferation (n=4-5; p=0.0078), reduced scar area (n=4-5; p=0.0088), lowered mortality (n=18-26; p=0.0338), and improved cardiac function (n=4; p=0.0317); ET-R A knockout produced similar effects. In organotypic ToF myocardial cultures, ambrisentan increased the number of proliferating CMs (n=3-4; p=0.0132). ET-1 upregulated p38 MAP kinase signaling, and the p38 MAP kinase inhibitor SB203580 reversed the ET-1-mediated anti-proliferative effects (n=3; p=0.0038) revealing the role of p38 MAP kinase in the mechanism. Conclusion: Cardiac injury and disease upregulate ET-1, which inhibits CM proliferation and heart regeneration. These effects can be reversed through ET-R A inhibition. Our study identifies ET-R A blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy for cardiac regeneration.

abstract: Background Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) is classically associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but may also occur in elderly patients with basal septal hypertrophy or sigmoid septum morphology. In patients with coexisting calcific aortic valve disease, distinguishing fixed valvular obstruction from dynamic LVOTO can be challenging, particularly when elevated Doppler gradients are attributed primarily to aortic stenosis (AS). Failure to recognize concomitant dynamic obstruction may lead to overestimation of AS severity and inappropriate referral for valvular intervention. Case An 88-year-old woman with hypertension, atrioventricular block status post pacemaker implantation and previously diagnosed moderate AS, undergoing evaluation for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) presented with progressive exertional dyspnea and chest discomfort. Vital signs and ECG were unremarkable. Physical examination revealed a systolic murmur at the aortic area. Symptoms were initially attributed to worsening AS and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Treatment with diuretics and metoprolol resulted in minimal improvement. Repeat echocardiogram revealed prominent basal septal hypertrophy with sigmoid septum morphology, and a calcified aortic valve (Image 1). Continuous-wave Doppler interrogation demonstrated a late-peaking, dagger-shaped waveform, with a resting LVOT peak gradient of 56 mmHg that increased to 75 mmHg with Valsalva, consistent with severe dynamic obstruction (Image 2 and 3). Adjustment of the probe toward the aortic valve showed a parabolic waveform consistent with valvular stenosis, with an aortic valve mean gradient of 16 mmHg and a calculated aortic valve area of 2.38 cm 2 , consistent with only mild AS. Planned TAVR was deferred after recognition that dynamic LVOTO, rather than AS, represented the predominant lesion. Her symptoms began to improve following up-titration of metoprolol. Discussion This case highlights an important diagnostic pitfall during TAVR evaluation. Exertional symptoms, calcific valve disease and elevated Doppler gradient created an anchoring bias toward symptomatic AS. However, sigmoid septum associated basal septal hypertrophy can produce severe dynamic LVOTO that mimics obstructive physiology and confounds assessment of concomitant valvular disease. In this patient, careful Doppler interrogation identified a late-peaking, dagger-shaped waveform with provoked gradient augmentation, establishing dynamic obstruction as the primary lesion. Reliance on peak gradients alone would have overestimated AS severity and potentially led to unnecessary valve intervention. Comprehensive Doppler assessment and waveform morphology are essential when evaluating elderly patients with coexisting septal hypertrophy and calcific aortic valve disease.
title: Abstract 16787: Sigmoid Septum Associated Dynamic LVOT Obstruction Masquerading as Symptomatic Aortic Stenosis During TAVR Evaluation

abstract: Background Rural populations experience a 40% higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease compared with urban counterparts. Yet rural hospitals face unique challenges, including low patient volumes and limited availability of tailored quality metrics for acute care. 1 To address these gaps, the American Heart Association implemented a national rural quality improvement initiative to expand access to evidence-based care through registry participation, rural-specific performance metrics, and targeted support. Methods The Rural Health Care Outcomes Accelerator (RHCOA), launched in July 2022, offering eligible rural hospitals access to 1:1 rural quality support, rural focused education and resources, peer collaboration and no-cost access to Get With The Guidelines®- Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) and/or Heart Failure (HF) registries this included novel metrics aligned with care provided in the resource limited rural setting and meaningful metric composite analysis methodology for lower patient volumes. Eligible hospitals include those located in Rural Urban Commuting Areas 4-10, and/or federally designated Critical Access Hospitals. We compared baseline (2023) and post-implementation (2025) performance on GWTG-CAD populations, including ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), Non-STEMI (NSTEMI), cardiac chest pain, and GWTG-HF preserved and reduced HF populations. Results Between July 2022 and December 2023, 125 new rural hospitals enrolled in GWTG-CAD, 52 in GWTG-HF. Among these early adopter participants, adherence improved for the Rural Acute STEMI composite score (69.6% to 74.4%); (p<0.001), the Rural Acute Non-ST Elevation (NSTE) -Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) including (cardiac chest pain and NSTEMI) composite score (66.9% to 73.8%); (p<0.001), and the HF composite score (70.2% to 81.9%); (p<0.001). Conclusion Participation in the Rural Health Care Outcomes Accelerator (RHCOA) was associated with significant improvements in evidence-based care for STEMI, chest pain/suspected ACS and HF patient populations. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of scalable, registry-based, and rural-tailored strategies to improve evidence-based cardiovascular care delivery in rural hospitals.
title: Abstract 16800: Improved Adherence to Evidence Based Acute Cardiovascular Care in Rural Hospitals: Early Adopter Findings from the Rural Health Care Outcomes Accelerator

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock (CS) complicates a minority of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarctions (STEMI) but remains the leading cause of mortality following acute myocardial infarction. Data regarding the long-term consequences of CS among young STEMI survivors are limited. We evaluated the association of CS with mortality, ventricular arrhythmia (VA) events, and heart failure (HF) hospitalizations among adults aged 18-50 years presenting with STEMI. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults aged 18-50 years with STEMI were identified and stratified by the presence or absence of CS within one day of the index event. Patients with pre-existing implantable cardioverter-defibrillators or permanent pacemakers were excluded. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed for demographics (age, sex, and race) and major comorbidities (Hypertension, Heart Failure, Pulmonary Hypertension, Diabetes Mellitus, Obesity, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Kidney Disease, Obstructive Sleep Apnea) Outcomes were assessed from 1 month to 1 year following the index event. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included a composite of ventricular tachycardia (VT), ventricular fibrillation (VF), ventricular flutter, or cardiac arrest, as well as HF hospitalization. Results: After propensity matching, young STEMI patients with CS experienced significantly higher all-cause mortality compared with those without CS (10.3% vs 3.7%; HR 2.9, 95% CI 2.26-3.72; p<0.01). The composite endpoint of VT/VF/cardiac arrest was also increased in the CS cohort (3.2% vs 2.1%; HR 1.8, 95% CI 1.16-2.75; p<0.01). HF hospitalization occurred more frequently among patients with CS (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.21-2.83; p=0.004). No significant differences were observed in ischemic stroke during follow-up. Conclusions: Among adults aged 18-50 years with STEMI, CS identifies a high-risk phenotype associated with substantially increased 1-year mortality, greater risk of major VA events, and increased HF hospitalization despite rigorous propensity matching. These findings highlight the need for enhanced longitudinal surveillance and risk-stratified post-discharge management among young STEMI survivors complicated by cardiogenic shock.
title: Abstract 16801: Long-Term Clinical and Arrhythmic Outcomes Among Young Adults with STEMI Complicated by Cardiogenic Shock: A Propensity-Matched Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Infective endocarditis (IE) caused by methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) carries high mortality through rapid valvular destruction and acute heart failure. Multivalvular disease with aorto-cavitary fistula (ACF) is exceedingly rare, occurring in 1.8% of native valve IE cases. We present a case of MSSA IE with recurrent aorto-cardiac fistulization despite aggressive surgical intervention. Patient Information: A 34-year-old woman with bicuspid aortic valve and recent MSSA bacteremia from a suspected odontogenic source presented with fever, confusion, dyspnea, and cough. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Vital signs revealed hypotension (104/31 mmHg), tachycardia (145 bpm), and elevated lactate (4.1 mmol/L). Creatinine was 1.93 mg/dL, BNP 3606 pg/mL, troponin 5046 ng/L. Blood cultures grew MSSA. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed tricuspid (15х15 mm) and aortic (8х8 mm) vegetations with aortic root-to-right atrium fistula. Computed tomography demonstrated splenic infarct. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: The patient met criteria for septic and cardiogenic shock with multivalvular IE, left-to-right fistulization, and septic embolic phenomenon. Therapeutic Interventions: She required vasoactive medications, mechanical ventilation, and broad-spectrum antimicrobials. Emergent surgery included aortic valve replacement, root abscess debridement, pericardial patch repair, fistula closure, and tricuspid vegetation excision. Postoperative prosthetic valve endocarditis resolved with targeted antibiotics. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: On postoperative day 19, she decompensated. Emergent TTE revealed recurrent aorto-cavitary fistula to the right ventricle with severe tricuspid regurgitation. Reoperation included septal defect closure and tricuspid valve replacement. Refractory biventricular failure ensued. Despite venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) and vasopressors, perfusion could not be maintained. The family elected comfort-focused care and the patient expired. Discussion & Synthesis: IE carries approximately 17% in-hospital mortality, rising to 40% at one year. ACF is associated with 41% in-hospital mortality despite surgery; residual fistulae carry 100% complication rates within two years. Staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis mortality reaches 40%–80%. High Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores, acute heart failure, and embolic complications are strong mortality predictors. This case illustrates all high-risk features proving fatal despite maximal support. Conclusion: This case demonstrates a catastrophic disease course despite advanced surgical and mechanical circulatory support. Dedicated multidisciplinary endocarditis teams may enable earlier diagnosis and intervention, potentially improving outcomes.
title: Abstract 16802: Recurrent Aorto-Cardiac Fistula in Fulminant Multivalvular Infective Endocarditis

abstract: Introduction: Contemporary diagnostic approaches to constrictive pericarditis (CP) increasingly emphasize echocardiography as the cornerstone of diagnosis. We present a patient with cirrhosis, severe hypothyroidism, and progressive volume overload in whom comprehensive echocardiography established the diagnosis of CP. Patient Information, Clinical Findings, and Timeline: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, cirrhosis, and ascites presented with progressive anasarca, scrotal edema, abdominal distension, and exertional dyspnea despite outpatient diuretic therapy. Abdominal imaging demonstrated cirrhotic liver morphology with moderate ascites, while severe hypothyroidism further complicated the clinical picture. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Diagnostic paracentesis removed 4.3 liters of fluid and demonstrated a serum-ascites albumin gradient >1.1 g/dL with ascitic protein >2.5 g/dL, raising suspicion for cardiac ascites. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated ventricular interdependence with respirophasic septal shift, marked respiratory variation in atrioventricular inflow velocities, annulus reversus, hepatic vein expiratory diastolic flow reversal, a dilated non-collapsible inferior vena cava, and lateral wall strain reduction. Collectively, these findings strongly supported CP. Right and left heart catheterization demonstrated elevated and equalized filling pressures with prominent x- and y-descents and a square-root sign. Cardiac CT confirmed circumferential pericardial thickening greater than 4 mm. Therapeutic Intervention: Following multidisciplinary evaluation, the patient underwent total circumferential pericardiectomy. Follow-Up, Outcomes, and Adverse Events: Intraoperative examination revealed a markedly thickened circumferential pericardium measuring approximately 8 mm, confirming the diagnosis. The postoperative course was complicated by cardiogenic shock, respiratory failure, renal failure requiring dialysis, and prolonged hospitalization. Discussion and Synthesis: This case highlights the diagnostic value of comprehensive echocardiography in constrictive pericarditis. Despite competing hepatic and endocrine explanations for severe volume overload, multiple concordant echocardiographic findings established the diagnosis before invasive evaluation. Consistent with contemporary ACC guidance, invasive hemodynamic assessment and advanced imaging served primarily as confirmatory tests, while echocardiography established the diagnosis. When multiple classic features of constrictive physiology are present, echocardiography may guide management while reserving invasive testing for equivocal cases.
title: Abstract 16816: When the Liver Looks Guilty but the Heart is the Culprit: Echocardiography-Guided Diagnosis of Constrictive Pericarditis

abstract: Introduction: Despite the clinical benefits of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), a substantial proportion of patients remain symptomatic after the procedure. The triglyceride-systemic immune-inflammation composite index (TSI) reflects combined metabolic and inflammatory burden and may provide additional prognostic value. Methods: This retrospective longitudinal cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent transfemoral TAVR at the Heart Center of Kaplan Medical Center between December 2010 and February 2025. TSI was calculated using preprocedural laboratory values and standardized as a z-score (TSI_z). The primary outcome was lack of symptomatic improvement, defined as persistent New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III-IV symptoms, heart failure hospitalization, or persistent NYHA class II symptoms in patients presenting with NYHA class II at baseline. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days and 1 year. Associations were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was used to assess predictive performance. Results: Among 1,032 patients, 190 (18.4%) showed no symptomatic improvement at 1 year. Higher TSI values were associated with increased risk of lack of symptomatic improvement at 30 days (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.01-1.24, P=0.025) and 1 year (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.08-1.28, P<0.001). After multivariable adjustment, the association remained significant at 1 year (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.05-1.25, P=0.003) but not at 30 days. Addition of TSI improved discrimination (AUC 0.68 vs 0.71; DeLong P=0.043). Conclusion: TSI is independently associated with a lack of functional improvement at 1 year after TAVR. Although adding TSI to the clinical model significantly improved discrimination, the incremental gain was modest.
title: Abstract 16839: Triglyceride-Immune Inflammation Composite Index Predicts Lack of Functional Improvement After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Background: The optimal revascularization strategy for chronic total occlusion (CTO) in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) remains uncertain. While CTO revascularization may improve symptoms and myocardial viability, its impact on long-term arrhythmic outcomes has not been well characterized. We compared mortality, ventricular arrhythmias, and heart failure (HF) outcomes among patients with ICM undergoing CTO percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) versus coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adult patients with ICM who underwent CTO PCI or CTO CABG within 3 months of CTO diagnosis were identified. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed for demographics (age, sex, and race) and major comorbidities (Heart Failure, Hypertensive Heart Diseases, Atrial Fibrillation and flutter, Pulmonary Hypertension, Diabetes Mellitus, Obesity, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Kidney Disease, Obstructive Sleep Apnea). Outcomes were assessed from 1 month to 1 year after the index procedure. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included a composite of ventricular tachycardia (VT), ventricular fibrillation (VF), ventricular flutter, or cardiac arrest; VT alone; implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation; and HF hospitalization. Kaplan-Meier analysis and hazard ratios (HRs) were used to compare outcomes.Results:After propensity matching, 1,411 patients remained in each cohort. Compared with CTO CABG, CTO PCI was associated with significantly higher all-cause mortality (HR 2.81, 95% CI 2.02-3.90; p<0.01). CTO PCI was also associated with a higher incidence of the composite ventricular arrhythmia endpoint (HR 2.76, 95% CI 1.81-4.19; p<0.01) and VT alone (HR 2.02, 95% CI 1.31-3.11; p<0.01). HF hospitalization was significantly more frequent following CTO PCI (HR 1.90, 95% CI 1.24-2.90; p=0.01). A trend toward increased ICD implantation was observed in the CTO PCI cohort (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.03-2.62; log-rank p=0.035).Conclusion:Among propensity-matched patients with ICM undergoing CTO revascularization, CTO PCI was associated with significantly higher mortality, VA burden, and HF hospitalization during 1-year follow-up compared with CTO CABG. These findings suggest that the revascularization strategy may influence long-term electrical and clinical outcomes in patients with ICM and CTO, and may warrant further prospective investigation.
title: Abstract 16860: Long-Term Arrhythmic and Heart Failure Outcomes Following CTO Revascularization in Patients with Ischemic Cardiomyopathy: A Propensity-Matched Analysis

abstract: Background: Patients with new or worsening peripheral artery disease (PAD) symptoms experience high rates of healthcare utilization within 12 months. However, risk stratification tools that adopt a multidimensional biopsychological framework of risk remain limited. Identifying key predictors of healthcare utilization may improve individualized risk assessment and inform value-based care models. Objective: To develop a random forest machine-learning model to identify key biopsychosocial predictors of 12-month hospital admissions and emergency department (ED) visits among patients with new or worsening PAD symptoms. Methods: We analyzed data from patients presenting with new or worsening PAD symptoms at U.S. vascular specialty clinics for evaluation in the international, multicenter PORTRAIT registry. The outcome was at least one hospital admission or ED visit within 12 months of enrollment. A total of 45 candidate predictors, including sociodemographic characteristics, comorbidities, cardiovascular risk management factors, PAD-related variables, and health status and psychological measures, were evaluated using a random forest model to identify variables with the highest relative importance (RI). Results: A total of 787 patients were included; the mean age was 68.5±9.6 years, and 42.1% were female. Hospital admission or ED visit within 12 months occurred in 46.3% (364/787), with a mean of 0.91±1.46 events per patient. The most common causes were peripheral vascular (35.0%), nonvascular (34.2%), and cardiovascular (25.5%). Psychological and health status variables were among the highest-ranked predictors. The Peripheral Artery Questionnaire (PAQ) Summary Score had the highest relative importance (RI = 100%), followed by the Perceived Stress Scale-4 (RI = 79%), Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (RI = 71%), EuroQol Visual Analog Scale (RI = 70%), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-2 (RI = 67%) scores. Perceived social support (ESSI) (RI = 76%) and age (RI = 72%) also ranked highly. Clinical history and PAD-related factors were also important, including participation in exercise therapy (RI = 92%), resting ankle-brachial index (RI = 81%), former smoking (RI = 80%), history of cancer (RI = 78%), sleep apnea (RI = 75%), cerebrovascular disease (RI = 75%), prior PCI/CABG (RI = 74%), and prior PVI (RI = 74%). Conclusion: Using a biopsychosocial framework of risk, psychological and health status factors emerged as the highest-ranked predictors of 12-month hospital admission and ED visits in patients with PAD, along with traditional cardiovascular risk factors and other comorbidities.These findings form the foundation for building novel, risk prediction models as a strategy to design value-based care frameworks to reduce health care utilization in individuals with a new or worsening PAD diagnosis.
title: Abstract 16862: Biopsychosocial Predictors of 12-Month Hospitalization Risk in Patients with New or Worsening Peripheral Artery Disease Symptoms: A Machine Learning Analysis from the PORTRAIT Registry

abstract: Background: Pulmonic valve infective endocarditis is exceedingly rare, particularly when caused by Aspergillus species. It carries high mortality, frequently presents with negative blood cultures, and may demonstrate disseminated disease. Case: A 58-year-old male with a past medical history of orthotopic heart transplantation (OHT) six months earlier, prior pulmonary embolism, latent tuberculosis, and chronic anemia presented with low-grade fever, acute hypoxic respiratory failure, hypotension, and atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Despite broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, he developed mixed distributive and cardiogenic shock requiring vasopressors. Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) revealed a large pulmonic valve vegetation causing severe right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, while blood cultures remained negative. Emergent redo sternotomy showed a massive cavitary vegetation extending into the interventricular septum and mediastinum with abscess formation. The patient underwent pulmonic valve replacement, RVOT reconstruction, and radical debridement. Mediastinal abscess cultures grew Aspergillus species, prompting initiation of liposomal amphotericin B; subsequent pathology confirmed invasive aspergillosis involving the pulmonic valve and mediastinum. His postoperative course was complicated by refractory respiratory failure, renal failure requiring continuous renal replacement therapy, coagulopathy, VV-ECMO dependence, and progressive multiorgan failure. Despite maximal support, he died on hospital day 12. Discussion: Aspergillus endocarditis is a rare but devastating complication in immunocompromised patients, particularly after solid organ transplantation. Diagnosis is often delayed because blood cultures are frequently negative and presentations may mimic bacterial infection or thromboembolic disease. Pulmonic valve involvement is exceptionally uncommon and may further obscure recognition. This case demonstrated aggressive invasive disease extending from the pulmonic valve into the RVOT, interventricular septum, and mediastinum with extrapericardial involvement, resulting in mechanical RVOT obstruction and cardiogenic shock. The cavitary appearance suggested an indolent process developing over months. Definitive management required extensive surgical debridement, RVOT reconstruction, and antifungal therapy; however, prognosis remains poor once extensive tissue invasion and multiorgan failure develop. Conclusion: Invasive Aspergillus pulmonic valve endocarditis following OHT is a rare but highly lethal condition that may present with culture-negative shock and RVOT obstruction. Early multimodality imaging, prompt diagnosis, and surgical source control are critical, though prognosis remains poor in advanced disease.
title: Abstract 16900: Invasive Aspergillus Pulmonic Valve Endocarditis with RVOT Obstruction Following Heart Transplantation

abstract: Introduction: Unicuspid aortic valve (UAV) is a rare congenital anomaly (~0.02% prevalence) presenting as acommissural or unicommissural subtypes. Raphae and calcification obscure true valvular anatomy, contributing to frequent misclassification as bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). UAV's abnormal orifice geometry generates turbulent flow and elevated shear stress, predisposing to endothelial injury and infective endocarditis (IE). When IE occurs, complications mirror those of BAV but manifest at younger ages and follow a more fulminant course. Clinical Findings: A 25-year-old male with a lifelong heart murmur presented after three weeks of dyspnea, fatigue, and cough, with hsTroponin 16,900-20,128 ng/dL, proBNP 11,891 pg/mL, and ECG showing anterior ST elevations with reciprocal changes. Despite resuscitation, he required vasopressors and intubation. PA catheter revealed elevated biventricular filling pressures with a Fick cardiac index of 1.5 L/min/m2, with a mixed venous saturation of 23%; Echocardiogram demonstrated an enlarged left ventricle with LVEF 15%, probable BAV with aortic insufficiency (AI) and moderate aortic stenosis. Diagnosis and Interventions: Coronary angiography excluded disease. Transesophageal echocardiogram revealed fused L-R cusps with severe calcification, consistent with BAV, severe AI (pressure half-time 149 ms), and moderate-severe AS (valve area 1.4 cm 2 , maximum velocity 3.5 m/s, mean gradient 32 mmHg). He was taken emergently to the OR where intraoperative findings revealed UAV with R-L commissure abscess. He underwent aortic valve replacement (AVR) with a 23 mm Inspiris Resilia bioprosthesis, annular debridement with bovine pericardial patch repair, and direct aortic Impella 5.5 for post-cardiotomy cardiogenic and vasoplegic shock. Outcomes: Postoperative course included vasoplegia, CVVH-dependent renal failure, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. LVEF improved from 10-15% to 35% at discharge after Impella explant and inotrope discontinuation. Blood cultures were negative; he completed 6 weeks of antibiotics for culture-negative endocarditis. He was doing well at 30-day follow up Conclusion: UAV endocarditis and perivalvular abscess leading to acute severe AI and ultimately profound cardiogenic shock managed with emergent AVR and Impella 5.5 is a previously unreported clinical entity. Notably, the combination emergent AVR and unloading with Impella was the treatment for profound cardiogenic shock from a structural valve issue that would have otherwise made mechanical circulatory support not a viable option.
title: Abstract 16907: Endocarditis Causing Acute Severe Aortic Insufficiency and Cardiogenic Shock Requiring Emergent Aortic Valve Replacement and Impella 5.5 Placement

abstract: Background: In patients with recent acute coronary syndrome (ACS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), coronary microvascular dysfunction (low coronary flow reserve; CFR) and reduced ejection fraction (EF) may coexist or occur in isolation, each with independent prognostic value. The molecular mechanisms underlying these pathological phenotypes, individually and in combination, remain incompletely understood. Research question: This study aimed to identify plasma protein patterns associated with CFR and EF phenotypes in patients with recent ACS. Methods: A total of 291 patients with recent ACS undergoing PCI within 4 weeks of the index event were prospectively recruited (mean age 64±9 years; 86% male). Patients underwent transthoracic Doppler echocardiography-derived CFR and left ventricular EF assessment using the Simpson’s biplane method based on 2D echocardiographic cine loops. Plasma proteins were analyzed using the Olink Target 96 Cardiovascular panel. Patients were categorized into four groups based on CFR and EF: CFR+ (≥2.5) and CFR– (<2.5), and EF+ (≥50%) and EF– (<50%), yielding four groups: CFR+/EF+, CFR+/EF–, CFR–/EF+, and CFR–/EF–. Group differences were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Proteins with FDR<0.05 were visualized as a heatmap of z-scaled group means with hierarchical row clustering. Results: Fourteen proteins differed significantly between groups (FDR<0.05). The CFR–/EF– group showed consistently higher levels of risk biomarkers related to cardiac stress (BNP, NT-proBNP, GDF-15), inflammation (IL-6, PTX3, EN-RAGE, CCL20, TNFSF14), vascular/endothelial dysfunction (VEGF-A, ADM, OPG), remodeling/repair (HGF, GDF-15, OPG), and metabolic dysregulation (resistin), indicating a broadly adverse molecular profile, potentially underlying this disease phenotype. Patients with preserved CFR showed overall lower risk biomarker levels regardless of EF status. Among patients with reduced EF, concomitant microvascular dysfunction (CFR–/EF–) was associated with markedly higher risk biomarker levels compared with CFR+/EF-. Isolated systolic dysfunction (CFR+/EF–) was associated with relatively lower risk biomarker levels, whereas isolated microvascular dysfunction (CFR–/EF+) displayed an intermediate profile. Conclusions: In patients with recent ACS after revascularization, combined microvascular and cardiac dysfunction is associated with higher levels of risk biomarkers reflecting cardiac stress, inflammation, and remodeling. CFR provides incremental biological risk stratification beyond EF and is associated with a high-risk molecular phenotype, particularly in patients with reduced EF.
title: Abstract 16910: Plasma Protein Signatures of Microvascular and Cardiac Function After Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Introduction: Aorto-left atrial fistula is an uncommon complication of valve surgery that may present with heart failure and can be challenging to diagnose. We report successful transcatheter closure guided by multimodality imaging. Case: A 61-year-old female with rheumatic heart disease presented with progressive dyspnea and underwent surgical mitral valve replacement, aortic valve replacement (AVR), and tricuspid valve repair 7 years prior to presentation. Her symptoms initially resolved after surgery. However, for the past two years, she had been experiencing progressive dyspnea with a continuous murmur noted on exam. Diagnostic Assessment: Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricle function, severely elevated right ventricle systolic pressure, and only trace mitral regurgitation (MR). A right heart catheterization (RHC) was performed which showed severe, combined pre and post-capillary pulmonary artery (PA) hypertension (PH): a mean PA pressure of 78 mmHg, wedge of 28 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) of 17.6 WU. Given her history of cardiac surgery, a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was obtained which demonstrated a continuous communication between the aortic root and left atrium adjacent to the prosthetic aortic valve consistent with aorta-to-left atrial fistula. There was also a paravalvular leak with moderate MR ( Panels A-C ). Therapeutic Intervention: Surgical intervention was deemed inappropriate for this patient due to her comorbidity burden and prior sternotomy. Accordingly, the patient underwent percutaneous interventions in two stages. First, an Amplatzer duct occluder was successfully delivered through the aortic root to close the aorto-left atrial fistula ( Panels D-F ). Four months later, an Amplatzer duct occluder II was delivered through transseptal access to close the paravalvular leak. Intraprocedural TEE demonstrated both complete occlusion of the fistula and marked reduction in flow across the paravalvular leak. Follow-up: Six months after intervention, patient reported significantly improved exertional capacity. RHC demonstrated significantly improved pre and post capillary pressures (mean PA 50 mmHg, wedge 35, PVR 7.0 WU). Discussion: In this case we highlight a unique complication of aorto-left atrial fistula following AVR. This case highlights the importance of considering occult structural complications in patients with heart failure symptoms and PH following cardiac surgery. Multimodality imaging was critical for diagnosis and procedural planning. Transcatheter closure may provide a feasible alternative to repeat surgery in selected patients with postoperative aorto-left atrial fistula.
title: Abstract 16918: Aorto-Left Atrial Fistula as a Rare Cause of Pulmonary Hypertension Following Multiple Valve Surgeries

abstract: Background: Current guidelines recommend an LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) target below 55 mg/dL for patients with very high-risk atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Yet, outcomes-based evidence directly validating this target relative to higher levels remains limited. Research Question: Does achieving very low LDL-C (less than 55 mg/dL) reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) compared with higher LDL-C levels in adults with established ASCVD? Methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis per PRISMA 2020. PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched through March 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials enrolling adults with established ASCVD that compared intensive lipid-lowering therapy to achieve LDL-C <55 mg/dL with less intensive therapy or placebo. The primary outcome was MACE (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke). Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, coronary revascularization, hospitalization for unstable angina, and safety outcomes. Pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using random-effects models. Evidence certainty was assessed using GRADE. Results: Five trials met inclusion criteria (FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, IMPROVE-IT, Ez-PAVE, REAL-CAD; N=80,093). Forest plot analysis showed intensive lipid-lowering significantly reduced MACE (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.80-0.93; GRADE: Low), non-fatal myocardial infarction (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.69-0.89; GRADE: Low), non-fatal stroke (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.74-0.98; GRADE: Moderate), and coronary revascularization (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.80-0.91; GRADE: Low). All-cause mortality (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85-1.04; GRADE: Very Low), cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.87-1.05; GRADE: Low), and hospitalization for unstable angina (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.72-1.05; GRADE: Very Low) were not significantly different. Safety outcomes, including new-onset diabetes (RR 1.01), neurocognitive events (RR 0.97), and adverse events (RR 1.01), did not differ significantly (all GRADE: Low to Very Low). Certainty was downgraded for risk of bias, heterogeneity, and imprecision. Conclusions: In adults with established ASCVD, achieving LDL-C below 55 mg/dL significantly reduces MACE, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, and coronary revascularization without excess safety risk. However, the certainty of the evidence is low to moderate. These findings support guidelines recommending intensive LDL-C targets in very high-risk patients
title: Abstract 16942: Cardiovascular Outcomes of Very Low LDL-Cholesterol Achieved versus Higher Levels in Patients with Established Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

abstract: Introduction: High-degree atrioventricular block (HAVB) occurs after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in 6.5%-25.9% of cases. Pacing strategies include left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP), which preserves physiologic conduction, and leadless pacemakers, which avoid transvenous lead- and pocket-related complications. This study’s objective was to compare outcomes of LBBAP vs leadless pacemaker implantation for HAVB after TAVR. Methods: This retrospective, single-system study included consecutive patients who underwent TAVR between March 2023 and September 2025 and received a pacemaker within 30 days of TAVR. Patients were grouped by device type (LBBAP or leadless pacemaker); recipients of other pacemakers were excluded. Device selection was made at the operator’s discretion. Primary endpoints were post-procedure left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), change in LVEF, and pacing dependency (>95% pacing). Secondary endpoints included complication rates through 6 months (pericardial effusion, vascular complication, pneumothorax, device or lead dislodgement, pocket infection/hematoma, and heart failure hospitalization). Results: 95 patients were included in the study, 63 LBBAP and 32 leadless pacemakers. The average age was 83.0 ± 6.3 years, and 52% were male. Baseline conduction abnormalities (LBBAP vs leadless pacing) included LBBB in 6/63 (9.5%) vs 4/32 (12.5%) (p=0.655), RBBB in 21/63 (33.3%) vs 9/32 (28.1%) (p=0.606), and bi-fascicular block in 13/63 (20.1%) vs 6/32 (18.8%) (p=0.828). Pre-existing HFrEF (9/63, 14.3%) and ESRD (4/63, 6.3%) were observed only in the LBBAP group. Baseline LVEF was 60.6 ± 11.8 for the LBBAP and 64.3 ± 6.6 for the leadless pacing group (p=0.049). Follow-up LVEF was 61.0 ± 11.7 for LBBAP and 62.2 ± 8.9 for leadless devices with a change in LVEF of +0.19 and -2.2, respectively (p=0.266). 29 patients in the LBBAP group vs 2 in the leadless pacemaker group had greater than 95% pacing dependency at 6 months (p<0.001). There were 5 complications in the LBBAP group (3 HF hospitalizations, 1 pericardial effusion, and 1 lead dislodgement) vs 1 pericardial effusion complication in the leadless pacemaker group (p=0.362). Conclusion: In this single-center experience, the change in LVEF was similar between the two groups. Pacing dependency was significantly higher in the LBBAP group, likely reflecting a clinical decision for physiologic pacing when pacemaker dependence was anticipated. The total number of complications was higher in the LBBAP group, although not statistically significant. However, the patient population that received LBBAP had more pre-existing HFrEF and ESRD than those who received leadless pacing and had a nominally lower baseline LVEF. Limitations include nonrandomized treatment allocation, confounding by indication, and inability to control baseline comorbidities. Larger randomized studies are needed.
title: Abstract 16986: Comparison of Left Bundle Branch Area Pacing Versus Leadless Pacing Following TAVR

abstract: Patient Presentation: A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with chills, fatigue, myalgias, and generalized weakness following ureteroscopy with basket extraction of left ureterolithiasis and temporary ureteral stent placement. Evaluation revealed anemia, and colonoscopy showed no gastrointestinal bleeding source. During hospitalization, he developed severe substernal chest pain associated with dyspnea and diaphoresis. Initial Workup: Troponin peaked at 199 ng/L, and ECG demonstrated anterior ST-segment elevations (V1-V6). Emergent coronary angiography revealed 100% ostial-to-proximal LAD occlusion, successfully treated with thrombectomy, restoring TIMI-3 flow.
