Methods and Results: We analyzed data from 427 patients (mean age, 83.7 years; 34.2% male) with severe aortic stenosis who underwent TAVI (balloon-expandable valve 71.0%, self-expandable valve 29.0%). Morning blood pressure (BP) and pulse pressure were measured at baseline and on postoperative days 1 (POD1) and 2 (POD2), and analyzed in conjunction with laboratory data obtained on the same days. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality after TAVI. Compared with baseline, BP decreased on POD1, but recovered by POD2 (systolic BP, 130.7, 124.3, and 132.2 mmHg; diastolic BP, 66.0, 49.0, and 65.0 mmHg; P < 0.001 for both). Pulse pressure increased on both POD1 and POD2 compared with baseline (63.0, 74.0, and 66.0 mmHg, respectively; P < 0.001). During a median follow-up period of 719 days after TAVI, 74 patients reached the primary endpoint. When patients were classified into quartiles of systolic BP, diastolic BP, and pulse pressure at each perioperative time point, Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that patients in the lowest quartile of systolic BP and pulse pressure at baseline and POD2 had the lowest survival rates ( Figures 1 , 2 , and 3 ). In multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis, the lowest quartiles of systolic BP and pulse pressure on POD2, but not at baseline, were associated with increased all-cause mortality after TAVI compared with the highest quartiles, after adjustment for confounders including same-day laboratory data. Conclusion: Low systolic BP and pulse pressure on POD2 were associated with increased mortality after TAVI.
title: Abstract 5689: Clinical Significance of Blood Pressure and Pulse Pressure in the Perioperative Period of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation

abstract: Background: Homelessness is associated with increased cardiovascular disease burden, yet its impact on access to advanced resuscitation therapies — particularly extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) — during cardiac arrest hospitalizations remains unexplored. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) 2016-2022, identifying adult hospitalizations with a principal or secondary diagnosis of cardiac arrest. Homelessness was defined by ICD-10 codes. The primary outcome was ECMO/ECPR receipt. Secondary outcomes included coronary angiography, PCI, mechanical circulatory support, in-hospital mortality, and discharge disposition. Multivariable logistic regression with survey-weighted adjustment for demographics, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics was performed. Results: Among 1,413,890 weighted cardiac arrest hospitalizations, 10,085 (0.71%) involved homeless patients. Homeless patients were younger (52.6 vs. 65.6 years), more frequently male, and had markedly higher rates of substance use disorder (48.1% vs. 8.8%) and psychiatric comorbidity. Contrary to our hypothesis, homeless patients had significantly higher odds of receiving ECMO (aOR 2.06, 95% CI 1.10-3.86; p=0.025). However, they were significantly less likely to undergo coronary angiography (aOR 0.75; p=0.009) and far more likely to leave against medical advice (aOR 2.19; p<0.001). In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly between groups (aOR 0.92; p=0.163). Conclusions: Homeless patients with cardiac arrest demonstrate a paradoxically higher likelihood of receiving ECMO, yet face pronounced barriers to coronary evaluation and higher rates of AMA discharge, revealing complex and inequitable patterns in advanced resuscitation care.
title: Abstract 5695: Impact of Homelessness on ECMO Utilization and Survival in Cardiac Arrest Hospitalizations: A Retrospective Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Cardiac catecholamines are classically considered to derive from sympathetic innervation and peripheral circulation; however, whether cardiomyocytes possess an intrinsic catecholaminergic system and its functional significance in cardiac stress responses remain unclear. Objective: To determine whether cardiomyocytes express a functional catecholamine biosynthetic and handling machinery and to define its role in myocardial injury and cellular homeostasis. Methods: Expression of catecholamine biosynthetic enzymes was explored in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs), isolated ventricular cardiomyocytes from adult wild-type CD1 mice, and H9C2 cells using western blotting and immunostaining. A rat regional ischaemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury model, through anterior descending coronary ligation, was used to evaluate in vivo regulation. Functional monoamine uptake and vesicular storage were examined using fluorescent false neurotransmitters. Pharmacological inhibition of catecholamine biosynthesis was performed to assess effects on viability, organelle function, and mTOR/energy-sensing pathways. Results: Cardiomyocytes demonstrated expression of the key catecholamine biosynthetic enzymes tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH), and phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT) across hiPSC-CMs, adult mouse cardiomyocytes, and H9C2 cells. In vivo I/R injury induced coordinated upregulation of TH (p=0.008), AADC (p=0.031), DBH (p=0.008), and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2; p=0.008), consistent with enhanced catecholamine biosynthesis and vesicular handling. Functional studies confirmed active monoamine uptake and vesicular storage within cardiomyocytes. Pharmacologic inhibition of catecholamine biosynthesis in H9C2 cells resulted in a dose-dependent reduction in cell viability (p<0.0001), increased cell death, and heightened susceptibility to oxidative stress. These effects were associated with mitochondrial depolarisation, ER stress, and lysosomal expansion. Mechanistically, catecholamine biosynthesis inhibition suppressed mTOR signalling while activating LKB1-dependent energy stress pathways and ULK1 phosphorylation, consistent with induction of autophagy. Conclusion: Cardiomyocytes possess a conserved and functional intrinsic catecholaminergic system that is dynamically upregulated following myocardial injury and is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and stress resilience. These findings identify a previously unrecognised, cell-autonomous catecholamine pathway in the heart with potential relevance to myocardial adaptation and injury responses.
title: Abstract 5701: An Intrinsic Cardiomyocyte Catecholaminergic System Regulates Myocardial Stress Responses and Cellular Homeostasis

abstract: Introduction: Clot-in-transit (CIT) traversing an atrial septal defect (ASD) causing pulmonary embolus (PE) is life-threatening, with only a handful of cases reported in the literature. Capturing a CIT crossing an ASD on Transthoracic Echochardiogram (TTE) represents a diagnostically rare event. We present one of the few documented cases in which TTE identified a serpentine CIT traversing an ASD, resulting in massive PE. Case: A 62-year-old male with chronic kidney disease status post renal transplant (2022), hypertension, and type II diabetes mellitus presented with five days of progressive dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. On arrival, he was tachypneic and hypoxic, with elevated troponin and proBNP of 11,000 pg/mL. Electrocardiogram demonstrated right bundle branch block with inferior T-wave inversions. CT angiography confirmed massive bilateral pulmonary emboli with significant clot burden, right heart strain, and patchy right-sided consolidations. TTE revealed a hyperdynamic left ventricle (EF 75%), severely dilated right ventricle, large pericardial effusion and a large serpiginous thrombus traversing a previously undiagnosed ASD, extending from the right atrium through the mitral valve into the left ventricular outflow tract. Given rapid hemodynamic detoriation, he was transferred to a tertiary care center where femoral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) was initiated. Percutaneous aspiration thrombectomy of the right pulmonary artery and pericardial drainage were performed; however, his course was complicated by recurrent ventricular fibrillation. He underwent emergent surgical intracardiac thrombectomy, left pulmonary thromboembolectomy, ASD repair and prophylactic left atrial appendage ligation. Post-operatively, acute inferior STEMI secondary to proximal right coronary artery thrombosis was identified and treated with mechanical thrombectomy and stenting. Persistent right ventricular failure necessitated transition from VA-ECMO to right ventricular assist device (RVAD) support, from which he was successfully weaned. Discussion: CIT traversing an ASD on TTE is exceedingly rare, as TEE is generally superior for interatrial septal imaging. CIT is identified in only 2-4% of acute PE cases and CIT across an ASD poses a 5 fold increase in PE mortality. Thin body habitus likely facilitated optimal acoustic windows in our patient. Surgical embolectomy and ASD closure remains the preferred strategy in hemodynamically unstable patients with CIT and ASD. Conclusion: Serpentine CIT traversing an ASD is a rare but catastrophic emergency with potential for paradoxical and systemic embolization. This case highlights the diagnostic value of TTE and the importance of early multidisciplinary interventions including mechanical circulatory support, surgical thrombectomy and ASD closure.
title: Abstract 5735: A Deadly Crossing: Transthoracic Echocardiographic Discovery of a Serpentine Right Heart Thrombus Bridging an Atrial Septal Defect in Massive Pulmonary Embolism

abstract: Background: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is causal in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors (PCSK9i) reduce events in secondary prevention, but their role in primary prevention was unresolved until the recent VESALIUS-CV trial. Hypothesis: Among high-risk adults without prior myocardial infarction (MI) or stroke, PCSK9i reduce LDL-C and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) with acceptable safety. Methods: We searched PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Google Scholar through May 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of PCSK9i versus placebo in adults at high cardiovascular risk without prior MI or stroke. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and assessed risk of bias (Cochrane RoB 2). Placebo-corrected percentage change in LDL-C was pooled using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model; heterogeneity was quantified with I 2 . MACE outcomes were synthesized narratively, anchored on the largest dedicated outcomes trial in this population. Results: Of 863 records screened, four placebo-controlled RCTs (n=1,848) of evolocumab or inclisiran in high-risk adults free of prior MI or stroke contributed to the quantitative LDL-C synthesis: RUTHERFORD-2 and ORION-9 in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, BANTING in type 2 diabetes, and MENDEL-2 in primary hypercholesterolemia. Pooled placebo-corrected LDL-C reduction was 54.4% (95% CI 49.9 to 58.8; I 2 =69%), consistent across populations, with heterogeneity explained by agent class (monoclonal antibody vs siRNA). Cardiovascular outcomes were defined by VESALIUS-CV, which randomized 12,257 adults with atherosclerosis or high-risk diabetes and no prior MI or stroke to evolocumab or placebo (median follow-up 4.6 years). Evolocumab lowered 3-point MACE (coronary heart disease death, MI, or ischemic stroke) by 25% (hazard ratio 0.75; 95% CI 0.65 to 0.86) and 4-point MACE by 19% (hazard ratio 0.81; 95% CI 0.73 to 0.89), with median LDL-C of 45 versus 109 mg/dL at 48 weeks and nominal reductions in cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Across trials, PCSK9i were well tolerated, with no excess of serious adverse events or new-onset diabetes; injection-site reactions were more frequent but predominantly mild. Conclusion: In high-risk adults without prior MI or stroke, PCSK9i achieve large, consistent LDL-C reductions, and evolocumab reduces first major cardiovascular events with a favorable safety profile. These findings support extending PCSK9 inhibition to ASCVD primary prevention.
title: Abstract 5744: PCSK9 Inhibitors for the Primary Prevention of Major Cardiovascular Events in High-Risk Adults Without Prior Myocardial Infarction or Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Current clinical practice relies on the 99th percentile binary cutoff (14 ng/L for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T [hs-cTnT]) to define myocardial injury, yet this diagnostic threshold fails to capture the continuous cardiovascular risk gradient observed in primary prevention populations with detectable-but-below-threshold troponin concentrations. The clinical significance of "normal but detectable" troponin levels remains poorly defined, limiting risk stratification in asymptomatic individuals. This analysis addresses whether a non-linear risk inflection point exists below the diagnostic threshold and proposes a novel risk framework for the micro-injury continuum. Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library from inception to March 2026 to identify relevant studies and performed restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis with four knots positioned at the 10th, 50th, 90th, and 97th percentiles of the continuous hs-cTn distribution below the 99th percentile diagnostic threshold. Data were synthesized from three large primary prevention cohorts: the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study (hs-TnI quintiles and hs-cTnT categories <6, 6-14, ≥14 ng/L), the Dallas Heart Study (n=3,276, median age 43 years), and the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). Primary outcomes included incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and incident heart failure (HF) over median follow-up periods ranging from 4.5 to 12 years. Results: RCS modeling revealed a non-linear risk gradient with a critical inflection point at approximately 4 ng/L for hs-cTnT, well below the 14 ng/L diagnostic threshold. In ARIC, the highest hs-TnI quintile (≥3.8 ng/L) versus the lowest (≤1.3 ng/L) demonstrated multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios of 4.20 (95% CI 3.28-5.37) for HF hospitalization, 2.20 (95% CI 1.64-2.95) for coronary heart disease, and 3.01 (95% CI 2.50-3.63) for global cardiovascular disease. One-year cardiovascular disease incidence increased stepwise across hs-cTnT categories: 1.0% (<6 ng/L), 1.7% (6-14 ng/L), and 5.7% (≥14 ng/L). The Dallas Heart Study confirmed log-linear associations with hazard ratios per 1-SD increase in log hs-cTnT of 1.65 (95% CI 1.40-1.95) for HF and 1.27 (95% CI 1.15-1.32) for global cardiovascular disease. Conclusion: A continuous, non-linear cardiovascular risk gradient exists across the full spectrum of detectable hs-cTn concentrations, with meaningful risk elevation beginning at approximately 4 ng/L—substantially below current diagnostic thresholds. These findings challenge the binary 99th percentile paradigm and support integration of the hs-cTn continuum into primary prevention risk algorithms, enabling earlier identification of subclinical myocardial injury and more precise cardiovascular risk stratification in asymptomatic populations.
title: Abstract 5761: The Micro-Injury Continuum: A Primary Restricted Cubic Spline Defining the Non-Linear Cardiovascular Risk Threshold of 'Normal' High-Sensitivity Troponin

abstract: INTRODUCTION: Permanent pacing after complex congenital heart surgery may be challenging when postoperative anatomy limits conventional transvenous access. We report successful percutaneous dual-chamber pacemaker implantation in a patient with severe Ebstein anomaly following one-and-a-half ventricle repair. PATIENT INFORMATION: A 21-year-old man with severe Ebstein anomaly (87% atrialization of the right ventricle), atrial septal defect (10 mm), ventricular septal defect (5 mm), Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, prior ischemic stroke, cyanosis (SpO 2 85%), and digital clubbing was referred for surgical correction. CLINICAL FINDINGS AND DIAGNOSTIC ASSESSMENT: Preoperative catheterization demonstrated favorable hemodynamics, including mean pulmonary artery pressure 16 mmHg, left ventricular end-diastolic pressure 12 mmHg, and cardiac output 3.94 L/min. Electrophysiological evaluation advised against accessory pathway ablation because it represented the only antegrade conduction pathway, with anticipated postoperative complete atrioventricular block. THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTION: The patient underwent tricuspid valve replacement with a 33-mm bioprosthesis, plication of the atrialized right ventricle, bidirectional cavopulmonary shunt, and closure of septal defects. Postoperatively, complete atrioventricular block developed with pacing dependence. A percutaneous dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted through right subclavian access. The ventricular active-fixation lead was advanced through the superior vena cava-right pulmonary artery-main pulmonary artery route and secured at the low interventricular septum. Atrial lead placement was challenging because of the cavopulmonary connection and prosthetic tricuspid valve. Using an Amplatz catheter and snare support, fixation was achieved at the high lateral right atrial wall. FOLLOW-UP AND OUTCOMES: A dual-chamber generator was programmed in DDD mode. Fluoroscopy confirmed stable lead positioning and appropriate device function. Oxygen saturation improved from 85% to 92%, digital clubbing resolved, and no device-related complications occurred. DISCUSSION: One-and-a-half ventricle repair creates unique challenges for permanent pacing. This case demonstrates that transvenous dual-chamber pacemaker implantation is feasible despite cavopulmonary connections and a prosthetic tricuspid valve when advanced catheter-based techniques are used. Percutaneous pacing may be a valuable alternative to epicardial systems in selected patients with surgically modified right-heart anatomy.
title: Abstract 5797: Percutaneous Dual-Chamber Pacemaker Implantation After One-and-a-Half Ventricle Repair in Severe Ebstein Anomaly

abstract: Introduction: Donation after circulatory death (DCD) provides an alternate strategy to donation after brain death (DBD) in pediatric cardiac donation to increase the donor pool and decrease waitlist times. Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) allows for assessment of cardiac function following circulatory arrest, though it is not available at all centers and is not suitable for all patient sizes. On-table reanimation (OTR) is a novel back-table reanimation technique previously described by our center that allows for ex-vivo assessment of cardiac function following circulatory death prior to transport and recipient implantation. Methods: A retrospective analysis of all isolated pediatric DCD heart transplants performed at our center from January 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025 was conducted. Patients were stratified based on method of reanimation (NRP vs. OTR). The primary outcome was severe primary graft dysfunction (PGD) at 24 hours; secondary outcomes included treated rejection, incidence of treated arrhythmia, and 6-month survival. Wilcoxon rank-sum or Fisher’s exact tests were used for group comparison as appropriate. Results: A total of 17 patients underwent DCD heart transplantation; OTR was used for reanimation in 4 (23.5%) cases. There were no differences in age, sex, race, listing indication, listing status, time on waitlist, use of mechanical ventilation, or mechanical circulatory support at time of transplant. There was a trend towards increased incidence of primary graft dysfunction in OTR recipients compared to NRP, though it did not reach statistical significance (50% vs 8%, p=0.12). Incidence of treated rejection in the first 6 months (25% vs 15%, p=0.58), arrhythmia (0% vs 39%, p=0.21), and 6-month survival (75% vs 92%, p=0.43) were similar among the two groups. Conclusions: Pediatric DCD cardiac transplantation with on-table reanimation demonstrates comparable outcomes to normothermic regional perfusion in its limited use thus far. OTR demonstrates a signal toward higher incidence of severe PGD compared to NRP, though this does not reach statistical significance in a limited sample size. 6 month survival, incidence of rejection, and arrhythmia are similar among the two groups. On-table reanimation may serve as a viable alternate for reanimation when NRP use is limited, thereby increasing the pool of available organs for donation.
title: Abstract 5832: On-Table Reanimation versus Normothermic Regional Perfusion in Pediatric Donation After Circulatory Death Heart Transplantation

abstract: Advanced cardiac therapies, including mechanical circulatory support and heart transplantation, have historically not been considered for patients with muscular dystrophy. With improved life expectancy, these therapies may now be implemented for select patients with muscular dystrophy and advanced heart failure. Here, we describe a 10-year-old male with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD)-associated cardiomyopathy treated with destination Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD). He was diagnosed with DMD at 9 months old (partial duplication of exons 52-61 in the dystrophin gene). Emflazacort was initiated at 6 years of age. Over the 5 years prior to LVAD implantation, he experienced progressive left ventricular dysfunction and began oral therapies with lisinopril, eplerenone, carvedilol, and dapagliflozin. The patient had preserved respiratory function with no oxygen or positive pressure requirement. He became wheelchair-dependent 5 months prior to admission. Despite optimized medical therapy, he progressed to severe left ventricular dilation and dysfunction associated with symptoms of heart failure. He was admitted for severe heart failure exacerbation requiring intravenous inotrope therapy. Evaluation was notable for severe left ventricular dilation and dysfunction (LVEF 16%), severe mitral valve regurgitation, moderate right ventricular dysfunction, and elevated nt-pro-BNP (11,102 pg/mL). With minimal clinical improvement, he was evaluated for LVAD placement. He underwent implantation of a Heartmate 3 LVAD as destination therapy. At time of implant, he weighed 44.2 kg with a body surface area of 1.35 m 2 . Implantation was complicated by ventricular arrhythmias and right ventricular dysfunction. Ventricular tachycardia was initially treated with lidocaine infusion and later transitioned to mexiletine with excellent control. Postoperative right ventricular dysfunction initially required inhaled nitric oxide and inotrope infusions, later transitioned to tadalafil and ambrisentan. He was extubated on postoperative day 13 and discharged home on nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure therapy with no daytime oxygen requirement. Anticoagulation was initially managed with bivalirudin, transitioned to apixaban and aspirin. He was discharged home 2 months after device implantation on medical therapy for heart failure with lisinopril, eplerenone, carvedilol, and dapapagliflozin. He has not had complications of bleeding, thrombosis, stroke, VAD malfunction or alarm. He was admitted for uncomplicated superficial driveline site infection requiring IV antibiotics 10 months after implantation. This represents the youngest patient described with DMD and LVAD implantation. As care of other DMD-related comorbidities improves, advanced cardiac therapies should increasingly be considered for improved quality of life and potential life prolongation.
title: Abstract 5836: Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation in a 10-Year-Old with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy-Associated Cardiomyopathy

abstract: Background: Data comparing left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) to contemporary oral anticoagulants (OAC) in atrial fibrillation remains uncertain. Hypothesis: We investigated the safety and efficacy of LAAO versus OAC in patients with atrial fibrillation. Methods: We conducted a systematic literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, EMBASE, Web of Science (WOS) from inception to April 2026, to identify eligible randomized controlled trials. The primary outcome was composite outcomes (a composite of all-cause mortality, stroke, systemic embolism, major bleeding). Secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, ischemic stroke, major and non-major bleeding, and systemic embolism. Pooled effect sizes were calculated using fixed or random effects models and expressed as risk ratios (RR) or mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence intervals. Results: Six RCTs comprising 7004 patients (LAAO: 3681; OAC: 3323) were included. There was no statistically significant difference in composite outcome between groups (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.76-1.27, p=0.99; I 2 =43.4%). LAAO was associated with a significantly higher risk of ischemic stroke compared to OAC (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.04-1.68, p=0.03; I 2 =0%). Non-major bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAO (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.43-0.58, p=0.002; I 2 =0%) with no statistical difference in the major bleeding outcome (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.73-1.16, p=0.38; I 2 =0%). We found no significant difference between groups in terms of all-cause mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.87-1.22, p=0.65; I 2 =0%), or systemic embolism (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.41-4.07, p=0.65; I 2 =0%). Conclusions: LAAO was associated with a significantly higher ischemic stroke risk, while reducing non-major bleeding, however with no significant reduction in the major bleeding outcome. Additionally, groups were comparable in terms of composite outcomes, all-cause mortality, and systemic embolism. Our findings support an individualized approach to LAAO adoption in clinical practice.
title: Abstract 5847: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion versus Oral Anticoagulation in Atrial Fibrillation: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials

abstract: Introduction: Statin therapy is standard for the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. However, the safety of high-intensity statin therapy remains debatable, including the potential risk of new-onset diabetes mellitus (NODM). Since ezetimibe provides an additional lipid-lowering effect, the combination with a lower statin dose may offer comparable stroke prevention and improves safety in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Purpose: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of statin/ezetimibe combination therapy compared to high-intensity statin monotherapy in a nationwide AF cohort. Methods: The analysis included a total of 644,811 patients with new-onset AF from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The primary endpoint was the 10-year incidence of net adverse clinical and cerebral events (NACCE), defined as a composite of stroke, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), major bleeding, and all-cause mortality. Risks were estimated using Cox hazards models, and inverse probability weighting was applied to reduce confounding. Results: In comparison with low-intensity statins, moderate-to-high intensity statin therapy demonstrated a significantly lower risk of NACCE (HR 0.919, 95% CI 0.848-0.997; p = 0.042), with a greater reduction when combined with ezetimibe (HR 0.877, 95% CI 0.800-0.963; p = 0.006). Only high-intensity statin therapy was associated with an increased risk of NODM (HR 1.253, 95% CI 1.083-1.449; p = 0.024). In direct comparison, moderate-intensity statin/ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with lower risks of NACCE (HR 0.894, 95% CI 0.845-0.945; p < 0.001) and NODM (HR 0.702, 95% CI 0.627-0.786; p < 0.001) than high-intensity monotherapy. No significant differences were observed for ischemic stroke (HR 0.926, 95% CI 0.834-1.028; p = 0.150), major bleeding (HR 0.913, 95% CI 0.752-1.108; p = 0.358), and all-cause mortality (HR 1.018, 95% CI 0.934-1.108; p = 0.691). Conclusion: In this nationwide AF cohort, moderate-intensity statin/ezetimibe combination therapy was associated with lower risks of NACCE and NODM than high-intensity statin monotherapy, with comparable risks of stroke, bleeding, and mortality. These findings suggest that the synergistic effect of ezetimibe co-administration could permit a reduction in statin intensity, thereby potentially mitigating statin-related adverse events without compromising stroke prevention.
title: Abstract 5868: Impact of Ezetimibe on Statin for the Prevention of Stroke and New-Onset Diabetes Mellitus in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: A Nationwide Investigation

abstract: Background: People with HIV (PWH) experience increased cardiovascular risk, yet outcomes following type 1 myocardial infarction (T1MI) remain poorly understood. While prior studies have examined acute coronary syndromes in PWH, data on incident T1MI and subsequent nonfatal cardiovascular outcomes remain limited. We compared one-year outcomes following T1MI between PWH and people without HIV (PWoH). Hypothesis: We hypothesized that PWH would experience worse post-T1MI outcomes than PWoH, including cardiovascular complications and mortality. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 137 individuals (45 PWH and 92 PWoH) diagnosed with incident T1MI at an academic medical center between 2000 and 2020, adjudicated by a cardiologist. The primary outcome was one-year nonfatal cardiovascular complication, defined as a composite of recurrent MI, stroke, heart failure hospitalization, or unstable angina. We used multivariable logistic regression to evaluate the association between HIV status and one-year nonfatal post-MI complications, adjusting for age, sex, race, ethnicity, diabetes, tobacco use, index T1MI treatment, and MI year (≤2012 as reference). Secondary outcomes included 30-day and one-year mortality. Results: PWH experienced T1MI at a younger age (median 54.6 vs 61.3 years) and had greater comorbidity burden. Among PWH, median CD4 was 499 cells/mm 3 (IQR 310-720), 66.7% had suppressed viral load (defined as HIV RNA <50 copies/mL), and 95.6% were on antiretroviral therapy. Prevalence of any nonfatal post-MI complication within one year was 22.2% among PWH and 19.6% among PWoH. Individual complication rates for PWH and PWoH were compared for recurrent MI (4.4% vs 4.3%), stroke (2.2% vs 1.1%), unstable angina (0.0% vs 3.3%), and heart failure hospitalization (15.6% vs 12.0%). Thirty-day and one-year mortality were higher among PWH (2.2% vs 0% and 11.1% vs 2.2%, respectively). HIV status was not independently associated with nonfatal post-MI complication (adjusted OR 1.51, 95% CI 0.51-4.48, p=0.45). Conclusion: Among individuals who experienced incident T1MI, HIV status was not independently associated with nonfatal cardiovascular complications, but one-year mortality was higher among PWH. These findings highlight important post-T1MI differences between PWH and PWoH and underscore the need to better understand mechanisms of post-MI risk among PWH.
title: Abstract 5920: Clinical Outcomes Following Type 1 Myocardial Infarction Among People With and Without HIV

abstract: Background: Newer lipid-lowering therapies (LLTs) increasingly enable patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) to achieve very low low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. Although intensive LDL-C lowering reduces ASCVD risk, concerns persist around potential neurocognitive adverse effects associated with extremely low LDL-C levels. Real-world data evaluating cognitive outcomes among these patients remains limited. Research Question: We evaluated whether achieving LDL-C <30 mg/dL is associated with an increased risk of incident cognitive impairment compared with LDL-C 30-55 mg/dL among adults with established ASCVD receiving LLT. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults aged ≥45 years with established ASCVD receiving LLT, including statins, ezetimibe, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors, inclisiran, or bempedoic acid, were identified. Patients achieving LDL-C <30 mg/dL were compared with those achieving LDL-C 30-55 mg/dL. The primary outcome was incident cognitive impairment, defined as a composite of mild cognitive impairment, cognitive decline, memory disorders, or dementia diagnoses. Secondary outcomes included Alzheimer’s disease (AD), vascular dementia, hemorrhagic stroke, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a composite of acute myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, and coronary revascularization. Outcomes were defined using validated ICD-10 codes and analyzed using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Propensity score matching was performed using 52 baseline variables. Results: After PSM, 173,804 patients were included in each cohort. Mean age was 69.3 years and 33.6% were women. Over a median follow-up of approximately 3.1 years, LDL-C <30 mg/dL was not associated with increased risk of incident cognitive impairment compared with LDL-C 30-55 mg/dL (HR 1.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.98-1.02, p=0.12). No significant increase was observed for vascular dementia (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.92-1.00, p=0.60). AD risk was lower among patients achieving LDL-C <30 mg/dL (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.89-0.98, p=0.01). No significant difference was observed in hemorrhagic stroke risk (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.96-1.04, p=0.91). MACE risk was similar between groups (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.05, p=0.19). Falsification analyses demonstrated no significant associations. Conclusions: Among adults with established ASCVD receiving LLT, achievement of LDL-C <30 mg/dL was not associated with increased risk of incident cognitive impairment, vascular dementia, or hemorrhagic stroke, but was associated with slightly lower hazard of AD. These findings provide reassurance regarding the neurocognitive safety of intensive LDL-C lowering.
title: Abstract 5926: Neurocognitive Safety of Achieving LDL-C <30 mg/dL in Patients with Established ASCVD

abstract: Background: Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a guideline-recommended secondary prevention program that reduces morbidity and mortality among patients with ischemic heart disease (IHD) yet remains underutilized. Over the past decade, the Veterans Health Administration (VA) has implemented strategies to increase CR participation, including automatic referral, CR liaisons, and virtual home-based CR (HBCR) programs as alternatives to traditional center-based CR (CBCR). Objective: To examine temporal trends and factors associated with CR participation among Veterans with IHD from 2012 through 2022. Design, Setting, and Participants: In this observational study, we examined national VA electronic health record data to evaluate CR participation among Veterans hospitalized for IHD, identified using ICD-9 or ICD-10 codes. Exposures: Availability of CR delivery models at VA facilities, including referral to community care programs only, VA CBCR, or VA HBCR. Main Outcomes and Measures: The main outcome was participation in CR within 12 months of the index event, identified using CPT codes and VA stop codes from VA-provided, purchased, or Medicare-claimed services. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with participation. Results: Among 405,907 Veterans with IHD, 63,185 (15.6%) participated in CR. Participation increased from 9.6% in 2012 to 17.1% in 2022 (P for trend <.001), with a peak of 19.7% in 2018. In 2022, participation was higher at facilities offering HBCR (20.0%) compared with those offering CBCR without HBCR (14.8%) or referral to community care programs only (14.3%). In adjusted analyses, Veterans treated at facilities offering HBCR had nearly double the odds of participation (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.90; 95% CI, 1.86-1.95), while those at facilities offering CBCR without HBCR had higher odds of participation (aOR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.24-1.29), compared with referral to community care programs only. As compared with those who did not participate, Veterans who participated in CR were slightly younger and more likely to be male, white, married, obese, and with higher income. They were more likely to have MI, PCI, CABG, COPD, diabetes, and kidney disease but less likely to have heart failure or peripheral vascular disease (p<0.01 for all). Conclusions and Relevance: Between 2012 and 2022, CR participation among Veterans with IHD nearly doubled, coinciding with the expansion of VA HBCR programs. However, fewer than 1 in 5 eligible Veterans received any CR and low CR participation remains a significant gap in care. Broader implementation of HBCR may be an effective strategy to improve CR participation within large health systems.
title: Abstract 5929: Trends in Cardiac Rehabilitation Participation and the Role of Home-Based Programs Among US Veterans Between 2012 and 2022

abstract: Background: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) remain first-line therapy for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (AF), but left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is increasingly used in patients with high bleeding risk or intolerance to chronic anticoagulation. Contemporary randomized data comparing LAAC with DOAC-based therapy remain evolving and require consolidated synthesis. Research Question: We evaluated the efficacy and safety of LAAC versus DOAC-based therapy in randomized trials of patients with high-risk nonvalvular AF. Methods: This PROSPERO-registered meta-analysis (CRD420261384938) included randomized controlled trials comparing LAAC with DOAC-based therapy in patients with high-risk nonvalvular AF. Risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using inverse-variance methods, with fixed- or random-effects models applied according to between-study heterogeneity assessed by the I 2 statistic. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Results: Five randomized controlled trials were included, comprising 6,239 patients randomized to LAAC (n=3,126) or DOAC-based therapy (n=3,113). LAAC did not significantly differ from DOAC-based therapy for composite efficacy outcomes, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, non-cardiovascular mortality, stroke, ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, or major bleeding. LAAC was associated with lower minor bleeding (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.40-0.58; p<0.001; I 2 =6.9%) and clinically relevant nonprocedural bleeding (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.48-0.65; p<0.001; I 2 =0.0%). However, systemic thromboembolism was higher with LAAC (RR 2.53, 95% CI 1.04-6.19; p=0.041; I 2 =28.9%), as were pericardial effusion (RR 2.35, 95% CI 1.15-4.83; p=0.019; I 2 =0.0%) and serious adverse events (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02-1.14; p=0.006; I 2 =0.0%). Conclusions: In contemporary randomized evidence, LAAC demonstrated broadly comparable major efficacy outcomes to DOAC-based therapy and was associated with lower nonprocedural bleeding, but with higher systemic thromboembolism, pericardial effusion, and serious adverse events. These findings support LAAC as a phenotype-selected alternative rather than a universal substitute for anticoagulation in high-risk nonvalvular AF.
title: Abstract 5972: Left Atrial Appendage Closure versus Direct Oral Anticoagulants in High-Risk Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation: A GRADE-Assessed Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials

abstract: Introduction: Gerbode defect, an abnormal left ventricular-to-right atrial (LV-RA) shunt, is a rare acquired complication of structural cardiac interventions. Post-TAVR Gerbode defects may present atypically, delaying diagnosis. We report a post-TAVR Gerbode defect presenting as progressive hepatic failure and cardiogenic shock despite preserved ventricular function. Patient Information: A 71-year-old male with coronary artery disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and severe bicuspid aortic stenosis underwent transfemoral TAVR with a 34 mm Medtronic Evolut valve complicated by complete heart block requiring permanent pacemaker implantation. Postprocedural TTE demonstrated preserved ventricular function and normal prosthetic valve function. He was discharged in stable condition. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Two weeks later, he presented with abdominal distention, transaminitis, coagulopathy, and acute kidney injury. Infectious evaluation was unrevealing. Despite intravenous diuresis for presumed congestive hepatopathy, he progressed to acute liver failure and oliguric renal failure. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Repeat TTE demonstrated preserved biventricular function despite progressive shock physiology. Right heart catheterization demonstrated elevated filling pressures with oxygen saturation step-up from the superior vena cava (57%) to pulmonary artery (75%) and Qp:Qs (pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio) 2.9, suggesting a significant left-to-right shunt. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) confirmed LV-to-RA shunting through a ventricular septal defect (Gerbode defect) related to recent TAVR. Therapeutic Intervention(s): A 14 mm Abbott Amplatzer ASD occluder device partially reduced shunt flow (Qp improved to 1.9) but was complicated by severe hemolysis, ongoing right-sided heart failure, and cardiogenic shock. He subsequently underwent emergent open ventricular septal defect repair, TAVR explantation, and surgical bioprosthetic valve replacement. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Postoperatively, the patient had refractory multiorgan failure requiring vasopressors, dialysis, and transfusions. He developed mesenteric ischemia requiring emergent bowel resection. Despite maximal therapy, he progressed to septic shock and multiorgan failure. After goals-of-care discussions, he was transitioned to comfort care and expired. Discussion & Synthesis: This case highlights a rare TAVR complication and important diagnostic pitfall. Preserved ventricular function and failure to visualize the VSD on TTE obscured severe shunt physiology, delaying diagnosis. After TAVR, unexplained right-sided heart failure or end-organ dysfunction should prompt consideration of occult intracardiac shunting. Hemodynamic assessment with right heart catheterization and TEE were essential for establishing the diagnosis.
title: Abstract 6000: A Diagnostic Dilemma Following TAVR: Occult Iatrogenic Gerbode Defect Presenting as Progressive Hepatic Failure and Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) such as semaglutide are widely used for obesity management. While gastrointestinal adverse effects are common, severe hemodynamic complications are rarely described. Patient Information: A 35-year-old man with obesity, hypertension, ADHD, and migraines presented with syncope after restarting semaglutide at the maximum dose (2.4 mg weekly) following several months of discontinuation. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Following semaglutide reinitiation, the patient developed several days of progressive nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention, and poor oral intake. He subsequently experienced syncope during routine exercise, prompting a presentation to the ED. Shortly after arrival, he developed recurrent syncope with profound hypotension (72/46 mmHg) and tachycardia (126 bpm), requiring central venous access, aggressive fluid resuscitation, and escalation to triple vasopressor therapy. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Laboratory studies revealed hemoconcentration, leukocytosis, and dynamic troponin elevation with EKG changes. TTE demonstrated preserved biventricular function without structural abnormalities. CT revealed marked gastric distention with compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC) and reduced caval cross-sectional area. Troponin elevation was attributed to demand ischemia in the setting of obstructive shock. Therapeutic Intervention: Despite rapid administration of intravenous fluids and multiple vasopressors, hypotension persisted. Following a large-volume emesis during attempted nasogastric tube placement, the patient experienced rapid hemodynamic improvement allowing complete vasopressor discontinuation within minutes. Recurrent hypotension later resolved again following successful nasogastric decompression. He was subsequently treated with bowel rest, metoclopramide, and antiemetics. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: The patient remained hemodynamically stable following gastric decompression and tolerated advancement of oral intake. He was discharged home without recurrent symptoms. Discussion & Synthesis: This case highlights a rare but severe complication of improper GLP-1 RA reinitiation. Abrupt resumption of high-dose semaglutide likely precipitated massive gastric distention causing IVC compression, impaired venous return, and obstructive shock physiology analogous to aortocaval compression. The reproducible resolution of hypotension following spontaneous emesis and nasogastric decompression strongly supports a mechanically mediated process. Early recognition of this physiology is critical, as gastric decompression may be lifesaving. Patient Perspective: The patient reported immediate relief in abdominal pressure and dizziness following decompression.
title: Abstract 6031: Hemodynamic Collapse Following High-Dose Semaglutide Reinitiation

abstract: Background: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with an initial shockable rhythm is frequently caused by acute coronary syndrome. Guidelines recommend immediate coronary angiography after OHCA only in the setting of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). However, traditional STEMI criteria may have limited sensitivity and specificity for occlusive myocardial infarction (OMI) in the post-OHCA setting. Artificial intelligence (AI) models have shown promise in detecting OMI from ECG, though their utility after OHCA is unknown. Research hypothesis: AI-ECG can detect occlusive myocardial infarction after shockable OHCA with comparable accuracy to cardiologist-assessed STEMI criteria. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at University of Washington of patients with OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm who underwent coronary angiogram and had a digital ECG available within 30 days post-arrest (2013-2023). Patients without an ECG prior to angiography were excluded. Coronary angiograms were adjudicated for OMI, defined as thrombotic lesion with abnormal TIMI flow, or an obstructive lesion with normal TIMI flow and a peak troponin ≥70 times the upper limit of normal. Each case was reviewed for STEMI or STEMI-equivalent criteria using all available clinical data leading up to angiography. The first available hospital ECG was analyzed by the AI model to predict presence of OMI. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and compared using the DeLong test. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were also calculated. Results: Of 295 OHCA cases undergoing angiography, OMI was present in 139 (47%). Compared to cardiologist-assessed STEMI criteria, AI-ECG showed superior discrimination for OMI (AUROC 0.83 [95% CI: 0.78-0.87] vs. 0.78 [95% CI: 0.73-0.82], p=0.047), higher sensitivity (70% vs. 63%), lower specificity (85% vs. 93%), lower PPV (80% vs. 89%) and higher NPV (76% vs. 74%). There were 52 OMI cases labeled by cardiologists as NSTEMI, of which the AI ECG model correctly predicted OMI in 21 (40%) cases. There were 42 OMI cases missed by the AI ECG model, of which cardiologists labeled STEMI or STEMI-equivalent in 11 (26%) cases. Conclusion: AI-ECG analysis after OHCA accurately predicts OMI with superior discrimination and comparable predictive accuracy compared to cardiologist-assessed STEMI criteria. AI-ECG identified 40% of individuals with OMI not meeting guideline-indication for urgent angiography after OHCA.
title: Abstract 6032: Artificial Intelligence ECG Accurately Predicts Occlusive Myocardial Infarction Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with Shockable Rhythm

abstract: Introduction: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) is an uncommon sterile valvular process associated with hypercoagulable and autoimmune conditions, particularly antiphospholipid syndrome (APLS). It is most commonly described on the mitral and aortic valves; predominant right-sided and multivalvular involvement is a rare entity and can mimic infective endocarditis. Patient information: 39-year-old female with a past medical history of provoked deep venous thrombosis (DVT), unprovoked pulmonary embolism (PE) requiring catheter-directed thrombectomy (CDT) on Rivaroxaban, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), and triple-positive APLS presenting with progressive dyspnea and decreased exercise tolerance. She denied history of intravenous drug use, indwelling catheters, or recent procedures. Clinical findings: On presentation, she was hemodynamically stable, afebrile and requiring 2L NC. Exam was notable for bilateral lower extremity edema. Diagnostic assessment: APLS panel with beta-2-glycoprotein and lupus anticoagulant was positive. Blood cultures and infectious work up was negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated new globular echo densities involving the tricuspid valve with severe tricuspid regurgitation. Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) revealed multiple >1 cm bulky echo densities involving all three tricuspid valve leaflets with severe regurgitation, mobile echo densities on the pulmonic valve (1cm), and small linear echo density on the aortic valve (3mm). Therapeutic Intervention: The patient was managed with diuresis for volume overload. Rivaroxaban was discontinued, heparin was initiated, and she was bridged to Warfarin. Follow-up and Outcomes: The patient demonstrated clinical improvement with resolution of dyspnea and reduction in lower extremity edema. She was discharged on warfarin. Multi-disciplinary consultant follow-up was arranged with plans for repeat outpatient TTE and INR monitoring. Discussion: This case illustrates a rare presentation of NBTE with predominant right-sided and multivalvular involvement in the setting of triple-positive APLS. The patient’s history of provoked DVT, unprovoked PE/DVT, and concomitant CTEPH reflects the high thrombotic burden of APLS. Additionally, initial treatment with DOAC was inefficient at mitigating the thrombotic risk, as the cornerstone of management is centered around vitamin K antagonists. Takeaways: NBTE should be considered in patients with APLS presenting with new valvular disease in the absence of infection; right-sided valvular involvement should not exclude this diagnosis. Anticoagulation with vitamin K antagonists remains the evidence-based treatment for this patient subset. Limitations include inability to obtain histopathological confirmation of NBTE, as the patient did not undergo surgical intervention.
title: Abstract 6036: Multivalvular Right-Sided Non-Bacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis in Antiphospholipid Syndrome: A Case Report

abstract: INTRODUCTION: As life expectancy in persons with hemophilia (PWH) approaches that of the general population, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease has become increasingly prevalent. While PCI in PWH with acute coronary syndromes has been described, no prior case has reported left main PCI complicated by cardiogenic shock in a hemophilia B patient — requiring simultaneous management of life-threatening ischemia and severe hemorrhagic risk. PATIENT INFORMATION: The patient was a 62-year-old male with moderate hemophilia B (baseline factor IX activity 8%), prior coronary artery bypass grafting (LIMA to LAD; radial artery to RCA), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes. He had a history of major bleeding after dental extractions without factor IX prophylaxis. CLINICAL FINDINGS & TIMELINE: He presented with acute chest pain and hemodynamic instability (blood pressure 86/50 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm). Electrocardiogram showed deep ST-segment depression in V2-V6, I, and aVL with T-wave inversions. Troponin I was 7.25 ng/mL and CK-MB 7.7 ng/mL. DIAGNOSTIC ASSESSMENT & REASONING: Findings were consistent with NSTEMI and cardiogenic shock. Urgent coronary angiography via radial access revealed a 95% calcified left main stenosis with patent bypass grafts and incomplete circumflex filling via retrograde LAD collaterals. THERAPEUTIC INTERVENTION: Hematology was consulted emergently and recommended factor IX concentrate (7,000 IU) before antithrombotic therapy. The patient then received unfractionated heparin, eptifibatide, aspirin, and clopidogrel 600 mg. An intra-aortic balloon pump provided hemodynamic support. Left main PCI was performed with a 4.0 х 15 mm bare-metal stent, achieving 5% residual stenosis with immediate circumflex flow restoration. Post-procedurally, factor IX infusions targeted 100% activity for 72 hours, then twice-weekly infusions maintaining trough levels of 15-20% throughout the six-week dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) course. FOLLOW-UP, OUTCOMES & ADVERSE EVENTS: The patient achieved full clinical recovery and was discharged without bleeding or thrombotic complications during the DAPT period. DISCUSSION & SYNTHESIS: To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of successful primary left main PCI in a hemophilia B patient with cardiogenic shock. Success relied on four principles: emergent hematology-cardiology collaboration; pre-procedural factor IX repletion; radial access to reduce bleeding risk; and a post-procedural factor IX bridging protocol aligned with DAPT duration. Antithrombotic therapy must be individualized to balance thrombosis and hemorrhage in PWH. Bare-metal stenting limited DAPT exposure; however, polymer-free drug-coated stents with abbreviated DAPT may be superior in future cases. This case highlights the need for prospective registries and consensus guidelines for acute coronary syndromes in PWH.
title: Abstract 6044: Primary Left Main Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in a Hemophilia B Patient Presenting with Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Introduction: Transcatheter tricuspid valve intervention (TTVI) is a novel treatment option for severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR), particularly those with high surgical risk. However, even after successful reduction of TR with TTVI, pulmonary hypertension (PH) may persist or occur in a subset of patients. No consensus exists on an effective approach for detecting underestimated PH or right ventricle-pulmonary artery (RV-PA) uncoupling after procedure. Hypothesis: This study aimed to develop a deep learning model capable of non-invasively identifying RV-PA uncoupling. Methods: Patients with symptomatic severe TR without severe PH who underwent TTVI were enrolled. Clinical characteristics, catheterization findings, and echocardiographic data were collected. The endpoints included all-cause mortality, ventricular systolic dysfunction, and PH at 1-year follow-up. Using statistical tests to assess feature significance, correlation, and redundancy. To predict post-TTVI PH, all analyses were performed using Python 3.6. The target variable was defined as postoperative PH. The data were split into training and test sets in a 7:3 ratio using stratified random sampling. L1-regularized logistic regression was used for feature selection and redundancy removal based on prior statistical analyses. The top three features were selected for model development. Multiple classifiers were trained on the selected features. The model performance was evaluated using accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), specificity, recall, precision, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), kappa, and p-value. Results: Overall, 144 patients from two centers underwent TTVI. The cohort consisted of older adults (mean age 70.3 ± 8.2 years), with a female predominance (60.4%). During the 1-year follow-up, the all-cause mortality rate was 4.9%. Ten patients developed mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (48.6 ± 4.3%). PH was observed in 44 patients. A non-invasive model was developed based on three predictive features. Among all classifiers, LightGBM achieved the best overall performance, yielding an AUC of 0.766, accuracy of 0.735, recall of 0.690, specificity of 0.752, and MCC of 0.412 (P = 0.069). Gradient Boosting also demonstrated competitive performance during training. In external validation, Gradient Boosting model demonstrated the best overall performance, achieving an accuracy of 0.835, AUC of 0.766, recall of 0.921, specificity of 0.62, and MCC of 0.577 (P < 0.0001). Conclusions: An AI-guided multimodal echocardiography framework effectively predicted post-TTVI PH and RV-PA uncoupling. These findings may improve individualized risk stratification and provide prognostic values. Keywords: transcatheter tricuspid valve intervention, tricuspid regurgitation, right ventricle-pulmonary artery uncoupling, machine learning
title: Abstract 6047: AI-Guided Framework for Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Vascular Uncoupling Following Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Intervention

abstract: Introduction: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is an established alternative to long-term anticoagulation for stroke prevention in selected patients with atrial fibrillation. Infective endocarditis involving LAAO devices is rare, likely because of progressive endothelialization after implantation. We describe an early case of methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infective endocarditis involving an Amplatzer Amulet device. Patient Information: A 58-year-old man with sick sinus syndrome status post dual-chamber pacemaker and paroxysmal atrial flutter/fibrillation status post cryoablation, redo pulmonary vein isolation, vein of Marshall ethanol ablation, and recent Amulet implantation presented two weeks after the procedure. Clinical Findings & Timeline: He presented with altered mental status, fever, confusion, and seizure-like activity. On arrival, he was febrile to 101.7°F and hypotensive to 98/58 mmHg with mild leukocytosis. Two sets of blood cultures grew MSSA. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Given MSSA bacteremia in the setting of recently implanted intracardiac hardware, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) was performed. TEE demonstrated a well-seated Amulet device without peri-device leak, with multiple mobile echodensities attached to the device, consistent with device-related infective endocarditis (Fig 1). Therapeutic Interventions: Antibiotics were narrowed to oxacillin and rifampin based on Infectious Disease recommendations. Given concurrent intracardiac hardware and MSSA bacteremia, the pacemaker system was removed. Follow-up & Outcomes: Repeat TEE after 12 days of targeted antibiotic therapy demonstrated interval reduction in vegetation size (Fig 2). He was discharged on prolonged intravenous antibiotics with a plan for repeat TEE in 8 weeks. Discussion & Synthesis: LAAO device-related infective endocarditis is exceedingly uncommon. In this case, early post-implant MSSA bacteremia likely seeded the device before complete endothelialization. This case highlights the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for LAAO device infection in patients with recent implantation and Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. Because optimal management remains uncertain, additional cases are needed to define when prolonged antibiotics are sufficient and when device removal should be considered.
title: Abstract 6070: A Rare Case of Bacterial Vegetation on an Amplatzer Amulet Left Atrial Appendage Occluder Device

abstract: Background: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) is a well-established intervention for severe aortic stenosis. However, cardiovascular and renal complications following the procedure are still prevalent and are linked to poorer prognoses. Although GLP-1 receptor agonists have shown cardiometabolic advantages in atherosclerotic disease, their effect on patients undergoing TAVR remains uncertain. This study investigates the relationship between pre-procedural use of GLP-1 receptor agonists and subsequent cardiovascular and renal outcomes post-TAVR. Hypothesis: Pre-procedural GLP-1 RA use in TAVR patients is associated with reduced cardiovascular and renal complications. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was performed utilizing the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adult individuals (aged 18 years and older) undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement(TAVR) were identified through CPT and ICD-10-PCS codes. Participants were stratified based on exposure to Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1 RA), including liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, and lixisenatide, within a 12-month period preceding the procedure. Propensity score matching at a ratio of 1:1, considering demographics, comorbidities and baseline medications, resulted in two cohorts of 2,550 patients each. The study evaluated outcomes such as myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, all-cause mortality, stroke, and acute kidney injury, with exclusion of patients with prior history of these outcomes. The analytical methods employed included risk difference, risk ratio, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, Cox proportional hazards models, and comparison of event frequencies. Results: GLP-1 RA use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (17.0% vs 27.9%; RR 0.61; p=0.001; ARR 10.9%), myocardial infarction (8.2% vs 11.9%; RR 0.69; p=0.001), and acute kidney injury (17.9% vs 22.9%; RR 0.78; p=0.001). No significant differences were observed in heart failure (30.3% vs 33.1%; p=0.293), arrhythmias (31.4% vs34.8%; p=0.110), or stroke (7.9% vs 9.4%; p=0.072). Kaplan-Meier analyses showed no significant time-to-event differences for most outcomes, with evidence of non-proportional hazards for mortality and AKI. Mean follow-up was shorter in the GLP-1 RA group (795 vs 1,239 days), which may have influenced time-dependent analyses. Conclusion: Pre-procedural GLP-1 RA use was associated with decreased risks of myocardial infarction, acute kidney injury, and all-cause mortality following TAVR. Although residual confounding may exist, these findings indicate potential benefits and underscore the need for prospective studies to establish causality and evaluate clinical utility.
title: Abstract 6083: Glucagon-Like Peptide- 1 Receptor Agonists Before Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Propensity-Matched Analysis of Mortality and Cardiorenal Protection

abstract: Background: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) reduces ischemic risk but imposes a haemorrhagic burden associated with increased morbidity. Major bleeding complicates long-term management across acute coronary syndromes (ACS) and chronic coronary syndromes, underscoring the need for safer antithrombotic strategies. P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy following short-term DAPT has been proposed as a safer alternative, yet reported outcomes across individual randomized trials have been inconsistent, and the optimal strategy remains incompletely defined. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched through April 2026 for randomized trials comparing P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy after short-term DAPT with standard DAPT (6 to 12 months) in adult patients undergoing PCI with drug-eluting stents for ACS or CCS. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Trial sequential analysis (TSA), prespecified subgroup analyses, and GRADE certainty assessment were performed. Results: Twelve trials enrolling 48,778 patients were included. P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy significantly reduced major bleeding (1.2% vs. 2.0%; RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.37–0.68; P<0.001), all bleeding (3.1% vs. 4.8%; RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.40–0.65; P<0.00001), and net adverse clinical events (NACE) (6.0% vs. 7.2%; RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.70–0.89; P<0.0002). No significant differences were observed in Major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), myocardial infarction, stroke, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, stent thrombosis, or target vessel revascularization. Trial sequential analysis confirmed the robustness of bleeding and NACE reductions and crossed the futility boundary for MACCE, providing reassurance against meaningful ischemic harm. The bleeding benefit was predominantly driven by ACS patients (P for interaction <0.0001), consistent across both early and delayed aspirin withdrawal strategies, and observed with all P2Y12 agent subtypes, though ticagrelor monotherapy uniquely demonstrated significant reductions in both NACE and MACCE. GRADE certainty was moderate for mortality and low for remaining outcomes, driven by open-label designs and heterogeneity. Conclusions: P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy after short-duration DAPT significantly reduced bleeding and improved net clinical outcomes without increasing ischemic events. These findings support P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy as an evidence-based antiplatelet de-escalation strategy after PCI, though the predominant bleeding benefit in ACS patients and the clinical superiority of ticagrelor underscore the necessity of individualized patient selection and deliberate agent choice in clinical practice.
title: Abstract 6087: P2Y12 Inhibitor Monotherapy Following Short-Duration Dual Antiplatelet Therapy After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials

abstract: Background: Aconite, AKA wolfsbane or monkshood, is used in traditional Chinese herbal preparations. It contains aconitine alkaloids that persistently activate voltage-gated sodium channels, producing malignant ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension, and neurotoxicity. Even small doses may be fatal, and electrical storm represents the most severe manifestation. We report two fatal cases of aconite-induced electrical storm following ingestion of OTC herbal preparations. Case 1: A 65-year-old woman ingested an OTC aconitum-based remedy for arthritis. She rapidly developed severe GI symptoms, hypotension, leukocytosis, AKI, hypokalemia, and lactate 17 mmol/L. ECG showed sinus tachycardia with QTc prolongation, progressing to pulseless polymorphic VT. She underwent extensive ACLS with >15 shocks, amiodarone and lidocaine boluses and infusions, electrolyte repletion, bicarbonate, epinephrine, and atropine. Despite transfer to an ECMO-capable center, she remained in refractory electrical storm with multiorgan failure. The family declined ECMO, and she died shortly thereafter. Case 2: A 56-year-old man ingested the same OTC aconitum-based remedy for arthritis. He developed immediate GI symptoms, diaphoresis, paresthesias, and hypotension. Labs revealed leukocytosis, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, and lactate 11.3 mmol/L. He progressed to recurrent polymorphic VT/VF requiring multiple shocks, epinephrine, lidocaine, amiodarone, bicarbonate, and magnesium. Antiarrhythmic infusions were initiated, and he was transferred for ECMO evaluation, but he remained in refractory shock with persistent electrical storm. The family elected comfort care, and he died shortly after arrival. Discussion: Aconite poisoning is a rare life-threatening cause of electrical storm. Electrical storm is 3 or more episodes of VT, VF, or appropriate shocks from an ICD within 24 hours. Both cases developed malignant ventricular arrhythmias within hours of ingestion and remained refractory to amiodarone, lidocaine, and magnesium. Case reports suggest lidocaine may be more effective than amiodarone due to its MOA, and flecainide has been proposed as an alternative. Management requires rapid stabilization, airway protection, vasopressor support, and repeated ACLS. ECMO may be lifesaving, and some reports describe benefit from hemoperfusion with CVVH, though outcomes remain poor in severe toxicity. Conclusion: Aconite ingestion can trigger rapid-onset electrical storm resistant to standard antiarrhythmics. Early engagement with intensivists, cardiologists, nephrologists, antiarrhythmic therapy, aggressive supportive care, and timely mechanical circulatory support may improve survival. These cases highlight the importance of a detailed drug/supplement history. Public education and regulation of herbal preparations are essential preventive strategies.
title: Abstract 6112: Aconite Poisoning Triggering Lethal Electrical Storm

abstract: Introduction: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction that can progress to myasthenic crisis requiring mechanical ventilation. Intravenous magnesium sulfate is contraindicated in MG due to inhibition of neuromuscular transmission, yet hypomagnesemia increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and stent thrombosis in patients with recent coronary stents. No guidelines address this clinical dilemma. We present the case of a patient with MG and recent coronary stent placement who developed myasthenic crisis following emergent surgery, requiring a novel threshold-based magnesium replacement strategy to balance competing neuromuscular and cardiovascular risks. Case Presentation: A 67-year-old man with MG managed with pyridostigmine and mycophenolate mofetil, and coronary artery disease status post two left anterior descending artery drug-eluting stents (DES) placed one month prior on dual antiplatelet therapy, presented with hypotension and shortness of breath. Computed tomography revealed pneumoperitoneum from a duodenal perforation, and emergent exploratory laparotomy with Graham patch repair was performed. On postoperative day (POD) 3, the patient developed respiratory acidosis (pH 7.244, PaCO 2 53 mmHg), bradycardia, hypotension, and bulbar weakness consistent with myasthenic crisis, requiring intubation. Serum magnesium progressively declined from 2.0 to 1.3 mg/dL (reference 1.7-2.4) during the intensive care unit course. A threshold-based replacement strategy was implemented: two grams of intravenous magnesium sulfate infused over two hours only when serum levels fell below 1.4 mg/dL, with continuous telemetry and serial neuromuscular assessments. Five sessions of plasma exchange were completed. The patient tolerated cautious magnesium repletion without cardiac arrhythmias or worsening weakness. After two failed extubation attempts (negative inspiratory force [NIF] –15 cmH 2 O each), successful extubation occurred on POD 15 (NIF –26 cmH 2 O). By POD 36, the patient was clinically stable with improved strength and discharged to inpatient rehabilitation. Discussion: This case demonstrates that individualized, threshold-based magnesium replacement can safely balance competing neuromuscular and cardiovascular risks when MG coexists with recent coronary stent placement. Low serum magnesium independently predicts major adverse cardiac events after DES implantation and acute stent thrombosis, while the FDA explicitly contraindicates magnesium sulfate in MG. The 1.4 mg/dL threshold represented a pragmatic compromise, permitting repletion at levels associated with highest cardiac risk while minimizing magnesium exposure. Plasma exchange likely improved the margin of safety by enhancing neuromuscular transmission. Formal guidelines addressing magnesium management in this population are needed.
title: Abstract 6130: Magnesium Management Challenges in Myasthenic Crisis Post-Graham Patch Repair with Recent Coronary Stents: A Case Report

abstract: Introduction: Chimeric Antigen Receptor-T cell (CAR-T) therapy has transformed outcomes for patients with hematologic malignancies, in particular Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). However, its cardiovascular toxicity is incompletely characterized, limiting patient optimization and risk-stratification strategies. We investigated Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE) incidence, associated risk factors, and mortality outcomes in a national Medicare cohort. Methods: This study used national 100% Medicare Fee-For-Service and Advantage claims data to identify beneficiaries over 65 who received inpatient CAR-T for DLBCL between 2017 and 2023. Patient demographics, baseline comorbidities, and chemotherapy exposures were assessed during the 12 months prior to CAR-T. The primary outcome, MACE during the CAR-T index hospitalization, was defined as a composite of acute heart failure (HF), cardiogenic shock, myocardial infarction (MI), cardiac tamponade, ventricular arrhythmia, complete heart block, or stroke. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of index MACE, and in-hospital and 1-year mortality. Results: Of 3324 patients (mean age 73.3, 40.1% female, 85.8% white, see Table) who received CAR-T in the study period, 194 (5.8%) experienced MACE. Patients with MACE were more frequently male and had higher rates of baseline cardiac comorbidities, such as HF, atrial fibrillation (AFib), hypertension, prior cerebrovascular accident (CVA) / intracranial bleed, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, peripheral artery disease, obesity, prior MI, and cytarabine exposure. In multivariable analyses, independent predictors of in-hospital MACE included HF (OR 2.27 [1.56-3.30]), prior CVA/intracranial bleed (OR 2.70 [1.42-5.13]), AFib (OR 1.45 [1.01-2.08]), cytarabine exposure (OR 1.90 [1.07-3.38]), and doxorubicin exposure (OR 1.38 [1.02-1.86]). In-hospital mortality occurred in 155 patients (4.7%); independent predictors included index MACE (OR 13.3 [9.00-19.57]), prior Ventricular Tachycardia (OR 3.32 [1.64-6.71]), doxorubicin exposure (OR 1.55 [1.12-2.17]). Post-discharge 1-year mortality occurred in 663 patients (20.0%); index MACE (OR 1.69 [1.12-2.55]), doxorubicin exposure (OR 1.64 [1.35-2.00]), and AFib (OR 1.42 [1.10-1.83]) were independent predictors. Conclusions: In the largest known cohort of older adults undergoing CAR-T therapy for DLBCL, MACE occurred in 5.8% of patients and predicted a 13-fold increase in index mortality and a 1.7-fold increase in 1-year mortality. Established cardiac comorbidities and prior doxorubicin exposure were independent risk factors; cytarabine emerged as a novel predictor. These findings may inform pre-treatment risk stratification and support prospective studies evaluating the cardiovascular impact of salvage therapy selection.
title: Abstract 6133: Cardiovascular Events Following Chimeric Antigen Receptor-T (CAR-T) Cell Therapy in Patients with Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL): A Medicare Claims-Based Analysis

abstract: Background: Early enteral nutrition (EN) is recommended in critically ill patients, but should be delayed or used cautiously in patients with uncontrolled shock or inadequate perfusion. Evidence is limited regarding early EN in cardiogenic shock patients supported with a microaxial flow pump (mAFP), in whom perfusion may be maintained despite severe circulatory failure. Objective: To evaluate the association between early EN and 180-day all-cause mortality in cardiogenic shock patients requiring mAFP support. Methods: We analyzed the UNLOADERS-PVAD registry, a Japanese multicenter registry of three high-volume mechanical circulatory support (MCS) centers, from April 2018 to December 2023. Of 501 patients, 69 who died or were weaned from MCS within 48 hours were excluded, leaving 432 patients for landmark analysis. EEN was defined as EN initiation within 48 hours after mAFP support. The primary endpoint was 180-day all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox regression was the primary analysis; center-stratified and propensity score-based analyses were sensitivity analyses. Results: Of 432 patients, 169 (39.1%) received EEN and 263 (60.9%) were classified as non-EEN, with marked variation across centers. Compared with non-EEN patients, EEN patients had lower baseline severity, with less concomitant VA-ECMO support and lower lactate, creatinine, APACHE II, and SAPS II scores. The EEN group had lower crude 30-day mortality than the non-EEN group (20% vs 38%; p<0.001), and Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower 180-day mortality in the EEN group (log-rank p<0.001). After adjustment for demographics, center, E-CPR status, MCS strategy, lactate, creatinine, APACHE II, and SCAI stage, EEN was associated with lower 180-day mortality (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.33-0.65). Additional adjustment for total 0-48-hour caloric delivery did not materially attenuate this association. The association remained consistent in center-stratified Cox analysis (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.67), stabilized inverse probability weighting (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.38-0.72), overlap weighting (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.39-0.72), and propensity score matching (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.39-0.76). Conclusions: In cardiogenic shock patients supported with an mAFP, EEN within 48 hours was consistently associated with lower 180-day mortality after adjustment for baseline severity, center-level practice variation, and treatment-selection bias. These findings support EEN as a potential early supportive strategy once perfusion is maintained.
title: Abstract 6168: Early Enteral Nutrition and Mortality in Microaxial Flow Pump-Supported Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Introduction: Managing pulmonary hypertension (PH) and limiting the progression of pulmonary vascular disease in patients with restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is vital to preserving their candidacy for heart transplant. CardioMEMS TM HF (Abbott Laboratories), an implantable pulmonary artery (PA) pressure sensor, may improve outcomes in these patients through real-time, invasive hemodynamic monitoring to inform titration of PH therapy. We present the first case of a CardioMEMS TM HF implant in a pediatric patient with PH secondary to RCM on mechanical circulatory support. Patient Information: A 9-year-old girl with a history of restrictive cardiomyopathy, previously managed with percutaneous atrial septal fenestration and home milrinone infusion, presented with frequent episodes of syncope. Clinical Findings: Her exam and data were notable for mild tachypnea and hepatomegaly with preserved end-organ function. Echocardiogram disclosed grade 2 diastolic dysfunction and a TAPSE of 1.2 cm (Z score = -5.5). Cardiac catheterization demonstrated right ventricular pressure of 103/24 mmHg, mean PA pressure of 70 mmHg, left ventricular end diastolic pressure of 29 mmHg, cardiac index of 2.1 L/min/sqm, and indexed pulmonary vascular resistance (PVRi) of 22 iWU. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Given her severe combined pre- and post-capillary PH and end-stage RCM, a Berlin Heart EXCOR left ventricular assist device (LVAD) with atrial cannulation was implanted as a bridge to potential heart-only transplant. Given the high-risk hemodynamics, intravenous treprostinil was initiated in the operating room and subsequently up titrated with close observation for side-effects. Therapeutic Intervention(s) and Timeline: Five months after LVAD implant, cardiac catheterization on treprostinil 60 ng/kg/min and enteral sildenafil and ambrisentan demonstrated PVRi acceptable for heart transplant. A CardioMEMS TM HF device was implanted in the distal left pulmonary artery without incident to record daily PA pressures and inform continued use of PH therapies while awaiting transplant. One month later, the patient underwent successful heart transplantation. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Treprostinil was discontinued shortly after transplant due to bleeding. CardioMEMS TM HF data enabled precise titration of pulmonary vasodilator therapies in the step-down unit. Four-week post-transplant catheterization on sildenafil monotherapy demonstrated improving PH with mean PA pressure of 28 mmHg and PVRi of 3.5 iWU. Discussion & Synthesis: CardioMEMS TM HF provided hemodynamic data enabling inpatient PH medication titration in a child with RCM on LVAD. Use of the device was safe, feasible and informed clinical management.
