Pediatric patients on advanced cardiac therapies, especially those with combined pre- and post-capillary PH, may benefit from CardioMEMS TM HF while awaiting transplant.

abstract: Background: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is an established stroke prevention strategy for patients with atrial fibrillation who are unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. While transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) are both utilized for intraprocedural guidance, high-quality comparative data on procedural performance and clinical outcomes remain limited. This study directly evaluates the procedural efficiency, safety profiles, and peridevice leak (PDL) rates between these two imaging modalities. Methods: We conducted a single-center, retrospective, observational study of 409 patients (ICE: n=205; TEE: n=204) who underwent LAAO between January 2024 and February 2026. Baseline demographics, clinical characteristics, and device types (Watchman vs. Amulet) were extracted. PDL was assessed by post-procedural TEE at 45 days and classified by jet width. Univariable and multivariable regression analyses identified factors associated with immediate complications and PDL, with statistical significance defined as a p-value <0.05. Results: Patient cohorts were well-matched, though the ICE group had a higher rate of concomitant ablation (55.4% vs. 10.8%) and higher baseline DOAC use (84.9% vs. 70.6%) (Figure 1). For LAAO-only procedures, ICE significantly reduced fluoroscopic time by 7.07 minutes (5.99 vs. 13.25 min, p<0.001) without altering total procedure time or patient radiation dose, a benefit most pronounced with the Watchman device (fluoroscopic time reduction: -6.50 min, p<0.001). In concomitant LAAO and ablation procedures, ICE reduced total procedure time by 28.33 minutes (126.87 vs. 155.27 min, p<0.001), driven primarily by cases using the Amulet device (procedure time reduction: -9.79 min, p=0.040) (Figure 2a, b). Multivariable analysis confirmed that imaging modality, device type, and concomitant ablation were not associated with immediate composite complications (including tamponade or vascular bleeds; p>0.05) (Figure 3a). At the 45-day follow-up, ICE guidance demonstrated a trend toward a 65% higher likelihood of visualizing any PDL (OR: 1.65, p=0.067), a 57% trend for leaks <3mm (OR: 1.57, p=0.128), and a 46% trend for leaks 3-5mm (OR 1.46, p=0.475), though none reached statistical significance (Figure 3b). Concomitant ablation procedures did not predict PDL presence or size (Figure 3c). Conclusions: ICE serves as a highly efficient alternative to TEE for intraprocedural LAAO guidance, offering superior procedural and fluoroscopic efficiency, particularly during concomitant ablation and specific device selections, with an identical safety profile. The borderline trend toward higher 45-day PDL rates is likely clinically insignificant and may reflect a procedural learning curve that improves with operator experience.
title: Abstract 6215: Close the Gap: A Head-to-Head Comparison of Intracardiac Echocardiography and Transesophageal Echocardiography for Peridevice Leak and Outcomes in Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion

abstract: Introduction: Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) is a rare cause of positional hypoxemia resulting from right-to-left shunting, most commonly through a patent foramen ovale (PFO). Case Presentation: An 83-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease (ILD), hypertension, coronary artery disease, mitral valve prolapse, obstructive sleep apnea on continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), and hypothyroidism presented with progressive dyspnea and severe hypoxemia despite home oxygen, requiring BiPAP and intensive care admission. Symptoms worsened in the upright position and improved when supine. Computed tomography angiography excluded pulmonary embolism and demonstrated only mild interstitial lung disease insufficient to explain the severity of hypoxemia. Previous Right heart catheterization indicated normal right-sided pressures without pulmonary hypertension. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study revealed a PFO with interatrial septal aneurysm and significant right-to-left shunting. Orthodeoxia testing confirmed POS. Due to the severity of her hypoxemia and absence of significant lung disease or pulmonary hypertension, a multidisciplinary team including cardiology, pulmonology, and cardiothoracic surgery recommended percutaneous PFO closure, however with the high possibility that even with closure, the patient's symptoms would not resolve. The patient underwent successful percutaneous PFO closure using a 30-mm Amplatzer device with marked improvement in oxygenation and resolution of positional desaturation. Discussion: Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) is a rare and underrecognized clinical condition characterized by dyspnea and arterial desaturation that worsen in the upright position and improve when supine. The syndrome results from positional right-to-left shunting and is most commonly associated with intracardiac defects such as patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defects, functional alterations of the interatrial septum, or less frequently intrapulmonary shunting due to pulmonary arteriovenous malformations or parenchymal lung disease. The appropriate diagnostic workup, including echocardiographic evaluation and assessment of a previous right heart catheterization, was pivotal in identifying the PFO as a likely cause of her positional desaturation and not to focus solely on the patients minimal ILD. The successful percutaneous closure of the PFO not only improved her oxygenation but also emphasizes the potential for significant recovery in patients with POS. Conclusion: POS should be considered in unexplained hypoxemia with positional desaturation. Careful diagnostic evaluation including echocardiography with bubble study is essential for identifying intracardiac shunting and Percutaneous PFO closure can provide substantial symptomatic and physiologic improvement in select patients.
title: Abstract 6225: Thinking Beyond the Lungs: Platypnea Orthodeoxia Syndrome from Patent Foramen Ovale Causing Refractory Hypoxemia

abstract: Background: Current guidelines provide a Class IA recommendation for an implantable cardiac defibrillator (ICD) in patients successfully resuscitated from a cardiac arrest (CA) due to ventricular fibrillation (VF) or hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia (VT), in the absence of a reversible cause. CA reportedly occurs less frequently in women, who are less likely to have typical risk factors and more likely to have an unexplained underlying etiology than men. While disparities in resuscitation post arrest is documented, gender disparities in secondary prevention (SP) ICD implantation is less well-known. Objective: To analyze and compare SP ICD implantation rates across genders in CA patients. Methods: We used the TriNetX research network to create a sex specific cohort with an index CA, using ICD codes for CA with VT and VF. We excluded patients with prior CA, prior ICD, or identifiable reversible causes, including acute coronary syndrome. As in-hospital mortality after CA is high, we only included patients alive at 90 days. The primary outcome was secondary prevention ICD implantation by 90 days in men vs. women, assessed using CPT procedural codes. We then compared rates of SP ICDs in the two groups. To adjust for comorbidities, we created 1:1 propensity score-matched (PSM) sex specific cohorts, utilizing parameters of the Charlson Comorbidity Index. To assess the robustness of our findings and inherent selection bias, we performed a sensitivity analysis assessing ICD implantation rates at 2 weeks from index CA. Results: Our final analysis included 34,695 men and 19,177 women. At 90 days, 24.3% of men and 22.4% of women had undergone ICD implantation. 17,585 men and women were included in our 1:1 PSM analysis. 24.2% and 22.6%, respectively, had a SP ICD by 90 days (p=0.003, absolute risk reduction (ARR) 1.6%). In our sensitivity analysis, a difference in ICD implantation was noted early after SCD, with 15.6% of men and 14.6% of women receiving an ICD at 2 weeks (p=0.006, ARR 1.05%). Conclusion: Women appear to have lower SP ICD implantation than men. However, despite strong recommendations, SP ICD implantation rates were suboptimal in both genders.
title: Abstract 6258: Gender Disparities in Defibrillator Implantation After Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) are at elevated risk for aortic valve calcification and stenosis, yet have been systematically excluded from major transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) trials. Real-world outcomes data for this population remain scarce. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) from 2017 to 2019. Adult patients undergoing TAVR were identified by ICD-10 codes. Advanced CKD was defined as stage 4 or greater. The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital complications, length of stay (LOS), and hospitalization cost. Weighted multivariable logistic and linear regression models were adjusted for Elixhauser comorbidities, age, and sex. Results: Of 67,670 patients undergoing TAVR, 4,912 (7.3%) had advanced CKD. The prevalence of advanced CKD among TAVR recipients increased from 1,360 in 2017 to 1,942 in 2019. Advanced CKD patients were significantly younger (mean age 76.1 vs 79.2 years; p<0.001), and female sex was inversely associated with advanced CKD (OR 0.73; p<0.001). Using White patients as the reference group, Black (OR 4.08), Asian (OR 2.11), and Hispanic (OR 1.92) patients with advanced CKD had significantly higher odds of in-hospital mortality (all p<0.001). Advanced CKD was independently associated with higher odds of acute kidney injury (OR 2.69), cardiogenic shock (OR 2.31), cardiac arrest (OR 2.08), ventricular tachycardia (OR 1.60), hypoxic respiratory failure (OR 1.40), atrial fibrillation (OR 1.83), acute myocardial infarction (OR 1.30), and hemorrhage (OR 1.27; all p<0.05). Hispanic patients with advanced CKD had significantly higher hospitalization costs (+$77,209; p<0.001) and longer LOS (+1.49 days; p=0.037) compared to White patients. Conclusions: Advanced CKD is independently associated with increased in-hospital morbidity and mortality following TAVR, with pronounced racial and ethnic disparities in outcomes, cost, and resource utilization. These findings underscore the need for prospective study inclusion, peri-procedural risk stratification, and targeted clinical interventions for this underrepresented population.
title: Abstract 6269: TAVR and Advanced Kidney Disease: A National Retrospective Analysis of Outcomes and Health Disparities

abstract: Background: Exertional angina and presyncope raise concern for myocardial ischemia, but ischemic symptoms are not synonymous with atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (CAD). Left main coronary artery (LMCA) atresia is a rare congenital anomaly characterized by the absence of the left coronary ostium, with the proximal left main trunk terminating blindly, without connection to the aorta. The distal left coronary tree remains present and is perfused retrogradely through congenital collateral vessels from the right coronary artery. Case Presentation: A 40-year-old man with class III obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a strong family history of premature cardiovascular disease presented with recurrent chest tightness, exertional dyspnea, and episodic presyncope limiting his work as a professional singer. Resting electrocardiography (ECG) showed sinus rhythm without ischemic ST-T changes. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved biventricular systolic function and no significant valvular disease. Coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) showed a calcium score of zero and no atherosclerosis, but revealed the absence of a direct LMCA connection to the aortic root. A moderately sized left anterior descending and circumflex arteries were reconstituted by collateral vessels arising from the right coronary artery and right posterior descending artery, consistent with LMCA atresia (Figure 1A, 1B) . Treadmill stress echocardiography reproduced chest tightness at peak exercise but showed no ischemic ECG changes, inducible wall-motion abnormalities, or ventricular arrhythmias. Management: Given preserved exercise capacity and absence of objective high-risk features, management was individualized through shared decision-making. Beta-blocker therapy was started to reduce myocardial oxygen demand, alongside aggressive risk-factor modification and close surveillance. Surgical revascularization was deferred, with reconsideration if symptoms progressed or objective ischemia or arrhythmia emerged. Conclusion: This case highlights LMCA atresia as a rare cause of exertional angina and presyncope in adulthood despite the absence of atherosclerotic coronary disease. CCTA was decisive in distinguishing congenital coronary anatomy from atherosclerotic CAD, while functional testing helped guide individualized management. Although surgical revascularization is recommended based on predominantly pediatric case reviews, select adults without inducible ischemia or arrhythmia may be managed medically with close follow-up (Figure 2) .
title: Abstract 6274: Chest Pain from an Uncommon Cause: Left Main Coronary Artery Atresia

abstract: Background: Myocardial infarction (MI) is one of the leading causes of death throughout the world. Despite advances in treatment, the molecular mechanisms underlying MI remain poorly understood. Changes in gene expression and DNA methylation, crucial for regulating cellular processes, have received limited exploration. Aims: This study aimed to investigate the role of Fc Gamma Receptor IIa (FCGR2A) and its regulatory mechanism in myocardial infarction, providing potential therapeutic insights. Methods: Our study combined human sample analysis with a rat ischemic model, using RRBS and RNA-Seq to identify and analyze candidate genes via GO and KEGG enrichment. FCGR2A overexpression and knockdown in H9C2 cells were used to assess its role in cell viability and apoptosis under hypoxia and serum deprivation. DNA methylation was analyzed by BSP, while calcium concentration and L-type calcium current density were measured using Fura-2 and patch clamp techniques. Dual-luciferase reporter assays and chromatin immunoprecipitation confirmed ATF3-mediated transcriptional regulation of FCGR2A. In vivo, myocardial infarction was induced by LAD ligation, and AAV9-mediated FCGR2A overexpression or ATF3 knockdown validated its protective effects on the ischemic heart. Results: We combined the analysis of genomic methylation sequencing (RRBS) and RNA-Seq and screened out FCGR2A as a potential target for treatment of myocardial infarction(Fig 1A-G). Hypermethylation in the CpG island of FCGR2A was associated with ischemic heart disease and induces downregulation of FCGR2A (Fig 1H-M). Overexpression of FCGR2A mitigated hypoxia-induced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, reduced L-type calcium channel current density, and alleviated intracellular calcium overload. Additionally, ATF3 was found to regulate FCGR2A transcription by promoting its promoter methylation(Fig 2A-F). In vivo, FCGR2A overexpression or ATF3 knockdown validated its cardioprotective effects and clarified their regulatory relationship in ischemic myocardial injury(Fig 2G-H). Conclusion: FCGR2A plays a critical role in protecting the ischemic heart and is epigenetically regulated by ATF3. Targeting FCGR2A may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for myocardial infarction.
title: Abstract 6275: Epigenetic Silencing of FCGR2A by Promoter Hypermethylation Exacerbates Cardiac Remodeling in Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: TAVR has transformed the treatment of severe aortic stenosis, yet the benefits of this therapy may not be experienced equally across racial and ethnic groups. Although disparities in access to TAVR are well described, whether differences in clinical outcomes persist post-procedurally remains unclear. This study evaluated racial and ethnic differences in post-TAVR mortality and complications. Methodology: This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359817). We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane, and CINAHL from database inception through May 1, 2026, for studies evaluating adult TAVR recipients with clinical outcomes stratified by race or ethnicity. White patients were used as the comparator group, with odds ratios comparing White patients against Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American patients. Eligible studies included observational studies and randomized controlled trials reporting post-TAVR outcomes, including mortality, myocardial infarction, permanent pacemaker implantation, vascular complications, stroke, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, and analyses were performed using Stata version 19.5 and R version 4.6.0. Results: This meta-analysis included 16 studies. White patients had lower odds of mortality than Hispanic patients (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.38-0.97), while other mortality comparisons were not significant. For cardiovascular outcomes, White patients had lower odds of myocardial infarction than both Black and Hispanic patients (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.60-0.72 and OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.83, respectively). White patients also had lower odds of vascular complications compared with Hispanic patients (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.71-0.92) and lower odds of stroke compared with Black patients (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.66-0.90); remaining comparisons were not significant. For systemic outcomes, White patients had lower odds of hemorrhage (OR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74-1.00) and acute kidney injury (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30-0.96) compared with Black patients. White patients also had lower odds of acute kidney injury compared with Native American patients (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03-0.52). Other group comparisons were not significant. Conclusion: Racial and ethnic differences in post-TAVR outcomes were observed across mortality, cardiovascular complications, and systemic complications. These findings highlight the need to better understand the underlying causes of these differences and develop strategies to improve post-procedural care. However, results should be interpreted with caution given the potential for residual confounding from disease severity, comorbidity burden, and access to care.
title: Abstract 6284: Racial Disparities in Clinical Outcomes Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND: Patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) face persistent thrombotic risk despite dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). Coagulation activation persists weeks beyond the acute phase, providing rationale for dual-pathway inhibition with low-dose rivaroxaban. In anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), left ventricular (LV) thrombus further increases embolic risk. No prior meta-analysis has synthesized randomized evidence across cardiovascular event reduction and LV thrombus prophylaxis in this population. Hypothesis: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily added to DAPT reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality after AMI, reduces LV thrombus in anterior STEMI, and increases bleeding versus DAPT alone. MethodS: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Embase (inception-March 2026). Eligible studies enrolled AMI patients post-PCI randomized to rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus DAPT versus DAPT alone. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs were pooled via DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed by I2. Cochrane RoB 2 evaluated bias. Protocol was prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD420261377182). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted for all outcomes. ResultS: Four RCTs (11,106 patients) were included: Mega 2012 (ATLAS ACS 2-TIMI 51), Zhang 2022, Puymirat 2026 (APERITIF), and Mennuni 2025 (ARISE-ARMYDA 7). Three trials were at low risk of bias; APERITIF carried some concerns. Rivaroxaban plus DAPT significantly reduced all-cause mortality (RR 0.67; 95%CI 0.62-0.73; P=0.002; I2=0%) and MACE (RR 0.83; 95%CI 0.72-0.95; P=0.028; I2=0%). Recurrent MI was not significantly reduced (RR 0.89; P=0.110). In the anterior STEMI subgroup (n=839), LV thrombus reduction was non-significant (RR 0.33; P=0.503; I2=78.8%), driven by divergent results: Zhang 2022 (RR 0.08; P=0.015) versus Puymirat 2026 (RR 0.83; P=0.34). Triple therapy increased major bleeding (RR 3.31; 95%CI 2.49-4.39; P<0.001; I2=0%) and minor bleeding (RR 1.92; 95%CI 1.35-2.74; P=0.010; I2=0%). ConclusionS: Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily added to DAPT significantly reduces all-cause mortality and MACE after AMI at the cost of a threefold increase in major bleeding. LV thrombus prophylaxis evidence in anterior STEMI remains inconclusive due to high heterogeneity. Selective use is supported in high-ischemic-risk, low-bleeding-risk patients; a well-powered CMR-based RCT with standardized P2Y12 allocation is the priority research need.
title: Abstract 6289: Low Dose Rivaroxaban Added to Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Following Acute Myocardial Infarction Impact on Cardiovascular Events Left Ventricular Thrombus and Bleeding Risk A Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Traditional approaches to improving cardiac rehabilitation (CR) participation often evaluate risk factors in isolation, limiting their real-world clinical implications. Rather than isolated risk factors, multiple risk factors can interact and exist in the same patient. We aimed to identify patients' phenotypes across the cascade of CR enrollment and completion using a dual-analytical framework. Methods: We analyzed 2,780 patients referred to CR within a large health system between 2018 and 2025. We performed a sequential analysis utilizing multivariable logistic regression and machine learning-based Classification and Regression Tree (CART) modeling to evaluate two outcomes: enrollment (attending ≥1 session) and completion (≥36 sessions). Models integrated clinical characteristics, social determinants, and geospatial real-world driving distances, with subgroup analyses for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and medically managed myocardial infarction (MI). Results: The cohort had median age of 68, (IQR 60 to 77), 38% women, 29% Black. Overall, 690 (25%) of referred patients enrolled, and only 115 (17%) of enrollees completed the program. Multivariable regression (Figure 1) revealed enrollment barriers including Medicaid, Medicare, or self-pay insurance, higher neighborhood deprivation, longer driving distance, and non-cardiac surgery discharging specialty. Conversely, program completion was driven by an older age. CART analysis unmasked distinct non-linear patient phenotypes: the cohort presenting the highest risk of non-enrollment comprised patients discharged from cardiac surgery who faced longer driving distances (Figure 2). For the medically managed MI subgroup (Figure 3), insurance type acted as the primary systemic gatekeeper, with Medicaid, Medicare, or self-pay defining the lowest enrollment phenotype. Conclusions: CR participation involves distinct phenotypic transitions, where factors driving initial enrollment differ fundamentally from those dictating long-term adherence. While driving distance represents a highly modifiable logistical barrier to entry, patient age demonstrates a paradoxical effect, hindering initial enrollment while increasing the likelihood for long-term completion. Deploying this phenotype-driven framework provides actionable insights for clinical practice and population health, enabling targeted strategies for patients at the highest risk of attrition.
title: Abstract 6311: Evaluating Patient Barriers and Phenotypes of the Cardiac Rehabilitation Participation Cascade: Decision Tree Analysis and Logistic Regression

abstract: Background: Myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) is more common among younger patients. Multimodality imaging with coronary optical coherence tomography (OCT) and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) can identify underlying mechanisms of MINOCA, but findings in relation to age have not been described. Research Question: How do MINOCA patients who present at younger ages differ from those who present at older ages in terms of clinical and imaging characteristics? Methods: We performed a secondary analysis of the prospective, multi-center Heart Attack Research Program evaluating underlying causes of suspected MINOCA. Patients were enrolled before or after coronary angiography for MI and had multivessel OCT and CMR within a week. Patients with ≥50% stenosis on angiography were excluded. Angiography, OCT and CMR were interpreted by independent core laboratories blinded to clinical data. Here, we stratified participants by age ≤60 versus >60 years. OCT findings, CMR diagnoses, and final adjudicated diagnoses were compared between groups using Wilcoxon rank-sum and chi-square/Fisher exact tests. Results: Among 754 enrolled participants, younger patients were less likely to screen fail with MI due to coronary artery disease than older patients (40% vs 47%, p=0.04) but there was a similar frequency of MINOCA (54% vs. 50%, p=0.24). Among 336 MINOCA patients with OCT, 187 (56%) were aged ≤60 years. Younger patients were less likely to have hypertension (41% vs 56% of older patients, P=0.004) or dyslipidemia (28% vs 51%, P<0.001) but diabetes was similar (15% vs. 21%, P=0.12). Normal coronary angiography was more common among younger patients (55% vs 36%, p<0.001) and OCT culprit lesions less common (34% vs 59%, p<0.001, Figure). Among 284 participants with CMR, younger MINOCA patients were more likely to have CMR-defined infarction (33% vs 20%, p=0.01) and less likely to have CMR-defined regional injury than older MINOCA patients (5% vs 23%, p<0.001). Normal CMR tended to be more common among younger versus older patients (41% vs 30%, p=0.06). A final adjudicated diagnosis of MI was less common in younger versus older patients (52% vs 64%, p=0.03), while idiopathic MINOCA (31% vs 19%, p=0.01) was more common in younger individuals (Figure). Conclusions: Older age was associated with higher prevalence of culprit lesions on OCT and greater likelihood of a final diagnosis of MI among patients presenting with suspected MINOCA. However, MI remained the most common final diagnosis among younger patients with suspected MINOCA, supporting the use of multimodality imaging regardless of patient age.
title: Abstract 6357: Age and Multimodality Imaging Findings Among Patients Presenting with MINOCA in the HARP Study

abstract: Background: Chest pain leads to ~7 million ED visits annually, with ECG as the first-line test, though non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is often missed due to subtle findings. Current pathways like the HEART are safe but depend on serial troponins, delaying decisions and increasing resource use. Troponin-free tools are faster but apply to too few patients. No existing approach provides fast, broadly applicable, and accurate risk stratification for all-risk chest pain patients. Hypothesis: An AI model applied to the initial 12-lead ECG can rapidly and safely stratify NSTEMI risk in acute chest pain patients, accurately identifying both low-risk patients suitable for early discharge and high-risk patients requiring urgent evaluation, with further improvement when combined with baseline troponin. Methods: Using retrospective Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist (AHWFB) data, we developed a multi-class 1D ResNet ECG-AI model to predict NSTEMI and STEMI within 30 days. Adults with chest pain, a clinical 12-lead ECG, and ≥30-day follow-up were included; data were split 8:1:1 at the patient level. The model was evaluated in a distinct ED cohort across five AHWFB facilities including patients with chest pain, ≥1 troponin measurement, and no STEMI on index ECG. Zero-shot rule-out and rule-in performance were assessed, including an ensemble approach combining ECG-AI with elevated 0-hour troponin. Results: The model was developed using 142,647 ECGs from 81,239 patients. In the holdout set (14,094 ECGs; 649 NSTEMI, 276 STEMI), AUCs for 30-day outcomes were 0.84 for no MI, 0.79 for NSTEMI, and 0.95 for STEMI. The ED NSTEMI registry, that was held out during model building, included 15,854 patients; 971 (6.1%) experienced MI/death at index and 1,126 (7.1%) within 30 days. ECG-AI identified 4,256 patients (27%) as low risk. In this group, MI/death rates were 0.75% at index ED visit and 1.15% within 30 days, enabling a modeled 5.1 ± 3.8 hours earlier discharge and reducing total ED stay by 24%. ECG-AI assigned 201 (1.3%) patients into very high-risk group. In this group, PPVs were 68% at index and 70% at 30 days. The ECG-AI + troponin ensemble identified 4,136 patients (26%) for rule-out with NPVs of 99.76% (index) and 99.47% (30-day) and 147 high risk patients with improved PPVs of 82% and 84% for index and 30-day outcomes, respectively, while reducing ED stay by 15%. Discussion: ECG-AI demonstrated strong zero-shot performance for rapid NSTEMI risk stratification using only the initial ECG. The model safely identified low-risk patients while accurately enriching a high-risk subgroup. Integration with baseline troponin further improved performance. These findings support its potential to enable faster, safer triage and prioritization in acute chest pain evaluation.
title: Abstract 6362: Fast and Scalable ECG-AI for Safe Rule-Out and High-Risk Prioritization of NSTEMI in Acute Chest Pain

abstract: Background: The HEAR score (History, ECG, Age, Risk factors) is used in the emergency department (ED) to risk-stratify patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS), particularly non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), while ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is usually straightforward to identify by ST-segment elevation on electrocardiogram (ECG). While the ECG is rapid and troponin-independent, it is partly subjective and may miss subtle ischemic ECG changes. ECG-based artificial intelligence (ECG-AI) may therefore provide additional prognostic value beyond standard assessment. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that an ECG-AI model would capture prognostic signals not represented by HEAR components or standard ECG interpretation, improving prediction of index visit myocardial infarction (MI) or death. Methods: We conducted a observational study of ED patients from the Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist (AHWFB) evaluated for suspected NSTEMI. Patients were stratified using a pre-built ECG-AI model into low- and high-risk groups and compared with HEAR score components and clinician ECG interpretation. Outcomes included index and 30-day MI/death, with assessment of concordance between ECG-AI and conventional risk stratification. Results: The model was trained on 142,647 ECGs from 81,239 patients. In a holdout set (14,094 ECGs; 649 NSTEMI, 276 STEMI), AUCs for 30-day outcomes were 0.84 (MI), 0.79 (NSTEMI), and 0.95 (STEMI).The ED NSTEMI cohort included 15,854 patients; 971 (6.1%) experienced MI/death at index and 1,126 (7.1%) within 30 days. Among 4,256 ECG-AI low-risk patients, most had elevated HEAR scores (65.8%) or traditional risk factors (72.7%), with abnormal ECGs (23.6%), yet event rates remained low (0.75% index; 1.15% 30-day).Conversely, 201 high-risk patients were clinically heterogeneous, with 12.0% HEAR <2 and 13.3% no risk factors, but showed high event rates (PPV 68% index; 70% 30-day). Notably, nearly one-third had normal ECGs (30.7%) yet still experienced events, indicating discordance with conventional assessment.Additional low- and high-risk group results are shown in Table 1. Discussion: ECG-AI provides prognostic information beyond HEAR-based risk stratification and standard ECG interpretation. It identifies low-risk patients despite abnormal clinical features and high-risk patients despite reassuring findings, suggesting it captures latent ECG signatures not reflected in conventional variables. These findings support ECG-AI’s potential role in ED ACS triage, enabling safer and larger scale rule-out and improved identification of high-risk patients.
title: Abstract 6366: Beyond HEAR: ECG-AI Unmasks Latent Risk in Suspected NSTEMI

abstract: Introduction: Magnetocardiography (MCG) is a non-invasive, radiation-free technology that measures the magnetic fields generated by the heart using a multi-channel sensor array in a clinical environment. Unlike EKG, which records voltage potentials subject to thoracic impedance, MCG captures depolarization and repolarization dynamics with greater spatial resolution and sensitivity. We present a case in which a pre-catheterization unshielded MCG scan correctly identified a true-positive acute coronary syndrome (ACS). The scan captured abnormal depolarization and repolarization biofeatures and detected a possible injury current not evident on 12-lead EKG. Case: A 73-year-old male with a medical history of diabetes presented to the ED with chest pain and was ruled in for Type 1 NSTEMI. Baseline EKG showed normal sinus rhythm with rightward axis; findings did not exclude an inferior infarct. High-sensitivity troponin trended upward (1,263, 2,534, and 48,875 ng/L). Initial ECHO demonstrated an EF of 47% with hypocontractility of the mid inferolateral wall and hypokinesis of the posterior wall. The patient underwent a same-day pre-catheterization MCG scan. Cardiac catheterization revealed 1-vessel CAD, 80-90% proximal and distal LCx stenosis, both successfully stented. The patient remained hemodynamically stable through discharge. Results/Discussion: The MCG scan yielded an 80% positive classification supported by magnetic biofeatures compared against a database of over 600 healthy subjects (95% CI). (1) The R and T wave field map angles fell outside the healthy range, indicating altered dominant depolarization and repolarization vectors relative to the tightly clustered up-and-rightward orientation observed in healthy subjects. (2) The R wave magnetic field map showed abnormal clockwise rotation across the ±10 ms window surrounding the R peak, where the dipole orientation is expected to remain stable, consistent with a disordered ventricular depolarization sequence. (3) Multipolar field patterns were present across both the R and T waves, reflecting regional electrical heterogeneity inconsistent with uniform myocardial activation. (4) A probable injury current was observed across both depolarization and repolarization, appearing as a low frequency baseline shift synchronized across all channels and consistent with current flow across injured myocardium. The observed shift was not consistent with noise patterns typical of an unshielded environment. Conclusion: This case demonstrates the value of MCG as a diagnostic tool in patients with suspected ACS. MCG captured abnormalities, including possible injury current, that were not detected on a standard 12-lead EKG. These findings support further investigation of MCG as a rapid, non-invasive adjunct to existing chest pain triage pathways, particularly for patients whose EKG does not clearly establish a diagnosis.
title: Abstract 6382: Non-Invasive Detection of Possible Injury Current by Magnetocardiography in a Patient with NSTEMI: A Case Report

abstract: Congenital absence of the inferior vena cava (CAI) is a rare vascular anomaly (<1% prevalence) from aberrant embryologic development of the posterior cardinal, subcardinal, and supracardinal veins between gestational weeks 6-10. Venous return reroutes through collaterals, most commonly the azygos-hemiazygos system. CAI often remains clinically silent until invasive femoral venous procedures are attempted, though early-onset DVT or unexplained lower extremity edema (LEE) may provide early diagnostic clues. As LAAO use expands, unrecognized venous anomalies carry important procedural implications. An 81-year-old woman with non-valvular atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, and chronic unexplained bilateral LEE was referred for Watchman implantation due to recurrent falls with prior hip fracture, conferring unacceptable long-term anticoagulation risk. Despite successful right femoral venipuncture, guidewire advancement along the expected IVC course failed. Intraprocedural venography revealed absence of the IVC with a markedly dilated azygos vein draining into the superior vena cava, consistent with azygos continuation. Venography demonstrated smooth, uninterrupted IVC absence with prominent azygos collateralization (Figure 1) , favoring CAI rather than acquired obstruction or thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced CT or MR venography can confirm the diagnosis. Retrospectively, chronic bilateral LEE likely represented an early manifestation of impaired venous return from this congenital anomaly. Given the absence of safe transfemoral access, transseptal puncture could not be performed and the LAAO procedure was aborted. The patient remained hemodynamically stable without access-site or pericardial complications and was discharged the next day. Transjugular or transhepatic approaches were discussed as alternative strategies, though each carries increased procedural complexity and risk. The patient was discharged without complications. Cross-sectional vascular imaging was recommended prior to future structural or EP procedures. Long-term anticoagulation management and fall-risk mitigation were addressed at follow-up. CAI is a rare but clinically significant cause of failed femoral-based LAAO. In this case, chronic bilateral LEE was an underrecognized pre-procedural clue. As Watchman utilization grows following landmark trials, atypical venous anatomy must be considered in patients with prior failed venous access, or atypical wire course. Pre-procedural CT or MR venography may guide access planning, prevent procedural failure, and identify the need for alternative approaches. The patient understood the anatomic finding and agreed with conservative planning, expressing willingness to pursue further evaluation for alternative approaches to reduce stroke risk.
title: Abstract 6399: Rerouting Required: Congenital Absence of IVC Disrupting Watchman LAAO Closure

abstract: Introduction/Background Patient selection and the utility of percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) remain areas of active debate. Practice guidelines do not clearly define who should undergo LAAO, which allows for substantial discretion in treatment decisions. While there is a perception that practice patterns regarding patient selection for LAAO procedures may vary, such heterogeneity has not been objectively assessed. Research Questions/Hypothesis We first quantified the extent of variation across Hospital Referral Regions (HRRs) that persisted after adjusting for patient characteristics and the local supply of cardiologists and LAAO implanters and then estimated the risk-standardized rates of receiving LAAO across HRRs. Methods/Approach The study cohort included Medicare Fee-For-Service beneficiaries aged ≥66 years with a first diagnosis of AF between January 1, 2017 and December 31, 2023, a CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score ≥3 for women or ≥2 for men, and continuous enrollment in Medicare Parts A, B, and D in the prior year. The outcome was LAAO implantation (ICD-10 02L73DK). Follow-up ended at earliest of LAAO, death, Medicare disenrollment, or December 31 st , 2023. We used multivariable, mixed-effects Poisson models with HRR random intercepts and person-time offsets to estimate adjusted rates of LAAO. The model included patient characteristics, cardiologist density, and electrophysiologist or interventional cardiologist density as fixed effects. We mapped patients’ ZIP codes to HRRs and derived adjusted HRR-level rates of LAAO using indirect standardization and visualized geographic variation with a choropleth map. Results/Data Among 525,917 beneficiaries with first AF (mean age 79.0; 52.5% women; 32.8% frail), 9,194 (1.8%) received LAAO during a median follow-up of 21.6 months (IQR 7.3-43.0). Table 1 shows factors associated with rates of LAAO. The highest decile general cardiologist density was associated with lower LAAO rates whereas the highest decile electrophysiology or interventional cardiology density was associated with higher LAAO rates. In the adjusted model, the median rate ratio was 1.59 (95% CI 1.52-1.68), which indicates that two otherwise identical individuals would differ by 59% in their rate of receiving LAAO if they resided in different, randomly selected HRRs. Adjusted rates of LAAO for each HRR across the continental US are shown in Figure 1 . Conclusion We found persistent geographic variation in LAAO rates after adjusting for patient case-mix and care access factors. Other factors, like clinician preferences, referral patterns, and local practice norms, likely play an important role in shaping treatment decisions. More definitive evidence regarding optimal patient selection and LAAO implanter characteristics, and consequently clearer clinical practice guidelines, remain an important unmet need.
title: Abstract 6409: Geographic Variation in Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Use Among Medicare Fee-for-Service Beneficiaries with Atrial Fibrillation

abstract: Introduction Congenital left main coronary artery atresia (LMCAA) is a rare anomaly in which the left coronary ostium fails to form and the proximal left main trunk ends blindly. Flow through the left coronary tree remains dependent on collateral circulation from the right coronary artery (RCA). Although a limited number of cases have been reported, the majority of adult cases present with angina, dyspnea, or sudden cardiac death. Patient Information A 31-year-old woman with hypertension and obesity reported progressive exertional dyspnea prior to collapsing while climbing stairs. Clinical Findings EMS documented ventricular fibrillation (VF) with return of spontaneous circulation after a single defibrillation. ECG was consistent with sinus tachycardia and left ventricular hypertrophy. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) of 40-45%. Troponin I was 0.084 ng/mL on presentation and peaked at 0.143 ng/mL (reference: <0.034 ng/mL). Diagnostic Assessment Coronary catheterization revealed a dilated RCA supplying the left system through collaterals, with no identifiable left main ostium. CT coronary angiography confirmed an absent LMCA origin with collateral reconstitution of the left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex arteries. After exclusion of acute thrombus, obstructive atherosclerosis, anomalous aortic origin, and myocardial bridging, VF arrest was attributed to congenital LMCAA. Therapeutic Interventio n s The patient underwent uncomplicated coronary artery bypass grafting (LIMA-to-LAD, saphenous vein graft-to-circumflex) and was started on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with mildly reduced EF. Follow-up Postoperative TTE showed a stable EF of 40-45%. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement was deferred after electrophysiology (EP) consultation, as VF was attributed to a reversible ischemic substrate corrected by revascularization. She recovered without neurologic deficit and was discharged to cardiac rehabilitation. She was seen as an outpatient 8 months after discharge after completing cardiac rehabilitation without angina, presyncope, or palpitations. Repeat TTE and outpatient EP evaluation were pending. Discussion Congenital LMCAA can remain silent for three decades before presenting as sudden cardiac arrest, and survival from VF arrest due to this anomaly is exceptionally rare. To our knowledge, this is the first reported adult survivor of out-of-hospital VF arrest secondary to congenital LMCAA treated with surgical revascularization. We conclude that it is important to consider congenital coronary anomalies in young adults with unexplained cardiac arrest and absence of atherosclerotic disease. Further, identification of LMCAA may prevent reflexive defibrillator implantation in patients with a reversible cause of cardiac arrest.
title: Abstract 6412: Congenital Left Main Coronary Artery Atresia Presenting as Out-of-Hospital Arrest in a Young Woman: A Case Report

abstract: Introduction: Globe luxation is a rare ocular emergency with direct implications for anticoagulation, hemodynamics, and sedation decisions in the cardiac intensive care unit (CICU). Case: A 65-year-old man was admitted to the CICU for management of cardiogenic shock complicating acutely decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, and atrial fibrillation. Treatments included milrinone, furosemide, and apixaban, with improving hemodynamics and congestion. One night at 3am, the critical care cardiology attending was called for acute ocular protrusion described as the patient’s “eye falling out.” Bedside evaluation revealed marked left eye proptosis with conjunctival injection. In the setting of systemic anticoagulation, initial concern centered on hemorrhage, and anchoring bias toward retrobulbar bleeding was explicitly recognized. This prompted a structured diagnostic approach considering hemorrhagic (retrobulbar hemorrhage), vascular (carotid-cavernous fistula), and mechanical (globe luxation) etiologies. Computed tomography angiography of the head and neck showed no hemorrhage or vascular lesion. Ophthalmologic examination demonstrated anterior globe displacement with elevated intraocular pressure and eyelid laxity consistent with suspected floppy eyelid syndrome; orbital compartment syndrome was clinically excluded. Anticoagulation was held during diagnostic uncertainty and resumed after exclusion of hemorrhage. The globe was successfully reduced at bedside without complication. Dexmedetomidine was used to limit agitation and Valsalva-related recurrence. Final diagnosis was spontaneous globe luxation in suspected floppy eyelid syndrome. Discussion: Spontaneous globe luxation is a rare ocular emergency in critically ill CICU patients that may mimic hemorrhagic orbital catastrophe, particularly in anticoagulated patients. This case highlights a key cognitive pitfall, anchoring on anticoagulation-associated hemorrhage, which may lead to inappropriate reversal or delay in definitive mechanical management. We propose a bedside CICU triage framework for acute, vision-threatening orbital emergencies, intentionally limited to immediately life- or vision-altering causes: hemorrhagic, vascular, and mechanical etiologies. This pragmatic framework is intended for time-sensitive ICU decision-making rather than exhaustive ophthalmologic differential diagnosis. Recognition of this structured approach facilitated timely diagnosis and avoided potential mismanagement in a high-stakes anticoagulated patient. Conclusion: Globe luxation in the CICU is a rare diagnosis that can mimic hemorrhagic orbital emergencies. Rapid structured triage is essential, as divergent management pathways directly impact cardiovascular care, including anticoagulation and sedation decisions.
title: Abstract 6432: Spontaneous Globe Luxation in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit: Diagnostic Pitfalls and Anticoagulation Decision-Making in an Acute Non-Cardiac Emergency

abstract: Introduction: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is associated with a 2.6-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Chronic neuroinflammation upregulates procoagulant pathways, while physical disability and glucocorticoid use further compound thromboembolic risk. We present a 59-year-old man with MS who developed a paradoxical embolic stroke - a diagnosis that risked misattribution to a new demyelinating lesion. Case Presentation: A 59-year-old male with MS, optic neuritis, and hypertension presented with left foot drop. Exam revealed left facial asymmetry, pronator drift, and leg lag. MRI brain showed restricted diffusion in the periventricular and subcortical white matter of the right cerebral hemisphere without gadolinium enhancement, favoring embolic stroke over active demyelination. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated early right-to-left shunting across the interatrial septum, suggestive of a patent foramen ovale (PFO). Lower extremity duplex was negative for DVT. The patient was started on aspirin and rosuvastatin with cardiology referral for TEE and PFO closure consideration. Discussion: PFO closure is favored in patients under 60 with cryptogenic stroke and high-risk anatomical features - large shunt, atrial septal aneurysm, or hypermobile septum - as demonstrated by the CLOSE, REDUCE, and RESPECT trials. In older patients or those with small, incidental PFOs, medical therapy alone is reasonable. When closure is deferred, the choice between anticoagulation and antiplatelets depends on underlying thrombotic risk. Antiplatelets are appropriate when DVT and hypercoagulable states are absent, as the embolic source is presumed transient. Anticoagulation is preferred when concurrent DVT, hypercoagulable disorder, or atrial arrhythmia is identified, or after recurrent events on antiplatelet therapy. The PICSS trial found no clear superiority of warfarin over aspirin in isolated PFO, suggesting anticoagulation is not routinely warranted without additional thrombotic risk factors. In this patient - under 60 with MS-related prothrombotic physiology and early right-to-left shunting - aspirin was initiated pending TEE to characterize PFO anatomy. High-risk features on TEE would favor closure as definitive therapy. If closure is deferred, MS-associated hypercoagulability may justify escalation to anticoagulation over antiplatelets alone.
title: Abstract 6437: A Step in the Wrong Direction: Foot Drop Reveals a Paradoxical Embolic Stroke

abstract: Background: In patients with cardiogenic shock requiring venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), increased left ventricular afterload may contribute to pulmonary congestion. ECPELLA, combining VA-ECMO with a microaxial flow pump (mAFP), provides both systemic perfusion and left ventricular unloading. However, the clinical impact of reducing VA-ECMO flow while maintaining total systemic perfusion during acute ECPELLA support remains unclear. Objective: This study examined whether VA-ECMO flow dependency at 48 hours, expressed as percent ECMO flow (%ECMO-flow), was associated with short-term outcomes in patients receiving ECPELLA support. Methods: The UNLOADERS-PVAD Registry is a multicenter observational registry enrolling consecutive patients with cardiogenic shock who received mAFP support at three high-volume Japanese centers between April 2018 and December 2023. Among 501 patients, 206 treated with mAFP alone were excluded, and 295 patients receiving ECPELLA support were screened. To evaluate VA-ECMO flow dependency at 48 hours, patients who died, were weaned from VA-ECMO or mAFP support, or lacked pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) data by 48 hours were excluded, leaving 226 patients. PAC-derived cardiac output (PAC-CO) was used to estimate native forward flow. Hybrid total systemic perfusion was defined as PAC-CO plus VA-ECMO flow in patients with detectable PAC-CO (≥1.0 L/min) and as VA-ECMO flow plus mAFP flow in those with undetectable PAC-CO (<1.0 L/min). %ECMO-flow was calculated as VA-ECMO flow divided by hybrid total systemic perfusion х100. Cox models assessed %ECMO-flow as a continuous variable for 30-day mortality. Results: The median %ECMO-flow was 57.4%, and patients were divided into low and high %ECMO-flow groups (n=113 each). Compared with the high %ECMO-flow group, the low %ECMO-flow group was younger and had a lower prevalence of chronic kidney disease, whereas other comorbidities, severity scores including APACHE II and SAVE scores, SCAI stage, and lactate levels were not significantly different. The low %ECMO-flow group had higher 30-day survival (67.3% vs. 42.5%, P<0.001), VA-ECMO weaning (85.8% vs. 63.1%, P<0.001), and mAFP weaning rates (78.4% vs. 51.8%, P<0.001). In multivariable Cox analysis, each 10% increase in %ECMO-flow was associated with higher 30-day mortality after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates, including hybrid total systemic perfusion index (adjusted HR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.07-1.37; P=0.003). Conclusions: In acute ECPELLA support, lower VA-ECMO flow dependency at 48 hours was associated with better short-term outcomes and successful MCS weaning. Higher %ECMO-flow at 48 hours was independently associated with increased 30-day mortality, suggesting that VA-ECMO flow dependency may serve as a marker of treatment response during ECPELLA de-escalation.
title: Abstract 6438: Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Flow Dependency at 48 Hours and Short-Term Outcomes in Cardiogenic Shock Patients Receiving Concomitant Microaxial Flow Pump Support

abstract: Background: Reperfusion delay is associated with higher mortality in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The time to reperfusion from the first medical contact (FMC) to device has traditionally been divided into transport time and door-to-balloon time. Emergency medical services (EMS) destination protocols prioritize transport to the nearest PCI-capable hospital to minimize prehospital delay. Since door-to-balloon times vary among PCI-capable hospitals, there may be populations with similar transport times to more than one PCI-capable hospital but potentially different reperfusion times. Defining the scale and distribution of these transport factors may inform strategies to optimize regional STEMI systems of care. Methods: For contiguous U.S. census block groups, we calculated road-network drive times to PCI-capable hospitals within a 90-mile straight-line radius using the OpenStreetMap Routing Machine (OSRM). PCI-capable hospitals (n=1,598) were identified from the 2024 CMS Provider of Services file by on-site cardiac catheterization laboratory service codes 1 or 3. Block groups with no PCI-capable hospital within the search radius (n=970; 741,166 adults) or with only one reachable PCI-capable hospital within the search radius (n=2,533; 2,237,857 adults), for whom the primary measure was undefined, were excluded. The primary measure was additional drive time to the second-nearest PCI-capable hospital, defined as the difference in drive time between the nearest and second-nearest PCI-capable hospitals. Analyses were weighted by adults aged ≥20 years from the 2019-2023 American Community Survey and stratified by U.S. Census Bureau region. Confidence intervals were estimated using block-group cluster bootstrap with 500 replicates. Prespecified sensitivity analyses varied traffic assumptions, geocoding precision, and PCI-center definitions. Results: Among 234,690 block groups representing 245.3 million adults, the population-weighted median additional drive time to the second-nearest PCI-capable hospital was 5.1 minutes (95% CI, 5.0-5.1; IQR, 2.0-11.9). Overall, 122 million adults (49%) lived within 5 additional minutes of a second PCI-capable hospital, 196 million (79%) within 15 minutes, and 226 million (91%) within 30 minutes. Median additional drive times were 4.3 minutes in the Northeast, 4.7 minutes in the Midwest, 4.9 minutes in the West, and 6.0 minutes in the South. Conclusions: Nearly half of U.S. adults live within 5 additional minutes of driving to a second PCI-capable hospital, and nearly 4 in 5 live within 15 additional minutes. Investigating transport strategies within these cohorts holds promise for reducing reperfusion delay but requires integrating hospital-level performance data, EMS operational protocols, and prospective evaluation.
title: Abstract 6456: A National Analysis of the Additional Drive Time to a Second Per-Cutaneous Intervention-Capable Hospital

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) commonly coexists with functional mitral regurgitation in patients undergoing transcatheter mitral valve repair (M-TEER). Concomitant tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is prevalent in this population and may reflect advanced right-sided remodeling and systemic congestion. While TR has been associated with adverse outcomes in valvular disease and heart failure, its impact after M-TEER in patients with AF remains unclear. We evaluated the effect of concomitant TR on long-term outcomes in patients with AF undergoing M-TEER using a large global federated electronic health record database. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adult patients with atrial fibrillation or flutter (ICD-10-CM: I48) undergoing transcatheter mitral valve repair (CPT: 33418, 33419, 0345T; ICD-10-PCS: 02QG3ZZ) were identified. Cohorts were defined by the presence or absence of rheumatic or nonrheumatic tricuspid regurgitation (I07.1, I36.1). The index event was the first M-TEER procedure, with outcomes assessed from 1 day through 5 years. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, stroke/transient ischemic attack/systemic embolism, major bleeding, heart failure hospitalizations, and AF hospitalizations. Propensity score matching (1:1) balanced demographics, hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and anticoagulant use. After matching, 3,865 patients remained in each cohort. Results: A total of 5,547 patients with TR and 4,335 without TR met inclusion criteria, with 3,865 patients per cohort after matching. All-cause mortality was similar between groups (25.5% vs 25.2%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.86-1.02; p=0.734). However, TR was associated with significantly higher thromboembolic events (11.5% vs 9.8%; odds ratio [OR] 1.21, 95% CI 1.02-1.42; p=0.028), major bleeding (16.4% vs 13.1%; OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.13-1.50; HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.03-1.35; p=0.014), and heart failure hospitalizations (22.2% vs 16.7%; OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.20-1.68; HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.13-1.53; p<0.001). AF-related hospitalizations were similar (86.0% vs 86.8%; p=0.694). Patients with TR also experienced a higher burden of recurrent heart failure events (mean 5.99 vs 4.37; p=0.011). Conclusions: Among patients with AF undergoing M-TEER, concomitant TR was associated with higher risks of thromboembolic events, major bleeding, and heart failure hospitalizations despite similar mortality. These findings suggest TR identifies a high-risk phenotype that may not be adequately addressed by isolated mitral intervention.

register_verdicts.note: Prognostic study of concomitant TR after M-TEER in AF patients does not test TEER against medical therapy in secondary MR outside COAPT criteria.

title: Abstract 6475: Impact of Concomitant Tricuspid Regurgitation on Clinical Outcomes in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation Undergoing Transcatheter Mitral Valve Repair: A Propensity-Matched Analysis from a Global Federated Database

abstract: Introduction: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) frequently coexists with mitral valve disease and may contribute to renal dysfunction through systemic venous congestion and impaired renal perfusion. Whether concomitant tricuspid valve (TV) intervention during mitral valve surgery is associated with improved postoperative renal function remains uncertain. We evaluated the association between concomitant TV intervention and one-year changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 311 consecutive patients who underwent mitral valve surgery at a single center between 2017 and 2024 and had available preoperative and one-year postoperative eGFR data. Patients were categorized into TV intervention (TV+, n=184; annuloplasty 163, reconstruction 15, replacement 6) and no TV intervention (TV–, n=127) groups. The primary outcome was ΔeGFR, defined as one-year postoperative minus preoperative eGFR. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using 11 covariates: age, sex, body surface area, EuroSCORE II, atrial fibrillation (AF) history, left ventricular ejection fraction, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP), baseline eGFR, mitral valve replacement, and renal dysfunction. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), multivariable linear regression adjusting for 13 covariates, and subgroup analyses by TR severity, AF status, baseline eGFR, mitral procedure type, and RVSP were also performed. Results: At baseline, TV+ patients had higher RVSP (42.2 vs 29.4 mmHg, P < 0.001), more frequent AF history (50.0% vs 20.5%, P < 0.001), and lower baseline eGFR (59.5 vs 65.2, P=0.004). In unadjusted analysis, TV+ showed greater eGFR improvement (ΔeGFR: +3.4 vs –1.0, P < 0.001). Improved eGFR was more frequent in TV+ (63.0% vs 43.3%, P < 0.001), whereas clinically significant eGFR decline (ΔeGFR < –10) was less frequent (7.6% vs 18.1%, P=0.005). After PSM (61 pairs), the association persisted (ΔeGFR: +2.8 vs –2.1, P=0.004). IPTW confirmed a significant treatment effect (coefficient: +3.20, 95% CI: 0.59-5.81, P=0.017). In multivariable regression, TV intervention remained independently associated with greater eGFR improvement (coefficient: +3.35, 95% CI: 0.42-6.27, P=0.025). Other predictors were younger age, lower EuroSCORE II, AF history, lower baseline eGFR, and higher total bilirubin. Subgroup analyses showed directionally consistent associations without significant interaction. Conclusions: Concomitant TV intervention during mitral valve surgery was independently associated with improved one-year renal function. This association was consistent across multiple analytic approaches and suggests that addressing concomitant TR during mitral valve surgery may have renal benefit, warranting prospective validation.
title: Abstract 6519: Concomitant Tricuspid Valve Intervention is Associated with Improved One-Year Renal Function After Mitral Valve Surgery

abstract: Introduction: Pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma (PAIS) is a rare and aggressive vascular malignancy that frequently mimics pulmonary thromboembolism and infectious pulmonary disease, resulting in delayed diagnosis and poor outcomes. Early recognition of atypical imaging findings is critical in emergency radiology practice. Patient information and clinical findings: A 36-year-old woman presented with a two-month history of persistent dry cough, pleuritic chest pain, and 8-kg unintentional weight loss. Initial chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a thick-walled cavitary lesion in the left upper lobe with small pleural effusion. Despite antibiotic therapy, symptoms progressed. Follow-up contrast-enhanced CT revealed multiple bilateral cavitary and subsolid pulmonary nodules, ground-glass opacities, and hepatic and splenic lesions, initially raising concern for disseminated fungal infection. Extensive microbiological evaluation, including bronchoalveolar lavage, tuberculosis testing, and cryptococcal antigen, was negative. Concurrent CT demonstrated a filling defect within the left lobar pulmonary artery consistent with pulmonary embolism, and anticoagulation therapy was initiated without clinical or radiological improvement. Diagnostic Assesment and Reasoning: Given the atypical evolution and treatment failure, multidisciplinary reassessment was performed. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG PET-CT) demonstrated intense hypermetabolic activity involving the pulmonary artery trunk and main branches, as well as multiple pulmonary nodules, favoring malignant vascular neoplasm over thromboembolic or infectious disease. Thoracoscopic biopsy and wedge resection revealed high-grade spindle cell sarcoma with marked atypia, necrosis, and elevated mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated MDM2 and CDK4 positivity, confirming pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma. Additional imaging demonstrated metastatic involvement of the left ventricle. Discussion: PAIS should be considered in patients with atypical or refractory pulmonary embolism, particularly when imaging demonstrates progressive intravascular lesions, cavitary pulmonary nodules, or absence of response to anticoagulation and antimicrobial therapy. Multimodal imaging, especially FDG PET-CT, plays a pivotal role in differentiating malignant vascular tumors from thromboembolic disease and may facilitate earlier diagnosis of this highly aggressive entity.
title: Abstract 6552: Refractory Pulmonary Embolism and Cavitary Lung Nodules as Manifestations of Pulmonary Artery Sarcoma

abstract: Introduction: Right atrial thrombus in transit is an uncommon but high-risk manifestation of acute pulmonary embolism. Early recognition is critical because it is associated with abrupt clinical deterioration and therapeutic uncertainty. Patient Information and Clinical Findings: A 43-year-old man arrived at the emergency department because of 2-hours of dyspnea and palpitations. On admission, he remained normotensive, but was tachycardic (126 bpm), tachypneic (RR 28/min), cyanotic, and severely hypoxemic, with an oxygen saturation of 71% while breathing room air. He had no prior history of venous thromboembolism, recent travel, or trauma. Left hip osteoarthritis with reduced mobility was the only relevant antecedent. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: The initial electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia and no other alterations. Laboratory studies included complete blood count (normal), kidney and liver function (normal), troponin (162,8 ng/L. Normal <45 ng/L) and arterial blood gas analysis, which showed moderate hypoxemia and hyperlactatemia (3,5 mmol/L). CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated saddle pulmonary embolism involving the main pulmonary artery bifurcation, with extension into bilateral lobar and segmental branches, signs of right ventricular overload, multilobar pulmonary infarction, and a tubular hypodense structure within the right atrium suspicious for thrombus in transit. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed right atrial thrombi forming a mobile conglomerate extending toward the right ventricle, measuring 5.2 х 1.4 cm, with right ventricular dilatation and systolic function at the lower limit of normal (TAPSE 12mm; TASV 8cm/s; FAC 37%). Therapeutic Intervention and Follow-up: The case was discussed by the pulmonary embolism response team (PERT). In view of the high thrombotic burden, mobile right-heart thrombus, positive biomarkers, hypoxemia, hyperlactatemia, and concern for early decompensation, the patient was taken for urgent endovascular treatment under general anesthesia. After thrombus debulking, right ventricular function, systemic perfusion, and oxygenation improved, and extracorporeal support was ultimately not required. Discussion: This case illustrates the value of integrating CT pulmonary angiography, echocardiography, and PERT-based decision-making in acute pulmonary embolism with thrombus in transit. Large-bore endovascular thrombectomy allowed rapid thrombus debulking and clinical stabilization in a patient with high-risk thrombotic burden and right-heart involvement, while avoiding systemic thrombolysis and extracorporeal support. In selected patients at risk of early decompensation, early multidisciplinary endovascular reperfusion may be decisive.
title: Abstract 6557: Caught in Transit: Right Atrial Thrombus and Saddle Pulmonary Embolism Treated with Large-Bore Endovascular Thrombectomy

abstract: Introduction: Coronary artery spasm (CAS) is commonly caused by endothelial dysfunction, cold exposure, or sympathetic nervous system activation. Phentermine, a weight-loss agent, is a sympathomimetic amine that suppresses appetite and may increase susceptibility to coronary vasoconstriction. We present a case of severe phentermine-induced CAS resulting in myocardial infarction, ventricular fibrillation (VF), and cardiogenic shock necessitating temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS). Case: A 48-year-old female with chronic angina and recent initiation (<60 days) of phentermine via an online pharmacy presented to the emergency department with episodic chest pain. Initially with an unremarkable ECG, high-sensitivity troponin (HsT), BNP, and lactate. She subsequently developed recurrent chest pain with repeat ECG demonstrating ST elevation in aVR and V1 with diffuse ST depressions involving the lateral, inferior, and anteroseptal leads. HsT rose from 7 ng/L to >6,000 ng/L. She became hypotensive during emergent coronary angiography, with an elevated LV end-diastolic pressure of 35 mmHg and was found to have diffuse spasm of all coronary vessels without obstructive coronary disease. Her course was complicated by VF requiring defibrillation, after which an Impella CP device was placed for hemodynamic support. Following stabilization, coronary spasm was resolved with intracoronary nitroglycerin. A right heart catheterization showed preserved cardiac indices after Impella placement. MCS was successfully weaned and removed within 24 hours, and anti-anginal medications were uptitrated. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal biventricular systolic function with an LVEF of 55-60%. She was discharged on diltiazem and isosorbide mononitrate. At 3-month follow-up, felodipine was added with improvement in angina frequency. Discussion: Previously, she was suspected to have coronary microvascular dysfunction (MVD) after coronary angiography demonstrated non-obstructive coronary arteries with sluggish flow, and metoprolol was initiated for symptom management. After excluding other causes of CAS, phentermine was identified as the most likely precipitant. This may have been caused by increased catecholamine release associated with phentermine which may promote coronary vasoconstriction through unopposed alpha-adrenergic activity. While prior reports have described an association between phentermine and CAS, the severity observed in this case with diffuse multivessel CAS, cardiogenic shock requiring MCS, and VF requiring defibrillation, represents an exceptionally severe constellation of complications. It also highlights that in patients with suspected or established MVD who are otherwise on appropriate medical therapy, phentermine can precipitate life-threatening exacerbations of CAS.
title: Abstract 6561: A Case of Phentermine-Induced Multi-Vessel Coronary Artery Spasm

abstract: Background: National-level data comparing healthcare disparities in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) are limited. Methods: The cohort was taken from the National Inpatient Sample from January 2016 to December 2022 using ICD-10-CM codes. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality for patients admitted for TAVR. The secondary outcomes were complication rates, length of stay (LOS), and total cost. Multivariate logistic regression with adjustment for age, race, and Elixhauser comorbidity index was used. Results: A total of 551,122 patients (mean age 78 years, 44% female sex) underwent TAVR. Most TAVR procedures were performed in large-bed hospitals (71%) and teaching hospitals (92%). The overall in-hospital mortality rate across the US was 1.22%. Larger and teaching hospitals had higher mortality rates (P<0.005 and P=0.03), with no difference across geographic locations (P=0.22). Larger hospitals had more procedural complications (Table 1). Larger hospitals, hospitals in the Northeast, and teaching hospitals had longer LOS (P=significant in all, Tables 1-3). Total cost was the highest in larger hospitals and teaching hospitals, with no difference based on geography (P<0.001, P=0.004, and P=0.54, respectively) (Tables 1-3). Conclusion: Despite the vast majority of TAVR procedures having been performed in large and teaching hospitals, these hospitals also had the highest mortality risk, vascular complications, total cost, and LOS. This may reflect larger and teaching hospitals performing TAVR on higher-risk individuals than smaller, non-academic hospitals. Additional studies comparing these disparities are needed.
title: Abstract 6568: Identifying National Healthcare Disparities and Outcomes in TAVR: A 7-year National Inpatient Sample Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Apixaban and rivaroxaban are the two most widely prescribed direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF). They have been compared head-to-head in other indications, including the recently published COBRRA trial for acute venous thromboembolism, which demonstrated markedly lower clinically relevant bleeding with apixaban, raising the question of whether this safety advantage extends to the AF population. Hypothesis: In propensity-matched adults with non-valvular AF, apixaban is associated with lower three-year risk of clinically relevant bleeding than rivaroxaban, with comparable rates of stroke, mortality, thromboembolic events requiring left atrial appendage closure (LAAC), and hospitalization. Methods: Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, we identified adults with non-valvular AF initiating apixaban or rivaroxaban, excluding patients with malignancy, secondary causes of AF, and prior venous or arterial thromboembolism. Among 201,398 apixaban and 50,911 rivaroxaban eligible patients, cohorts were 1:1 propensity-matched on more than 80 baseline variables spanning demographics, comorbidities, concomitant medications, and laboratory values. Six outcomes were assessed over three years: all-cause mortality, need for LAAC, stroke, a bleeding composite capturing International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) major and clinically relevant non-major bleeding, ISTH major bleeding alone, and all-cause hospitalization. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals were computed; post-match standardized mean differences were under 0.10 for all covariates. Results: Analysis yielded a population of 101,822 patients (50,911 per group). Apixaban was associated with lower three-year risk of the bleeding composite (4.1% vs 4.6%; RR 0.881, 0.830-0.935; p<0.001) and ISTH major bleeding (2.7% vs 2.9%; RR 0.928, 0.862-0.999; p=0.047). Mortality (9.8% vs 10.1%; RR 0.969, 0.934-1.006; p=0.098), need for LAAC (0.6% vs 0.6%; RR 1.110, 0.948-1.301; p=0.195), stroke (3.2% vs 3.0%; RR 1.062, 0.988-1.141; p=0.101), and hospitalization (75.0% vs 74.7%; RR 1.004, 0.997-1.012; p=0.219) did not differ. Conclusions: In the largest contemporary real-world head-to-head comparison of apixaban and rivaroxaban in non-valvular AF, apixaban was associated with significantly lower three-year risk of both ISTH major bleeding and the broader bleeding composite, without any difference in stroke, mortality, thromboembolic events requiring LAAC, or hospitalization. These findings are consistent with a bleeding-safety signal previously observed in the randomized COBRRA trial and extend this association to the AF population.
title: Abstract 6580: Does the Choice of Direct Oral Anticoagulant Matter for Bleeding in Atrial Fibrillation? A Real-World Head-to-Head Comparison of Apixaban and Rivaroxaban

abstract: Introduction: Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) remains a life-threatening complication. Large vegetations causing functional prosthetic mitral stenosis are uncommon and may present predominantly with decompensated heart failure rather than classic infectious symptoms. Case Presentation: A 61-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30-35%), multivessel coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass grafting, bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and cardiac resynchronization therapy-defibrillator presented with progressive dyspnea and lower-extremity edema despite outpatient diuretic therapy. Blood cultures grew Enterococcus faecalis . Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a large mobile vegetation measuring 3.12 х 1.46 cm attached to the bioprosthetic mitral valve. The vegetation prolapsed into the left atrium during systole and produced functional mitral stenosis with a mean transmitral gradient of 13 mmHg. Right-heart catheterization revealed severe pulmonary hypertension and elevated filling pressures (RA 24 mmHg, PA 71/51 mmHg, PCWP 45 mmHg) with a cardiac index of 1.93 L/min/m 2 .Intravenous ampicillin and ceftriaxone were initiated, and follow-up blood cultures cleared. Evaluation suggested an odontogenic source, supported by imaging demonstrating dental caries involving the right maxillary central incisor and canine. Despite antimicrobial therapy, the large vegetation, prosthetic valve obstruction, and progressive heart failure prompted surgery.The patient underwent redo sternotomy with explantation of the infected prosthesis, annular debridement, and replacement with a 33-mm bioprosthetic mitral valve. Because of severe cardiomyopathy and anticipated postoperative instability, temporary mechanical circulatory support with an Impella 5.5 was implanted via a right axillary graft. Operative findings confirmed severe prosthetic valve endocarditis with multiple vegetations. The postoperative course was notable for successful Impella explantation on postoperative day eight, clearance of bacteremia, and completion of six weeks of intravenous antibiotics. Discussion: Functional mitral stenosis caused by large prosthetic valve vegetations is an uncommon manifestation of E. faecalis endocarditis. This case highlights how obstructive valvular physiology can result in severe pulmonary hypertension, low-output heart failure, and the need for advanced surgical and mechanical circulatory support despite microbiologic control. Conclusion: Enterococcus faecalis prosthetic mitral valve endocarditis may present as functional mitral stenosis with progressive heart failure. Early recognition of obstructive physiology and multidisciplinary management are essential to optimize outcomes.
title: Abstract 6589: When Endocarditis Mimics Mitral Stenosis: Giant Enterococcus faecalis Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis Requiring Redo Mitral Valve Replacement and Impella 5.5 Support

abstract: Intro: Left ventricular thrombus (LVT) in newly diagnosed HFrEF carries significant cardioembolic risk. Unlike venous thromboembolism, LVT cannot be mechanically intercepted, making sustained therapeutic anticoagulation the only embolic defense. We present a case of recurrent cardioembolic stroke from persistent LVT complicated by an anticoagulation monitoring gap, prompting consideration of enhanced surveillance in high-risk patients. Patient Information: A 50-year-old male with hypertension, CKD stage 3, sleep apnea, and asthma presented with dyspnea and reduced exercise tolerance. Timeline: Six weeks prior, an ED presentation for chest pain, fatigue, and tachycardia with EKG showing LVH was diagnosed as costochondritis. On admission (HD1), BNP was 808 with pulmonary congestion. TTE revealed LVEF 22%, severe LV dilatation, and apical LVT. Angiography showed nonobstructive disease. Heparin was initiated HD2.On HD3, the patient was found aphasic with right hemiplegia and left gaze preference; NIHSS 23. Anti-Xa was <0.04; heparin IV was found dislodged. CTA confirmed L M1 occlusion. Thrombectomy achieved TICI 3 reperfusion but course was complicated by L ICA dissection, malignant edema requiring hemicraniectomy, hemorrhagic conversion, and ventriculoperitoneal shunting. TTE on HD32 showed persistent LVT, LVEF 21%.
