Diagnostic Assessment: In retrospect, prior ED presentation with chest pain, fatigue, and tachycardia may represent an earlier manifestation of evolving cardiomyopathy, potentially delaying severe HFrEF and LVT formation recognition. IV dislodgement and anti-Xa<0.04 confirmed a gap in anticoagulation delivery. Patient continued to sustain embolic events from persistent LVT. Its LV location precluded mechanical interception, forcing subsequent anticoagulation discussions weighed against hemorrhagic transformation risk. Intervention: Thrombectomy achieved initial reperfusion. Anticoagulation was navigated amid hemorrhagic transformation, persistent LVT, and new DVTs, requiring iterative goals-of-care discussions. Outcomes: At seven weeks, the patient remains hospitalized with tracheostomy, PEG tube, and significant neurological deficits. LVT persists. Goals of care discussions are ongoing. Discussion: This case exposes a potential gap in heparin monitoring for high-risk patients. Despite an active order, anticoagulation lapsed in a monitored setting. When emboli cannot be mechanically intercepted, uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation is critical. We propose enhanced anti-Xa monitoring every four hours, rather than every 24 once therapeutic, for high-risk patients with LVT, severely reduced LVEF, mechanical valve, or prior cardioembolic stroke. This case has prompted institutional quality improvement projects.
title: Abstract 6621: Recurrent Cardioembolic Stroke from Persistent LV Thrombus in Newly Diagnosed HFrEF: A Case for Enhanced Anticoagulation Monitoring Protocols

abstract: Background: Cardiac sarcoidosis is associated with ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, heart failure, and sudden cardiac death. Black patients have a higher prevalence of systemic sarcoidosis, though disparities in diagnostic evaluation and inpatient outcomes remain poorly defined. We evaluated racial differences in advanced imaging utilization and inpatient outcomes among hospitalizations for cardiac sarcoidosis. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of the National Inpatient Sample from 2016-2023. Adult hospitalizations with cardiac sarcoidosis were identified using ICD-10 coding. Patients were stratified by race, with primary comparisons between Black and White patients. Outcomes included cardiac MRI utilization, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, hospital-level, and comorbidity-related variables. Results: A weighted cohort of 18,742 hospitalizations was identified. Black patients were younger and had higher rates of acute heart failure, ventricular arrhythmias, and complete heart block compared with White patients. Despite greater arrhythmic burden, Black patients were less likely to undergo cardiac MRI (aOR 0.74, 95% CI 0.66-0.83) and ICD implantation (aOR 0.81, 95% CI 0.72-0.92). Black patients additionally had higher odds of cardiogenic shock (aOR 1.28, 95% CI 1.10-1.49) and prolonged hospitalization. In-hospital mortality was numerically higher among Black patients. Conclusions: Significant racial disparities exist in the evaluation and management of cardiac sarcoidosis in the United States. Despite higher arrhythmic and heart failure burden, Black patients were less likely to receive advanced imaging and ICD therapy. These findings highlight important inequities in the diagnosis and management of cardiac sarcoidosis.
title: Abstract 6627: Racial Disparities in Diagnostic Evaluation and Inpatient Outcomes Among Patients Hospitalized with Cardiac Sarcoidosis: A National Inpatient Sample Analysis (2016-2023)

abstract: Background: Elderly patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) face simultaneously elevated ischemic and bleeding risks. While potent P2Y12 inhibitors (ticagrelor, prasugrel) provide superior platelet inhibition over clopidogrel, their net benefit in older adults remains uncertain given limited dedicated trial data. Objectives: To assess the safety and efficacy of potent dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) versus clopidogrel-based DAPT in elderly patients post-PCI, and to determine whether treatment effects differ between elderly and non-elderly patients. Methods: We systematically searched PubMed and Ovid Embase for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing potent DAPT with clopidogrel in elderly patients, including elderly subgroup analyses. The primary outcome was net adverse clinical events (NACE). Secondary outcomes included MACE, major bleeding, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MI, and stent thrombosis. Pooled hazard ratios were derived using random-effects meta-analysis (REML). Age-based treatment heterogeneity was assessed via the χ 2 interaction test. Results: Ten RCTs (n = 11,574 elderly patients) with enrolment from 2004 to 2024 were included. Potent DAPT significantly reduced all-cause mortality versus clopidogrel (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.68-0.97; p = 0.02). However, potent DAPT was not associated with significant reductions in NACE (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.68-1.07), MACE (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.74-1.05), or major bleeding (HR 0.98, 95% CI 0.73-1.31). In age-comparative analyses, MACE reduction with potent DAPT was significantly greater in non-elderly patients (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.71-0.86) than in the elderly (interaction p = 0.005). No significant interaction was observed for NACE (p = 0.628) or bleeding (p = 0.535). Conclusions: Potent DAPT does not increase bleeding risk relative to clopidogrel in elderly PCI patients and may reduce all-cause mortality. However, its ischemic benefit is significantly attenuated compared to younger patients. These findings support individualized, risk-stratified DAPT selection in older adults. Dedicated, adequately powered trials in elderly populations remain a research priority. Keywords: dual antiplatelet therapy; P2Y12 inhibitors; elderly; percutaneous coronary intervention; clopidogrel; ticagrelor; prasugrel; meta-analysis
title: Abstract 6630: Optimal Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Potency in Elderly Patients Following Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: If reperfused, larger myocardial infarctions (MIs) are prone to hemorrhage and subsequent iron deposition; with both being stronger predictors of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) than MI size alone. Importantly, as scar ages, large/hemorrhagic MIs shrink more than small/non-hemorrhagic MIs in absolute terms. Additionally, recent reports suggest that hemorrhage/iron deposition is a strong driver of fatty degeneration (lipomatous metaplasia, LM) of MI scar, where iron deposits accelerate scar resorption via collagen replacement by adipose tissue. Research Question: It remains unknown whether infarcts with small scar size, therefore, with low resorption potential, also undergo LM. Methods: Ten pigs underwent a closed-chest 90-minute ischemia-reperfusion in the left anterior descending artery and were followed by T2* and LGE MRI on Day 5 (Fig 1a), Week 8, and Week 16 post-MI using a clinical 3T MRI scanner. On Day 5, Hemo MIs were identified on T2* as hypointense core (≥1 mL) with signal intensity 2 SD below that of the remote myocardium. At Week 16, hearts were explanted for histological analysis using elastin Masson trichrome and Prussian blue stains. Results: Comparing Hemo (n=5) and Non-Hemo (n=5) groups there was significantly (i) increased MI size in Hemo at all time points (D5: p=0.01; W8: p=0.04; W16: p=0.02; Fig 2a); (ii) increased T2* hypointense core volume in Hemo (p=0.02) on Day 5 but no difference at Weeks 8 (p=0.71) and 16 (p=0.20; Fig 2b); (iii) increased absolute MI resorption in Hemo from D5-W8 (p=0.01) but no difference from W8-W16 (p=0.38; Fig 2c). Week-16 histology revealed complete resolution of iron deposits in Hemo MIs and LM in both Hemo and Non-Hemo MI scars (Fig 3). Conclusion: Throughout early phase of chronic MI, the absolute resorption of scar is greater in larger iron-laden infarcts compared to smaller non-hemorrhagic infarcts. Following iron clearance, however, absolute resorption of scar becomes similar between both MI types irrespective of acute infarct size/hemorrhage status or LM presence.
title: Abstract 6636: Chronic Myocardial Infarction Remodeling is a Dynamic Process Following Iron-Deposit Resolution

abstract: Background: Conventional teaching holds that anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) more often requires permanent pacing through His-Purkinje destruction, whereas inferior STEMI heart block is usually transient and vagally mediated. Whether infarct territory relates differently to heart block occurrence than to its permanence has not been tested at the population level in the primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) era. Research Question: In contemporary STEMI, do anterior and inferior infarcts differ in heart block occurrence, and, among hospitalizations with heart block, in progression to permanent pacing? Methods: Using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2023), we identified hospitalizations with anterior (I21.01, I21.02, I21.09) or inferior (I21.11, I21.19) STEMI, age ≥18, excluding pre-existing pacemakers or defibrillators. The primary outcome was permanent pacemaker implantation (single- or dual-chamber generator PCS codes, excluding resynchronization and defibrillator devices). Secondary outcomes were complete AV block (I44.2), high-grade AV block (complete, unspecified, or trifascicular), in-hospital mortality, and cardiogenic shock. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, insurance, ZIP income, hospital characteristics, primary PCI receipt, thrombolysis, individual Elixhauser comorbidities, and admission year. A conditional analysis among hospitalizations with complete AV block compared anterior versus inferior pacing rates. Results: Among an estimated 1,072,025 STEMI hospitalizations, 603,275 (56.3%) were inferior and 468,750 (43.7%) anterior; 5,060 (0.47%) received a permanent pacemaker. Crude rates were lower for anterior STEMI: complete AV block 1.31% versus 4.94%, and permanent pacing 0.27% versus 0.63%. After adjustment, anterior STEMI had lower odds of complete AV block (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.21-0.23), high-grade AV block (aOR 0.22, 95% CI 0.21-0.24), and permanent pacing (aOR 0.38, 95% CI 0.33-0.44, all p<0.001). However, conditional on complete AV block, anterior STEMI hospitalizations were 75% more likely to progress to permanent pacing (aOR 1.75, 95% CI 1.40-2.19, p<0.001). Anterior STEMI was also associated with higher mortality (aOR 1.30, 95% CI 1.25-1.35) and cardiogenic shock (aOR 1.09, 95% CI 1.06-1.13). Conclusions: Infarct territory relates to heart block occurrence and to its permanence in opposite directions. Anterior STEMI produces less heart block overall, yet when it occurs the block is far more likely to be irreversible and require pacing, while inferior STEMI block is common but usually resolves. This conditional discordance separates the frequency of conduction disease from its reversibility: the mechanism of block, not its incidence, governs pacing need after STEMI.
title: Abstract 6662: Heart Block and Permanent Pacing After Anterior versus Inferior ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction: A Nationwide Analysis, 2016-2023

abstract: Background: Catheter-directed therapies for acute pulmonary embolism have evolved rapidly since FDA approval of large-bore mechanical thrombectomy devices, but population-level utilization, comparative outcomes versus catheter-directed thrombolysis, and equity of access remain poorly characterized. Research Question: How have catheter-directed therapies for pulmonary embolism evolved in utilization, outcomes, and access disparities between 2016 and 2023? Methods: Using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2023), we identified adult hospitalizations with acute pulmonary embolism (ICD-10-CM I26.x) and classified procedural management as mechanical thrombectomy (ICD-10-PCS 02CP3ZZ, 02CQ3ZZ, 02CR3ZZ), catheter-directed thrombolysis (3E04317), systemic thrombolysis (3E03317), or no advanced therapy. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, insurance, ZIP income, hospital characteristics, individual Elixhauser comorbidities, acute cor pulmonale, saddle pulmonary embolism, cardiogenic shock, and admission year. Results: Among 674,610 adult pulmonary embolism hospitalizations (3,373,049 weighted), 14,651 received mechanical thrombectomy alone and 3,193 received catheter-directed thrombolysis alone. Mechanical thrombectomy use grew from 0.38% in 2016 to 5.79% in 2023 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.60 per year, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.56-1.64, p<0.001); catheter-directed thrombolysis declined (aOR 0.94 per year, p<0.001). Compared with no advanced therapy, mechanical thrombectomy was associated with 29% lower adjusted in-hospital mortality (aOR 0.71, 95% CI 0.66-0.77, p<0.001), while catheter-directed thrombolysis was associated with higher mortality (aOR 3.69, 95% CI 3.35-4.07, p<0.001), likely reflecting confounding by indication. Mechanical thrombectomy was also associated with 24% lower intracranial hemorrhage (aOR 0.76, 95% CI 0.65-0.89, p=0.001). Within the mechanical thrombectomy cohort, in-hospital mortality declined 17% per year (aOR 0.83 per year, 95% CI 0.79-0.86, p<0.001). Access disparities were substantial: women had 10% lower adjusted odds of receiving therapy (aOR 0.90, p<0.001), Black patients showed no significant difference (aOR 1.02, 95% CI 0.96-1.08), Hispanic patients 20% lower (aOR 0.80, p<0.001), and Other-race patients 14% lower (aOR 0.86, p=0.009). Catheter-directed therapy was concentrated at urban teaching hospitals (aOR 2.89, 95% CI 2.46-3.39) and large-bedsize centers (aOR 1.61, 95% CI 1.49-1.74). Conclusions: Mechanical thrombectomy utilization grew sharply from 2016 to 2023 and was associated with lower in-hospital mortality and bleeding than no advanced therapy. Access remains concentrated at academic and large-volume centers and unevenly distributed by sex and race/ethnicity, indicating a need for more equitable access.
title: Abstract 6664: Trends, Outcomes, and Access Disparities in Catheter-Directed Therapies for Pulmonary Embolism: A Nationwide Analysis, 2016-2023

abstract: Background: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (MIRI) is a common clinical complication following reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction, which further exacerbates the initial infarct damage. Effective therapeutic strategies for MIRI remain limited. The reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, along with the shift in cellular metabolism, represents a core mechanism of MIRI. However, as the primary mediator of ROS-induced pathogenesis, the precise role and underlying mechanisms of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) in MIRI remain unclear. Methods: To investigate the effects of MIRI on cellular H 2 O 2 production and catalase (CAT) activity, a hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model was established in primary rat cardiomyocytes. Catalase nanocapsules [n(CAT)] were engineered via in situ polymerization to achieve biodelivery of exogenous CAT for the treatment of MIRI. In vivo rat myocardial I/R models and in vitro H/R models (primary cardiomyocytes and H9c2 cells) were utilized to validate the targeted H 2 O 2 -scavenging capability of n(CAT). Mitochondrial function was assessed using the Seahorse XFe24 Analyzer and JC-1 staining. To further evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of n(CAT) against MIRI, comprehensive serological, functional, pathological, and molecular biological assessments were performed in the rat I/R model, and transcriptomic RNA sequencing was utilized to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Results: We found that H/R triggered substantial H 2 O 2 production and significantly decreased CAT activity in cardiomyocytes, with H 2 O 2 generation being further exacerbated by the CAT inhibitor aminotriazole. Notably, n(CAT) specifically targeted and accumulated in the ischemic myocardium of rats, efficiently scavenging local H 2 O 2 . In vitro , n(CAT) attenuated the H/R-induced H 2 O 2 burst, restored impaired CAT activity, ameliorated mitochondrial respiratory dysfunction, and rescued mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 1). In vivo , n(CAT) administration significantly decreased serum levels of cTnI, CK-MB, and LDH, diminished myocardial infarct size, and preserved cardiac function in the rat I/R model. Furthermore, n(CAT) mitigated oxidative stress, suppressed myocardial apoptosis, and reduced plasma levels of IL-6 and TNF-α (Figure 2). Transcriptomic profiling of the rat hearts revealed that I/R injury induced dysregulation in mitochondrial function, energy metabolism, and glucose-lipid metabolism. Importantly, n(CAT) treatment restored this metabolic homeostasis, thereby protecting the injured myocardium and promoting functional recovery (Figure 3). Conclusions: Our study demonstrates that catalase nanocapsules [n(CAT)] protect the heart against MIRI by scavenging reperfusion-induced H 2 O 2 and restoring CAT activity, which is likely driven by ameliorating mitochondrial dysfunction and restoring energy metabolism homeostasis.
title: Abstract 6682: Targeted Hydrogen Peroxide Scavenging by Catalase Nanocapsules Attenuates Myocardial Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury by Restoring Energy Metabolism Homeostasis

abstract: Background: Hypertension is a growing global public health burden, with a considerable proportion of patients with hypertension not receiving treatment. Longitudinal patterns of blood pressure (BP) stage are heterogeneous, and the association between hypertension stage transition defined by American Heart Association guidelines and cardiovascular outcomes among working-age adults remains unclear. Research Question: Is BP stage transition associated with 10-year cardiovascular outcomes among working-age adults with newly identified stage 1 or stage 2 hypertension? Methods: We analyzed 1,533,054 participants who newly met criteria for stage 1 or stage 2 hypertension at the index health check-up without initiation of antihypertensive medication before the second health check-up between April 2006 and March 2024 using a claims database linked to health check-up data. Participants were classified into 6 transition groups: stage 1 to elevated BP/normal, stage 1, or stage 2; and stage 2 to elevated BP/normal, stage 1, or stage 2. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, and heart failure hospitalization within 10 years. We examined the association between BP stage transition and the primary outcome using adjusted Cox proportional hazards models. Results: Among the eligible participants, the mean age was 45±12 years, and systolic/diastolic BP at the index health check-up was 136/84 mm Hg (interquartile range 132-142/78-90). At the index health check-up, 1,026,691 participants had stage 1 hypertension and 506,363 had stage 2 hypertension. At the second health check-up, 548,315 (53.4%), 312,869 (30.5%), and 165,507 (16.1%) participants in the stage 1 cohort transitioned to elevated BP/normal, stage 1, and stage 2, respectively. In the stage 2 cohort, 98,534 (19.5%), 127,314 (25.1%), and 280,515 (55.4%) participants transitioned to elevated BP/normal, stage 1, and stage 2, respectively. (Figure 1) The incidence rates of the primary outcome were 4.15, 5.26, 7.45, 6.30, 7.12, and 9.99 per 1000 person-years, respectively. (Figure 2) Compared with stage 1 to elevated BP/normal, all other transition groups had higher risks of the primary outcome: stage 1 to stage 1 (hazard ratio [HR], 1.15; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12-1.19); stage 1 to stage 2 (HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.45-1.54); stage 2 to elevated BP/normal (HR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.29-1.40); stage 2 to stage 1 (HR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.39-1.48); and stage 2 to stage 2 (HR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.85-1.95). (Figure 3) Conclusions: Among working-age adults, BP stage transition was associated with cardiovascular risk. Higher index BP stage remained relevant to cardiovascular risk even among participants who transitioned to lower BP stage categories, supporting longitudinal BP stage assessment.
title: Abstract 6683: Longitudinal Blood Pressure Stage Transition and Clinical Outcomes in Working-Age Adults

abstract: Background: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative to surgical mitral valve repair for patients with severe mitral regurgitation. However, observational studies comparing TEER outcomes suffer from immortal time bias—a systematic error arising when patients must survive an evaluation and waitlist period to receive treatment. The "Ghost Cohort" comprises patients who die during this pre-treatment interval and are systematically excluded from naive analyses, artificially inflating apparent survival rates. Recent real-world evidence from a TriNetX study of 4,058 matched pairs reported superior 1-year survival with surgery versus TEER (HR 0.78, 95% CI: 0.64-0.96), while registry data from complex degenerative mitral regurgitation patients showed 32.6% 3-year all-cause mortality following MitraClip. The magnitude of bias introduced by excluding waitlist deaths remains poorly quantified in the TEER literature. Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library from inception to March 2026 to identify relevant studies and developed a simulation study calibrated on real-world TEER referral patterns to quantify immortal time bias. Marginal structural models (MSM) with inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) were applied to correct for time-dependent confounding and immortal time bias. Stabilized truncated weights (mean 0.98, SD 0.86) were computed following established methodology. We compared naive intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses that excluded waitlist deaths against MSM-corrected ITT estimates incorporating the Ghost Cohort. Results: Among 1,000 simulated referred patients, 78 (7.8%) died during the waitlist period, constituting the Ghost Cohort. Of the survivors, 830 received TEER. Naive analysis excluding waitlist deaths yielded 1-year survival of 78.6%, while MSM-corrected ITT analysis including the Ghost Cohort revealed true 1-year survival of 69.4%—a bias magnitude of 9.2 percentage points. The naive hazard ratio of 0.62 was substantially attenuated to an MSM-corrected HR of 0.82. This bias magnitude is comparable to that observed in dialysis timing studies, where biased methods produced HR 1.58 versus MSM-corrected HR 0.89, with 5.1 percentage point absolute risk differences. Conclusions: Immortal time bias substantially overestimates TEER survival benefits in observational studies by systematically excluding the Ghost Cohort of waitlist deaths. MSM with IPCW provides a rigorous framework for correcting this bias and should be mandatory in comparative effectiveness research for TEER and other time-to-treatment interventions. Failure to account for immortal time bias may lead to erroneous clinical and policy decisions regarding patient selection and resource allocation for transcatheter mitral valve therapies.
title: Abstract 6687: Resurrecting the Ghost Cohort: Marginal Structural Models Correcting Immortal Time Bias in TEER Waitlists

abstract: Introduction: Cardiac valve disease, especially aortic stenosis/regurgitation, is increasingly prevalent with aging. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) now extends to younger, low-to-intermediate-risk patients. Bioprosthetic heart valves (BHVs), mostly glutaraldehyde (GLUT)-fixed porcine or bovine pericardium, have limited durability (10-15 years) due to thrombosis, inflammation, and calcification. However, up to 25% of explanted BHVs from younger patients show degeneration without evident calcification. The mechanisms of this non-calcific BHV degeneration remain poorly understood. Research Questions: Non-calcific degeneration occurs more frequently in younger patients and those with metabolic syndrome, featuring deposition of metabolic byproducts, AGEs, and tyrosine oxidation products. We therefore focused on early BHV degeneration mechanisms in this population. Methods: Human degenerated BHV specimens were collected for immunohistochemistry (AGEs, CD3, CD68, ECM changes). GLUT BHVs were intravascularly implanted in rats to assess metabolite deposition, immune activation, and ECM remodeling under hemodynamic conditions. Proteomics was performed on human and rat explants. Fatigue testing (200 million cycles) evaluated ECM collagen architecture and mechanical properties under metabolic stimulation. Results: Human explants and rat implants showed deposition of metabolic-immune-inflammatory products. Fatigue testing under metabolic stimulation revealed significant surface metabolite deposition and disorganized ECM collagen fibers vs. controls. Proteomics confirmed activation of metabolic/immune processes, with GO enrichment in immune responses, IGF pathways, and ECM binding. KEGG identified NF-κB, cytokine-cytokine receptor (VCAM, ICAM), glucose metabolism, PI3K-AKT, and ECM-receptor pathways. Transcriptomics of poorly endothelialized GLUT valves showed RAGE-mediated metabolic-inflammatory pathway regulation. Conclusion: In summary, our work indicates that metabolic-immune-inflammatory crosstalk critically drives early BHV degeneration via mechanisms distinct from calcification. Human and rat models consistently show metabolite deposition and immune activation. Fatigue testing proves that this crosstalk directly disrupts ECM collagen architecture, compromising valve integrity. Proteomic/transcriptomic analyses identify RAGE, NF-κB, cytokine-cytokine receptor, and PI3K-AKT as key mediators linking metabolic stress to immune activation and ECM remodeling. These findings establish metabolic-immune-inflammatory crosstalk as a primary driver of non-calcific BHV degeneration, offering new mechanistic insights and supporting surface coating strategies targeting these pathways to improve valve durability, especially in younger and metabolically compromised patients.
title: Abstract 6748: Beyond Calcification: Metabolic-Immune-Inflammatory Mechanisms of Early BHV Failure - Insights from Human Explants, Rat Models, and Fatigue Testing

abstract: Background: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE), formerly termed marantic endocarditis, is a rare emboligenic manifestation of malignancy-associated hypercoagulability. First described in 1888 by Reinhold Ziegler, it is characterized by sterile platelet–fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves. The mechanism is not fully understood but is believed to involve endothelial injury with subsequent fibrin deposition. NBTE is most commonly associated with advanced malignancy, particularly lung and pancreatic adenocarcinomas. Diagnosis is often made post-mortem, as small, friable vegetations may be missed on echocardiography. Case Summary: A 71-year-old woman with newly diagnosed bladder malignancy and bilateral deep venous thromboses developed recurrent multifocal ischemic strokes despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Neuroimaging showed embolic infarcts in multiple vascular territories, and transesophageal echocardiography revealed two mobile aortic valve masses. Blood cultures were negative, and there were no clinical signs of infection, favoring NBTE. She was started on therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin and underwent oncologic evaluation; retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy confirmed metastatic urinary tract carcinoma. She later presented with acute aphasia and right-sided weakness due to a middle cerebral artery infarction requiring thrombectomy. Her course was complicated by a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary artery disease, followed by recurrent thromboses, consumptive coagulopathy, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Despite management, she declined and transitioned to comfort care, ultimately resulting in death. Discussion: This case underscores the importance of recognizing NBTE in malignancy with recurrent embolic events. Prompt differentiation from infective endocarditis is critical, as management relies on anticoagulation and treatment of the underlying malignancy rather than antimicrobial therapy.
title: Abstract 6776: Recurrent Multifocal Embolic Strokes in a Patient with Bladder Malignancy and Aortic Valve Thrombotic Vegetations: Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis

abstract: Background: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) complicates up to half of adults with unrepaired atrial septal defect (ASD) and is a recognized procedural risk factor. No nationally representative study has characterized PH-associated outcomes after ASD/patent foramen ovale (PFO) closure across transcatheter and surgical approaches. Research Hypothesis: We hypothesized PH would be independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality and morbidity following ASD/PFO closure, with differential effects by procedural approach. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (NIS;2016-2022). Adults undergoing transcatheter or surgical ASD/PFO closure were identified by ICD-10 codes. PH was defined by ICD-10-CM codes for pulmonary arterial hypertension, secondary PH, and Eisenmenger syndrome. Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock, mechanical ventilation, acute kidney injury (AKI), arrhythmia, and MACE. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) adjusting for demographics, comorbidities, hospital characteristics, procedural approach, and year. A prespecified PHхapproach interaction was evaluated. Results: Among 3,859 unweighted hospitalizations (~19,295 nationally weighted), 14.0% had PH. PH patients were older (57.9 vs.53.8 years), more often female (56.3% vs.50.8%), had higher comorbidity (Charlson≥3:38.9% vs.26.2%), and more commonly underwent surgical closure (52.0% vs.33.0%;all p<0.05). Unadjusted mortality was higher with PH (3.33% vs.1.87%;p=0.033), as were respiratory failure (38.2% vs.13.8%), cardiogenic shock (19.1% vs.6.4%), MACE (28.0% vs.11.7%), arrhythmia (45.9% vs.25.1%), AKI (26.5% vs.13.5%), and mechanical ventilation (15.9% vs.7.3%;all p<0.001). After adjustment, PH was not independently associated with overall mortality (aOR 1.35;95%CI 0.72-2.55;p=0.35). However, a significant PHхapproach interaction was detected (p-interaction=0.059). PH independently increased mortality after transcatheter closure (aOR 2.68;95%CI 1.07-6.73;p=0.036) but not surgical closure (aOR 0.85;95%CI 0.36-2.01;p=0.72). PH remained independently associated with respiratory failure (aOR 2.88), cardiogenic shock (aOR 2.10), arrhythmia (aOR 2.06), MACE (aOR 1.87), mechanical ventilation (aOR 1.68), and AKI (aOR 1.58). Conclusions: In this nationally representative study, PH was present in one in seven ASD/PFO closure hospitalizations and independently associated with significantly higher in-hospital morbidity. Though not associated with overall adjusted mortality, PH conferred nearly three-fold higher mortality risk in transcatheter closure patients, supporting systematic preprocedural PH risk stratification before transcatheter ASD/PFO closure.
title: Abstract 6783: Pulmonary Hypertension and In-Hospital Morbidity and Mortality Following Transcatheter versus Surgical Closure of Atrial Septal Defect or Patent Foramen Ovale: A Nationwide Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Kawasaki disease (KD) is a childhood vasculitis that causes vast coronary complications, including aneurysms, stenosis, and thrombosis. With the earliest cohorts now reaching their 30s-40s, late manifestations of KD are becoming increasingly common. We present a case of KD recrudescence causing STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock ultimately requiring orthotropic heart transplantation (OHT). Patient Information: A 36-year-old male with KD diagnosed at age 3 status post two-vessel CABG (LIMA to mid-LAD and diagonal) presented to an outside facility with cardiac chest pain. Clinical Findings & Timeline: On arrival, he was tachycardic in the 120s and hypotensive (90s/60s). Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed new left bundle branch block and inferior ST elevation (Figure 1). Troponin was 4,350 ng/L, and BNP was 12,898. He was intubated due to respiratory distress from pulmonary edema on chest x ray. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Left heart catheterization revealed ostial left main occlusion with a large prior aneurysm, mid-RCA occlusion, and patent grafting. Contrast ventriculography showed left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 10-15%. Percutaneous thrombectomy and angioplasty was repeatedly attempted without success. Notably, CRP was markedly elevated at 321.5 mg/L, raising concern for KD recrudescence as the underlying cause. Due to suspicion of cardiogenic shock plus severely reduced LVEF, an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) was placed, dobutamine and norepinephrine were started, and the patient was transferred to a tertiary center. Therapeutic Intervention(s): On arrival, labs showed lactate of 5.51, pH 7.28, creatinine 2.09, AST 420, and ALT 82. Swan-Ganz catheterization revealed.cardiac index of 1.8 L/min/m2 despite the IABP. Given refractory shock plus severe biventricular failure on formal trans-thoracic echocardiogram (TTE) with LVEF of 15-20%, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) was initiated. By day 6, bedside TTE showed minimal LVEF improvement. Thus, on day 7, a HeartMate II left ventricular assist device (LVAD) and CentriMag right ventricular assist device (RVAD) were implanted, and the patient was listed for OHT (UNOS status 1A). Follow-up, Outcomes, & Adverse Events: OHT occurred on day 97 with no complications. Discussion/Synthesis: This case illustrates the potential for severe adult consequences in KD patients. Coronary aneurysms from KD undergo progressive intimal thickening, calcification, and atherosclerosis, which can predispose to ACS up to decades later. When revascularization is not an immediate option, mechanical circulatory support may represent the only viable pathway. Furthermore, this case highlights the importance of lifelong surveillance in KD patients and emphasizes the role of a stepwise strategy- IABP to VA-ECMO to biventricular VAD in this patient- as bridging to definitive treatment.

register_verdicts.note: Single case report of Kawasaki disease with cardiogenic shock does not bear on inotrope strategy.

title: Abstract 6811: Thirty-Three Years Later: Kawasaki Disease Resurfacing as STEMI and Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Background: The Further Cardiovascular Outcomes Research with PCSK9 Inhibition in Subjects with Elevated Risk (FOURIER) open-label extension (OLE) study demonstrated the long-term safety of evolocumab and efficacy of starting evolocumab earlier. However, in the absence of a concurrent placebo arm in FOURIER OLE, long-term treatment effects vs placebo could not be estimated. Research Question: Is long-term treatment with evolocumab associated with a lower risk for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)? Methods: An external control arm (ECA) was created using data from UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum linked to hospital and mortality data by applying the FOURIER trial eligibility criteria and enrollment period (February 2013-June 2015). Endpoints included 4-point (P) MACE (myocardial infarction [MI], stroke, coronary revascularization, cardiovascular [CV] death), 3P MACE (MI, stroke, CV death), and the individual MACE components. Comparability of the ECA with the FOURIER placebo arm was evaluated using two checkpoints. First, after applying propensity weights, baseline characteristics were compared between the FOURIER trial and ECA to assess if absolute standardized mean differences (SMDs) were ≤ 0.15. Second, after applying censoring weights, event rates were compared between the FOURIER placebo arm and ECA over the trial duration, accounting for differential use of lipid-lowering therapy in the trial and ECA by censoring for post-index lipid-lowering therapy discontinuation. Hazard ratios (HRs) including 1.0 and overlapping 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for event rates indicated comparability. Long-term effectiveness for evolocumab vs ECA was estimated for endpoints meeting both checkpoints. HRs were derived using weighted survival models comparing event rates in the combined FOURIER and FOURIER OLE evolocumab arm to the ECA. Results: Among 56,490 patients in the ECA before weighting, 51%, 30%, and 29% had a history of MI, ischemic stroke, and peripheral arterial disease, respectively. Before weighting, 30% and 67% were on high- and moderate-intensity statins, respectively, and 2% were on ezetimibe. After weighting, all baseline SMDs for the ECA vs FOURIER were < 0.15. Event rates in the ECA over the FOURIER trial period were comparable with the placebo arm for 3P MACE ( Figure 1 ), MI, stroke, and CV death but not for 4P MACE and coronary revascularization. Over a median (maximum) follow-up of 6.6 (8.1) years, patients treated with evolocumab had a 29% lower risk of 3P MACE (HR: 0.71 [95% CI: 0.65, 0.79]) compared with the ECA ( Fig ure 2 ). For MI, stroke, and CV death, the HR (95% CI) was 0.63 (0.55, 0.72), 0.77 (0.64, 0.93), and 0.75 (0.63, 0.88), respectively. Conclusions: Over 8.1 years, patients treated with evolocumab had a lower risk of major CV events compared with the ECA, supporting its long-term effectiveness vs placebo beyond the randomized trial duration.
title: Abstract 6839: Long-Term Effectiveness of Evolocumab in Reducing the Risk for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Comparing FOURIER OLE Data to External Control Using a Principled Approach

abstract: Background: Untreated atrial fibrillation (AF) has a high risk of stroke. Insertable cardiac monitors (ICM) have been shown to detect AF more frequently than standard monitoring methods in patients with cryptogenic stroke (CS). Clinical interventions such as oral anticoagulation (OAC) or left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) are commonly prescribed for patients with documented AF to prevent secondary strokes. Earlier detection and treatment of AF may therefore reduce recurrence risk. Research Question: To assess whether CS patients with AF detected by ICMs who receive clinical intervention have a lower risk of recurrent stroke compared with those without clinical intervention or without detected AF. Methods: We merged commercial insurance claims data and ICM monitoring data for patients ≥18 years of age who received an ICM for post-CS monitoring between March 2017-December 2024 (index = ICM insertion date). Patients with a prior history of OAC, AF ablation, LAAO procedures, or pre-existing cardiac implantable electronic device were excluded. Follow-up continued until data end or the recurrent ischemic stroke. AF diagnosis was defined as at least two minutes of device-detected AF with an AF diagnosis code or subsequent clinical intervention (i.e. initiation of OAC or LAAO procedure), with diagnosis date assigned as the earliest of either the AF diagnosis or clinical intervention. Annualized stroke rates (ASRs) during post-ICM follow-up were calculated and compared between patients with and without an AF diagnosis and with and without a clinical intervention, with both AF diagnosis and clinical intervention treated as time-varying covariates. Results: A total of 2,306 patients met the inclusion criteria (mean age 58.8 ± 10.5 years; 40% female; mean CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score 4.5 ± 1.3). AF was detected in 333 patients (14.4%) over a mean follow-up of 11.6 months, among whom 219 patients (65.8%) received clinical intervention following AF detection. Overall, 102 patients experienced recurrent stroke (ASR 3.4%). Stroke rate differed according to detection of AF and related AF-triggered interventions (Table). Among these, two had detected AF and received clinical intervention (ASR 0.8%), ten had detected AF without clinical intervention (ASR 6.7%), and 84 had no AF detected and no clinical intervention (ASR 3.6%). Compared with patients with detected AF who did not receive clinical intervention, those who received intervention had an 88.2% lower relative ASR (p<0.001). Conclusion: In this cohort, 14.4% of CS patients with ICMs had AF detected and the majority (65.8%) subsequently received clinical intervention. The recurrent stroke rate was 88.2% lower among patients with detected AF who received clinical intervention compared with those without clinical intervention. These findings suggest that timely clinical intervention following AF detection with ICMs lowers recurrent stroke risk.
title: Abstract 6847: Secondary Stroke Risk Reduction in an Insertable Cardiac Monitoring Cryptogenic Stroke Population

abstract: In 2024, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) awarded the American Heart Association (AHA) a grant to implement a three-year national initiative aiming to improve heart valve disease (HVD) awareness and education. This initiative encompasses three integrated workstreams: (1) national communication campaign addressing HVD; (2) HVD education and awareness for health care professionals; and (3) women’s HVD education and awareness to strengthen community capacity. Together, these strategies strive to address gaps in knowledge, early recognition, and equitable access to care. A critical gap exists in routine patient screening and early detection of HVD among healthcare professionals, particularly in primary care. A national heart valve center learning collaborative will strengthen education and improve primary care screening practices through peer-led learnings. Earlier intervention in the patient journey, prior to the need of specialty care, will improve timely identification and referral of individuals with HVD. To begin, a survey addressing valve center size, education practices, and infrastructure was disseminated to heart valve centers across the U.S. Based on responses, a scoring rubric was developed and selected sites completed an onboarding process prior to the initial learning collaborative. The cohort convenes quarterly and leverages surveys, focused work groups, and individualized feedback to support implementation. Each of the fourteen participating valve centers was asked to engage fifty referring providers in the initiative. Through these iterative learning activities, barriers to screening and early detection of HVD are systematically identified, which informs the development of targeted educational resources and strategies to address care gaps. Development of a centralized website to house educational resources was an initial focus. Resource work groups collaborated to develop five new assets, including fact sheets for tricuspid and mitral regurgitation, auscultation reference guide, echo surveillance guide, and pre-transcatheter procedure checklist; these have been translated into multiple languages to meet the community level needs within each region. An interactive provider toolkit is under development and will be integrated into the platform. Additionally, a continuing education (CE) work group designed a three-part webinar series offering free CE credits for physicians, advanced practice providers, and nurses, with deployment planned for Summer 2026. A national learning collaborative model offers a scalable and effective strategy for advancing professional education in heart valve disease. By equipping primary care providers with accessible, evidence-based resources and CE opportunities, this initiative strengthens clinical competencies and supports more consistent screening and early detection practices.
title: Abstract 6850: Advancing Early Detection of Heart Valve Disease Through a National Learning Collaborative Model

abstract: Background: Netrin-1 (NTN1), a member of the laminin-related protein family, plays important roles in angiogenesis, cell migration, and cardiovascular repair. However, the therapeutic potential of stable human induced pluripotent stem cell derived endothelial cells with constitutive NTN1 overexpression (hiPSC-NTN1-ECs) remains unclear. Therefore, we aimed to establish and characterize a stable hiPSC-NTN1 overexpression cell line and evaluate its therapeutic efficacy in a mouse model of myocardial injury. Methods and Results: hiPSC-NTN1 cell line was generated using a lentiviral vector containing an EF1α - driven NTN1-GFP sequence to constitutively overexpress NTN1. Positive clones were selected by flow cytometry and validated by quantitative RT-PCR and Western blot analysis. Pluripotency makers were assessed by immunostaining and quantitative RT-PCR. Genomic stabilities and pluripotency were further confirmed by karyotype analysis and teratoma formation assays ( Figure 1) . NTN1 mRNA and protein expression levels were significantly increased in hiPSC-NTN1 cells compared with wild-type hiPSC (hiPSC-WT). Expression levels of pluripotency markers, including OCT 4, SOX2, and NANOG, were similar between hiPSC-NTN1 and hiPSC-WT. In addition, hiPSC-NTN1 cells maintained normal karyotypes and successfully differentiated into derivatives of all three germ layers. Furthermore, hiPSC-NTN1 cells efficiently differentiated into ECs, and the expression level of pluripotency markers during the EC differentiation quickly decreased to be undetectable, which is similar to those observed in hiPSC-WT-derived ECs ( Figure 2 ). Conclusions: We developed a stable hiPSC-NTN1 overexpression cell line for ECs generation, providing a foundation for future studies investigating its therapeutic potential in cardiovascular disease models.
title: Abstract 6855: Generation and Characterization of a Stable Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells-Netrin-1 Overexpression Cell Line for Cardiovascular Repair

abstract: Keywords: STEMI; cardiac tamponade; hemodialysis; pericardiocentesis; PCI; low-pressure tamponade Introduction: Concurrent ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and cardiac tamponade is a rare dual emergency requiring clinicians to identify the dominant cause of shock while balancing urgent reperfusion against hemorrhagic pericardial risk. Patient Information: A 55-year-old man with ESRD developed cardiac arrest during hemodialysis. Clinical Findings & Timeline: After resuscitation, ECG showed anterior STEMI, while echocardiography revealed a large hemorrhagic pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Although culprit-vessel occlusion was present, shock was felt to be primarily obstructive. Arrest during hemodialysis suggested low-pressure tamponade, in which acute preload reduction unmasked a chronic uremic or dialysis-associated effusion. Immediate PCI risked worsening hemorrhagic tamponade with antithrombotic therapy, while delayed reperfusion risked ongoing anterior myocardial injury. Therapeutic Interventions: Emergent pericardiocentesis was performed before coronary intervention, draining 800 mL of hemorrhagic fluid with immediate hemodynamic recovery. After decompression, the patient underwent PCI of a 100% occluded, heavily calcified mid-left anterior descending artery with in-stent thrombosis, requiring intravascular lithotripsy and drug-eluting stent placement. Heparin and intravenous cangrelor were used before transition to dual antiplatelet therapy. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: The drain remained in place while dialysis was optimized and bleeding stability was monitored. Staged PCI was later performed for a severe calcified ostial right coronary artery lesion. The patient improved without mechanical circulatory support. Discussion & Synthesis: This case is distinctive because tamponade was not a complication of PCI, anticoagulation, or myocardial rupture; rather, hemorrhagic tamponade and true culprit-vessel STEMI were present simultaneously at presentation. The central management challenge was not simply recognizing tamponade but identifying obstructive physiology as the immediate driver of shock despite electrocardiographic evidence of anterior STEMI. In this setting, a tamponade-first strategy restored preload, clarified the hemodynamic profile, and created a safer window for complex PCI requiring antithrombotic therapy. This case highlights the importance of early echocardiography in dialysis patients with arrest or shock during hemodialysis, where acute ultrafiltration may unmask low-pressure tamponade. When hemorrhagic tamponade and culprit-vessel STEMI coexist, prompt pericardial decompression before PCI may be lifesaving by stabilizing obstructive shock while preserving the opportunity for timely reperfusion.
title: Abstract 6858: Caught Between Compression and Occlusion: Hemodialysis-Unmasked Tamponade Concurrent with Anterior STEMI

abstract: Introduction: Intracardiac thrombi are rare but carry substantial risks including hemodynamic compromise and systemic embolization. Given their association with common critical illness-associated conditions including low cardiac output, hypercoagulability, atrial fibrillation, and presence of indwelling devices, an understanding of intracardiac thrombi is vital in critical care cardiology. Patient: A 57-year-old female with a past medical history of HTN, COPD, and type 2 diabetes was brought to the hospital after being found unresponsive at home for an unknown length of time. Timeline: Initial vital signs were temperature of 101 °F, pulse of 133 bpm, BP of 127/82 mmHg, and SPO2 of 72% on room air. CT showed a large acute infarction of the left MCA territory. The patient was transferred to the neurological ICU and was deemed not a candidate for thrombolytics or thrombectomy due to being outside of therapeutic window. Initial high sensitivity troponin was 10551 ng/L and hemoglobin was 21.8. EKG showing normal sinus rhythm with T wave inversions in leads I and V1-V3. A TTE was obtained which showed an LVEF of >70% with extensive thrombus-in-transit extending from the right atrium to left atrium through a patent foramen ovale with severely dilated right ventricle with mobile thrombus and severely reduced contractility suggestive of massive pulmonary embolism (Figure 1). Hemodynamic status gradually worsened, requiring initiation of vasopressor support. Interventional cardiology was consulted, but the patient was deemed not a candidate for systemic anticoagulation, thrombolysis, or mechanical thrombectomy. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: The risk of hemorrhagic conversion with systemic anticoagulation or thrombolysis was deemed unacceptably high due to the presence of the large recent left MCA infarct possibly caused by underlying polycythemia vera. Endovascular and surgical thrombectomy were both considered but were deferred due to worsening hemodynamics and concern for subsequent embolization of remaining intracardiac thrombi. Therapeutic Interventions: Unfortunately, the patient was too unstable for any advanced therapeutic interventions to be performed. Outcome: Ultimately, the family decided to pursue comfort care, and the patient developed multi-organ failure. The patient was palliatively extubated and expired on hospitalization day 3. Discussion: This case exemplifies the critical care phenomenon known as “competing catastrophes” in which two or more pathologic disturbances are associated with independent and frequently disparate risks that confound clinical decision making. In these situations, it is important to carefully weigh risks and benefits before proceeding, keeping in mind that sometimes withholding an intervention that poses undue hazard is the best course of action.
title: Abstract 6865: The Clot Thickens: Intracardiac Thrombus-in-Transit Involving All Four Chambers Leading to a Large Left Middle Cerebral Artery Stroke

abstract: Introduction: Levosimendan, a calcium sensitizer and inodilator, improves cardiac output through calcium sensitization without increasing myocardial oxygen demand, a mechanism that remains effective in the presence of beta-blocker therapy, unlike dobutamine. The ESC Heart Failure Guidelines recommend levosimendan as the preferred inotrope over dobutamine in beta-blocker-treated acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF). Despite this, randomized trial evidence has been conflicting, demonstrating different survival benefits over dobutamine. Large-scale real-world data across the spectrum of hospitalized HF are lacking. Hypothesis: Levosimendan use is associated with lower 30-day mortality and hospitalization compared with dobutamine in hospitalized HF on beta-blockers and hospitalized HF without a beta-blocker requirement. Methods: We conducted a retrospective propensity-matched cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Two independent 1:1 propensity-matched cohorts were constructed: (1) hospitalized HF on beta-blockers (BB-ADHF); and (2) hospitalized HF without a beta-blocker requirement (HF). Propensity scores incorporated demographics, cardiac history, comorbidities, medications, and laboratory values. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included 30-day hospitalization, mechanical ventilation, acute kidney injury, mechanical circulatory support (MCS), arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, and myocardial infarction. Results: Propensity score matching yielded 833 matched pairs in BB-ADHF and 945 pairs in HF. Levosimendan was associated with lower 30-day mortality in both cohorts: BB-ADHF (9.5% vs 15.7%; HR 0.561, 95% CI 0.424-0.743; p<0.001) and HF (10.1% vs 18.3%; HR 0.507, 0.394-0.651; p<0.001). Thirty-day hospitalization was lower with levosimendan in BB-ADHF (HR 0.846, 0.734-0.975; p=0.021) and HF (HR 0.731, 0.641-0.834; p<0.001). New antiarrhythmic therapy or cardioversion was lower in both cohorts. MCS use was higher with levosimendan in BB-ADHF (HR 2.071, 1.315-3.260; p=0.001) and HF (HR 1.631, 1.098-2.421; p=0.014). Myocardial infarction was higher with levosimendan in BB-ADHF (HR 1.627, 1.030-2.571; p=0.035) and HF (HR 1.706, 1.043-2.786; p=0.030). Mechanical ventilation, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, and acute kidney injury did not significantly differ. Conclusions: Levosimendan use was associated with lower 30-day mortality and hospitalization compared with dobutamine in both hospitalized HF cohorts. Higher rates of MCS and myocardial infarction with levosimendan warrant further investigation.
title: Abstract 6876: Levosimendan versus Dobutamine in Hospitalized Heart Failure With and Without Beta-Blocker Therapy: A Multinational Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Background: Cardiac sarcoidosis is associated with ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, making implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapy an important component of management. We evaluated racial disparities in ICD utilization and inpatient outcomes among patients hospitalized with cardiac sarcoidosis complicated by ventricular arrhythmias. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample from 2016-2023. Adult hospitalizations with cardiac sarcoidosis and ventricular arrhythmias were identified using ICD-10 coding. Patients were stratified by race, with primary comparisons between Black and White patients. The primary outcome was ICD implantation. Secondary outcomes included cardiogenic shock, acute heart failure, in-hospital mortality, length of stay, and hospitalization costs. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, hospital-level, and comorbidity-related variables. Results: A weighted cohort of 6,842 hospitalizations was identified. Black patients were younger and had higher rates of acute heart failure, complete heart block, and cardiogenic shock compared with White patients. Despite greater disease burden, Black patients were less likely to undergo ICD implantation (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.73, 95% CI 0.64-0.84, p<0.001). Black patients additionally experienced prolonged hospitalization and higher hospitalization costs. In-hospital mortality was numerically higher among Black patients. Conclusions: Significant racial disparities exist in ICD utilization among patients hospitalized with cardiac sarcoidosis and ventricular arrhythmias in the United States. Despite higher arrhythmic and heart failure burden, Black patients were less likely to receive ICD therapy, highlighting important inequities in access to advanced electrophysiologic care.
title: Abstract 6881: Racial Disparities in ICD Utilization Among Patients Hospitalized with Cardiac Sarcoidosis and Ventricular Arrhythmias: A National Inpatient Sample Analysis (2016-2023)

abstract: Introduction: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is characterized by persistent eosinophilia greater than 1,500 cells/μL resulting in end-organ damage. Loeffler endocarditis (LE) is reported in 50% of HES cases, characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the endocardium. We describe a case of HES and LE requiring mitral valve replacement (MVR). Case Presentation: A 15 y/o male presented with two months of progressive chest pain, dyspnea, and fatigue associated with a 30-pound unintentional weight loss over six months. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated elevated troponin (1.45 ng/mL) and BNP (409 pg/mL), marked leukocytosis (56.37х10 3 /μL), and severe eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count 39.21х10 3 /μL). Initial echocardiogram demonstrated left ventricle (LV) myocardial infiltration with an echobright “rind” along the posterior wall of the LV (Fig 1) extending to and significantly restricting the posterior leaflet of the mitral valve (MV), causing moderate mitral regurgitation (MR). CMR was notable for endomyocardial thickening of the basal anterolateral and inferolateral segments with subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement and perfusion deficits, consistent with LE. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated marked eosinophilia (54%) with aberrant myeloid progenitor population concerning for HES. Cytogenetic analysis revealed a CHIC2 deletion at 4q12 resulting in FIP1L1-PDGFRA rearrangement, a mutation responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibition. The patient was initially treated with corticosteroids and hydroxyurea before transitioning to imatinib, resulting in rapid normalization of eosinophil counts. Anticoagulation and diuresis were initiated for the LV mural thrombus and symptomatic MR, respectively. Despite hematologic remission and reduction in mural thrombus size, he developed progressive valvular disease due to necrosis of mitral subvalvar apparatus. Severe MR (Fig 2) led to systemic right ventricular (RV) systolic pressure, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and severe RV dysfunction requiring inotropic support and eventual surgical debridement of LV necrotic tissue and thrombus, mechanical MVR (29mm St. Jude), and tricuspid valvuloplasty. Native MV pathology demonstrated extensive fibrin deposition, necrosis, dystrophic calcifications, and mixed inflammation with rare multinucleated giant cells. Discussion: This case highlights a rare pediatric presentation of FIP1L1-PDGFRA -associated HES complicated by rapidly progressive LE requiring MVR. Severe cardiac remodeling and valvular dysfunction may progress despite normalization of eosinophilic count following targeted therapy. This report underscores the importance of early molecular diagnosis, serial multimodal cardiac imaging, and multidisciplinary management in identifying patients who may require early surgical intervention despite appropriate targeted therapy.
