abstract: Background: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a heritable, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and it is not meaningfully reduced by statins or ezetimibe. Whether elevated Lp(a) translates into measurable residual cardiovascular and limb ischemic risk in patients who have achieved an LDL-C goal of <70 mg/dL on these therapies has not been well established, and the magnitude of this risk in primary versus secondary prevention populations remains uncertain. Research Question: Is elevated Lp(a) associated with higher residual cardiovascular and limb ischemic risk in patients with LDL-C <70 mg/dL on statin and/or ezetimibe therapy? Methods: We used the TriNetX Research Network to identify adults (≥18 years) with at least one LDL-C <70 mg/dL on statin and/or ezetimibe therapy and a documented Lp(a) measurement. Patients on PCSK9 inhibitors were excluded. We defined elevated Lp(a) as ≥50 mg/dL or ≥125 nmol/L and matched cohorts 1:1 by propensity score on demographics, comorbidities, medications, and BMI. The primary outcome was MACE (acute myocardial infarction [AMI], ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack [TIA], or coronary revascularization). Secondary outcomes were the individual components of MACE, major adverse limb events (MALE), heart failure hospitalization, and all-cause mortality. We tested for a dose-response across Lp(a) quartiles and used lower extremity fracture and pneumonia as falsification endpoints. Results: Of 69,059 eligible patients, 41,750 were included after matching (20,875 per group; mean age, 61.7 years; 42.3% female; all SMDs <0.1). Over a median follow-up of 2.6 to 3.1 years, patients with elevated Lp(a) had higher rates of MACE (HR 1.08; 95% CI 1.04-1.12; P<.001), AMI (HR 1.19; 1.12-1.26), coronary revascularization (HR 1.24; 1.14-1.35), MALE (HR 1.43; 1.23-1.66), and heart failure hospitalization (HR 1.13; 1.05-1.22) (Figure 1). Stroke/TIA and all-cause mortality did not differ between groups. Risk rose stepwise across Lp(a) quartiles for MACE, AMI, coronary revascularization, and MALE (Figure 2). The association held in both the primary prevention (MACE HR 1.13; 1.09-1.18) and secondary prevention (MACE HR 1.07; 1.03-1.11) subgroups. Falsification endpoints did not differ between groups. Conclusions: In patients who reached LDL-C <70 mg/dL on statin and/or ezetimibe therapy, elevated Lp(a) was associated with higher rates of coronary and limb ischemic events and heart failure hospitalization, with a graded dose-response across Lp(a) levels and consistent signals in primary and secondary prevention. These data support routine Lp(a) measurement and identify a population with controlled LDL-C but elevated Lp(a) as a high-yield target for emerging Lp(a)-lowering therapies to address residual risk.
title: Abstract 6899: Lipoprotein(a) and Residual Vascular Risk Among Patients Achieving Optimal LDL-C: A Real-World Cohort Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Colchicine is commonly used for pericarditis and post-pericardiotomy syndrome but has a narrow therapeutic index, particularly in patients with renal dysfunction. While gastrointestinal, hematologic, and neuromuscular toxicities are well recognized, central nervous system manifestations are rarely reported. We present a case of rapidly reversible encephalopathy attributed to colchicine toxicity in a patient with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on peritoneal dialysis following cardiac surgery. Case Presentation: A 63-year-old man with coronary artery disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and ESRD on peritoneal dialysis initially presented with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and underwent coronary angiography with staged revascularization. He later developed cardiac tamponade requiring coronary artery bypass grafting with a concomitant pericardial window. Operative findings showed severe hemorrhagic fibrinous pericarditis, and colchicine was started for post-pericardiotomy pericarditis at a renally adjusted dose of 0.3 mg every 72 hours. Several weeks later, he was readmitted with mediastinitis complicated by Klebsiella bacteremia and septic shock requiring vasopressors. His course was further complicated by atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation arrest. Despite resolution of shock and discontinuation of sedation, he remained encephalopathic with a GCS of 7T. Brain MRI and continuous EEG were unrevealing.Given ongoing colchicine exposure and an otherwise negative workup, colchicine neurotoxicity was suspected. Colchicine was discontinued, and the patient rapidly improved. He was successfully extubated and, within 24 hours, was awake, alert, following commands, and had returned to a GCS of 15. Discussion: Colchicine is cleared through both hepatic and renal pathways and is poorly removed by dialysis because of its large volume of distribution and intracellular binding. As a result, toxicity may occur even with renal dose adjustment. In critically ill patients, encephalopathy is often attributed to sepsis, hypoxia, medications, or metabolic abnormalities, which can delay recognition of drug toxicity. In this case, the negative neurologic workup, lack of another clear cause, and rapid recovery after colchicine discontinuation support colchicine-associated encephalopathy as the most likely diagnosis. Conclusion: As colchicine use expands in cardiovascular medicine, clinicians should consider neurotoxicity in patients with renal dysfunction who develop unexplained encephalopathy, even when receiving adjusted dosing. Early recognition and discontinuation may lead to rapid and complete neurologic recovery.
title: Abstract 6915: An Unusual Cause of Postoperative Encephalopathy: Colchicine Toxicity in End-Stage Renal Disease

abstract: Background: Vasoplegia is a frequent and morbid complication after Total Artificial Heart (TAH) implantation, often leading to end-organ hypoperfusion. Mesenteric arterial vasospasm causing bowel ischemia is an underrecognized and highly lethal sequela in this population. We report the first successful use of prolonged catheter-directed intra-arterial papaverine as targeted therapy in this setting. Case Presentation: A 48-year-old man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy (baseline LVEF 20%), severe functional mitral regurgitation (s/p two MitraClips), and left ventricular thrombus presented in refractory SCAI Stage E cardiogenic shock. Despite maximal medical therapy, he required VA-ECMO with Impella CP (ECPELLA configuration), upgraded to Impella 5.5, followed by TAH implantation on hospital day 13. Post-TAH Course: The patient developed profound vasoplegia requiring high-dose norepinephrine and vasopressin. On post-operative day 2, he manifested rising lactate (>20 mmol/L) and abdominal distension. CT angiography demonstrated severe diffuse vasospasm of the celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), and renal arteries with multiorgan hypoenhancement, consistent with visceral ischemia secondary to vasopressor-induced vasospasm rather than thromboembolic disease. Intervention: A multidisciplinary shock team performed emergent bedside exploratory laparotomy, confirming patchy bowel ischemia without frank necrosis. A 6.5 Fr catheter was positioned in the SMA/celiac axis for continuous intra-arterial papaverine infusion (150 mg/50 mL at 1-2 mg/hr). Systemic vasodilators were avoided due to hemodynamic instability. TAH settings were optimized (rate 130 bpm, increased vacuum -17/-15 mmHg) to improve output (5.8-6.5 L/min), alongside methylene blue, stress-dose steroids, broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and CRRT with bicarbonate. Outcome: Intra-arterial papaverine resulted in rapid angiographic improvement in mesenteric perfusion within 12 hours, with lactate declining from >20 to <4 mmol/L within 48 hours and stabilization of bowel viability on repeat evaluation. The patient achieved temporary hemodynamic recovery on minimal vasopressors. Unfortunately, recurrent fungemia and multiorgan failure ultimately led to transition to comfort care per family wishes on hospital day 18. Discussion: This case highlights mesenteric vasospasm as a critical, underreported complication of post-TAH vasoplegia. Catheter-directed intra-arterial papaverine delivery provides targeted vasodilation while minimizing systemic hypotension, a strategy not previously described in the TAH population. Combined with aggressive MCS optimization and multidisciplinary care, it can serve as a bridge in select patients with refractory cardiogenic shock. Further studies are warranted to define its role in advanced heart failure mechanical support algorithms.
title: Abstract 6931: Successful Use of Catheter-Directed Intra-Arterial Papaverine for Refractory Mesenteric Vasospasm in a Patient with Total Artificial Heart: A Novel Salvage Strategy in Post-TAH Vasoplegia

abstract: Introduction: Obesity and overweight characterize many patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). In the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial, alirocumab reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) post-ACS compared with placebo, with protocol-driven dose up-titration from 75 to 150 mg to achieve target LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C). Whether body mass index (BMI) influences LDL-C response, drives the need for up-titration, and modifies MACE benefit has not been examined. Hypothesis: Baseline BMI predicts the magnitude of LDL-C lowering, the likelihood of dose up-titration, and the cardiovascular benefit of alirocumab post-ACS. Methods: In this post hoc analysis of alirocumab vs. placebo on top of maximally tolerated statin in 18,924 post-ACS patients (ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial), independent predictors of alirocumab up-titration to achieve an LDL-C level <50 mg/dL were identified by logistic regression. LDL-C reduction by BMI category (<25, 25-<30, 30-<35, ≥35 kg/m 2 ) was assessed after 2 months’ treatment and subsequent follow-up. Treatment effect on MACE (coronary death, nonfatal MI, ischemic stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina) was assessed with adjusted Cox models including a treatment-by-BMI interaction (continuous and categorical). Treatment-emergent adverse events were summarized by BMI. Results: Mean (±SD) baseline LDL-C was 92±31 mg/dL. Independent predictors of need for up-titration of alirocumab dose included higher BMI (OR 1.31, 1.67, 2.13 for BMI 25-<30, 30-<35, and ≥35 vs <25 kg/m 2 ), higher baseline LDL-C or Lp(a), female sex, diabetes, younger age, and intensity of background statin therapy (all p<0.001). On alirocumab 75 mg, LDL-C reduction was attenuated with increasing BMI; however, following protocol-driven up-titration to 150 mg, there were no significant differences in LDL-C reduction across BMI categories throughout the follow up. In adjusted Cox models with continuous BMI, the treatment-by-BMI interaction on LDL-C reduction was significant (Figure; interaction p=0.017); a spline-based model adjusted for region, age, sex, race, smoking status, high-intensity statin use, baseline LDL-c, eGFR, and diabetes status showed a consistent linear pattern (interaction p=0.059). Across BMI categories, alirocumab hazard ratios for MACE were 0.98, 0.85, 0.80, and 0.74 (trend interaction p=0.071). Treatment-emergent adverse events, including injection-site reactions, did not differ by BMI. Conclusions: In this post hoc analysis, higher BMI was associated with attenuated initial LDL-C reduction on alirocumab 75 mg and predicted the need for up-titration to 150 mg. Despite convergence of on-treatment LDL-C across BMI categories after up-titration, higher BMI was associated with reduction in the relative risk for MACE with alirocumab versus placebo. These findings suggest BMI may be a clinically relevant modifier of PCSK9 inhibitor benefit post-ACS.
title: Abstract 6938: Body Mass Index, LDL-Cholesterol Response, and Cardiovascular Outcomes with Alirocumab After Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Background: Delirium is a common complication among older patients hospitalized with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and is associated with impaired recovery, functional decline, and adverse clinical outcomes. Malnutrition contributes to frailty and vulnerability to acute stressors and may therefore increase the risk of delirium during hospitalization. However, the association between nutritional status and delirium in patients with ACS has not been well established. The Mini Nutritional Assessment-Short Form (MNA-SF) is a simple nurse-administered nutritional screening tool that may facilitate early identification of patients at increased risk for delirium. Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center observational study including 185 consecutive patients admitted with ACS between April 2024 and December 2025. Nutritional status was assessed using the MNA-SF at admission. Patients were categorized as having normal nutritional status (12-14 points), being at risk of malnutrition (8-11 points), or being malnourished (0-7 points). The primary outcome was in-hospital delirium. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed using MNA-SF score, age, sex, and cardiogenic shock requiring intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) support as explanatory variables. Results: A total of 185 patients with ACS were included. The incidence of delirium increased progressively with worsening nutritional status, occurring in 11.0% of patients with normal nutritional status, 29.0% of those at risk of malnutrition, and 68.0% of malnourished patients (p<0.001).In multivariable logistic regression analysis, lower MNA-SF score remained independently associated with delirium (OR 0.79 per 1-point increase, 95% CI 0.68-0.91, p=0.001). Older age was also independently associated with delirium (OR 1.08 per year, 95% CI 1.04-1.13, p<0.001). Cardiogenic shock requiring IABP support was strongly associated with delirium (OR 14.7, 95% CI 3.70-58.1, p<0.001). Sex was not significantly associated with delirium (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.55-3.45, p=0.497). Conclusions: Lower MNA-SF scores were independently associated with in-hospital delirium in patients hospitalized with ACS. This association remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, and cardiogenic shock requiring IABP support. Routine nutritional screening at admission may help identify patients at increased risk for delirium and support early multidisciplinary prevention strategies.
title: Abstract 6990: Lower Mini Nutritional Assessment-Short Form Scores Are Independently Associated with In-Hospital Delirium in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Background: Eosinophilic myocarditis (EM) is a rare inflammatory cardiomyopathy that can mimic acute coronary syndromes, including ST-elevation myocardial infarction. EM has been linked to drug hypersensitivity, hyper-eosinophilic syndrome, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and paraneoplastic processes. There are only isolated case reports in the literature for EM. We report a case of a patient with multiple myeloma (MM) on Lenalidomide who was diagnosed with fulminant eosinophilic myocarditis. Case Presentation: A 65-year-old male with stage III IgA kappa MM, on daratumumab, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (DRd, cycle 8), presented with chest pain, troponin of 16,000 ng/L and ST-elevation in aVR with ST-depression in V4-V6. Coronary angiogram showed no obstructive disease and CT angiography was negative for aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism. He developed cardiogenic shock requiring norepinephrine and milrinone. Subsequent echocardiography showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45-55% with asymmetric apical thickening (17 mm) suspicious for infiltrative cardiomyopathy with superimposed thrombus. Peripheral blood eosinophil count was markedly elevated at 19 x 10 9 /L. Given high suspicion for eosinophilic myocarditis, cardiac magnetic resonance was pursued and demonstrated extensive non-vascular territory sub-endocardial late gadolinium enhancement with myocardial edema and a 2.1 x 2.1 cm apical LV thrombus, consistent with eosinophilic myocarditis/Loeffler endocarditis. Lenalidomide was discontinued and high-dose IV methylprednisolone (starting at 250 mg up to 1000 mg daily) was initiated for a total of 8 days to achieve significant clinical improvement. Repeat TTE 1 week after CCU admission showed significant reduction in thrombus size and recovery of EF to 55%. Bone marrow biopsy subsequently revealed plasma cell leukemia with plasmablastic features (50-60% marrow cellularity) with 25% eosinophils and precursors. Patient afterwards was started on Dexamethasone 40 mg weekly, Apixaban 5 mg BID and received hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Patient eventually was treated with multi-drug salvage therapy and hematopoietic stem cell transplant. Conclusion: This case highlights EM presenting as a STEMI mimic with cardiogenic shock and Loeffler endocarditis in a patient with MM with progression of disease. The etiology of EM in this context is likely secondary to paraneoplastic eosinophilia driven by underlying plasma cell leukemia, and less likely, but possibly secondary to lenalidomide-mediated hypersensitivity. This case underscores the importance of early recognition of eosinophilic myocarditis and the diagnostic utility of CMR in promptly recognizing EM. The management of EM described in the literature mostly centers around high dose steroids in the early phase as well as treatment of underlying case.
title: Abstract 6993: A Case Report of Eosinophilic Myocarditis Presenting as ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction in a Patient with Multiple Myeloma Undergoing Leukemic Transformation

abstract: Introduction: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a key driver of cardiovascular risk, yet data across diverse populations with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) remain limited. Research Question: The Understanding Racial and Ethnic Variations in Lipoprotein(a) (UNRAVEL) Study evaluated racial and ethnic variation in Lp(a) and the feasibility of a decentralized, single-IRB study approach. Methods: UNRAVEL was a decentralized, cross-sectional study of U.S. adults with medically confirmed ASCVD. Participants self-identifying as Hispanic/Latino, Black, South Asian, or White were recruited through electronic health record (EHR) patient-portal outreach, social media and community engagement, and clinician referrals, with Spanish-language materials available throughout the study. Following electronic informed consent, participants completed remote study procedures and underwent a one-time blood draw and anthropometric assessment at local collection sites. Lp(a) concentrations were measured in nmol/L. Differences across racial and ethnic groups were evaluated using Kruskal-Wallis tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Results: From November 2024 to December 2025, 2,463 individuals completed prescreening, and 1,695 (68.8%) were eligible. A total of 921 participants were enrolled (median age 64 years [IQR, 57-71]; 37.9% female), including 65.8% White, 15.3% Hispanic/Latino, 14.7% Black, and 4.2% South Asian individuals. EHR patient-portal outreach was the primary recruitment strategy, accounting for 68.0% of reported referral sources. Overall, 61.5% had a history of myocardial infarction or prior coronary stent placement or coronary artery bypass grafting, 33.4% had ischemic stroke, and 5.3% had symptomatic peripheral artery disease. The median Lp(a) was 40 nmol/L (IQR, 11-163), 27.3% had Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L, and 24.1% had Lp(a) ≥150 nmol/L. Black participants had the highest median Lp(a) level (118 nmol/L [IQR, 40-182]), while South Asian participants had the highest observed prevalence of elevated Lp(a) (≥125 nmol/L) at 38.5%, followed by Black (32.6%), White (26.9%), and Hispanic/Latino participants (20.6%). Notably, 82.2% of exit survey respondents rated their overall experience as highly favorable. Exit survey responses indicated favorable post-study perceptions of Lp(a) testing: 61.5% rated Lp(a) measurement as very important, and approximately half strongly endorsed family testing and future targeted Lp(a)-lowering therapies. Conclusions: UNRAVEL characterized Lp(a) distribution among adults with established ASCVD while demonstrating the feasibility of a decentralized cardiovascular research model integrating EHR-based identification, patient portal outreach, remote consent, and decentralized biomarker assessment.
title: Abstract 6997: Racial and Ethnic Variation in Lipoprotein(a) Among Adults with Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: Initial Findings from the UNRAVEL Decentralized Study

abstract: Background: Primary cardiac tumors are exceedingly rare, with an autopsy incidence ranging from 0.001% to 0.03%, of which 10 to 25% are malignant. Cardiac sarcomas represent the majority, of which undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas (UPS) have an incidence of 10-30%, therefore highlighting the overall rarity of occurrence. Cardiac UPS is considered a highly aggressive mesenchymal malignancy that arises in the left atrium and presents as nonspecific cardiopulmonary symptoms. Here we discuss a case of a 49-year-old female who presented with acute respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock and was subsequently found to have a golf ball-sized cardiac UPS. Case Presentation: A 49-year-old female with no significant previous medical history presented to the hospital with an acute onset of shortness of breath, chest heaviness, and presyncope with venous blood gas suggestive of hypoxemia. She failed BiPAP support and was eventually intubated with concurrent hypotension requiring vasopressor support with norepinephrine and vasopressin. CTA pulmonary was negative for pulmonary embolism but showed an enlarged left atrium with a hypodense filling defect. The transthoracic echocardiography was suggestive of a medium mobile mass attached to the intra-atrial septum (Figure 1). Subsequent transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a left atrial appendage mass of ~4.33 cm x 3.46 cm (Figure 2). Interestingly, a TTE done 1 month ago was negative for any atrial mass. Given the size of the mass, Cardiothoracic Surgery was consulted, and the patient underwent sternotomy and resection. Her post-op period was complicated with intermittent Atrial flutter and symptomatic junctional rhythm requiring pacemaker placement. The pathology of the atrial mass was suggestive of a focally spindled sarcomatous tumor with extensive necrosis and tumor present at the epicardial margin. Given the positive margins, the patient was started on radiation and adjuvant photon therapy. Despite the above therapy, she developed left axillary lymphadenopathy with the biopsy suggestive of regionally metastatic disease with MDM2 amplification and was thus started on immunotherapy with Pembrolizumab. Discussion: Cardiac UPS remains an exceptionally rare and highly aggressive malignancy with non-specific clinical symptoms, which may mimic benign atrial masses. This case highlights a unique course characterized by rapid tumor development, presenting as cardiogenic shock and respiratory failure, post-resection conduction abnormalities requiring a pacemaker, and early regional metastatic spread despite resection and adjuvant therapy. Therefore, highlighting the need for a high index of clinical suspicion and improved therapeutic guidelines.
title: Abstract 7021: Cardiac Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma Presenting as a Golf Ball-Sized Left Atrial Mass and Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Background: Ischemia with nonobstructive coronary arteries (INOCA) is estimated to affect 30%-50% of patients undergoing invasive coronary angiography. Professional society guidelines recommend noninvasive diagnostic testing prior to invasive coronary function testing (CFT). The use and diagnostic utility of noninvasive testing in patients with INOCA undergoing CFT have not been comprehensively evaluated. Research question: What noninvasive diagnostic tests are used before invasive CFT in patients with INOCA, and are they associated with the CFT-determined physiologic diagnosis? Methods: DISCOVER INOCA is a prospective, multicenter registry of patients with INOCA enrolled at 9 US centers. All patients underwent protocol-guided invasive CFT, including acetylcholine provocation, bolus thermodilution to measure coronary flow reserve (CFR) and index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR), and intravascular imaging. Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) was defined as IMR ≥25 and/or CFR ≤2.5. Vasospastic angina (VSA) included epicardial vasospasm (≥90% narrowing with angina/ischemic electrocardiographic [ECG] changes) or microvascular spasm (angina/ischemic ECG changes without epicardial spasm) during acetylcholine testing. Data regarding demographics, pre-CFT noninvasive testing, and post-CFT phenotypes were obtained. Results: 500 participants were enrolled (78% female, age 57±12 years). Post-CFT phenotypes were CMD in 17%, VSA in 36%, mixed CMD/VSA in 28%, other disorders in 14%, and normal physiology in 6%. Overall, 390/500 participants (78%) underwent ≥1 noninvasive diagnostic test; among them, 66% had 1 test, 31% had 2, and 3% had ≥3. Pre-CFT testing included stress testing in 65%, coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) in 31%, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) in 10%. Among the 327/500 participants who underwent stress testing, 80% had 1 test, 18% had 2, and 2% had ≥3; nuclear stress imaging was most common (64%), followed by stress echocardiography (27%), exercise treadmill testing (27%), and stress CMR (5%). Use of pre-CFT noninvasive testing was similar across phenotypes for ≥1 noninvasive test (p=0.35) and stress testing (p=0.39). Among participants with ≥1 noninvasive test, 167/390 (43%) had an abnormal result (CCTA 44%, CMR 16%, stress testing 33%), with no difference across phenotypes (p=0.56). The presence of an abnormal result on CCTA (p=0.26), CMR (p=0.37), or stress testing (p=0.52) was not associated with a specific INOCA phenotype. Conclusions: Pre-procedure noninvasive diagnostic testing was frequently performed in patients with INOCA, but most patients did not have an abnormal result. There was no association between abnormal results on noninvasive testing and the final diagnosis determined by invasive CFT.
title: Abstract 7022: Use of Noninvasive Diagnostic Testing in Patients with Ischemia with Nonobstructive Coronary Arteries Prior to Coronary Function Testing: Insights from the DISCOVER INOCA Multicenter Registry

abstract: Background: Women are underrepresented in venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) trials. To what extent sex influences post-ECMO outcomes beyond mortality remains uncertain in contemporary practice. Hypothesis: Female sex is associated with distinct complication profiles and lower escalation to durable advanced heart failure therapies after VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock, despite comparable mortality. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (173 healthcare organizations). Adults aged ≥18 years with cardiogenic shock who underwent VA-ECMO were stratified by sex and matched 1:1 on 27 propensity score covariates including demographics, cardiovascular comorbidities, and acute illness markers, yielding 3,258 women and 3,258 men. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days, 90 days, and 1 year, including all-cause mortality, organ-specific complications (acute kidney injury [AKI], renal replacement therapy [RRT], ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, major bleeding, vascular complications, sepsis), and escalation to durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation or heart transplantation (HT). Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from Kaplan-Meier analyses with log-rank testing. Results: All-cause mortality did not differ significantly at 30 days (46.0% vs. 44.5%; HR 1.055, 95% CI 0.981-1.134; p=0.148), 90 days (HR 1.054, 95% CI 0.984-1.129; p=0.131), or 1 year (55.1% vs. 55.0%; HR 1.016, 95% CI 0.952-1.086; p=0.635). Despite comparable mortality, complication profiles diverged markedly. Women had lower risk of AKI (30-day HR 0.813, 95% CI 0.748-0.884; p<0.001) and RRT (30-day HR 0.899, 95% CI 0.816-0.990; p=0.028), persisting to 1 year. Conversely, women had higher risk of ischemic stroke at 30 days (HR 1.217, 95% CI 1.031-1.437; p=0.019) and hemorrhagic stroke through 1 year (30-day HR 1.356, 95% CI 1.082-1.701; 1-year HR 1.250, 95% CI 1.013-1.542; p<0.05 at each interval). Major bleeding did not differ significantly at 30 days (HR 1.004, 95% CI 0.925-1.090; p=0.895), whereas risks of escalation to durable LVAD (1-year HR 0.539, 95% CI 0.422-0.689) and HT (1-year HR 0.566, 95% CI 0.441-0.726) was substantially lower in women. Conclusions: In propensity-matched adults receiving VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock, women and men had comparable mortality through 1 year, but post-ECMO trajectories diverged: women experienced fewer renal complications, higher hemorrhagic stroke risk through 1 year, and substantially lower escalation to durable advanced heart failure therapies. These findings support sex-specific neurologic monitoring and structured pathways for advanced therapy referral in women with cardiogenic shock, while highlighting the need to evaluate whether anticoagulation strategies contribute to observed stroke differences.
title: Abstract 7038: Sex Differences After VA-ECMO for Cardiogenic Shock: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve outcomes in heart failure, but their association with mitral regurgitation (MR) reduction and reverse remodeling after mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (MTEER) remains unclear. Aim: The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether baseline SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with post-MTEER MR response and echocardiographic remodeling across MR mechanisms. Methods: Patients undergoing MTEER were stratified by baseline SGLT2-inhibitor use. MR severity was assessed at baseline and one-year follow-up. Change in MR severity was calculated as follow-up minus baseline grade, with more negative values indicating greater MR reduction. Outcomes included follow-up MR severity, residual MR ≥ moderate, follow-up MR ≤ mild, any MR improvement, and changes in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left atrial volume index (LAVI), left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (LVEDVi), left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVi), left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD), left ventricular end-systolic diameter (LVESD), and left ventricular mass index (LVMi). Multivariable models were adjusted for relevant clinical and echocardiographic characteristics. Results: Among 361 patients (mean age 79.2 ± 10.3 years; 51.8% female), 58 (16%) were receiving SGLT2 inhibitors and 303 (84%) were not. Baseline MR severity was similar between groups. At one year follow-up, SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with lower MR severity (1.29±0.83 vs 1.65±0.80; p=0.003), greater MR reduction (-2.13±1.08 vs -1.81±0.93; p=0.009), lower residual MR ≥ moderate (38% vs 60%; p=0.006), and more frequent follow-up MR ≤ mild (62% vs 38%; p=0.002). After adjustment, SGLT2-inhibitor use remained associated with lower odds of residual MR ≥ moderate (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21-0.92; p=0.030). By mechanism, the association was most evident in secondary MR, where SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with greater MR reduction (-2.20±0.97 vs -1.88±0.90; p=0.043) and more frequent follow-up MR ≤ mild (58% vs 38%; p=0.048), with numerically lower residual MR ≥ moderate (42% vs 61%; p=0.074). In primary MR, SGLT2-inhibitor use was associated with more frequent follow-up MR ≤ mild (63% vs 31%; p=0.023). SGLT2-inhibitor use was not significantly associated with changes in LVEF, LAVI, LVEDVi, LVESVi, LVEDD, LVESD, or LVMi. Conclusions: Baseline SGLT2-inhibitor use was independently associated with lower residual MR after MTEER at one-year follow-up. This association appeared most prominent in secondary MR, without significant independent associations with echocardiographic reverse remodeling. These findings support prospective evaluation of SGLT2 inhibitors as potential modifiers of post-MTEER MR response.
