title: Abstract 7041: Association of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitor Use with Mitral Regurgitation Reduction and Cardiac Remodeling After Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair Across Mitral Regurgitation Mechanisms

abstract: Introduction: Valve-in-Valve Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (ViV-TAVI) and surgical explantation are two widely used methods to manage failed transcatheter aortic valves. Both methods differ significantly in invasiveness and long-term complications. Previous studies are mostly focused on use of ViV-TAVI in management of failed surgical valves. This review compares outcomes of surgical explantation versus ViV-TAVI following failed transcatheter aortic valves. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that ViV-TAVI would demonstrate superior short-term procedural safety outcomes compared to surgical explantation in patients with failed transcatheter aortic valves. Methods: A thorough search was done for relevant studies on PubMed, EMBASE, SCOPUS, Cochrane Library and Clinicaltrials.org. The search included studies from inception to25/06/2025. The mean differences for continuous and risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes were combined using RevMan 5.4.1 software, with a 95% confidence interval using the random effects model. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was used to ensure quality assessment of cohorts. Results: The pooled meta-analysis showed a statistically significant lower incidence of stroke (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.17, 0.63, I 2 =0%, P=0.0009), major bleeding (OR 0.08, 95% CI 0.06, 0.11, I 2 =0%, P< 0.00001), new-onset atrial fibrillation (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.16, 0.28, I 2 =0%, P< 0.00001) and a shorter length of postprocedural hospital stay (MD -5.67, 95% CI -7.47, -3.87, I 2 =0%, P< 0.00001) in the patients who underwent ViV-TAVI. ViV-TAVI was associated with significantly higher risk of major vascular complications compared to surgical explantation (OR 12.20, 95% CI 3.73, 39.87, I 2 =0%, P<0.0001), major valve event-free survival and 5-year survival. Incidence of new pacemaker implants (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.35, 4.36, I 2 =80%, P=0.74), acute kidney injury (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.21, 1.17, I 2 =50%, P=0.11) and all-cause mortality (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.48, 1.67, I 2 =25%, P=0.72) in both groups showed no statistically significant difference. Conclusion: ViV-TAVI showed distinct short-term procedural benefits including significantly lower rates of stroke, major bleeding, atrial fibrillation, and hospital stay, while maintaining equivalent short-term mortality, acute kidney injury, and pacemaker implantation rates. Our hypothesis was partially supported; while ViV-TAVI demonstrated superior short-term safety on several endpoints, surgical explantation showed significantly lower vascular complications and superior long-term outcomes including major valve event-free survival and 5-year survival. Surgical explantation carries higher early procedural risk but may offer better hemodynamic and durability outcomes. Treatment decisions must therefore be individualized by a multidisciplinary heart team weighing short-term procedural risk against long-term durability.
title: Abstract 7058: ViV-TAVI Reduces Short-Term Stroke and Bleeding versus Surgical Explantation for Failed Transcatheter Aortic Valves: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Patients with severe acute myocardial infarction (MI) often progress to heart failure, which remains a major public health challenge. Our recent studies demonstrated follistatin (FST), a paracrine factor secreted by a unique hiPSC line derived cardiomyocyte (CMs), promotes endogenous CM proliferation in porcine hearts. Given the high cost of recombinant FST protein, FST gene therapy may be a cost-effective therapeutic strategy for cardiac regeneration in adult mammalian hearts. Recognizing that FST is a secreted protein and that CMs are resistant to nanoparticle-mediated gene therapy, we propose using nanoparticles (NPs) to deliver the FST gene, under the control of the CDH5 promoter (i.e., an endothelial cell [EC]-specific promoter), into ECs. These ECs will then secrete FST into the extracellular matrix, thereby stimulating the proliferation of adjacent CMs. Methods and Results: Polyethyleneimine (PEI)-based nanoparticles (PEI-NPs) were formulated with GFP or FST -encoding plasmids driven by the endothelial-specific CDH5 promoter at an optimized PEI: plasmid = 8: 1 mass ratio, validated using PEI-GFP control NPs. NP size and zeta potential were measured, and morphology was assessed by transmission electron microscope (TEM). Therapeutic efficacy of PEI-NPs was evaluated in a murine model of MI following intramyocardial delivery. CM cell cycle activity was quantified at 4 days and 4 weeks post-treatment via immunofluorescence staining. Cardiac function was determined by echocardiography at 1 and 4 weeks, while scar size and wall thickness were evaluated by Masson’s trichrome staining at 4 weeks after MI induction and treatment. PEI-GFP and PEI-FST nanoparticles exhibited average sizes of 48.9 ± 0.8 nm and 66.7 ± 1.7 nm, with zeta potentials of 14.8 ± 24.3 mV and 9.79 ± 3.31 mV, respectively. The peak concentration of secreted FST protein from PEI-FST-transfected mouse cardiac ECs was 164.69 ±37.64 ng/mL, as measured using an FST ELIKA kit, on day 4 after transfection, which was approximately 126-fold higher than that of PEI-GFP transfected mouse cardiac ECs. Mouse studies showed that PEI-FST NP administration significantly increased cardiomyocyte mitosis and cytokinesis compared to PEI-GFP administration at 4 days post-treatment. At 4 weeks after treatment, PEI-FST NP treatment further enhanced endogenous cardiomyocyte proliferation ( p < 0.001), improved cardiac function, reduced infarct size ( p = 0.0382), and increased wall thickness compared to PEI-GFP treatment ( p = 0.0162). Conclusions: PEI-based FST gene delivery represents a promising strategy for cardiac regeneration.
title: Abstract 7071: Nanoparticle-Mediated Endothelial Targeting of Follistatin Gene Therapy for Enhanced Cardiac Regeneration

abstract: Patient Presentation: A 78-year-old woman with hypertension, chronic low back pain, glaucoma, and prior gastric bypass presented with acute substernal chest pain and dyspnea. Four days earlier, she had undergone percutaneous spinal biopsy. Initial Workup: She was tachycardic (103 bpm) and hypoxemic requiring 6 L nasal cannula. High-sensitivity troponin T was 205 ng/L and NT-proBNP 3,118 pg/mL. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia with S1Q3T3 and anterior T-wave inversions. CT pulmonary angiography revealed a large saddle pulmonary embolism with extensive bilateral clot burden and right ventricular (RV) strain (RV/LV ratio 1.5). Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed a severely dilated, hypokinetic RV, TAPSE 1.3 cm, and estimated RV systolic pressure of 50 mmHg. Diagnosis and Management: The patient was diagnosed with intermediate high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) (AHA/ACC category C3). Following activation of the PE response team, she underwent percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy. Initial hemodynamics demonstrated low cardiac output (cardiac index [CI] 1.3 L/min/m 2 ), prompting initiation of dobutamine. Thrombectomy achieved substantial clot extraction with modest improvement in CI and pulmonary artery pressures.Following the procedure, she developed worsening hypotension and lactic acidosis despite escalation of dobutamine to 10mcg/kg/min and initiation of norepinephrine, raising concern for persistent RV shock. Multidisciplinary shock team evaluation with pulmonary artery catheterization and repeat TTE demonstrated improved RV hemodynamics but new systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO). Given concern for inotrope-induced LVOTO, dobutamine was discontinued and intravenous fluids were administered. Follow-Up: Within hours, hemodynamics and perfusion rapidly improved. Cardiac index increased to 3.0 L/min/m 2 , lactate normalized, and vasopressors were discontinued. Repeat TTE 48 hours later demonstrated resolution of LVOTO and improved RV function. The patient was discharged home on systemic anticoagulation one week later. Conclusion: This case highlights an uncommon cause of persistent shock following PE thrombectomy: inotrope-induced dynamic LVOTO. Acute PE can produce a small, hyperdynamic left ventricle through impaired RV output and reduced LV preload. Inotropic therapy may further decrease LV cavity size and increase contractility, precipitating SAM of the mitral valve and dynamic LVOTO, particularly in patients with LV hypertrophy. Recognition of this physiology is critical because management differs fundamentally from isolated RV failure. Integration of invasive hemodynamics, echocardiography, and multidisciplinary evaluation enabled prompt diagnosis, while withdrawal of inotropic therapy and volume resuscitation resulted in rapid clinical recovery.
title: Abstract 7092: The Importance of Cardiogenic Shock Phenotyping: Iatrogenic Inotrope-Induced Obstructive Shock Following Pulmonary Embolism Thrombectomy

abstract: Background: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a key inflammatory cytokine implicated in heart failure (HF) pathophysiology, yet its prognostic significance in high-risk post-acute coronary syndrome populations with type 2 diabetes remains incompletely defined. Hypothesis: We hypothesised that elevated baseline IL-6 would be independently associated with increased risk of HF hospitalization (HFH) in patients with type 2 diabetes who are post-ACS. Methods: We analyzed 5,131 participants from EXAMINE with available baseline IL-6 measurements obtained using the Olink Cardiovascular II proteomics panel. Associations between IL-6 and HFH were assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards and Fine-Gray competing risk models, with IL-6 analyzed per 1-standard deviation (SD) increase. Restricted cubic spline analyses characterized the relationship between IL-6 and HFH risk across the full spectrum of IL-6 values, and prespecified subgroup analyses assessed consistency across major clinical phenotypes including sex, body mass index, diabetes duration, renal function, and prior HFH status. Results: During follow-up, 185 participants experienced HFH, with event rates increasing progressively from 1.9% in the lowest IL-6 tertile to 6.4% in the highest tertile. Higher IL-6 levels were independently associated with increased HFH risk in adjusted Cox models (HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.22-1.53, p<0.001) and competing risk analyses accounting for death without HFH (SHR 1.34, 95% CI 1.21-1.48, p<0.001) (Figure 1A). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated a progressive increase in HFH risk across the spectrum of IL-6 values (Figure 1B). Among participants without prior HFH (n=3,659), IL-6 remained independently associated with future HFH (adjusted HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.03-1.52, p=0.025) (interaction P >0.15). Associations were broadly consistent across subgroups, including BMI category, diabetes duration, renal function, prior HFH status, and sex. Conclusions: In patients with recent ACS and type 2 diabetes, elevated IL-6 demonstrated a significant association with HFH risk. Notably, persistence of this association among participants without prior HFH suggests inflammatory pathways may contribute to early HF vulnerability in this particularly vulnerable, optimally treated post-ACS population. Further studies are warranted to determine whether IL-6 may improve early HF risk stratification and identify residual inflammatory risk amenable to targeted intervention.
title: Abstract 7094: Interleukin-6 and Heart Failure Hospitalization in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Post Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Background: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has emerged as an increasingly utilized treatment strategy for acute pulmonary embolism (PE). However, comparative data evaluating hospitalization burden, procedural complexity, and postprocedural resource utilization versus catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) remain limited. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing hospitalization- and procedure-related outcomes between MT and CDT. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted using studies identified through searches of PubMed , Embase , Scopus , and Cochrane Library . Studies comparing MT and CDT in patients with acute PE were included. Random-effects models were primarily used to pool standardized mean differences (SMD) and risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Outcomes included hospital length of stay (LOS), intensive care unit (ICU) LOS, fluoroscopy duration, procedure time, estimated blood loss, and postprocedural ICU admission. Results: Nine studies reporting hospital LOS demonstrated no significant difference between MT and CDT (SMD 0.02, 95% CI –1.12 to 1.17; p=0.969). ICU LOS was also comparable between groups (SMD 0.14, 95% CI –0.27 to 0.56; p=0.501). MT was associated with significantly longer fluoroscopy duration compared with CDT (SMD 1.78, 95% CI 0.91-2.64; p<0.001). Procedure time numerically favored CDT but did not reach statistical significance (SMD 6.51, 95% CI –3.84 to 16.87; p=0.218). Estimated blood loss was greater with MT in the available studies. Postprocedural ICU admission was significantly lower with MT compared with CDT (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.34-0.87; p=0.012). Conclusions: MT and CDT demonstrated comparable hospitalization duration outcomes in patients with acute PE. MT was associated with longer fluoroscopy duration and increased estimated blood loss, while demonstrating lower postprocedural ICU admission rates. These findings highlight potential tradeoffs between procedural complexity and downstream resource utilization with MT. Further prospective randomized studies are needed to better define optimal procedural strategies in acute PE.
title: Abstract 7128: Procedural Efficiency and Hospital Resource Utilization in Mechanical Thrombectomy versus Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis for Acute Pulmonary Embolism: An Updated Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Isolated splenic infarction in young patients may represent an atypical manifestation of systemic embolism and should prompt evaluation for an underlying right-to-left shunt. Patient Information: A 19-year-old male with a history of asthma and familial possibility of sickle cell trait (SCT) with no prior thrombotic history presented to the ED with acute left-sided abdominal pain immediately following a bowel movement. He reported a viral prodrome two weeks prior with fever, rhinorrhea, diarrhea, and poor oral intake. Clinical Findings & Timeline: In the ED, he was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory evaluation was notable for leukocytosis of 15,200 cells/μL and lactate of 2.5 mmol/L. Physical exam revealed diffuse left-sided abdominal tenderness. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed multiple wedge-shaped hypodensities within the spleen consistent with splenic infarcts. He was started on heparin and admitted for further evaluation and treatment. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Hypercoagulable workup was negative for antiphospholipid antibodies and inherited thrombophilias; hemoglobin electrophoresis confirmed SCT. Given unclear etiology of splenic infarcts, a transthoracic echocardiogram with bubble study was obtained to evaluate for cardioembolic source and demonstrated a hypermobile interatrial septum with a large (>20 bubbles) right-to-left shunt. Transesophageal echocardiogram confirmed a complex patent foramen ovale (PFO) with 0.8 cm tunnel length and 0.67 cm maximal excursion. Duplex ultrasound of the upper and lower extremities showed no deep vein thrombosis. Therapeutic Interventions: Anticoagulation with heparin was transitioned to enoxaparin, followed by apixaban at discharge. Follow -up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: He was discharged on three months of anticoagulation with apixaban with hematology and cardiology follow-up with planned PFO closure. Ambulatory rhythm monitoring showed no atrial fibrillation. No complications occurred during hospitalization or immediate follow-up. Discussion & Synthesis: This case illustrates an unusual visceral presentation of paradoxical splenic infarcts in a young patient, likely driven by a multifactorial “two-hit” mechanism. Firstly, the SCT may have contributed to a prothrombotic state, while the complex, hypermobile PFO provided an anatomic pathway for ‘paradoxical’ systemic embolization. The timing of symptom onset immediately following a bowel movement suggests that a transient Valsalva-induced increase in right atrial pressure facilitated right-to-left shunting of an occult venous thrombus. These findings support the necessity of considering a cardioembolic workup, including echocardiography with a bubble study, in young patients presenting with cryptogenic visceral infarction. Management includes anticoagulation with individualized consideration of PFO closure.
title: Abstract 7131: Atypical Systemic Embolism: Splenic Infarction Associated with Patent Foramen Ovale in a Young Patient with Sickle Cell Trait

abstract: Background: The contemporary epidemiology and outcomes of cardiogenic shock (CS) complicating transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) remain incompletely characterized, particularly as TAVR has expanded to lower-risk populations. Research Question: Among TAVR hospitalizations, how common is CS, what outcomes does it carry, how is mechanical circulatory support used, and have outcomes changed over time? Methods: Using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2023), we identified TAVR hospitalizations (ICD-10-PCS 02RF[3-4]), age ≥18, and assessed CS (R57.0, any position), mechanical circulatory support (MCS; intra-aortic balloon pump, Impella, VA/VV-ECMO), and in-hospital outcomes. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, insurance, ZIP income, hospital characteristics, and individual Elixhauser comorbidities, with a separate model testing temporal change in CS-TAVR mortality. Results: Among an estimated 582,910 TAVR hospitalizations, annual volume increased 2.65-fold from 40,265 in 2016 to 106,830 in 2023, while CS prevalence remained stable at 1.97% (p=0.72 for trend). CS-TAVR patients were younger (mean 74.9 vs 78.5 years), had higher comorbidity burden (mean Elixhauser score 7.38 vs 5.45), and were more often Medicaid-insured. CS was independently associated with markedly higher in-hospital mortality (16.38% vs 0.88%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 13.49, 95% confidence interval [CI] 11.42-15.94), acute kidney injury (aOR 10.38, 95% CI 9.34-11.52), and stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 2.67, 95% CI 2.21-3.22, all p<0.001); mechanical ventilation (33.19% vs 1.49%) and length of stay (14.6 vs 3.2 days) were also higher. MCS use among CS-TAVR patients was modest at 21.7% (intra-aortic balloon pump 12.5%, Impella 7.9%, ECMO 4.6%) and did not increase over the study period (peaking near 2020, returning to baseline by 2023). After adjustment, in-hospital mortality among CS-TAVR patients declined over time (aOR 0.92 per year, 95% CI 0.86-0.98, p=0.011), approximately 8% relative annual reduction. Conclusions: Cardiogenic shock complicating TAVR remained uncommon and stable in prevalence even as TAVR volume grew 2.65-fold, and it carried very high in-hospital mortality. Mortality nonetheless fell by roughly 8% per year while MCS use did not rise, suggesting that procedural refinement and patient selection, rather than greater mechanical support, are driving improved survival in this high-risk group.
title: Abstract 7144: Cardiogenic Shock Complicating Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Nationwide Analysis, 2016-2023

abstract: Background: Thrombus in transit occurs in approximately 4% of patients with pulmonary embolism (PE) and is associated with increased mortality. When a thrombus traverses a patent foramen ovale (PFO), termed thrombus straddling a foramen ovale (TSFO), the risk of paradoxical embolism further complicates management. Optimal treatment remains unclear, as available evidence are limited to retrospective studies and case series. Case Presentation: A 39-year-old man with obesity and a family history of unprovoked venous thromboembolism presented with three days of nausea and fatigue. Evaluation revealed new-onset atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, mild hypotension, acute kidney injury, elevated troponins and BNP, along with lactic acidosis. Computed tomography demonstrated bilateral pulmonary emboli with right ventricular (RV) strain. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severe RV dilation and dysfunction with large mobile masses in both atria. Duplex ultrasonography identified an occlusive left femoral deep vein thrombosis. Cardiac computed tomography confirmed a bi-atrial thrombus extending through a PFO, establishing the diagnosis of TSFO. Management and Outcome: How distal and extensive the clot burden was limited catheter-based and surgical based interventions. Given patient’s hemodynamic instability, a treatment option needed to be rapidly chosen. A multidisciplinary team including the pulmonary embolism response team, cardiac critical care, and cardiothoracic surgery ultimately elected to pursue systemic thrombolysis. Following treatment, hemodynamics rapidly normalized, oxygen requirements resolved, and repeat echocardiography demonstrated complete resolution of the bi-atrial thrombi with marked recovery of RV function. The patient was discharged on apixaban with plans for outpatient hypercoagulability evaluation and consideration of PFO closure. Discussion: TSFO is a rare and life-threatening manifestation of venous thromboembolism. Management is challenging because comparative evidence among systemic thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, catheter-based intervention, and anticoagulation remains limited. Treatment decisions must account for thrombus morphology, PE burden, bleeding risk, and procedural feasibility. This case demonstrates successful treatment with systemic thrombolysis in a patient whose distal clot burden complicated alternative interventions. Conclusion: Systemic thrombolysis can be an effective treatment option for TSFO in carefully selected patients. Early recognition, multidisciplinary collaboration, and individualized risk assessment are essential to optimize outcomes in this rare but high-risk condition.
title: Abstract 7158: Paradoxical Bi-Atrial Thrombus in Transit: Thrombus Straddling a Patent Foramen Ovale Successfully Treated with Systemic Thrombolysis

abstract: Background: The clinical benefit of chronic total occlusion (CTO) revascularization in patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) remains uncertain. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing CTO revascularization with medical therapy in adults with CTO and reduced LVEF. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched through 2025 for studies comparing successful CTO revascularization with medical therapy in adults with at least one angiographically confirmed CTO (TIMI 0 flow, ≥3 months duration) and baseline LVEF <50% with at least 12 months of follow-up. Pooled risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were generated using restricted maximum likelihood random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic. Results: Five observational cohort studies, including a total of 2,211 patients, met the inclusion criteria. Among studies with extractable baseline demographics, mean age ranged from 58.0 to 68.4 years, and women comprised approximately 11% to 25% of participants; included cohorts were predominantly male with LVEF thresholds ≤50%. The composite endpoint, major adverse cardiac events (MACE) or major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), was analyzed in 866 patients undergoing revascularization and 1,345 receiving medical therapy, while the all-cause mortality and cardiac mortality analyses included 741 versus 995 and 822 versus 1,076 patients, respectively. Compared with medical therapy, successful CTO revascularization was associated with significantly lower risks of all-cause mortality (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.45-0.66, p<0.00001; I 2 =0%; Figure 1A), cardiac mortality (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.39-0.62, p<0.00001; I 2 =0%; Figure 1B), and MACE/MACCE (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.93, p=0.01; I 2 =74%; Figure 1C). Conclusion: In patients with reduced LVEF and coronary CTO, successful revascularization is associated with an approximately 46% relative reduction in all-cause mortality and 51% reduction in cardiac mortality compared with medical therapy alone. Revascularization was also associated with a significant reduction in MACE/MACCE, though with substantial heterogeneity across studies.
title: Abstract 7169: Chronic Total Occlusion Revascularization versus Medical Therapy in Patients with Reduced Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Acute intermediate-high risk pulmonary embolism — defined by preserved hemodynamics with RV dysfunction and myocardial injury — carries significant risk of hemodynamic collapse despite anticoagulation. Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) delivers fibrinolytics directly into the pulmonary artery, enabling faster RV offloading with potentially lower hemorrhagic risk than systemic thrombolysis. Prior meta-analyses were limited by retrospective data and lacked recent trials, including HI-PEITHO, STRATIFY, and CANARY. Hypothesis: CDT would significantly improve hemodynamic and clinical outcomes versus anticoagulation alone without a proportional increase in major bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage. Methods: Five databases were searched from inception through 2026 per PRISMA and Cochrane guidelines. Eligible studies compared CDT to anticoagulation in hemodynamically stable patients with RV dysfunction. A random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation was used. Primary outcomes included RV/LV ratio, pulmonary artery pressure, thrombus burden, and short- and long-term mortality. Secondary outcomes included clinical deterioration, bleeding, and length of stay. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, with subgroup analyses comparing ultrasound-assisted versus standard CDT and RCTs versus observational studies. Results: Eighteen studies (11,542 patients; 2,744 CDT, 8,798 anticoagulation; 4 RCTs, 14 observational) were included. CDT significantly reduced RV/LV ratio (MD = –0.06; 95% CI [–0.10, –0.03]; p<0.001), mean pulmonary artery pressure (MD = –2.93 mmHg; p<0.05), and thrombus burden (SMD = 0.86; p<0.001). Short-term mortality fell 55% (RR = 0.45; p<0.001) and long-term mortality 49% (RR = 0.51; p<0.01). RCTs showed a 64% reduction in clinical deterioration (RR = 0.36; p<0.01). CDT did not significantly increase major bleeding (RR = 1.59; p=0.08) or intracranial hemorrhage (RR = 1.77; p=0.19), though minor access-site bleeding was higher (RR = 3.08; p<0.001). No differences were observed between ultrasound-assisted and standard CDT. Conclusion: In acute intermediate-high risk PE, CDT accelerates RV recovery, reduces pulmonary pressures, and lowers short- and long-term mortality without meaningfully increasing major bleeding or intracranial hemorrhage. Ultrasound facilitation confers no additional benefit, supporting standard catheters as the more cost-effective approach.
title: Abstract 7186: Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis Compared to Anticoagulation Alone in Acute Intermediate-High Risk Pulmonary Embolism: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Resistant hypertension (RH), defined as blood pressure (BP) remaining above goal despite > 3 antihypertensive drug classes at maximally tolerated doses or controlled on > 4 antihypertensive drugs, poses a therapeutic challenge. Despite optimal medical therapy, achieving BP control is difficult in this population. Ultrasound-based renal denervation (URDN) has emerged as a promising adjunctive intervention. The timing of the BP drop remains under investigation. There are some concerns in the literature about the regrowth of nerves and the long-term effects of denervation in the real world. This study evaluates the impact of URDN on BP and antihypertensive medication burden in patients with RH in real life at successive intervals of 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year. Methods: In our RH clinic, an IRB-approved registry is maintained for all patients seen in the clinic. Of the 172 patients, 33 underwent URDN and were then followed prospectively with home BP monitoring. Diagnosis of true RH was confirmed via office and home BP evaluations. Secondary causes of hypertension were excluded in this population with assessment of plasma renin and aldosterone levels, as well as renal artery ultrasound. The procedure was offered to patients with no identifiable secondary etiology and an eGFR > 40 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Procedural efficacy was assessed by comparing changes in systolic and diastolic BP (office measurements) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-URDN. Changes in the total number of antihypertensive medications were noted. Renal safety was evaluated by monitoring changes in eGFR and serum creatinine at the same time points. Results: A total of 33 patients underwent URDN. Mean change in systolic BP was -13.25 + 21.55 mmHg (p = 0.0015) at 3 months (n = 32), -14.48 + 17.84 mmHg (p = 0.001) at 6 months (n = 22), and -13.55 + 16.98 mmHg (p < 0.0001) at 1 year (n = 10). Mean change in diastolic BP was -5.45 + 10.61 mmHg (p = 0.0067) at 3 months, -8.42 + 12.76 mmHg (p = 0.0055) at 6 months, and -9.10 + 10.62 mmHg (p = 0.028) at 1 year. Mean total antihypertensive medication count decreased by 0.76 + 1.12 medications (p < 0.001). Furthermore, 50% of patients (17/34) achieved a reduction of ≥ 1 antihypertensive medication dose. Changes in eGFR were not statistically significant: +0.48 + 9.73 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (p = 0.81) at 3 months, -0.20 + 9.41 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (p = 0.94) at 6 months, and -5.13 + 14.08 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (p = 0.34) at 1 year. Changes in serum creatinine were not statistically significant: +0.01 + 0.19 mg/dL (p = 0.79) at 3 months, +0.13 + 0.31 mg/dL (p = 0.15) at 6 months, and +0.19 + 0.32 mg/dL (p = 0.20) at 1 year. Reduced sample sizes at later time points reflect available follow-up data. Conclusion: URDN provides sustained 1-year reductions in BP and antihypertensive medication burden in patients with RH, without compromising renal function. These findings support URDN as an effective and renal-safe adjunctive intervention in the management of RH.
title: Abstract 7224: 1-Year Outcomes of Ultrasound-Based Renal Denervation for Resistant Hypertension: Real World Reduction in Blood Pressure and Antihypertensive Medication Burden

abstract: Background: With the expansion of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), lifetime management of aortic stenosis (AS) has become increasingly important. Accurate assessment of treatment response requires evaluation of left ventricular (LV) function and the mechanical load imposed by AS. The pressure-volume area (PVA) obtained from pressure-volume loops reflects total ventricular mechanical energy and serves as an index of LV load (Fig. 1A), but cannot be directly measured in clinical practice. We constructed a cardiovascular (CV) simulation model of AS and performed patient-specific CV simulations to evaluate how LV contractility (end-systolic elastance, Ees) and diastolic stiffness (β) influence changes in PVA after TAVR (ΔPVA), hypothesizing that ΔPVA is determined by the interaction between Ees and β. Methods: In-silico CV Simulation Analysis: A lumped-parameter CV model with a 5-element systemic/pulmonary resistance-capacitance network and four time-varying elastance chambers was used to simulate severe AS and TAVR. Severe AS was represented by fixing the aortic valve area (AVA) at 0.4 cm 2 , and TAVR was simulated by increasing AVA to 4.0 cm 2 . LV-Ees (1.0-20.0 mmHg/mL) and β (0.01-0.10) were systematically varied (Fig. 1B). For each Ees-β combination, hemodynamics, pressure-volume loops, and PVA were computed before and after TAVR. Patient-Specific CV Simulation Analysis: A total of 43 consecutive patients who underwent TAVR between December 2021 and April 2022 were included. For each patient, a CV simulation was constructed before and after TAVR using the same model, with 13 hemodynamic and ventricular parameters optimized by Bayesian optimization (Fig. 2). Pressure-volume loops were reconstructed, and LV-Ees, β, and PVA were estimated. Results: In the in-silico analysis, high Ees and low β conditions produced large reductions in PVA after TAVR (ΔPVA 6,000-9,000 mmHg·mL), whereas low Ees and high β conditions showed limited reductions (Fig. 3A). In the patient-specific CV simulations, the reproducibility of simulated hemodynamics was 7.7±5.6% before TAVR and 8.9±8.0% after TAVR. When patients were stratified by the fitted Ees-β relationship line (β = 0.033 х Ees + 0.022), those with relatively higher β exhibited significantly smaller ΔPVA than those with relatively lower β [4,232 (2,088-6,303) vs. 7,750 (4,558-9,704) mmHg·mL, p<0.01]. The three-dimensional Ees-β-ΔPVA surface (r=0.58, p<0.01, Fig. 3B) derived from clinical data closely matched the β-dependent gradient observed in the in-silico simulation. Conclusions: Both in-silico and patient-specific CV simulations showed that the mechanical benefit of TAVR is determined by the interaction between LV contractility and diastolic stiffness. Simulation-based estimation of cardiovascular properties may support prediction of mechanical benefit after TAVR.
title: Abstract 7226: Cardiovascular Simulation Reveals Systolic-Diastolic Interaction as a Determinant of Mechanical Benefit After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Background: Cardiac involvement by lymphoma, though well-documented, is an uncommon presentation that can closely mimic acute coronary syndrome, posing a significant diagnostic challenge in differentiating tumor-related myocardial injury from true ischemic events. Case: A 35-year-old male with primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBCL) on active chemotherapy presented with two weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea. He denied chest pain, palpitations, or constitutional symptoms. Examination revealed diminished left basilar breath sounds. Initial evaluation demonstrated an elevated high-sensitivity troponin with stable kinetics (100 → 91 ng/L), cytopenias, and hyperlactatemia (4.3 mmol/L) that resolved with fluid resuscitation. ECG revealed new downsloping ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversions in leads I, II, aVL, and V2-V6. CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but identified a large left mediastinal mass with effacement of left pulmonary artery branches and suspected left ventricular myocardial invasion. Transthoracic echocardiography was nondiagnostic due to a limited acoustic window. Cardiac MRI provided definitive characterization: a large necrotic left mediastinal mass extending from the chest wall into the mediastinum, abutting the anterolateral heart with loss of pericardial fat planes, restricted anterolateral wall motion, and positive epicardial late gadolinium enhancement; collectively confirming direct epicardial and myocardial infiltration. Biventricular size was preserved with mildly reduced systolic function (LVEF 50%, RVEF 46%). The combination of absent ischemic symptoms, non-dynamic troponin trend, multi-territory ECG changes, and CMR findings supported tumor-related myocardial injury rather than an acute coronary event. Per patient preference, cardiothoracic surgery was deferred. He completed five fractions of palliative radiotherapy and was discharged with cardiology follow-up for hemodynamic surveillance and monitoring of treatment-related cardiac toxicity. Conclusion: Lymphomatous cardiac involvement can present with ACS-like features driven by direct epicardial and myocardial infiltration. When echocardiography is non-diagnostic, CMR is indispensable for tissue characterization, injury mechanism differentiation, and treatment planning. This case underscores the necessity of a multimodality imaging strategy in oncologic patients with new electrocardiographic and biomarker abnormalities.
title: Abstract 7232: Epicardial and Myocardial Infiltration by Primary Mediastinal B-Cell Lymphoma Presenting as an Acute Coronary Syndrome Phenotype: Diagnostic Utility of Multimodality Cardiovascular Imaging

abstract: Introduction: Structural valve degeneration (SVD) remains a major limitation of bioprosthetic heart valves (BHVs), particularly among patients with diabetes mellitus, in whom inflammation, oxidative stress, and advanced glycation accelerate valve deterioration. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors exert pleiotropic anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects that may favorably influence SVD. We evaluated the association between SGLT2 inhibitor use and valve re-intervention and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with diabetes and BHVs. Methods: We performed a retrospective multicenter cohort study using the TriNetX federated electronic health record network. Adults (≥18 years) with diabetes who underwent surgical or transcatheter BHV implantation (aortic, mitral, or tricuspid) between 2014 and 2023 were included. Patients were stratified by post-procedural SGLT2 inhibitor use. Primary outcome was repeat valve intervention. Secondary outcomes included acute heart failure hospitalization, myocardial infarction, ventricular tachycardia, cardiac arrest, and atrial fibrillation. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed. Time-to-event outcomes were plotted using Kaplan-Meier methods, logistic regression of propensity-score matched cohorts yielded odds ratios (ORs). All tests were two-sided (p< 0.05). Results: Among 28,575 eligible patients, 1,958 received SGLT2 inhibitors. After matching, 1,832 patients remained in each group with well balanced baseline characteristics. Over approximately 2.8±1.8 years of follow-up, repeat valve intervention occurred in 2.5% of SGLT2 inhibitor users versus 3.7% of non-users (OR 0.67; 95% CI 0.46-0.98). Convergence of rates of valvular re-intervention were observed starting after 3 years of follow-up. SGLT2 inhibitor use was also associated with lower odds of cardiac arrest (OR 0.55; 95% CI 0.41-0.75), atrial fibrillation (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.69-0.89), acute heart failure hospitalization (OR 0.63; 95% CI 0.55-0.72), and acute myocardial infarction (OR 0.64; 95% CI 0.53-0.77). Conclusions: In patients with diabetes and BHVs, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with reduced valve re-intervention and fewer adverse cardiovascular events. These findings support a potential role for SGLT2 inhibitors in improving BHV durability and clinical outcomes and warrant prospective validation.
title: Abstract 7233: SGLT2 Inhibitor Use and Bioprosthetic Valve Re-Intervention in Patients with Diabetes

abstract: Introduction: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is a nonpharmacologic alternative to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation (AF). Comparative data in patients with autoimmune diseases, who have elevated thrombotic and bleeding risks, remain limited. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX multinational database. Adults with AF meeting indication for anticoagulation, and autoimmune disease were included and stratified by treatment with LAAO or DOACs. Patients with antiphospholipid syndrome, rheumatic mitral stenosis, mechanical valves or prior valve replacement, concurrent cardiac surgery, alternative indications for chronic anticoagulation, or recent major bleeding were excluded. Propensity score matching was performed 1:1. Outcomes were assessed from 3 months after LAAO implantation through 36 months. Cox regression estimated hazard ratios (HRs). Results: After matching, 2,713 patients were included in each cohort from 2020 to 2024. Baseline characteristics were well balanced, with mean age 76.7±8.7 versus 76.6±10.0 years and female sex 49.2% versus 48.8% in the LAAO and DOAC cohorts, respectively. Over 36 months, LAAO was associated with similar risks of all-cause mortality (LAAO 14.2% vs DOACs 15.9%; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.01; p=0.07), hospitalization (53.3% vs 52.9%; HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.92-1.07; p=0.79), ischemic stroke (10.2% vs 10.8%; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.08; p=0.32), systemic embolism (0.9% vs 1.2%; HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.43-1.20; p=0.20), AMI (10.7% vs 11.2%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.80-1.10; p=0.45), cardiac arrest (2.2% vs 2.7%; HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.58-1.15; p=0.25), and MACEs (21.9% vs 21.5%; HR1.01, 95% CI 0.90-1.13; p=0.86). LAAO was associated with lower major bleeding (6.2% vs 8.2%; HR 0.77; 95% CI 0.60-0.99; p=0.04) and acute heart failure exacerbation (23.5% vs 26.8%; HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.76-0.94; p=0.001). Conclusions: In patients with AF and autoimmune disease, LAAO was associated with comparable stroke prevention and cardiovascular outcomes versus DOACs over 36 months, with lower major bleeding and acute heart failure exacerbation. These findings support LAAO as a potential nonpharmacologic alternative in this high-risk population, warranting validation in prospective studies.
title: Abstract 7235: Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion versus Direct Oral Anticoagulants for Stroke Prevention in Atrial Fibrillation Patients with Autoimmune Disease

abstract: Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery (AAOCA) includes a heterogeneous group of congenital coronary anomalies with variable clinical significance. The configuration in which all three coronary arteries arise from separate ostia within the right coronary cusp, without a left main coronary artery, is rarely reported. We describe a 48-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis who underwent regadenoson nuclear perfusion imaging as part of routine pre-transplant evaluation. The study demonstrated inferolateral perfusion abnormalities of uncertain significance. Invasive coronary angiography showed no obstructive coronary artery disease and demonstrated separate origins of the right coronary artery, left anterior descending artery (LAD), and left circumflex artery (LCX) from the right coronary cusp. Coronary computed tomographic angiography demonstrated an LAD course most consistent with a prepulmonic trajectory anterior to the pulmonary artery, a course generally regarded as low risk. The LCX followed a retroaortic course. Coronary calcium score was zero, and echocardiography was normal. Given the rarity of the anatomy, the uncertainty regarding the physiologic significance of the perfusion findings, and the implications for transplant candidacy, the patient was referred to a specialized congenital cardiac surgical center for further evaluation. At the time of this report, he remains asymptomatic and is awaiting that assessment, with no interim cardiac events. The renal transplant evaluation remains ongoing pending cardiology clearance. This case highlights the importance of careful CCTA characterization of anomalous coronary anatomy, the clinical significance of coronary course subtype classification, and the challenges of managing incidentally discovered coronary anomalies with discordant functional and anatomic findings in the pre-transplant setting. Key message: Careful CCTA characterization can distinguish lower-risk prepulmonic coronary courses from high-risk interarterial AAOCA and help avoid overinterpretation of discordant functional testing in asymptomatic patients undergoing pre-transplant evaluation.
title: Abstract 7243: When the Left Goes Right: Three Separate Coronary Ostia from the Right Coronary Cusp with a Prepulmonic LAD and Retroaortic LCX

abstract: Background: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) targets during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) vary across institutions, and the optimal perfusion pressure remains uncertain. Although low MAP during CPB has been linked to acute kidney injury (AKI), the impact of cumulative hypotension burden on outcomes after cardiac surgery is poorly understood. We examined the association between the burden of CPB hypotension and postoperative outcomes. Methods: This retrospective, bi-institutional study analyzed adults undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB between 2016 and 2025. After excluding patients undergoing heart transplantation, LVAD implantation, preoperative mechanical circulatory support (MCS), deep hypothermic circulatory arrest, or redo surgery, 13,927 patients were included. Associations between CPB blood pressure metrics and in-hospital mortality were explored by restricted cubic splines. Hypotension burden was quantified as the area under the curve (AUC) of MAP <65 mmHg during CPB. Patients were stratified into AUC quartiles for descriptive analyses and visualization (Figure 1-2), whereas outcome analyses modeled CPB hypotension as a continuous variable (Figure 3). Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations between AUC MAP <65 mmHg and AKI, postoperative MCS, stroke, in-hospital mortality, and new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) among patients without preexisting AF. Recovery outcomes were analyzed using Fine-Gray competing-risk models accounting for in-hospital death, with ICU and hospital discharge, extubation, and vasopressor weaning defined as recovery events. Estimates are presented such that values >1 reflect delayed recovery. All regression models were adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, CPB duration, LVEF, and procedure category. Results: Unadjusted spline analyses demonstrated a U-shaped relationship between mean CPB MAP and in-hospital mortality, with the lowest predicted mortality occurring at approximately 63 mmHg (Figure 2). Higher hypotension burden was associated with in-hospital mortality (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01-1.32; Figure 3), stroke (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.12-1.57), postoperative MCS (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.1-1.38), and NOAF (OR 1.82, 95% CI 1.67-1.98). Higher hypotension burden was also associated with prolonged recovery, including longer ICU stay (sHR 1.27, 95% CI 1.22-1.32), hospital stay (sHR 1.19, 95% CI 1.14-1.23), time to extubation (sHR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07), and vasopressor weaning (sHR 1.07, 95% CI 1.03-1.1). No association was observed for AKI (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.95-1.1). Conclusions: Cumulative hypotension during CPB was independently associated with increased postoperative mortality, complications, and delayed recovery. These findings suggest that minimizing hypotension burden during CPB may improve postoperative outcomes and support prospective evaluation of optimal CPB perfusion pressure targets.
title: Abstract 7268: Cumulative Hypotension Burden During Cardiopulmonary Bypass and Postoperative Outcomes After Cardiac Surgery

abstract: Background: Post-infarction ventricular septal rupture (PI-VSR) remains a major contributor to myocardial infarction-related mortality. Surgical repair has limited effectiveness in patients with cardiogenic shock and when performed early after infarction. Evidence on percutaneous closure (PC) using occluder devices remains scarce, leaving its role in PI-VSR management insufficiently defined. We evaluated clinical outcomes and predictors of in-hospital mortality after PC for PI-VSR. Methods: This single-center, retrospective cohort included all patients with PI-VSR who underwent PC at the Chazov National Medical Research Center of Cardiology, Moscow, Russia, between 2020 and 2025. The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality. Secondary endpoints included 30-day mortality, in-hospital and 30-day cardiovascular mortality, procedural and technical success, and complications. Predictors of in-hospital mortality were assessed using multivariable Firth logistic regression. Results: Between 2020 and 2025, 48 patients with PI-VSR were included (mean age, 71.9 ± 12.0 years; 35.4% men). Anterior-wall myocardial infarction with apical rupture was observed in 58.3% (28/48). Cardiogenic shock on the day of PC was present in 83.3% (40/48). Among patients with shock, SCAI stage D was most common (24/40, 60.0%). Cardiac arrest before intervention occurred in 12.5% (6/48).Mechanical circulatory support was used in 79.2% (38/48), including VA-ECMO in 33.3% (16/48). Median time from myocardial infarction onset to PC was 8.0 [IQR, 4.0-19.8] days. Atrial septal defect occluders were used in 70.8% (34/48), and ventricular septal defect occluders in 29.2% (14/48). Open surgical ventricular septal repair after PC was performed in 16.7% (8/48).In-hospital mortality was 72.9% (35/48). Thirty-day mortality was 64.6% (31/48). In-hospital and 30-day cardiovascular mortality were 45.8% (22/48) and 39.6% (19/48), respectively. The most common complications of PC were cardiac arrest (15/48, 31.3%), tricuspid valve chordal rupture (12/48, 25.0%), and hemopericardium (8/48, 16.7%). Technical and procedural success were achieved in 87.5% (42/48) and 50.0% (24/48), respectively. Maximum SCAI cardiogenic shock stage throughout follow-up (OR, 11.60; 95% CI, 3.87-93.85) and septic shock (OR, 21.64; 95% CI, 2.92-96.36) were associated with higher in-hospital mortality in multivariable analysis. Conclusion: This study represents one of the largest real-world single-center cohorts of PC for PI-VSR. In-hospital mortality after PC remained high, with frequent procedural complications; more than one-third of deaths were non-cardiac. These findings highlight the need for careful patient selection, procedural optimization, and strategies targeting non-cardiac complications.
title: Abstract 7272: Percutaneous Closure of Post-Infarction Ventricular Septal Rupture: A Single-Center Cohort Study from Russia

abstract: Background: Patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary artery disease require long-term antithrombotic therapy that balances ischemic protection with bleeding risk. Although guidelines favor oral anticoagulation monotherapy beyond the early post-revascularization period, clinical practice remains variable. Prior randomized trial meta analyses did not include the most recently published trial evidence. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that single antithrombotic therapy (SAT) with oral anticoagulation monotherapy reduces bleeding without increasing ischemic events compared with dual antithrombotic therapy (DAT) with oral anticoagulation plus antiplatelet therapy. Methods: We performed an updated systematic review and meta analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing single versus dual antithrombotic therapy in adults with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary artery disease. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through November 24, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Co-primary outcomes were all cause mortality and major bleeding. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, net adverse clinical events, and clinically relevant non major bleeding. Pooled hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Results: Five randomized trials including 5,052 patients were analyzed; 2,531 were assigned to SAT and 2,521 to DAT. In time to event analyses, SAT was not associated with a significant difference in all-cause mortality (HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.60-1.02; p=0.06), cardiovascular death (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.53-1.08), ischemic stroke (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.62-1.44), or myocardial infarction (HR, 1.37; 95% CI, 0.73-2.55). SAT significantly reduced major bleeding (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.42-0.72; p<0.0001), net adverse clinical events (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.54-0.75; p<0.00001), and clinically relevant non major bleeding (HR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.43-0.63; p<0.00001). Conclusion: This updated meta analysis of all available randomized evidence supports oral anticoagulation monotherapy as the preferred long term strategy in patients with atrial fibrillation and stable coronary artery disease, providing lower bleeding and net adverse clinical event rates without a significant increase in ischemic outcomes.
title: Abstract 7287: Oral Anticoagulation Monotherapy versus Combination Antithrombotic Therapy in Atrial Fibrillation with Stable Coronary Artery Disease: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta Analysis

abstract: Background: Hypoattenuating thickening after transcatheter aortic valve replacement is a marker of valve thrombosis, which typically manifests as hypoattenuating leaflet thickening (HALT) and less commonly in perivalvular regions. These lesions have been associated with thromboembolic events, most commonly cerebral vascular events, and rarely coronary embolism. We report a case of myocardial infarction due to annular thrombosis in a self-expanding bioprosthetic aortic valve and secondary coronary embolism, highlighting the role of multimodality cardiac imaging. Case:: An 88-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and severe aortic stenosis status post bioprosthetic transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a self-expandable valve eight months prior presented with a sudden-onset severe chest pain radiating to the jaw and back following exercise. Electrocardiography demonstrated biphasic T waves in anterolateral leads and ST-depression in lateral leads. High-sensitivity troponin increased from 0.072 ng/mL on presentation to a peak of 35.7 ng/mL. Coronary angiography revealed acute thrombotic occlusion of the posterolateral branch of the right coronary artery without underlying atherosclerotic disease. Aspiration thrombectomy successfully restored TIMI-3 flow non-obstructive coronary artery disease. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed preserved valve function with a peak velocity of 1.9 m/s, a mean gradient of 6 mmHg, a valve area (VTI) of 0.88 cm 2 , and a dimensionless index (DI) of 0.43. Subsequent cardiac CT demonstrated circumferential hypoattenuating annular thickening consistent with bioprosthetic valve thrombosis (image 1-2). The patient was started on long-term therapeutic anticoagulation. Conclusion: This case highlights the potential for TAVR-associated valve thrombosis to cause coronary embolization despite normal prosthetic valve hemodynamics. Cardiac CT was critical for diagnosing annular thrombosis when echocardiography was unrevealing. Early recognition of attenuating lesions in patients with unexplained thromboembolic events may guide antithrombotic therapy and reduce the risk of recurrent embolization.
title: Abstract 7307: Coronary Embolization Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Secondary to Annular Thrombosis

abstract: Background: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) in patients with severe aortic stenosis and pre-existing Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) is high risk due to rapid pacing and cardiac arrest (CA) risk during valve deployment. Periprocedural Mechanical Circulatory Support (MCS) devices may be used prophylactically or as bail-out for hemodynamic stability. The clinical profile and short-term outcomes of this population remain poorly characterized. This study provides the first large-scale analysis of TAVR patients requiring early periprocedural MCS using real-world data. Methods: Using the TriNetX Health Network, we included adults who underwent TAVR for severe aortic stenosis with HFrEF to identify a subcohort with early periprocedural MCS placement (within 72 hours, including intra or post-TAVR) from September 2013 to December 2025. Demographics, comorbidities, MCS device use, and 30-day outcomes were quantified. Results: A total of 509 MCS-TAVR-HFrEF patients were identified from 20,428 TAVR-HFrEF patients. Demographics and MCS device use are in Table 1 . The cohort was predominantly male (357/509, 70.1%), older (mean age 71.5 ± 12.6 years), with high cardiovascular comorbidity ( Table 2 ) including coronary artery disease (418/509, 82.1%) and atrial fibrillation (291/509, 57.2%). A majority had prior cardiogenic shock (CS) (255/509, 50.1%) or CA (69/509, 13.6%), likely prompting MCS use. Intra-aortic balloon pump was used in 269/509 (52.8%), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in 152/509 (29.9%), Impella in 152/509 (29.9%), and other devices in 107/509 (21.0%); at least 171/509 (33.6%) required ≥2 device types.At 30 days, all-cause mortality was 29.27% (149/509) with new-onset CS in 244/509 (47.94%), acute kidney injury in 131/509 (25.74%), major bleeding in 158/509 (31.04%), blood transfusion in 165/509 (32.42%), new dialysis in 93/509 (18.27%), mechanical ventilation in 174/509 (34.18%), CA in 168/509 (33.01%), stroke in 39/509 (7.66%), and new permanent pacemaker in 30/509 (5.89%) ( Figure 1 ). Conclusion: To our knowledge, this is the first and largest real-world study characterizing MCS use on the day of or within 72 hours of TAVR in HFrEF patients, establishing 30-day clinical benchmarks. Most had prior cardiogenic shock (50.1%) or cardiac arrest (13.6%) before TAVR, likely prompting MCS use. Because MCS placement and outcomes were captured from the day of TAVR, acute intraoperative events fall within the 30-day window, capturing the full periprocedural burden. At 30 days, there was substantially elevated mortality (29.3%), cardiogenic shock (47.9%), acute kidney injury (25.7%), and major bleeding (31.0%). About one-third required ≥2 device types. These findings underscore the elevated risk of this subgroup and the need for dedicated risk-stratification and surveillance protocols.
title: Abstract 7309: Incidence and Outcomes of Early Mechanical Circulatory Support Use During Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Population-Based Study

abstract: Background: Severe aortic stenosis and coronary artery disease frequently coexist in patients referred for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Whether planned percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) before valve intervention improves outcomes compared with conservative or deferred management remains uncertain. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that planned PCI before TAVR would reduce ischemic events and revascularization but may increase bleeding. Methods: We conducted a PRISMA-adherent systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing planned PCI before TAVR with conservative, deferred, or no-PCI strategies in adults with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis and significant coronary disease (PROSPERO: CRD420261397950). PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through April 2026. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Results: Three randomized trials, including 1,156 patients, were included. Planned PCI before TAVR did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality (16.2% vs 18.0%; RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.70-1.15; P=0.40), major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (24.7% vs 27.6%; RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.70-1.18; P=0.47), cardiovascular death (7.4% vs 10.1%; RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.51-1.08; P=0.12), myocardial infarction (6.4% vs 8.3%; RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.45-1.63; P=0.64), stroke (6.9% vs 9.9%; RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.48-1.03; P=0.07), rehospitalization (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.87-1.32; P=0.52), or acute kidney injury (RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.34-4.31; P=0.76). Planned PCI reduced urgent revascularization (2.6% vs 8.2%; RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.13-0.87; P=0.03) and any revascularization (3.7% vs 15.6%; RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.07-0.87; P=0.03), but increased major bleeding (15.7% vs 9.9%; RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.07-2.32; P=0.02) and any bleeding (37.1% vs 20.5%; RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.27-2.47; P<0.01). Conclusions: In patients with severe aortic stenosis and concomitant coronary disease undergoing TAVR, planned PCI did not improve mortality or major ischemic outcomes but reduced subsequent revascularization at the cost of increased bleeding. These findings support a selective, individualized PCI strategy rather than routine pre-TAVR revascularization.
title: Abstract 7324: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Before Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients with Aortic Stenosis and Coronary Disease: A Meta-Analysis of RCTs

abstract: Introduction: High output heart failure may present similarly to heart failure with preserved or reduced ejection fraction, but the distinction is critical due to differences in etiology and management. Here we describe a case in which a simple bedside maneuver provided diagnostic clarity in a patient with worsening undifferentiated shock and unclear physiology. Clinical Case: A 51-year-old male with end stage renal disease, failed living donor kidney transplant on hemodialysis via left brachiobasilic arteriovenous fistula (AVF) and bioprosthetic aortic valve (AV) presented to an outside hospital where he was admitted to the floor for presumed community-acquired pneumonia and asthma exacerbation. Despite treatment with ceftriaxone, doxycycline, bronchodilators, and corticosteroids, he developed worsening hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring ICU transfer. TTE revealed newly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF 35% from 63% eighteen months prior) and prosthetic AV stenosis (peak velocity 4.5 m/s from 2.9 m/s). He was transferred to a tertiary care center for consideration of AV intervention. ICU course was complicated by influenza A infection, undifferentiated shock requiring escalating vasopressors, and mechanical ventilation. Serial TTE demonstrated further decline in LVEF and worsening AV hemodynamics (peak velocity 5.0 m/s, mean gradient 60 mmHg, dimensionless index 0.16). Ultrasound of the AVF demonstrated patency with flow rates up to 2.6 L/min. Following transfer to the cardiac ICU, bedside manual compression of the AVF produced an immediate 30-40 mmHg increase in systolic blood pressure on invasive monitoring. Simultaneously, central venous oxygen saturation decreased from 95% to 75%, indicating a substantial reduction in cardiac output. Repeat TTE performed during AVF occlusion demonstrated improved AV hemodynamics (peak velocity 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 47 mmHg, dimensionless index 0.27), implicating high-output physiology in the patient's hemodynamic deterioration. AVF ligation was performed the following day, leading to discontinuation of vasopressors on postoperative day 1 and extubation on postoperative day 2. Valve-in-Valve TAVR was later performed during admission. Unfortunately, the patient suffered a large intracranial hemorrhage complicated by subfalcine herniation in the setting of coagulopathy (INR 1.37, PTT 50.6) and DAPT. The family elected to transition to comfort focused care, and the patient subsequently expired. Discussion: This case demonstrates how a simple bedside maneuver, the Nicoladoni-Branham sign, can provide critical diagnostic clarity and guide appropriate intervention. High-output physiology should be considered in patients with AVF, particularly when echocardiographic findings suggest rapid changes in valvular hemodynamics that are difficult to explain by structural valve deterioration alone.
title: Abstract 7325: Back to the Bedside: High-Output Heart Failure in a Patient with Severe Bioprosthetic Aortic Stenosis

abstract: 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (15-HETE) is the endogenous agonist for GPR39. We have previously shown that pharmacological inhibition of GPR39 reduces brain infarct size during middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) in the mouse. Because 15-HETE is a potent vasoconstrictor we hypothesized that pharmacological inhibition of GPR39 reduces brain infarct by increasing cerebral blood flow (CBF). CBF was measured using a laser speckle camera (Pericam PSI Z system) with a resolution of 0.075 mm and imaging rate of 0.4 Hz. After baseline imaging, 0.05 mg/kg of VC108, a non-brain penetrating inhibitor of GPR39, or vehicle, was injected directly into the cerebral ventricle of mice (n=14 in each group). Right MCAO (45 min) was performed 24 hours later and perfusion imaging repeated. Imaging was also repeated 24 hours later, just prior to euthanasia and brain infarct size measurement. CBF in the right hemisphere (normalized to baseline) was significantly higher in VC108 versus vehicle treated animals after MCAO (0.70±0.07 vs 0.51±0.05, p=0.04). CBF was also significantly higher in the left non-occluded bed (0.97±0.07 vs 0.69±0.06, p=0.007). Figure 1 depicts baseline and post MCAO images from a vehicle treated animal, while Figure 2 shows similar images from a VC 108 treated animal. A global CBF index including the entire brain was significantly different between VC108 and vehicle treated animals (0.73 ±0.05 vs. 0.66±0.06, p=0.002) and correlated with cortical as well as total cerebral hemisphere infarct size (r=0.56, p=0.02 and r=0.49, p=0.05) during MCAO. Cortical and total brain infarct size was significantly smaller in the VC108 versus vehicle treated animals (31.9±4.7% vs 71.9±5.2%, p=0.004 and 34.4±4.3% vs. 68.4±2.9 %, p=0.0004) The difference in CBF between VC108 and vehicle was no longer significant 24 hours later, by which time brain drug levels had declined. These results indicate that pharmacological inhibition of GPR39 favorably affects CBF not only in the occluded bed during MCAO, but also in the non-occluded contralateral region, thus reducing cerebral infarction. Therefore, a brain-penetrating GPR39 inhibitor may offer a novel pharmacological treatment of stroke.
title: Abstract 7333: Pharmacological Inhibition of GPR39 Reduces Stroke by Enhancing Cerebral Blood Flow During Middle Cerebral Artery Occlusion

abstract: Background: Anemia is prevalent among patients with cardiovascular disease and is independently associated with adverse outcomes in acute coronary syndromes and heart failure. Prior studies linking hemoglobin to outcomes in cardiogenic shock (CS) have measured hemoglobin during the acute hospitalization, when values may be confounded by fluid resuscitation, hemodilution, and procedural blood loss. Whether hemoglobin measured before shock onset independently predicts outcomes remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, a federated electronic health record database. Adults hospitalized with CS and concomitant vasoactive medication use were identified between January 2016 and December 2025. Baseline hemoglobin was defined as the most recent value obtained 7-28 days prior to the index CS event and stratified by a prespecified threshold of ≤10.9 g/dL versus ≥11.0 g/dL, consistent with WHO moderate-to-severe anemia classification. Patients with prior CS within two years, major bleeding, transfusion, or dialysis dependence were excluded. 1:1 propensity score matching balanced demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, and medication exposures. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes included mechanical circulatory support (MCS), renal replacement therapy (RRT), mechanical ventilation, stroke or TIA, readmission, and cardiac arrest. Urinary tract infection served as a falsification endpoint. Results: Among 10,399 eligible patients, 2,955 had hemoglobin ≤10.9 g/dL and 7,444 had hemoglobin ≥11.0 g/dL. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 2,556 patients remained per cohort. Lower pre-shock hemoglobin was associated with higher 30-day all-cause mortality (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.06-1.28; p=0.002). Anemic patients were less likely to receive MCS (HR 0.58; p<0.001) but more likely to require RRT (HR 1.41; p=0.001) and mechanical ventilation (HR 1.18; p=0.023). No significant associations were observed for stroke or TIA, readmission, or cardiac arrest. The falsification endpoint was null. Findings were consistent in sensitivity analyses redefining baseline hemoglobin using measurements obtained 1 to 3 months prior to the index event and at 1-year follow-up. Conclusions: In this propensity-matched observational cohort, lower pre-shock hemoglobin was independently associated with higher short-term mortality and greater organ-support requirements in CS. The paradoxical reduction in MCS utilization despite worse outcomes raises important questions about whether hemoglobin influences therapeutic escalation decisions in this high-risk population. These hypothesis-generating findings support prospective investigation of pre-shock hemoglobin as a prognostic marker and potential therapeutic target in CS.
title: Abstract 7360: Pre-Existing Anemia and Short-Term Outcomes in Cardiogenic Shock: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study

abstract: Background: Ceramides are lipid species comprising sphingosine and fatty acid moieties carried by lipoprotein particles and influencing their function. CERT2 is a score (0 to 12 points) derived from concentrations and ratios of several ceramide and phospholipid species. CERT2 has been shown to predict the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with stable coronary heart disease or with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) within 1 month. However, shortly after ACS ceramides may be perturbed by an acute phase response and lipid-lowering therapy may be in flux. Research Question: It is not known whether CERT2 predicts MACE and death independent of conventional risk factors and biomarkers in patients stabilized after ACS on intensive lipid-lowering therapy. We addressed this question in a post hoc analysis of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial that compared PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab with placebo, each added to optimized statin therapy. Methods: At baseline 1-12 (median 2.6) months after ACS, ceramides and phospholipids were measured by mass spectrometry and CERT2 was calculated in 4285 trial participants. Natural cubic splines adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, estimated glomerular filtration rate, LDL cholesterol, lipoprotein(a), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein related CERT2 to 4-year risks of MACE (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, unstable angina, and ischemia-driven coronary revascularization) and all-cause death. Results: In the placebo group, CERT2 predicted both MACE ( Figure left ; P=0.012) and death ( Figure right ; P=0.004) independent of key demographic and clinical risk factors. Alirocumab significantly reduced CERT2 by approximately 2 risk-score points compared with placebo at 4-month follow-up. In the alirocumab group, higher baseline CERT2 was no longer associated with MACE (P=0.49) or death (P=0.13). Conclusion: In patients stabilized after ACS on optimized statin treatment, CERT2 predicts the risk of MACE and death independent of conventional clinical characteristics and biomarkers. Alirocumab significantly lowered CERT2 and CERT2-associated risk was attenuated in the alirocumab group, thus indicating that intensive lipid-lowering therapy with a PCSK9 inhibitor may modify ceramide-associated residual risk.
title: Abstract 7379: Ceramides, Cardiovascular Risk After Acute Coronary Syndrome, and the Effect of PCSK9 Inhibition with Alirocumab

abstract: Background: Unprotected left main (ULM) coronary artery disease represents a high-risk clinical subset associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Contemporary guidelines recommend the use of intravascular imaging (IVI) to optimize ULM percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), with the 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI guideline update strengthening these recommendations. However, real-world patterns of IVI utilization, and potential disparities in IVI adoption among patients undergoing ULM PCI remain poorly characterized. Research Question: Among patients undergoing unprotected left main (ULM) PCI, is intravascular imaging (IVI) utilization independently associated with improved in-hospital outcomes, and are there disparities in IVI adoption across patient and hospital characteristics? Methods: We analyzed National Inpatient Sample (2016-2023) adults undergoing ULM-PCI. Patients with prior/concurrent bypass grafting was excluded. The primary exposure was recipes of IVI. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate factors associated with IVI utilization and its association with in-hospital outcomes after adjustment for patient demographics, hospital characteristics, and clinical acuity. Interaction analyses compared temporal trends and disparities in IVI adoption before and after the 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI guideline update (2016-2021 vs. 2022-2023). Results: Analysis included 1,513,555 weighted patients. Overall IVI use was 10.53%, increasing from 5.94% (2016) to 19.85% (2022). High-income quartile (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.32-1.51) and large hospitals (aOR 1.41) were associated with higher IVI use, whereas female sex (aOR 0.96) and self-pay (aOR 0.85) were associated with lower use. Higher acuity was associated with reduced IVI use (STEMI aOR 0.73, NSTEMI aOR 0.81, shock aOR 0.84; P<0.01), while mechanical support favored IVI use (aOR 2.00). IVI was associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.72, 95% CI 0.65-0.79, P<0.001) and similar stroke rates (aOR 0.95, P=0.388). Documented coronary complications were higher (aOR 1.69, P<0.001), likely reflecting enhanced detection. Post-guideline analysis demonstrated widening IVI utilization gaps among Hispanic patients (interaction aOR 0.83, P=0.019). Conclusion: IVI use was independently associated with improved ULM-PCI survival, supporting guideline-concordant care. However, socioeconomic and racial disparities in adoption persist, with widening gaps among Hispanic patients after guideline updates. Targeted strategies are needed to promote equitable access to IVI.
title: Abstract 7386: Disparities in Intravascular Imaging Adoption and Clinical Outcomes in Unprotected Left Main Coronary Intervention

abstract: Background: ICI-Myocarditis is a severe toxicity of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), antibodies that target inhibitory T-cell checkpoints. While T cells are central to disease pathogenesis, the specific mechanisms and relative contributions of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells remain unclear. Methods: We used a novel genetic mouse model of ICI-myocarditis ( Lag3 -/- ,Pdcd1 -/- ), in which key checkpoint pathways are deleted, to define pathogenic T-cell subsets and signaling pathways. Mice underwent histology, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA-sequencing, antibody-mediated depletion, and genetic perturbation. Results: Lag3 -/- ,Pdcd1 -/- mice demonstrate an expansion of both cardiac CD4 + and CD8 + T-cells. Antibody-mediated depletion of T-cell subsets highlighted the necessity of both CD4 + and CD8 + T lymphocytes for myocarditis and pre-mature mortality. Flow cytometry and cardiac CD4 + sorted scRNA-seq identified activated CD4 + T-cell subsets with Th1 and Gzmk signatures. Blockade of the CD4 + T-cell costimulatory molecule, CD40L, attenuated pre-mature lethality, myocarditis and activated CD8 + T-cells in Lag3 -/- ,Pdcd1 -/- mice, indicating that CD4 + T-cells signal through CD40L to potentiate CD8 + T-cell-mediated myocardial injury. In contrast, genetic loss of the CD8 + T-cell cytotoxic protein, Perforin-1 ( Prf1 ), in Lag3 -/- ,Pdcd1 -/- mice markedly improved survival and arrhythmias despite evidence of significant myocardial inflammation. While Prf1 -/- , Lag3 -/- ,Pdcd1 -/- mice developed cardiac inflammation, troponin levels were minimally elevated - suggesting that the Perforin-1 pathway through direct perforin-mediated cytotoxicity is required for cardiomyocyte injury. Conclusions: These findings highlight that CD4 + T-cell CD40L signaling and CD8 + T-cell perforin-mediated cardiomyocyte cytotoxicity represent distinct but complementary drivers of ICI-myocarditis. Together, these results decouple inflammation from tissue injury and identify targetable pathways that may enable more precise diagnosis and treatment for ICI-myocarditis, without broadly suppressing immune activation.
