abstract: Background: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a prevalent clinical condition, affecting approximately 20-22% of older adults over age 60, with prevalence increasing substantially with age and reaching 30% or higher in those over 70 years, which places a significant strain on the healthcare systems worldwide. Managing OH is often challenging, particularly in elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, and treatment options remain limited. In this study, we compare the efficacy and clinical utility of midodrine and droxidopa in patients with OH. Hypothesis: This study aims to compare the incidence of new-onset cardiac arrhythmia among midodrine and droxidopa receiving patients, as well as the incidence of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), stroke, all cause hospitalization and all cause mortality. Methods: We did a retrospective cohort analysis using the TriNetX database from April 5, 2006 to April 5, 2026 of OH patients and created two cohorts: midodrine and droxidopa, Cohort 1 comprised patients treated with midodrine without droxidopa, while cohort 2 comprised patients treated with droxidopa without midodrine (Fig1-A. Propensity score matching was employed based on age, race, sex, comorbidities and medications to reduce baseline disparities (Fig1-B). Outcomes were new-onset cardiac arrhythmia events, acute coronary syndrome (ACS) incidence, stroke incidence, all cause hospitalization and all cause mortality. Results: After matching, 947 patients were included in each cohort (midodrine and droxidopa). New-onset cardiac arrhythmia occurred more frequently in the midodrine group (12.5%) compared to the droxidopa group (6.6%) (HR: 1.846; 95% CI: 1.268-2.689, P = 0.002). Receiving midodrine was also associated with higher rates of all cause hospitalization (HR: 1.521; 95% CI: 1.071-2.161, P= 0.030). On the other hand, acute coronary syndrome (HR: 1.806; 95% CI: 0.894-3.650, P= 0.13), stroke (HR: 1.098; 95% CI: 0.615-1.962, P= 0.883) and all cause mortality (HR: 1.360; 95% CI: 0.998-1.855, P= 0.07) showed no difference between the two groups (Fig2-A/B). Conclusions: Our findings suggest increased risk of new-onset cardiac arrhythmia and all cause hospitalization in OH patients who are receiving midodrine compared to patients receiving droxidopa. These results highlight a potential difference between midodrine and droxidopa in patients with OH. Emphasizing the need for prospective, standardized studies to validate these findings.
title: Abstract 7408: Comparative Cardiovascular Outcomes of Midodrine versus Droxidopa in Patients with Orthostatic Hypotension: A Retrospective Cohort Study

abstract: Introduction: The 2018 heart allocation policy assigns lower transplant priority to candidates bridged with durable left ventricular assist devices (LVAD) compared to those supported with temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS), potentially disadvantaging subgroups directed toward durable LVAD. While previous studies have documented higher rates of durable LVAD use and prolonged wait times among obese candidates, it remains unclear whether these disparities are attributable to clinical necessity or to systemic design. Hypothesis: Structural inequities in transplant access for obese candidates are driven by system design, as evidenced by (1) consistent funneling across centers into a durable LVAD pathway and (2) routing into that pathway is associated with worse and more variable outcomes. Methods: We cohort-analyzed adult heart transplant candidates listed between October 2018 and June 2024 who were supported by mechanical circulatory support at listing, utilizing the United Network for Organ Sharing registry (n=10,819). The cohort comprised 6,560 non-obese candidates and 4,259 obese candidates, with obesity defined as a body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m 2 . Center-level coefficients of variation (CV) were calculated to assess institutional practice patterns. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to adjust for baseline patient- and center-level characteristics. Results: After adjusting for clinical severity, centers demonstrated more uniform use of durable LVAD bridging among obese patients (CV 0.34) compared to non-obese patients (CV 0.48, Figure 1A ). Obesity remained associated with twice the odds of durable LVAD assignment (odds ratio [OR] 2.03, 95% CI 1.78-2.32), and this durable LVAD pathway exhibited two- to threefold greater cross-center variability in transplant rates compared to tMCS across all BMI groups (non-obese CV 0.35 vs 0.10; BMI 30-35, n=3,063, CV 0.37 vs 0.16; BMI greater than 35, n=1,196, CV 0.41 vs 0.17; Figure 1B ). Adjusted transplant access was consistently lower for durable LVAD than for tMCS in every BMI group (non-obese OR 2.58, BMI 30-35 OR 2.54, BMI greater than 35 OR 1.83; all p<0.001). Specifically, among Status 4 durable LVAD patients, obese candidates had higher adjusted odds of remaining waitlisted (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.08-1.56) without increased mortality compared to non-obese candidates. These findings persisted after confirming equivalent volume distributions between pathways (p=0.89). Conclusions: Obese candidates are uniformly funneled into a durable LVAD pathway that carries greater center outcome variability and lower transplant access, disadvantaging them through device assignment. This may call for further evaluation of status criteria for obese patients.
title: Abstract 7414: Policy-Driven Constraints versus Clinical Necessity in Device Allocation for Obese Heart Transplant Candidates Post-2018

abstract: Background: South Asians bear a disproportionate burden of cardiovascular disease, yet conventional single-timepoint glycemic thresholds poorly capture risk in this population. Whether longitudinal glycemic trajectories, derived from routine serial measurements, add prognostic value for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) beyond baseline glycemia is unknown. Methods: We analyzed 8,837 participants (53.9% women, mean age 42.8 years) from the Center for cArdiometabolic Risk Reduction in South Asia (CARRS) prospective cohort, categorized at baseline as normal glucose tolerance (NGT), prediabetes (PreDM), or diabetes using standard ADA criteria. We used latent class linear mixed models (LCMMs) for data-driven identification of subgroups of individuals with similar longitudinal profiles to identify glycemic trajectory classes within each baseline stratum. LCMMs with quadratic time terms, class-specific fixed effects, correlated random effects (unstructured covariance), and class-varying residual variances were fitted for 1-5 classes. Optimal class number was selected using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), entropy, and the Integrated Classification Likelihood (ICL). Trajectory classes were named descriptively based on their observed patterns. Survey-weighted cause-specific Cox models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for MACE (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and revascularization), with NGT-Stable as reference. Results: Seven FPG trajectory classes were identified: NGT-Stable (27.8%), NGT-Progressors (2.1%), PreDM-Slow Progressors (32.9%), PreDM-Rapid Progressors (2.3%), DM-Slow Progressors (14.7%), DM-Moderate Progressors (10.6%), and DM-Rapid Progressors (9.6%). Notably, individuals with similar baseline glycemia followed different longitudinal trajectories associated with substantially different cardiovascular risk. Over a median follow-up of 11.5 years (IQR 10.3-12.1), 791 MACE occurred. MACE incidence ranged from 2.6 (NGT-Stable) to 27.1 (DM-Rapid Progressors) per 1,000 person-years across FPG classes. Per SD increase in baseline FPG and HbA1c, aHRs for MACE were 1.32 (95%CI 1.26-1.39) and 1.40 (1.32-1.48). Compared to NGT-Stable, DM-Rapid Progressors had the highest MACE risk (FPG aHR 4.89 [3.38-7.09]), with a monotonic risk gradient across trajectory classes. Elevated risk among prediabetes trajectory classes did not reach statistical significance. HbA1c analyses revealed six analogous trajectory classes with similar risk gradients and event rates. Trajectory class assignment provided incremental discrimination beyond baseline glycemic values (ΔAUC +0.008 for FPG and +0.006 for HbA1c; both p<0.001). Conclusions: Trajectory-based glycemic phenotyping using serial measurements offers a practical approach to cardiovascular risk stratification in South Asians.
title: Abstract 7423: Trajectories of Glycemic Measures and Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in South Asians of the CARRS Cohort

abstract: Introduction/Background: Sepsis and atrial fibrillation (AF) are each associated with adverse outcomes in critical illness, yet the relationship between sepsis, electrical cardioversion (ECV) success, and survival among patients with cardiogenic shock (CS) and AF undergoing ECV remains incompletely characterized. Research Questions/Hypothesis: We evaluated whether sepsis was associated with increased mortality and reduced ECV success among patients with CS and AF undergoing ECV. Methods/Approach: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with CS and AF who underwent ECV at our institution in 2025. Patients were stratified by the presence or absence of concomitant sepsis. Outcomes included all-cause mortality and ECV success, defined as immediate restoration and maintenance of sinus rhythm for 24 hours and at the time of discharge. Mortality was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression, while ECV success was assessed using logistic regression. Models were evaluated both unadjusted and adjusted for age and sex. Results/Data: Among 68 patients with CS and AF who underwent ECV, 11 (16%) had sepsis. Baseline SCAI stage distribution did not differ significantly between patients with and without sepsis (p=0.562). ECV success was similar between groups (81.8% vs 78.9%, p=1.00). Sepsis was not associated with ECV success in unadjusted analysis (OR 1.20, 95% CI 0.23-6.31, p=0.83) or after adjustment for age and sex (OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.23-6.88, p=0.80) (Table 1). In contrast, mortality was significantly higher among patients with sepsis compared with those without sepsis (91% vs 46%, p=0.005). Sepsis was associated with increased mortality in unadjusted Cox regression (HR 3.19, 95% CI 1.52-6.70, p=0.002) and after adjustment for age and sex (HR 3.10, 95% CI 1.47-6.54, p=0.003). Pre-cardioversion Vasoactive-Inotropic Score (VIS) was similar between groups (13.95 ± 20.65 vs 8.14 ± 13.03, p=0.229), while post-cardioversion VIS was higher among patients with sepsis (21.74 ± 25.07 vs 9.05 ± 14.58, p=0.025). Inotropic support was similar between patients with and without sepsis, including epinephrine (3.25 ± 4.57 vs 3.25 ± 5.07, p=1.00), dobutamine (2.50 ± 4.33 vs 0.68 ± 1.44, p=0.091), and milrinone (0.08 ± 0.14 vs 0.04 ± 0.09, p=0.434). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated worse survival among patients with sepsis (log-rank p=0.0013) (Figure 1). Conclusion: In patients with AF and CS undergoing ECV, concomitant sepsis was associated with significantly increased mortality but not with reduced ECV success. These findings suggest that ECV remains feasible in patients with sepsis, AF, and CS, although sepsis identifies a high-risk phenotype associated with worse survival.
