title: Abstract 7756: Atrioventricular Node Ablation versus Atrial Fibrillation Ablation in Patients with Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy: A Propensity Matched Outcomes Analysis

abstract: Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) commonly coexists with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and is associated with worsening symptoms, recurrent hospitalization, and increased mortality. Both atrioventricular node (AVN) ablation and AF ablation are used in this population; however, comparative long-term outcomes remain poorly defined. We compared clinical outcomes following AVN ablation versus AF ablation in patients with AF and HFpEF. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, including 168 healthcare organizations. Adults aged >18 years with AF and HFpEF were included. Patients undergoing AVN ablation were compared with those undergoing AF ablation. Patients with prior AF ablation were excluded from the AVN cohort, while those with prior AVN ablation were excluded from the AF cohort. Outcomes were assessed from 1 day after the index procedure through 1 and 3 years. Primary outcomes included all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization. Secondary outcomes included AF hospitalization, cardiogenic shock, stroke or transient ischemic attack, bleeding, and cardioversion. Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 fashion using demographics, cardiovascular comorbidities, AF characteristics, baseline anticoagulant and antiarrhythmic therapy, and left ventricular ejection fraction. Before matching, 6,124 patients underwent AVN ablation and 33,629 underwent AF ablation. After matching, 5,365 patients remained in each cohort. Results: At 1 year, AF hospitalization was similar between groups (46.9% vs 42.9%; p=0.722). Heart failure hospitalization was higher after AVN ablation (19.4% vs 13.9%; OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.27-1.76; p<0.001). All-cause mortality was significantly higher after AVN ablation (13.9% vs 4.6%; HR 3.00, 95% CI 2.60-3.47; p<0.001). Cardiogenic shock was also increased (2.2% vs 1.3%; HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.26-2.33; p=0.001). Cardioversion was less frequent following AVN ablation (1.2% vs 9.8%; HR 0.12, 95% CI 0.08-0.17; p<0.001).At 3 years, AF hospitalization remained similar (68.8% vs 61.9%; p=0.511). Bleeding was higher after AVN ablation (13.0% vs 10.6%; HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.04-1.34; p=0.010). Mortality remained significantly higher (26.3% vs 10.4%; HR 2.46, 95% CI 2.23-2.72; p<0.001), as did cardiogenic shock (4.0% vs 2.3%; HR 1.65, 95% CI 1.31-2.07; p<0.001). Cardioversion remained lower following AVN ablation (1.8% vs 14.2%; HR 0.12, 95% CI 0.09-0.16; p<0.001). Conclusions: Among patients with AF and HFpEF, AVN ablation was associated with higher mortality, heart failure hospitalization, cardiogenic shock, and bleeding compared with AF ablation, while cardioversion was less frequently required. These findings suggest AF ablation may be associated with more favorable long-term outcomes in selected patients with HFpEF.
title: Abstract 7776: Atrioventricular Node Ablation versus Atrial Fibrillation Ablation in Patients with Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Propensity Matched Outcomes Analysis

abstract: Background: Transcatheter left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) provides an alternative to anticoagulation for preventing thromboembolic events in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). The optimal post-LAAC antithrombotic therapy, including type and duration, remains debated, with some studies favoring short-term anticoagulation while others support dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). Purpose: This study aims to assess the net clinical benefit of using direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) compared to DAPT in patients undergoing LAAC. Methods: We systematically searched major databases for trials comparing DOAC with DAPT in patients who underwent LAAC. The primary endpoints included major and clinically significant non-major bleeding and a composite efficacy endpoint involving death, stroke, bleeding, or device-related thrombus (DRT). Individual patient data were reconstructed from Kaplan-Meier curves. Hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using Cox regression. Time-to-benefit analysis was performed to determine when clinically meaningful differences emerged. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.5.0. Results: ANDES and ADALA trials were included, with 600 patients, among whom 297 (49%) received DOAC. The average age was 76.5 years, with 394 (65%) male participants. The use of DOAC significantly reduced the risk of major and clinically significant non-major bleeding compared to DAPT (HR 0.56, 95% CI: 0.37-0.83, P=0.005), indicating a 46% relative risk reduction. The time-to-benefit analysis showed a cumulative absolute risk reduction (ARR) peaking at 7.48% on day 44 (NNT=14). For the composite endpoint, low-dose DOAC also demonstrated superior outcomes (HR 0.53, 95% CI: 0.37-0.76, P<0.001, ARR 9.16%; NNT=11). Conclusion: In patients undergoing LAAC, DOAC was associated with a lower risk of bleeding and superior outcomes compared to DAPT, with significant implications for clinical practice. The findings suggest that DOAC may offer a safer alternative in the management of thromboembolic risk following LAAC. Further studies with larger sample sizes are warranted to confirm these results and explore the long-term outcomes associated with each treatment strategy.
title: Abstract 7777: Time to Benefit of DOAC versus Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Following Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Secondary Analysis of ANDES and ADALA Trials

abstract: Background: Guidelines support invasive hemodynamic assessment in cardiogenic shock (CS), yet right heart catheterization (RHC) utilization in underserved populations is poorly characterized. We examined RHC utilization, timing, and outcomes at an urban academic medical center serving a predominantly Black, socioeconomically disadvantaged population. Methods: Retrospective cohort study of 128 adult patients with adjudicated CS treated between 2022-2025 at an urban safety-net academic center. Patients were stratified by RHC use. Main descriptors: time to RHC and group phenotype. Primary outcome: in-hospital mortality. Statistical Analysis: Group comparisons used Chi-square/Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests. Multivariable logistic regression assessed independent association of RHC with mortality, adjusting for age, admission lactate, and pre-existing HF; treatment variables (inotropes, vasopressors) were not included to avoid collider bias. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) reported with 95% CI. Analyses were performed and independently verified using R. AI-assisted tools (Claude, Anthropic) were used for initial code drafting and figure generation. Results: Cohort: 95% Black, mean age 67±15, 48% female. RHC was performed in 23.4% (30/128) — above the ~10% rate reported in national administrative datasets but below the ~79% reported at specialized CS centers. Median time from admission to RHC was 4 days (IQR 2-7); only 10% occurred within 24h and 23% within 48h, well beyond published early-RHC thresholds (≤6h to <2 days) linked to improved outcomes. RHC patients had advanced-HF phenotype: higher pre-existing HF (80.0% vs 55.7%, p=0.029), lower nadir LVEF (20% vs 30%, p=0.031), higher BNP (3137 vs 1177 pg/mL, p=0.002) and more temporary MCS use (16.7% vs 3.1%, p=0.025). Unadjusted mortality was numerically lower among patients undergoing RHC (33.3% vs. 51.1%, p =0.10); however, RHC was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment (aOR 0.60, 95% CI 0.22-1.64, p =0.32). This finding should be interpreted cautiously given modest RHC group size. Conclusions: RHC utilization exceeded rates reported in national administrative datasets but was implemented late (median 4 days) and selectively in advanced-HF phenotypes rather than as early risk stratification — substantially exceeding published early-RHC thresholds. This highlights an important quality-improvement target and opportunity to improve implementation of guideline-supported CS care in underserved patient populations. Limitations: single-center retrospective design; modest sample size; SCAI stage not systematically assigned given incomplete documentation of stage-defining variables.
