title: Abstract 7809: Right Heart Catheterization in Cardiogenic Shock: Utilization, Timing, and Outcomes in an Underserved Urban Academic Cohort

abstract: Introduction: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is a cardiac emergency and requires urgent intervention, but some noncardiac conditions such as acute gastric distention can mimic STEMI on electrocardiography (ECG). These conditions need to be identified early to avoid unnecessary interventions. We present a case of bowel obstruction-induced gastric distention causing inferior ST elevations and Q waves, resolving after naso-gastric (NG) tube decompression. Case Description/Methods: A 63-year-old male presented for elective left maxillectomy for squamous cell carcinoma of left maxilla. Initial ECG was within normal limits. Post-operative surgical course was complicated by ileus causing severe distention. Repeat ECG showed new Q waves, and ST elevations in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) (Figure 1). Stat echocardiography demonstrated normal ejection fraction and subtle inferior hypokinesis (nondiagnostic). Serial high-sensitivity troponins remained negative (<0.01 ng/mL). Abdominal imaging showed massive gastric distention (Figure 2 a and b). Stat NG tube insertion achieved decompression, yielding >2L aspirate. Follow-up ECG post-decompression showed improved ST elevations and echocardiography showed resolved inferior wall motion abnormality, supporting gastric compression as the etiology. No antiplatelet therapy or catheterization was pursued given negative biomarkers and clinical improvement. Discussion: STEMI is a life-threatening condition and an emergent diagnosis that needs prompt treatment. An ECG is the most readily available early diagnostic method. Besides myocardial infarction, there are several other causes for ST elevations such as pericarditis, myocarditis, and some intra-abdominal processes as small bowel obstruction (SBO), pancreatitis, and cholecystitis. The mechanism of ST elevations in SBO is not well understood. Proposed mechanisms include intra-abdominal distention causing myocardial irritation; displacement of intrathoracic structures leading to leftward QRS axis shift; a viscero-cardiac reflex increasing vagal tone and reducing coronary perfusion; and stress-induced cardiomyopathy due to catecholamine-mediated microvascular dysfunction. Regardless of mechanism, this case highlights a rare but important ECG mimic of STEMI caused by severe gastric distention. Conclusion: Recognition of this phenomenon is critical to avoid unnecessary cardiac interventions. Prompt gastric decompression not only relieves the underlying mechanical stress but also results in rapid resolution of ECG abnormalities.
title: Abstract 7810: Inferior ST-Elevation Mimic from Malignancy-Related Gastric Distention: A Case Report

abstract: Introduction: Nitroglycerin is typically therapeutic in coronary vasospasm due to its vasodilatory effects; however, paradoxical vasospasm is rare and may lead to life-threatening arrhythmias(1). Patient information: A 71-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and prior tobacco use underwent elective coronary angiography for unstable angina. Clinical findings and timeline: Initial angiography showed small caliber vessels with no clear evidence of stenosis (Figure 1). After administration of 200 mcg intracoronary nitroglycerin, she developed worsening chest pain, bradycardia, and hypotension. Repeat angiography demonstrated diffuse vasoconstriction of the left main and left anterior descending coronary arteries (Figure 2), followed by ventricular fibrillation. Therapeutic intervention: She underwent brief cardiopulmonary resuscitation, received epinephrine, atropine, phenylephrine, amiodarone, and defibrillation with return of spontaneous circulation. Follow-up and outcome: Repeat angiography showed resolution of vasospasm and patent coronary arteries. The patient fully recovered without residual complications. Discussion: Nitroglycerin is a potent vasodilator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and dilates the coronary arteries. During cardiac catheterization, intracoronary nitroglycerin is routinely administered to distinguish fixed atherosclerotic stenosis from reversible coronary vasospasm, particularly when diffuse narrowing limits angiographic interpretation. Although nitroglycerin typically relieves coronary spasm, paradoxical coronary vasospasm has rarely been reported, and the literature on this phenomenon remains limited (2)(3). The mechanism by which nitroglycerin induces coronary vasospasm remains unclear(3). In the present case, administration of intracoronary nitroglycerin was followed by severe vasoconstriction of left main coronary artery and left anterior descending artery, resulting in transient but profound myocardial ischemia. This was complicated by hemodynamic instability characterized by hypotension, bradycardia, and progression to ventricular fibrillation. Conclusion: This case highlights a rare, severe presentation of paradoxical vasospasm after intracoronary nitroglycerin, a phenomenon with limited literature despite nitroglycerin’s usual role in relieving coronary spasm.
title: Abstract 7824: When a Vasodilator Constricts: Diffuse Coronary Vasospasm and Ventricular Fibrillation Following Intracoronary Nitroglycerin

abstract: Background: Neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with cardiovascular disease incidence and mortality, yet whether it predicts disease progression after an index atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event, independent of traditional risk factors, remains unknown. We evaluated the association between neighborhood socioeconomic status (nSES) and adverse cardiovascular outcomes in a large secondary prevention cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults aged 18-89 years with established ASCVD receiving care within a large, integrated healthcare system. Patients with an index ASCVD event between 2015 and 2019 were followed through 2024. Neighborhood socioeconomic status was derived from a validated composite index based on American Community Survey data linked to residential ZIP codes and categorized as high versus low using the national median. Outcomes included incidents of heart failure (HF), stroke, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; myocardial infarction or coronary revascularization). Marginal Cox proportional hazards models accounting for ZIP-level clustering were adjusted for demographics, healthcare utilization, comorbidities, and time-dependent treatment variables including statin and antihypertensive use. Results: Among 41,890 adults with established ASCVD (mean age 64.1±13.0 years; 53.3% male), 51.2% resided in higher socioeconomic neighborhoods. During a median follow-up of 66 months, 8,816 patients (21.1%) developed HF, 2,539 (6.1%) experienced stroke, and 4,621 (11.0%) experienced MACE. In fully adjusted models, higher nSES was independently associated with lower risk of incident HF (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.98) and stroke (aHR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78-0.95). No significant association was observed between nSES and MACE (aHR 1.07, 95% CI 0.95-1.21); the absence of an effect on acute coronary events may in part reflect more uniform treatment intensity for obstructive coronary disease across socioeconomic strata. In sensitivity analyses restricted to patients with index myocardial infarction, higher nSES remained associated with lower HF risk (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.63-0.95). Conclusions: Lower neighborhood socioeconomic status is independently associated with increased risk of incident heart failure and stroke among adults with established ASCVD, despite adjustment for traditional cardiovascular risk factors and treatment variables. These findings suggest that neighborhood socioeconomic context may augment risk stratification in secondary prevention populations and represent a potential target for cardiovascular risk reduction beyond conventional clinical factors.
title: Abstract 7845: Incident Heart Failure and Stroke Risk by Neighborhood Socioeconomic Status Among Adults with Established ASCVD

abstract: Introduction: For patients with concomitant aortic valve disease and coronary artery disease, the optimal combined revascularization and valve replacement strategy remains uncertain. Real-world comparative effectiveness data spanning short- and long-term follow-up are limited. Hypothesis: Clinical outcomes after TAVR/PCI versus SAVR/CABG differ across early and long-term follow-up windows. Methods: We conducted a retrospective propensity-matched cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network in adults with aortic valve disease and coronary artery disease. Exclusions included acute myocardial infarction, endocarditis, and prior valve replacement. 1:1 propensity score matching on 50+ covariates including patient characteristics, medications, comorbidities, and laboratory values. Outcomes were compared at 30 days, 90 days, 1 year, and at 5 years. Hazard ratios were used for primary outcomes including all-cause mortality, MACE-plus, stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and cardiac arrest; risk ratios were used for secondary outcomes including acute kidney injury, hospitalization, and pacemaker insertion. Results: Analysis 1 yielded 1,698 matched pairs; TAVR/PCI was associated with lower 30-day mortality (2.6% vs 4.5%; HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.40-0.84; p=0.004) and lower 90-day mortality (4.1% vs 6.5%; HR 0.62, 0.46-0.83; p=0.001). Mortality did not differ at 1 year (8.8% vs 9.9%; HR 0.87, p=0.227). At 5 years, TAVR/PCI was associated with higher mortality (23.7% vs 19.2%; HR 1.50, 1.29-1.74; p<0.001) and higher MACE-plus (42.7% vs 39.3%; HR 1.32, 1.09-1.60; p=0.004). Acute kidney injury was lower with TAVR/PCI at every window (30-day RR 0.28, 0.22-0.35; 5-year RR 0.66, 0.58-0.75; all p<0.001). Hospitalization was lower with TAVR/PCI across all windows. Pacemaker insertion, heart failure, myocardial infarction, and stroke did not significantly differ. Conclusions: TAVR/PCI was associated with lower early mortality and consistently lower acute kidney injury compared with SAVR/CABG, while SAVR/CABG was associated with lower 5-year mortality and MACE-plus.
title: Abstract 7847: TAVR with PCI versus SAVR with CABG in Patients with Aortic Valve Disease and Coronary Artery Disease: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis Across Short- and Long-Term Follow-Up

abstract: Introduction: For patients with aortic stenosis and concomitant coronary artery disease undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), the optimal timing of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) relative to TAVR remains uncertain. Observational comparative effectiveness data at scale are lacking. Hypothesis: Clinical outcomes after PCI performed before TAVR differ from those after PCI performed after TAVR when both procedures are staged within 40 days. Methods: We conducted a retrospective propensity-matched cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network in adults with aortic valve disease who underwent TAVR with PCI staged within 40 days. Patients with acute myocardial infarction prior to the applicable timing window were excluded. 1:1 propensity score matching on demographics, cardiac history, comorbidities, medications, and laboratory values. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days and 3 years. Hazard ratios were used for primary outcomes including all-cause mortality, MACE-plus, stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and cardiac arrest; risk ratios were used for secondary outcomes including acute kidney injury, hospitalization, and pacemaker insertion. Results: Analysis yielded 380 matched pairs; PCI before TAVR was associated with higher pacemaker insertion (15.3% vs 7.0%; RR 2.20, 95% CI 1.33-3.65; p=0.002), higher hospitalization (89.9% vs 80.7%; RR 1.11, 1.05-1.19; p<0.001), and higher MACE-plus (34.8% vs 19.7%; RR 1.76, 1.03-3.00; p=0.031). Thirty-day all-cause mortality and acute kidney injury did not differ. At 3 years, PCI before TAVR was associated with higher pacemaker insertion (23.0% vs 12.7%; RR 1.82, 1.27-2.60; p=0.001), higher myocardial infarction (9.2% vs 4.8%; HR 1.91, 1.03-3.53; p=0.035), and higher MACE-plus (61.2% vs 38.6%; HR 2.11, 1.35-3.28; p=0.001). Three-year all-cause mortality, acute kidney injury, stroke, and bleeding did not significantly differ. Conclusions: PCI before TAVR was associated with higher pacemaker insertion, myocardial infarction, and MACE-plus rates compared with PCI after TAVR at both short- and long-term follow-up.
title: Abstract 7855: Before or After? Timing of PCI Around TAVR: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Background: Renal denervation (RDN) has re-emerged as an adjunctive therapy for resistant hypertension, with current AHA/ACC guidelines acknowledging modest but clinically meaningful reductions in blood pressure. Since FDA approval of the Paradise and Symplicity Spyral systems, commercial use has begun to expand, yet real-world safety data remain sparse. We used the FDA MAUDE database to characterize the adverse events being reported as the technology moves into everyday practice. Methods: MAUDE is the FDA's post-market surveillance system for device-related adverse events in the United States. On May 2, 2026, we queried the database for all RDN-related reports submitted since device approval. Duplicates were removed, and the remaining reports were reviewed to extract and categorize adverse events, mechanisms of injury, management strategies, and clinical outcomes. Results: Thirty-three adverse event reports were identified. Renal artery injury was the most common complication, accounting for 13 cases (39.4%), followed by device or catheter malfunction (10 cases, 30.3%), hemodynamic events (6 cases, 18.2%), and vascular access complications (2 cases, 6.1%); two additional reports (6.1%) lacked enough diagnostic detail to classify. Reported mechanisms of renal artery injury included arterial dissection, vasospasm, thrombosis, and renal subcapsular hematoma. Injuries were reported slightly more often with the Paradise system (7/13, 53.8%) than the Symplicity Spyral system (6/13, 46.2%), but the pattern of subtypes differed: vasospasm was reported exclusively with Symplicity Spyral, while subcapsular hematoma was reported exclusively with Paradise. No deaths were reported. Conclusion: In this national post-marketing analysis, renal artery injury was the dominant adverse event signal associated with commercial RDN, with mechanisms ranging from dissection to subcapsular hematoma. The absence of reported mortality is reassuring. Sustained surveillance and operator-level analyses will be essential as RDN moves from controlled trials into broader clinical practice
title: Abstract 7866: Percutaneous Intervention for Renal Artery Injury Following Commercial Renal Denervation Insights from FDA MAUDE

abstract: Background: Recent clinical trials have suggested potential benefits of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) following acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, patients with cardiogenic shock requiring mechanical circulatory support (MCS) were excluded from these trials, leaving their effectiveness in this population uncertain. We investigated the association between discharge SGLT2i therapy and 180-day outcomes in patients with AMI-related cardiogenic shock (AMICS) requiring MCS. Methods: We analyzed the Q-HEART Retrospective Shock Registry (6 hospitals, 2020-2025). Consecutive AMI patients requiring MCS, including intra-aortic balloon pump, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, or Impella, were enrolled. Exclusion criteria were dialysis dependence, in-hospital death, or missing data. Patients who received SGLT2i therapy at discharge were included in the SGLT2i group, and the others were in the non-SGLT2i group. The primary endpoint was the 180-day composite of all-cause mortality and heart failure rehospitalization. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using age, sex, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), body mass index (BMI), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and guideline-directed medical therapy. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards regression. Results: Among 523 patients with AMICS requiring MCS in this registry, 314 survived to discharge and were eligible for this study (SGLT2i group, n=119 [38%]; non-SGLT2i group, n=195 [62%]). Median age was 72 years and 78% were male. Compared with the non-SGLT2i group, the SGLT2i group had a higher prevalence of diabetes (58% vs 32%, p<0.001), a higher proportion of male sex (85% vs 74%, p=0.028), and lower LVEF (43% vs 48%, p<0.001). In the overall cohort, Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated higher 180-day event-free survival in the SGLT2i group compared with the non-SGLT2i group (96% vs 88%; log-rank p=0.031). Cox proportional hazards regression confirmed the association between SGLT2i use and reduced risk of the 180-day composite endpoint (univariate: HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.14-0.95, p=0.038; adjusted for age and sex: HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.13-0.90, p=0.030). After PSM (72 matched pairs), 180-day event-free survival in the SGLT2i group was higher compared with the non-SGLT2i group (96% vs. 80%; log-rank p=0.004). Cox proportional hazards regression demonstrated a lower risk of the 180-day composite endpoint in the SGLT2i group (HR 0.20, 95% CI 0.06-0.60, p=0.004). Conclusion: Among AMICS patients requiring MCS, initiation of SGLT2i therapy at discharge was associated with improved 180-day clinical outcomes. These findings suggest that SGLT2i therapy may benefit patients with AMICS requiring MCS, a population historically excluded from post-AMI trials, and support further prospective investigation.
title: Abstract 7888: Clinical Impact of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitor Therapy at Discharge in Patients with Acute Myocardial Infarction-Related Cardiogenic Shock Requiring Mechanical Circulatory Support

abstract: BACKGROUND: May-Thurner Syndrome is a phenomenon in which the right common iliac artery compresses left common iliac vein that more often than not is an asymptomatic disease but in severe cases, may cause extensive deep venous thrombosis, compressive symptoms and post thrombotic complications. High index of suspicion along with timely diagnosis and intervention with pharmaco-mechanical thrombolysis with minimally invasive interventions (venoplasty with iliac vein stenting) will minimize morbidity and post thrombotic syndromes. CASE PRESENTATION: This case report details a 20-year-old male without any known comorbid illnesses came in with a 2-year history of left leg pain and swelling, which was eventually diagnosed as deep venous thrombosis and was managed conservatively with Apixaban however, 2 months later had recurrence of the swelling and discomfort. A CT scan of both lower extremities revealed large saccular aneurysms involving both superficial femoral arteries and the right iliac artery was shown compressing the left iliac vein highly suggestive of May-Thurner Syndrome. He underwent bilateral femoral-popliteal bypass revealing multilobulated popliteal aneurysms of both left and right lower extremities. A venogram with venoplasty and stenting using an Abre 10x40 mm self-expandable stent of the left common iliac to the left external iliac vein was also done showing good post procedural venous outflow. DISCUSSION: This case highlights an uncommon presentation of MTS in a young male complicated by recurrent extensive DVT despite therapeutic anticoagulation and associated bilateral peripheral arterial aneurysms. Persistent or recurrent unilateral lower extremity swelling despite adequate anticoagulation should prompt evaluation for underlying anatomic venous obstruction. Early recognition of MTS is essential, as anticoagulation alone may be insufficient when significant mechanical venous compression is present. CONCLUSION: May-Thurner syndrome should be considered in young patients presenting with recurrent or extensive left-sided DVT, particularly when symptoms persist despite anticoagulation. Multimodality imaging facilitates diagnosis, while a combined approach involving anticoagulation and endovascular or surgical intervention may improve venous patency, reduce recurrence, and minimize long-term post-thrombotic complications.
title: Abstract 7895: Extensive Deep Venous Thrombosis Secondary to May-Thurner Syndrome in a 20 Year-Old Male Patient: A Case Report

abstract: Background: Balancing ischemia and bleeding during PCI remains challenging. MT1002 is a 32-amino acid peptide dual antagonist targeting thrombin and GPIIb/IIIa, offering simultaneous anticoagulation and antiplatelet effects with rapid onset and offset. Purpose: To evaluate safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) of MT1002 in healthy subjects from two Phase I trials in US and China and assess consistency of its effects across populations. Methods: Data were analyzed from two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind (China)/open-label (US), single-ascending-dose Phase I trials, with registration# NCT04116840. US Study (n=30): Cohorts 1-5 received MT1002 as a bolus + 4h infusion at dose levels of: Cohort 1: 0.15 mg/kg + 0.3 mg/kg/h; Cohort 2: 0.3 mg/kg + 0.6 mg/kg/h; Cohort 3: 0.6 mg/kg + 1.2 mg/kg/h; Cohort 4: 0.9 mg/kg + 1.8 mg/kg/h; Cohort 5: 1.2 mg/kg + 2.3 mg/kg/h. China Study (n=20): Cohort A received 0.6 mg/kg + 1.2 mg/kg/h. Following protocol-defined criteria (APTT >105s) in two subjects, Cohort B received a reduced dose of 0.45 mg/kg + 0.9 mg/kg/h.Safety, PK, and PD (ACT, aPTT, PT, INR, TT, platelet aggregation [PA]) were assessed. Safety: MT1002 was generally safe and well-tolerated. All treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were mild or moderate. No serious AEs or discontinuations occurred. In the US study, bleeding-related TEAEs (e.g., injection site hemorrhage, mouth hemorrhage) were observed in Cohorts 4 and 5, suggesting these doses may exceed the optimal range for healthy subjects. In contrast, no bleeding events were reported in any Chinese cohort. PD: MT1002 showed rapid onset of action (<5 min) with dose-dependent prolongation of aPTT, PT, TT, INR, and ACT, and inhibition of PA. In the Chinese 0.45 mg/kg + 0.9 mg/kg/h cohort, ACT and PA reached levels considered effective for PCI immediately post-dose. All PD parameters returned to near baseline within 24 hours. PK & Ethnic Consistency: MT1002 exposure (Cmax and AUC) increased in a slightly greater than dose-proportional manner. PK parameters were consistent across doses with a mean t1/2 of approximately 1.2-1.4h. Quantitative PK/PD modeling demonstrated that under the same dosing regimen (e.g., 0.9 mg/kg + 1.8 mg/kg/h), the typical values and 95% confidence intervals for ACT and APTT were highly consistent between US and Chinese populations, confirming comparability across ethnicities. Conclusion: MT1002 demonstrated a favorable safety profile with rapid, reversible, and dose-dependent anticoagulant and antiplatelet effects in healthy subjects. Its PK/PD characteristics are highly consistent between US and Chinese populations. The dual-targeting mechanism offers the potential to address the longstanding challenge of balancing ischemic and bleeding risks. These findings support its continued development as a promising therapeutic strategy for patients undergoing PCI.
title: Abstract 7898: First-in-Class Dual Thrombin and GPIIb/IIIa Inhibitor MT1002: Pooled Phase I Safety, PK, and PD Results from US and Chinese Healthy Subjects

abstract: Background: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, is associated with systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, accelerated atherosclerosis, and increased cardiovascular risk. Chronic inflammation may promote plaque formation and instability, increasing susceptibility to acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, outcomes among patients hospitalized with ACS remain incompletely characterized, particularly with respect to the impact of systemic corticosteroid exposure. We evaluated short-term outcomes in patients hospitalized with ACS with and without IBD and assessed the influence of corticosteroid use among patients with IBD. Methods: We performed a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study using the TriNetX Analytics Network (>139 million patients across 110 U.S. healthcare organizations). Adults aged 18-100 years hospitalized with ACS (STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina) were stratified by IBD status. After 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics, comorbidities, and medications, 33,201 patients remained in each cohort. Thirty-day outcomes included all-cause mortality, cardiogenic shock, acute heart failure, atrial fibrillation/flutter, ventricular arrhythmias, ischemic stroke, acute kidney injury (AKI), percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and mechanical ventilation. Outcomes were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models. A prespecified subgroup analysis compared corticosteroid-exposed versus non-exposed patients with IBD+ACS (4,076 matched pairs). Results: Patients with IBD hospitalized with ACS had lower 30-day mortality than those with ACS alone (4.5% vs. 5.5%; HR 0.795, 95% CI 0.743-0.852; p<0.001). However, they had higher rates of AKI (3.0% vs. 2.4%; HR 1.174, 95% CI 1.050-1.312; p=0.001) and lower PCI utilization (1.4% vs. 1.6%; HR 0.845, 95% CI 0.746-0.958; p=0.015). No significant differences were observed in cardiogenic shock, heart failure, atrial fibrillation/flutter, ventricular arrhythmias, ischemic stroke, or mechanical ventilation. In the corticosteroid subgroup, exposure was associated with increased risks of ventricular arrhythmias (HR 1.847; p=0.007) and mechanical ventilation (HR 1.389; p=0.006), without differences in mortality or other major cardiovascular outcomes. Conclusion: Patients with concomitant IBD and ACS experienced lower short-term mortality despite higher rates of AKI and lower PCI utilization. Among patients with IBD, systemic corticosteroid exposure identified a subgroup at increased risk for ventricular arrhythmias and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, suggesting corticosteroid use may be an important marker of adverse inpatient risk and supports enhanced cardiac and respiratory monitoring in such patients.
title: Abstract 7899: Influence of Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Systemic Corticosteroid Exposure Among Patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Propensity Score-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Background: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is the standard of care for severe aortic stenosis. However, conduction disturbances requiring permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) remain a significant complication, particularly with self-expanding valves. While self-expanding valve implantation depth relative to the membranous septum (MS) length is a recognized predictor of PPI, the actual anatomical relationship between the deployed valve and the MS has rarely been evaluated. Postprocedural contrast-enhanced cardiac computed tomography (CCT) offers a unique opportunity to precisely define this relationship and its impact on clinical outcomes. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that the actual transcatheter valve position relative to the MS, as accurately assessed by postprocedural CCT, is directly associated with the incidence of new conduction disturbances requiring PPI. Methods: This single-center retrospective observational study included 159 consecutive patients (mean age 84 ± 5 years; 62.9% women) who underwent TAVR with self-expanding valves (120 Evolut [75.5%]; 39 Navitor [24.5%]) and had postprocedural CCT available between March 2018 and April 2025. The transcatheter valve position relative to the MS was evaluated at the commissural plane between the non-coronary and right-coronary cusps. Patients were classified into two groups: the Within-MS group (valve edge located within the MS region) and the Outside-MS group (valve edge positioned below the MS). The primary outcome was the incidence of new PPI within 1 month post-TAVR. Categorical variables were compared using the Fisher's exact test. Results: The transcatheter valve was positioned within the MS in 105 patients (66.0%) and outside the MS in 54 patients (34.0%). New-onset complete left bundle branch block immediately after TAVR occurred in 58 patients (36.5%), which decreased to 22 patients (13.8%) at 48 hours and 10 patients (6.3%) at 1 month, with no significant differences between the Within-MS and Outside-MS groups at any time point. However, the requirement for new PPI within 1 month was significantly lower in the Within-MS group compared to the Outside-MS group (3.8% [4/105] vs. 13.0% [7/54]; P=0.046). Notably, in the Outside-MS group, 50% (5 of 10) of patients with baseline complete right bundle branch block required PPI. Conclusion: This study provides direct anatomical evidence using postprocedural CCT that actual transcatheter valve deployment beyond the MS is significantly associated with a higher incidence of new PPI. These anatomical findings validate the critical importance of preprocedural MS length assessment and individualized implantation depth planning to minimize conduction complications in TAVR.
title: Abstract 7923: Impact of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Position Relative to the Membranous Septum on Conduction Disturbances: A Postprocedural Computed Tomography Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Clot-in-transit (CIT) is a transient phenomenon of thrombus in the right heart. CIT in the setting of a patent foramen ovale (PFO) is rare and associated with increased mortality. Patient Information: A 60-year-old male presented after a ground-level fall in the setting of new onset chest pain and shortness of breath. He had a medical history notable for traumatic brain injury complicated by physical disability and seizures. He resided in an assisted living facility. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Upon arrival, HR was 115 beats/minute, BP was 152/124 mmHg, RR was 25 breaths/minute, and SpO2 was 88% on room air. Physical examination revealed coarse breath sounds and trace edema in the bilateral lower extremities. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: The differential diagnosis included ACS, PE, heart failure, and pneumonia. Initial EKG showed sinus tachycardia with right axis deviation. Given high suspicion for PE, CT of the pulmonary arteries was obtained and revealed bilateral PE, an RV/LV ratio of 1.1cm, and a filling defect in the right atrium (RA). A subsequent contrast-enhanced CT also revealed a left common femoral DVT. Initial transthoracic echocardiography did not identify a PFO, but transesophageal echocardiography revealed an ill-defined, at least 6cm, echogenic mass in the RA traversing a tunnel-type PFO into the left atrium with mobile components crossing the mitral valve. Therapeutic Interventions: An urgent multi-disciplinary meeting was held to guide management. He was deemed a poor surgical candidate due to his functional status, and thus catheter-based thrombectomy was attempted. Prior to thrombectomy, a cerebral protection device was placed. Under TEE guidance, an Inari FlowTriever T24 device was used to aspirate clot from the RA and across the PFO. Aspiration thrombectomy was then performed in the bilateral pulmonary arteries. Given the left lower extremity DVT, PFO closure was performed with an Amplatzer Cribriform Occluder device. The cerebral protection device was removed and no clot was noted. Intra-operatively, continuous epinephrine and milrinone were initiated for hemodynamic support. He returned to the cardiac intensive care unit intubated and a continuous heparin infusion was started. Follow-up & Outcomes: By post-operative day one, he was weaned off of milrinone and epinephrine. Repeat echocardiography showed improvement in RV size and function. By post-operative day two, he was extubated, noted to be at his baseline mental status, and transitioned from continuous heparin to oral apixaban and clopidogrel. He was discharged on post-operative day seven with planned follow-up in cardiology clinic. Discussion & Synthesis: Management of CIT traversing a PFO lacks consensus. This case highlights the importance of team-based decision-making and demonstrates catheter-based therapy as a feasible alternative to surgery or systemic thrombolysis.
title: Abstract 7933: Pulmonary Embolism with Bi-Atrial Thrombus Straddling Across a Patent Foramen Ovale: A Percutaneous Management Case Report

abstract: Background: Optimal lipid management after femoropopliteal endovascular therapy (EVT) is a key component of secondary prevention in lower extremity peripheral artery disease. Although statin therapy has been associated with improved patency, it remains unclear whether baseline LDL-C or achieved LDL-C during follow-up is more relevant to lesion-related outcomes. We investigated the association between achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL at 1 year and late target lesion revascularization (TLR) after femoropopliteal EVT. Methods: This multicenter retrospective study used data from the Clinical Outcomes of Multi-center Monitoring and Analysis of Endovascular Therapy for Femoropopliteal Arterial Disease: A Retrospective Study (COMMAND study) and included 2,543 patients undergoing femoropopliteal EVT. To account for potential immortal time bias, a 1-year landmark analysis was performed among patients who were alive, free from TLR at 1 year, and had LDL-C measurements at both baseline and 1 year. The primary endpoint was TLR beyond 1 year. Patients were stratified by achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL at 1 year. Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards modeling were performed. The multivariable model adjusted for TASC II classification, chronic total occlusion, severe calcification (PACSS >3.4), Rutherford category 4-6, age, hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus, prior EVT, and baseline LDL-C <70 mg/dL. Results: Among 1,159 patients in the landmark cohort, 493 achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL at 1 year and 666 did not. Late TLR occurred in 85 patients with LDL-C <70 mg/dL and 163 with LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL. Patients with achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL had a significantly lower risk of late TLR (log-rank p=0.0065). In multivariable analysis, achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL was independently associated with lower late TLR (adjusted HR 0.64; 95% CI 0.47-0.86; p=0.003), whereas baseline LDL-C <70 mg/dL was not significantly associated with late TLR. Conclusions: Among patients undergoing femoropopliteal EVT who survived and remained free from TLR for 1 year, achieved LDL-C <70 mg/dL at 1 year was independently associated with lower late TLR. These findings highlight the importance of postprocedural LDL-C target attainment and suggest that longitudinal lipid optimization may be more relevant to long-term lesion-related outcomes than baseline LDL-C status.
title: Abstract 7937: One-Year Achieved Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol and Late Target Lesion Revascularization After Femoropopliteal Endovascular Therapy

abstract: Background: The optimal role of Factor XI inhibitors in reducing thromboembolic risk while minimizing bleeding complications in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) remains unclear. Objectives: The study aims to compare clinical outcomes of AF patients treated with Factor XI inhibitors versus Factor X inhibitors based on published data. Methods: We identified relevant studies by performing a systematic search in the MEDLINE and Cochrane Central databases. Studies reporting primary outcomes (stroke or systemic embolism and major bleeding [ISTH-defined]) and secondary outcomes (all-cause mortality, ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, major or CRNMB bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, fatal bleeding, minor bleeding, and BARC classification) were included, while case reports were excluded. Risk ratios (RR) between factor XI inhibitors and factor X inhibitors were estimated for dichotomous outcomes using the Mantel-Haenszel method in a random-effects model. Results: The analysis included 3 studies comprising 16,852 AF patients. Factor XI/XIa inhibitors were associated with a higher risk of stroke or systemic embolism (RR: 2.28; p=0.02) and ischemic stroke (RR: 3.14; p < 0.00001) compared with Factor Xa inhibitors. However, Factor XIa inhibitors were associated with a lower risk of major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding (RR: 0.41; p < 0.00001) and minor bleeding (RR: 0.58; p < 0.00001). There were no significant differences in all-cause mortality (RR: 0.82; p = 0.11), cardiovascular mortality (RR: 1.04; p = 0.83), or intracranial hemorrhage (RR: 0.42; p = 0.13). Conclusions: Pooled results suggest that Factor XI/XIa inhibitors may not reduce mortality among patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation compared with Factor Xa inhibitors. While they are associated with a lower risk of major and minor bleeding, this benefit appears to come at the expense of an increased risk of stroke and other thromboembolic events. Further prospective studies and randomized trials are needed to validate these findings.
title: Abstract 7939: Efficacy and Safety of Factor XI Inhibitors versus Factor X Inhibitors Among Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Meta Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Optimal anticoagulation following mitral valve repair or replacement remains a clinical challenge. While Vitamin K Antagonists (VKAs) are the traditional standard, Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) have emerged as a potential alternative. However, their comparative safety and efficacy, particularly regarding time-dependent outcomes after surgery, require further clarification. Research Question/Hypothesis: This systematic review and meta-analysis sought to compare the safety and efficacy of DOACs versus VKAs in patients undergoing mitral valve interventions, including both mechanical and bioprosthetic valves, using a time-stratified approach to assess early (≤30 days) and late (≥1 year) outcomes. Methods: Registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261292947) and following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane, and EMBASE databases through January 2025. Nine randomized and observational studies were identified. Data extraction was conducted rigorously, and a random-effects model was used for meta-analysis. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Results: A total of 9 studies comprising 16,917 patients were included. DOACs were associated with a significantly lower risk of major bleeding (RR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.54-0.89; p=0.02; I 2 =0.0%). In time-stratified analyses, early major bleeding (≤30 days) showed no significant difference (p=0.09), whereas late major bleeding (≥1 year) was significantly lower with DOACs (RR: 0.70; p=0.02). All-cause mortality was significantly lower in the DOAC group (RR: 0.74; 95% CI: 0.56-0.97; p=0.03; I 2 =34.5%). No significant difference was observed in stroke risk (RR: 0.79; p=0.50) or thromboembolic events. Any bleeding and non-major bleeding favored DOACs but did not reach statistical significance. GRADE certainty ranged from very low to moderate, with moderate evidence supporting reductions in major bleeding and mortality. Conclusion: DOACs demonstrate superior safety and survival profiles compared with VKAs following mitral valve interventions. These benefits appear time-dependent, characterized by early reductions in overall bleeding and sustained long-term reductions in major bleeding, without increasing stroke risk. These findings support DOACs as a viable alternative to VKAs in this population. Further randomized research is warranted to confirm these findings and optimize clinical management.
title: Abstract 7941: Direct Oral Anticoagulants versus Vitamin K Antagonists After Transcatheter or Surgical Mitral Valve Intervention: A Systematic Review and Time-Stratified Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Left ventricular systolic function emerges from the integration of cardiomyocyte contraction at the microscale into global pump function at the macroscale. How myocardial units mechanically interact at the intermediate mesoscale to shape global function remains unresolved. Hypothesis: Mechanical interactions between adjacent millimeter-sized myocardial units are intrinsic to left ventricular performance, constituting a myocardial "tug-of-war" that pervades the healthy heart and impairs contraction in the diseased heart after myocardial infarction (MI). Methods: Motion-encoded cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (tissue phase mapping) was performed in 20 healthy individuals and 20 patients with prior ST-elevation MI (Fig. 1a). Circumferential strain was resolved in ~427 transmural units per heart (~2.6 mm width) (Fig. 1b). An analytical framework was developed to classify contraction patterns as simple shortening or tug-of-war (containing transient elongation phases) (Fig. 1c,d). Finite element computational models of left ventricular mechanics were employed to interrogate underlying mechanisms. Results: Tug-of-war was present in 45±11% of myocardial units in healthy hearts and was significantly more prevalent following MI (58±9%; P<0.001) (Fig. 1e). In the infarcted heart, elevated tug-of-war persisted in non-infarcted viable remote myocardium (52±10%; P=0.02) (Fig. 1f) and scaled with infarct size (r=0.75; P<0.001) (Fig. 1g) and NT-proBNP (r=0.52; P=0.02) (Fig. 1h). At the regional level, tug-of-war correlated with regional contraction in both healthy hearts (r=0.97; P<0.001) and following MI (r=0.78; P=0.002) (Fig. 2a,b). At the global level, tug-of-war correlated with reduced ejection fraction (r=–0.65; P<0.001) (Fig. 2c), impaired global strain (r=0.71; P<0.001) (Fig. 2d), and prolonged isovolumetric contraction and relaxation phases (r=0.79 and r=0.51; both P<0.001) (Fig. 2e,f). Notably, tug-of-war was attenuated at coarser resolutions, rendering it macroscopically invisible in most myocardial segments (Fig. 2g,h). Computational modeling identified the heart's fiber structure and electrophysiological propagation as sufficient drivers of tug-of-war, with simulated tissue heterogeneity, as can be induced by pathological remodeling, markedly amplifying its severity (Fig. 3). Conclusions: Myocardial tug-of-war is a mesoscale determinant of left ventricular efficiency and performance that is invisible to conventional macroscale imaging and worsens following MI. These findings support a new conceptual framework for understanding left ventricular failure, with potential implications for diagnostics.
title: Abstract 7944: Myocardial Tug-of-War as a Mesoscale Determinant of Left Ventricular Performance

abstract: Introduction: Acute myocarditis is an inflammatory cardiac disease that may deteriorate into fulminant presentation and lead to early mortality. Although immune cell infiltration is a hallmark of myocarditis, the detailed architecture and clinical relevance of spatial immune organization within the injured myocardium remain incompletely defined. Aims: We sought to define the spatial immune microenvironment in acute lymphocytic myocarditis and determine its clinical impact. Methods: We enrolled 28 patients with biopsy-proven acute lymphocytic myocarditis diagnosed by endomyocardial biopsy. Multiplexed proteomic imaging mass cytometry (IMC) was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded myocardial biopsy sections using a 23-antibody panel ( Figure 1 ). We developed single-cell segmentation and phenotyping using an AI-assisted image analysis pipeline. Clinical information and 90-day mortality were assessed. Results: Among the 28 patients (age 50.4±19.3 years; 18 men), 15 presented with fulminant myocarditis requiring mechanical circulatory support. IMC revealed that the abundance of conventional immune-cell populations or lineage-level immune-cell composition did not significantly differ according to fulminant presentation ( Figure 2A and 2B ), and neither measure was associated with peak serum troponin I, creatine kinase, or left ventricular ejection fraction. In contrast, GranzymeB + Ki-67 + NK cell counts showed a positive correlation with peak serum troponin I levels (Spearman ρ=0.49; P=0.009), suggesting a link between proliferative cytotoxic immune activation and myocardial injury. Then, we generated a total of 10211 neighborhood features from patient-level neighborhood matrices. Clustering of the most variable spatial neighborhood features identified three spatial immune-pattern classes and partial enrichment of fulminant cases in one cluster ( Figure 2C) . We further constructed a count-distance integrated spatial high-risk module reflecting spatial coupling among injured cardiomyocytes, macrophage/APC-lineage cells, CD4/cytotoxic T cells, and CitH3-positive extracellular trap-like inflammatory structures. A higher injury-centered module score was associated with significantly worse 90-day survival ( Figure 3 ). Conclusion: IMC-based spatial immune profiling identified injury-centered immune neighborhoods associated with early mortality in acute lymphocytic myocarditis, beyond immune-cell abundance alone.
title: Abstract 7964: Spatial Immune Neighborhood Signatures Identify High-Risk Injury-Centered Niches in Human Acute Lymphocytic Myocarditis

abstract: Introduction: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) is increasingly utilized during high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), while heart failure (HF) remains a common comorbidity. National data characterizing age-modified contributions of MCS use and HF to in-hospital PCI outcomes are limited in the contemporary era. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that MCS utilization and HF each increase with age and are independently associated with worse in-hospital outcomes, and that HF's prognostic effect is modified by selection bias. Methods: Using discharge-level weighted National Inpatient Sample data (2021-2023), patients undergoing PCI were stratified by age (<65, 65-79, ≥80). MCS modalities such as Impella, intraaortic balloon pump (IABP), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and HF comorbidity were identified using ICD-10 codes. Primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and major bleeding; secondary outcomes were length of stay (LOS) and total charges. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, presentation type, insurance, and hospital characteristics with a significance level of p<0.001. Cochrane-Armitage trend testing was used to assess MCS utilization and HF prevalence across age strata. Results: The analytic sample included 445,050 PCI hospitalizations; 43.3% had HF, 3.6% Impella, 3.1% IABP, and 0.3% ECMO. Mortality was 2.1% (<65), 3.7% (65-79), and 5.6% (≥80; all with p<0.001). Each MCS modality was independently associated with mortality: Impella (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.43, 95% CI 3.15-3.73), IABP (aOR 2.40, 95% CI 2.19-2.63), and ECMO (aOR 2.34, 95% CI 1.81-3.03; all p<0.001). HF paradoxically reduced adjusted mortality (aOR 0.84, 95% CI 0.79-0.90, p<0.001), consistent with survivor bias. Major bleeding occurred in 3.8% overall; HF independently increased bleeding risk (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 1.19-1.31, p<0.001). MCS and HF rose with age: Impella 2.5% to 5.3%, IABP 2.8% to 3.7%, ECMO 0.4% to 0.1%, HF 36.9% to 55.0% (all p<0.001). HF independently prolonged LOS (+1.34 days), as did ECMO (+5.20 days) and IABP (+1.41 days; all p<0.001). Age ≥80 was associated with +$2.30M and 65-79 with +$1.08M higher total charges vs. <65 (both p<0.001); IABP added +$2.48M (p=0.006). Conclusions: MCS escalates with age and is independently associated with higher mortality, Impella conferring the greatest risk, and prolonged LOS. HF paradoxically reduces adjusted mortality due to survivor bias while increasing major bleeding and LOS. Advanced age drives markedly higher charges. These findings highlight the complexity of PCI risk stratification and the resource burden in high-acuity PCI.
title: Abstract 7971: Mechanical Circulatory Support Utilization and Heart Failure Morbidity in PCI Hospitalizations: Age-Stratified Analysis from the National Inpatient Sample 2021-2023

abstract: Background: Environmental stressors, as air pollution or temperature changes, can trigger acute coronary syndromes, yet their influence on plaque progression and plaque characteristics remains incompletely documented in humans. We investigated the association between multiple environmental exposures and progression of coronary atherosclerosis on serial CCTA. Hypothesis: Adverse environmental exposures are associated with accelerated plaque progression, particularly towards high-risk plaque phenotypes. Methods: We included consecutive patients undergoing serial CCTA for chronic chest pain evaluation at University Hospital Brussels, Belgium, between 2016 and 2025, with ≥1 year between scans. Coronary plaque burden was quantified using the AI-Enabled Coronary Plaque Analysis (AI-CPA, Heartflow Inc.), including total plaque, vessel-specific plaque (left main [LM], left anterior descending [LAD], left circumflex [LCX], and right coronary artery [RCA]), and plaque composition (calcified plaque [CP], non-calcified plaque [NCP], and low-attenuation plaque [LAP]). Residential environmental exposures, including air pollution (PM2.5, PM10, NO 2 ), temperature, green space, road proximity, airport proximity, and neighborhood income and educational level, were estimated at residential addresses using high-resolution interpolation models. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for cardiovascular risk and socioeconomic factors were used to evaluate associations with plaque progression risk. Results: A total of 574 patients were included (60 [IQR 52-67] years; 53% male). Over a median follow-up of 3.6 (2.3-5.1) years, median plaque burden increased from 89 (19-234) mm 3 to 116 (27-312) mm 3 , and plaque progression occurred in 362 patients (63%). Median residential exposure to PM2.5 and NO 2 was 10.7 (9.9-11.7) μg/m 3 and 15.9 (13.0-19.0) μg/m 3 . Higher PM2.5 and PM10 exposure were associated with overall plaque progression (PM2.5: HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.06-1.49 per IQR increase, p=0.008). No other stressors were associated. In vessel-specific analyses, PM2.5 and PM10 were consistently associated with plaque progression in all vessels. NO 2 exposure was associated with LM plaque progression (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.13-1.77, p=0.002). For plaque composition, PM2.5 and PM10 were associated with CP, NCP and LAP progression. The strongest associations were observed for LAP progression (PM2.5: HR 4.23, 95% CI 1.69-10.6, p=0.002). NO 2 was not associated with CP or NCP progression but demonstrated a strong association with LAP progression (HR 10.6, 95% CI 3.2-35.5; p<0.001). Conclusions: In this longitudinal CCTA cohort using AI-CPA, residential air pollution exposure was associated with coronary plaque progression risk, particularly pronounced for left main coronary and low-attenuation plaque, a high-risk phenotype linked to future acute coronary syndromes.
title: Abstract 7977: Associations of Environmental Stressors with Coronary Plaque Progression on CCTA: Results from Serial AI-Enabled Coronary Plaque Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Takayasu arteritis (TA) is a rare large-vessel vasculitis that can present with nonspecific symptoms. In this case we describe a previously healthy Caucasian adolescent girl whose first recognized manifestation of TA was acute ischemic stroke from extensive aortic arch and cervicocerebral involvement, with imaging initially concerning for type A aortic dissection. This atypical presentation contrasts with the classic profile of a young woman of Asian ancestry. Patient Information: A previously healthy 16-year-old Caucasian girl with a recent diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia (IDA) on iron supplementation. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Symptoms started with several months of fatigue, headaches and presyncope. Initially, she was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. She presented acutely to the emergency room after awakening with right facial droop, right-sided weakness, aphasia, and visual deficits. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Given patient’s neurologic presentation Brain imaging was ordered that showed acute left MCA territory infarction. CTA demonstrated bilateral common carotid occlusion, distal left ICA /left MCA occlusion, right subclavian and proximal right vertebral occlusion, and aortic arch wall thickening, raising concern for type A aortic dissection. Therapeutic Intervention: Initially, she was taken emergently to surgery for aortic dissection. However, Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) imaging showed marked inflammatory aortic wall thickening without dissection, supporting chronic inflammatory aortitis. Patient underwent mechanical thrombectomy of carotid artery. Patient was treated with pulse steroids followed by prednisone taper, methotrexate, then infliximab. Patient was also treated with anticoagulation with long term aspirin therapy. The diagnosis was supported by systemic inflammation, iron deficiency anemia, positive ANA and the vascular distribution involving carotid, subclavian, celiac, superior mesenteric, renal, and iliac arteries on MRI. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: At 6-month follow-up, she had returned to school with about 90% neurologic recovery and with very mild residual right-hand weakness. Repeat MRA showed chronic occlusion/slow flow of bilateral common carotids, innominate artery, and proximal right subclavian artery with residual but improved vessel-wall inflammation. Discussion & Synthesis: This case is a unique presentation of TA due to initial imaging pointing towards aortic dissection. This case highlights the importance of having high index of suspicion for Takayasu arteritis in young patients with unexplained stroke and antecedent constitutional symptoms.
title: Abstract 7993: Takayasu Arteritis Mimicking Acute Aortic Dissection in an Adolescent Presenting with Ischemic Stroke

abstract: Introduction: (Context & Rationale) Coronary artery fistulas (CAFs) are rare coronary anomalies characterized by abnormal communications between coronary arteries and cardiac chambers or venous structures that bypass the myocardial capillary bed. Bilateral fistulas with coronary sinus drainage constitute an uncommon and anatomically complex subgroup for which objective frameworks defining physiological significance and guiding management remain limited.Patient InformationA 66-year-old man with no known congenital or acquired heart disease was referred for evaluation of a systolic murmur, exertional chest pressure, dyspnea, and episodic palpitations. Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Physical examination revealed a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border without a continuous component. Initial transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved ventricular function, biatrial dilation, a dilated right coronary artery, and Doppler findings concerning for an interatrial shunt. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Multimodality imaging identified a complex bilateral CAF consisting of a dominant, diffusely ectatic right coronary artery with distal left circumflex contribution draining into the coronary sinus. Four-dimensional flow cardiac magnetic resonance imaging excluded an atrial septal defect and demonstrated a mild left-to-right shunt (Qp/Qs 1.37). Coronary computed tomography angiography defined the bilateral arterial anatomy and common drainage pathway. Positron emission tomography demonstrated preserved global coronary flow reserve (2.62) without inducible ischemia. Exercise testing showed preserved functional capacity (10.7 METs) without ischemic changes, while ambulatory patch monitoring revealed no clinically significant arrhythmias.Therapeutic Intervention(s)The case was reviewed in a multidisciplinary adult congenital and structural heart disease setting. Given the absence of objective physiological compromise despite complex anatomy, conservative management with metoprolol therapy and longitudinal surveillance was recommended. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: At 1-month follow-up, the patient reported improvement in exertional chest pressure, dyspnea, and palpitations. No adverse events occurred. Discussion & Synthesis: This case highlights a diagnostic pitfall: fistulous drainage may mimic interatrial shunting on echocardiography. Despite high-risk anatomy, integrated assessment across shunt burden, myocardial perfusion, functional capacity, and arrhythmic risk demonstrated limited hemodynamic and ischemic significance. Concordant physiological findings supported a conservative management strategy and avoided the potential procedural risks associated with intervention in the setting of marked coronary ectasia.
title: Abstract 7994: Bilateral Coronary Artery Fistula with Coronary Sinus Drainage: Anatomy-Physiology Discordance Guiding Conservative Management

abstract: Introduction: Post stem-cell transplant cardiovascular complications are difficult to manage given hematologic derangements and the overall engraftment process. Patient Information: A 65-year-old male with acute myeloid leukemia presented for an allogeneic stem-cell transplant. Prior TTEs demonstrated a LVEF in the mid-50%s with severe left atrial dilation. His hospital course prior to the transplant was notable for paroxysmal AFib with intermittent RVR, which improved with metoprolol. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Roughly two weeks after his stem-cell infusion, he developed respiratory failure, altered mental status, weight gain, fever, and more frequent AFib with RVR. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Imaging showed pulmonary edema and pleural effusions with focal coronary calcification near the left main coronary artery origin. TTE showed a newly decreased LVEF to 34% with interval development of apical, anterior, and anterolateral hypokinesis. Laboratory values were significant for severe pancytopenia (though white blood cells and platelets were no longer undetectable), newly elevated transaminases, a marked decrease in renal function, and a stable high-sensitivity troponin of around 40 ng/dL. Severe thrombocytopenia, impaired renal function, encephalopathy, and general clinical instability precluded a thorough cardiomyopathy and ischemic work-up with subsequent treatment, including invasive coronary angiography or CCTA, cardiac MRI, and anti-platelet therapy. Rhythm control was deferred given the inability to clear the left-atrial appendage with TEE. The patient met criteria for engraftment syndrome. Therapeutic Interventions: Engraftment syndrome criteria was met and steroids were started. He underwent diuresis with significant urine output. Intravenous rate control was pursued given mucositis limiting oral access. Follow-up, Outcomes, and Adverse Events: The patient’s work of breathing, arrhythmia burden, renal and hepatic function, and mental status recovered over days. Subsequent TTE showed a LVEF of 51% with similar wall motion abnormalities. On discharge, the patient underwent myocardial perfusion PET which showed no perfusion defects, though with globally decreased coronary flow reserves. Discussion and Synthesis: The differential for cardiomyopathy was broad, including engraftment syndrome with major cytokine release following neutrophil recovery, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, stress cardiomyopathy precipitated by engraftment syndrome and chemotherapy, and coronary ischemia given the echocardiographic findings and calcification distribution. Work-up was limited by the patient’s condition; treatment focused on congestive heart failure, atrial tachyarrhythmias, and engraftment syndrome. Managing the sequelae of cardiomyopathy despite the unknowable etiology was essential.
title: Abstract 7998: A Complex Case of New-Onset Cardiomyopathy Following an Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplant Complicated by Engraftment Syndrome: Diagnostic Challenges in the Setting of Multiple Potential Etiologies

abstract: Background: In chronic aortic regurgitation (AR), increased preload and afterload confound measures of systolic function. Because of increased preload and total stroke volume, standard ejection fraction (LVEF) may be preserved despite reduced net systemic output. Effective LVEF (eLVEF), defined as net forward stroke volume/end-diastolic volume, integrates AR severity, LV output, and remodeling into a single hemodynamic metric. Methods: We evaluated patients with moderate or severe chronic AR on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), excluding concomitant valvular disease, prior valve intervention, or cardiomyopathy/shunts. eLVEF was calculated as ([LV stroke volume - AR volume]/LVEDV) x 100; MR volume subtracted in mild coexisting MR. Using guideline-defined LVEF (55%) and the cohort median eLVEF (33%), patients were categorized as Concordant Preserved (LVEF ≥55%, eLVEF >33%), Discordant (LVEF ≥55%, eLVEF ≤33%), or Reduced LVEF (LVEF <55%). The primary outcome was death or heart failure hospitalization under medical management, censored at aortic valve replacement (AVR). Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed. Results: Among 598 patients (median age 69 [IQR 58-78], 79.6% male, 29.8% bicuspid), 275 (46%) were Concordant Preserved, 109 (18.2%) Discordant, and 214 (35.8%) Reduced LVEF. Standard LVEF (median 58%) and eLVEF (median 33%) showed wide dispersion (Figure 1). Median eLVEF was lower in patients with events (28.9% vs 34.7%, p<0.001), with greater separation than LVEF (55.0% vs 59.1%, p<0.001). Each 1% decrease in eLVEF independently conferred higher hazard (HR 1.027, p=0.029). Compared to Concordant Preserved, Discordant patients had higher AR fraction (47% vs 34%), LVESVi (48.9 vs 37.7 mL/m 2 ), AVR rates (60% vs 36%), lower forward stroke volume (69 vs 87 mL) and cardiac output (4.6 vs 5.7 L/min), all p<0.001. The Discordant group had threefold higher risk versus Concordant Preserved (HR 3.00, 95% CI 1.92-4.68, p<0.001), approaching the risk seen in Reduced LVEF (HR 3.40, 95% CI 2.35-4.91, p<0.001) (Figure 2), and remained independently associated with adverse outcomes after adjustment for age, sex, EuroSCORE II, NYHA class, late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and LV end-systolic volume index (HR 2.55, 95% CI 1.62-4.02, p<0.001). Findings were consistent using the regression derived eLVEF threshold of 32% (predicted eLVEF at LVEF=55%, R 2 =0.65). Conclusion: Effective LVEF on CMR integrates AR severity, LV remodeling, and net forward output into a single hemodynamic metric, identifying a higher-risk phenotype not captured by standard LVEF assessment. Among patients with preserved LVEF ≥55%, approximately one in four patients have reduced eLVEF and exhibit adjusted risk approaching patients with reduced LVEF. eLVEF may provide incremental prognostic value in chronic AR.
title: Abstract 8011: Effective LV Ejection Fraction by Cardiac MRI: A Hemodynamic Efficiency Metric for Risk Stratification in Chronic Aortic Regurgitation

abstract: Introduction: Despite advances in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), the relative impact of hospital factors, metabolic status, and socioeconomic determinants on contemporary in-hospital outcomes remains unclear. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that hospital teaching status, bed size, weekend admission, obesity, and socioeconomic disadvantage independently influence in-hospital mortality and major bleeding following PCI. Methods: We analyzed weighted National Inpatient Sample data (2021-2023) for PCI hospitalizations (n=445,050). Exposures included hospital teaching status, bed size, admission timing, obesity, sex, insurance type, and median household income quartile. Primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and major bleeding; secondary outcomes were length of stay (LOS) and total charges. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic and linear regression models adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics (p<0.001). Results: Urban teaching hospitals performed 77.7% of PCIs, and 24.1% of admissions occurred on weekends. Hospital teaching status was not independently associated with mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.00; p=0.974), and the apparent mortality advantage of small hospitals was attenuated. The weekend mortality signal was eliminated after adjustment (aOR 0.99; p=0.704). Obesity (24.8%) was independently associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.69; p<0.001). Compared with Medicaid beneficiaries, self-pay patients had higher mortality (aOR 1.46; p<0.001), whereas privately insured patients had lower mortality (aOR 0.79; p<0.001). Residence in the highest-income quartile was associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.75; p<0.001). For major bleeding, teaching status and weekend admission were not independently associated with risk, whereas obesity was associated with lower odds of bleeding (aOR 0.88; p<0.001). Higher income independently predicted shorter LOS (β –0.27 days; p<0.001). Self-pay patients also had shorter LOS than Medicaid beneficiaries but incurred higher charges (+$3.28M; p=0.025). Conclusion: Hospital structural characteristics and weekend admission were not independent predictors of adverse in-hospital outcomes after risk adjustment. In contrast, obesity was associated with lower mortality and major bleeding, while socioeconomic disadvantage, particularly self-pay status and lower income, remained associated with worse outcomes. These findings suggest that metabolic phenotype and socioeconomic factors exert greater influence on contemporary PCI outcomes than hospital structural characteristics.
title: Abstract 8029: Structural, Temporal, Metabolic, and Socioeconomic Determinants of In-Hospital Outcomes Following Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A National Inpatient Sample Analysis (2021-2023)

abstract: Background: Social determinants of health, particularly unhoused individuals and housing instability, may significantly influence access to medical care, medication adherence, follow-up, and management among patients with heart failure. Individuals experiencing homelessness often have a higher burden of comorbidities, limited healthcare access, and increased barriers to continuity of care, which could lead to adverse hospital outcomes. In this study we explored the impact of homelessness on adverse outcomes among heart failure hospitalizations. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that adverse hospital outcomes will be higher among heart hospitalizations with homelessness. Methods: This study is a retrospective analysis of National Inpatient Sample data, 2019-2022. Hospitalizations ≥41 years of age admitted with heart failure diagnosis were included in the analysis. The outcomes of the study were in-hospital mortality, prolonged length of stay, mechanical ventilation, mechanical circulatory support, and vasopressors use. Propensity score matched logistic regression analysis were used to compare the outcomes between hospitalizations with and without homelessness. Results: A total of 4,705,274 primary heart failure hospitalizations were included in the analysis. Of these, 42,090 (0.9%) reported homelessness. In-hospital mortality (P<0.001), mechanical ventilator use (P=0.001), mechanical circulatory support (P<0.001), and vasopressors use (P=0.004) were significantly lower among hospitalizations reporting homelessness, while prolonged length of stay did not differ between the groups. Regression analysis showed that hospitalizations with homelessness had significantly lower odds for in-hospital mortality (aOR, 0.48, 95% CI: 0.37-0.63, P<0.001), mechanical ventilator use (aOR, 0.55, 95% CI: 0.46-0.65, P<0.001), mechanical circulatory support (aOR, 0.31, 95% CI: 0.18-0.53, P<0.001), and vasopressors use (aOR, 0.51, 95% CI: 0.37-0.70, P<0.001). Though univariate analysis did not show significant association, prolonged length of stay was significantly associated with homelessness in the regression analysis (aOR, 1.20, 95% CI: 1.14-1.26, P<0.001). Conclusion: Our findings show a paradox where unhoused heart failure patients demonstrated lower in-hospital mortality and reduced need for advanced interventions yet experienced longer adjusted lengths of stay. This could be due to admission threshold bias where unhoused patients with lower acuity levels are admitted due to lack of safe discharge environment, rather than a true survival advantage. The prolonged length of stay in this group further supports discharge planning barriers rather than medical complexity. Robust transitional care and community-based interventions are required to address these disparities among the unhoused population.
title: Abstract 8043: The Unhoused Paradox: Lower In-Hospital Mortality but Longer Stays Among Heart Failure Hospitalizations

abstract: Introduction: Long-term antiplatelet monotherapy after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains an important strategy for secondary cardiovascular (CV) prevention following completion of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). However, American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines favor aspirin, diverging from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines, which increasingly support clopidogrel. Given the publication of three recent studies, including two extended follow-up analyses, we performed an updated meta-analysis comparing clopidogrel versus aspirin monotherapy after PCI to evaluate their comparative efficacy and safety profiles. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through May 7, 2026, for RCTs and observational studies evaluating clopidogrel versus aspirin as maintenance monotherapy after completion of DAPT following PCI. Studies were included if they reported comparative CV or bleeding outcomes in adult patients undergoing PCI treated with clopidogrel or aspirin monotherapy after a defined period of DAPT. Statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 19. For comparative analyses, pooled effect estimates were expressed as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, while pooled estimates were calculated using a random-effects model with the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) method for effect size estimation. Results: Nine studies (5 observational studies and 4 RCTs; N = 48,666; mean follow-up time of 4.3 years) were included. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, with predominantly male patients with a mean age of 65.1 years and high prevalences of acute coronary syndrome, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and prior myocardial infarction. Clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with a lower risk of major adverse CV events (MACE) (HR: 0.82 CI 0.74-0.92; p<0.001; I 2 = 39%), myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and hemorrhagic stroke compared with aspirin monotherapy. No statistical differences were observed regarding net adverse clinical events (NACE) (HR: 0.90 CI 0.82-1.00; p = 0.06; I 2 = 47%), BARC type 3 or 5 bleeding (HR: 0.92 CI 0.73-1.15; p = 0.46; I 2 = 46%), all-cause mortality, CV mortality, non-CV mortality, definite or likely stent thrombosis, ischemic stroke, target-lesion revascularization, non-target-lesion revascularization, BARC 2, 3, or 5 bleeding, TIMI major bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding, and intracranial bleeding. Conclusion: Our findings suggest that clopidogrel monotherapy after PCI following completion of DAPT may be more effective than aspirin in reducing CV risk while demonstrating a comparable safety profile regarding major bleeding risk.
title: Abstract 8044: Clopidogrel versus Aspirin for Maintenance Monotherapy After Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: An Updated Meta-Analysis with 10-Year Follow-Up Data

abstract: Introduction: Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair (MTEER) is an effective treatment for mitral regurgitation (MR). Multiple studies have demonstrated significant ethnic disparities in outcomes for patients undergoing transcatheter interventions. We seek to characterize ethnic disparities in heart-failure hospitalizations (HFH) in our single-center MTEER patient cohort. Methods: Patients with complete HFH outcome data were included in this study. Multivariable Cox proportional hazard analyses were conducted for overall time to HFH by ethnicity (white, black, Hispanic, or other) and for risk of HFH in patients who were HFH-free at one year post-MTEER. Results: 339 patients were included. Median follow-up time by reverse Kaplan-Meier analysis was 777 days (95% CI 673-921 days). 39.5% of included patients had primary MR, while 54% had functional MR and 6.5% had mixed MR pathology. The type of MR varied significantly by ethnicity (p=0.0045), with greater proportions of Black, Hispanic, and Other races experiencing functional MR as compared to White patients. 30.2% of white patients (n=189) experienced HFH, while 39.1% of black patients (n=46), 48.8% of Hispanic patients (n=43), and 39.3% of other ethnic groups (n=61) experienced HFH (p=0.095). Overall HFH-free survival probability differed by ethnic group (p=0.03). Multivariable Cox analysis revealed a significantly higher risk of HFH for Hispanics as compared to White patients (HR 1.9, 95% CI 1.11-3.24, p = 0.019). Additionally, functional MR, as compared to primary, conferred a significantly increased risk of HFH (HR 1.69, 95% CI 1.08-2.63, p=0.02). Secondary analysis of 194 patients who survived HFH-free for one year (118 white, 23 black, 23 Hispanic, and 30 patients of other ethnicities) revealed Hispanic ethnicity to be an independent predictor of HFH one year after MTEER (HR 3.94, 95% CI 1.58-9.8, p = 0.003). Discussion: We demonstrate increased risk of HFH for Hispanic patients undergoing MTEER at our center, corroborating ethnic disparities identified for transcatheter procedural outcomes in the literature. Importantly, we also show that a large proportion of HFH burden in the Hispanic population may occur one year post-MTEER, suggesting early post-procedural complications alone may not account for disparities in outcomes in our patient cohort. Further studies should explore patient education, language barriers, and access to long-term care to address disparate long-term complications.

title: Abstract 8046: Ethnic Disparities in Heart Failure Hospitalization Following Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair: A Single-Center, Retrospective Study

abstract: Introduction: Left ventricular (LV) dysfunction during chemotherapy is frequently attributed to anthracycline cardiotoxicity, potentially overlooking reversible alternative etiologies. We present a pediatric case in which multimodality imaging was essential in identifying an alternate diagnosis as the true cause of acute heart failure during leukemia treatment. Patient Information, Clinical Findings & Timeline: A previously healthy 5 year old boy with newly diagnosed acute biphenotypic leukemia was referred for cardiac evaluation prior to bone marrow transplant. His chemotherapy regimen included cumulative daunorubicin 150 mg/m 2 and mitoxantrone 48 mg/m 2 (doxorubicin equivalent ~317 mg/m 2 ). Baseline echocardiography showed LVEF of 70% that declined to 41% after second cycle of chemotherapy (~6 weeks). He presented with poor oral intake, emesis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and fatigue, prompting pediatric ICU admission, where LVEF had further declined to 30%. He required intravenous milrinone and initiation of guideline-directed heart failure therapy. His course was complicated by atrial ectopy requiring antiarrhythmics. BMT candidacy was held pending cardiac recovery. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: The etiology was initially thought to be anthracycline cardiotoxicity, but infectious workup was positive for rhinovirus/enterovirus. Cardiac catheterization showed normal filling pressures and cardiac index. Endomyocardial biopsy showed minimal perivascular inflammation with interstitial fibrosis. Cardiac MRI (CMR) revealed septal myocardial edema on T2-weighted imaging, patchy mid-wall and epicardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in the basal, mid anteroseptal and inferolateral segments, consistent with myocarditis - distinct from the diffuse, nonedematous myocardial injury pattern typically seen in anthracycline cardiotoxicity. These findings, with concurrent viral infection, supported acute viral myocarditis as the primary etiology. Therapeutic Interventions: Chemotherapy was modified to reduce cardiotoxic exposure. Follow-Up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: LVEF progressively normalized at follow up over 14 months, and he was successfully weaned off heart failure therapies, consistent with the reversible natural history of viral myocarditis. He was then able to receive all appropriate leukemia chemotherapy. Discussion: This case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis when LV dysfunction develops during chemotherapy, even with clinically relevant cumulative anthracycline exposure. In this case, CMR tissue characterization identified a fully reversible etiology after endomyocardial biopsy was insufficient to establish the diagnosis, underscoring the complementary role of CMR when biopsy findings are equivocal, and guiding appropriate cardio-oncologic management. Consent: Obtained.
title: Abstract 8073: Left Ventricular Dysfunction During Chemotherapy: Pediatric Viral Myocarditis Masquerading as Anthracycline Cardiotoxicity - Case Report

abstract: Background: Emerging valve-integrated and miniaturized pacing systems may enable treatment of conduction disturbances associated with transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, the electrophysiologic properties of potential pacing sites within the paravalvular aortic root have not been systematically characterized in humans. Objective: To compare ventricular capture, pacing thresholds, and ventricular activation patterns during pacing from the right coronary cusp (RCC), left coronary cusp (LCC), non-coronary cusp (NCC), and left-sided His bundle (LV His) region. Methods: Twenty-five consecutive patients undergoing clinically indicated left-sided electrophysiology procedures underwent sequential bipolar pacing from the RCC, LCC, NCC, and LV His region following completion of the index procedure. Pacing sites were localized using 3-dimensional electroanatomic mapping, fluoroscopy, and intracardiac echocardiography. Capture thresholds (1-ms pulse width), electrogram amplitudes, and paced QRS characteristics were assessed. Results: Ventricular capture was achieved in all patients from the LV His region (25/25, 100%), compared with 23/25 (92%) from the RCC and 19/25 (76%) from the LCC, while no ventricular capture was observed from the NCC. LV His pacing demonstrated significantly lower capture thresholds than coronary cusp pacing (4.6±2.1 mA vs. 13.3±5.1 mA for RCC and 14.2±4.7 mA for LCC) and produced the narrowest paced QRS duration (137.5±15.6 ms vs. approximately 165 ms for cusp pacing). An RBBB-like morphology in lead V1 was frequently observed during LV His capture. In contrast, pacing from the NCC resulted in atrial capture in 8/25 patients (32%) without ventricular capture. Conclusions: The left-sided His region represents a uniquely favorable pacing substrate within the aortic root, combining universal ventricular capture, lower pacing thresholds, and more physiologic ventricular activation than coronary cusp pacing.
