Subsequently, medical therapy was initiated with unfractionated heparin and transitioned to apixaban. Marked clinical improvement was observed during the hospital course. Follow-up, Outcomes and adverse Events: Clinical improvement was noted. Two weeks later, EF increased to 25%, and at one month, it improved to 50-55%. No intracardiac thrombus was observed. Discussion and synthesis: Viral myocarditis due to EBV is a rare but serious complication, potentially causing cardiomyopathy and biventricular failure. In this case, EBV-related myocarditis likely led to severe dysfunction and a left ventricular thrombus. EBV-associated hypercoagulability may have contributed to pulmonary embolism. The simultaneous occurrence of cardioembolic stroke and PE complicates management. Negative coronary angiography, autoimmune, hypercoagulability workup, and PET/CT excluded other causes such as ischemic disease, autoimmune myocarditis, prothrombotic disorders, and malignancy. This case underscores the importance of considering viral myocarditis, particularly EBV, in patients with cardioembolic and thromboembolic events. Timely diagnosis and investigation are crucial for optimal outcomes.
title: Abstract 8349: A Perfect Storm: Epstein-Barr Virus-Associated Venous Thromboembolism, Severe Biventricular Dysfunction Leading to Left Ventricular Thrombus, and Stroke

abstract: Background: Pulmonary embolism (PE) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has emerged as an important reperfusion strategy for intermediate-high-risk and high-risk PE; however, comparative data regarding the procedural and efficacy outcomes between the most common modalities of aspiration (large bore aspiration thrombectomy (LBAT) and computer assisted vacuum thrombectomy (CAVT)) remain limited. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a large academic medical center including patients with intermediate-high-risk or high-risk acute PE treated with MT using either the Inari FlowTriever© (LBAT) or Penumbra Lightning© (CAVT) systems from January 1, 2018, through August 1, 2025. Device selection was at the discretion of the treatment team. Primary efficacy endpoints included reduction in right ventricular-to-left ventricular (RV/LV) ratio assessed by transthoracic echocardiography and reduction in mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP). Secondary outcomes included procedural parameters, length of stay, and readmission rates. Categorical variables were compared using chi-squared analysis, and odds ratios were calculated for binary outcomes. Results: A total of 229 patients were included (57.28±17.14 years; 50.66% female; high-risk PE 21.83%, intermediate-high-risk PE 78.17%). MT was performed using LBAT in 170 (74.24%) patients and CAVT in 59 (25.76%) of patients. There were no significant differences in demographic or co-morbid risk factors between groups. Comparable improvements in RV/LV ratio (21.60%±19.07% vs 26.17%±17.85%, p=0.78) and mPAP (23.35%±19.63% vs 20.36%±18.15%, p=0.74) were observed between the LBAT and CAVT cohorts, respectively. Radiation exposure, fluoroscopy time, and procedure time were similar between both groups as well. Furthermore, this study found no difference in intensive care or hospital length of stay between either cohort (4.67±8.23 vs 6.15±12.55, p=0.68; 11.13±12.78 vs 12.41±13.54, p=0.60). Readmission rates at 30 days showed a trend towards a higher rate for patients undergoing LBAT as compared to CAVT (8.82% vs 1.69%, p=0.10), but this was not observed at 1 year (25.88% vs 23.73%, p=0.74). Conclusion: Among patients with intermediate-high-risk and high-risk PE undergoing MT, LBAT and CAVT demonstrated similar hemodynamic improvement, procedural metrics, and clinical outcomes. Both systems appear to provide comparable efficacy, supporting individualized device selection based on patient and procedural factors.
title: Abstract 8351: Comparative Procedural and Efficacy Outcomes of Large Bore Aspiration and Computer Assisted Vacuum Thrombectomy Devices in Intermediate-High- and High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism

abstract: Introduction: Intranasal phenylephrine (IN PE) is a topical vasoconstrictor commonly administered before nasal endoscopy (NE) to reduce mucosal congestion and bleeding via alpha-1 adrenergic receptor stimulation. Cardiovascular complications are uncommon given limited systemic absorption, and medical literature addressing this interaction is scarce. We describe two cases of non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) from coronary vasospasm attributed to compounded topical anesthetic containing IN PE and tetracaine. Case Presentations: Case 1: A 46-year-old woman developed sudden chest, back, shoulder pain and diaphoresis briefly after receiving IN PE prior to NE evaluation for allergies. She was treated with intramuscular epinephrine due to initial concern for anaphylaxis. Electrocardiogram (ECG) on admission showed no ST changes. High sensitivity-Troponin I (hsTn) peaked at 1,449 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated septal and inferior left ventricular regional wall motion abnormalities (LV RWMA) with an ejection fraction (EF) of 50%. Cardiac catheterization showed no obstructive disease or dissection. She discharged on daily aspirin and metoprolol in stable condition. Case 2: A 54-year-old woman developed acute onset-headache, chest pressure, nausea and vomiting after NE preceded by IN PE administration. She took full dose aspirin prior to presenting to the ER for persistent symptoms. ECG on presentation had no ischemic changes. hsTn trended up from 426 to 1,318 ng/L. TTE revealed inferior and lateral LV RWMA with an EF of 68%. Follow-up angiography showed minimal proximal right coronary artery plaque and no obstructive disease or dissection. She was discharged in stable condition on daily aspirin. Discussion: IN PE-associated NSTEMI is an underrecognized phenomenon that may result in extensive and potentially invasive cardiac workup. Our two patients developed acute anginal symptoms immediately following IN PE exposure. The combination of their symptoms and markedly elevated hsTn levels prompted early invasive evaluation to exclude obstructive coronary artery disease. Despite topical administration, IN PE may cause systemic alpha-1 adrenergic activation due to rapid absorption through the highly vascular nasal mucosa. Awareness of this may prompt clinicians to avoid compounded phenylephrine-based decongestants in at-risk individuals. It may also limit excessive downstream testing while ensuring appropriate acute coronary syndrome evaluation.
title: Abstract 8371: Not Just a Nasal Spray: Two Cases of Intranasal Phenylephrine-Associated Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) improves functional capacity and cardiovascular outcomes in multiple cardiac conditions; however, its impact following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) remains incompletely characterized in real-world practice. We evaluated the association between participation in CR after TAVR and subsequent cardiovascular outcomes. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network including adults undergoing TAVR between 2015 and 2025. Patients participating in CR within 3 months following TAVR (n=5,163) were compared with TAVR patients without CR participation (n=61,494). Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed for demographics and major cardiovascular comorbidities, yielding 5,161 patients in each cohort. Baseline characteristics were well balanced after matching, with all standardized mean differences (SMDs) <0.1, indicating adequate covariate balance. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 1 year. Secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA), heart failure (HF), new atrial fibrillation/flutter, and depression/anxiety. Results: The matched cohorts had similar mean age (77.7 vs 77.5 years) and female representation (41.2% vs 40.7%). CR participation following TAVR was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality compared with no CR participation (3.9% vs 8.9%; HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35-0.49; p<0.001). One-year survival probability was higher in the CR cohort (95.7% vs 90.1%). Secondary outcomes were also improved in the CR cohort, including lower rates of MI (7.2% vs 9.3%; HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.64-0.84; p<0.001), HF (46.5% vs 61.6%; HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.53-0.59; p<0.001), and new atrial fibrillation/flutter (6.6% vs 9.4%; HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.55-0.79; p<0.001). Stroke/TIA rates were numerically lower in the CR cohort (9.2% vs 10.1%; p=0.134) but did not reach statistical significance. Rates of depression/anxiety were similar between groups (3.3% vs 3.2%; p=0.826). Conclusion: Participation in cardiac rehabilitation following TAVR was associated with substantially improved survival and lower cardiovascular event rates in a large real-world cohort. While these findings suggest a potential benefit of cardiac rehabilitation after TAVR, they should be considered hypothesis-generating. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm these associations and inform strategies to optimize rehabilitation participation in this population.
title: Abstract 8387: Cardiac Rehabilitation Participation and Clinical Outcomes After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Cohort Study

abstract: Background: The coronary anatomy captured during cardiac catheterization is rarely used to predict subsequent complications. Acute kidney injury (AKI), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and heart failure (HF) affect ~8%, ~11%, and ~4% of patients, respectively, representing a substantial burden of preventable morbidity. No validated risk scores are routinely applied for MACE or HF, while the Mehran score for contrast-induced AKI depends on manual variable extraction: a laborious process blind to the angiogram. AI now enables automated angiographic reading at scale, opening the path toward efficient and clinically applicable risk models. Hypothesis: Automated AI angiographic reading improves complication prediction, and a compact model can rival validated manual scores. Methods: We linked a registry of coronary catheterizations (Montreal Heart Institute, 2017-2024) with pre-procedure laboratories, electrocardiograms, comorbidities, procedural data and automated deep-learning angiographic interpretations (ventricular function, stenosis, calcification, occlusion, SYNTAX). Outcomes were 48-hour KDIGO AKI, 1-year MACE (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke) and 1-year heart-failure (HF) hospitalization. For each outcome, clinical and AI variables were ranked by LASSO regression; sparse logistic models were assessed by AUROC and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) with 95% bootstrap CIs on a held-out test set. The compact AKI model was compared with the Mehran score, in an identical percutaneous coronary intervention subset, by paired DeLong test. Results (preliminary): Among 6 383 (AKI, 6%), 11 790 (MACE, 12%), and 11 292 (HF, 4%) patients, hybrid models using only 5-6 variables discriminated well: AKI AUROC 0.80 [0.78-0.82], AUPRC 0.26 [0.22-0.31]; MACE 0.82 [0.81-0.83], AUPRC 0.40 [0.37-0.43]; HF 0.82 [0.79-0.84], AUPRC 0.24 [0.19-0.28]. AUPRCs were 3-6x outcome prevalence, confirming strong precision for these rare events. A single AI-derived measure, predicted left ventricular ejection fraction, was the leading angiographic variable for MACE and HF, whereas AKI did not clearly benefit from AI input. The 5-variable AKI model equaled the Mehran score (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.79; p=0.96) without manual entry of hypotension, shock or heart failure. At a Youden threshold, NPVs reached 0.98-0.99 for AKI and HF, identifying a low-risk majority who could forgo prophylaxis and monitoring. Conclusion: Compact models combining routine variables with AI-generated angiographic measures accurately predict MACE, HF and AKI, even matching the Mehran score, without requiring manual data entry. At our center only (~5,800 catheterizations/year), these models could flag several hundred patients annually for targeted prevention, supporting prospective and calibration testing before point-of-care use.
title: Abstract 8400: Parsimonious Models Integrating Routine Clinical Data and Artificial Intelligence-Derived Angiographic Phenotypes to Predict Acute Kidney Injury, Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events and Heart Failure After Cardiac Catheterization

abstract: Introduction: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) such as Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (VA-ECMO) and Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP) is vital in refractory cardiogenic shock. While these therapies can be lifesaving, their combined use alters hemodynamics in ways that may predispose patients to rare, devastating neurologic events such as spinal cord infarction (SCI) resulting in permanent paraplegia. Patient Information: A 53-year-old male with nonischemic cardiomyopathy presented in severe cardiogenic shock. Despite maximal inotropic and vasopressor support, he remained in refractory shock, prompting IABP placement. Due to persistent hemodynamic instability, support was escalated to femoral-femoral VA-ECMO. Clinical Findings & Timeline: On day 7 of combined MCS support, he acutely developed bilateral lower extremity weakness and sensory loss, with preserved upper extremity strength. Neurological examination revealed a T10 level of injury, ASIA Grade C, consistent with acute SCI. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: In patients supported with VA-ECMO and IABP, the spinal cord is vulnerable to multiple insults leading to localized cord ischemia. We hypothesize the etiology of SCI in this setting to be multifactorial, driven by altered aortic flow dynamics, mechanical obstruction, and thromboembolism. First, retrograde femoral VA-ECMO flow directly competes with anterograde native cardiac output, creating a stagnant “watershed zone” in the descending aorta. When this zone localizes near the Artery of Adamkiewicz, spinal cord perfusion is critically compromised. Secondly, IABP positioning may physically occlude spinal feeding arteries during 1:1 inflation cycles. Third, the traditional lower MAP goal to reduce risk of LV dilation and cardiogenic pulmonary edema may exacerbate regional ischemia. Lastly, the presence of foreign hardware dramatically increases thromboembolic risk to the spinal vasculature. Therapeutic Interventions: Despite prompt IABP removal and higher MAP target for cord perfusion, motor and sensory deficits persisted. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: The patient subsequently underwent orthotopic heart transplantation and continues physical rehabilitation with limited lower extremity function. Discussion & Synthesis: SCI is a devastating, underrecognized complication of combined VA-ECMO and IABP therapy. Early recognition via frequent neurological assessments is crucial, as prognosis for functional recovery remains poor. Mitigating strategies include maintaining higher MAP targets to optimize spinal cord perfusion, enforcing meticulous anticoagulation protocols, and earlier transition from ECMO or preferentially utilizing alternative LV venting strategies (such as Impella or central ECMO) to avoid competitive retrograde flow and maintain physiologic antegrade blood flow for spinal cord perfusion.
title: Abstract 8412: The Price of Perfusion: Spinal Cord Infarction During Combined Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation and Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Support

abstract: Background: Patients with cardiogenic shock (CS) requiring temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) are frequently transferred from regional hospitals to CS hub centers (HCs). Whether associations exist between transfer time (TT), tMCS-related adverse events (AEs), and clinical outcomes is poorly defined. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients with tMCS for CS transferred from referral centers to a CS HC from 8/2021-8/2024. TT was defined as time from referral center transfer initiation to HC arrival. Patients were stratified by > vs ≤ median TT. Baseline characteristics were compared. Outcomes including in-hospital survival, survival to discharge or heart replacement therapy, and adjudicated tMCS-related AEs were compared using chi-square testing. TT was also analyzed continuously using logistic regression. A sensitivity analysis by location of tMCS placement was performed. Results: A total of 227 patients with CS transferred from referral centers were included. Overall, 63.4% had SCAI stage D/E CS and heart failure CS was the most common etiology (63.0%). A total of 90 (39.6%) patients had tMCS placed prior to HC transfer (31.1% IABP, 68.9% microaxial flow pump). TT ranged from 2.4-112.5 hours (median 9.0 [6.1,17.9] hours). Baseline characteristics including SCAI stage were similar between those > vs ≤ median TT. Patients with > median TT were less likely to have Impella CP at any time during the hospitalization, more likely to have Impella 5.5 at any time during the hospitalization, and had lower baseline alanine transferase and creatinine (Table). Total tMCS device days were higher in those with > median TT (Table). The incidence of any tMCS-related AE was similar between those with > vs ≤ median TT (41.6% vs 43.0%, respectively; p=0.83). Individual tMCS-related AEs were also similar between groups (11.5 % vs 12.3% for bacteremia, 17.7% vs 16.7% for bleeding, 2.7% vs 0.9% for stroke, 11.5% vs 11.4% for vascular injury, 3.5% vs 3.5% heparin induced thrombocytopenia; p>0.05 for all). Overall, in-hospital survival was 72.7%, while 17.2% underwent heart replacement therapy. There was no significant difference in in-hospital survival (69.5% vs 75.4%; p=0.35) or survival to discharge or heart replacement therapy (70.8% vs 77.2%; p=0.27) between groups. When analyzed as a continuous variable, TT was not significantly associated with survival or tMCS-related AEs. Findings from the main analysis were consistent in the sensitivity analyses of those who underwent tMCS placement prior to (n=90) or after (n=137) HC transfer (Figure). Conclusions: Among patients with tMCS for CS transferred from a referral center to a HC, patients with ≤ median TT had more end-organ dysfunction but similar CS severity as those with > median TT. Referral center to HC TT was not associated with tMCS-related AEs, in-hospital mortality, or survival to discharge or heart replacement therapy.
title: Abstract 8415: Referral Center to Hub Center Transfer Times and Clinical Outcomes in Patients with Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support for Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Introduction: Pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronary artery dissection (P-SCAD) is a leading cause of peripartum myocardial infarction, with a more severe phenotype than non-pregnancy SCAD. Its concurrence with pulmonary embolism (PE) and preeclampsia is rare and forces directly conflicting therapeutic imperatives. Subsequent pregnancy after SCAD with severely reduced ejection fraction (EF) is scarcely described. Patient Information: A 35-year-old woman G17P7 (7 prior deliveries with 10 pregnancy losses) presented one week postpartum with anterolateral STEMI. She had no atherosclerotic risk factors and a normotensive antenatal course. Investigations: Coronary angiography demonstrated SCAD of the distal left main, left anterior descending, and circumflex arteries, with a normal right coronary artery. CT angiography revealed bilateral segmental PE. Postpartum hypertension, transaminitis, and hemoconcentration confirmed preeclampsia. Echocardiography showed an EF of 31-35%, declining to a nadir of 25%. Management and Outcome: The dissection was managed conservatively, given hemodynamic stability and preserved flow. The coexisting PE created an antithrombotic dilemma, as recent data identify oral anticoagulation as the strongest independent predictor of adverse events in SCAD (adjusted HR 3.8). This was resolved with a time-limited strategy: therapeutic anticoagulation for the provoked PE, ceased at three months, then aspirin monotherapy. Serial echocardiography was chosen over repeat angiography to avoid iatrogenic injury to fragile vessels. Persistently low EF despite maximally tolerated therapy, constrained by chronic hypotension, prompted an extravascular ICD. Despite counseling, she conceived again at EF 26-30% (modified WHO Class IV). A multidisciplinary Pregnancy Heart Team carried the gestation to 29 weeks, when intraamniotic infection necessitated vaginal delivery under inotropic support, complicated by postpartum hemorrhage. Mother and neonate survived; a contraceptive implant was placed before discharge. Discussion: This case shows that even severe multi-vessel left main P-SCAD with concurrent PE and preeclampsia can be managed conservatively with favorable outcomes. The co-occurrence of SCAD, PE, and preeclampsia may reflect a shared substrate of postpartum endothelial dysfunction and hypercoagulability. The antithrombotic conflict between PE and SCAD is the most generalizable lesson, resolved here by time-limited anticoagulation. The successful subsequent pregnancy demonstrates that coordinated multidisciplinary care can navigate even extreme-risk gestation, a scenario for which published guidance is limited. This case underscore the value of preconception risk stratification; registries capturing subsequent pregnancies after SCAD with reduced EF are needed to guide counseling for this rare population.
title: Abstract 8427: Successful Conservative Management of Postpartum Multi-Vessel Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection with Concurrent Pulmonary Embolism and Preeclampsia, and a Subsequent Extreme-Risk Pregnancy

abstract: Background: Statin intolerance is a recognized barrier to sustained lipid-lowering therapy (LLT), yet its clinical phenotype, management patterns, and cardiovascular consequences in contemporary practice remain incompletely characterized. Objective: To characterize statin intolerance at scale and determine whether its cardiovascular consequences are driven by the intolerance label or by the LLT discontinuation that often follows. Methods: Among patients with a new statin prescription in the Mass General Brigham health system, we characterized the prevalence, phenotype, and temporal trends of incident statin intolerance, described post-intolerance LLT management, and examined cardiovascular outcomes using time-varying Cox models. Analyses were conducted overall, separately by primary- and secondary-prevention, and within intolerant patients comparing those who discontinued all LLT with those who continued any LLT. Results: Of the 254,035 new statin users, 68.4% were treated for primary prevention and 31.6% for secondary prevention. Statin intolerance was documented in 10,644 (4.2%) over a median (IQR) of 3.1 (1.0-6.9) years, modestly more frequently in secondary than primary prevention (4.5% vs 4.1%). Documented statin intolerance rose through the late 2000s before declining and plateauing at approximately 4 per 1,000 active statin users in recent years ( Fig 1A ). Intolerance was predominantly musculoskeletal (68.1%). More than one third of intolerant patients discontinued all LLT, including 39.5% of those in secondary prevention ( Fig 1B ). Ezetimibe was the most common nonstatin alternative (38.0% secondary, 31.1% primary), followed by PCSK9 inhibitors (10.6% and 7.7%), while bempedoic acid was rarely used (<2%). Discontinuation led to a mean (standard deviation) low-density lipoprotein-C (LDL-C) increase of 6.8 (36.3) mg/dL versus a 4.9 (41.8) mg/dL decrease among LLT continuers (P<0.001). Compared with tolerant patients, intolerance was associated with increased risk of coronary artery bypass grafting (HR 1.55 [95% CI 1.35-1.77]), percutaneous coronary intervention (1.37 [1.24-1.53]), myocardial infarction (1.21 [1.13-1.30]), and ischemic stroke (1.12 [1.04-1.20]). Among intolerant patients, discontinuing all LLT was associated with substantially higher risk than continuing therapy across every outcome, with HRs ranging from 1.38 for mortality to 2.14 for venous thromboembolism, consistent across prevention groups. Between 13% and 31% of cardiovascular events among intolerant patients were attributable to discontinuation. Conclusions: Statin intolerance is frequently followed by discontinuation of LLT, contributing to worsening LDL-C trajectories and substantial risk of cardiovascular disease. The findings highlight post-intolerance treatment decisions as a critical, modifiable determinant of cardiovascular outcomes.
title: Abstract 8446: Statin Intolerance, Treatment Gaps, and Cardiovascular Outcomes: A 24-Year Health System Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Giant coronary artery aneurysms are rare and most commonly associated with atherosclerosis or systemic vasculitis, including IgG4-related disease. We present an unusual case of diffuse multi-vessel coronary aneurysms and recurrent myocardial infarctions ultimately attributed to genetically confirmed Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS), initially mimicking inflammatory vasculitis. Case Description: A 45-year-old African American male with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and prior myocardial infarctions in 2012, 2013, and 2021 presented with exertional chest pain and dyspnea. Coronary angiography demonstrated severe diffuse coronary aneurysmal disease (Figure1A) involving the LM, LAD and LCx coronart arteries iwith chronic total of the proximal RCA containing a prior stent with collateral circulation supplying the distal vessel. During his 2021 MI, distal OM occlusion was suspected to represent coronary embolization from proximal aneurysms. Inflammatory markers were persistently elevated (ESR peak 87 mm/hr; IgG 1942 mg/dL), raising concern for medium-vessel vasculitis or IgG4-related disease; however, IgG4 subclasses, ANA, ANCA, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. Cardiac CT demonstrated diffuse coronary ectasia (Figure1B) with severe periarterial thickening and a giant distal LM aneurysm measuring 16х17 mm, later progressing to 18 mm. Progressive aortic root dilation was also noted with the sinus of Valsalva progressing from 4.8 to 5.2 cm over 14 months. FDG-PET/CT demonstrated no active coronary or systemic inflammation, prompting genetic evaluation, which revealed a pathogenic SMAD2 mutation confirming LDS. Management: Immunosuppressive therapy was deferred following genetic confirmation. The patient was maintained on clopidogrel and rivaroxaban given recurrent myocardial infarctions and presumed embolic risk from giant coronary aneurysms. Due to progressive aortic root dilation, he was referred for elective aortic root replacement and underwent comprehensive MRI/MRA vascular surveillance. Conclusion: LDS may rarely present with giant multi-vessel coronary aneurysms and periarterial thickening closely mimicking inflammatory vasculitis. Negative inflammatory imaging and unrevealing autoimmune serologies should prompt consideration of genetic aortopathies especially in the presence of aortic dilatation as in this case. Early genetic diagnosis is critical, as it significantly alters management, surveillance, and surgical planning. Abbreviations: LAD (Left Anterior Descending artery), LM (Left Main Artery), LCx (Left Circumflex Artery), RCA (Right Coronary Artery), OM (Obtuse Marginal artery). ANA (Antinuclear Antibody), Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies (ANCA), MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging), MRA (Magnetic Resonance Angiography), FGD PET (Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography)
title: Abstract 8458: Recurrent Myocardial Infarctions and Giant Multi-Vessel Coronary Artery Aneurysms: Loeys-Dietz Syndrome Mimicking Inflammatory Vasculitis

abstract: Background: Intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) is increasingly used to guide left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) because it may reduce dependence on general anesthesia, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) imaging personnel, and procedural resource utilization. However, comparative procedural and safety outcomes between ICE and TEE remain incompletely defined. Research Question: How does ICE compare with TEE for procedural success, procedural duration, resource utilization, and periprocedural complications during LAAO? Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was performed using PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases through December 1, 2025. Twenty-four observational studies involving 132,398 patients undergoing LAAO were included. Outcomes included procedural success, procedure time, in-lab time, cost, periprocedural complications, stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA), pericardial effusion/tamponade, peri-device leak, and residual iatrogenic atrial septal defect (iASD). Odds ratios (OR) and mean weighted differences (MWD) with 95% confidence intervals were pooled using random-effects models. Results: Among 132,398 patients, 6,287 (4.75%) underwent ICE-guided LAAO. Procedural success was similar between ICE and TEE (98.8% vs 98.5%; OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.84-1.51; p=0.426). Procedure time was not significantly different (MWD -2.75 minutes; p=0.384), although ICE significantly reduced total in-lab time (83.7 ± 34.3 vs 110.3 ± 40.0 minutes; MWD -26.59 minutes; p<0.001). Total procedural cost was similar (MWD $2,539; p=0.207), while professional fees were lower with ICE (MWD -$5,415; p=0.008). ICE was associated with higher overall periprocedural complications (6.1% vs 5.4%; OR 1.17; p=0.031), including pericardial effusion/tamponade (2.5% vs 1.9%; OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.06 - 1.76; p=0.016) and stroke/TIA (0.56% vs 0.29%; OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.23 - 4.13; p=0.008). Residual iASD was more common with ICE (36.6% vs 27.3%; OR 1.62; p=0.002), whereas peri-device leak was similar between groups. Conclusions: ICE-guided LAAO provides comparable procedural success with meaningful reductions in in-lab time and professional resource utilization, supporting its role as an efficient alternative imaging strategy as structural heart procedure volumes continue to expand. However, ICE was also associated with increased periprocedural complications, including pericardial effusion/tamponade and stroke/TIA. Although the absolute event differences were small, these findings remain clinically relevant because LAAO is a preventive procedure performed in otherwise stable patients with a low margin for procedural risk. Continued advances in ICE technology, procedural standardization, and increasing operator experience may help mitigate these safety concerns and further define the role of ICE-guided LAAO.
title: Abstract 8493: Intracardiac versus Transesophageal Echocardiography for Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: Meta-Analysis of Clinical Outcomes and Resource Utilization

abstract: Background and Hypothesis: Early identification of ischemic insult to the myocardium is critical as it can allow for timely intervention and improve patient outcomes. Native myocardial T1 maps from cardiac MRI may offer opportunities for detecting early myocardial tissue changes. However, whether T1 changes occur in response to early ischemia and if so, what cellular mechanisms would be at play are yet to be investigated. We hypothesized that acute ischemia results in rapid T1 elevations prior to perceptible high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) elevation and are associated with early metabolic changes characterized by compromises in mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes. Methods: No flow ischemia was created in canines (n=16) by occluding left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery for 3 hours. Serial native T1 mappings were performed every 5-10 minutes after induction of ischemia. Circulating hs-cTnI measurements were made at baseline and across increasing duration of ischemia (5-90 min). PET images were acquired at 120 min to determine area-at-risk. Studies were also performed in cultured cardiomyocytes exposed to ischemia (0-90 min). T1 values of culture, intracellular pH, total ATP production, mitochondrial respiration, and spare respiratory capacity were measured. Results: Canines : Myocardial native T1 values increased progressively and significantly with increasing ischemic duration in vivo , rising from 1182.19 ± 12.81 ms at baseline to 1324.32 ± 16.00 ms at 90 min of ischemia ( p <0.0001). Importantly, significant elevations in native T1 were detectable by 5 min of ischemia, while ischemia thresholds based on hs-cTnI levels were not breached until after 35 mins of ischemia. PET images allowed for visualization of area-at-risk within which T1 values evolved. Cultured Cardiomyocytes : ischemia induced a time-dependent increase in T1 values, rising from 2243.36 ± 7.77 ms at baseline (n = 5) to 2324.27 ± 14.18 ms after 90 min of ischemia (n = 5; p <0.002). Notably, these T1 changes paralleled progressive intracellular acidification, reduced total ATP production, impaired mitochondrial respiration, and declining spare respiratory capacity. The temporal association between T1 increases and metabolic deterioration suggests that native T1 elevation reflects early bioenergetic stress before overt myocardial injury and biomarker release. Conclusions: Native T1 mapping has the sensitivity to detect early ischemic myocardial changes prior to significant hs-cTnI elevation. T1 prolongation closely reflects underlying metabolic derangements, including intracellular acidosis, ATP depletion, and mitochondrial dysfunction. These findings support native T1 mapping to evolve as a noninvasive cardiac MRI approach for the early detection of myocardial ischemia from compromised myocardial energetics.
title: Abstract 8503: Native Myocardial T1 Elevations During Acute Ischemia Reveals Early Energetic Failure and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Cardiomyocytes

abstract: Introduction: Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy), widely used for GVHD prophylaxis after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), is associated with early cardiac events in up to 19% of recipients. We present a case of fulminant PTCy-associated perimyocarditis, highlighting therapeutic barriers of the post-transplant period. Patient Information: A 45-year-old male with T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (prior anthracycline treatment, cumulative 225 mg/m 2 , ~50% of lifetime max) in remission developed treatment-related myelodysplastic syndrome. He had no cardiac history and underwent haploidentical stem cell transplant with fludarabine/melphalan/TBI conditioning, PTCy/mesna (50 mg/kg, days +3 /+4), tacrolimus, and mycophenolate for GVHD prophylaxis. Pre-transplant LVEF was 60-65%. Clinical Findings & Timeline: On day +7, he developed hemorrhagic cystitis and low QRS voltages (Figure 1). TTE showed preserved function with small circumferential pericardial effusion. Over subsequent days, TTEs showed progressive pericardial effusion with worsening systolic dysfunction, requiring pericardiocentesis and right and left heart catheterization. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Cardiac catheterization on day +10 revealed elevated filling pressures, reduced cardiac index of 1.7 L/min/m 2 , and no obstructive CAD, consistent with fulminant perimyocarditis. Within 24 hours, systolic function rapidly declined, leading to severe cardiogenic shock with LVEF < 20%. Troponin peaked at 68,920 ng/L on day +13. Therapeutic Interventions: Inotropes, IABP, and VA-ECMO were initiated. Given suspected cytokine-mediated component, tocilizumab was empirically trialed and troponin declined to 1,613 ng/L (Figure 2). Myocardial recovery did not occur and he remained ECMO-dependent for 57 days. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Bone marrow biopsy confirmed engraftment, but persistent thrombocytopenia prevented left ventricular assist device implantation. Heart transplant was precluded by oncologic uncertainty. The patient expired from refractory cardiogenic shock. Discussion: PTCy-associated cardiogenic shock is a severe complication of allo-HSCT that can progress rapidly, leaving a narrow and often undetected window for intervention. Injury is mediated by acrolein, the same toxic metabolite causing hemorrhagic cystitis, with downstream cytokine activation. Cytopenias and oncologic uncertainty often preclude advanced cardiac therapies. ICU mortality is 47%, primarily from refractory cardiogenic shock, and survivors may not show LVEF recovery until a median of 33 days. The tocilizumab-associated troponin decline observed here raises the question of cytokine involvement but remains unknown, and warrants prospective study, alongside biomarker validation for earlier recognition and intervention before irreversible cell death.
title: Abstract 8504: Fulminant Perimyocarditis and Refractory Cardiogenic Shock from Post-Stem Cell Transplant Cyclophosphamide Cardiotoxicity: A Therapeutic Challenge

abstract: BACKGROUND: Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (AA) is a rare HACEK organism associated with infective endocarditis (IE), delayed culture positivity, and embolic complications. Extensive periannular infection involving the aorto-mitral curtain with histopathologic sparing of the valve leaflets is uncommon. CASE: A 32-year-old man with obesity and tobacco use presented with fever, chills, and chest pain. Several days earlier, he underwent non-cardiac evaluation at an outside hospital for shoulder pain, arm paresthesias, and chest discomfort and was discharged on corticosteroids without cardiac evaluation. Examination revealed a new diastolic murmur. TTE demonstrated a 0.8х1.0 cm mobile mass associated with the aortic valve, mild aortic regurgitation, and preserved left ventricular systolic function. Blood cultures obtained on admission remained negative initially but became positive after approximately 103 hours of incubation in all four bottles for AA.TEE demonstrated a previously undiagnosed bicuspid aortic valve, severe aortic regurgitation, vegetation involving the aorto-mitral curtain, and periannular abscess formation. Brain MRI revealed multiple subacute cerebral infarcts consistent with septic embolization. Dental evaluation revealed only mild gingivitis without a clear odontogenic source.The patient underwent surgical intervention. Intraoperative TEE demonstrated vegetations arising from the aorto-mitral curtain with extension into the LVOT. Surgical inspection revealed grossly normal bicuspid valve leaflets without evidence of infection, while vegetations and abscess formation were confined to the aorto-mitral curtain and LVOT. Extensive debridement and patch reconstruction were performed. Because of severe aortic insufficiency, bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement was required. Histopathology of the excised valve leaflets demonstrated only mild degenerative changes without evidence of inflammation or IE. The patient completed six weeks of intravenous ceftriaxone with clinical recovery. DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION: This case illustrates an unusual presentation of AA IE characterized by an initially misleading presentation prompting extensive non-cardiac evaluation, delayed culture positivity, septic cerebral embolization, and extensive aorto-mitral curtain infection with histopathologic sparing of the aortic valve leaflets. Surgical and histopathologic findings confirmed destructive periannular infection with leaflet sparing, while the absence of a clear odontogenic source further complicated source identification. Recognition of this atypical pattern is important, as aggressive invasive IE may occur beyond the valve itself; early TEE should be pursued when clinical suspicion remains high despite initially nondiagnostic findings
title: Abstract 8537: Beyond the Valve: Aggregatibacter Actinomycetemcomitans Endocarditis Causing Destructive Aorto-Mitral Curtain Infection with Pathologic Leaflet Sparing

abstract: Introduction: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an increasingly recognized cause of acute coronary syndrome in women without traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Although most patients are managed conservatively, long-term coronary remodelling after SCAD remains incompletely understood. Patient Information: A 53-year-old woman with prior non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) secondary to SCAD presented two years later with intermittent exertional and emotionally triggered chest discomfort without atherosclerotic risk factors. Clinical Findings & Timeline: The index NSTEMI occurred during intense psychosocial stress and was characterized by chest pressure, dyspnea, and left arm pain. Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed no ischemic changes, while high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 1,453 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved biventricular function. Coronary angiography revealed Type 2 SCAD involving the mid-LAD and first obtuse marginal branch, and vascular imaging demonstrated no fibromuscular dysplasia. Conservative management was pursued given the absence of ongoing ischemia or hemodynamic compromise. Intermittent chest discomfort persisted over the ensuing two years. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: Exercise treadmill testing for recurring chest pain reproduced symptoms without ischemic ECG changes. CCTA demonstrated a calcium score of 0, no coronary plaque or recurrent dissection, and bridging collateral vessels connecting the distal LAD and LIMA. Findings were consistent with adaptive post-SCAD vascular remodelling resulting in a spontaneous LIMA-LAD arterial connection. Therapeutic Intervention(s): Long-acting nitrates and calcium channel blockers were not tolerated. Ranolazine was initiated and titrated to 1,000 mg twice daily along with conservative management. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: At one-month follow-up, chest pain frequency and severity were markedly reduced, with only rare mild symptoms. Discussion & Synthesis: This case highlights a rare manifestation of post-SCAD healing, with spontaneous development of a LIMA-LAD collateral pathway functioning as a native arterial bypass. CCTA was instrumental in excluding recurrent dissection and identifying this unique collateral network. This case expands the spectrum of post-SCAD healing by demonstrating spontaneous native arterial bypass formation and highlights the role of CCTA in characterizing long-term coronary remodelling.
title: Abstract 8540: A Natural Bypass: Spontaneous LIMA-to-LAD Collateralization Following SCAD

abstract: Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) is an uncommon cause of dyspnea and refractory hypoxemia resulting from positional right-to-left shunting. Positional changes promote right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defect, resulting in hypoxemia that worsens when upright and improves when supine. Recognition of POS is especially important in acute care settings where intubation is being considered. We present a case of POS due to a PFO that highlights an important diagnostic and management consideration in cardiovascular critical care. A 76-year-old female with a history of PFO diagnosed in 2016, chronic hypoxemia requiring 6 L home oxygen, hypertension, and bipolar disorder presented with worsening dyspnea. On presentation, she was normotensive with an oxygen saturation of 87% despite 100% FiO 2 via a non-rebreather mask. Arterial blood gas demonstrated severe hypoxemia with a PaO 2 of 43 mmHg. CTA of the chest showed no evidence of pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or pleural effusion, with only chronic interstitial opacities. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved LVEF, an aneurysmal atrial septum, and an interatrial shunt on bubble study. She was transferred to the cardiac intensive care unit for structural heart evaluation. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a patent foramen ovale with significant right-to-left shunting. During hospitalization, she developed profound positional hypoxemia consistent with platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome. Oxygenation improved when supine, allowing continued support with a high-flow nasal cannula and avoiding intubation. Given refractory hypoxemia and oxygen dependence out of proportion to pulmonary findings, she underwent successful placement of a 30 mm PFO closure device. Post-procedural TEE demonstrated no significant residual shunt. Oxygen requirements improved substantially, and she was discharged on 2 L nasal cannula. POS is frequently missed, mainly because it can present later in life despite being associated with a congenital intracardiac shunt, such as a PFO. It should be considered in cases where patients become increasingly hypoxic despite escalating oxygen delivery methods. Early identification of this physiology is particularly important in critically ill patients, as positive-pressure ventilation may exacerbate right-to-left shunting and worsen hypoxemia. Recognition of POS facilitated definitive treatment with percutaneous closure, resulting in a marked reduction in this patient's long-term oxygen requirements.
title: Abstract 8549: The Supine Solution: Avoiding Mechanical Ventilation Through Recognition of PFO Related Platypnea Orthodeoxia Syndrome

abstract: Introduction: Combined overdose of long-acting calcium channel blockers (CCBs) and alpha-2 agonists can cause profound vasoplegic and cardiogenic shock. However, delayed recurrent hemodynamic collapse after apparent recovery remains poorly described. Patient Information: A 61-year-old woman with schizophrenia and hypertension presented after intentional ingestion of 300 mg amlodipine and an unknown quantity of clonidine. Clinical Findings & Timeline: On presentation, blood presssure was 70/40 mmHg and heart rate 74 bpm. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated lactic acidosis (lactate 3.6 mmol/L; peak 9.0 mmol/L) and acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.3 mg/dL). Despite aggressive fluid resuscitation, she developed refractory mixed vasoplegic and cardiogenic shock requiring norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin, and phenylephrine. Vasopressor requirements improved and were discontinued by hospital day 2. Unexpectedly, profound hypotension recurred on hospital day 3, necessitating re-escalation to triple-pressor support before eventual recovery. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: EKG demonstrated intermittent sinus node exit block with accelerated junctional rhythm, and left anterior fascicular block (Figure 1). Transthoracic echocardiography obtained while receiving four vasopressors revealed hyperdynamic left ventricular (LV) systolic function with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve chordae without LV outflow tract obstruction (Figure 2). Therapeutic Interventions: Treatment included activated charcoal to prevent further drug absorption, intravenous calcium gluconate to counteract amlodipine-induced L-type calcium channel blockade, and naloxone to counteract central sympatholysis and associated bradycardia and hypotension. High-dose insulin euglycemic therapy was initiated to augment myocardial glucose utilization and contractility in the setting of severe calcium channel blocker toxicity along with vasopressor support in an intensive critical care setting. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Following recurrent shock and repeat vasopressor escalation, hemodynamics and organ dysfunction gradually stabilized without cardiovascular sequelae. Discussion & Synthesis: Amlodipine-induced vasoplegia and myocardial dysfunction from L-type calcium channel blockade, compounded by clonidine-mediated central sympatholysis, resulted in severe refractory shock. The delayed recurrence of shock likely reflected prolonged amlodipine half-life and redistribution kinetics, revealing a clinically underrecognized biphasic toxicodynamic profile. Conclusion: Long-acting CCB toxicity may produce delayed rebound hemodynamic collapse despite apparent early stabilization. Recognition of this biphasic shock pattern is critical to avoid premature de-escalation of vasoactive support and intensive care monitoring.
title: Abstract 8565: Biphasic Refractory Cardiogenic and Vasoplegic Shock in Combined Amlodipine and Clonidine Overdose

abstract: Abstract: We describe a patient with nonischemic cardiomyopathy who presented in cardiogenic shock with a left ventricular (LV) apical thrombus. The patient acutely decompensated necessitating escalation in mechanical support. Left atrial veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (LAVA-ECMO) was utilized as a bridge to transplant. Introduction: Venoarterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) raises LV pressures and impedes ejection. LV venting and unloading can be employed to reduce pulmonary congestion, clot formation, and myocardial oxygen demand. Common strategies include intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) and temporary microaxial flow pump, with the latter contraindicated in intracardiac thrombus. In this situation, the ECMO circuit was reconfigured to provide venting and unloading via a left atrial (LA) cannula, a strategy known as LAVA-ECMO. Patient Information: A 48-year-old male with advanced NICM presented with progressively worsening dyspnea. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Vitals were initially unremarkable. Examination revealed jugular venous distension, edema, and cool extremities. Laboratory studies showed lactic acidosis and kidney injury. He was started on dobutamine with no improvement, so milrinone was added. TTE revealed LV ejection fraction < 20% and an apical LV thrombus measuring 4x3.3cm. While on dual inotropes, right heart catheterization revealed elevated filling pressures and a Fick cardiac output of 2.9 L/min. Femoral IABP was placed for additional support. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) with hemodynamic compromise necessitated VA-ECMO. Reconfiguration was performed to LAVA-ECMO. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: The patient’s presentation was consistent with SCAI C cardiogenic shock, which stabilized on dual inotrope and single agent MCS. Instability, escalating to SCAI E, prompted the need for VA-ECMO. LV venting and unloading was needed with patient hemodynamics and imaging findings but complicated by LV thrombus (Figure). LAVA-ECMO was an appropriate strategy. Therapeutic Intervention(s): Ultimately, the patient was able to be stabilized for transplantation with dual inotropic support, LAVA ECMO, and right axillary IABP. Followup, Outcomes & Adverse Events: The patient underwent a successful heart transplant. Discussion & Synthesis: VA-ECMO increases LV afterload and impedes LV ejection via retrograde arterial flow. LV venting and unloading refer to strategies employed to reduce left-sided filling pressures, clot formation, and myocardial oxygen demand. LAVA-ECMO is a potential strategy in patients with LV thrombus that allowed for successful bridge to transplant in this case.
title: Abstract 8633: Left Atrial Venting and Unloading with Reconfigured Extracorporeal Support as a Bridge to Transplantation: When Extensive Intracardiac Thrombus Complicates Biventricular Heart Failure

abstract: Background: The formation of coronary collateral circulation is a critical compensatory mechanism in patients with coronary chronic total occlusion (CTO), yet its regulatory mediators remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to investigate the association between plasma levels of Copine III (CPNE3))and coronary collateralization in CTO patients, and to evaluate the functional role of CPNE3 in angiogenesis. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that higher circulating CPNE3 is associated with better coronary collateralization in CTO patients and that CPNE3 promotes endothelial angiogenic responses under ischemic conditions. Methods: Plasma CPNE3 was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay in 206 patients with coronary chronic total occlusion. Patients were classified as having poor or good collateral circulation according to the Rentrop classification. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells were exposed to hypoxia and subjected to CPNE3 gain- and loss-of-function experiments. Endothelial proliferation, migration, invasion, and tube formation were assessed using EdU incorporation, wound-healing, Transwell, and tube formation assays. VEGFR2, PI3K, and AKT signaling components were examined by Western blot. In a mouse hindlimb ischemia model, recombinant CPNE3 protein or phosphate-buffered saline was administered. Perfusion recovery was monitored by laser Doppler imaging, and capillary density was evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Results: Plasma CPNE3 levels were higher in patients with good collateral circulation than in those with poor collateral circulation (3371.13±1415.61 vs 2204.29±824.84 pg/mL; P <0.001). In hypoxic endothelial cells, CPNE3 overexpression enhanced proliferation, migration, invasion, and tube formation. CPNE3 increased VEGFR2 expression and AKT phosphorylation without a detectable increase in PI3K phosphorylation. In vivo, recombinant CPNE3 protein improved perfusion recovery after hindlimb ischemia and increased capillary density in ischemic muscle compared with phosphate-buffered saline control. After adjustment for clinical covariates, higher CPNE3 remained associated with good collateral circulation (adjusted OR=3.591, 95% CI 2.396-5.383, P =0.002). Conclusion: Circulating CPNE3 is associated with better coronary collateralization in patients with coronary chronic total occlusion and promotes endothelial angiogenic activity. These findings support CPNE3 as a candidate biomarker of collateral development and a potential regulator of ischemia-induced angiogenesis.
title: Abstract 8652: Association and Functional Role of Copine III in Coronary Collateral Formation in Chronic Total Occlusion

abstract: Background: Therapeutic angiogenesis remains an attractive strategy for Ischemic heart disease (IHD), yet clinical translation has been limited by the inability to generate durable and functional vascular networks. Increasing evidence suggests that successful vascular repair depends not only on endothelial activation but also on preservation of endothelial identity during remodeling. However, the molecular regulators governing this process remain poorly defined. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that ADAM10 supports EC identity maintenance during ischemic repair and that reduced ADAM10 is associated with impaired collateral formation, maladaptive fibrosis, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Methods: Plasma proteomics was performed in 148 patients with chronic total occlusion (CTO) and validated in an independent dual-center cohort of 712 CTO patients. Endothelial-specific Adam10 knockout mice ( Adam10 ΔEC ) were subjected to myocardial infarction (MI). Mechanisms were examined using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), lineage trajectory mapping, and intercellular crosstalk analysis of the cardiac ECs at serial time points after MI. Therapeutic potential of ADAM10 was evaluated using AAV-mediated gene delivery. Results: In patients, circulating ADAM10 was associated with coronary collateral circulation (CCC) and outcomes. ADAM10 discriminated favorable CCC formation with an ROC of 0.781. Low ADAM10 levels independently predicted major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCEs) (HR 0.772, 95% CI 0.666-0.895, P < 0.001), with significantly higher MACCE incidence observed in the low-ADAM10 group (30.0% vs 16.8%). In mice, endothelial-specific Adam10 knockout ( Adam10 ΔEC ) increased post-MI mortality (66.67% vs 17.65%) and impaired cardiac function (LVEF: 10.54% vs 56.00%, P = 0.001). and increased fibrosis (45.82% vs 14.53%, P < 0.001). scRNA-seq identified expansion of a mesenchymal-like endothelial population co-expressing endothelial and profibrotic genes, consistent with an EndoMT-like transition. ADAM10 deficiency promoted fibronectin-1-mediated fibroblast activation and maladaptive fibrotic remodeling. AAV-mediated ADAM10 expression improved cardiac function after MI (LVEF: 46.76% vs 9.60%, P < 0.001). Conclusions: ADAM10 acts as a key endothelial regulator during ischemic repair, supporting EC identity maintenance and limiting pathological profibrotic remodeling. Together, clinical and experimental findings suggest that endothelial competence, beyond endothelial proliferation alone, may be important for effective revascularization and cardiac recovery.
title: Abstract 8653: Endothelial ADAM10 Preserves Fate Stability to Coordinate Collateral Remodeling and Cardiac Repair After Ischemic Injury

abstract: Background: Chronic total occlusion (CTO) is a complete coronary artery occlusion lasting >3 months. Distal myocardial perfusion depends on collateral circulation, yet collateral development varies significantly among patients. No effective pro-collateral therapy currently exists. ADAM10 expression in peripheral blood correlates with collateral status and patient prognosis, suggesting a functional role in collateral remodeling. However, targeted ADAM10 delivery for collateral angiogenesis remains unexplored. Hypothesis: Localized, ultrasound-triggered delivery of ADAM10 active peptide promotes collateral circulation formation and improves blood flow recovery. Methods: ADAM10 active peptide and perfluorohexane (PFH) were co-encapsulated into PLGA nanovesicles, then integrated into methacryloyl hyaluronic acid hydrogel microspheres via microfluidic chip (HAMA@PA@A10/P). The system was validated in hindlimb ischemia and coronary collateral models. Ultrasound triggered PFH cavitation for on-demand ADAM10 release. Three groups were compared: (1) PFH-only microspheres with ultrasound (HAMA@PA@P); (2) PFH+ADAM10 microspheres without ultrasound (HAMA@PA@A10/P); (3) PFH+ADAM10 microspheres with ultrasound (HAMA@PA@A10/P+LIFU). Outcomes included collateral formation, blood flow recovery, and HUVEC migration/chemotaxis/sprouting. Results: In vitro, the HAMA@PA@A10/P+LIFU group significantly enhanced HUVEC migration, chemotaxis, and sprouting capacity versus both controls. In the hindlimb ischemia model (28 days), laser Doppler imaging showed blood flow recovery ratios of 0.84 (HAMA@PA@A10/P+LIFU) vs. 0.69 and 0.75 in controls ( P <0.05). In the coronary collateral model, the treatment group showed significantly improved cardiac function, reduced infarct size, and decreased cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Echocardiography confirmed significantly better ejection fraction and fractional shortening in the HAMA@PA@A10/P+LIFU group ( P <0.05). Conclusion: Localized, ultrasound-triggered ADAM10 delivery via HAMA@PA@A10/P microspheres effectively promotes endothelial function, enhances collateral circulation, restores perfusion, and improves cardiac function, offering a novel on-demand therapeutic strategy for CTO.
title: Abstract 8657: A Novel Ultrasound-Responsive Hydrogel Microsphere System for Controlled Delivery of ADAM10 Active Peptide to Promote Collateral Circulation Formation

abstract: Background: Mitral transcatheter valve edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) has become a treatment option for heart failure (HF) patients with mitral regurgitation (MR) at high surgical risk. However, limited data exist for the association between hospitalization at a center providing advanced HF therapy and clinical outcomes in patients after M-TEER. Research Question: Is treatment at an advanced HF care center associated with improved clinical outcomes among HF patients undergoing M-TEER? Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients undergoing M-TEER between April 2018 and December 2021 using the J-MITRA Registry data. The primary outcome was major cardiovascular adverse events during a 2-year follow-up period after the procedure. The association between advanced HF care status (hospitals performing heart transplantation and/or VAD implantation) and the outcomes was evaluated with a mixed-effects Cox model. Results: Among 4,351 patients, 986 (23%) patients were treated at advanced HF care centers. The use of HF medications increased across fiscal years at both advanced HF centers and non-advanced centers. Cumulative incidence of primary outcome developed 9.26 per 100 person-years in the advanced HF centers and 10.57 per 100 person-years in the non-advanced HF centers. The Advanced HF status was associated with a lower risk of the primary outcome than the non-advanced HF status after adjustment (hazard ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval, 0.54-0.96). In subgroup analyses, the association was consistent across age, sex, New York Heart Association class, left ventricular ejection fraction, MR etiology, and case volume strata. Conclusion: Advanced HF care status was associated with better outcomes among HF patients after M-TEER. Our findings suggest that multidisciplinary heart team management performed at advanced HF centers may be important for patients undergoing M-TEER.
title: Abstract 8662: Advanced Heart Failure Care Status and Outcomes in Patients Undergoing Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair

abstract: Background: Cardiac anxiety is a specific form of psychological distress, characterized by fear, hypervigilance to cardiac-related sensations, recurrence, and avoidance behaviors in patients with cardiovascular disease. It affects approximately one-third of patients after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and is associated with poorer quality of life (QoL), impaired recovery, poorer adherence to lifestyle recommendations and adverse cardiovascular prognosis. In a prior randomized controlled trial (RCT) we demonstrated that digital exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy for cardiac anxiety (CA-CBT) reduced cardiac anxiety and improves disease-specific health status after ACS. Building on these findings, we evaluated CA-CBT n patients following ACS, against a therapist-guided lifestyle intervention, serving as an active comparator to account for non-specific treatment effects. Methods: In this RCT, patients with prior ACS (≥6 months post STEMI, NSTEMI or unstable angina) and significant cardiac anxiety, as per clinical interview, were randomized to eight weeks of therapist-guided digital CA-CBT or to a therapist-guided, digital cardiac lifestyle intervention (CLI). CA-CBT included psychoeducation, interoceptive and situational exposure to feared cardiac-related sensations and activities. CLI included psychoeducation and behavior change-support for health behaviors, including physical activity, without exposure components. The primary outcome was change in cardiac anxiety measured by the Cardiac Anxiety Questionnaire (CAQ) at post-treatment. Secondary outcomes included disease-specific QoL (HeartQoL). Analyses were conducted using mixed-effects models. Results: A total of 178 participants (mean age 64.3 years, 61% men) were randomized to CA-CBT (90) or CLI (88). Participants receiving CA-CBT demonstrated greater reductions in cardiac anxiety compared with CLI (B=-6.77, 95% CI [-8.16, -5.39], d=0.78; P<.001), along with greater improvements in both emotional and physical QoL domains (emotional domain: B=0.24, 95% CI [0.11, 0.37], d=0.31; P<.001; physical domain: B=0.20, 95% CI [0.11, 0.29], d=0.29; P<.001) at posttreatment. Treatment credibility ratings were similar between groups. Conclusions: Among patients with clinically significant post-ACS cardiac anxiety, therapist-guided digital exposure-based CBT resulted in greater improvements in cardiac anxiety and disease-specific emotional and physical QoL compared with a lifestyle-focused intervention. These findings support exposure-based CBT as a promising adjunctive strategy to improve psychological recovery and QoL following ACS. Ongoing analyses will further evaluate long-term outcomes, additional patient-reported outcomes, and adherence to secondary prevention lifestyle recommendations.
title: Abstract 8677: Digital Exposure-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Cardiac Anxiety Following Acute Coronary Syndrome Compared with a Lifestyle-Focused Intervention: A Randomized Controlled Trial

abstract: Introduction: VEGF-A 165 b, the anti-angiogenic VEGF isoform, is overexpressed in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and those with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (MI). Stable angina pectoris due to atherosclerotic coronary artery disease (CAD) results in significant morbidity in 9 million people in the US and is a predictor of major adverse coronary events, such as an MI. It has been associated with poor coronary collateral blood flow, but the reason for poor collateralisation is unknown. Hypothesis. VEGF-A 165 b is raised in stable angina, and is correlated with clinical condition. Methods: We measured VEGF-A 165 b and the angiogenic isoform VEGF-A 165 a in plasma from 18 patients with confirmed CAD and 18 healthy individuals with no history of chest pain (source, Europa Biosite), using isoform specific ELISAs. Results: VEGF-A 165 a was no different between angina (22±9.6pg/ml) and control subjects (24±7.2pg/ml). VEGF-A 165 b was significantly higher in angina patients (114±43 pg/mL, n=18) than controls (22±9.6 pg/mL, n=18, p<0.0001 Kruskal Wallis, p<0.05, Dunn’s post-hoc test). VEGF-A 165 b concentration was significantly higher than VEGF-A 165 a in angina patients (p<0.05, Wilcoxon) but lower in healthy individuals (p=0.055). The ratio of VEGF-A 165 b to VEGF-A 165 a (ratio>1 - more anti-angiogenic, <1 - more angiogenic) was significantly higher in angina (median±IQR 4.0±9.5, N=13) compared with controls (0.06±0.26, N=14). Exercise stress electrocardiogram results (time on modified Bruce treadmill stress test) were significantly negatively correlated with VEGF-A 165 b concentration (r=0.394, p<0.05, Spearman). Conclusions: These data indicate that VEGF-A 165 b is raised in patients with stable angina pectoris and suggest that VEGF-A 165 b could be a potential target for pro-angiogenic therapy in patients with chronic stable angina.
