abstract: Background: Premature acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity. Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] has been recognized as a genetic risk factor for premature cardiovascular disease, whereas malondialdehyde-modified low-density lipoprotein (MDA-LDL), remnant cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B (ApoB) have emerged as markers of residual cardiovascular risk. However, the clinical and plaque characteristics of patients with premature ACS in contemporary Japanese practice remain poorly understood. Objective: We aimed to characterize the clinical and plaque phenotypes of patients with premature ACS using comprehensive lipid profiling and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) assessment of culprit lesions. Methods: This was a prospective single-center observational study including 153 consecutive patients with ACS who underwent emergency coronary angiography. Premature ACS was defined as age <55 years in men and <65 years in women. Clinical characteristics, lipid parameters including Lp(a), MDA-LDL, remnant lipoproteins, and ApoB, as well as culprit lesion morphology assessed by IVUS, were compared between patients with premature and non-premature ACS. Results: Among 153 patients with ACS, 29 had premature ACS and 124 had non-premature ACS. Despite lower HbA1c levels, patients with premature ACS exhibited a distinct metabolic and oxidized lipid phenotype. Compared with non-premature ACS patients, they had significantly higher BMI (27.9 ± 4.4 vs 23.0 ± 4.5 kg/m 2 ), triglycerides (193.3 ± 96.5 vs 130.0 ± 109.8 mg/dL), LDL-C (134.2 ± 37.0 vs 114.3 ± 38.4 mg/dL), MDA-LDL (110.2 ± 45.0 vs 82.8 ± 38.8 U/L), and remnant lipoprotein levels (4.6 ± 3.0 vs 3.2 ± 2.8 mg/dL), all p<0.01. In contrast, Lp(a) levels were not significantly different between the two groups (19 [9-29] vs 16 [8.8-31.5] mg/dL, p=0.67). IVUS analysis demonstrated that lipid-rich plaques tended to be more frequently observed in patients with premature ACS (83.3% vs 61.3%, p=0.057), whereas calcified plaques tended to be less common (12.5% vs 27.9%, p=0.13). In exploratory logistic regression analyses, MDA-LDL (OR 1.01, p<0.01), remnant lipoproteins (OR 1.16, p=0.02), and ApoB (OR 1.02, p=0.01) were independently associated with premature ACS in separate models including Lp(a). In contrast, Lp(a) was not significantly associated with premature ACS in these models. Conclusion: Premature ACS was characterized by a metabolic and oxidized lipid phenotype, including elevated MDA-LDL, remnant lipoproteins, and ApoB levels. These findings suggest that factors other than Lp(a) may contribute to premature disease onset and provide novel insights into risk stratification and potential targets for primary prevention.
title: Abstract 8699: Premature Acute Coronary Syndrome Is Characterized by a Metabolic and Oxidized Lipid Phenotype Beyond Lipoprotein(a)

abstract: Key Words: cardio-oncology; myocarditis; heart block; cardiogenic shock; immunosuppressive therapy. Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis is a rare but potentially fatal complication of cancer immunotherapy. Conduction abnormalities and cardiogenic shock may occur despite preserved ventricular function early in the disease course. We report a case of Pembrolizumab-associated Triple-M syndrome and biopsy-proven myocarditis presenting with complete heart block (CHB) and cardiogenic shock requiring VA-ECMO. A 55-year-old man with metastatic melanoma received his first Pembrolizumab infusion three weeks prior to presentation. Additional history included obesity status post sleeve gastrectomy, COPD, and HLD. The patient presented with dyspnea, dizziness, and visual disturbances. ECG demonstrated a new left bundle branch block followed by CHB. TTE initially showed preserved left ventricular systolic function. Despite pulse-dose corticosteroids, he developed lactic acidosis, ventricular arrhythmias, and progressive shock with evolving biventricular dysfunction. Coronary angiography revealed no obstructive CAD. Right heart catheterization demonstrated elevated filling pressures and impaired cardiac index. The relationship to Pembrolizumab exposure, CHB, and hemodynamic compromise raised suspicion for ICI myocarditis. Endomyocardial biopsy demonstrated lymphohistiocytic myocarditis. Concurrent neurologic and skeletal muscle involvement led to a diagnosis of immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated triple-M syndrome. A temporary transvenous pacemaker was placed for CHB. The patient received high-dose intravenous Methylprednisolone, Abatacept, Ruxolitinib, intravenous Immunoglobulin, and guideline-directed critical care support. Due to refractory cardiogenic shock and multiorgan dysfunction, he underwent VA-ECMO cannulation and was transferred to a tertiary center. After immunosuppressive therapy and mechanical circulatory support, ventricular function recovered sufficiently for ECMO decannulation. Repeat TTE demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55-60%. Although partial recovery of native conduction occurred, intermittent Mobitz II atrioventricular block persisted, requiring permanent pacemaker implantation. The patient was discharged and was transferred for rehabilitation. ICI myocarditis remains an uncommon but highly lethal immune-related adverse event. This case highlights its ability to present with a new bundle branch block and CHB before rapidly progressing to cardiogenic shock. Biopsy confirmation, early recognition, aggressive immunosuppression, and timely escalation to VA-ECMO were critical to survival. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for ICI myocarditis in patients presenting with new conduction abnormalities after checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
title: Abstract 8715: Fulminant Triple-M Syndrome Following Pembrolizumab: Biopsy-Proven Myocarditis with Complete Heart Block and Cardiogenic Shock Requiring VA-ECMO

abstract: Background: Hypercoagulable disorders are associated with increased risk of thrombosis. However, their impact on patients with left ventricular assist device (LVAD) is uncertain. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study utilizing the TriNetX database. We identified the adult patients who underwent LVAD implantation with and without hypercoagulable disorders then we did propensity score matching. The study assessed 5-year outcomes (thrombotic events, bleeding, mortality, and cardiovascular events) using hazard ratios (HR). We performed a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients who were treated after 2019, corresponding to the adoption of the HeartMate 3 device as a standard of care. Results: After propensity matching, 438 patients were included in each cohort with well-balanced baseline characteristics. Patients with hypercoagulable disorders had significantly higher rates of pulmonary embolism (HR 2.19, 95% CI 1.43-3.32), deep vein thrombosis (HR2.13, 95% CI 1.65-2.75), right heart failure (HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.15-1.86), and arterial thrombosis (HR 1.69, 95% CI 1.08-2.64). There were no significant differences between both cohorts in LVAD thrombosis (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.89-1.61), all-cause mortality (HR 1.17, 95%CI 0.94-1.47), or gastrointestinal bleeding (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.86-1.38). In the post-2019 sensitivity analysis, these findings remained consistent, with increased risks of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, and right heart failure. Conclusions: Hypercoagulable disorders in LVAD recipients are associated with increased thromboembolic complications. These results remained consistent in sensitivity analysis limited to the HeartMate 3 device, which highlights the need for specific anticoagulation strategies for these high-risk patients.
title: Abstract 8720: Outcomes of Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation in Patients with Hypercoagulable Disorders: A Propensity-Matched Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) accounts for 5-6% of acute myocardial infarctions (AMI) and is often considered lower-risk, fostering false reassurance that may lead to delayed presentation and undertreatment. Ventricular septal rupture (VSR) is a rare mechanical complication of AMI (~0.3% of cases), with only approximately ten post-MINOCA VSR cases reported. We present a case in which delayed presentation after weeks of undertreated symptoms culminated in cardiogenic shock requiring venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) and open-heart VSR repair. Case: A 56-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis, hyperlipidemia, and active tobacco use presented with three weeks of intermittent chest pain and two days of acute worsening, having self-treated with aspirin. The initial electrocardiogram showed no ST-segment elevation; high-sensitivity troponin was markedly elevated (17,000 ng/L). A repeat electrocardiogram showed anterior ST-segment elevation consistent with evolving transmural infarction. Left heart catheterization revealed non-obstructive coronary arteries with an LVEDP of 38 mmHg. The LAD and LCx arteries arose from separate aortic ostia, and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) confirmed the absence of obstructive pathology. Echocardiography showed an LVEF of 35-40%, a 1.7 cm apical VSR, an LV apical thrombus, and moderately-to-severely reduced RV function. Cardiac MRI confirmed LAD-territory infarction with an apical septal defect. Right heart catheterization demonstrated cardiogenic shock (cardiac index 1.6 L/min/m 2 ) with biventricular failure and a significant oximetric step-up at the ventricular level with a Qp:Qs of 4:1. After IABP support proved insufficient, central VA-ECMO was initiated via a right innominate artery graft. On hospital day 9, the patient underwent successful double-patch VSR repair with ECMO decannulation. The postoperative course was complicated by bilateral pulmonary emboli and multi-site deep vein thrombosis. She was discharged ambulatory on hospital day 31 with an LVEF of 42% and no residual VSR. Discussion: This case illustrates how MINOCA can produce transmural infarction of sufficient magnitude to cause catastrophic complications. The delay in presentation likely reflects false reassurance accompanying a perception of "non-obstructive coronaries." The ensuing course and complications were indistinguishable from the most severe obstructive MI presentations. Although angiography and IVUS confirmed non-obstructive coronary arteries, spontaneous recanalization of an initially occlusive thrombus cannot be excluded given the three-week interval between symptom onset and catheterization. MINOCA warrants the same clinical vigilance and guideline-directed follow-up as obstructive AMI to prevent fatal complications.
title: Abstract 8729: Ventricular Septal Rupture Complicating Myocardial Infarction with Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries: A Case for Heightened Clinical Vigilance

abstract: Background: In patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), the optimal duration of "triple therapy" is shifting toward "ultra-short" durations to mitigate bleeding. However, the ischemic safety of discontinuing aspirin within 7 days remains debated. Purpose: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of an "ultra-short" aspirin strategy (≤ 7 days) compared to conventional durations in patients with AF undergoing PCI, specifically assessing whether the significant reduction in major bleeding outweighs potential periprocedural ischemic risks. Methods: We performed a review of data from major randomized controlled trials (AUGUSTUS, SAFE-A, COACH-AF) and high-volume clinical registries (Danish National Registry, South Yorkshire Registry). This systematic review was conducted in strict accordance with PRISMA guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was performed. Title, abstract, and full-text screening were conducted to ensure blinded, rigorous study selection. Following the application of predefined inclusion criteria, we included 14 major studies comprising a total of 6,854 patients. The intervention was "ultra-short" aspirin (periprocedural to < 7 days) followed by dual antithrombotic therapy (DOAC + P2Y12 inhibitor). The comparator was conventional aspirin duration (> 1 month). Primary outcomes included International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) major/Clinically Relevant Non-Major (CRNM) bleeding and a composite of ischemic events (stent thrombosis [ST], myocardial infarction (MI), and stroke). Results: Data from 6,854 patients (Mean CHADS-VASc: 4.1; Mean HAS-BLED: 2.1) were analyzed. Ultra-short aspirin (median 3 to 6 days) was associated with a significant reduction in ISTH major/CRNM bleeding compared to 1-month therapy (e.g., 3.3% vs. 9.3% in the South Yorkshire cohort; HR 0.58 pooled across trials). Regarding ischemic safety, there was a slight numerical increase in early ST frequency within the first 30 days (0.85% vs. 0.19% in AUGUSTUS), but no significant difference in long-term MI, stroke, or cardiovascular death (COACH-AF: 2.5% vs 1.9%). Net clinical benefit consistently favored the < 7-day strategy. Across all datasets, the substantial reduction in bleeding events resulted in a consistent net clinical benefit for the ultra-short strategy, as the excess in bleeding events with conventional therapy (approx. 60 per 1000) outweighed the periprocedural ischemic signals. Conclusion: Dropping aspirin at hospital discharge (< 7 days) in AF patients undergoing PCI significantly reduces major bleeding with a manageable ischemic risk profile. These findings support a default ultra-short aspirin strategy in the contemporary drug-eluting stent (DES) era.
title: Abstract 8762: Safety and Efficacy of Ultra-Short Aspirin in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation Undergoing PCI: An Analysis of RCTs and Real-World Registries

abstract: Background: Despite strong guideline recommendations supporting sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) for patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and established cardiovascular disease, implementation in routine clinical practice remains suboptimal. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) clinical encounters may present an opportunity to improve implementation of cardioprotective therapies among high-risk patients. Methods: REMIND-DM was a multi site, pragmatic, prospective, cluster randomized quality improvement implementation study in patients with type 2 diabetes undergoing PCI within the BMC2 PCI Collaborative. Following a 6 month “baseline period”, the 23 participating PCI sites (caring for 7,045 patients over the study period) were randomized to usual care (12 sites) or a QI intervention (11 sites) consisting of a templated PCI report “reminder” of medication eligibility linked to a decision support tool. Sites were followed for a 6 month “evaluation period”. The primary outcome was new discharge prescription of SGLT2i or GLP-1RA. We assessed the consistency of the intervention effect on prespecified subgroups: age, sex, race, inpatient/outpatient encounter, elective/non-elective PCI, and insurance type. Results: Patients in the intervention arm were older, more often White or Asian, more often had HF and had private insurance or dual eligibility for Medicaid/Medicare. Rates of new discharge prescription in the entire cohort increased from 11.1% (baseline) to 12.9% (evaluation period), a 16.4% relative increase. The rate of new discharge prescription increased by 17.1% and 14.0%, over baseline, among usual care and intervention sites, respectively. The QI intervention was not associated with a change in new discharge prescription (aOR 0.91[0.78-1.06] p = 0.54); Figure 1 . Among patients undergoing elective PCI, the intervention was associated with a numerically greater likelihood of new discharge prescription (aOR 1.65, 95% CI 0.91-2.98) whereas among those undergoing non-elective PCI, the intervention was associated with a lower likelihood of prescription (aOR 0.69, 95% CI 0.48-0.97); P Interaction =0.023). The effect of the intervention was consistent across prespecified subgroups of age, sex, race, PCI setting, and insurance type (P Interaction >0.05 for all). Conclusions: A low touch reminder-based QI intervention implemented during a period of already increasing prescription of SGLT2i or GLP-1RA did not significantly increase new discharge prescriptions in high-risk patients with T2D undergoing PCI. Reminder-based nudges may be more effective in controlled environments of planned elective encounters, a signal that warrants further investigation to inform future implementation strategies.

abstract: Introduction: Identifying the primary driver of acute heart failure decompensation (ADHF) in patients with multiple concurrent cardiac insults is challenging. We present a case of progressive left bundle branch block (LBBB) as the predominant contributor to ADHF in a patient with mixed aortic valve disease (MAVD), highlighting the value of multimodality imaging and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) in this complex clinical scenario. Case Presentation: An 80-year-old man with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 43%), permanent atrial fibrillation, prior chemotherapy for B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, quadricuspid aortic valve with moderate aortic regurgitation (AR) and moderately severe low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (AS), and chronic LBBB presented for 1 month of progressive exertional dyspnea and intermittent chest pain. ECG demonstrated slow AF and LBBB (QRS 172 ms) meeting Strauss criteria. CXR revealed bilateral pulmonary edema. Repeat TTE showed new reduced LVEF 15-20% with unchanged MAVD severity ( Image 1 ). Coronary angiography identified severe ostial D1 and mid LCx disease, out of proportion to the degree of LV dysfunction. Workup for TAVR/PCI vs. SAVR/CABG was initiated. TEE redemonstrated no valvular lesion meeting standalone guideline severity criteria. Further imaging was pursued given newly recognized severe LV dilation: cardiac CT revealed moderate AS by planimetry (AVA 1.4 cm 2 ) and a wide coaptation gap (measured at 0.254 cm 2 ), while cardiac MRI demonstrated end-diastolic reverse aortic flow velocity 25-30 cm/s and aortic regurgitant fraction 58% ( Image 2 ), favoring SAVR over TAVR for severe AR given low coronary ostia and mild AV calcifications. However, serial ECG review revealed gradual LBBB progression over prior four years (QRS from 120 ms to 172 ms, image 3 ), temporally correlating with adverse remodeling and ADHF, while MAVD had remained stable on annual surveillance. After multidisciplinary discussion, CRT with biventricular pacing was offered as the primary intervention. Post-CRT ECG showed adequate LV capture ( image 3 ). At yearly follow-up, patient returned to unrestricted physical activity. LVEF improved to 39% ( image 3 ), LV volumes nearly normalized, with otherwise stable MAVD. Discussion: This case underscores the diagnostic complexity of ADHF with concurrent structural, electrical, and ischemic contributors. Serial ECG analysis identified LBBB progression as the primary culprit, while multimodality imaging enabled accurate characterization of MAVD severity. CRT produced significant clinical and hemodynamic recovery, deferring high-risk valve surgery. This case supports the systematic ECG trend review and a multimodality imaging strategy when managing multifactorial cardiomyopathy, and demonstrates the therapeutic potential of CRT when progressive LBBB coexists with chronic severe AR and borderline AS.
title: Abstract 8771: When the Bundle Breaks the Heart: Progressive Left Bundle Branch Block Unmasking Severe Cardiomyopathy in the Setting of Mixed Aortic Valve Disease - A Multimodality Imaging Approach

abstract: Introduction: In the phase 3 EXPLORER-HCM study (NCT03470545), mavacamten, a cardiac myosin inhibitor (CMI), improved symptoms, exercise capacity and health status compared with placebo in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). A 27-protein proteomic cardiovascular (CV) risk score, the CV Risk SomaSignal® Test (SST), has been previously established using large multicohort data and predicted risk of CV outcomes (4-year likelihood of myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, or death) in studies of various classes of drugs (e.g. GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors). However, the effect of CMI on the CV Risk SST has not been reported. Aim: To assess the effect of 30 weeks of mavacamten treatment versus placebo on the CV Risk SST in patients with obstructive HCM. Methods: The CV Risk SST was measured from EXPLORER-HCM patients at baseline and week 30 using SomaScan (v4.1). Pharmacodynamic analyses of the CV Risk SST were performed on paired data using an ANCOVA model with fixed effects for baseline biomarker value, treatment and study stratification factors. Additional subgroup analyses of the CV Risk SST were conducted using a separate ANCOVA model with fixed effects for baseline biomarker value, treatment, subgroup, and treatment-by-subgroup interaction terms. Results: Baseline CV Risk SST scores did not differ significantly between the mavacamten (n=92) and placebo (n=105) arms (median [IQR]: 9.8 [5.4, 18.8] vs 8.4 [4.8, 17.0], respectively; P=0.23). At week 30, mavacamten treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the CV Risk SST compared with a trend towards an increase in the placebo arm (Figure 1A). The model-adjusted percent decrease (mean [95% CI]) in CV Risk SST from baseline was -23.0% [-13.1, -31.9] with mavacamten; in contrast, there was a 10.9% [-1.2, 24.4] increase with placebo. The relative reduction in CV Risk SST for mavacamten vs placebo was -30.6% [-19.6, -40.1], P <0.001. Furthermore, subgroup analyses demonstrated a consistent reduction in CV Risk SST at week 30 with mavacamten versus placebo across baseline variables including age, gender, BMI, LVEF, history of hypertension or atrial fibrillation, sarcomere gene mutation status, disease duration, beta-blocker use and disease severity (Figure 1B). Conclusions: In patients with obstructive HCM, mavacamten treatment significantly reduced the proteomic CV Risk SST score compared with placebo, with consistent results across various patient subgroups.
title: Abstract 8797: The Effect of Mavacamten Treatment on Proteomic Cardiovascular Risk Score in Patients with Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy in the EXPLORER-HCM Study

abstract: Keywords: STEMI; Apple Watch; wearable ECG; coronary artery disease; digital health. Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) devices are increasingly utilized for arrhythmia detection, but their role in identifying acute coronary syndromes remains less established. These devices may facilitate earlier recognition of ischemic events and prompt timely medical evaluation. We report a case in which serial Apple Watch ECG recordings identified ischemic changes that led to the diagnosis of acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). A 52-year-old man with HTN, HLD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and prior ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm repair presented with acute, severe chest pain. He routinely checks his ECG using his Apple Watch but during these ongoing symptoms, he noticed a change in the shape of his ECG recordings prompting him to seek medical attention. Although symptoms partially improved, concern regarding the abnormal ECG recordings prompted presentation to the emergency department. On arrival, he was hypertensive and tachycardic. 12-Lead ECG demonstrated ST-segment elevation in the anterior and high-lateral leads with reciprocal inferior changes. Point-of-care ultrasound revealed anteroseptal and anterolateral wall motion abnormalities. Given a history of prior aortic surgery, CT angiography was performed and ruled out acute aortic pathology. Emergent coronary angiography demonstrated 100% occlusion of the ostial-to-mid left anterior descending artery and 95% stenosis of the third obtuse marginal artery, confirming acute anterior STEMI. The patient received Aspirin, Ticagrelor, and Intravenous heparin before undergoing successful percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent placement to the left anterior descending artery, followed by staged intervention of the obtuse marginal branch. Guideline-directed medical therapy for ischemic cardiomyopathy was initiated. TTE demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% with extensive apical and septal hypokinesis and a small left ventricular apical thrombus. Anticoagulation with Apixaban was initiated in addition to dual antiplatelet therapy. The patient remained clinically stable and was discharged with close cardiology follow-up. This case highlights the emerging role of wearable ECG technology in the early recognition of acute coronary syndromes. Prior studies have shown that wearable ECGs can detect ischemic and infarction-related changes using lead I and bipolar-derived precordial lead configurations. In this case, serial Apple Watch recordings demonstrating ST-segment elevation prompted emergency evaluation and subsequent diagnosis of a STEMI. Earlier recognition of ischemia may reduce delays to diagnosis and revascularization. Further investigation is warranted to define the role of wearable ECG devices in the detection of cardiovascular emergencies.
title: Abstract 8810: Consumer Wearable ECG Identification of Ischemic ST-Segment Abnormalities Leading to Diagnosis of Acute Anterior STEMI Diagnosed by Apple Watch

abstract: Background: Whether percutaneous ventricular assist devices (pVAD) improve outcomes over intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) or standard care during high-risk PCI (HRPCI) or cardiogenic shock (CS) remains contested. Two recent meta-analyses reached opposite conclusions after the DanGer Shock trial. Methods: We searched PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL through May 2026 for RCTs comparing pVAD (Impella 2.5/CP/5.0 or TandemHeart) with IABP or standard care in adults undergoing HRPCI or with CS. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2. Outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR) by Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect and DerSimonian-Laird random-effects methods. TSA used O'Brien-Fleming alpha-spending (alpha 2.5%, beta 10%, anticipated RRR 20%). Certainty was graded with GRADE. Results: Seven RCTs (n=969) were included. In the pre-specified CS-only primary analysis, 30-day mortality did not differ between pVAD and IABP (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.75-1.53; I2=0%; k=5); adding HRPCI did not change this (RR 1.13, 0.82-1.57). Long-term (>=6 month) mortality favored pVAD over control (RR 0.81, 0.67-0.97; p=0.026; k=2), but was contributed 89% by DanGer Shock, nullified on leave-one-out, and did not cross the O'Brien-Fleming boundary on TSA (39% of required information size accrued; observed |z|=2.24 vs required 3.12). A pre-specified subgroup analysis showed null effect against IABP head-to-head (RR 1.00, 0.57-1.76) and benefit only against standard care (RR 0.78, 0.64-0.96), resolving the contradiction between recent meta-analyses. pVAD was associated with more major bleeding (RR 2.27, 1.60-3.24), limb ischemia (RR 5.32, 1.93-14.69), and AKI/RRT (RR 1.42, 1.08-1.88); no harm signal crossed TSA boundaries. Conclusions: Randomized evidence is best read as a single positive trial in a narrowly selected STEMI-CS phenotype rather than a robust pooled benefit. The long-term effect is driven by one trial, nullified on its removal, and not trial-sequentially robust. The pVAD carries consistent excess bleeding, limb ischemia, and renal injury. Phenotype-specific, not universal, adoption is supported.

register_verdicts.note: Pooled randomised trials of pVAD do not address transportability by emulation in unselected registry populations.

title: Abstract 8818: Updated Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis of Percutaneous Ventricular Assist Devices in Cardiogenic Shock and High-Risk Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

abstract: Background: Coronary obstruction is a feared complication of valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement (ViV-TAVR), especially with low coronary height, narrow sinuses, externally mounted leaflets, or short virtual valve-to-coronary distance. BASILICA, chimney/snorkel stenting, ShortCut, UNICORN, and leaflet-modification strategies are used, but evidence is fragmented. We evaluated pooled short-term outcomes after these strategies in high-risk ViV-TAVR. Methods: We searched MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library through April 2026 for adult human studies of high-risk ViV-TAVR treated with BASILICA, chimney/snorkel stenting, ShortCut, UNICORN, or other leaflet-modification strategies. Eligible designs were cohorts, registries, comparative studies, and series with at least 3 patients and extractable outcomes. Case reports, native-valve-only studies without extractable ViV data, imaging-only studies, and duplicate cohorts were excluded or narratively synthesized. The primary outcome was acute coronary obstruction or related coronary event; secondary outcomes were 30-day mortality, stroke/TIA, and bailout PCI/rescue stenting. Single-arm proportional meta-analysis used a random-intercept logistic model with logit transformation. Because strategy subgroups were small and clinically heterogeneous, subgroup estimates were interpreted descriptively rather than as comparative efficacy. No direct comparative trials were found. Results: Seven studies including 188 patients contributed to the primary analysis. Acute coronary obstruction or related coronary events occurred in 14 patients, with a pooled random-effects proportion of 5.68% (95% CI, 1.99%-15.17%; I^2=0.0%) and prediction interval of 0.94%-27.70%. Estimates were 11.63% for BASILICA, 5.00% for ShortCut, and 3.13% for UNICORN; subgroup differences were not significant (p=0.3825). The chimney/snorkel subgroup included one small zero-event study and was not reliable for comparison. Six studies (178 patients) contributed to 30-day outcomes: mortality was 1.69% (95% CI, 0.54%-5.09%; 3 events), and stroke/TIA was 1.69% (95% CI, 0.54%-5.09%; 3 events). Bailout PCI/rescue stenting occurred in 13 of 188 patients, with a pooled proportion of 3.65% (95% CI, 0.67%-17.55%). Sensitivity analyses were consistent: strict ViV 5.06%, broad 4.26%, and no-abstract 3.80%. Conclusions: Contemporary coronary protection and leaflet-modification strategies for high-risk ViV-TAVR appear feasible and were associated with low 30-day mortality and neurologic event rates, but coronary events were not eliminated. Evidence does not support ranking individual strategies because studies are small, observational, heterogeneous, and variably define outcomes. These findings support computed tomography-based selection and individualized procedural planning.
title: Abstract 8835: Coronary Protection and Leaflet Modification in High-Risk Valve-in-Valve Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Coronary endarterectomy (CE) is an adjunctive procedure performed during coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) for patients with diffuse coronary artery disease. Perioperative blood loss during CABG with CE is a modifiable risk factor impacting wound complications, hospital stay, and total costs; however, the differential impact of on-pump versus off-pump techniques remains poorly characterized. This study investigated perioperative bleeding-related parameters, stratified by perfusion strategy and specific coronary vessels. Eligible patients who underwent CABG with CE at our center between January 2016 and January 2025 and had complete perioperative data were retrospectively enrolled. The primary endpoints included the red blood cell transfusion rate and the reduction in hemoglobin (Hb) levels from preoperative to both immediate postoperative and day-1 postoperative states, with specific primary outcomes further stratified via subgroup analyses according to the coronary targets of endarterectomy (left anterior descending [LAD], right coronary artery [RCA], left circumflex artery [LCX], multiple vessels, and other sites). A total of 1,106 patients (age: 61.1 ± 9.1 years; male: 79.4%) were included. Overall, off-pump CABG with CE was associated with a significantly smaller reduction in pre-to-postoperative Hb compared with the on-pump group (median 10 g/L [IQR 1, 18] vs. 24 g/L [IQR 15, 33], P < 0.0001). Similarly, the pre-to-postoperative day-1 reduction in Hb was significantly lower in the off-pump group than in the on-pump group (median 22 g/L [IQR 13, 31] vs. 30 g/L [IQR 19, 40], P < 0.0001). Regarding blood product utilization, while the overall blood transfusion rates remained comparable between the two cohorts (28.7% vs. 30.6%, P = 0.5041), the off-pump technique yielded a statistically significant reduction in the red blood cell transfusion rate (21.0% vs. 27.7%, P = 0.0099). Stratified analyses based on CE target sites revealed that off-pump CABG significantly reduced both pre-to-postoperative and pre-to-postoperative day-1 Hb drops in patients receiving LAD-CE or RCA-CE (all P < 0.0001), while the red blood cell transfusion rate was markedly lower among patients with RCA-CE undergoing off-pump procedures ( P = 0.0079). Regarding major clinical outcomes, the off-pump group was associated with a significantly lower incidence of perioperative myocardial infarction (POMI) within 48 hours compared with the on-pump group (7.9% vs. 12.4%, P = 0.015). In patients undergoing CABG with CE, the off-pump strategy is associated with superior overall blood preservation and favorable early clinical outcomes compared with the conventional on-pump approach.
title: Abstract 8870: Reduction of Perioperative Blood Loss in Off-Pump versus On-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Combined with Coronary Endarterectomy: A Cohort Study

abstract: Introduction: Salmonella is one of the most common causes of foodborne illness in the USA. Salmonella serogroup C has a disproportionately high propensity of extraintestinal manifestations. Perimyocarditis, defined as primary myocardial inflammation associated with secondary extension into the pericardium, is a rare extraintestinal complication, with only 2 cases reported in the literature associated with Salmonella serogroup C. Case Description: 39-year-old healthy immunocompetent male presented to the emergency department with fever, chest pain and diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. Electrocardiogram revealed inferolateral ST segment elevation. (Figure 1). Troponin I was elevated to 11.2 ng/mL (abnormal if >0.119). He was with given 325 mg of aspirin and 180 mg of ticagrelor and transferred for urgent cardiac catheterization. On arrival to the coronary intensive care unit, the patient had persistent chest pain, and remained afebrile with stable vital signs. Electrocardiogram showed persistent ST elevation, and bedside echocardiogram showed grossly normal biventricular function. Given the clinical context, a decision was made to order stool and blood cultures, and a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Both stool and blood cultures were positive for Salmonella serogroup C. Cardiac MRI showed left ventricular (LV) dilatation and a LVEF of 45%, myocardial edema and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) of anterior, anterolateral and inferolateral walls. Delayed enhancement of the pericardium was also present (Figure 2). The patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone for 7 days and oral ciprofloxacin for an additional 7 days. In addition, colchicine was started for treatment of pericarditis. Patient felt improvement of chest pain within 1 day and was discharged on hospital day 10. Repeat cardiac MRI at 4 months showed normal LV volume and systolic function, mild subepicardial and mid-myocardial LGE involving the basal to mid-anterior, inferolateral and anterolateral wall segments, and no evidence of myocardial edema or pericardial inflammation. Colchicine was discontinued at that time. At 9-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic and had resumed his work as a firefighter. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of history of present illness to diagnose and treat perimyocarditis, a potentially fatal extraintestinal manifestation of Salmonella serogroup C, and avoid iatrogenic interventions. Given the overlap of those symptoms with other infectious causes of myocarditis, a high index of suspicion is necessary.
title: Abstract 8875: Salmonella Perimyocarditis Presenting as an Acute Coronary Syndrome Phenocopy

abstract: Intro: Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) is a major cause of graft dysfunction after orthotopic heart transplantation (OHT). Although endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is central for diagnosis, histopathology may miss clinically significant antibody-mediated injury. Case: A 68-year-old woman with end-stage heart failure from nonischemic cardiomyopathy, status post OHT 5 years earlier, complicated by chronic kidney disease, mitral regurgitation, and mild left ventricular dysfunction, was hospitalized with dyspnea, cough, and fatigue. She was febrile and tachycardic, with elevated NT-proBNP and chest radiography showing a left lower lobe infiltrate. She received antibiotics for presumed sepsis. Mycophenolate mofetil was temporarily held then resumed, sirolimus was reduced for supratherapeutic levels, and a new right popliteal venous thromboembolism prompted apixaban initiation. She re-presented shortly after discharge with hematochezia and melena. Anticoagulation was held, but her endoscopy was complicated by hypoxia and PEA arrest. Post-arrest transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) noted left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 45-50%, new right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, and moderate-severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR). CT angiography (CTA) was initially deferred due to acute kidney injury, and ventilation-perfusion scan was intermediate probability for pulmonary embolism (PE). Repeat TTE showed LVEF 34%, RV dilation with reduced function, and septal flattening. Later, CTA ruled out PE. Right heart catheterization with EMB showed elevated biventricular filling pressures and low output consistent with cardiogenic shock. Coronary angiography ruled out cardiac allograft vasculopathy. EMB was negative for cellular rejection (0R), with negative C4d staining and no significant intracapillary CD68-positive monocytes. However, donor-specific antibody (DSA) testing revealed de novo reactivity against HLA-Cw10, HLA-B60, HLA-DR53, and HLA-DQ8, absent 6 months ago. She was treated for presumed biopsy-negative AMR with pulse-dose methylprednisolone, anti-thymocyte globulin, plasmapheresis, and intravenous immunoglobulin. Temporary mechanical circulatory support was deferred given goals of care. She ultimately died from refractory cardiogenic shock. Discussion: This case illustrates the limitations of relying on EMB alone to exclude AMR. Despite negative EMB, her de novo DSAs, biventricular failure, and low cardiac output supported AMR cardiogenic shock. New RV failure with worsening TR appropriately raised concern for PE, but persistent shock with progressive graft dysfunction should prompt reassessment for rejection while mimics are excluded. In retrospect, the left lower lobe infiltrate may have reflected pulmonary edema, and her transition from tacrolimus to sirolimus months earlier may have contributed to subsequent rejection.
title: Abstract 8898: Biopsy-Negative Antibody-Mediated Rejection Mimicking Pulmonary Embolism After Heart Transplantation

abstract: Background: Cardiac troponin (cTn) elevations above the 99th percentile upper reference limit (URL) are central to the diagnosis of myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA); however, limited data exist on the relationship between the magnitude of cTn elevation and multimodality imaging findings. Research Question: Are cTn values associated with imaging findings in patients presenting clinically with MINOCA? Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of participants enrolled in the Heart Attack Research Program (HARP, NCT02905357), a prospective multicenter MINOCA cohort who underwent coronary angiography, multivessel optical coherence tomography (OCT), and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) within 1 week of MI. Images were interpreted by independent core laboratories Patients were stratified by peak cTnI or cTnT (contemporary and hs-cTn assays) ratios (relative to the sex-specific 99th percentile URL) into the top tertile (N=112) versus the bottom two tertiles (N=224). Associations between initial and peak cTn ratios, OCT-defined culprit lesion morphology, and CMR diagnoses were evaluated. Results: Among 336 participants (80% female, median age 58) with MINOCA, median initial and peak cTn ratios were 6.92х URL (IQR 2.27-32.90) and 32.48х URL (IQR 10.76-111.00), respectively. Both were higher in the top tertile than in the bottom two tertiles (initial: 69.98х vs. 3.89х; peak: 193.33х vs. 15.03х URL; both p<0.001). Participants in the top tertile of peak cTn were more likely to be female (88% vs. 76%, p=0.009) and less likely to have hypertension (38% vs. 52%, p=0.017) or diabetes (7% vs. 23%, p<0.001). STEMI was more frequent in the top tertile (9% vs. 3%, p=0.022). Presenting symptoms, angiographic findings, and OCT culprit lesion frequency or type did not differ between groups. The frequency of 3-vessel OCT was the same similar (66% vs. 63%). CMR findings (n=284) differed markedly: CMR-confirmed MI (51% of top tertile vs. 16% bottom two tertiles), ischemic findings (64% vs. 28%), infarct size (3.75g vs. 0.66g), and normal CMR (15% vs. 48%) all differed significantly ( p<0.001), with no differences in regional ischemic injury or MINOCA mimics ( Figure ). CMR was performed earlier in the top tertile (median 5 vs. 7 days, p=0.001) Conclusions: In MINOCA, higher initial and peak cTn ratios were associated with CMR-confirmed myocardial infarction and larger infarct size, but not with angiographic findings or OCT-defined culprit lesion morphology.
title: Abstract 8917: Relationship Between Cardiac Troponin and Multimodality Imaging Findings in MINOCA

abstract: Background: Desmoplakin cardiomyopathy (DSP-CM) is a high-risk genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy characterized by myocardial fibrosis, ventricular dysfunction, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. A distinctive feature is the occurrence of myocarditis-like "hot-phase" episodes, which may precede overt cardiomyopathy and are frequently misdiagnosed as acute myocarditis. Recognition of these episodes is critical because they carry important prognostic implications and may prompt genetic testing, family screening, and disease-specific management. Case Presentation: A 34-year-old man presented with acute substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia with first-degree atrioventricular block, inferior Q waves, diffuse ST-segment depression, and T-wave inversions. High-sensitivity troponin peaked at 100,283 ng/L. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 45-50%).Coronary angiography demonstrated an anomalous circumflex artery arising from the proximal right coronary artery without obstructive coronary artery disease. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) revealed extensive late gadolinium enhancement involving the interventricular septum and inferior wall with associated regional hypokinesis. T2 mapping demonstrated increased myocardial signal consistent with active inflammation. Acute myocarditis was initially suspected, and the patient was treated with pulse-dose corticosteroids. Endomyocardial biopsy was nondiagnostic.Given the extensive pattern of myocardial injury, genetic testing was pursued and identified a pathogenic desmoplakin (DSP) mutation, establishing the diagnosis of DSP cardiomyopathy presenting as a hot-phase inflammatory episode. Conclusion: This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing acute myocarditis from inflammatory presentations of DSP cardiomyopathy. In young patients presenting with chest pain, marked troponin elevation, nonobstructive coronary arteries, and extensive myocardial fibrosis on CMR, underlying genetic cardiomyopathy should be considered. Recognition of DSP-associated hot-phase disease is important because affected patients are at increased risk for ventricular arrhythmias, progressive ventricular dysfunction, and heart failure. Early diagnosis facilitates genetic counseling, cascade screening of relatives, risk stratification, and implementation of appropriate long-term surveillance and therapeutic strategies.
title: Abstract 8923: Desmoplakin-Associated Cardiomyopathy Presenting as Severe Myocarditis

abstract: Introduction: Mechanical complications post-acute myocardial infarction (AMI) are uncommon, especially in the percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) era. Right ventricular (RV) free-wall rupture is even rarer, most commonly from right coronary (RCA) ischemia. RV free wall rupture from left main (LM) ischemia is even more exceedingly rare with only a few reported cases. We present the first case of RV free wall rupture from LM ischemia and wrap-around left anterior descending (LAD) causing RV apical aneurysm with pseudoaneurysm within the aneurysm. Case Presentation: An 81-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (AF) presented with crushing chest pain after days of gastrointestinal discomfort. Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed AF, right bundle branch block, ST elevation in aVR/V1, and diffuse ST-segment depression (no q-waves) (Figure 1), suggesting acute LM ischemia. The patient developed profound hypotension, vasopressors were initiated. Bedside TTE revealed an RV apical aneurysm (Figure 2) with an extending pseudoaneurysm, local hemopericardium, and new severe LVEF reduction; contrast confirmed contained rupture with no extravasation beyond the pseudoaneurysm. Emergent invasive coronary angiography revealed 99% distal LM stenosis extending to branch ostia with TIMI 2 flow (Figure 3). An intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) was placed for cardiogenic shock. Emergent interdisciplinary discussion with cardiology and cardiothoracic surgeons deferred surgery due to profound shock and contained RV rupture. Emergent PCI with drug eluting stent to the distal LM was performed. Right heart catheterization showed elevated filling pressures and borderline cardiac index, prompting exchange of IABP for Impella CP. Follow-up/Outcomes: Despite PCI, refractory cardiogenic shock developed. Repeat TTE showed a stable, contained pseudoaneurysm but worsening biventricular failure. On hospital day 5, she suffered asystolic cardiac arrest and expired. Discussion: This is the first reported case of LM ischemia-induced RV apical free-wall aneurysm, with pseudoaneurysm. One prior case report described RV free-wall rupture following an anterior wall ST-elevation MI (STEMI) from LAD occlusion but did not involve aneurysm formation. Our case highlights the capacity for critical LM ischemia to cause RV apical free-wall infarction without EKG evidence of anterior wall STEMI. RV free-wall rupture by AMI is exceedingly rare and typically occurs with RCA occlusion. The incidence of AMI-induced RV free-wall rupture is ill-defined given only a few reported cases of this phenomenon. Contrast-enhanced TTE was pivotal in identifying the RV apical aneurysm/pseudoaneurysm, essential for planning potential operative intervention, though this was ultimately not attempted for this patient. RV infarction and mechanical complications are rare but clear potential complications of LM and LAD AMI.
title: Abstract 8932: Acute Myocardial Infarction from Critical Left Main Disease Complicated by Pseudoaneurysm within an Apical Right Ventricular Aneurysm

abstract: Introduction: Endovascular treatment of calcified common femoral artery (CFA) disease remains challenging because of the CFA’s biomechanical environment and traditional status as a no-stent zone. Intravascular lithotripsy (IVL), atherectomy, and hybrid vessel-preparation strategies may expand endovascular options, but contemporary evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Research Question/Hypothesis: This study evaluated procedural effectiveness and acute safety of endovascular calcium-modification strategies for symptomatic calcified CFA lesions. Methods: We conducted a systematic review of adult studies and conference abstracts from January 2018 through April 2026 evaluating atherosclerotic CFA disease treated with IVL, atherectomy, or hybrid calcium-modification approaches. Eligible reports included cohorts, registries, comparative observational studies, and case series with extractable CFA-specific outcomes; open endarterectomy-only reports, single-patient case reports, reviews, and duplicate cohorts were excluded. A single-arm proportional meta-analysis used a random-effects model with logit transformation. Primary endpoints were technical success, bailout stenting, and acute periprocedural complications; follow-up patency and target lesion revascularization were summarized descriptively when definitions or timepoints varied. Results: Eighteen studies met inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis, and 13 contributed to the primary pooled analysis. Technical success was achieved in 725 of 779 cases, with a pooled proportion of 96.65% (95% CI, 89.20%-99.02%; I 2 =89.5%). Bailout stenting occurred in 74 of 966 treated lesions or limbs, with a pooled proportion of 8.16% (95% CI, 5.22%-12.53%; I 2 =59.5%). Distal embolization occurred in 9 of 750 cases (1.87%; 95% CI, 1.05%-3.30%; I 2 =0.0%), perforation in 10 of 807 cases (2.07%; 95% CI, 1.08%-3.91%; I 2 =7.0%), and flow-limiting dissection in 4 of 507 cases (1.90%; 95% CI, 0.88%-4.05%; I 2 =0.0%). Descriptive strategy-specific estimates showed technical success of 97.50% for IVL-based approaches and 94.35% for atherectomy-based approaches, with bailout stenting rates of 9.73% and 7.76%, respectively; formal head-to-head pooling was not performed due to limited comparative evidence. Sensitivity analysis excluding abstract-only studies remained directionally consistent. Conclusion: Endovascular calcium-modification strategies for symptomatic calcified CFA disease demonstrate high acute technical success, infrequent bailout stenting, and low periprocedural complication rates in the no-stent zone. These findings support acute procedural feasibility in selected lesions; however, prospective comparative studies with standardized definitions and longer follow-up are needed to define the optimal strategy and clarify durability.
title: Abstract 8934: Endovascular Calcium-Modification Strategies for Calcified Common Femoral Artery Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) is a leading cause of global mortality from plaque rupture/thrombosis. Blood-based transcriptomic research seeking signatures is limited by “noise” from variability, heterogeneous cohorts and platform bias failing to separate acute events from chronic/stable CAD (sCAD). We built an AI/ML pipeline for a consensus gene panel distinguishing CAD and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) from stable disease and atherosclerosis. Methods: We harmonised 45 public datasets: GEO transcriptomic (30 microarray, 10 RNA-seq) and PRIDE proteomic (5 LC-MS/MS) from blood, PBMCs, plasma/serum and arterial/plaque tissue spanning healthy controls, stable CAD, unstable angina (UA), AMI and recurrent AMI (Re-AMI). Differential expression used limma (microarray, LC-MS/MS) and DESeq2 (RNA-seq); effect sizes were combined by random-effects meta analysis (metafor) and Robust Rank Aggregation across four contrasts (AMI vs control, vs stable CAD, vs UA, vs Re-AMI). Genes were tiered as core consensus (FDR<0.05, directionally concordant in ≥3/4 contrasts), AMI specific by removing chronic sCAD noise, severity(vs UA) and recurrence associated(vs Re-AMI), followed by Meta-GSEA. Consensus proteins were tested for concordant abundance (cross omics validation); the core panel is trained by multi-ensemble model, evaluated by AUC in held-out validation. Results: The core tier showed AMI upregulation of ADAMDEC1, PLA2G4A, CCNA1, OLFM4, AQP9, SOCS3, TNFAIP6, CR1, S100A9 and HP, and downregulation of SNCA and SELENBP1. The AMI specific tier (vs controls and sCAD) was enriched for innate-immune/neutrophil-activation markers (AQP9, RNASE3, SOCS3, TNFAIP6, CR1, HP, OLFM4, S100A9). Severity (AMI vs UA) and recurrence (AMI vs Re-AMI) signatures converged on SOCS3, AQP9, TNFAIP6, S100A9, CR1 and HP, with persistent innate-immune dysregulation. Meta-GSEA revealed inflammatory-metabolic reprogramming: Interferon-Gamma Response (NES=+2.18) and Oxidative Phosphorylation (NES=+2.10) were most enriched, with TNF-alpha/NF-kB, MTORC1, Inflammatory Response and E2F/MYC activation, and downregulation of Heme Metabolism and KRAS signalling. At protein level, Haptoglobin (HP), Calprotectin (S100A8/A9) and Olfactomedin-4 (OLFM4) showed concordant abundance in independent LC-MS/MS cohorts, confirming reproducibility. The ensemble classifier discriminated AMI from healthy controls and stable CAD and maintained cross-platform performance, complementing markers such as cardiac troponin and myoglobin. Conclusions: This multi-omics framework yields a tiered panel distinguishing acute infarction from chronic CAD and resolving ACS severity and recurrence, reflecting the inflammatory-metabolic reprogramming central to AMI, and offers a scalable basis for blood-based point-of-care ACS diagnostics before irreversible myocardial damage.
title: Abstract 8962: An Integrative Multi-Omics Machine Learning Framework for Cross-Platform Identification of Diagnostic Gene Panels in Coronary Artery Disease and Acute Coronary Syndrome

abstract: Background: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) can progress to cardiogenic shock requiring advanced therapies, including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD), or heart transplantation. National patterns of illness severity, advanced therapy use, and disparities in outcomes remain incompletely characterized. Methods: Adult female hospitalizations with PPCM were identified in the National Inpatient Sample from 2016-2023 using ICD-10-CM. The primary outcome was composite advanced therapy use, defined as ECMO, durable LVAD, or heart transplantation. The secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Survey weights generated national estimates. Multivariable survey-weighted logistic regression assessed associations with advanced therapy use and mortality, adjusting for demographics, payer, income quartile, hospital characteristics, year, shock, respiratory failure, acute kidney injury (AKI), cardiac arrest, and comorbidities. Results: A weighted 36,380 PPCM hospitalizations were identified. Annual hospitalization volume remained stable, while illness severity increased: shock rose from 5.75% to 9.75%, AKI from 12.47% to 17.92%, and mean charges from $69,332 to $130,075. Overall in-hospital mortality was 1.62% and did not show a significant adjusted temporal trend. Advanced therapy use remained uncommon overall (2.83%), increasing from 1.74% in 2016 to 3.04% in 2023 and peaking at 4.17% in 2022. Use was concentrated in urban teaching hospitals (3.41%) compared with urban non-teaching hospitals (0.32%), with no events observed in rural hospitals. Advanced therapy use was similar among Black and White patients (3.07% vs 2.52%) and lower among Hispanic patients (2.23%), but race/ethnicity was not independently associated with advanced therapy use after adjustment. Large hospital bed size was associated with greater advanced therapy use (aOR 6.86, 95% CI 2.02-23.35; p=0.002), as were shock (aOR 10.65; p<0.001), coagulopathy (aOR 4.09; p<0.001), AKI (aOR 1.64; p=0.037), arrhythmias (aOR 1.79; p=0.015), and Elixhauser burden (aOR 1.22; p=0.012). Hispanic patients had higher adjusted mortality than White patients (aOR 2.92, 95% CI 1.33-6.39; p=0.008). Conclusions: Advanced therapy use remained rare and was concentrated in large urban teaching hospitals, suggesting dependence on hospital capability and regional access. Hispanic patients experienced higher adjusted mortality, while severe complications were major mortality drivers. These findings support regionalized cardio-obstetric shock pathways and equitable access to advanced heart failure therapies.
title: Abstract 8973: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy Hospitalizations in the United States: Rising Severity and Concentrated Advanced Therapy Use 2016-2023

abstract: Background: Pregnancy-associated acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is rare but associated with substantial maternal morbidity. Contemporary national trends and differences in invasive management remain incompletely characterized. Methods: Female hospitalizations aged 15-54 years with AMI and pregnancy-associated diagnoses were identified in the National Inpatient Sample from 2016-2023. The primary outcome was percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Secondary outcome was severe cardiovascular complication, defined as death, shock, cardiac arrest, or mechanical circulatory support use. Survey weights generated national estimates. Multivariable survey-weighted logistic regression evaluated predictors of PCI and severe complications, adjusting for demographics, payer, income, hospital characteristics, preeclampsia/eclampsia, complications, and comorbidities. Results: A weighted 6,995 pregnancy-associated AMI hospitalizations were identified, increasing from 540 in 2016 to 1,340 in 2023. Severe maternal cardiovascular morbidity was frequent, including shock in 9.5%, respiratory failure in 25.8%, AKI in 16.3%, and MCS/ECMO use in 5.0%. Preeclampsia/eclampsia was more common among Black and Hispanic patients than White patients, while PCI use was lower. PCI declined from 12.96% in 2016 to 5.22% in 2023, a temporal pattern that persisted after adjustment (aOR 0.88 per calendar year; p=0.036). Compared with White patients, Black patients (aOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.28-0.88; p=0.016) and Hispanic patients (aOR 0.46, 95% CI 0.21-0.98; p=0.044) had lower adjusted odds of PCI. Race/ethnicity was not independently associated with severe cardiovascular complications. Conclusions: Pregnancy-associated AMI hospitalizations increased with substantial morbidity. PCI use declined over time and was lower among Black and Hispanic patients, but this may reflect evolving AMI phenotypes, including greater recognition of nonatherosclerotic causes, rather than undertreatment alone. Phenotype-specific cardio-obstetric AMI pathways are needed.
title: Abstract 8988: Rising Burden, Declining PCI: Contemporary Trends and Disparities in Pregnancy-Associated Acute Myocardial Infarction

abstract: Background: Neo-left ventricular outflow tract (neo-LVOT) obstruction is a clinically important complication of transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR). Although computed tomography (CT) simulation is central to TMVR planning, reported obstruction risk, imaging thresholds, and predictive performance vary across valve-in-mitral annular calcification (ViMAC), mitral valve-in-ring (MViR), and mitral valve-in-valve (MViV) anatomy. Research Question: Does the risk of clinically significant LVOT obstruction (LVOTO) after TMVR differ by mitral phenotype, and how well do CT- and echocardiography-based neo-LVOT measurements support procedural-risk assessment? Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, and Wiley Online Library were searched for adult TMVR studies reporting neo-LVOT prediction, imaging comparison, or clinically significant LVOTO. Eligible studies required extractable denominators for LVOTO events or extractable correlation data for imaging-based neo-LVOT measurements. Random-effects generalized linear mixed models were used to pool LVOTO event proportions. Prespecified subgroup analyses examined TMVR phenotype and LVOTO definition class. Fisher z random-effects meta-analysis was used for correlations between 3D TEE/TOE and CT, and between CT-predicted and observed neo-LVOT. Quantitative synthesis was restricted to clinically and statistically comparable subsets. Results: The primary analysis included 11 studies, 477 treated patients, and 63 LVOTO events. Pooled clinically significant LVOTO incidence was 13.4% (95% CI, 9.6%-18.5%; I 2 =19.2%); a broader sensitivity analysis was similar at approximately 12% (95% CI, 8%-18%; I 2 =34.0%). Phenotype-specific risk differed significantly (p=0.0008): ViMAC, 34% (95% CI, 8%-75%; I 2 =76.8%); MViR, 10% (95% CI, 3%-27%; I 2 =0%); and MViV, 2% (95% CI, 0.1%-27.8%; I 2 =0%). LVOTO definition class was not associated with significant subgroup differences (p=0.5645). Meta-analysis of three studies showed high correlation between 3D TEE/TOE and CT-derived neo-LVOT measurements (pooled r=0.97; 95% CI, 0.95-0.98), while three CT-based studies showed strong predicted-versus-observed neo-LVOT correlation (pooled r=0.82; 95% CI, 0.67-0.90). Conclusions: Clinically significant LVOTO after TMVR occurs in approximately 12%-13% of analyzable cases and is strongly phenotype-dependent, with highest pooled point estimate in ViMAC. Imaging-based planning is supported, but imperfect predicted-versus-observed CT correlation, heterogeneity within ViMAC, and variable LVOTO definitions highlight the need for standardized definitions, prospective phenotype-specific thresholds, and multimodality planning in high-risk anatomy. These findings may inform consideration of leaflet-modification or other preventive strategies and closer peri-procedural monitoring after TMVR.
title: Abstract 9013: Neo-Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction After Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement: Phenotype-Specific Risk and Imaging Prediction

abstract: Background: Intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) in ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is associated with extensive infarct expansion, loss of myocardial salvage, and marked cardiac troponin I elevation within the first 24 hours of reperfusion. However, the cell/molecular basis of this observation is not known. Heme is an early breakdown byproduct of red blood cells and may preferentially drive cardiomyocyte death in hemorrhagic MI. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that heme and the associated cardiac troponin I concentrations ([hs-cTnI]) in reperfused STEMI patients with IMH are higher than those without IMH; and that heme is toxic to cardiomyocytes in culture. Methods/Approach: Reperfused STEMI patients (n=12) underwent LGE and T2* CMR. T2* CMR was used to identify those with IMH and LGE was used to measure infarct size. Total heme and [hs-cTnI] (a known marker of cardiomyocyte injury) were measured from baseline and up to 24 hours after reperfusion. In addition, human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) were exposed to graded exogenous heme concentrations (0-120 μM). Cell viability and [hs-cTnI] were quantified. Results: CMR classified 7 patients as hemorrhagic and 5 as non-hemorrhagic. Infarct size was greater in patients with IMH than those without (52.1±7.4% vs 15.2±6.8%; p<0.0001). From baseline and up to 24 hours after reperfusion, those with IMH showed higher fold of total heme than those without IMH (24.8 ± 4.22 vs 1.39 ± 2; p<0.0001) and a higher peak of hs-cTnI release (418.4 ±34 vs 164.3±37.5 p<0.0001). In hiPSC-CMs, exogenous heme caused concentration-dependent cardiomyocyte injury with an estimated IC50 of ~15±4.5μM, along with hs-cTnI release that increased sharply between 15 and 30 μM and plateaued after 60μM. Conclusion: Our collective findings identify heme as a key driver of cardiomyocyte death in hemorrhagic STEMI, linking red blood cell breakdown after reperfusion to amplified myocardial injury. Targeting heme toxicity in hemorrhagic STEMI may provide a new strategy to limit infarct expansion and adverse remodeling after MI.

abstract: Background: The Impella 5.5 provides temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS) for cardiogenic shock and advanced heart failure and is FDA-approved for up to 14 days. In practice, prolonged support is often required as a bridge to transplantation or recovery. Decompensated heart failure is associated with skin failure from hypoperfusion, immobility, and prolonged hospitalization. As axillary Impella 5.5 use increases, greater mobility combined with sustained device-skin contact increases risk of PSI-03, including medical device-related pressure injuries (MDRPIs) and decubitus ulcers, an emerging and potentially preventable safety concern. Data describing PSIs during prolonged Impella 5.5 support remain limited. Research Question: To describe the incidence and pattern of PSIs among patients receiving Impella 5.5 support beyond 14 days. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult patients in a tertiary cardiothoracic transplant ICU who received Impella 5.5 support for >14 consecutive days between August 2020 and October 2025. PSI events were identified using Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality definitions and confirmed by manual chart review to determine timing and device association. For PSI-03, the first documented stage ≥3 wound was considered the index event; multiple PSIs per patient were recorded as separate events. PSIs present on admission or occurring after Impella removal were excluded. Clinical characteristics, transplant outcomes, and mortality were summarized descriptively and stratified by PSI occurrence. Results: Among 149 patients, 16 (10.7%) experienced at least one PSI. Pressure injury (PSI-03) occurred in 8 patients (5.4%), accounting for 10 injuries, including 3 MDRPIs at the right anterior chest wall cannula-skin interface and 7 decubitus ulcers. Patients with pressure injuries commonly had diabetes mellitus (75%) and malnutrition (50%) and required advanced support, including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation or intra-aortic balloon pump (63%) and continuous renal replacement therapy (25%). Other PSIs included sepsis (PSI-13, 6.3%), pneumonia (PSI-04b, 6.3%), respiratory failure (PSI-11, 6.3%), and hemorrhage/hematoma (PSI-09, 6.3%). Patients with PSIs had longer hospital and ICU stays, and higher in-hospital mortality compared with those without PSIs. Conclusions: MDRPIs localized to the cannula-skin interface and clustered in patients with high comorbidity burden and prolonged Impella 5.5 support. These findings support targeted prevention bundles, including cannula padding, routine skin checks, nutritional optimization, and multidisciplinary device rounds.
title: Abstract 9044: Safety Indicators Among Patients with Impella 5.5 Support for More Than 14 Days: A Focus on Device-Skin Interface Injuries

abstract: Background: While multidisciplinary prehabilitation (prehab) is associated with improved postsurgical outcomes, prehab availability has been mostly limited to high-risk patients (e.g., frailty, multimorbid conditions) who meet requirements for specialty referrals. However, providing prehab to all cardiac surgery patients is important for preoperative physical and mental optimization. Therefore, a nurse-led prehab program (Table 1) was created based on the recommendations from the Enhanced Recovery after Cardiac Surgery group and implemented for patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery who previously did not meet requirements for prehab. The overall purpose of this study was to compare post-operative complications, length of stay (LOS), and discharge disposition of patients who received nurse-led prehab to those who received usual care. Hypotheses: Patients who received nurse-led prehab, compared to usual care, would have 1) less occurrences of major morbidities (i.e., stroke, renal failure, reoperation, prolonged ventilation, sternal infection); 2) a shorter LOS; and 3) higher percentage of discharges to home vs. rehab. Methods: This single-center, retrospective cohort study included elective cardiac surgery patients from March to December 2025. Inclusion criteria were English-speaking adults undergoing elective coronary artery bypass graft and/or valve surgery with ≥ 2-weeks wait time. Exclusion criteria were unstable angina, < 2-week myocardial infarction, Stage 3 or 4 chronic kidney disease, or limiting physical, neurological, or psychiatric conditions. Major morbidity was measured using Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) definitions. Data were collected using the STS Adult Cardiac Surgery database and chart reviews. Independent t-tests and Chi-squared tests were used to test the hypotheses. Results: Of the 587 patients who met the eligibility criteria, 76 patients (13%, 1-4 patients/week) received prehab due to the availability of the facility's part-time prehab nurse (Figure 1). Patient characteristics and results are presented in Table 2. For Hypothesis 1, patients who received prehab, compared to usual care, did not have less occurrences of major morbidity. For Hypothesis 2, patients who received prehab, compared to usual care, had a shorter average LOS (6.12±1.63 vs. 7.14±4.42 days, p <.001). For Hypothesis 3, patients who received prehab, compared to usual care, had a higher percentage of patients discharged to home vs. rehab (94.7% vs. 83.8%, p =.010). Conclusions: Preliminary findings of nurse-led prehab for elective cardiac surgery showed a promising result in reducing LOS, despite having similar occurrences of major morbidity as the usual care group. Although findings were limited by small sample size, future studies are warranted to examine nurse-led prehab in a larger, more comprehensive sample with a prospective research design.
title: Abstract 9064: Nurse-Led Prehab for Patients Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery and/or Heart Valve Surgery

abstract: Introduction: The goal of transcatheter left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is to reduce bleeding risk associated with oral anticoagulation (OAC) while providing protection against ischemic stroke. Patterns of short-term changes in medications after LAAO have been described, but longer-term OAC discontinuation, OAC reinitiation, and associations with stroke and bleeding events remain unknown. Methods: We evaluated patients who received a Watchman device (2.5 or FLX) in the NCDR LAAO Registry from 2016 to 2021 with linked Medicare Part D data. Medicare Part D prescription fills for OAC were used to determine long-term discontinuation and reinitiation of OAC after LAAO hospital discharge. We also evaluated incidence of registry-adjudicated stroke and major bleeding for combined person-time spent on and off OAC following LAAO, and performed comparisons using multivariable logistic regression. Time on or off OAC was determined from prescription fills during follow-up, allowing individual patients to contribute time to both categories in the analysis. Results: The study cohort included 53,984 Medicare patients who underwent LAAO with mean age 77 (SD 6) years, 43.2% women, mean CHA 2 DS 2 VASc score 4.7 (SD 1.4) and mean HAS-BLED score 3.0 (SD 1.1). At discharge, 90.6% were reported to be discharged on OAC using registry data, whereas 67.9% had a filled prescription for OAC available prior to admission or within one day of discharge. OAC use rapidly declined early after discharge, falling to 7.7% at 6 months. OAC use remained low in long-term follow-up ( Figure 1 ). After discharge, 8.1% of patients were newly initiated on OAC after a period of not taking the medication. Among patients who remained off OAC at 2 years post-discharge, subsequent OAC use remained low out to 5 years ( Figure 2 ). During 2-year follow-up after LAAO, there was no significant difference in person-time spent off vs. on OAC for rates of ischemic stroke (1.21 vs. 1.21 events per 100 person-years; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.07, 95% CI 0.87-1.32; p = 0.52) or any stroke (aOR 0.92, 95% CI 0.77-1.09; p = 0.33). In the two years following LAAO, person-time spent off OAC was associated with significantly lower rates of total major bleeding (4.91 vs. 16.15 events per 100 person-years; aOR 0.29, 95% 0.27-0.31; p <0.001), as well as intracranial hemorrhage (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.46-0.74; p <0.001) and gastrointestinal bleeding (aOR 0.27, 95% CI 0.25-0.29; p<0.001). Conclusions: Among patients who undergo transcatheter LAAO in the U.S., long-term use of OAC remains low out to 5 years of follow up and OAC reinitiation is infrequent. Rates of bleeding after LAAO are significantly lower during person-time spent off OAC, with no differences in ischemic stroke observed for person-time spent off vs. on OAC. These findings confirm that the vast majority of patients who undergo LAAO remain off OAC during long-term follow-up and likely benefit from lower bleeding.
title: Abstract 9072: Oral Anticoagulation Use and Clinical Outcomes After Transcatheter Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion in the United States: A Report from the NCDR LAAO Registry

abstract: Introduction: Noonan syndrome is associated with congenital pulmonary valve disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, yet limited literature guides pregnancy-related decision-making in women with progressive right ventricular outflow tract disease. Patient Information: A 34-year-old woman with Noonan syndrome, childhood pulmonary valvuloplasties, bioprosthetic pulmonary valve replacement in 2016, and hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) presented with chest pressure after several days of vomiting, nausea, and dizziness. Clinical Findings and Timeline: She had elevated troponin and dynamic electrocardiographic changes. Echocardiography demonstrated severe bioprosthetic pulmonary regurgitation, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Coronary computed tomography angiography and invasive angiography showed no obstructive coronary artery disease but confirmed chronic right coronary artery ostial occlusion with extensive left-to-right collaterals. Right heart catheterization and pulmonary angiography confirmed severe pulmonary regurgitation. Her symptoms were attributed to dynamic LVOT obstruction and altered loading conditions in the setting of dehydration, HOCM physiology, and severe bioprosthetic valve degeneration. Therapeutic Intervention: She improved with intravenous hydration and beta-blockade. Given her young age, prior sternotomy, desire to avoid lifelong anticoagulation with a mechanical valve, and future pregnancy considerations, a multidisciplinary adult congenital and structural heart team recommended elective valve-in-valve transcatheter pulmonary valve replacement (TPVR). Follow-up and Outcomes: She was discharged in stable condition on beta-blocker therapy with outpatient adult congenital heart disease follow-up, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, and TPVR planning. Discussion: This case highlights the long-term pulmonary valve sequelae of Noonan syndrome in women of childbearing age. Early pregnancy-centered counseling is important because severe pulmonary regurgitation may reduce hemodynamic reserve during pregnancy. Valve-in-valve TPVR may provide a less invasive, patient-centered strategy for severe bioprosthetic pulmonary valve failure while avoiding repeat sternotomy and lifelong anticoagulation in appropriately selected young women.
title: Abstract 9140: Pregnancy at the Crossroads: Valve-in-Valve Transcatheter Pulmonary Valve Replacement for Severe Pulmonary Regurgitation in Noonan Syndrome

abstract: Myocarditis in children is rare and has a variable course, ranging from mild or asymptomatic inflammation to cardiogenic shock. For children with severe hemodynamic compromise, veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) may provide temporary circulatory support during myocardial recovery or as a bridge to durable mechanical circulatory support or heart transplantation (HT). However, contemporary multicenter data describing ECMO use and outcomes in pediatric myocarditis remain limited. We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study using the Pediatric Health Information System (PHIS) database to identify children hospitalized with myocarditis from 2015 through 2025. Patients were stratified by receipt of VA-ECMO. Continuous variables were compared using Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, and categorical variables using chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and HT. Adjusted hospitalization charges was a secondary outcome. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with ECMO use. Over the course of 10 years, we identified 5,925 children hospitalized with myocarditis. The median age was 14 years (IQR 7-16), 30.3% were female, and the majority were non-Hispanic White. In hospital mortality occurred in 3.1% (N=182) of patients and HT in 1.1% (N=67). VA-ECMO was used to support 7.3% (N=430) patients. ECMO patients were younger [7y (IQR 1-13 vs 14y (IQR 8-16)], more frequently female (48% vs 29%), and more often Black race (28% vs 20%). Mortality (27.4% vs 1.2%), HT (6.7% vs 0.7%), and adjusted median cost [$305,731 IQR ($165,794—$558,522) vs. $5,770 ($669—$34,107)] were all substantially higher in the ECMO cohort (P<0.001 for all). Younger age (aOR 0.96 [0.94-0.98]), female sex (aOR 1.4 [1.10-1.77]), Black race (aOR 1.56 [1.12-2.16]), intubation at admission (aOR 5.22 [3.91-6.97]), vasopressors at admission (aOR 4.77 [3.55-6.42], p<0.001), and vasodilators at admission (aOR 2.26 [1.71-2.98]) were independently associated with ECMO use (p<0.05 for all). In this large, contemporary, multicenter cohort of children hospitalized with myocarditis, VA-ECMO was used in approximately 7% of patients and was associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and resource utilization. Markers of illness severity at presentation, including intubation and vasoactive medication use, were strongly associated with ECMO utilization. Black race was independently associated with increased ECMO use, a finding that merits further investigation into the mechanisms underlying racial disparities in myocarditis presentation and management. More than one in four ECMO-supported patients died during hospitalization, highlighting the need for early recognition of high-risk patients and further study of strategies to improve outcomes in this population.
title: Abstract 9156: Contemporary Use and Outcomes of VA-ECMO in Children Hospitalized with Myocarditis

abstract: Introduction: Sinus venosus atrial septal defect (SV ASD) is an uncommon congenital lesion associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR) and requiring surgical repair. Although paradoxical embolization is a recognized complication of atrial septal defects, progressive systemic embolization from right atrial thrombus through an SV ASD has rarely been described. We report a case of simultaneous pulmonary and systemic embolization complicated by brain abscess and intracranial hemorrhage that created a challenging intervention dilemma. Case Presentation: A 33-year-old female presented with seven days of nausea and vomiting. Imaging showed a 2.4 х 2.9-cm basal ganglia abscess with midline shift (figure 1), a 2.6-cm right atrial (RA) mass (figure 2), subsegmental pulmonary embolism, and embolic lesions involving the liver, spleen, and right kidney. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) revealed a superior SV ASD with PAPVR and two fixed RA masses (1.0 х 1.7 cm and 1.3 х 1.1 cm) (figure 2). Panorex X-ray showed multiple dental abscesses. Brain abscess drainage and dental extractions were performed; cultures grew Streptococcus intermedius and Fusobacterium species, while serial blood cultures remained negative.
