Compared with usual care, CR did not show statistically significant improvements in 6-minute walk distance (8 comparisons; n=727; MD 15.1 m; 95% CI –19.0 to 49.3; p=0.40), peak oxygen consumption (6 comparisons; n=158; MD 1.0 mL/kg/min; 95% CI –0.5 to 2.4; p=0.20), or Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score (4 comparisons; n=199; MD 7.8 points; 95% CI –1.9 to 17.4; p=0.10). However, CR was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (5 studies; n=1,044; RR 0.52; 95% CI 0.32-0.85; P=0.009). Programs lasting ≥8 weeks produced greater improvements in peak oxygen consumption than shorter programs (interaction P=0.001). Conclusions: Following surgical or transcatheter AVR, cardiac rehabilitation was associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality. Although overall improvements in functional capacity and health status were not statistically significant, longer rehabilitation programs were associated with greater cardiopulmonary benefit. These findings support structured CR as an important component of post-AVR recovery.
title: Abstract 9626: Impact of Cardiac Rehabilitation Post-Surgical and Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Comparative Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Pulmonary embolism carries high mortality when unrecognized, making early identification essential. This urgency is amplified in heart failure (HF) patients, whose reduced physiologic reserve renders them least tolerant of a missed diagnosis. In HF, PE hides behind decompensation: shared symptoms mislead clinicians, and standard risk stratification tools may suppress true PE probability. This case illustrates how structured multimodal RV strain assessment serves as a diagnostic bridge when clinical scoring tools fail. Case Presentation: A 59-year-old male with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF 20%) presented with dyspnea and volume overload. Vital signs: HR 120, RR 28, SpO 2 93% on room air, BP 130/60 mmHg. Wells score was 1.5. POCUS raised concern for RV strain, prompting TTE, which showed TAPSE 1.4 cm, diastolic septal flattening, dilated RA, and elevated PA pressures. ECG showed T-wave inversions in V1-V3. Troponin was 300 ng/L; prior coronary angiography was normal, excluding obstructive CAD. CT-PA confirmed PE with bilateral main PA emboli (RV/LV ratio 1.17). After PERT activation, the patient underwent percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy via right CFV access and was discharged on anticoagulation. Discussion: HF patients represent the highest-risk subgroup for missed PE—reduced physiologic reserve makes them least tolerant of hemodynamic burden, yet paradoxically most diagnostically vulnerable. Dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, and RV dysfunction are shared features of both conditions, allowing PE to masquerade as decompensation. Standard pre-test probability tools are ill-equipped for this population—the Wells score assigns a 3-point penalty when an alternative diagnosis exists, a criterion neutralized in HF where decompensation serves as a competing explanation. When scoring tools fail, multimodal RV strain assessment becomes the diagnostic bridge. TAPSE <1.7 cm carries sensitivity up to 94%, diastolic septal flattening specificity of 98%, combined anterior and inferior T-wave inversions sensitivity 98% and specificity 92% for PE versus MI; elevated troponin signals RV myocardial injury. When RV strain converges across echo, ECG, and CT, with positive troponin, adverse event OR rises to 8.8 . No single modality suffices; convergence is key. Conclusion: In HF patients, algorithmic scores alone are insufficient to exclude PE. When clinical trajectory is unexplained, structured multimodal RV strain assessment should guide decision-making. A validated HF-specific PE risk stratification tool is urgently needed. Reference: Carroll BJ, Heidinger BH, Dabreo DC, Matos JD, Mohebali D, Feldman SA, McCormick I, Litmanovich D, Manning WJ. Multimodality Assessment of Right Ventricular Strain in Patients With Acute Pulmonary Embolism. Am J Cardiol. 2018;122(1):175-181.
title: Abstract 9638: When the Score Fails: Multimodal RV Strain Assessment Unmasks Saddle PE in a Heart Failure Patient

abstract: Background: Congenital unilateral pulmonary artery abnormalities are rare vascular anomalies typically diagnosed during childhood. Adult presentation is uncommon and may mimic pulmonary embolism (PE), leading to misdiagnosis and inappropriate anticoagulation. Case: A 33-year-old male with a history of childhood ventricular septal defects that reportedly closed spontaneously presented with two weeks of cough, intermittent hemoptysis, left-sided chest pain, and progressive dyspnea on exertion. He reported exertional limitation since adolescence. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography was initially interpreted as extensive right-sided PE involving segmental and subsegmental branches with severe narrowing of the right pulmonary artery. Additional findings included right lung volume loss and pleural thickening. Therapeutic anticoagulation was initiated. Despite the reported clot burden, the patient remained hemodynamically stable. Troponin and BNP were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated preserved right ventricular size and function without evidence of right heart strain. Decision-Making The absence of right ventricular strain, normal biomarkers, and stable hemodynamics were discordant with extensive acute PE. Multidisciplinary review involving cardiology, pulmonology, and radiology prompted reconsideration of the diagnosis. Right heart catheterization demonstrated normal right-sided filling pressures and normal pulmonary artery pressures (mean PA pressure 22 mmHg, PCWP 5 mmHg, cardiac output 6.5 L/min), findings inconsistent with extensive PE. Repeat review of CT imaging demonstrated absence of the proximal right pulmonary artery with associated right lung hypoplasia. Given the patient's lifelong symptoms, preserved oxygenation, normal hemodynamics, and imaging findings, the treating teams concluded the findings were most consistent with congenital right pulmonary artery atresia. Anticoagulation was discontinued and the patient was referred for adult congenital heart disease evaluation. Conclusion: Congenital right pulmonary artery atresia may remain undiagnosed until adulthood and can closely mimic PE. When imaging suggests a large thromboembolic burden but biomarkers, echocardiography, and invasive hemodynamics remain normal, congenital pulmonary vascular anomalies should be considered. Multidisciplinary review and multimodality imaging are essential to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary anticoagulation.
title: Abstract 9644: Congenital Right Pulmonary Artery Atresia Masquerading as Extensive Pulmonary Embolism: A Diagnostic Pitfall

abstract: Background: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) is increasingly recognized as a distinct clinical entity, often presenting in younger patients and women. However, its long term prognosis is currently not well defined. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that clinical outcomes in patients with MINOCA differ by sex. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies reporting sex-specific outcomes in MINOCA. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched through May 2025. Primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included long-term MI, stroke, and all-cause mortality. Analyses were performed using RStudio with heterogeneity assessed by I 2 statistics. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the influence of individual studies.Results: Fourteen studies comprising 38,521 women and 27,917 men with MINOCA were included. The mean age was 55.8 years for women and 48.6 years for men. Hypertension was present in 46.8% of women and 40.5% of men, while diabetes was reported in 13.2% of women and 12.7% of men. In-hospital all-cause mortality was significantly lower in women compared to men with MINOCA (risk ratio 0.87; 95% CI, 0.78-0.96; p = 0.008; I 2 = 0%). Long-term all-cause mortality over a mean follow-up of 42 months was significantly lower in women compared to men with MINOCA (risk ratio 0.95; 95% CI, 0.92-0.98; p < 0.001; I 2 = 0%). At 31-month follow-up, long-term MI rates were similar (RR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.80-1.03; p = 0.15; I 2 = 37.2%). At 32-month follow-up, stroke risk was similar (RR 1.14; 95% CI, 0.90-1.44; p = 0.29; I 2 = 68.5%). Leave-one-out analysis showed consistent results for in-hospital and long-term mortality, while estimates for long-term myocardial infarction were moderately stable, while stroke outcomes showed greater variability and heterogeneity, indicating less consistent findings across studies. Conclusion: Among patients with MINOCA, women had significantly lower in-hospital and long-term all-cause mortality compared to men. However, rates of long-term myocardial infarction and stroke were similar between sexes. More research with long-term follow up is required to determine clinical course and management.
title: Abstract 9664: Sex Based Differences in Clinical Outcomes Among Patients with Myocardial Infarction with Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

abstract: Background: Heart failure (HF) is increasingly recognized among lung transplant recipients and may influence perioperative and post-transplant outcomes. However, national data evaluating outcomes by HF subtype remain limited. We aimed to evaluate the association of HF phenotypes with in-hospital outcomes among lung transplant hospitalizations. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that HFrEF, but not HFpEF, would be independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality and major cardiovascular complications after lung transplantation. Methods: Adult lung transplant hospitalizations were identified from the National Inpatient Sample. Patients were stratified into no HF, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Survey-weighted analyses compared baseline characteristics and outcomes. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, race, pulmonary hypertension (PH) group, pulmonary circulation disorders, obesity, and complicated hypertension. Results: Among 17,350 weighted lung transplant hospitalizations, 96.1% had no HF, 2.5% had HFpEF, and 1.4% had HFrEF. HFpEF patients were older, whereas HFrEF patients had lower female representation. Group 1 PH prevalence increased progressively across no HF, HFpEF, and HFrEF groups (6.9%, 12.6%, and 20.0%, respectively; p<0.01). In-hospital mortality was higher in HFrEF hospitalizations (16.0%) than in HFpEF (4.6%) and no HF (4.4%) groups. After multivariable adjustment, HFrEF remained independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.0, 95% CI 1.4-6.5, p<0.01) and cardiogenic shock (aOR 2.8, 95% CI 1.5-5.2, p<0.01). Group 1 PH (aOR 1.7, p=0.047) and Group 2 PH (aOR 4.3, p=0.02) were also independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: HFrEF was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality and cardiogenic shock among lung transplant hospitalizations. These findings underscore the importance of cardiovascular risk stratification and perioperative optimization in lung transplant recipients with pre-existing systolic heart failure.
title: Abstract 9666: Impact of Heart Failure Subtypes on In-Hospital Outcomes Following Lung Transplantation: A National Analysis

abstract: Introduction: The coexistence of adult congenital heart disease and obstructive coronary artery disease is uncommon and presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Decision making becomes particularly complex in patients with elevated surgical risk and complex coronary anatomy. Patient Information: A 45 year old woman with a history of Ebstein’s anomaly, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension, with irregular cardiology follow up, presented with progressive exertional chest pain associated with New York Heart Association functional class II symptoms. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated right heart chamber enlargement, mild biventricular systolic dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction 53%, right ventricular ejection fraction 49%), and moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Given persistent symptoms, invasive coronary evaluation was performed. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Coronary angiography revealed complex triple vessel coronary artery disease. The left anterior descending artery exhibited multiple severe stenoses of up to 90% involving a diagonal branch with TIMI 2 flow. The right coronary artery demonstrated a proximal lesion causing up to 80% stenosis with TIMI 2 flow. Considering the patient’s congenital heart disease, ventricular dysfunction, and elevated surgical risk, a multidisciplinary team favored a percutaneous approach. Therapeutic Intervention(s): A staged percutaneous coronary intervention strategy was undertaken. Initial intervention targeted the right coronary artery with implantation of a sirolimus eluting stent, achieving an optimal angiographic result. Subsequently, the left anterior descending artery bifurcation lesion was treated with predilation followed by sequential implantation of sirolimus and everolimus eluting stents. Adequate stent expansion and apposition were achieved, with final TIMI 3 flow in all treated vessels. Follow Up, Outcomes, and Adverse Events: The patient experienced an uneventful recovery without periprocedural complications or immediate adverse cardiovascular events. Clinical symptoms improved following complete revascularization. Discussion and Synthesis: Coronary artery disease is increasingly encountered in adults with congenital heart disease as survival improves. However, reports describing complex multivessel coronary intervention in patients with Ebstein’s anomaly remain scarce. This case illustrates that staged percutaneous revascularization can be a feasible and effective strategy in selected high risk patients, even in the presence of complex bifurcation lesions. Individualized management by a multidisciplinary heart team is essential to optimize outcomes in this growing population.
title: Abstract 9672: Staged Percutaneous Revascularization for Triple Vessel Coronary Artery Disease in a Patient with Ebstein's Anomaly

abstract: Background: GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have demonstrated cardiometabolic benefits in patients with diabetes and heart failure. However, their impact on outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) remains unknown. We evaluated the association between GLP-1 RA use and post-TAVR outcomes using a large real-world dataset. Method: Using the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adult patients who underwent TAVR across 100 healthcare organizations. Two cohorts were defined: TAVR patients with (n=2,399) and without (n=2,399) GLP-1 RA use. Patients with eGFR <25 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were excluded. Propensity score matching was applied to balance baseline characteristics. Outcomes included 1-year all-cause mortality (primary), heart failure exacerbations, acute kidney injury (AKI), myocardial infarction (MI), ischemic stroke, and electrolyte disturbances. Risk and survival analyses were performed. Results: GLP-1 RA use was associated with significantly lower 1-year mortality (3.1% vs. 5.8%; risk ratio 0.53 [95% CI 0.40-0.70]; p<0.001) and fewer heart failure exacerbations (36.8% vs. 40.2%; risk ratio 0.92 [95% CI 0.85-0.99]; p=0.018). There were no significant differences in AKI, MI, stroke, or arrhythmias. Kaplan-Meier analysis confirmed improved survival in the GLP-1 cohort (HR 0.52, p<0.001). Conclusion: GLP-1 receptor agonist use at the time of TAVR is associated with significantly lower 1-year mortality and reduced heart failure exacerbations without increased risk of other complications. These findings support further investigation of GLP-1 RAs as adjunctive therapy in TAVR populations.
title: Abstract 9677: Impact of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Post-TAVR Outcomes: A Propensity-Matched National Cohort Study

abstract: Introduction: Platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome (POS) is a rare cause of positional hypoxemia characterized by dyspnea and oxygen desaturation in the upright position that improves when supine. Although a patent foramen ovale (PFO) is commonly implicated, additional anatomical factors are often required to facilitate clinically significant right-to-left shunting in the absence of elevated right-sided pressures. Patient Information and Clinical Findings: An 80-year-old woman with an ascending aortic aneurysm (5.3 cm), moderate aortic regurgitation, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and bronchiectasis presented with progressive exertional dyspnea and intermittent oxygen desaturation. Symptoms began one year prior and progressed from occurring during singing to limiting routine activities, including gardening and yoga. Oxygen saturation was 95-99% while supine but fell to 86% when upright despite high-flow nasal cannula oxygen. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Computed tomography demonstrated mild basilar subpleural scarring without pulmonary embolism or extracardiac shunting. Pulmonary evaluation was otherwise unrevealing. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a small PFO with minimal shunting in the supine position, preserved left ventricular systolic function, moderate aortic regurgitation, and a dilated aortic root. Right heart catheterization revealed normal right-sided filling pressures, excluding pressure-mediated shunting. Upright bubble study demonstrated increased right-to-left shunting across the PFO, confirming platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome. Therapeutic Intervention and Outcomes: The patient underwent percutaneous PFO closure using a 25-mm Amplatzer occluder under transesophageal echocardiographic and fluoroscopic guidance. Device stability was confirmed with a negative push-pull test. Post-procedural imaging demonstrated complete defect coverage without residual shunt or complications. Positional hypoxemia resolved immediately following closure with marked improvement in exertional symptoms. Discussion: This case highlights a geometry-dependent mechanism of POS in which ascending aortic dilation altered atrial septal orientation and redirected venous inflow toward a small PFO, producing severe hypoxemia despite normal right-sided pressures. The diagnosis was only apparent with positional assessment, emphasizing the importance of upright oxygen measurements and contrast echocardiography when evaluating unexplained hypoxemia. Recognition of this reversible cause of hypoxemia enabled definitive treatment with percutaneous PFO closure and rapid symptomatic recovery.
title: Abstract 9704: When a Small PFO Causes Severe Hypoxemia: Platypnea-Orthodeoxia Syndrome Driven by Aortic Root Dilation

abstract: Introduction/Background: False-positive catheterization lab activations occur in 14-65% of Code STEMI responses. To reduce these at Los Angeles General Medical Center (LAG), an urban STEMI receiving center with >130,000 annual ED visits, a tiered activation protocol was introduced in August 2024. Pathway 1 retained the full Code STEMI bundle page mobilizing the entire interventional team and catheterization lab staff, while Pathway 2 triggered an urgent interventional cardiology consult—without reflex catheterization lab staff activation—for patients with ACS and high-risk ECG changes or complex presentations (Figure 1). The protocol reduced the false-positive STEMI activation rate from 40% to 22%. We sought to characterize the patient characteristics and outcomes of Pathway 2 activations. Methods: Patient characteristics and procedural outcomes of Pathway 2 activations from August 2024 to December 2025 were obtained retrospectively. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test and are presented as median (IQR); categorical variables were compared using the Fisher exact or χ 2 test and are presented as n (%). A two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Among 186 Pathway 2 activations, 78 (42%) underwent catheterization lab activation and 108 (58%) did not (Table 1). Of those catheterized, 34 (44%) underwent PCI; obstructive coronary disease was present in 58 (74%)—multivessel in 35 (45%) and single-vessel in 23 (29%)—with non-obstructive disease in 10 (13%) and normal coronaries in 8 (10%). Final diagnosis of STEMI was identified in 10 (13%) catheterized patients, highlighting STEMIs not recognized at initial ECG triage. The median time to the catheterization lab for these patients was 79 minutes. Cath patients had markedly higher cardiac biomarkers (median initial troponin 210 vs 43 ng/L; peak troponin 969 vs 60 ng/L; both p<0.001) and were younger (62 vs 66 years, p=0.03), though sex did not differ between groups (p=0.11). Cath patients also had longer hospital (4 vs 2 days) and ICU (3 vs 0 days) stays (both p<0.001). Race/ethnicity (p=0.01) and primary discharge diagnosis (p<0.001) also differed, with chest pain and ACS diagnoses concentrated among catheterized patients. IABP (16 vs 0, p<0.001) and mechanical thrombectomy (5 vs 0, p=0.01) occurred exclusively in catheterization patients, whereas vasopressor use, intubation, and central-line placement were similar between groups. In-hospital mortality was 24 (13%) overall and did not differ significantly (9% vs 16%, p=0.19). Conclusion: A tiered STEMI activation pathway identified high-risk ACS at an urban safety net hospital. 42% of Pathway 2 patients required catheterization, of which 44% underwent PCI, including STEMIs unrecognized at the initial ECG triage. This protocol reduced false-positive activations and avoided unnecessary reflexive full-team mobilization.
title: Abstract 9745: Characteristics and Outcomes of Patients Triaged Through a Tiered STEMI Activation Pathway at an Urban Safety Net Hospital

abstract: Introduction/Background: Early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) risk is essential for prevention. The AHA-PREVENT score integrates cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic domains, but its laboratory requirements may limit immediate use in resource-constrained or first-contact settings. Phase angle (PhA), derived from bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), reflects cell membrane integrity, body cell mass, and metabolic reserve; however, its value for discriminating elevated PREVENT-estimated risk in Mexican adults has not been established. Research Question/Hypothesis: We evaluated whether PhA measured by BIA is associated with 10-year AHA-PREVENT risk and whether sex-specific PhA thresholds can identify intermediate-to-high risk, supporting its use as a practical adjunct for cardiovascular risk screening. Methods/Approach: We performed a cross-sectional study of 113 first-time Mexican cardiology outpatients. Patients with previous acute coronary syndrome or unavailable estimated glomerular filtration rate were excluded. The reference standard was 10-year AHA-PREVENT risk, dichotomized at ≥7.5%. PhA was measured using an mBCA 554 dry-electrode bioimpedance platform. Discrimination was assessed with receiver operating characteristic curves, and optimal sex-specific thresholds were selected using the Youden index. AUCs with 95% CIs, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and accuracy were calculated from 2х2 tables. Results/Data: Intermediate-to-high PREVENT risk was present in 60 patients (53.1%). PhA correlated inversely with PREVENT score (r=-0.52; p<0.001). In men, PhA showed strong discrimination (AUC 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.97). The optimal cutoff was ≤5.55°, yielding 88.24% sensitivity, 81.82% specificity, 88.24% positive predictive value, and 81.82% negative predictive value. In women, discrimination was moderate (AUC 0.75; 95% CI, 0.63-0.88). The optimal cutoff was ≤4.95°, yielding 88.24% sensitivity, 58.06% specificity, 63.89% positive predictive value, and 85.71% negative predictive value. Overall, PhA had 88.33% sensitivity, 67.92% specificity, 75.71% positive predictive value, 83.72% negative predictive value, and 78.76% accuracy. Conclusion(s): In Mexican adults undergoing first-time cardiology evaluation, lower PhA discriminated intermediate-to-high 10-year PREVENT risk, with stronger performance in men and useful rule-out performance in women. Sex-specific PhA thresholds may provide a rapid, noninvasive screening approach that complements conventional CKM risk assessment, particularly when laboratory-based risk calculation is not immediately available.
title: Abstract 9825: Phase Angle as a Screening Tool for Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk in Mexican Adults

abstract: Introduction: Cardiogenic shock (CS) carries high in-hospital mortality but data from safety-net hospitals remain limited. Pulmonary artery catheterization (PAC) use with hemodynamic profiling is associated with lower CS mortality but utilization at safety-net hospitals has not been characterized. Additionally, the prognostic value of Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) within uniformly high-vulnerability populations is not well studied. Hypothesis: PAC and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) utilization at a safety-net hospital are lower than reported in multicenter registries, and SVI does not discriminate mortality in a uniformly high vulnerability CS population. Methods: This was a single-center, retrospective observational study of adults (≥18 years) admitted with CS (SCAI Stage ≥ C) over 10 months. Data were collected via chart review including demographics, comorbidities, shock etiology, and cardiac arrest status. Admission and peak lactate were documented. PAC-derived hemodynamics (pulmonary artery pulsatility index [PAPi], pulmonary capillary wedge pressure [PCWP], cardiac index [CI]) and MCS device use (Impella, intra-aortic balloon pump [IABP], and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation [ECMO]) were recorded. Statistical analysis was performed using chi-square test, Fisher's exact test, Welch's t-test, and Pearson correlation coefficient. Results: Among 100 CS patients (mean age 65, 74% male, mean SVI 0.83), comorbidity burden was high (HF 82%, DM 50%). Shock etiology was predominantly HF-CS (59%). PAC was utilized in 54% and MCS in 15% of the cohort (IABP 11%, Impella 3%, ECMO 1%). Overall mortality was 27% and in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) was associated with significantly higher mortality compared to out-of-hospital arrest (OHCA) (77.8% vs. 33.3%, p=0.004). Among PAC-monitored patients, PAPi <1 (41% mortality), PCWP >18 (39%), and CI <2.2 (37%) identified higher-risk subgroups. MCS use was associated with higher mortality (47% vs. 20%, p=0.043). Non-survivors had higher mean admission lactate (5.14 vs. 2.78, p=0.017) and peak lactate (9.23 vs. 4.20, p<0.001). Mean SVI was high among non-survivors and survivors (0.79 vs 0.84, p=0.33). Conclusion: The cohort had a typical HF-CS predominance, but PAC utilization (54%) and MCS (15%) use were lower than reported in multicenter CS registries. Higher MCS mortality likely reflects rescue deployment rather than early intervention. Among PAC-monitored patients, PAPi <1 identified the highest-risk subgroup, highlighting the value of invasive hemodynamic profiling. SVI did not discriminate mortality, suggesting a ceiling effect in which clinical severity, rather than incremental differences in social vulnerability, drives outcomes. Limitations include single-center design and sample size. These findings support expanded access to hemodynamic monitoring and early MCS at safety-net hospitals.
title: Abstract 9839: Cardiogenic Shock at a Safety-Net Hospital: A Retrospective Analysis of Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring and Mechanical Circulatory Support in a Socially Vulnerable Population

abstract: Introduction: Prinzmetal angina is a transient coronary vasospasm that can mimic acute coronary syndrome, presenting with chest pain and transient ST-segment changes that resolve spontaneously or with nitrates. Although usually benign, Prinzmetal angina can rarely cause ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest. We report a rare case of ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest secondary to Prinzmetal angina in a patient with Sjogren’s syndrome (SS). Patient Information: A 45-year-old female with SS, asthma, hypertension (HTN), and hyperlipidemia (HLD) presented with substernal burning chest pain radiating to the jaw and tongue. Hydroxychloroquine noncompliance raised concern for a Sjögren’s flare. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Initial troponin levels showed <0.010 ng/mL. CTA chest was negative for pulmonary embolism. Electrocardiogram demonstrated anterolateral ST-segment elevation with symptom improvement after nitroglycerin and morphine. However, 105 minutes later, chest pain recurred with diaphoresis. A repeat electrocardiogram showed marked anterolateral ST-segment elevation (Figure 1), followed by ventricular fibrillation. CPR and defibrillation restored circulation. Diagnostic Assessment: Emergent left heart catheterization demonstrated no obstructive coronary artery disease and normal left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 70-75% (Figure 2). Findings supported Prinzmetal angina. Therapeutic Intervention: The patient was treated with verapamil, isosorbide mononitrate, and prednisone. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was placed for secondary prevention. Follow-Up & Outcomes: Over 5 years of follow-up, she experienced intermittent chest pain related to stress or infection without recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or cardiac arrest. Discussion: Prinzmetal angina can cause life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias despite the absence of obstructive coronary disease. Multivessel spasm, HTN, and HLD may increase arrhythmia risk. Although no direct association between SS and Prinzmetal angina has been established, chronic systemic inflammation, autoimmune-mediated endothelial dysfunction, and impaired vascular repair may promote vasospasm. This case emphasizes the need to consider Prinzmetal angina in the differential diagnosis in the setting of uncontrolled SS, as prompt recognition and treatment may prevent cardiac arrest.
title: Abstract 9856: The Spasm That Nearly Killed: A Rare Case of Prinzmetal Angina with Sjogren's Syndrome

abstract: Background: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common among patients with aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and may contribute to cardiac conduction abnormalities through intermittent hypoxia, autonomic dysfunction, and cardiac remodeling. Whether OSA severity and treatment adherence modify these risks following TAVR is unknown. Hypothesis: Increasing OSA severity is associated with higher rates of post-TAVR conduction abnormalities and permanent pacemaker (PPM) implantation, while adherence to OSA therapy is protective. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of 252 patients undergoing TAVR at an urban academic medical center (2018-2025). Patients were stratified by OSA severity (none, mild, moderate, severe) and treatment adherence (treated/adherent vs. untreated/nonadherent).. Primary outcomes were post-TAVR conduction abnormalities and PPM implantation at index hospitalization, 6 months, and 12 months. Secondary outcomes included mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Baseline characteristics were compared using Kruskal-Wallis tests and chi-squared tests. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated associations between OSA severity and PPM implantation, adjusting for demographics, body mass index (BMI), and clinically relevant comorbidities. Results: Among 252 patients, 59 had OSA: mild (n=13), moderate (n=17), or severe (n=29). Severe OSA was associated with higher BMI (p < 0.001) and male predominance (p=0.001). Conduction abnormalities at 6 months increased with OSA severity (p=0.044), with a similar trend at 12 months (p=0.056). No differences were observed in secondary outcomes. In multivariable regression, increasing OSA severity was associated with increased PPM placement at 12 months (OR 3.45, p=0.027). Among patients with available adherence data (n = 57), untreated/nonadherent (n=44) had increased odds of PPM at 6 months (OR 24.14, p=0.021), 12 months (OR 15.38, p=0.023), and any time point (OR 3.80, p=0.033). Conclusions: Increasing OSA severity and treatment nonadherence are associated with greater odds of post-TAVR conduction abnormalities and PPM implantation. These findings support OSA screening and treatment optimization in pre-TAVR evaluation to reduce conduction-related complications.
title: Abstract 9862: Don't Sleep on It: Obstructive Sleep Apnea as a Predictor of Conduction Abnormalities and Permanent Pacemaker Implantation After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Background: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is an established alternative to long-term anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. Device embolization is a rare and serious complication yet limited data is available on advanced percutaneous retrieval strategies for embolized devices. Cases: Case 1: A 74-year-old male developed acute post-procedural embolization of a WATCHMAN device into the LVOT, resulting in hemodynamic instability and a transaortic flow velocities >3 m/s. Emergent transfemoral arterial retrieval was performed. The device was first mobilized from the LVOT into the descending aorta using snare techniques, followed by stabilization with a retrieval basket. After failure of conventional snaring and capture attempts, definitive extraction was achieved using a bioptome through large-bore arterial access. Retrieval was successful without complications. Case 2: An 82-year-old male experienced near-complete device migration into the left atrium following LAAO implantation, with partial anchoring at the appendage ostium. A transseptal approach using a steerable venous platform was employed. A multimodal retrieval strategy combining snare catheterization, retrieval basket stabilization, and Raptor grasping forceps was required to secure and extract the device into the sheath. Subsequent attempts at LAAO re-implantation with multiple Amplatzer Amulet devices failed due to unfavorable appendage anatomy and extrinsic compression beneath the pulmonary artery, and no replacement device was implanted. Discussion: LAAO device embolization is uncommon (0.07-1.5%) but can result in significant morbidity. Embolization location dictates procedural risk and retrieval strategy; LVOT embolization represents a time-sensitive, high-risk scenario requiring prompt intervention. In both cases, conventional snaring alone was insufficient, highlighting the limitations of single-device retrieval approaches. Successful extraction required a multimodality strategy combining snare techniques, retrieval basket stabilization, and grasping/bioptome devices. Device stabilization was the critical technical step, allowing controlled manipulation and safe retrieval through large-bore sheaths. Unfavorable LAA anatomy may contribute to both device embolization and failure of repeat LAAO implantation, emphasizing the importance of reassessing anatomy after retrieval. Conclusion: Advanced multimodal percutaneous techniques can effectively manage complex LAAO device embolization and may avoid surgical extraction. A stepwise strategy and familiarity with multiple retrieval tools are critical for procedural success.
title: Abstract 9863: Advanced Percutaneous Retrieval Strategies for Embolized Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion Devices: Technical Insights from Complex Cases

abstract: Background: Registry studies of acute kidney injury (AKI) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) often ascertain AKI from ICD-10 administrative codes and dichotomize chronic kidney disease (CKD), which may misclassify events and mask a graded biological risk gradient. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that continuous baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), rather than binary CKD status, predicts laboratory-defined AKI, and that ICD coding substantially undercounts AKI relative to KDIGO criteria. Methods: Single-center retrospective cohort of 183 consecutive adults undergoing TAVR for severe native aortic stenosis (October 2022 to December 2024). The primary outcome was in-hospital AKI by KDIGO serum creatinine criteria (peak/baseline ratio of at least 1.5 or an absolute rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL); a secondary definition used ICD-10 N17.x. Continuous baseline eGFR (per 10 mL/min/1.73 m2 decrement) was modeled in the 182 patients with complete baseline laboratory data by Firth-penalized logistic regression adjusted for hemoglobin, diabetes, and heart failure. Concordance between definitions was assessed by sensitivity, specificity, and Cohen's kappa; discrimination by area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC). Results: KDIGO criteria identified 36 AKI events (19.7%) versus 11 by ICD coding (6.0%); ICD sensitivity was 27.8%, specificity 99.3%, kappa 0.37. KDIGO AKI was more frequent in CKD than non-CKD patients (30.6% vs 14.0%; p=0.0075), a difference undetectable by ICD coding (9.7% vs 4.1%; p=0.19). Each 10 mL/min/1.73 m2 decrement in baseline eGFR raised adjusted odds of KDIGO AKI by 34% (odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.60; p=0.0016; AUC 0.69, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.78). KDIGO AKI was associated with longer length of stay (median 3.8 vs 1.5 days; p less than 0.0001); binary CKD status was not (2.1 vs 2.2 days; p=0.71). Conclusions: Laboratory KDIGO criteria identified more than three-fold the AKI events captured by ICD coding alone. Baseline eGFR is an independent, continuous predictor of post-TAVR AKI, whereas AKI, not binary CKD status, drives length of stay. Registry surveillance based on ICD-10 coding substantially undercounts post-TAVR AKI and may bias estimates toward the null.
title: Abstract 9881: Administrative Coding versus Laboratory Criteria for Acute Kidney Injury After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Introduction: While pericarditis is a known cardiovascular manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), acute multi-valve failure from an active flare is exceptionally rare. This case highlights the rapid progression of fulminant lupus valvulitis to multi-organ failure and the multidisciplinary interventions necessary for surgical salvage. Patient Information: A 21-year-old male with SLE, nonadherent to hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolate mofetil, presented with three days of chest pain and dyspnea. This followed a recent admission for an upper respiratory infection complicated by pericarditis. Clinical Findings: Upon presentation, the patient exhibited rapidly progressing cardiovascular collapse and profound volume overload. Diagnostic Assessment: Labs showed significant troponemia (4,481 ng/L), concerning for myocarditis. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrated preserved left ventricular systolic function (EF 62%) but revealed new torrential aortic regurgitation, severe mitral regurgitation, and moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation, findings highly consistent with profound lupus valvulitis. Therapeutic Interventions: Advanced heart failure, rheumatology, and cardiothoracic surgery consultations were obtained. Hemodynamic instability required dobutamine. Pulse-dose corticosteroids and immunomodulators were initiated to suppress systemic inflammation. Despite medical management, his clinical course deteriorated with acute kidney injury requiring continuous veno-venous hemofiltration and acute hypoxic respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation. He then developed right-sided weakness secondary to a left sylvian M2 ischemic stroke, receiving tenecteplase with complete resolution of deficits. On hospital day 10, he underwent mechanical aortic valve replacement, alongside mitral and tricuspid valve repairs. Follow-Up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Postoperative TTE showed a reduced EF of 30% with resolution of aortic insufficiency and only mild residual mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. A new-onset atrial flutter was successfully converted to normal sinus rhythm via transesophageal echocardiography-guided cardioversion. Renal function normalized without further dialysis. He was discharged on immunosuppressives, guideline-directed medical therapy, and warfarin. Discussion: SLE nonadherence can rapidly precipitate life-threatening cardiovascular collapse. This case illustrates how active SLE can rapidly progress to fulminant multi-valve valvulitis, cardiogenic shock, and systemic complications despite preserved ventricular systolic function. Despite catastrophic complications requiring thrombolysis, aggressive medical optimization bridged with timely multidisciplinary surgical intervention yields successful outcomes in fulminant lupus valvulitis.
title: Abstract 9892: Fulminant Triple-Valve Lupus Valvulitis Complicated by Cardiogenic Shock and Acute Stroke: A Multidisciplinary Surgical Salvage

abstract: Introduction: Mechanical prosthetic valve obstruction is a life-threatening condition most commonly caused by thrombus or pannus. Differentiating between these etiologies is critical, as management strategies differ significantly. Case Presentation: A woman in her 50s with rheumatic bivalvular disease status-post mechanical bileaflet mitral and aortic valve replacement 20 years prior, atrial fibrillation on warfarin (with prior subtherapeutic INRs), HFpEF, prior cardioembolic MCA stroke, CKD stage 3, hypertension and diabetes, underwent elective cholecystectomy. Warfarin was held preoperatively, with bridging anticoagulation, and was restarted postoperatively. Routine postoperative TTE showed markedly elevated gradients across the mechanical aortic valve (peak velocity >6 m/s, mean gradient 80 mmHg), increased from prior, concerning for valve thrombosis. Fluoroscopy revealed restricted, asymmetric, beat-to-beat variable leaflet motion of the aortic prosthesis. The opening angular motion of each leaflet differed with every cardiac cycle, giving the appearance of “wobbly” or “dancing” valve leaflets. Cardiac CT demonstrated a well-seated mechanical aortic valve with hypoattenuating leaflet thickening (HALT) and hypoattenuation affecting motion (HAM), along with subvalvular pannus extending from the endomyocardium into the neo-sinus leaflet; valve area was 0.34 cm 2 , consistent with severe aortic stenosis. Comparison to prior imaging revealed likely progression of pannus, favoring pannus over thrombus as the primary etiology of valve obstruction. Clinically the patient remained at her baseline state with chronic exertional dyspnea throughout this course. CT had additionally revealed a right hepatic subcapsular hematoma (post-surgical) without active extravasation, with associated hemoglobin drop requiring transfusion, prompting temporary cessation of anticoagulation. Given the high surgical risk, intervention was deferred. The patient remained stable, anticoagulation was resumed, and she was discharged with plans for outpatient surgical AVR revision to correct the pannus-mediated obstruction. Discussion: This case highlights the importance of multimodality imaging in differentiating pannus from thrombus in mechanical valve obstruction. Recognition of chronic pannus as a cause of severe obstruction is essential, particularly in the postoperative setting, as it guides management away from thrombolysis toward surgical intervention. Pannus formation arises from the chronic growth of fibroelastic tissue over the valve. The beat-to-beat variability or “dancing” leaflet motion on fluoroscopy, occasionally referred to as “obstruction alternans” in some case reports, is likely from differing stroke volumes in each cardiac cycle due to valvular atrial fibrillation, although could be from thrombus as well if present.
title: Abstract 9895: When It’s Not Thrombus: Chronic Pannus Causing Severe Mechanical Aortic Valve Obstruction with Abnormal Leaflet “Dancing” Motion Seen on Fluoroscopy

abstract: Introduction/Background: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) caused by bleeding within the media of the epicardial coronary artery. SCAD affects predominantly women (>90% of cases), who are on average 44-53 years old. SCAD causes ~40% of ACS in pregnant and postpartum women (P-SCAD). P-SCAD has a higher severity than non-P-SCAD. These patients represent a significant management challenge for clinicians as recommendations to avoid pregnancy after SCAD are based on small case numbers in observational data. Research Questions/Hypothesis: Do genetic factors contribute to the higher severity of clinical presentation in P-SCAD compared to non-P-SCAD? Methods/Approach: The Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute (VCCRI) arteriopathies and SCAD cohort (VASC) has ~700 cases of SCAD, the majority with core lab angiographic confirmation. P-SCAD cases are identified through clinical history acquired at the time of enrolment and stored in the secure Redcap database. DNA is prepared from buccal cell mouthwash, saliva or blood samples. Cases are whole genome sequenced (WGS) using Illumina HiSeq X Ten platform with 30X coverage. Reads are aligned to the human reference genome. Tiered gene lists allow reporting on predicted damaging variants in genes already linked to SCAD, aortopathies or connective tissue disorders, and variants in novel genes are also reported. The validated SCAD polygenic risk score is calculated for all P-SCAD cases. Comparison is made to non-P-SCAD controls from previously published data to assess for overall relative burden of predicted damaging variants and polygenic risk. Results/Data (descriptive and inferential statistics): There are 38 P-SCAD cases recorded in the VASC database and 31 are angiographically confirmed. From the 38 cases, two cases were during pregnancy and 12 cases each were within one month, two-five months and six-twelve months post-partum. There were seven cases of recurrent SCAD. Mean age was 36 years (range 28-42 years). There were pregnancy complications of gestational diabetes in five and pre-eclampsia in one. Of the 38 cases, 30 had a previous pregnancy without SCAD and three had a pregnancy without SCAD after the P-SCAD pregnancy. Four P-SCAD cases had a family history of SCAD. From 17 cases that already have WGS data, there were seven predicted damaging variants in Tier 1 or 2 genes, including variants in ADAMTS2 , COL5A2 , PRKG1 , ACVR1 , COL4A1 (two cases) and FBN1 . A further 9 cases have been sent for WGS, with data pending. The preliminary predicted damaging variant yield in P-SCAD for Tier 1 or 2 genes is 7/17 (41%) which is greater than the yield in a non-P-SCAD cohort of 8/81, 10% (p=0.0097). Conclusion(s): The predicted damaging variant yield in SCAD, aortopathy and connective tissue disorder genes may be higher in P-SCAD than non-P-SCAD.
title: Abstract 9905: Genetic Features of Pregnancy-Associated Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection

abstract: Background: VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock carries substantial neurologic morbidity and resource utilization. Despite the high prevalence of chronic coronary disease in this population, its impact on neurologic outcomes and resource utilization remains poorly defined. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that pre-existing ischemic burden would independently predict neurologic complications, resource utilization, and discharge outcomes among VA-ECMO recipients. Methods: Using the HCUP National Inpatient Sample (2016-2022), we identified 37,425 adult hospitalizations with cardiogenic shock undergoing VA-ECMO, excluding post-cardiotomy shock, durable left ventricular assist device implantation, and prior transplant. Ischemic burden comprised five chronic coronary markers: prior myocardial infarction, coronary artery bypass grafting, percutaneous coronary intervention, ischemic cardiomyopathy, and chronic total occlusion, categorized as none, single, or two or more markers. Primary outcomes were ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. Secondary outcomes included discharge to home, vascular complications, length of stay, and total hospitalization charges. Survey-weighted multivariable regression adjusted for demographics, hospital characteristics, cardiac arrest, active myocardial infarction, and Elixhauser comorbidity burden. Results: Greater ischemic burden was independently associated with lower odds of ischemic stroke in a graded fashion (single marker: OR 0.66 [0.52-0.84], P=0.001; ≥2 markers: OR 0.59 [0.41-0.86], P=0.005). Hemorrhagic stroke demonstrated a similar directional trend but did not reach statistical significance. Vascular complications were comparable across groups. Greater ischemic burden was also associated with shorter length of stay (single marker: –4.6 days; ≥2 markers: –6.3 days; both P<0.001), lower hospitalization charges (single marker: –$126,397; ≥2 markers: –$197,250; both P<0.001), and higher odds of discharge to home, reaching significance at ≥2 markers (OR 1.70 [1.29-2.23], P<0.001). In contrast, active myocardial infarction independently increased ischemic stroke risk (OR 1.52 [1.26-1.83], P<0.001), suggesting distinct pathophysiology between acute and chronic coronary states. Conclusions: Pre-existing ischemic burden demonstrated a paradoxical, dose-dependent association with lower stroke risk, reduced resource utilization, and improved discharge disposition among VA-ECMO recipients. Potential mechanisms include survival selection, antecedent antiplatelet exposure, and ischemic preconditioning. These findings suggest that ischemic burden may identify a distinct risk phenotype not captured by current ECMO risk stratification models and warrant prospective investigation.
title: Abstract 9915: Pre-Existing Coronary Substrate and Outcomes in Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Cardiogenic Shock: A National Inpatient Sample Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Blood culture-negative endocarditis (BCNE) accounts for up to 31% of infective endocarditis (IE) cases. In immunosuppressed patients with rheumatic heart disease (RHD), inflammatory valve pathology can mimic IE on echocardiography, creating diagnostic uncertainty with therapeutic consequences. Patient Information: A 49-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on abatacept and leflunomide, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, right nephrectomy for renal-cell carcinoma, and left thalamic stroke presented with dyspnea, orthopnea, leg edema, night sweats, and fatigue without fever. Clinical Findings and Timeline: Examination revealed pitting edema, RUQ tenderness, severe tricuspid regurgitation, moderate mitral/aortic regurgitation, and no endocarditis findings. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed severe rheumatic mitral stenosis/regurgitation with restricted posterior leaflet and 1-cm anterior mitral leaflet echodensity. ESR 61 mm/h, CRP 2.4 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 6,000 pg/mL without leukocytosis. Blood cultures x3 (fungal, mycobacterial) negative at 96 hours; Bartonella, Brucella, Coxiella, Tropheryma whipplei, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. CT head: multifocal subacute strokes; CT abdomen: old splenic infarct. Right-heart catheterization confirmed severe pulmonary hypertension (PAP 57, PCWP 44 mmHg). Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: Differential: BCNE, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and rheumatic valvulitis exacerbation. The echodensity and multiterritory embolic events in an immunosuppressed host raised concern for IE; negative cultures and RHD suggested noninfective etiologies. 18F-FDG PET/CT was not performed due to hemodynamic instability. Therapeutic Interventions: Empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin were stopped after 5 days given negative cultures and nephrotoxicity risk (solitary kidney). Antirheumatic drugs held. Mitral valve replacement and tricuspid repair followed team discussion. Follow-Up, Outcomes, and Adverse Events: Histopathology showed acute and chronic inflammation, myxoid degeneration, and microcalcifications without organisms or microabscesses, confirming rheumatic valvulitis with superimposed inflammation. Postoperative cardiogenic shock required VA-ECMO; the patient died. Discussion and Synthesis: The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria improved IE diagnostic sensitivity (84% vs. 75%) by incorporating PET/CT; however, PET/CT has limited sensitivity for native valve IE (as low as 22%) and may yield false-positive uptake in inflammatory valve disease. Surgical pathology served as the definitive diagnostic discriminator. Clinicians should recognize that not all mobile valve lesions with embolic events represent infection, and tissue diagnosis remains essential when noninvasive criteria are inconclusive.
title: Abstract 9941: Valvulitis Masquerading as Culture Negative Endocarditis in an Immunosuppressed Patient A Case Report

abstract: Background: Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) is foundational in HFrEF, but its benefit may be partly tied to neurohormonal activation under chronic pressure overload. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) abruptly relieves valvular afterload, raising an important question: does ARNI retain incremental benefit over ACE inhibitors/ARBs (ACEi/ARB) after mechanical afterload relief? Real-world comparative data for ARNI versus ACEi/ARB after TAVR remain limited. Methods: In a federated EHR network of 110 health care organizations, we identified adults with systolic HF who initiated ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACEi/ARB within 3 months of TAVR from January 2015 onward. Cohorts were 1:1 propensity-score matched on demographics, comorbidities, renal function, concurrent HF therapies, and severity markers including NT-proBNP and LVEF. The primary outcome was 1-year acute HF event; secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality and MACE. Patients with the outcome before the assessment window were excluded. Outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Results: ARNI recipients (n=630) were markedly sicker at baseline than ACEi/ARB recipients (n=1,455), with higher rates of cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension, and advanced HF therapy use, reflecting real-world channeling of ARNI to higher-risk patients. After matching (499 per arm; all standardized differences <0.1), 1-year acute HF events were comparable between ARNI and ACEi/ARB (9.0% vs 8.4%; HR 1.15, 95% CI 0.68-1.96; p=0.60). Findings were concordant for all-cause mortality (7.0% vs 7.0%; HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.69-1.76) and MACE (9.6% vs 11.0%; HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.58-1.57). The primary estimate was unchanged after additional matching on NT-proBNP and LVEF. Conclusions: Despite preferential use in sicker, more-remodeled patients, ARNI was not associated with superior 1-year outcomes compared with ACEi/ARB after TAVR, and findings were robust to severity matching. As residual confounding may have favored the comparator, a modest ARNI benefit cannot be excluded. These real-world comparative data suggest that the incremental value of ARNI over ACEi/ARB after mechanical afterload relief with TAVR remains uncertain and warrants prospective evaluation, with direct implications for the growing post-TAVR HFrEF population.
title: Abstract 9946: Neprilysin Inhibition After Afterload Relief: ARNI versus ACE Inhibitors/ARBs in HFrEF Following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract: Background: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a non-atherosclerotic cause of acute coronary syndrome predominantly affecting women, accounting for up to 35% of acute coronary syndromes in women under 50. Consensus statements favor single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT), but prior observational studies have compared dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) only against aspirin-based SAPT regimens. The direct comparison of DAPT with clopidogrel monotherapy in SCAD has not been reported. We hypothesized that DAPT would not be associated with improved cardiovascular outcomes compared with clopidogrel monotherapy in SCAD. Methods: Using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network (2015-2024), we identified adults with SCAD (ICD-10-CM I25.42), excluding iatrogenic dissection (I97.51). Patients initiated on DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel) or clopidogrel monotherapy within 7 days of diagnosis were 1:1 propensity score matched on demographics, comorbidities, medications, laboratory values, and healthcare utilization. Outcomes from day 7 to 365 included a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; mortality, MI, or stroke), acute MI (AMI), percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), recurrent SCAD, and all-cause mortality. Bleeding and stroke events were too infrequent at one year for reliable hazard ratio estimation in this cohort. Hazard ratios were calculated using Cox proportional hazards models, and E-values were computed for robustness to unmeasured confounding. Results: After matching, 504 patients per arm were available; women comprised 64% of the cohort. Compared with clopidogrel monotherapy, DAPT was associated with significantly higher rates of MACE (HR 1.45, 95% CI 1.17-1.79; E-value 2.25), AMI (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.14-1.81; E-value 2.22), and all-cause mortality (HR 1.86, 95% CI 1.03-3.35; E-value 3.11). PCI (HR 1.62, 95% CI 0.95-2.76) and recurrent SCAD (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.85-1.43) trended in the same direction. Conclusions: In this propensity-matched real-world analysis of patients with SCAD, DAPT was associated with higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events and mortality compared with clopidogrel monotherapy, robust to substantial unmeasured confounding by E-value analysis. These findings, in a comparator not previously studied in SCAD, align with prior observational evidence and support ongoing equipoise for randomized trials of antiplatelet strategy in this disease.
title: Abstract 9947: Dual versus Single Antiplatelet Therapy with Clopidogrel in Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection: A Propensity-Matched Real-World Analysis

abstract: Background: Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAC) is increasingly used for stroke prevention in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, yet the optimal postprocedural antithrombotic regimen remains unclear. Purpose: To systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) compared with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) as postprocedural antithrombotic regimens following LAAC. Method: A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, and Clinicaltrials.gov through January 2026. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing DOACs with DAPT after LAAC was performed, with Risk Ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated and a trial sequential analysis to assess the conclusiveness of evidence. Heterogeneity was assessed using Higgins’ I 2 statistic. Statistical analyses were performed using R statistical software, version 4.4.2. Results: Three randomized trials including 704 patients (DOAC, n=368; DAPT, n=336) were analyzed. The median age of the participants was 77.3 years, with 34.5% being female. DOAC therapy significantly reduced device-related thrombosis compared with DAPT (0.5% vs 4.5%; RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.05-0.59; P < 0.01; I 2 = 0%) and was associated with a lower risk of the composite endpoint of mortality, stroke, bleeding, and device-related thrombosis (18.4% vs 30.0%; RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.89; P < 0.01; I 2 = 16%). Major bleeding occurred less frequently with DOACs (8.4% vs 12.2%; RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.39-0.95; P = 0.03; I 2 = 0%). There were no significant differences in stroke (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.06-4.58; P = 0.45; I 2 = 0%), all-cause mortality (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.24-1.53; P = 0.29; I 2 = 0%), or any bleeding (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.38-1.03; P = 0.11; I 2 = 54%). Trial sequential analysis suggested benefit favoring DOACs but indicated that the required information size was not fully reached. Conclusion: Post-LAAC antithrombotic therapy with DOACs significantly reduces device-related thrombosis and major bleeding, offering a superior net clinical benefit compared with DAPT. While trial sequential analysis confirms these favorable safety and efficacy trends, the required information size has not been fully met, emphasizing the need for larger, definitive randomized trials.
title: Abstract 9953: Direct Oral Anticoagulation vs Dual Antiplatelet Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials and Trial Sequential Analysis

abstract: Background: Cardiogenic shock (CS) carries a high mortality burden, yet national trends in premature CS-related deaths remain poorly understood. Research Question: We hypothesized that CS-related mortality among U.S. adults aged 25-64 years increased from 2018 to 2024, with a disproportionate burden among males, older working-age adults, Black adults, and individuals residing in the South. Methods: U.S. mortality data from 2018 to 2024 were analyzed using the CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death database. CS-related deaths were identified using ICD-10 code R57.0 as a contributing cause. Outcomes included annual deaths, age-adjusted mortality rates (AAMR) per 100,000, subgroup analyses by sex, age, race/ethnicity, and Census region, and log-linear annual percentage change (APC). Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. Results: During the study period, 69,228 premature CS-related deaths were recorded. Annual deaths increased from 8,356 in 2018 to 10,340 in 2024, with the AAMR rising from 4.1 to 5.1 per 100,000 (APC 3.84%; 95% CI 0.37-7.43; p=0.036). Males accounted for 64.7% of deaths and had a higher 2024 AAMR than females (6.7 vs. 3.5 per 100,000). Adults aged 55-64 years experienced the greatest burden (43,267 deaths; crude rate 15.5 per 100,000). Black adults had more than twice the 2024 AAMR of White adults (9.9 vs. 4.4 per 100,000). The South had the highest regional AAMR (5.9 per 100,000). The leading underlying causes were acute myocardial infarction, unspecified (14.8%), atherosclerotic heart disease (8.1%), and unspecified cardiomyopathy (5.1%). Circulatory diseases accounted for 58.0% of deaths. Conclusions: Premature CS-related mortality increased significantly in the United States from 2018 to 2024, with the greatest burden among males, adults aged 55-64 years, Black adults, and individuals residing in the South. These findings underscore the urgent need for earlier cardiovascular risk identification and targeted prevention in high-risk populations.
title: Abstract 9971: Increasing Premature Cardiogenic Shock Mortality in the United States: Analysing National Trends and Disparities

abstract: Case Presentation: A woman in her 50s with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus was found collapsed at home from suspected, but unwitnessed, cardiac arrest by her son who subsequently started chest compressions. Emergency medical service personnel delivered a defibrillation shock; however, spontaneous circulation was not restored. After the insertion of a laryngeal tube as an esophageal obturator-type supraglottic airway device, the woman was transported to the emergency department where the laryngeal tube was exchanged for an endotracheal tube. Although spontaneous circulation was restored the patient’s hemodynamics remained unstable. Because bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation had been initiated and the initial rhythm was shockable, we initiated venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Thus, unfractionated heparin was administered before the completion of cannulation for venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Differential Diagnosis: Head computed tomography performed immediately thereafter revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage suggestive of a rupture of a left middle cerebral artery aneurysm, corresponding to modified Fisher grade 4. Treatment and Management: On the day of presentation, following discussions with her family and medical team, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was discontinued. Computed tomography angiography was not performed because the patient’s condition was extremely poor and no definitive intervention for the suspected ruptured aneurysm was considered feasible. Emergency coronary angiography was also not performed. Outcome: The patient eventually died on day 3 of hospitalization. Discussion/Teaching Points: Typically, unfractionated heparin is administered before the completion of cannulation to initiate extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. However, most causes of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remain unclear when venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is initiated in an emergency setting. This means that anticoagulation may worsen intracranial hemorrhage or acute aortic syndrome if these conditions are the cause of the cardiac arrest. Therefore, following the initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, it may be worth considering anticoagulation at least after severe subarachnoid hemorrhage and acute aortic syndrome have been ruled out by emergency computed tomography. Further research is needed to evaluate the utility of this strategy in clinical practice.
title: Abstract CR04: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Detected After Initiation of Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Case Report

abstract: Background: Biventricular intracardiac thrombi are rare clinical entities associated with severe ventricular dysfunction and substantial thromboembolic risk. Simultaneous right and left ventricular thrombi complicated by ischemic stroke remain infrequently described in the literature. Case: A 43-year-old male with severe nonischemic cardiomyopathy presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, multifocal pneumonia, hemoptysis, and decompensated heart failure. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe biventricular systolic dysfunction with a large right ventricular intracardiac mass suspicious for thrombus. Transesophageal echocardiography further demonstrated a mobile tricuspid cord-associated mass concerning for thrombus versus vegetation. During hospitalization, the patient developed an acute embolic left posterior cerebral artery ischemic stroke requiring emergent mechanical thrombectomy. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated mobile intracardiac lesions involving both ventricles consistent with biventricular thrombi. The patient was treated with systemic anticoagulation and guideline-directed medical therapy with subsequent clinical stabilization. Conclusion: This case highlights the diagnostic complexity and embolic risk associated with biventricular intracardiac thrombi in severe nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Multimodality imaging was essential for diagnosis and management. Early recognition and anticoagulation remain critical to reduce catastrophic thromboembolic complications.
title: Abstract CR05: Biventricular Intracardiac Thrombi Presenting with Ischemic Stroke in Severe Nonischemic Cardiomyopathy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

abstract: Case Presentation: A 51-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and prior proximal right coronary artery (RCA) drug-eluting stent presented after presyncope. Initial testing showed negative troponin and new inferior T-wave inversions. She became unresponsive during a 7.5-second sinus pause, requiring temporary transvenous pacing and leadless pacemaker placement for presumed sick sinus syndrome. Two days later, she again became unresponsive and hypotensive while ventricularly paced at 40 beats/min. ECG showed new anterolateral ST elevations, and echocardiography revealed right ventricular (RV) dilation and dysfunction. Differential Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism, pacemaker malfunction, bradyarrhythmia-mediated shock, acute coronary syndrome, and RV infarction were considered. CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism. Coronary angiography showed acute in-stent thrombosis of the prior RCA stent with normal left coronary circulation, establishing RCA STEMI with RV infarction as the diagnosis. Treatment and Management: Before percutaneous coronary intervention, she developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arrest requiring defibrillation. She underwent emergent RCA PCI. Given biventricular failure and refractory cardiogenic shock, veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was initiated. Outcome and Follow-Up: After PCI and mechanical circulatory support, she stabilized and was decannulated. Her course was complicated by pneumonia-related respiratory failure requiring antibiotics and tracheostomy. She was transferred to the floor for recovery and disposition planning. Teaching Points: Sinus arrest may reflect ischemia of the sinoatrial nodal artery, particularly in RCA disease. Although chronic coronary disease has been proposed as a contributor to intrinsic sinus node dysfunction, acute sinus arrest during progression to critical coronary obstruction remains less well described. For resuscitation teams, new sinus dysfunction with ischemic ECG changes should be viewed as a pre-arrest warning sign of evolving coronary occlusion rather than attributed only to intrinsic conduction disease. Earlier recognition may accelerate coronary evaluation and prevent progression to STEMI, arrest, and shock.
title: Abstract CR10: The Pause Before the Arrest: Sinus Arrest as a Warning Sign of RCA In-Stent Thrombosis Leading to Cardiac Arrest and VA-ECMO-Supported Shock

abstract: Case: An octogenarian woman with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting performed 34 years earlier was admitted for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction caused by a culprit lesion in the left circumflex artery. Immediately after successful percutaneous coronary intervention, she developed cardiac arrest and underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation followed by initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-A ECMO) and intra-aortic balloon pump support. Diagnostic reasoning: On hospital day 2, left ventricular systolic function was considered sufficient for an ECMO weaning attempt, and V-A ECMO weaning was attempted. During ECMO clamp testing, right atrial pressure increased abruptly in association with a marked decline in systemic arterial pressure. Notably, pulmonary artery pressure remained unchanged despite the marked increase in right atrial pressure. This discordant right-sided hemodynamic response suggested extrinsic obstruction of the pulmonary artery. The pulmonary artery catheter findings prompted focused reassessment of the right-sided circulation. Echocardiography demonstrated focal compression and stenosis of the pulmonary artery, and computed tomography identified a localized anterior mediastinal hematoma compressing the pulmonary artery. Management and Outcome: Emergency surgical evacuation of the hematoma was subsequently performed, enabling successful decannulation from V-A ECMO. The patient was discharged on hospital day 46 without neurological sequelae. Discussion: This case demonstrates a rare mechanism of V-A ECMO weaning failure in which chest-compression-related vascular injury resulted in a localized mediastinal hematoma, likely confined by postoperative adhesions after prior sternotomy. More importantly, this case highlights the physiological significance of pulmonary artery catheter assessment during ECMO clamp testing. The combination of unchanged pulmonary artery pressure and elevated right atrial pressure provided an important clue suggesting extrinsic pulmonary artery obstruction rather than persistent biventricular failure. Careful interpretation of right-sided hemodynamics during ECMO weaning may facilitate early recognition of occult extracardiac causes of circulatory collapse and guide definitive intervention.
title: Abstract CR12: Difficult Weaning from Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Due to Pulmonary Artery Compression by a Chest Compression Related Mediastinal Hematoma: A Case Report

abstract: Background: High-voltage electrocution produces a spectrum of cardiac effects ranging from ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest to transient arrhythmias. Although myocardial stunning is a recognized consequence, ST-segment elevation after electrocution is uncommon and may mimic STEMI, potentially leading to unnecessary activation of emergent coronary angiography pathways. Case Presentation: A previously healthy 22-year-old male sustained a high-voltage electrical shock while manipulating a ladder that contacted an active power line. He collapsed immediately, and CPR was initiated by bystanders. EMS found him pulseless in ventricular tachycardic arrest and achieved return of spontaneous circulation after three defibrillations and approximately 10 minutes of downtime. Following ROSC, ECG demonstrated marked ST-segment elevation in V1-V4 with deep T-wave abnormalities and a wide QRS morphology suggestive of diffuse myocardial injury rather than focal coronary occlusion. Within minutes, these abnormalities rapidly resolved with normalization of sinus rhythm and repolarization changes. The patient remained hemodynamically stable without recurrent malignant dysrhythmias and was discharged home on hospital day 4. Discussion: Electrical injury may cause direct myocardial injury, coronary vasospasm, global myocardial stunning, and arrhythmogenesis. Although uncommon, ST-segment elevation after electrocution can closely mimic acute STEMI. Unlike ischemic STEMI, electrical-injury-related ST elevation often demonstrates diffuse precordial involvement, atypical QRS-T morphology, rapid spontaneous resolution, and absence of reciprocal ST depression. In this patient, the transient ECG abnormalities were most consistent with electrical myocardial stunning rather than acute coronary occlusion. Recognition of this pattern is important when the mechanism strongly suggests electrocution. Conclusion: This case demonstrates a reversible pattern of transient ST-segment elevation following high-voltage electrocution that mimicked STEMI but resolved within minutes. Awareness of this presentation may prevent unnecessary invasive coronary angiography and help clinicians correctly attribute ECG abnormalities to electrical myocardial injury rather than ischemic infarction. Serial ECGs remain essential in the immediate post-ROSC period after electrical injury.
title: Abstract CR13: Lightning Strikes Twice: Transient ST-Segment Elevation Following High-Voltage Electrocution Causing Reversible Myocardial Stunning Mimicking STEMI in 22 y/o Male

abstract: Introduction: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is increasingly being used to manage out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. However, significant debate remains regarding the hemodynamic effects of VA-ECMO. Research Questions: 1. What happens to cardiac hemodynamics upon VA-ECMO commencement in a large animal model of cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest? 2. In humans that survive to a weaning study, how do invasive cardiac hemodynamics change when VA-ECMO flow is manipulated? Methods: We simultaneously conducted two prospective physiologic studies where we performed serial invasive hemodynamic and echocardiographic evaluations to define cardiac hemodynamics with VA-ECMO flow variations. The first study was a porcine study where we induced cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest via coronary balloon occlusion and significant fluid loading in 60-65 kg Yorkshire pigs. The second study involved performing simultaneous left and right heart catheterization with three-dimensional echocardiography in humans cannulated for ECPR while sequentially weaning VA-ECMO flow. Serial hemodynamic comparisons were evaluated within each study using mixed effects models. Results: There were 15 animals in the porcine study (11 experimental and four controls) and 28 humans in the clinical study. In the animal study, VA-ECMO was commenced at a median of 2L/minute flow after cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest were induced. The initiation of VA-ECMO led to reductions in left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic volume (p<0.001 for all stages of VA-ECMO support compared to measurements taken prior to cardiac arrest), LV end-diastolic pressure (p<0.001 for all stages), LV stroke work (p<0.05 for all stages), LV pressure-volume area (p<0.05 for all stages), and right atrial pressure (p<0.01 for all stages) (Figure 1). Mean pulmonary arterial pressure was not significantly different. In our clinical study, 28 humans completed the entire hemodynamic protocol at a median of 3.0 days after VA-ECMO cannulation. Reduction in VA-ECMO flow led to increases in LV end-diastolic pressure, end-diastolic volume, stroke work and pressure-volume area (Figure 2) as well as right atrial and mean pulmonary arterial pressures (all p<0.001 for lowest flow compared to baseline). Conclusions: Higher VA-ECMO flow reduces LV end-diastolic pressure, end-diastolic volume, and cardiac work both at the time of VA-ECMO commencement in an experimental model of cardiac arrest, but also in humans able to tolerate a weaning study.
title: Abstract Or004: Cardiac Hemodynamics in Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation

abstract: Introduction: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) time is one of the strongest predictors of outcomes in cardiac arrest patients treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). Yet, a subset of patients with prolonged CPR still achieve favorable neurological recovery (“super-responders”), while others do not despite shorter CPR duration. Hypothesis: There are pre-arrest and intra-arrest characteristics that distinguish ECPR super-responders from those with poor neurological outcomes. Aims: To characterize the clinical profile of the ECPR super-responders. Methods: This retrospective study included adult out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest patients treated with ECPR at the University of Minnesota between 2015-2023. Favorable neurological outcome was defined as Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) 1-2 at discharge. Two pre-specified comparisons were performed: 1) super-responders, defined as patients with CPR duration >45 minutes and favorable CPC, versus patients with CPR duration >45 minutes and unfavorable CPC; 2) super-responders versus patients with CPR duration ≤ 45 minutes and unfavorable CPC. Pre-specified multivariable logistic regression analyses included age, presenting rhythm, ischemic cause of arrest, intermittent return of spontaneous rhythm (ROSC) and initial lactate. Results: CPR duration exceeded 45 minutes in 355 patients; 53 had favorable while 302 had unfavorable neurological outcomes (Table 1). After multivariable adjustment, younger age (p=0.001), lower initial lactate (p<0.001), intermittent ROSC (p=0.001), and ischemic cause of arrest (p=0.042) were independently associated with favorable neurological recovery (Table 2A). When comparing the super-responder cohort to the 92 patients with unfavorable outcomes despite CPR duration ≤45 minutes (Table 3), super-responders were younger (p=0.005), more likely to have shockable rhythm (p=0.001), and intermittent ROSC (p=0.007) (Table 2B). Conclusion: ECPR super-responders have a distinct clinical phenotype characterized by younger age, lower serum lactate, shockable initial rhythm, intermittent ROSC, and ischemic cause of arrest. These findings may help guide real-time resuscitation decision-making by identifying patients who may benefit from continued resuscitative efforts and escalation to ECPR despite ongoing, prolonged CPR.
