title: Abstract Or008: The Super-Responder Phenotype: Who Recovers Neurologically After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Despite Prolonged Resuscitation?

abstract: Background: Ventricular arrhythmias (VA) remain a leading cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) during ST-elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI). Risk stratification for VA during STEMI remains elusive. Genetic risk for malignant arrhythmias, including out-of-hospital SCD, are well established for individuals with rare, pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in arrhythmia (AR) and cardiomyopathy (CM)-associated genes. Whether this risk extends to VA in other clinical contexts, such as during a STEMI, remains uninvestigated. Research Hypothesis: In a population genomic screening context, individuals with a rare, P/LP, AR- or CM-associated variant (G+) have higher odds of VA during a STEMI event compared to individuals without such a variant (G-). Methods: We curated a retrospective cohort of STEMI events in the Geisinger MyCode Community Health Initiative (n=230,070 with exomes and EHR). VA was determined as a composite of ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, SCD, or CPR during the STEMI encounter. P/LP status was assigned in 37 AR/CM genes according to gene-specific loss of function (LOF) or missense mechanisms based on Variant Effect Predictor and ClinVar annotations. Statistical comparisons were made with Firth’s bias-reduced logistic regression adjusted for sex, infarct location, admission LVEF, and peak troponin T, or t-test. Results: In 230,070 MyCode participants, there were 2,385 who experienced a STEMI and 441 with VA during the STEMI encounter (STEMI+VA; 17%). In 2,161 total MyCode participants with rare, P/LP genetic variants (0.9% of MyCode), 13 were STEMI without VA (0.6% of G+) and four were STEMI+VA (0.19%). Harboring a P/LP variant did not associate with VA risk during STEMI after accounting for patient sex, infarct location, and peak troponin (Odds Ratio 1.63 [0.3-6.3], P = 0.5). Variants in STEMI+VA were all LOF variants in four different genes, MYH7 , TTN , DSG2 , and ALPK3 . This was similar to variants detected in non-VA STEMI, which were identified in TTN (n=4 G+), ALPK3 (n=3), DSC2 , DSG2 , DSP , MYH7 , PLN , and SCN5A (all n=1). Age at STEMI+VA did not differ by P/LP status (G+ age 67 ± 10; G- 63 ± 13; P = 0.4), nor did LVEF at STEMI admission (G+ 48 ± 9.6%; G- 42 ± 13.5%; P = 0.4). Conclusions: Elucidating risk factors for VA during STEMI is a first step towards improving survival rates. Preliminary analyses suggest that harboring a rare, pathogenic genetic variant in AR/CM genes does not associate with increased risk of VA during STEMI. This is limited by lower yield of genetic testing in a population screening context and incomplete EHR data. It is likely that the role of genetics in STEMI+VA is multifactorial and encompasses polygenic risk and/or environmental factors that interplay with arrhythmic etiology in addition to monogenic risk from rare, pathogenic variants.
title: Abstract Or013: Evaluating Monogenic Ventricular Arrhythmia Risk During STEMI in a Population Cohort

abstract: Introduction/Background: Mature extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) programs can improve survival in patients with refractory ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (VT/VF OHCA) by supporting visceral perfusion and allowing time to identify the inciting cause. While ischemic etiologies account for approximately 70% of refractory VT/VF OHCA, the long-term outcomes of non-ischemic causes remains poorly explored. Research Questions: 1. Among patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR, are there differences in outcomes between ischemic and non-ischemic etiologies? 2.Among patients with non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR, are there differences in outcomes across distinct non-ischemic phenotypes? Aims: 1. Compare outcomes between ischemic and non-ischemic etiologies2. Compare outcomes among non-ischemic phenotypes. Methods/Approach: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA referred to the Minnesota Mobile Resuscitation ECPR protocol. Patients were classified as ischemic or non-ischemic based on angiographic, biomarker, and clinical evaluation. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier and adjusted survival analyses were done to compare outcomes between ischemic and non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA. Results/Data: Among 412 patients, 289 (70.1%) had ischemic and 123 (29.9%) had non-ischemic etiologies. All-cause mortality occurred in 83.3% of patients after 345.7 person-years follow-up. In unadjusted Cox proportional hazard and Kaplan-Meier analyses, ischemic cause of refractory VT/VF OHCA was not associated with the hazard of all-cause mortality (HR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.69-1.08 and log-rank, p=0.19; Figure 1). In adjusted analyses, ischemic cause of refractory VT/VF OHCA was not associated with the hazard of mortality in the total cohort (HR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.61-1.08) as well as the subset of patients who survived the index hospitalization (HR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.34-3.27). Among non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA phenotypes with >5 patients, patients with known genetic cardiomyopathy, illicit drug use, and arrhythmic sudden cardiac death without known cardiomyopathy had relatively better outcome (Figure 2). Conclusions: Among patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA requiring ECPR, there is a broad array of non-ischemic pathologies. These patients have comparable outcomes to patients with ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA. However, among patients with non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA, outcomes differ significantly by phenotype.
title: Abstract Or016: Phenotypes of Non-Ischemic Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Treated with Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation

abstract: Background: The "July Effect" refers to a potential deterioration in patient outcomes and hospital efficiency coinciding with the annual turnover of trainees in U.S. academic medical centers. In-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) represents a high-acuity scenario where frontline providers are often early-career trainees, yet the influence of academic-year timing on CPR outcomes has not been systematically characterized. Research Question: We hypothesized that patients requiring in-hospital CPR during Q3 (July-September) — the period of maximal trainee inexperience — would demonstrate worse outcomes compared to other academic quarters. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS, 2016-2019), identifying adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent in-hospital CPR (ICD-10-PCS: 5A12012). Patients with COVID-19 were excluded. Calendar quarters were defined as Q1 (January-March), Q2 (April-June), Q3 (July-September; reference), and Q4 (October-December). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital complications: cardiogenic shock, ventricular tachycardia (VT), and acute respiratory failure (ARF). Multivariable logistic regression was performed adjusting for age, sex, and Elixhauser comorbidities. Survey-weighted analyses used HCUP-NIS discharge weights to generate national estimates. All analyses were performed in Stata 17. Results: Among 123,253 patients requiring CPR, distribution across quarters was 24.01% (Q3 July-September), 26.65% (Q4 October-December), 25.55% (Q1 January-March), and 23.79% (Q2 April-June). Compared to Q3, Q4 had significantly higher odds of mortality (OR: 1.08; p<0.001). The likelihood of developing cardiogenic shock was lower in Q4 (OR: 0.95; p=0.04), while Q1 was associated with lower odds of acute respiratory failure (OR: 0.93; p<0.001) and ventricular tachycardia (OR: 0.95; p=0.029). No significant mortality difference was observed in Q1 or Q2. Conclusions: Contrary to the classic July Effect hypothesis, mortality was highest in Q4, not Q3. This paradox — higher mortality alongside fewer severe complications in Q4 — suggests that factors beyond initial trainee inexperience, including seasonal illness burden and evolving clinical decision-making across the academic year, may shape CPR outcomes. These findings challenge a binary framing of the July Effect and underscore the need for longitudinal quality-improvement strategies in high-acuity resuscitation care.
title: Abstract P1002: Staying Alive: A Retrospective Analysis of the July Effect and In-Hospital Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Outcomes

abstract: Background: Patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for sepsis are at high risk for hemodynamic collapse, as sepsis can precipitate acute-on-chronic cardiac decompensation through myocardial depression, altered loading conditions, and neurohormonal dysregulation. We sought to identify early clinical predictors of Cardiogenic Shock (CS) among HFrEF patients admitted to the ICU with sepsis. Aim: To identify predictors of ICU-acquired CS in HFrEF patients with sepsis. Methodology: We performed a retrospective multicenter cohort study using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (2014-2015) as the discovery cohort and MIMIC-IV (2008-2022) for external validation. Adult patients admitted to the ICU with concurrent HFrEF and sepsis were included, while those presenting with CS at ICU admission were excluded. Candidate predictors available within the first 24 hours of ICU admission included demographics, hemodynamics, laboratory values, illness severity, and vasopressor use. Univariate logistic regression was performed on all candidate predictors, and significant variables (P<0.10) were entered into a multivariable model. Results: The eICU-CRD discovery cohort comprised 2,452 patients (131 [5.3%] developed ICU-acquired CS). The MIMIC-IV validation cohort comprised 3,229 patients (566 [17.5%] with ICD-coded CS). ICU-acquired CS was associated with nearly twofold higher hospital mortality (44.3% vs. 22.2%; P<0.001) and more than twofold higher ICU mortality (30.5% vs. 14.0%; P<0.001) in the discovery cohort. CS patients were younger (median 68 vs. 73 years; P=0.008), more likely male (67.9% vs. 52.3%; P<0.001), and had higher illness severity (APACHE IV 83.5 vs. 68.0; P<0.001). Eight predictors independently associated with CS on univariate analysis (all P<0.05): vasopressor requirement within 24 hours (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.13-1.44), peak troponin elevation (OR 1.25, 95% CI 1.10 -1.42), maximum serum lactate (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.06 -1.42), APACHE IV score (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.05 -1.38), initial serum lactate (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.04 -1.39), maximum anion gap (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.01 -1.34), mean arterial pressure (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.75-0.99), and minimum serum bicarbonate (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73-0.96). The composite multivariable model achieved an AUROC of 0.778 (95% CI 0.716-0.839). In a prespecified sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with documented systolic HF, discrimination improved to an AUROC of 0.836 (95% CI, 0.753-0.914). The MIMIC-IV cohort confirmed a similarly high CS-attributable mortality burden (hospital mortality 31.9%), consistent with the discovery cohort findings. Conclusion: ICU-acquired cardiogenic shock occurs in a significant subset of HFrEF patients with sepsis, is associated with substantially increased mortality, and can be predicted using early clinical and laboratory markers.
title: Abstract P1005: Clinical Predictors of Cardiogenic Shock in Patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit for Sepsis - A Multicenter Discovery and External Validation Study

abstract: Background: The 2025 AHA Pediatric Advanced Life Support guidelines recommend epinephrine every 3–5 minutes during cardiac arrest (Class IIb), yet supporting evidence remains limited and hemodynamic effects of repeated dosing are not well characterized. Epinephrine raises coronary perfusion pressure via α 1 -mediated vasoconstriction and a resulting rise in diastolic blood pressure, quantifiable by computing the pressure–time integral (PTI) of the arterial diastolic waveform. In preclinical models, PTI attenuates with subsequent doses, likely due to receptor desensitization and arrest progression. Whether this decay occurs in humans, and whether its magnitude predicts resuscitation failure, is unknown. Hypothesis: The hemodynamic response to epinephrine boluses, quantified as the PTI of arterial diastolic pressure, declines with repeated dosing during cardiac arrest, characterized by exponential decay constant k. Methods: A single-center retrospective cohort of pediatric cardiac ICU arrests (2024–2026) receiving ≥2 epinephrine doses with continuous invasive arterial monitoring were identified. For each bolus, the PTI of arterial DBP above a 30-second pre-bolus baseline was computed over the subsequent 2 minutes. An exponential decay model was fit across bolus number (ln [PTI] ~ –k х dose index) to estimate each patient's per-bolus decay. The primary outcome was failed conventional resuscitation (ECPR < 20 minutes or death). Results: Twenty-one arrests met inclusion criteria and contributed 137 epinephrine boluses. All arrests had a measurable positive PTI of the arterial DBP. Median first-dose PTI was 524 mmHg·s (IQR 291-1336) and decreased to median 172 mmHg·s (IQR 105-595) by dose 5. In 14 out of 21 arrests (67%), last dose PTI was lower than first dose. Across all arrests with at least two analyzable boluses (n=20), the per-patient decay constant did not differ significantly from zero (Wilcoxon, p=0.17). Thirteen arrests (65%) had a positive exponential decay (k > 0; median k 0.47 per dose, IQR 0.10–0.54) and seven arrests (35%) had k < 0 (median k –0.21 per dose, IQR –0.37 to –0.12), indicating no consistent dose-related attenuation. In exploratory comparisons, arrests with ROSC (n=6) had higher first-dose PTI than those with ECPR/death (n=15) (median 1444 vs 495 mmHg·s), though not significant (Mann-Whitney, p=0.095). Conclusions: In this pilot cohort of pediatric in-hospital arrests, PTI computation of invasive arterial monitoring was feasible and revealed substantial interindividual variability in hemodynamic responsiveness to epinephrine across boluses. Most patients showed attenuation of response with successive doses, but effect magnitude and decay kinetics varied widely. These findings support validation of PTI-based decay metrics in larger cohorts to assess whether kinetics can inform individual resuscitation strategy or timing of escalation to ECPR.
title: Abstract P1017: Quantifying Hemodynamic Responses to Epinephrine Administration During Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Older patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) witnessed by family members in Japan are less likely to receive bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in the prehospital setting and have worse neurological outcomes than those witnessed by non-family bystanders. However, differences in in-hospital management remain unclear. Aim: To examine how in-hospital management differs according to bystander-patient relationship. Methods: Older patients (aged ≥65 years) with OHCA of cardiac origin witnessed by a lay bystander and registered in the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (JAAM-OHCA) registry between 2014 and 2022 were analyzed. Patients were divided into two groups: the family member-witnessed group and the non-family bystander-witnessed group. The primary outcomes were the proportions of patients receiving extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), intra-aortic balloon pumping (IABP), coronary angiography (CAG), percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and target temperature management (TTM). Associations between bystander-patient relationship and in-hospital management were assessed using multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for 14 covariates available at hospital arrival. Results: Among 11,861 patients (the family member-witnessed group: 7,547; the non-family bystander-witnessed group: 4,314), ECPR was performed in 387/7,547 (5.1%) in the family member-witnessed group and 291/4,314 (6.7%) in the non-family bystander-witnessed group, with no significant difference between groups (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.72-1.08). Similarly, there was no significant difference in IABP use (383/7,547 [5.1%] vs. 314/4,314 [7.3%]; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.71-1.05). In contrast, the family member-witnessed group was significantly less likely to receive CAG (780/7,547 [10.3%] vs. 669/4,314 [15.5%]; aOR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67-0.93), PCI (415/7,547 [5.5%] vs. 380/4,314 [8.8%]; aOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.63-0.97), and TTM (569/7,547 [7.5%] vs. 488/4,314 [11.3%]; aOR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Conclusions: Older patients with family member-witnessed OHCA were less likely to receive CAG, PCI, and TTM than those with non-family bystander-witnessed OHCA. The observed differences may be partly attributable to unmeasured factors, such as arrest location (e.g., at home vs. in public place), which may affect CPR quality but were unavailable in this registry. The authors used ChatGPT (OpenAI) exclusively for English language editing and not for data analysis. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the abstract.
title: Abstract P1021: Association Between Bystander-Patient Relationship and In-Hospital Management Among Older Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Multicenter Observational Study in Japan

abstract: Background: Sex-based differences in the clinical presentation of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) may influence downstream cardiovascular evaluation and treatment. Evidence on in-hospital cardiovascular interventions among patients who survive OHCA to hospital discharge remains limited. Hypothesis: Among hospital-discharge survivors after OHCA, cardiovascular diagnoses and in-hospital interventions differ between females and males. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry linked to provincial administrative and clinical databases. Adults with EMS-treated, nontraumatic OHCA from 2011 to 2017 who survived to hospital discharge were included. Cardiovascular diagnoses and in-hospital interventions were compared by sex using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Results: Among 9,982 EMS-treated OHCA cases, 1,325 patients survived to hospital discharge. After excluding 47 patients with missing covariate data, the final analytic cohort included survivors: 284 females (22.2%) and 994 males (77.8%). Females were less likely than males to have documented coronary artery disease (29.6% vs 56.6%; P<0.001) or ST-elevation myocardial infarction (18.3% vs 34.0%; P<0.001). Females were also less likely to undergo diagnostic angiography (52.8% vs 74.0%; P<0.001), percutaneous coronary intervention (26.1% vs 39.6%; P<0.001), or coronary artery bypass graft surgery (1.8% vs 12.3%; P<0.001). Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement was similar between females and males (22.2% vs 25.8%; P=0.22). Conclusions: Among patients discharged alive after OHCA, females underwent fewer coronary diagnostic and revascularization procedures than males. These unadjusted findings may reflect differences in arrest etiology, clinical presentation, or treatment patterns. Further multivariable analyses are needed to determine whether sex is independently associated with post-arrest cardiovascular care.
title: Abstract P1023: Sex Differences in Cardiovascular Interventions Among Survivors of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Temperature control is a pivotal component of post-cardiac arrest care for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Therapeutic hypothermia (TH), a subset of temperature control, may provide benefits in selected patients. Meanwhile, enteral nutrition (EN) for the patients with critical condition is advoacated. However, the effectiveness of EN during TH, remain uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the association between EN during TH and clinical outcomes in patients with OHCA. Methods: This study was a secondary analysis of the SAVE-J II study, a multicenter retrospective cohort of patients with OHCA who received veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and were treated with TH. The duration of TH was defined as the sum of the hypothermia and rewarming periods after ICU admission. Patients were categorized based on the timing of EN initiation during TH. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of infection and gastrointestinal complications, such as vomiting or ischemic colitis. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) and propensity score matching (PSM) were used to adjust for potential confounders. Results: Of the 2,157 enrolled patients, 345 were eligible for analysis (EN during TH, n = 122; EN after TH, n = 223). GEE analysis showed that initiation of EN during TH was not associated with a significant difference in survival to discharge compared with initiation after TH (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.46-1.54, p = 0.57). After PSM, 188 patients were matched (94 in each group), and conditional logistic regression analysis similarly showed no significant difference in survival to discharge between the groups (68.1% vs. 72.3%; OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.45-1.52, p = 0.54). The incidence of infection (54.2% vs. 63.8%; OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.35-1.20, p = 0.17) and gastrointestinal complications (1.1% vs. 2.1%; OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.05-5.51, p = 0.57) did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Although EN during TH was not associated with improved survival to discharge among patients with OHCA, the proportion of infection and gastrointestinal complication did not differ. These findings suggest that EN during TH may be feasible without increasing adverse events. Prospective studies are warranted to determine the optimal nutritional strategy during temperature management.
title: Abstract P1032: Effectiveness and Safety of Enteral Nutrition During Therapeutic Hypothermia for Patient Who Received Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation

abstract: Background: Hemoglobin targets are absent from post-cardiac arrest guidelines. New trials suggest that patients with brain and myocardial injury, injuries common post-arrest, may benefit from liberal transfusion strategies. Trends in post-arrest hemoglobin and real-world practices remain poorly characterized. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adult cardiac arrests at three academic hospitals. Patients who survived the initial resuscitation and had a hemoglobin value measured were included. All post-arrest hemoglobin values and red blood cell transfusions were collected through 30 days; descriptive statistics and graphical visualization were used to present hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices. Associations between hemoglobin level and in-hospital mortality were assessed with logistic regression for the initial post-arrest hemoglobin value, and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models for hemoglobin values through 30 days. Results: Of 2,634 cardiac arrests, 958 met inclusion criteria, with 152 (15.9%) out-of-hospital arrests and 806 (84.1%) in-hospital. The mean initial post arrest hemoglobin was 9.75 g/dL (SD 2.60), with hemoglobin levels declining progressively over the first 20 days post-arrest. Red cell transfusions were delivered for 369 (38.5%) patients in the 30 days post-arrest, with 1,253 total transfusions. The mean pre-transfusion hemoglobin value was 6.96 g/dL (SD 1.06). A restrictive transfusion strategy (pre-transfusion hemoglobin of < 7 g/dL) was used for 772 (61.6%) of transfusions, and a liberal strategy (pre-transfusion hemoglobin of ≥ 7 g/dL) for 481 (38.4%). Over 30 days, the highest proportion of patients transfused was in the first 48 hours. Patients with initial post-arrest hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL had lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.62, 95%CI 0.46-0.84, p<0.01). In time-varying analysis, post-arrest hemoglobin through 30 days demonstrated an L-shaped association with mortality, with 95% of the total reduction in mortality hazard captured below 9.20 g/dL. Conclusions: Anemia is common after cardiac arrest, worsening in initial survivors. There is substantial variation between liberal and restrictive transfusion strategies, reflecting clinical equipoise. Clinical trials are needed to disentangle anemia as a driver versus a marker of outcomes, and test whether the risk is modifiable.
title: Abstract P1034: Hemoglobin Trends and Transfusion Practices After Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Simulation-based medical education increasingly incorporates strategies to improve realism and learner immersion during high-acuity training. Moulage enhances visual and environmental fidelity, but evidence regarding its influence on clinical reasoning and decision-making during cardiac emergencies and resuscitation remains limited. Objective: To evaluate the influence of advanced moulage on clinical decision-making, diagnostic accuracy, and team performance during simulated cardiac emergencies and resuscitation training. Methods: A prospective observational simulation study was conducted with 20 healthcare professionals participating in advanced cardiovascular emergency and resuscitation training at a tertiary academic simulation center. Participants included physicians, nurses, and multidisciplinary emergency providers trained in ACLS. Teams participated in two high-fidelity simulation scenarios involving cardiac arrest and severe cardiogenic shock. Scenarios incorporated advanced moulage techniques reproducing cyanosis, diaphoresis, peripheral hypoperfusion, bleeding patterns, and progressive physiological deterioration. Primary endpoints included recognition of clinical deterioration, initiation of critical interventions, diagnostic accuracy, adherence to ACLS algorithms, and overall resuscitation performance. Results: Advanced moulage was associated with improved situational awareness and faster recognition of physiological instability. Median time to initiation of life-saving interventions decreased by 18% compared with institutional historical simulation benchmarks. Diagnostic accuracy increased from 72% to 90% in scenarios requiring differentiation between cardiogenic, obstructive, and hypovolemic etiologies. Teams exposed to enhanced realism demonstrated improved adherence to ACLS protocols and earlier escalation of critical interventions. Participants reported high immersion and realism scores (9.3 ± 0.5). Non-technical skills also improved, particularly leadership behavior and communication during resuscitation efforts. Conclusion: Advanced moulage enhanced realism, clinical reasoning, and team dynamics during simulated cardiac emergencies and resuscitation scenarios. Structured moulage techniques may improve recognition of critical illness, accelerate decision-making, and optimize adherence to resuscitation protocols. Findings support the incorporation of advanced moulage into cardiovascular simulation programs aimed at improving emergency preparedness and resuscitation performance.
title: Abstract P1050: The Influence of Moulage on Clinical Decision-Making in Simulated Cardiac Emergencies and Resuscitation

abstract: Background: High-quality chest compressions are the cornerstone of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), yet whether mechanical chest compressions delivered by the LUCAS device consistently generate effective forward blood flow remains uncertain. Transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) enables direct visualization of the cardiac structures compressed during ongoing CPR. We investigated the association between compression site and outcomes in patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). Methods: We conducted a single-centre retrospective observational study of consecutive adult patients with refractory OHCA admitted under ongoing mechanical CPR to the Cardiac Arrest Center of IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy, and subsequently treated with ECPR. TEE was performed immediately upon hospital arrival. An expert echocardiographer, blinded to outcomes, classified the compressed structure as the left ventricle (LV) body, LV outflow tract (LVOT), aortic valve/root, or left atrium. Ideal positioning was defined as LV body compression without LVOT, aortic valve, or aortic root compression, a configuration expected to maximize forward flow. Patients were categorized as having ideal or non-ideal compression. Results: Ninety patients were included (median age 54 years, 86% male, 64% presenting with a shockable rhythm). Twenty-two patients (24.4%) had ideal compression, whereas 68 (75.6%) had non-ideal compression. Survival to hospital discharge was significantly higher in the ideal group (22.7% vs 2.9%; p=0.009). Favourable neurological outcome at six months was also more frequent (14.3% vs 2.9%; p=0.083). After multivariable adjustment, ideal compression remained independently associated with survival to hospital discharge (adjusted OR 9.28, 95% CI 1.62-53.07; p=0.012) and showed a similar, borderline-significant association with favourable neurological outcome (adjusted OR 5.42, 95% CI 0.82-35.88; p=0.079). Conclusions: Among patients with refractory OHCA undergoing ECPR, TEE-confirmed compression of the LV body, without compression of the LVOT or aortic root, was strongly associated with survival to hospital discharge. These findings suggest that the anatomical target of mechanical chest compressions may substantially influence haemodynamic effectiveness and clinical outcomes. title: Abstract P1066: Transoesophageal Echocardiographic Assessment of Mechanical Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Positioning and Outcomes in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Prehospital critical care response units (CCRUs) that respond to out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA) and administer advanced interventions such as extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) may shorten treatment delays and improve patient outcomes. We sought to examine the feasibility of a planned prehospital CCRU program in southern Ontario, Canada and quantify potential benefit for OHCAs. Methods: We included adult (age 18+), EMS-assessed OHCAs occurring within one of three regions in southern Ontario, Canada (Toronto, Peel, Halton) between January 1, 2022 and December 31, 2023. We computed estimated response times by a CCRU crew (defined as the time between 9-1-1 call and CCRU crew arrival on scene) dispatched from one of two paramedic bases, accounting for CCRU crew availability at the time of dispatch and stand-down protocols (e.g., TOR before CCRU arrival). We defined OHCAs as ECPR-eligible if they had a CCRU response time ≤45 mins and met clinical inclusion criteria from one of three previous ECPR trials (ARREST, Prague, INCEPTION). Characteristics and distributions of CCRU response times were determined for each cohort of ECPR-eligible patients. Analyses were repeated to consider limiting CCRU availability to one base and/or to between 8:00am-8:00pm on weekdays based on potential operational constraints. Results: A total of 5,469 OHCAs were included. CCRU crews arrived on scene to 5,422 (99.1%) OHCAs with a median response time of 21.6 mins [IQR: 15.5-28.6]. The number of ECPR-eligible OHCAs was 206 (3.8%) following inclusion criteria from ARREST, 366 (6.8%) from Prague, and 106 (2.0%) from INCEPTION. Assuming CCRU availability between 8:00am-8:00pm on weekdays yielded a total of 2,315 OHCAs: CCRU crews arrived on scene to 2,257 (97.5%) OHCAs with a median CCRU response time of 22.1 mins [IQR: 15.6-29.3]. The number of ECPR-eligible OHCAs during this timeframe were 87 (3.9%) following inclusion criteria from ARREST, 142 (6.3%) from Prague, and 47 (2.1%) from INCEPTION. Proportions of ECPR-eligible OHCAs significantly differed by clinical inclusion criteria used (p<0.001) but did not differ across CCRU crew availability scenarios. Conclusion: Deployment of prehospital CCRU crews can provide timely ECPR access and may shorten delays to ECPR initiation. However, proportions of ECPR-eligible OHCAs remain relatively low.
title: Abstract P1070: Assessing Feasibility of Prehospital Critical Care Response Units for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Southern Ontario, Canada Using Geospatial Modeling

abstract: Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with low survival and poor neurological outcomes despite advances in resuscitation care. Guidelines advocate for centralization of post-resuscitation care in specialized cardiac arrest centers with 24/7 access to advanced resources and expertise for all patients with OHCA. Treatment in such centers appears to improve survival and outcome across the broader OHCA population. The Minnesota Mobile Resuscitation Consortium (MMRC) is a metropolitan-wide hub-and-spoke extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) program that directs selected patients with OHCA to three expert Cannulation Hospitals for potential extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Research Question: Whether patients who achieve prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) benefit from care within such a system, despite not requiring cannulation, remains unknown. Aim: To describe outcomes of patients with prehospital ROSC treated within an expert cardiac arrest and ECPR program, and to compare these outcomes with those of patients treated at hospitals without similar expertise. Methods: We conducted a retrospective descriptive study of patients with VF/VT OHCA meeting entry criteria for the MMRC protocol but achieving prehospital ROSC and transported to three expert ECMO centers between September 2020 and December 2025. A case control cohort of patients transported to other hospitals in the same metropolitan area were identified from the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES). The primary outcomes were survival to hospital discharge and functionally favorable survival. Results: Ninety-four patients met inclusion criteria in the MMRC cohort and 365 in the case control cohort. Survival to hospital discharge was 79/94 (84%) and 245/365 (67%) in the MMRC and case control cohorts, respectively, p<0.001. Functionally favorable survival to hospital discharge was similar between the MMRC and case control cohorts with 67/94 (71%) and 228/365 (62%), respectively, p=0.11. Conclusion: Among patients with VF/VT OHCA who achieved prehospital ROSC, treatment within the MMRC ECPR system, even in the absence of subsequent ECMO use, was associated with higher survival to discharge with no change in functionally favorable survival compared to the cohort outside the ECPR program.
title: Abstract P1072: Survival After Prehospital Return of Spontaneous Circulation Within an Expert Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation System

abstract: Background: Although outcomes of patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain poor, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has been reported to potentially improve outcomes in selected patients with OHCA. However, it remains unclear whether priority should be given to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) pump-on or endotracheal intubation (ETI) during ECPR implementation for OHCA patients. This study evaluated the association between ECMO pump-on prior to ETI and favorable neurological outcome for patients with OHCA who received ECPR. Methods: This study was a secondary analysis of the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (JAAM-OHCA) registry between June 2014 and December 2022, a multicenter retrospective registry study. Patients with OHCA who remained in cardiac arrest on hospital arrival and underwent ECPR were enrolled. Patients with a time from cardiac arrest to ETI or ECMO pump-on exceeding 60 minutes were excluded. Patients were divided into two groups depending on whether or not they underwent ECMO pump-on prior to ETI (the ECMO-first group and the ETI-first group). The primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome defined as Cerebral Performance Category scores of 1 or 2 at 30 days. Results: Of 95,902 patients registered in the JAAM-OHCA registry, 1,003 patients were enrolled in this study. The median age was 60 (IQR, 49-69) years, 85% were male. The median time from cardiac arrest to ECMO pump-on was 49 (IQR, 43-54) minutes, and the median time from cardiac arrest to ETI was 33 (IQR, 27-40) minutes. There were 73 patients in the ECMO-first group and 930 patients in the ETI-first group. The proportion of favorable neurological outcome at 30 day was 17.8% (13/77) vs. 13.0% (121/930). Multivariable logistic regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, witnessed cardiac arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and time from collapse to ECMO pomp-on, showed that the ECMO-first group was not associated with favorable neurological outcome at 30 days (Odds ratio: 0.84; 95% confidence interval: 0.37-1.91, p = 0.69). This trend was also found even for the patients with shockable rhythm on admission (OR: 1.06; 95%CI: 0.45-2.49, p = 0.90). Conclusions: ECMO pump-on prior to ETI for patients with OHCA who received ECPR was not associated with favorable neurological outcome at 30 days.
title: Abstract P1073: Timing of Endotracheal Intubation and Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Pump-On in Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Who Received Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation

abstract: Introduction: ACLS involves CPR and other resuscitation procedures that may cause iatrogenic injuries but unless the patient achieves sustained ROSC to evaluate for underlying cause of arrest and possible injuries, it is difficult to quantify these potential risks. HYPOTHESIS: What are the rates and types of ACLS injuries that are found post ECPR in non-trauma patients? Methods: Review of the ECLS Registry to identify all ECPR patients that survived for sufficient time to evaluate for possible post-ACLS injuries. The EMR was further used for review of radiological studies, laboratory tests, and physician notes. Results: We identified 17 ECLS patients who survived for adequate time to evaluate for iatrogenic injures due to ACLS efforts; there were 6 additional ECPR patients who died before achieving sustained ROSC so that no post-ACLS evaluation was possible. 7W/10M; IHCA 10/OHCA 7; Avg Age 58.4 (range 32-71); Avg ECMO Run: 3.4 d; Survival to D/C 5 (29.4%); Survival to Decan 4 (23.5%); Died before off ECMO 8 (47.1%); Patients without any injuries/hemorrhage: 3 (17.6%) vs significant injuries: 14 (82.4%); Injuries found: rib fractures with associated pneumothorax (4) and hemothorax (2), hemopericardium (1), liver lacerations (3), splenic laceration (1), bladder rupture (1), arterial injury [not due to ECPR] (1), massive hemorrhage [either diffuse bleeding or not due to trauma such as UGIB] (5). Total of six patients were given thrombolytics as part of ACLS prior to ECPR initiated. Only 1 patient (5.9%) who achieved sustained ROSC had an injury due to ECPR [CFA side branch repaired]. Conclusions: A large percentage of our ECPR patients who survived cardiac arrest have iatrogenic injuries presumably due to resuscitation efforts but ECPR itself appears to result in few vascular injuries. Thrombolytic administration during ACLS appears to be associated with significant hemorrhage. After sustained ROSC is achieved after ECPR, it is important to evaluate for the cause of the primary arrest and for potential iatrogenic injuries.
title: Abstract P1074: ACLS Injuries Revealed Post ECPR

abstract: Background: Earlier reperfusion in patients receiving extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (rVT/VF OHCA) is associated with improved neurologically favorable survival. By giving immediate circulatory and respiratory support, it allows time to stabilize the patient and investigate and treat a potential reversible cause of cardiac arrest. Despite the demonstrated association between shorter reperfusion time and improved neurologically favorable in patients with refractory OHCA requiring ECPR, there is limited data to evaluate the association between ECPR reperfusion time and post-arrest morbidity. Research Questions: Is there an association between reperfusion time and outcomes of post-arrest morbidity including biomarkers, clinical outcomes, and resource utilization in patients with rVT/VF OHCA requiring ECPR ? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with rVT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR between 2015-2023. We evaluated the association between reperfusion time and outcomes of non-fatal post-arrest morbidity, including biomarkers, clinical outcomes, and resource utilization. Results of adjusted regression analyses were reported as beta coefficients, odds ratios (ORs), and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). Analyses were adjusted for age and occurrence of bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Results: The study cohort included 332 patients with a median age of the cohort was 60.7 (50.9, 67.1) years and a majority of male patients (82.5%). Median reperfusion time was 63.0 (interquartile range: 54.0, 74.0) minutes. In adjusted analyses, every additional minute of reperfusion time was associated with greater peak lactate (Beta=1.04, 95% CI: 1.01-1.07); greater odds of chest trauma on admission chest CT (OR 1.02, 95% CI: 1.01-1.03); and prolonged intensive care unit admission stays (IRR: 1.01, 95% CI 1.006-1.02). No clinical outcome was associated with reperfusion time in the adjusted analyses. Conclusion: Longer reperfusion time, from 911 call to V-A ECMO, in patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR was associated with greater metabolic derangement, CPR-related thoracic trauma and longer ICU length of stay. These preliminary findings support system-level efforts to shorten time to VA-ECMO reperfusion.
title: Abstract P1075: Reperfusion Time and Non-Fatal Morbidity in Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation

abstract: Background: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiac arrest and severe shock. Although cannulation strategies are standardized, decannulation decisions remain variable. When hemodynamic collapse occurs after decannulation, emergent re-cannulation may be the only life-saving option. Outcomes after a second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization are poorly defined, particularly among extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) patients, a group often presumed to have especially poor prognosis. Hypothesis: A second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization is associated with meaningful survival to discharge. Aim: To evaluate survival and predictors of outcome after repeat VA-ECMO cannulation during the same hospitalization. Methods: This is a retrospective single-center study of patients who underwent two VA-ECMO runs during a single hospitalization between 2016-2024. Among 1,000 patients treated with VA-ECMO, 40 required emergent re-initiation after initial decannulation. Clinical characteristics, indications for re-cannulation, survival to hospital discharge and predictors of outcome at the time of re-cannulation were analyzed. Results: Survival to hospital discharge after repeat VA-ECMO was 32.5% (Table 1). The most common indications for re-cannulation were refractory cardiogenic shock (52%) and cardiac arrest requiring ECPR (40%) (Table 2). Patients re-cannulated for ECPR had survival comparable to, and numerically higher than, those re-cannulated for other indications, including refractory cardiogenic shock (44% versus 24%; p=0.29). Survivors were younger and less likely to have a history of coronary artery bypass grafting (Table 1). At the time of re-cannulation, survivors had lower serum lactate, international normalized ratio levels and higher platelet counts (Table 2). On multivariable analysis, older age and higher serum lactate were independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: Repeat VA-ECMO cannulation was associated with meaningful survival after post-decannulation hemodynamic collapse. The observation that patients re-cannulated for ECPR had outcomes similar to, and numerically better than other major re-cannulation groups, challenges the assumption that repeat ECPR is uniformly futile and suggests that carefully selected patients may still derive substantial benefit. Younger age and less severe metabolic derangement at the time of re-cannulation were associated with improved outcomes.
title: Abstract P1076: Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Re-Cannulation: Patient Characteristics, Clinical Outcomes, and Predictors of Success at a High-Volume Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Center

abstract: Background: Significant heterogeneity exists in pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) populations that suffer in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). While individual registries provide sizable cohorts, they lack diagnostic and procedural granularity. We propose a novel linkage of national cardiac arrest and pediatric cardiac critical care quality registries to evaluate IHCA in children with heart disease, characterize cardiac disease profiles, and identify unique outcome-related risk factors. Methods: We linked the American Heart Association’s Get With the Guidelines-Resuscitation (GWTG-R) and the Pediatric Cardiac Critical Care Consortium (PC 4 ) registries. We included medical (MC) and surgical (SC) cardiac patients < 18 years of age admitted to CICUs between 8/1/2014-2/13/2023 with an index IHCA event. Cross-referencing identified 22 centers participating in both registries (Fig. 1). Primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge (SHD). Secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), return of circulation via extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ROC), and survival with a favorable neurologic outcome (FNO) from GWTG-R, defined by pediatric cerebral performance category (PCPC) scores. A composite survival with FNO variable was created by adding neurologic complications collected in PC 4 to GWTG-R’s definition. Generalized linear mixed-effects models accounting for hospital clustering examined associations between illness categories, and within MC subgroups, with outcomes. Adjustment covariates included single ventricle (SV) and congenital heart disease (CHD) status derived from PC 4 . Results: A total of 1,012 children were evaluated (418 MC; 594 SC); 42% were infants, 27% were SV, 85% had CHD, and 51% of SC patients had STAT 4-5 operations (Table 1). IHCA cumulative incidence was 0.91% for STAT 1-3 and 4.6% for STAT 4-5. Median CPR duration was similar between groups (MC 9 [IQR 3-35] vs SC 13 [IQR 3-38] mins, p=0.10). Overall, SHD was 55%, FNO in survivors was 62%, and composite FNO in survivors was 53%. In multivariable models, MC patients had lower odds of SHD (OR 0.45 [0.32-0.62]), ROSC (OR 0.43 [0.27-0.69]) and ROC (OR 0.38 [0.24-0.58]) compared to SC groups (Table 2). Among MC cohorts, having CHD was associated with lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.35 [0.14-0.88]) and ROC (OR 0.44 [0.20-0.96]), but similar SHD versus those with structurally normal hearts. No differences in FNO or composite FNO were seen between MC and SC cohorts. Conclusion: In this linkage analysis, adjusted for covariates including SV and CHD status, MC patients had higher hospital mortality compared with SC patients. Although MC cohorts with CHD had lower rates of ROSC and ROC, SHD was similar to MC patients without CHD. This study framework enables new procedure- and complexity-specific insights not feasible in either registry alone to more accurately predict outcomes.
title:
Abstract P1077: Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Cardiac ICUs: Benefit of Linking AHA GWTG

                    4

abstract: Background: Adult and pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) have historically differed in baseline characteristics, etiologies, event features, interventions, and outcomes. Advances in arrest prevention and resuscitation practices may have narrowed these gaps, but contemporary comparisons are limited. We evaluated differences in characteristics and outcomes between pediatric and adult IHCA in a large national registry in North America. Methods: Using the GWTG-Resuscitation database, we identified index IHCA events requiring chest compressions for at least 1 minute between 2015 and 2024, excluding pandemic years 2020-2022. The exposure was age group (pediatric <18 years vs adult). Outcomes included survival to hospital discharge, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurological outcome (adult cerebral performance category [CPC] 1–2 or pediatric CPC 1–3). Generalized estimating equations were used for clustering by hospital and event year; pre-arrest factors were treated as mediators. Standard mean differences (SMDs) with SMD >0.1 or <-0.1 indicated meaningful differences. Results: The cohort included 161,162 adults and 3,749 children with IHCA. Adults had lower odds of survival to discharge (26% vs 46%; odds ratio [OR] 0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41-0.47), favorable neurological outcome (18% vs 33%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.46-0.57), and ROSC (73% vs 78%; OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.74–0.88) compared with children. Adults were more likely to present with VF/pVT (16% vs 10%, SMD -0.17), yet lower adult survival persisted after stratifying by initial rhythm: for non-shockable rhythms, survival was 22% vs 44% (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.48–0.52), and for shockable rhythms, 45% vs 52% (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78–0.97) for adults and children respectively. Children were more likely than adults to arrest in an ICU (69% vs 38%; SMD 0.66), receive calcium during CPR (44% vs 35%; SMD 0.18), and undergo ECPR (12% vs <1%; SMD 0.50). Adults more commonly received sodium bicarbonate (55% vs 48%; SMD 0.15) and amiodarone (20% vs 5%; SMD 0.49) during CPR. Conclusion: In this large IHCA registry, adults had approximately half the odds of survival to discharge and favorable neurological outcome compared with children, despite only modestly lower odds of ROSC. These survival differences were not explained by initial rhythm and occurred in the setting of marked differences in care setting, pre-arrest support, and resuscitation practices, highlighting age-specific targets to improve outcomes. Future directions include contrasting etiology of arrest and post-arrest care practices.
title: Abstract P1082: Characteristics and Outcomes of Adult and Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest affects over 500,000 Americans annually and remains a major public health challenge. Post-cardiac arrest shock—defined as inadequate oxygen delivery to vital organs—occurs in over 70% of initial survivors and contributes substantially to mortality and organ dysfunction. While post-arrest shock following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has been extensively studied, data on in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is limited. Research Objectives: The objectives of this study are to characterize the epidemiology, treatment patterns, and trajectory of shock following IHCA, including progression/resolution, evaluate associations with organ dysfunction, vasopressor selection, organ support, and clinical outcomes Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with IHCA using the Discover-IHCA registry. Post-arrest variables included vasoactive medication use, organ support methods, and cardiac sequential organ failure assessment score (cSOFA). The primary exposure was post-arrest shock; the primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included organ dysfunction requiring organ support, survival at 24, 48 and 72 hours. We present descriptive statistics as means or medians where appropriate. Paired comparisons between pre- and post-arrest organ support were performed using McNemars where appropriate. A covariate-adjusted logistic regression model was also developed. Results: We included 955 adult patients across 69 hospitals. Of these, 339 (35.5%) were female. The majority (42.2%) of individuals were age > 70 (Table 1). Primary respiratory causes were the most common etiology of arrest (n = 316, 33.1%), followed by primary cardiac (n = 250, 26.2%). A total of 742 patients (77.7%) experienced post-arrest shock, defined as any use of vasopressor/inotrope (n = 666, 69.7%), mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump/impella) (n = 30, 3.14%), or initiation of VA-ECMO (n = 46, 4.82%). Norepinephrine was the most common vasopressor (n = 709, 74.2%). Comparison of pre- versus post-arrest organ support showed significant increases in multiple interventions (Table 2). Higher weighted cSOFA burden was associated with higher odds of in-hospital death (OR =1.95, 95% CI 1.73-2.19, p < 0.001) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Over three-quarters of patients with IHCA suffer post-arrest shock. Significant increases in organ support occur after IHCA. Higher cSOFA scores post-arrest was strongly associated with in hospital death. Future analyses will explore patient centered outcomes and variations in IHCA management.
title: Abstract P1086: Shock Trajectories and Practice Variation After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Retrospective Analysis of the Discover-IHCA Registry

abstract: Background: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is a catastrophic complication of cardiogenic shock, yet predictors of arrest and subsequent mortality remain poorly characterized. We evaluated the incidence, determinants, and outcomes of IHCA among critically ill patients with cardiogenic shock. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database. Adult ICU patients with cardiogenic shock were identified using ICD-9 code 785.51 and ICD-10 code R57.0. IHCA was identified using ICD-9 code 427.5 and ICD-10 codes I46, I46.2, I46.8, and I46.9. Laboratory, hemodynamic, and cardiovascular phenotype data were extracted from the first 24 hours of ICU admission. Prespecified Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of IHCA and predictors of in-hospital mortality among patients who experienced cardiac arrest. Model discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results: Among 3,875 ICU admissions with cardiogenic shock, 11.4% experienced IHCA. Patients with IHCA had significantly higher in-hospital mortality compared with those without IHCA (63.6% vs. 33.4%, p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, VT/VF was the strongest independent predictor of IHCA (adjusted odds ratio[aOR]4.25,95% CI 3.36-5.39, p<0.001). Additional independent predictors included higher lactate, lower bicarbonate and lower minimum MAP. HFrEF was associated with lower odds of IHCA (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.44-0.72, p<0.001). The prediction model demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.77). Among patients with IHCA, mortality varied by phenotype and was highest among patients with HFpEF (79.5%) and lowest among those with HFrEF (53.5%). Mortality was 56.9% among VT/VF-associated arrests versus 70.2% among non-VT/VF arrests. However, in multivariable analysis, VT/VF was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality following cardiac arrest (aOR 0.91, 95% CI 0.55-1.52, p=0.71). Instead, older age, higher lactate concentration, and lower bicarbonate c independently predicted mortality following cardiac arrest. HFrEF remained independently associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.98, p=0.041), whereas VT/VF, acute myocardial infarction, minimum mean arterial pressure, sex, and HFpEF were not independently associated with mortality after adjustment. Post-arrest mortality model: AUC = 0.801. Conclusions: IHCA occurred in approximately one in nine ICU patients with cardiogenic shock and was associated with markedly increased mortality. VT/VF and markers of severe hypoperfusion and metabolic derangement independently predicted cardiac arrest, whereas post-arrest mortality was primarily driven by age, lactate elevation, and metabolic acidosis. Early identification of high-risk patients may facilitate enhanced monitoring and timely escalation of support.
title: Abstract P1087: Determinants of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest and Post-Arrest Mortality in Cardiogenic Shock

abstract: Introduction: Low-income patients experience worse outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Little is known about disparities in post-arrest hospital care that may contribute to these outcome disparities. We sought to identify income-based disparities in post-arrest care. Hypothesis: Lower income patients have worse hospital outcomes and receive post-arrest care less often. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the 2019-2022 National Emergency Department Sample, a national claims database. We included adult patients who survived to admission and excluded those with missing data. We stratified patients based on their household income quartile. We defined outcomes as post-arrest care, survival to discharge, and discharge to home (a surrogate for a good neurologic outcome). Using ordinal logistic regression, we evaluated the association between decreasing income quartile and outcomes with the top income quartile defined as the reference. We adjusted the analyses for age, sex, and race. Results: Of 359,652 OHCAs, 198,785 survived to admission. We included 188,627 patients; 32,534 from the top, 40,661 from the 2 nd , 49,751 from the 3 rd , and 65,681 from the lowest income quartile. Discharge to home rates for each group were 19.6% for 1 st , 19.1% for 2 nd , 17.9% for 3 rd , and 16.4% for 4 th income quartiles. Decreasing income was associated with decreased odds of left heart catheterization (OR 0.81 [0.77-0.85]), percutaneous coronary intervention (OR 0.85 [0.81-0.89]), ventricular assist device (OR 0.77 [0.71-0.83]), automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement (OR 0.85 [0.81-0.89]), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (OR 0.55 [0.45-0.68]), coronary artery bypass graft (OR 0.84 [0.75-0.94]), echocardiography (OR 0.85 [0.76-0.95]), central line placement (OR 0.93 [0.89-0.97]), arterial line placement (OR 0.86 [0.79-0.97]), therapeutic hypothermia (OR 0.70 [0.56-0.86]), survival (OR 0.90 [0.87-0.93]) , and survival with discharge to home (OR 0.87 [0.83-0.90]). Decreasing income was not associated with decreased odds of Head CT, electroencephalogram, body CT, or do not resuscitate orders. Conclusion: Decreasing income was associated with decreased odds of cardiac procedures, resuscitative procedures, and OHCA outcomes. Our findings suggest that income-based disparities in post-arrest care exist and warrant further investigation.
title: Abstract P2031: National Income-Based Disparities in Post-Arrest Care After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Background: For refractory ventricular fibrillation (rVF), two strategies have been studied in separate clinical trials: intra-arrest transport (IAT) to Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (ECPR) and Double Sequential External Defibrillation (DSED). However, some systems have both treatments available, and the optimal time to stop DSED and start IAT to ECPR remains unclear. Aim: We aimed to describe the probability of prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with ongoing DSED in patients still pulseless at three time points in the resuscitation and the proportion of pulseless patients already undergoing IAT at these times. Methods: We included patients randomized to DSED in secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial who did not have prehospital termination of resuscitation, vector change shocks prior to DSED, or a missing time of fourth defibrillation. We calculated the probability of prehospital ROSC at or beyond minute 5, 10, and 15 post-fourth defibrillation (first randomized DSED shock) in those still pulseless and the proportion already undergoing IAT. Results: Of 125 patients, 118 were included after applying exclusion criteria. Of these 118 patients, 58 (49%) achieved prehospital ROSC with 53/58 (91%) occurring on scene. At minutes 5, 10, and 15 post-fourth-defibrillation the probability of ROSC with continued resuscitation was 32/96 (33%), 16/80 (20%), and 7/71 (10%) respectively. At these same time points, the proportion of pulseless patients undergoing IAT was 2/96 (2%), 10/80 (13%), and 23/70 (33%) were actively undergoing IAT. Conclusions: The optimal timing of IAT in a system providing both ECPR and DSED may be from minutes 10-15, as the proportion of patients who will get ROSC falls below 10% at 15 minutes post-fourth-defibrillation; however, 32% of patients were receiving IAT at this timepoint, potentially underestimating the yield of continued on-scene resuscitation.
title: Abstract P2035: Optimizing Transport Timing in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation: A Secondary Analysis of the DOSE-VF Trial

abstract: Introduction: Ischemic spinal cord injury and strategies for its protection have received comparatively little attention in global ischemia and reperfusion research. We investigated the therapeutic effects of hypothermia on the spinal cord in our extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) rat model after 8 min of untreated ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest (VFCA) and hypothesized that immediate hypothermic temperature (HT) control (33°C for 12 hours) would reduce spinal cord dysfunction and histological damage, whereas delayed initiation of cooling after 2 hours would attenuate these protective effects after 72 hours of survival. Methods: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=39) were subjected to 8 min of VFCA and resuscitated with ECPR and drugs (epinephrine, bicarbonate, heparin). After defibrillation and restoration of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), rats were randomized into normothermic (NT) (n=16), immediate HT (n=9) and delayed HT (DHT) group (n=8). Hind leg paralysis (HLP) and urinary bladder retention (UR) were recorded and after 72h, the spine was fixed in formalin. Transverse sections of cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal cord (NT n=6, HT n=5, DHT n=5, Sham n=5) were embedded in paraffin. In Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-staining neuronal necrosis (NN) was evaluated semi-quantitatively (mild, moderate, marked). Microglia activation was assessed semi-quantitatively (mild, moderate, marked, malacia) utilizing Iba1- immunohistochemistry. Results: All animals achieved ROSC, but 8 NT animals died before the study endpoint. All surviving NT animals showed HLP. In the HT group only 2/9 animals exhibited HLP (p=0.002 vs. NT) while the DHT group showed less recovery (6/8 HLP; p=0.47 vs. NT, p=0.057 vs. HT, Sham 0/6). Urinary retention was not significantly different between groups (NT 3/8, HT 1/9, DHT 2/8, Sham 0/6). In HE-staining, 3/5 HT animals showed mild NN in the gray matter, while all animals of the NT group showed marked NN (p=0.0006 vs. Sham, p<0.0134 vs HT). Variable NN (mild to marked) was present in the DHT group. Sham animals showed physiological Iba1-expression. All VFCA groups exhibited microglia activation, reaching significance in NT (p=0.0003 vs. Sham) and DHT (p=0.0429 vs Sham). HT animals showed significantly less microglia activation compared to NT (p=0.0487). Conclusions: We found consistent NN in the spinal cords of NT rats 72 hours after 8 minutes of untreated VFCA followed by ECPR. In the HT group, these lesions were significantly reduced, correlating with improved neurological outcomes, whereas DHT group showed less pronounced protective effects. In addition, microglial responses after 72 hours of survival differed between the VFCA groups.
title: Abstract P2042: Spinal Cord Injury and Neurological Outcome in a 72-Hour Survival Rat Model of 8-Minute Ventricular Fibrillation Cardiac Arrest Resuscitated with ECPR and Immediate 12-Hour Hypothermic Temperature Control vs 2 Hour Delayed Temperature Control

abstract: Introduction: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is responsible for more than 300,000 deaths per year in the United States and is the third leading cause of death worldwide. It is well established that the presence of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction increases mortality in PE. Despite advancements in therapies for massive pulmonary embolism (PE) some patients with refractory cardiogenic shock will still require additional hemodynamic support. Such support is typically available at specialized referral centers where veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is commonly used to stabilize cardiogenic stages (D-E) associated with PE. In this case series, we describe the use of temporary pRVAD support with a micro-axial flow pump (RP Impella Flex) following aspiration thrombectomy and or systemic thrombolysis. Purpose: We describe and report the characteristics of eight patients with ultra high-risk PE, defined as category E1 or E2 who were treated with a temporary pRVAD micro-axial flow pump for refractory cardiogenic shock. Methods: We included patients aged 18 or older who presented from 01/2024 to 12/2025 with PE who received pRVAD. IRB (IRB00144384) approved the study and waived consent. Statistical Analysis: Data from all patients evaluated by the PE Response Team during the study period were analyzed. Baseline age, sex, BMI, Charlson comorbidity index, pulmonary embolism related shock stage, RVSP, TAPSE, and RV/LV ratio were summarized for patients who received RVAD support in Table 1. Descriptive statistical methods were used to summarize baseline characteristics among the included patients. Results: Six out of 8 patients were males with mean age of 59 (95% CI 54.1-64.1), BMI of 32.5 (95% CI 26-39). All 8 patients were stage E cardiogenic shock. A total of four out of 8 patients had cardiac arrest.All patients were on multiple vasoactive medications. The NEE (norepinephrine equivalents) use mean was 4.13 mcg/kg/min (95% CI 2.46-5.29). Their RV/LV ratio mean by CT was 1.63 (95% CI 0.85-2.41) and mean RVSP of 44.9 (95% CI 55.3-54.5). Six out of 8 patients survived hospitalization. Discussion: Patients with PE in cardiogenic shock stage E—with or without cardiac arrest—remain an extremely challenging population, with reported mortality rates nearing 70%. Our findings indicate that early pRVAD intervention may provide stabilization in select scenarios, compared to the conventional practice of stabilizing patients on VA-ECMO to achieve maximal hemodynamic support. The retrospective design and limited cohort size of this study preclude any broad generalization. Conclusion: In summary, temporary pRVAD support, combined with mechanical aspiration thrombectomy, appears to be a promising strategy for managing stage E cardiogenic shock in PE. Future prospective studies with larger cohorts are warranted to refine patient selection and optimize treatment protocols.
title: Abstract P2052: Microaxial Pump Support in Ultra High Risk Pulmonary Embolism

abstract: Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality and represents a keystone outcome in cardiovascular pathology, since it often occurs without warning. Existing risk stratification tools fail to identify many at-risk individuals. Circulating biomarkers reflecting myocardial injury, hemodynamic stress, and systemic inflammation may improve SCD risk prediction by capturing subclinical pathophysiology.We systematically searched PubMed, AHA Journal, BMC Journal, Sage Journal, Oxford Academic, ScienceDirect, and other major cardiology journal platforms from inception through October 2025. Primary statistical and observational studies of biomarker data, supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), were evaluated to identify biomarkers most strongly associated with SCD. Biomarkers related to inflammation, stress, and myocardial injury were prioritized due to their direct role in SCD development. Eligible studies included adult populations with measurements of one or more cardiovascular biomarkers and healthy controls. Meta-analyses used random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and Cochran’s Q, publication bias with funnel plots, and Egger’s regression test. Analyses were performed in Python, and study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS).Twenty studies comprising >240,000 participants met the inclusion criteria. Populations included healthy adults and individuals with known cardiac disease. Biomarkers were grouped as myocardial injury (troponins), hemodynamic stress (BNP/NT-proBNP), and inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6). Higher troponin levels were associated with ~2.8-fold increased SCD risk (HR≈2.84, 95% CI 1.94-4.14; I 2 ≈0%). Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP showed the strongest association (HR≈4.2, 95% CI 2.2-8.7; I 2 ≈84%). CRP exhibited a modest association (HR≈1.19, 95% CI 1.09-1.29; I 2 ≈45-50%). These associations generally persisted after adjustment for demographic factors, LVEF, coronary artery disease, and other cardiovascular risk factors. Troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP remained independently predictive, whereas CRP and IL-6 primarily functioned as supportive inflammatory markers.In this meta-analysis, biomarkers of hemodynamic stress (BNP/NT-proBNP) and myocardial injury (troponins) were strong independent predictors of SCD, while inflammatory markers such as CRP provided weaker but complementary information. Incorporating troponin and especially BNP/NT-proBNP into multimodal risk stratification frameworks may improve early identification of SCD and guide future prevention strategies.
title: Abstract P2055: Circulating Biomarkers of Myocardial Injury, Hemodynamic Stress, and Inflammation for Predicting Sudden Cardiac Death: A Meta-Analysis

abstract: Introduction: Despite recent reductions in US-based overdose death, drug overdose remains the leading cause of death in persons 18-44 years of age. Victims of overdose who experience cardiac arrest are a largely understudied population. To date, randomized clinical trials in cardiac arrest outcomes have actively excluded this patient population. The Influence of Cooling Duration in Cardiac Arrest Patients (ICECAP) trial was the first prospective randomized clinical trial in out of hospital cardiac arrest to include patients with overdose-associated cardiac arrest. Objective: To describe the population with overdose associated OHCA in the ICECAP Trial and compare their outcomes to those with other etiologies of arrest. Methods: All study participants from the ICECAP trial were analyzed in a planned a priori secondary analysis. Enrollments between April 2020 and June 2025 were assessed for etiology of arrest. Patient and arrest characteristics as well as initial laboratory results and outcomes were compared via the following two distributions; overdose vs. non-overdose; and overdose vs. cardiac vs. respiratory. Results: Among 71 participating hospitals, 1158 patients were enrolled into the ICECAP trial and 24.4% (n=283) of the study participants experienced an overdose-associated OHCA. When compared to the non-overdose cohort, overdose patients were younger [50 yrs (IQR 34,60) vs. 65 yrs (IQR 55,73)], male [65.4% (185) vs. 58.8% (493)] and more commonly Black [42.8% (121) vs. 37.8% (317)] and/or Hispanic/Latino [13.1% (37) vs. 8.5% (71)] (Table 1). The overdose cohort received less layperson CPR (48.4% vs. 53.6%), less AED use (11.3% vs. 16.4%), and presented with predominantly non-shockable rhythms at EMS/ED arrival (83.0% vs. 69.6%) (Table 2). Of note, 6.7% of persons in the overdose cohort presented with STEMI on initial EKG. Patients with overdose experienced slightly worse neurologic recovery versus those with non-overdose defined as a modified Rankin Score of 0-3 (15.2% vs. 18.0%); though no difference was appreciated in unadjusted 90-day mortality (75.6% vs.75.1%) for overdose versus non-overdose victims in the ICECAP trial (Figure 1). Conclusion: In this descriptive secondary analysis of the ICECAP participants who experienced OHCA due to overdose, overdose-associated OHCA victims were younger, Black and Hispanic, Male persons who received less bystander CPR and AED application. Overall survival outcomes were similar however, there is trend towards slightly worse neurologic recovery. Further study in this patient population is necessary to examine the role of neuroprotective strategies, variability in neuro-prognosis and use of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy and to identify targets to improve outcomes in this growing population of younger adults.
title: Abstract P2057: Incidence and Outcomes of Overdose-Associated Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Large US-Based Clinical Trial Network

abstract: Background: Thrombus formation is a feared complication of veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) treatment in patients requiring extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Research Questions: What are the incidence, subtypes, and prognostic implications of clinically detected incident thrombi in patients receiving ECPR for refractory ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation (rVT/VF) OHCA? Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study in patients with rVT/VF OHCA requiring ECPR. All patients were treated with a standardized anticoagulation strategy as per our previously published ECPR protocols. The primary objective was to determine the frequency and anatomic distribution of clinically detected incident thrombi during VA-ECMO support or within 7 days after the VA-ECMO treatment course. The secondary objectives was to evaluate the association between any incident thrombus and in-hospital mortality. The results were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: During 2015-2023, 418 patients were referred to our program for ECPR for rVT/VF OHCA (median age 60.8 years, 79.9% male, 78.7% witnessed, 69.1% ischemic cause of VT/VF OHCA). In this cohort, 63.6% (266/418) had an unloading device during the VA-ECMO run, with the vast majority being an intra-aortic balloon pump (260/266). There were 33 patients who were diagnosed with 40 incident thrombi (24 arterial and 16 venous). The presence of any thrombus was not statistically associated with in-hospital survival in unadjusted analyses (OR 1.59, 95% CI: 0.75-3.22) or after adjustment for adjustment for history of heart failure and presence of unloading device (OR: 1.87, 95% CI: 0.87-3.86). Conclusion: In a high-volume ECPR program using standardized anticoagulation, clinically detected incident thrombi occurred in approximately 8% of patients treated for rVT/VF OHCA. Arterial thrombi, particularly left ventricular thrombi, were the most common subtype. Incident thrombus detection was not statistically associated with in-hospital survival.
title: Abstract P2070: Incidence and Prognostic Implications of Thrombus in Patients Receiving Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Refractory Ventricular Tachycardia/Ventricular Fibrillation Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest

abstract: Introduction: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has improved survival significantly in refractory cardiac arrest in recent years, yet mortality remains high. When ECPR does not achieve patient survival, organ donation may be pursued. The 2025 American Heart Association Guidelines recognize ECPR patients as a potential source of donor organs, however data on transplant recipient outcomes is limited. Hypothesis: Kidneys donated from ECPR donors have comparable short- and long-term function as those from non-ECPR donors and thus have the potential to expand the donor pool. Aims: To assess short- and long-term outcomes in kidney transplant recipients from ECPR versus non-ECPR donors. Methods: In this retrospective study, ECPR and non-ECPR donors from the University of Minnesota and their corresponding recipients were identified between 2016 and 2023. Donor and recipient baseline characteristics, transplant variables and post-transplant outcomes were compared between groups. Primary outcomes included graft failure and patient mortality. Secondary outcomes included serum creatinine at discharge and at 6-, 12-, 24- and 36-month follow-up. Results: Overall, 23 ECPR donors and 24 non-ECPR donors were identified, donating kidneys to 39 and 45 recipients, respectively. Recipients were transplanted across multiple regions, with 41% (16/39) of ECPR and 49% (22/45) of non-ECPR recipients residing in Minnesota. Donor age was similar between groups, and ECPR donors had significantly higher serum creatinine at the time of organ procurement (p=0.002) (Table 1). Recipients had similar baseline characteristics (Table 2). Recipients from ECPR donors had significantly higher creatinine at discharge and at 6-, 12-, and 36-month follow-up, though graft failure rates were low and not significantly different between groups (5% versus 7%, p=1.0). Mortality rates were similar (p=0.62), and no deaths were attributable to graft dysfunction. Median follow-up was shorter in the ECPR group (Table 3). Conclusion: Kidney recipients from ECPR donors had consistently higher creatinine, however, they had similar graft and patient survival with those from non-ECPR donors. These findings show that in cases when patient recovery is not feasible, organ donation can extend the benefit of ECPR from one individual to multiple recipients per donor, across geographic regions.
title: Abstract P2071: Kidney Donation Outcomes After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation

abstract: Background: Hemolysis during veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-A ECMO) support is an important complication associated with acute kidney injury and increased transfusion requirements. Mechanical stress within the ECMO circuit is thought to contribute to the development of hemolysis; however, the association between circuit pressure parameters and hemolysis during V-A ECMO support has not been sufficiently investigated. This study examined the association of drainage pressure and pump head pressure with hemolysis in patients treated with V-A ECMO for cardiogenic shock. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective observational study including 23 patients who underwent V-A ECMO support between October 2022 and June 2024. Serum haptoglobin levels were measured at intensive care unit admission and at 12 and 24 hours thereafter. Hemolysis was defined as a minimum serum haptoglobin level <19 mg/dL at any of the three time points. ECMO circuit pressures were obtained from pressure monitoring values displayed on the ECMO console. Drainage pressure was defined as the pre-pump pressure, and pump head pressure was calculated as the difference between the pre-oxygenator pressure and the pre-pump pressure. Results: Twenty-three patients were included (median age, 73 years; 69.6% male). Most patients had advanced cardiogenic shock, with SCAI stage E accounting for 65.2% of the cohort (stage C, 13.0%; stage D, 21.7%; stage E, 65.2%). Hemolysis was observed in 19 of 23 patients. At 12 hours after intensive care unit admission, a visual trend was observed whereby patients with greater pre-ECMO shock severity tended to exhibit more negative drainage pressures and lower serum haptoglobin levels (Figure A). In addition, serum haptoglobin levels decreased over time from intensive care unit admission to 12 and 24 hours thereafter (Figure B).
